summary: Scaffolded the Vite, React and TypeScript client and the Express API in one repo, with a health route and a Postgres connection that works locally and on Render.
body:
Started the project from an empty folder. The client lives in web/ and the API in server/, with a shared tsconfig base. The API has one route, GET /health, which runs select 1 against Postgres and returns ok.

The Vite dev server proxies /api to port 4000, so the client needs no CORS setup during development. Added a .env.example with DATABASE_URL and PORT, and a small script that starts both processes.

Created the Render web service and a Postgres instance on the smallest plan. The first deploy failed because Render ran npm install without the server workspace, so I changed the build command to build both parts. The health route answers on the Render URL now. Next is the schema for shipments.

summary: Created the shipments schema and a seed script with 5,000 fake shipments, plus the first paginated GET /api/shipments endpoint that the table will use.
body:
Wrote the first migrations: shipments (id, reference, origin, destination, status, carrier, cost_cents, picked_up_at, delivered_at), carriers, and depots. Costs are stored as integer cents because float sums drifted in a quick test. Indexed delivered_at and status, since the dashboard will filter on both.

The seed script generates 5,000 shipments over the last 18 months with a realistic spread. Most are delivered, a few percent are delayed, and a handful are lost. Delivery times follow a skewed distribution so that the charts will not look flat. Running the seed takes about four seconds.

The endpoint GET /api/shipments takes page, pageSize and sort. It uses limit and offset for now, which is fine at this size. I capped pageSize at 200 and return a total count in the same response.

Validation uses a small zod schema, and bad input returns 400 with the field name. I wrote six Vitest tests against a test database that is recreated per run. They cover paging edges, an unknown sort column and an empty result.

One snag was that count(*) with the filters doubled the query time on the seed data. It is still only 12 ms, so I left it alone. If the real data grows, I may cache the count. Next is the table component.

summary: Built the first shipments table in React with sorting and paging against the API, and it renders 50 rows in under 100 ms on the seed data.
body:
The ShipmentsTable component fetches from /api/shipments and keeps page, pageSize and sort in component state. Clicking a header toggles ascending and descending, and the arrow shows the direction. I wrote a small useFetch hook with an abort controller so that quick clicks do not show stale pages.

Status is a colored badge: green for delivered, amber for in transit, red for delayed. Priya sent colors this morning, and I used her hex values in a CSS variables file instead of hardcoding them.

Durations are shown as hours and minutes. The API returns timestamps, and the client computes the difference. The money column uses Intl.NumberFormat with the euro, since Acme bills in euros.

Found a bug where changing the page size left the page number too high, which gave an empty table. The fix resets the page to 1 on a size change. Added a Vitest test for that reducer.

The table has no filters yet. That is next, after the date picker.

summary: Added a date range picker with presets such as last 7 days, and wired it to the shipments API through from and to query parameters.
body:
Jonas wants dispatchers to look at a week or a month quickly, so the picker has presets: today, last 7 days, last 30 days, this quarter, and a custom range. I wrote it by hand instead of pulling in a big library, because the library I tried added 90 kB.

The state is a pair of ISO dates in the URL query string. That way a dispatcher can send a link to a colleague and they see the same range. A hook, useDateRange, reads and writes the URL through the history API.

On the server, GET /api/shipments accepts from and to and filters on picked_up_at. Both are inclusive on the day level. I first made the end exclusive and got off-by-one results for shipments on the last day, which a test caught.

Time zones were the tricky part. Acme works in one zone, so day boundaries have to be computed in that zone and not in UTC. I put the zone in a config value and use it in the SQL with at time zone.

Keyboard use works: arrow keys move between days, and Enter selects. I have not tested it with a screen reader yet, and I noted that for later.

Tests: eight for the range helpers, including the daylight saving change week. All pass. Next I will build the first chart using the same range.

summary: Added the first ECharts chart, deliveries per day as a line, fed by a new aggregate endpoint that respects the date range.
body:
The new endpoint GET /api/stats/deliveries-per-day groups delivered shipments by day in the Acme time zone and returns date and count. Days without deliveries are filled with zero on the server, otherwise the line skips them and looks wrong.

On the client I added a thin DeliveriesChart wrapper around ECharts. I import only the line chart, grid, tooltip and canvas renderer parts, which keeps the bundle about 400 kB smaller than the full import.

The chart resizes with its container through a ResizeObserver. Without that, it stayed at the first width after the sidebar collapsed.

The range comes from the same URL state as the table, so both update together. For 18 months of seed data the query takes 9 ms. Next are a chart for average delivery time and one for costs.

summary: Added average delivery time and cost-per-carrier charts, and moved the chart code into a shared base so that colors and tooltips are the same everywhere.
body:
Two new endpoints: /api/stats/delivery-time, which returns the average and the 90th percentile per week, and /api/stats/cost-by-carrier, which sums cost per carrier for the range. The percentile uses percentile_cont in Postgres.

After writing the second chart I saw that I had copied the option setup three times. I pulled out a baseChartOptions function with the palette, the tooltip format and the axis styling. The palette comes from Priya's CSS variables, read at runtime, so a later dark theme is possible.

The cost chart is a horizontal bar chart sorted by value. With 12 carriers the labels fit, but a long name overflowed. I set a label width and a truncation with the full name in the tooltip.

The delivery time chart shows two lines, average and p90. Jonas asked on chat whether p90 is understandable for dispatchers. I added a short help text under the title: nine out of ten shipments are faster than this.

I also tested empty ranges. The charts show a message, no data in this range, instead of an empty grid. This was missing in the first chart too, so I fixed it there.

Performance: all three stats queries together take about 35 ms on seed data. I did not add caching. A Playwright smoke test now loads the dashboard and checks that three canvases exist. It runs in 6 seconds.

Next is the layout of the page and the settings page.

summary: Built the dashboard layout with a sidebar and a settings page for company name, time zone and default date range, stored in a settings table.
body:
The layout has a left sidebar with Dashboard, Shipments, Costs placeholder and Settings, and a top bar with the date picker. I used CSS grid, and on narrow screens the sidebar collapses into a menu button. Priya's mockup had icons, so I added an inline SVG set rather than an icon font.

The settings page has a form with three fields: company name, time zone and default date range. A settings table with one row per key holds them. The API has GET and PUT /api/settings, with zod validation. An unknown time zone is rejected, using Intl.supportedValuesOf to check.

The time zone setting now replaces the config value I used earlier for day boundaries. All stats queries read it once per request. I added a small in-process cache with a 60 second lifetime, and a PUT clears it.

The default date range is used when the URL has no range. I had to be careful about the order: the URL wins, then the setting, then last 30 days.

While testing I found that saving the form twice quickly created a race that showed the older value. The save button is now disabled while a request runs.

I wrote tests for the settings validation, six in total, and one Playwright test that changes the time zone and checks the chart range. Both pass.

Form errors are shown under each field with aria-describedby. That is not a full accessibility pass, but it is a start.

There is no permission model yet; anyone with the link can edit settings. Next is login, since this cannot go to Acme like this.

summary: Added email and password login with a session cookie held by the Express session middleware, with passwords hashed using bcrypt.
body:
Added a users table with email, password_hash, role and created_at. Roles are dispatcher, manager and admin. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt at cost 12.

POST /api/login checks the password and sets a session through express-session. For now the store is the default in-memory one, which is fine for development and for one instance. The cookie is httpOnly, sameSite lax and secure in production.

A requireLogin middleware protects every /api route except login and health. The client redirects to a login page when the API answers 401.

I also added a rate limit of ten login attempts per minute per IP. A seed script creates the first admin. The in-memory store will lose sessions on every deploy, so a Postgres store is the next step.

summary: Investigated why Jonas keeps getting logged out after Render deploys and planned how to keep sessions across restarts, without changing the login yet.
body:
Jonas told me he was logged out twice in one afternoon, and I could reproduce it quickly. Every Render deploy restarts the Node process, and the Express session middleware keeps its sessions in memory, so every restart wipes them. Nothing is broken in the login code itself. The store is the problem.

I read through the options for a persistent store. The one that looks best is connect-pg-simple, because Postgres is already there and no new service is needed. A sessions table would hold sid, sess as json and expire. My plan is to create the table with a migration of our own and not let the library create it, so that all schema changes stay in one place. An index on expire would be needed for the cleanup of old rows.

I also wrote down the settings I want to try. The session lifetime would be 14 days with a rolling cookie, so active users stay logged in. Pruning expired rows every 15 minutes should be good enough for now.

I looked at what a proxy means for the cookie. Render terminates TLS in front of the app, so Express will think the connection is not secure and may refuse to set a secure cookie. I added a note to try trust proxy set to 1 and to check that requests after login do not turn into 401 responses.

For tests, I sketched a Vitest integration test that starts two app instances against the same database and checks that a login on one is valid on the other. A logout test is also on the list: the old cookie should get a 401 afterwards.

One cost to keep in mind is an extra database read on every API request. At the current size that should be around 1 ms. I did not start the change today. First I want to talk it through with Jonas, since he is the one who noticed it, and then do the invite flow afterwards.

summary: Built the user invite flow: an admin enters an email, the API creates a one-time invite link, and the invited person sets a password.
body:
Added an invites table with email, role, a hashed token, expiry after 7 days, and used_at. The raw token is only shown in the link and in the email, and the database keeps a sha256 hash of it.

POST /api/invites is admin only. It creates the invite and sends an email through the provider Acme already has. For development the link is printed in the server log instead.

The page /accept-invite reads the token from the URL and shows a password form with a minimum of ten characters. On submit the API checks hash, expiry and used_at, creates the user, marks the invite used, and logs the person in.

I made the token check constant-time by looking up through the hash, so that no comparison of raw secrets happens.

Edge cases I covered with tests: an expired invite, a used invite, an email that already has a user, and two invites for the same address, where the old one is cancelled. Eleven tests, all passing.

The settings page now has a users section with the list and a button to invite. Revoking an invite is a simple delete. Resending is not done yet, since Jonas said it is not needed for the first group of users.

summary: Added filters to the shipments table for status, carrier and a free text search on reference, all kept in the URL.
body:
Dispatchers mostly look for one shipment or for the delayed ones, so the filters are status as a multi-select, carrier as a select, and a text box for the reference.

On the server, GET /api/shipments takes status, carrier and q. The status list is checked against the known values. The search uses ilike with a prefix pattern. I added a text_pattern_ops index on reference so that prefix searches use it.

The text box is debounced by 300 ms, so that typing does not send a request per letter. State goes to the URL like the date range, and the page resets to 1 on any filter change. I forgot that first, and an old page number gave empty results again.

A row of chips shows the active filters, and each can be removed with a click. Priya asked for a clear all link, which I added.

Totals changed with the filters, and the count query was slower: 40 ms with the filters and the full range. It is acceptable for now.

Tests: server tests for each filter and their combination, and a Playwright test for the whole path from typing to the URL. Next is the first round of feedback from Jonas.

summary: Handled the first round of feedback from Jonas: a totals row, the rename of columns to Acme's wording, a fix for delayed-status logic, and slower rows on his laptop.
body:
Jonas went through the dashboard with two dispatchers and sent a list. I did the items one by one.

First, the wording. Acme says consignment, not shipment, in the table headers, and pickup instead of picked up. I put all labels in one labels.ts file, so that the next change is one edit. The API names did not change.

Second, the delayed status. I had derived it in the client by comparing delivered_at to a promised time, but the dispatchers count a shipment as delayed as soon as the promised time has passed, even when it is not delivered. I moved the logic to the server, into a SQL expression, so that the filter and the badge agree. Before, the filter for delayed missed in-transit shipments past their time. A test with four cases covers it.

Third, a totals row under the table. It shows the number of consignments and the sum of the costs for the current filters, not just for the page. This needs one more query, which I combined with the count query to avoid an extra round trip.

Fourth, slowness on a dispatcher's laptop. It had 4 GB of memory and an old browser. I profiled with the CPU throttled 6 times. The slow part was the charts redrawing on every filter change, even when the range had not changed. They now refetch only when the date range changes, which is a separate dependency.

Fifth, the cost column was right-aligned but the header was not. A small fix.

I sent Jonas a link to the staging deploy and asked him to check the delayed filter against a list he knows. He said he would do it tomorrow.

Still open from his list: an export to a file, which I will do as a CSV later, and a print layout, which I will ask about again, since only one person asked.

summary: Fixed the totals row, which showed the sum for the page and not for the filtered set, after Jonas spotted a mismatch with his spreadsheet.
body:
Jonas compared the total cost with his own sheet for last week and was off by a few thousand euros. The totals query joined the carriers table and counted rows twice for shipments with two carrier entries from a data import quirk.

I removed the join from the totals query, since the sum does not need carrier names. The result now matches his sheet to the cent.

I also added a test with a duplicate carrier row to guard against it. A cleanup of the duplicate carriers in the staging data is on my list, and I will ask Jonas whether production has the same.

summary: Wrote the CSV export of the shipments table for the current filters, built in memory on the server, fine for the seed data and a few thousand rows.
body:
Added GET /api/shipments/export.csv. It takes the same filters as the table, runs the query without paging, builds the full CSV as a string and sends it with a content-disposition header.

I used a small hand-written escape function for quotes, commas and line breaks. Dates are formatted in the Acme time zone, and money in decimal euros with a dot, since their spreadsheet program expects it that way. A byte order mark at the start makes Excel read umlauts correctly.

With 5,000 rows the export takes 200 ms and the file is 600 kB. I did not test with much more. Acme's real data will be bigger, so I wrote down that large exports need a look later.

The button sits above the table and uses the active filters. A Vitest test checks the escaping with nasty input, and a second one checks the header row.

summary: Added a dark theme switch and an accessibility pass on the table and the filters, after Priya's review of contrast and focus states.
body:
Priya reviewed the app and sent notes on contrast and on focus rings. I did both topics in one session.

For the theme, the colors were already CSS variables, so the dark set is a second block under a data-theme attribute on the html element. The charts read the variables at runtime, but only when they are created, so they did not change on a switch. I added a listener that disposes and recreates the charts when the theme changes. The choice is saved in local storage, and the first visit follows prefers-color-scheme.

Contrast: three of the status badge colors failed the 4.5 to 1 ratio in the light theme, with the amber worst at 2.8. Priya gave me darker text colors. I checked every pair with a small script that reads the variables and computes the ratio, and it now fails the build if one is below 4.5.

Focus: the default outlines were removed by a reset I wrote on the first day, which was a mistake. I restored a visible two pixel ring on all interactive elements, using focus-visible so that mouse clicks do not show it.

Table: header cells now have aria-sort, and the sort buttons have labels that say what they do. The filter chips are buttons with a remove label that names the filter.

I also tried the table with a screen reader on the Mac. The totals row was read badly, because it was only divs. I made it a proper tfoot.

Open: the date picker still needs a real screen reader test, and the charts have no text alternative. A summary line below each chart would help, and I will ask Priya for wording.

The Playwright suite passes in both themes, 14 tests.

summary: Added text summaries under the charts for screen readers and a data table toggle, using the wording Priya proposed.
body:
Each chart now has a short sentence below it, generated from the data: for example the total deliveries in the range and the busiest day. Priya wrote the templates, and I filled in the values.

There is also a show data link that swaps the chart for a plain table of the same numbers. It uses the same API response, so there is no second request. The toggle is a button with aria-pressed.

The date picker got the screen reader test I owed. Month changes were not announced. I added an aria-live region that says the month and year when it changes, and I gave the grid cells full date labels.

One bug: the live region announced on the first render too, which was noisy. I skip the first update.

Tests: a Playwright check that the summary text exists and that the toggle shows a table with the right number of rows. All 17 tests pass.

That closes the accessibility notes for the first version.

summary: Built the first version of the costs breakdown, with cost per depot and per week, plus a first look at slow queries when the seed data grows to 200,000 rows.
body:
Jonas wants managers to see where the money goes. I added two stats endpoints: cost by depot, and cost per week split by carrier. Both take the date range.

The page uses a stacked bar chart for the weeks and a sorted bar chart for the depots. I reused baseChartOptions, so the colors and tooltips match. With twelve carriers the stack gets busy, so the smallest ones are grouped into other.

To see how it behaves with real volumes, I raised the seed to 200,000 shipments. The weekly cost query went from 15 ms to 380 ms, which is too slow for a page that fires four queries. The plan showed a sequential scan, since the filter was on picked_up_at while the only date index was on delivered_at.

I added a composite index on picked_up_at and carrier. The query dropped to 70 ms. The depot query needed an index on depot_id and picked_up_at, and it now takes 55 ms.

The table endpoint with offset paging is still fast for the first pages but slows near the end. Page 3,000 takes 250 ms. Nobody will go there, since dispatchers filter, so I leave it.

The count query with filters is 90 ms at this size. If it gets worse, I will cache it for a few seconds.

The totals row works unchanged. A short note went to Jonas that the costs page is ready for him to try on staging.

Open: the costs are shown without tax. I will ask Jonas whether the managers want gross numbers.

summary: Wrote the user settings and role checks, so dispatchers cannot edit company settings or invite people, and added a profile section where users change their own password.
body:
Until now, every logged-in user could call every settings endpoint. That was fine while only I used it, but not for Acme. I added a requireRole middleware that takes a list of roles and answers 403 otherwise.

Permissions now are: dispatchers read everything and change only their own profile. Managers also see the costs page. Admins do everything, including invites and company settings. The costs endpoints are closed to dispatchers, and the sidebar hides the entry for them as well. The server check is the one that counts, and the hidden entry is only a courtesy.

The profile section has a change password form. It asks for the current password, and the new one must be at least ten characters and differ from the old one. On success, the API destroys all other sessions of that user by deleting the rows in the sessions table where the user id matches, and keeps the current one. To do that, I now store the user id in the session data, and the query filters on the json field. An index on that expression keeps it quick.

I wrote a test for each role against each protected endpoint, using a table of cases. That gave 36 checks and found one miss: the invite list was readable by managers, which I had not intended. Now it is admin only.

Jonas asked for one more thing, a last login time shown in the users list. I added last_login_at to the users table and set it at login. The list shows it as a relative time.

One thing I decided against was a lockout after failed logins. The rate limit already slows guessing, and a lockout would let anyone block a dispatcher by typing wrong passwords. I put this in the notes for Jonas.

All tests pass, 63 in total on the server and 19 end to end.

Next I want to look at error handling on the client, because a failed request currently shows nothing.

summary: Added a global error handling pattern on the client, with toasts for failed requests and a retry button on charts and tables.
body:
Before this, a failed request left a blank chart or an endless spinner. I added an ApiError class that the fetch helper throws, carrying status and a message from the server.

Each chart and the table now have three states: loading, error and data. The error state shows a short message and a retry button, which calls the fetch again. For 401, the helper sends the user to the login page and remembers the current URL, so the user comes back to the same view after logging in.

A toast area at the bottom shows errors from actions such as saving settings. It uses role status so screen readers read it.

The server now returns errors as json with a message field in every case. Two older routes still sent plain text, which I fixed. A final Express error handler logs the stack and returns 500 without details.

Tests: I simulated a failing stats endpoint in Playwright and checked that the retry button works.

summary: Wrote the first Render production setup for Acme, with environment variables, a staging service, database backups and a migration step before each deploy.
body:
The dashboard is about to go to real users, so I cleaned up the hosting.

There are now two Render services, staging and production, each with its own Postgres instance. Staging deploys from every push to main, and production deploys from a manual promote. This was Jonas's wish, so that nothing changes on his dispatchers' screens without a reason.

Migrations run as a pre-deploy command, using the same script as locally. If a migration fails, the deploy stops and the old version keeps running. I tested it with a deliberately broken migration on staging, and the old version stayed up.

Environment variables: DATABASE_URL, SESSION_SECRET, the mail provider key, and the time zone default. I documented each one in the README. The session secret is different on both services.

Backups: Render's daily backups are on for production, and I tested a restore into a scratch database. It took eleven minutes for the current data. I wrote the steps in docs/restore.md.

I also added a /health check that Render uses, and it now returns the git commit hash so that I can see which version runs.

The seed script refuses to run when NODE_ENV is production. That is a small guard, but I once nearly ran it against the wrong database in my head, so it is there now.

The import of Acme's real data is the next step. Jonas will send an export of last year's consignments.

summary: Imported Acme's real consignment export into staging, which found three data problems: duplicate carriers, missing delivery times and costs with commas.
body:
Jonas sent a file with about 140,000 consignments. I wrote an import script that reads the file in a stream and inserts in batches of 1,000 inside a transaction.

Three problems showed up. First, the carrier names have spelling variants, such as DHL Freight and DHL freight, which created duplicates. I now normalize by trimming and lower-casing for matching, and keep the first spelling as the display name. Second, about 2,300 rows have no delivery time even though the status says delivered. I import them as is, and the charts skip them, with a note to Jonas. Third, the costs use a comma as decimal separator in some rows and a dot in others. The parser handles both and rejects values that are ambiguous, which were 14 rows, listed in a log file.

The import takes about 50 seconds. All pages now show real numbers, and the slow count query is at 110 ms, which I accept.

summary: Wrote a small script that rebuilds the staging database from the seed and the cleaned consignment import, so a broken staging state can be reset in about two minutes.
body:
After the real consignment import into staging, every experiment left the data in a slightly different state, and twice I could not tell whether a odd number came from the code or from leftovers. So this session went into a reset script, scripts/reset-staging.ts, run with npm run staging:reset.

The script does four things in order. It refuses to run unless DATABASE_URL points at the staging host, which I added after nearly pointing it at the wrong database during a test run. It drops and recreates the public schema, runs all migrations, and then loads the seed data. Last it applies the cleanup rules we wrote after the import: merging duplicate carriers by a normalized name, filling missing delivery times with null instead of zero, and converting costs written with a comma into numbers.

The first run took almost eleven minutes, which was too slow to use. The cause was one insert per row for the 5,000 seed shipments and for the imported consignments. I switched both to batched inserts of 1,000 rows with a single multi-row statement, and the run dropped to about two minutes. The carrier merge was also slow at first, because it did a lookup per row; keeping a map of normalized names in memory fixed that.

I compared row counts before and after the reset and they matched: the same carrier count after the merge, and the same total cost as the last manual import to the cent. One check still fails: the sessions table is wiped too, so everyone who is logged in on staging has to sign in again. That is fine for staging, but I wrote it at the top of the script output so nobody is surprised.

Next I want a lighter variant that keeps users and settings and only resets shipments, since Jonas has an account on staging and gets annoyed when it disappears. I also need to describe the script in the README so that it is clear it must never run against production.

summary: Improved the chart legend and carrier colors, so that twelve carriers are distinguishable and a click on a legend entry highlights that carrier across charts.
body:
Jonas said at the call that he could not tell some of the carrier colors apart. I looked at the palette with a color blindness simulator, and four pairs were close for the most common kinds.

Priya made a new palette of twelve colors, chosen for distance in the simulator as well. I put it in the shared base. Colors are now assigned by carrier id, so that a carrier has the same color on every chart and does not change when the range changes. Before, colors were assigned by position in the result, which moved them around.

For the legend, I replaced the built-in ECharts legend on the stacked bar chart with an own one beside the chart. It lists carriers sorted by cost, with a small color square and the total. The built-in one wrapped badly at twelve entries.

Clicking an entry highlights that carrier in all charts on the page, and dims the others. The state lives in a small context, and the charts dispatch the highlight action of ECharts when it changes. Clicking again clears it. I also made the entries real buttons, with aria-pressed, so that keyboard and screen reader users can use them.

One bug: the highlight was lost when a chart reloaded after a range change. I now reapply it after each data update.

Pattern fills for the bars would help too, but Priya thought the palette is enough for now, and I agree for the first version.

Tests: a Playwright test clicks a legend entry and checks aria-pressed on it and the dimmed state through a data attribute that I set for testing. Contrast of the legend text passes the build check.

Next is the delayed consignments per carrier chart that Jonas asked for.

summary: Added a keyboard shortcut and a hover state to the carrier legend, after Priya noticed that the click highlight could not be reached without a mouse.
body:
Priya's review of the new legend showed that the highlight only worked on click. I made the legend entries real buttons with aria-pressed and a visible focus ring. Enter and Space now toggle the highlight, and Escape clears it.

The hover state dims the other carriers to 30 percent opacity, using the same highlight action that the click uses, so there is only one code path. I first tried a CSS-only dim, but ECharts draws on canvas, so it had to go through dispatchAction.

One glitch appeared: after a tab switch the highlight stayed on a carrier that was no longer in the data. I clear the highlight whenever the series list changes. Vitest got two new tests for the toggle logic. Next is a check with Priya on the dark theme colors of the dimmed state.

summary: Slow shipments queries on 200,000 rows were caused by a missing composite index and a count over the whole table; two indexes and a capped count brought the list from 1.8 s to 90 ms.
body:
Since the seed grew to 200,000 rows, the shipments list took about 1.8 seconds with filters set. I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query behind GET /api/shipments. It did a sequential scan, and then sorted by delivered_at in memory.

I added an index on (carrier_id, delivered_at) and one on (status, delivered_at), in a new migration. The planner picked them for the common filters. The list query fell to about 140 ms.

The second cost was the total count for paging, which scanned all matching rows each time. For unfiltered requests I now read the estimate from pg_class. For filtered requests I keep the exact count, but it uses the same indexes now.

The free text search on reference was still slow because of ILIKE with a leading wildcard. I added a pg_trgm index on reference, which needed the extension enabled on Render staging. It worked there without a plan change.

After all of this, the list is at about 90 ms and the count at 25 ms. I wrote the before and after numbers into the migration comment. The aggregate endpoints for charts are next, since they still scan by date only.

summary: Added indexes for the chart aggregate endpoints, so deliveries per day and cost per carrier answer in under 100 ms on 200,000 rows.
body:
The chart endpoints grouped by day and carrier, and they took 600 to 900 ms on the large seed. I added a covering index on (delivered_at, carrier_id, cost) so the planner can use index-only scans.

The average delivery time chart still did a cast on a text column, which blocked the index. I changed the seed and the schema to store the duration as integer minutes, with a migration that fills it from the old column.

All three chart endpoints are now under 100 ms. I kept the query text in the repo notes so the numbers can be repeated.

summary: Wrote the first Playwright tests for login, the shipments table filters and the date picker, and found that the date range reset after a reload.
body:
Until now the only tests were Vitest unit tests. I set up Playwright with a config that starts the API against a test database and the Vite dev server, and a global setup that runs the seed script with 500 rows so the runs stay fast.

The first tests cover three flows. Login with the seeded admin lands on the dashboard. Setting the status and carrier filters changes the URL and the row count. Picking the preset last 7 days changes the chart request parameters.

The third test found a real bug. After a page reload the date range fell back to the default from the settings page, while the URL still had from and to. The picker read its state from settings first and only then from the URL. I changed the order so the URL wins, then the settings default.

I also added a helper that waits for the chart canvas to finish drawing, because the first version of the test was flaky. It listens for the ECharts finished event and sets a data attribute on the container.

The suite runs in about 40 seconds locally. I did not add it to the Render deploy step yet; that needs a decision about where the test database runs. Next I will add the invite flow as a test.

summary: Added a cache layer for the chart aggregate endpoints and a cheap refresh path, so the dashboard opens fast while totals still match the shipments table.
body:
After the indexes for the aggregate endpoints, the dashboard still fired five chart requests on every load and every date range change. This session added a small in-process cache on the API, keyed by endpoint, from, to, time zone and the active filters. Entries live for 60 seconds, which is short enough that dispatchers see new shipments within a minute.

The cache is cleared whenever a shipment is written through the API or the import script runs, so nobody sees stale numbers after an edit. I first tried a longer lifetime of five minutes, but Jonas would have noticed a delivered shipment missing from the count, so I dropped that idea. The key includes the settings time zone, because the midnight fix from last week made the queries depend on it.

I measured with the 200,000 row seed. A cold dashboard load takes about 380 ms for all five charts together, and a warm one takes about 40 ms. Repeating the date presets back and forth no longer hits Postgres at all.

I wrote Vitest tests for the key builder, for expiry and for the clearing on write. One test failed at first because two requests with the same filters in a different parameter order produced different keys. The key now sorts the parameters before it is built.

I compared the numbers of every chart with direct SQL for three date ranges, and they match to the last digit. Memory use of the cache stays below 5 MB with the current seed data, and I capped it at 200 entries with the oldest removed first. Still open: the cache is per process, so with two Render instances each would hold its own copy. That is fine for Acme's single instance today, and I noted it in the README. Next step is a small cache hit counter in the logs, so we can see whether the cache is useful in real use.

summary: Jonas asked why the delayed count on the dashboard differs from his spreadsheet; the cause was time zones at midnight, and the settings time zone is now used in all queries.
body:
Jonas reported 212 delayed shipments in the dashboard and 205 in his own sheet for the same week. I compared the lists and the seven extra ones were all delivered between midnight and 02:00.

The API grouped and filtered by date in UTC, while Acme works in its own time zone from the settings page. The date range filter used from and to as UTC midnights, so shipments near the edge fell on the wrong day.

I changed the queries to convert delivered_at with AT TIME ZONE using the company setting, in the list, the totals and the chart aggregates. A small helper builds the range boundaries once so the endpoints cannot disagree.

I added tests with shipments at 23:30 and 00:30 around a boundary, in two time zones. After the change the dashboard shows 205 and matches the sheet. I told Jonas and asked him to check two more weeks.

summary: Built the saved views feature: users can store a set of filters and a date range under a name and reopen it from the sidebar.
body:
Dispatchers repeat the same filters every morning, so Jonas asked for saved views. I added a saved_views table with user_id, name and the query string of the table filters, plus a unique constraint on user and name.

The API has GET, POST and DELETE under /api/views. A user can only see their own views. The role checks from before apply, so nothing special was needed for dispatchers.

On the client, a Save view button in the filter bar opens a small dialog for the name. The sidebar lists the views, and a click navigates to the shipments page with the stored query string. Because the filters already live in the URL, this was simple.

One edge case: a view with a relative preset such as last 7 days should stay relative. I store the preset name instead of fixed from and to values when a preset is active, and expand it when the view opens.

I wrote Vitest tests for the API and one Playwright test for saving and reopening. Deleting a view asks for confirmation. Rename is not done yet; Jonas said it can wait.

summary: Added rename for saved views and a limit of 20 per user, then fixed a bug where a view saved with a search term lost the term on reopening.
body:
Rename was a small PATCH route and an inline edit in the sidebar. The unique constraint on user and name returns a 409, which the client shows as a message under the field.

I added a limit of 20 views per user, checked in the API, with a clear error message. The sidebar was getting long for people who saved many.

The bug: a view saved with a free text search on reference reopened without the search. The save dialog built the query string from the filter state, but the search box is debounced, so a quick click on Save took the old value. I now read the value from the input directly when saving.

A test for it types and clicks Save at once. It failed before the fix and passes now.

Priya asked for an icon and a tooltip on the sidebar entries. I noted it for the next design pass.

summary: Fixed the sidebar so that long saved view names are cut with an ellipsis and show the full name in a tooltip.
body:
Priya sent a screenshot where a view named after a long carrier list pushed the delete button out of the sidebar. I set a max width and text-overflow ellipsis on the label, and added a title attribute with the full name.

The tooltip also works with keyboard focus, so I used the same accessible tooltip component as the legend. I checked the dark theme and the narrow layout. Both look right. The change is small and has one visual test.

summary: Measured the memory use of the in-memory CSV export on staging, found that large exports are a risk, and added a row limit as a stopgap.
body:
Jonas mentioned that an export of a whole quarter felt slow. I ran the export on staging with the imported real data, which has about 60,000 shipments in that range.

The request took 14 seconds and the Node process went up to about 300 MB, because the export builds all rows as objects and then joins one big string. The Render staging instance has 512 MB, so two exports at once could kill the service.

For now I added a row limit of 100,000 with a clear error message, so nobody takes the server down. The better fix is to stop building the file in memory, but that needs a change of how the query reads rows, so I only wrote it down as a task for later and did not start it.

I wrote the numbers into the notes. Quick wins like removing the second copy of the rows saved about 20 percent, which helps a little but does not change the basic problem.

summary: Added the first scheduled-looking report page: a printable weekly summary with totals, top carriers and delayed shipments, laid out for A4.
body:
Jonas wants a weekly summary he can print for meetings. I made a Report page that takes a week and shows three blocks: totals, the top five carriers by volume, and the list of delayed shipments.

The data comes from the existing endpoints, with one new route for the top carriers. The time zone helper from the earlier fix is used, so the numbers match the dashboard.

For printing I added a print stylesheet. The sidebar and the filter bar are hidden, charts get fixed sizes, and page breaks avoid cutting a table row. ECharts canvases printed blurry at first. Setting devicePixelRatio to 2 before printing fixed it.

Priya reviewed the layout and asked for larger numbers in the totals and Acme's wording for the headings. Both are done.

The page has no way to choose blocks yet. That is the idea for a report builder later, but I kept this version fixed on purpose.

summary: Mobile app agency asked how their driver app can log in against our API; I wrote down options and the constraints of the cookie login, and the user will decide.
body:
The agency building the driver app wrote to ask how the app should authenticate. Today the API only knows the session cookie that the Express session middleware sets after the email and password login. That works in a browser, but a native app has no good cookie handling and no CSRF context.

I listed what they need: login with the same driver accounts, calls to the shipments and status endpoints, and staying logged in for a work shift or more. They cannot easily store a cookie jar across app restarts.

Options I wrote up:
- keep sessions and let the app send the session id as a header. This is simple, but it mixes two ways of using the same value.
- issue signed access tokens on login and check them on each request, with no server lookup.
- use a long-lived API key per device, which is easy but hard to revoke cleanly.

The second option fits best for the app, because the checks are cheap and the app only has to send a header. Its weakness is revoking one token before it expires. I noted that we would need to pick a lifetime and a way to log out.

I also checked what the web client would need to change. The fetch wrapper adds credentials today, and it would send the header instead. The role checks read the user from the session, and they would read it from the token claims.

I sent the summary to the user. The decision is theirs, and I did not start any code.

summary: Wrote the API contract for the driver app: endpoints for assigned shipments and status updates, with example payloads and error codes for the agency.
body:
While the login choice is open, the agency asked for the rest of the contract. I wrote an OpenAPI file in the repo and served it as a page on staging.

Three endpoints are new. GET /api/driver/shipments returns the shipments assigned to the logged-in driver for today. POST /api/driver/shipments/:id/status takes a status of picked_up, in_transit or delivered with an optional note. GET /api/driver/me returns the profile.

Validation uses zod on the server, and the error body has a code and a message, such as invalid_status or not_assigned. I wrote an example for each case in the file.

A question came up about the order of status changes. A driver cannot mark delivered before picked_up. The API returns 409 with the code bad_transition. I added a small table of allowed transitions and tests for each.

I also added a role named driver to the role checks, with no access to the dashboard routes. The tests check that a driver gets 403 on the settings and invite endpoints.

The agency can now build against staging with a test driver account. Authentication is still the open point.

summary: Reviewed the first Acme user feedback on the dashboard charts and sorted it into quick fixes, design questions for Priya and wishes that need a decision from Jonas.
body:
Jonas sent a list of 17 remarks after two weeks of using staging with the real consignment data. I went through them one by one and grouped them so that nothing gets lost between the user, Priya and Jonas. Seven are quick fixes that I can do within a day or two. Five are design questions that Priya should look at, and five are wishes that change the scope.

The quick fixes are small things. The tooltip on the cost chart shows costs without a thousands separator, so 12400 is hard to read. The average delivery time chart labels its axis in minutes, while the dispatchers think in hours. Two column headers in the table still use the old wording and one empty state says only no data.

For Priya I collected the questions about the chart colors in dark theme, the spacing of the filter bar and whether the totals row should be sticky. I attached screenshots of the current state to each question, so she can answer without opening staging. She said she will answer in the next days.

The wishes are the ones with a cost. Jonas would like a comparison with the previous period in every chart, a map of the depots and a way to mark shipments as checked. None of them is small. I wrote a rough estimate for each, from half a day for the comparison up to about a week for the map.

I sent the list back to Jonas with the estimates and asked him to put the five wishes in an order. I also started on the quick fixes with the thousands separator and the axis units, and both are in the main checkout and tested.

summary: Looked into slow rows on Jonas's laptop and found that the table re-rendered every row on each hover; memoizing rows and a stable key cut scripting time by about 70 percent.
body:
Jonas had said before that the table felt slow on his laptop. I borrowed the case with a 6-year-old CPU profile setting, meaning a 6x throttle in the Chrome profiler, and recorded a hover across the table.

Every mouse move over a row changed a hovered-row state in the table component, and that rerendered all 50 rows with their cells. Scripting took about 90 ms per move on the throttled run.

I moved the hover highlight into CSS, so no state is needed. I also wrapped the row component in React.memo and made sure that the props are stable: the column definitions were created inline on each render, so I moved them into a useMemo.

The row key had used the array index, which made sorting remount rows. It uses the shipment id now.

After the change a hover costs almost nothing, and a sort took 60 ms instead of 210 ms on the throttled run. A test checks that rows do not rerender on hover by counting renders with a mock.

I asked Jonas to try the staging build. If it is still slow, we need virtual scrolling for the page size of 200 that he sometimes picks.

summary: Added virtual scrolling to the shipments table for page sizes of 100 and 200, which keeps scrolling smooth and the DOM below 40 rows.
body:
Jonas confirmed that the hover fix helped, but with a page size of 200 the scroll still stuttered on his laptop. The DOM had 200 rows with about 10 cells each.

I used @tanstack/react-virtual for the body. The table has a fixed row height of 44 px, which makes the math simple. The header stays sticky, and the totals row is outside the scrolled area.

Several things needed care. The column widths came from the content before, and with virtual rows they would jump while scrolling. I set explicit widths with a default per column, and the carrier column gets the rest.

Keyboard navigation broke at first, because rows that are not in the DOM cannot get focus. I added a roving focus on the visible rows and scrollToIndex on arrow keys, and I checked the screen reader labels with aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex, so that the position is still read correctly.

Printing is a problem, since only the visible rows exist. The print view turns virtual scrolling off and renders all rows of the page.

The measurements on the throttled profile: 200 rows scroll at 55 fps, the DOM has 34 rows, and the first render takes 80 ms instead of 400 ms. The Playwright tests for the table needed a small change to scroll before counting rows.

I also kept the old simple path for page sizes of 50 or less. It has no dependencies on measuring and fewer places to break.

summary: Added audit columns and a change log for shipment edits after a dispatcher's status change could not be traced, so every edit now records who made it and what changed.
body:
A dispatcher at Acme reported that a shipment had changed from in transit to delayed, and nobody could say who did it or when. The data was right in the end, but the missing trace bothered Jonas, so this session added an audit trail. I started with the question of what has to be recorded: the user, the time, the field, the old value and the new value.

A migration added a shipment_changes table with those columns and an index on the shipment id. The API endpoint for status updates now writes the change in the same transaction as the update, so the two cannot drift apart. I chose not to use a database trigger, because the user id lives in the application and would not be available there without extra work.

The shipment detail panel got a History section, which lists the last 20 changes with the name of the user and a relative time. Old shipments have no history, and the panel says so and not just an empty list. The import script writes its changes with the system as the user, which is clearer than a blank.

I wrote tests for three cases: a normal edit, an edit that changes nothing, which must not write a row, and an edit that fails halfway, where nothing may be written. The third case caught a bug in my first version, where the change row was saved even though the update was rolled back. Moving both into one transaction fixed it.

On the seed data the update endpoint still answers in about 12 ms. Open points are how long to keep the changes and whether managers should see the history for all shipments in one view. I wrote both as questions for Jonas.

summary: Prepared the changes for the report builder: a list of blocks, a settings shape stored per report, and a first spike that renders totals and a chart from a saved config.
body:
Jonas asked again for choosable blocks in the printed weekly report, so I started a spike for a report builder. This session was only about the shape of the data and a render test.

A report is a title plus an ordered list of blocks. Each block has a type and a small config. The types for now are totals, top_carriers, delayed_list and chart, where the chart config names one of the three existing charts.

I added a reports table with user_id, title and a JSON column for the blocks. Zod validates the shape on save, so an unknown block type is rejected with a clear message.

On the client, a registry maps each block type to a component and to the endpoint that feeds it. The existing weekly report page became the first report, defined as a config instead of fixed markup. This was a nice test of the idea: the output was the same, and the print stylesheet still worked.

I ran into a problem with the chart block. The charts read the date range from the URL, but a report has its own range. I made the range a prop that the block passes down, and the URL is only the default.

There is no editor yet. For the test I stored two reports by script and rendered them. One of them had the blocks in a different order, and the layout handled it.

Things to do: the editor with add, remove and reorder, a preview, and permission checks so a dispatcher cannot change shared reports. I also have to decide whether reports are private by default. I asked Jonas, who thinks managers should share them.

summary: Built the first editor for reports: add and remove blocks, move them up and down, and a live preview next to the form.
body:
With the data shape in place, the editor was the next step. It is a two-column page, the block list on the left and the preview on the right.

The left side has a select to add a block type and, for each block, buttons to move it up or down and to remove it. I did not add drag and drop. Buttons are easier to use with a keyboard, and Priya asked for that in the accessibility pass earlier.

The preview uses the same registry as the report page, so what you see is what is printed. Changes are held in local state and saved with a Save button, which sends a PUT with the whole block list.

Two bugs came up. The chart block lost its config when moved, because I used the index as the key. I switched to a generated id per block. The second was a stale preview after removing the last block, since an empty list was treated as no config and the old one was shown.

I wrote tests for the reducer behind the editor, covering add, remove and moves at the ends of the list. Next are the permissions, the sharing and the page that lists the reports.

summary: Planned the access token login for the dashboard and the driver app, listing what must change in the login route, the middleware and the web client, without building any of it yet.
body:
I started from the decision I wrote down earlier this week: the cookie cannot work for a native app, so the API will have to issue signed access tokens. Today I turned that into a written plan and did not change any login code.

The plan for the login route is that it keeps checking the email and password, and then returns a signed token with the user id and role as claims. The signing secret would be an environment variable on Render, and I made a note to add it to staging first. I looked at the existing role checks and confirmed that they all read from req.user, so a middleware that verifies the signature and the expiry and sets req.user should not need changes in them. For the transition, the middleware would also accept the session cookie for one more week, so nobody is logged out in the middle of work.

The lifetime is the open point. I sketched 30 days, which is long, but it matches how the drivers work and the user wants the first step to stay simple. I wrote this into the notes as something to review later.

For the web client, I read through the fetch wrapper and listed what would change: it would add an Authorization header from a stored token, and a 401 response would send the user to the login page. Local storage is the easy place for the token, but any script on the page can read it, so I noted that as a risk.

I also noted that logout would only delete the token on the client, because the server cannot take a token back. That is a known gap, and I plan to write a test that documents it so it is not forgotten.

For tests I listed the cases to cover in Vitest: valid, expired, tampered, missing header and wrong role. The Playwright login test will need to read the token instead of the cookie.

I sent the agency of the mobile app a short description of the planned route and asked for a test driver account. Next I will start with the login route and the middleware on a branch of the main checkout.

summary: Investigated a crash on the invite page and the sidebar of the web client and wrote down a plan for the login work that the driver app needs.
body:
Jonas saw the sidebar flash and then a white page on a fresh login on staging. The console showed Cannot read properties of undefined reading role. At this point the dashboard still logs in with the session cookie, so I first checked whether the crash came from the cookie flow itself.

The auth provider reads the user role from the session response during the first render, and the fetch of the session user runs in an effect afterwards. On a fresh load the user is undefined for one render, and the sidebar reads the role at once. That explains the flash and the white page. It only shows on a slow connection, which is why it never appeared on my machine and only on staging.

I did not change the provider yet. I wrote a short note on how it should work: the provider should resolve the user before the routes render, and a missing or invalid session should count as logged out at that point. The same shape will matter when the driver app agency asks for a login that works without a cookie, so I want the provider to be ready for a different source of the user.

I also reproduced the crash in a Playwright test that throttles the network and checks for console errors on a fresh login. It fails as expected and stays red for now. While looking around, I found a leftover check in the invite page that reads the old session user directly, and I put it on the list for the cleanup.

summary: Replaced the hand-written fetch calls in the client with one small API module, after a bug where an error from the server was handled differently on three pages.
body:
Yesterday a failed save on the settings page showed no message, while the same kind of failure on the shipments page showed a toast. The cause was that every page called fetch itself and read the error body in its own way. This session replaced all of that with a single module in the client, api.ts, that every request goes through.

The module sets the base path, sends JSON and reads the response. On a non-2xx status it throws a typed ApiError that holds the status, the error code from our API contract and the message. Pages catch that one error type, and the global handler from the error pattern shows the toast, so the behavior is the same everywhere.

The login is going to change soon, because the driver app needs a way to call the same API. For that reason the module is the only place where credentials are handled. Today it sends the session cookie with every request, and I put that in one spot with a comment, so the later change to the login only has to touch this file. That removed five copies of the same fetch options. A 401 answer is handled in one spot too, where the client clears its login state and goes to the login page. Before, only two of the pages did that, and the others just showed an empty table.

I moved the calls page by page, starting with settings and ending with the charts. The chart components needed the most care, because they cancel requests when the date range changes. The module accepts an AbortSignal and passes it on, and an aborted request is not treated as an error and shows no toast.

I added Vitest tests with a mocked fetch for success, a JSON error, a text error from a proxy and an abort. The Playwright tests for login and filters still pass, and the diff removes about 220 lines more than it adds. Still to do is the CSV export link, which uses a plain download and still builds its own URL. I left it as it is for now and wrote a note, because the export is due for a separate look.

summary: Wrote down the decision for the driver app login: the cookie cannot work for a native app, so the API will issue signed access tokens from a login endpoint.
body:
The mobile agency asked again yesterday for a date, so I put the options into one decision note in docs/auth-driver-app.md. The cookie login depends on the browser cookie jar and the Express session middleware, which keeps sessions in Postgres. A native app can keep a cookie, but the agency said their HTTP client drops it on some Android versions and they do not want to depend on it.

The note lists three options. First, keep the cookie and ask the agency to handle it by hand. Second, issue a long random key per driver and store it in a table. Third, issue signed access tokens that the API checks without a database call. I wrote down what each costs us: the key table adds a lookup on every request, while signed tokens are cheap to check but hard to revoke before they expire.

I also sketched the endpoint shape. A POST to /auth/login would take email and password and return the token plus an expiry time. The dashboard would send it in the Authorization header instead of the cookie. Existing cookie users would keep working for one release so nobody is logged out on deploy.

I listed the risks plainly. A token stored on the device can be lost with the phone. A long lifetime makes that worse, and there is no way to log out one device early. I suggested a lifetime of 30 days for now, since drivers complained in the first feedback round that they hate typing a password on a phone, and said we can shorten it later if it hurts.

I did not change any code today. The middleware stays as it is, and the role checks from the settings work are the part to reuse, since they read the user role from the request. The next step is the user's decision on the note. If it is the token option, the first piece of work is the login endpoint with tests, then moving the web client off the cookie. I also noted that the staging database has two test drivers that I can use for the agency's first calls.

summary: Added a refresh button and a last updated time to the dashboard header, because dispatchers did not know if the numbers were current.
body:
Jonas mentioned that dispatchers keep reloading the whole page to see whether the numbers changed. I added a small refresh button to the header that refetches the chart and table queries without a full reload. Next to it the header shows the time of the last successful fetch, taken from the response and not from the browser clock.

While doing this I found that the cache layer from earlier returns its own timestamp, so the label shows the cache age, which is the honest value. The button calls the cheap refresh path and then invalidates the client queries. A failed refresh keeps the old time and shows the usual error toast.

I added one Vitest test for the label formatting and one Playwright step that clicks the button and waits for the label to change. Both pass. Nothing is left open, but Priya may want a different icon.

summary: Planned the token login for the driver app: read the cookie login code, wrote down the endpoint shape and the tests I want, and wrote no endpoint code yet.
body:
Started the preparation for the driver app login in the main checkout. I read through the cookie login route in server/routes/auth.ts and found that the password check is already one function that compares hashes. The new login should reuse it, so there stays one place that compares hashes.

I wrote a short plan in the notes file for the API contract. The response should carry a signed token, the expiry as a timestamp and a small user object with name and role, so the driver app does not need a second call after login. Errors keep the codes from the contract: 401 for a wrong password and 403 for a disabled user. The message for an unknown email must be the same as for a wrong password, so the caller cannot learn whether an email exists.

I also looked at the lifetime. A long lifetime is simplest for the drivers, who dislike logging in again, so I wrote 30 days as the first proposal and listed the cost: a token cannot be taken back before it expires. I will bring that point to Jonas and the agency before I settle it.

For the secret, I decided it should come from an environment variable and that the server should refuse to start in production if it is missing. I have not added it to Render yet. I only checked where the staging service keeps its settings and what the local .env example looks like.

The cookie login has a limit of ten tries per minute per address, set in middleware on /login. A new route would need the same limit, so I added it to the list of tests to write: good login, wrong password, unknown email, disabled user, missing body, and the eleventh attempt getting a 429.

Nothing in the code has changed today, and the cookie route is untouched. Next I will write the failing tests first, then decide the lifetime with Jonas.

summary: Planned the middleware that will read an access token from the Authorization header next to the cookie session, and wrote the first tests, without wiring it into the routes yet.
body:
Nothing about the token login exists yet except a plan. The login endpoint that will return a signed access token is not written, so today I treated the token as a thing the middleware will have to accept once the endpoint exists. This was the start of the second step on paper, the middleware that will read that token. I sketched server/middleware/requireUser.ts, but it is not mounted on any route and the app still runs on the old session lookup alone.

The plan is that the middleware looks for a bearer token first and for the session cookie second. If the token is valid, it will set req.user with the id and role from the token claims. If there is no token, the old session lookup has to run exactly as before, so current users stay logged in.

The order needs care. A request with both a cookie and a token should use the token, because the new clients will send both for a while and I do not want two identities in one request. I wrote that case down as a test to be filled in.

The role checks from the settings work read req.user.role, so they should need no change. I went through each route that touches company settings and invites, and all of them go through the same helper. That was a relief, because a route that read the session directly would have been a hole.

For errors, I decided that an expired token will return 401 with a code token_expired and a broken signature will return 401 with token_invalid, so the client can tell them apart later.

I wrote the test list: a valid token, an expired one, a bad signature, a token for a disabled user, cookie only, token only, both together and neither. The disabled user case is the one I thought about longest. A signed token does not know that the user was disabled after it was issued. One option is a check against the users table for that one flag, which would cost one cheap indexed query but weakens the no database call idea a little. I did not settle it and will put it to the user as a decision.

The existing suite still runs green, 142 tests, and the Playwright login test still uses the cookie and passes. Left to do: write the login endpoint, finish the middleware, mount it, then the web client change and the logout, which today destroys the session and will need a new meaning for tokens.

summary: Planned the move of the web client to a future token login and prepared the client API module and auth store on paper, without switching the web client over or writing any endpoint.
body:
I spent the session preparing the client for a token login that does not exist yet, without changing how the web client logs in. The dashboard still uses the cookie, and the API has no login endpoint that returns a signed access token. That endpoint is only planned, so nothing in the client can call it today.

First I read through the client API module that came out of the earlier cleanup. Every request goes through one function, so attaching an Authorization header later is a change in one place. I wrote a short plan in the decision note: an auth store that holds the token and the expiry, a header added only when a token exists, and the cookie kept as the fallback so nobody is logged out during the change.

I thought about where the token should live, and I did not decide yet. Local storage survives a reload but a script injected into the page could read it. Memory only is safer but logs users out on every reload. The dashboard has no user generated HTML except the saved view names, which React escapes, so the risk looks small. I listed both options with this reasoning in the note so the user can choose before I build it.

I also noted the logout problem in advance. If the tokens live 30 days and are checked without a database call, clearing one on the client will not end it on the server. I wrote this down as an open question and did not try to solve it.

For tests, I sketched the Playwright cases I want: login sends the header, a reload keeps the user logged in, an expired token goes back to the login page. I also wrote down that the sidebar must read the role only after login has finished, because of the crash fixed earlier. Next I want to finish the endpoint plan and its tests, so that the two test drivers can try it on staging before I touch the web client.

summary: Read the mobile agency's sample client script and planned the token login for the driver app, noting a likely clock skew risk and a CORS gap, without writing any endpoint or middleware code yet.
body:
The agency sent a small script that calls our API the way the driver app will. I read through it this evening and compared it with the cookie login code and the endpoint shape I wrote down earlier. Nothing has been built or deployed yet. Two risks stood out on paper.

The first is clock skew. My plan for the signed access token was to set a not-before claim equal to the issue time. The two Render instances can differ by a second or two, so a token checked on the slower instance right after login could be rejected as not yet valid. I have not seen this fail, because there is no token code to run yet. I decided to leave the not-before claim out, since we do not need it, and to plan a tolerance of five seconds in the check. I put this in the notes as the first item for the later staging run.

The second is CORS. The browser will send a preflight request for the Authorization header, and the API's list of allowed headers does not include it. The old cookie flow never needed that. The agency script is not a browser, so it will not show the problem, but the dashboard will. I noted that Authorization has to be added to the allowed headers, with the preflight cache set to about ten minutes.

I also wrote the checks I want to run once the endpoint and middleware exist:
- login from the script returns a token and a user object
- the assigned shipments endpoint answers with the token and gives 401 without it
- a status update from the script is written with the right driver id in the audit columns
- the web dashboard works after a reload
- an old cookie session still works

I also want to compare response times for the shipments list with the token and with the cookie. The cookie version is about 90 ms, and the token version should match it, since no database call is needed.

The agency asked about the token lifetime. I answered that it will be 30 days for now and that the app should handle a 401 by sending the user back to login. I started a note for them with the header format and the error codes, to be finished later.

Next is writing the endpoint tests, including a small test for the tolerance so a skew bug cannot come back. The staging run and the release plan come after that.

summary: Prepared the token login for release by writing a checklist for the deploy and a test plan with the mobile app agency, without releasing anything yet.
body:
I went through the token login branch and wrote a release checklist for the deploy. It lists the migration step, the environment variable for the signing secret on Render, and the log lines to watch for 401 responses in the first hour. Nothing was deployed, and production still runs the cookie login only.

I checked the staging database with a copy of the real user table and ran the migration there twice, to be sure it can be repeated without errors. It ran clean both times and took a few seconds.

I also sent the agency a short plan for testing the driver app against the live API once the release is out. I asked them for a real driver account to use, and I asked what the app shows in its header after login. They answered that the header shows the depot name of the driver, and I noticed that the user object in our login response does not contain it yet. I added a note to the checklist to add the depot name to the response before the release, with a test, so that the agency does not find it first.

The cookie route is planned to stay for one release, so users who are logged in by cookie are not thrown out. I wrote a reminder for myself to look at the count of cookie only sessions after the release, and to think about what logout should do with tokens, since a token cannot simply be deleted on the server.

summary: Fixed the carrier legend overflowing on narrow screens by wrapping it under the chart and limiting it to two rows with a show more link.
body:
Priya sent a screenshot from a small laptop where the legend with twelve carriers pushed the chart to a thin strip. The legend was laid out to the right of the chart with a fixed width. I changed the layout so that below 900 px the legend moves under the chart.

Twelve entries still took four rows, so I limited it to two rows and added a show more link that expands the rest. The highlight on click and the keyboard shortcut still work in the collapsed state, and a highlighted carrier that is hidden in the collapsed part expands the list so the user sees which one is active.

I checked the layout at 800, 1024 and 1440 px by hand and added a Playwright screenshot test for the narrow case. Priya approved the look. The ECharts legend config is now built by one function, which will help for new charts later.

summary: Looked into how logout could really work once the token login exists, measured the options in a script, and wrote a plan to choose from, without changing any login code.
body:
The planned token login will only clear the token on the client at logout. A copied token would keep working until it expires, up to 30 days. Jonas asked yesterday whether a manager who leaves the company would be cut off at once under the new login, and the honest answer for the plan as it stands is no, unless we disable the user, which the middleware would check.

I spent the session finding out what the options cost. I wrote a small script that issues test tokens and calls a scratch copy of the API, to test each idea against real behavior. Nothing in the real login code changed, and nothing was deployed.

Option one is a deny list. Every logout stores the token id in a Postgres table, and the middleware checks the table on each request. It works, but it adds one query per request and the table grows by one row per logout until old rows are cleaned. With about 300 active users and a few logouts per day the growth is small. The query is by primary key and measured 0.6 ms in staging.

Option two is a token version on the user row. A logout increments the number, and tokens with an older number are rejected. It needs one read of the user per request, which we already do for the disabled flag, so the cost is almost zero. The problem is that it logs out every device at once, including the driver phone, which is not what a user pressing logout on the laptop wants.

Option three is shorter token lifetimes. A lifetime of 15 minutes limits the damage but needs a way to renew, which means a second kind of token and a second storage. That is more work and more moving parts, and the mobile agency would need to change their app.

Option four is to do nothing and accept the risk. The dashboard shows shipment and cost data of one client, not payments, and Jonas said the risk is acceptable for a short time, but not for long.

I tried the version number idea in a branch of my working copy and found a nasty detail. The read of the user row happens after the signature check, so a token for a deleted user gives a 500 unless the null case is handled. I wrote a test that shows it. The same gap exists in the planned disabled check, so I noted the fix in the plan.

My recommendation is option one for logout of a single token, and to revisit short lifetimes when the mobile app has its first update. I wrote the numbers and the recommendation into docs/auth-logout.md and sent a short summary to the user.

The next step waits for a decision. If the user agrees, I will design the deny list table with an expiry column and a cleanup query, and build the null user handling together with the middleware.

summary: Removed the old cookie login route after the count of cookie only sessions dropped to two, and cleaned out the session middleware code that served it.
body:
The reminder from the release was to remove the cookie path once nobody used it. I queried the sessions table and found two rows with activity in the last week, both from one dispatcher who had not opened the dashboard since the token release. I asked Jonas to have her log in again, and by noon her row was gone.

I removed the cookie fallback in requireUser.ts. The middleware now only accepts the bearer token. I deleted the old /login route, the session store setup and the cookie options. The sessions table stays for now in the schema, because dropping it is a migration that I prefer to do separately.

The tests had many places that logged in by cookie. I changed the test helper to create a token directly, which also made the suite faster, from 41 s to 33 s. Three Playwright tests needed their login step rewritten to use the form.

I checked the invite flow, which sends an email with a link. It created a session at the end of accepting the invite. I changed it to return a token like the login does. This was easy to miss, and I found it only by grepping for the session helper.

The password change in the profile section also destroyed the session and logged the user in again. Now it returns a fresh token. The old token is still valid after a password change, which is a weak spot, and I added it to the notes next to the logout problem.

On staging I tried login, invite, password change and logout by hand. All work. Production deploy is planned for this afternoon.
