The new table login_events has user id (nullable for unknown emails), the email as typed, the result (success, wrong_password, locked, unknown_user), the IP address, the user agent string and a timestamp. For privacy the IP is stored as is, but only for 90 days, and a weekly job removes older rows, like the cleanup of invite tokens that I added before.

The login handler writes the event after the check, in the same request. I took care that a failure to write the event does not fail the login. It logs the error and goes on, since an audit problem should not stop dispatchers from working.

The mobile app logs in through the same handler, so driver logins appear as well. I mark them with a source field taken from the app's user agent. The agency's agent string is stable, so the match is simple.

The rate limiter I added for the login already counts failures per email and IP. I considered reading the counts from the new table, but decided against it, since a limiter should not depend on a table that can be cleaned. They stay separate.

For the admin page I added a small read-only list of the last 100 events with a filter for the user. Only admins can open it, and the endpoint checks the role on the server. There is a test that a dispatcher gets a 403.

One issue appeared in testing. The user agent can be long, and a test with a 3,000 character string failed on the column length. I cut it at 300 characters before saving.

The migration is small and runs fast on the production size. I tested it on a copy with the real number of users.

Open points: showing the events to the user themselves in the settings page, which would be useful for people who want to see their own logins, and an alert for many failures. I put both in the notes. Jonas can look at the admin list tomorrow.

summary: Answered Jonas's question how many dispatchers log in per day using the new login events: about 55 on weekdays, and noted the data only goes back a few hours.
body:
Jonas asked, as soon as the admin list was available, how many people really use the dashboard each day. I wanted to give him a real number, but the login events table is only a day old, so I could only count what it has.

For the one full day, there were 52 distinct dispatchers and managers with a successful login, and 118 driver logins from the mobile app. Failed attempts were 9, of which 6 came from one person who forgot the password and then used the reset.

I told Jonas that one day is not a trend, and that I would give him a better number after two weeks. A subtlety is that the token lasts 30 days, so a user with a valid token does not log in and does not appear. The count of logins therefore understates the real use of the dashboard.

For active users, the better source is the API request log, which has the user id for each call. I ran a query on it for the last 30 days and got 71 distinct users, which is closer to the truth. I sent both numbers with this explanation.

summary: Fixed a chart tooltip that showed the wrong carrier name after the legend was used to hide a series, by looking up the name by series id instead of index.
body:
Priya found that in the costs by carrier chart the tooltip showed a different carrier name than the bar under the mouse after she clicked a legend entry to hide one carrier. I reproduced it in the dashboard with three carriers.

The tooltip formatter used the series index to find the name in our own array. ECharts keeps the indices of all series, but my array was built from the visible ones, so the index shifted after hiding. I changed the formatter to use the series id that is set when the option is built.

The same pattern was in two other charts that use chartBase, and I checked them: one had it, the delivery time chart, and I fixed it there too. I wrote a Vitest test for the formatter with a hidden middle series.

I took screenshots in both themes and Priya confirmed that the tooltips are right.

summary: Reviewed the pull-request-sized change of the user list paging with a fresh eye and found that searching by name ignored the page, so results beyond page one were missing.
body:
While answering a question of an admin who could not find a user, I looked again at the settings page user list, which got paging a few weeks ago. The search box filtered only the loaded page on the client. A user on page three never appeared in the results.

I moved the search to the server. The users endpoint takes a q parameter, matched with ILIKE on name and email, and returns the page of the matching rows with the right total. The search is debounced for 300 ms on the client.

For the ILIKE on about 4,000 users no index is needed, and the query takes a few milliseconds. I checked the plan to be sure.

One more edge case: a search text with a percent sign or an underscore would act as a pattern. I escape both before building the query, and there is a test with an email containing an underscore.

Changing the search resets the page to the first one. That was the same kind of bug as the one in the shipments table cursor.

Playwright covers a search for a user that is on page three of the full list. Deployed after the tests.

summary: Wrote the plan for the token lifetime and refresh design with the mobile agency, comparing a refresh token approach with other options, and Jonas chose to wait a few weeks.
body:
After the answers of the agency I wrote a proper plan for how to fix the long lifetime of the token. The problem is the same as before: a stolen or copied token works for 30 days, and a logout does nothing on the server.

Option A is short access tokens of about 15 minutes with a refresh token. The refresh token is long, stored per device in Postgres, and is replaced on each use. If an old one is used again, the whole family can be revoked. This gives real logout, since the refresh token can be deleted. The costs are a new endpoint, a table, and work in both clients. The agency needs about two weeks.

Option B is the token version per user. It is cheap and gives logout of all devices at once, but one device only is not possible. It also needs a database read per request, though a cache solves most of that.

Option C is a deny list of token ids. It gives a precise logout and needs a check per request. The table grows with every logout until the tokens expire, and after 30 days that means many rows to clean up. I do not like it for the long lifetime.

My ranking: A for the long term, B as a stopgap if the shared computer case becomes urgent. I stated that A has the most moving parts, especially the race when two tabs refresh at the same moment, which needs a small lock or a grace window on the client side.

I also described what the web client would look like. The refresh token would live in an httpOnly cookie, so local storage is no longer holding anything long lived. The access token stays in memory. This fixes the private mode complaint partly: the user would still need to sign in after closing the tab in private mode, but at least the secrets are safer.

For the mobile app, the refresh token lives in the keychain, and the agency adds a call on 401. I made a short sequence list of the calls for them, with the error codes.

Jonas read the plan and decided to do A, but not now. The agency is busy with a release for a new depot, and he does not want two changes in the same weeks. He asked me to keep the shared computer warning and to come back to it in a few weeks. I put the plan in the repository docs as a decision draft with open questions: lifetime of the refresh token, and whether an idle limit is wanted.

No code was changed. I listed which parts could be prepared without the agency, such as the table and the endpoint behind a feature flag.

summary: Prepared the report builder for number formats and column widths in table blocks, the two items left from the column work, and fixed PDF cells that overflowed with long carrier names.
body:
The two items I noted after the column work were widths and number formats. Dispatchers wanted costs with two decimals and a currency sign, delays in hours with one decimal, and narrow columns for ids. This session did both.

Each column in the block config can now have a format: plain, integer, decimal1, decimal2, currency, percent or duration. The formatter functions live in one module that the preview, the PDF and the CSV of a report block all use, so a number looks the same everywhere. That module took the most care, since a difference between the preview and the PDF would be visible at once.

Currency uses the report's locale setting. For Acme this is German style formatting with a comma as the decimal separator. The CSV of the block keeps a dot and no thousands separators, because a spreadsheet import breaks otherwise. I wrote this rule as a comment in the module.

Column widths are a choice of narrow, normal and wide, not free pixels. The PDF layout maps them to shares of the page width. Free sizing would again be hard to do with the keyboard.

The PDF problem appeared in a test report: long carrier names like 'Nordwest Spedition und Logistik GmbH' ran over into the next cell. I set a word break and a maximum of two lines with an ellipsis in the PDF, and the preview shows the full name in a title attribute. The row height is now fixed per block, which also helps the 40 rows per page rule.

An old report without format values uses plain for all columns, the same migration on load as before. A test checks three old shapes again, and one new test checks that unknown format names fall back to plain and do not crash.

Vitest cases for the formatters: negative amounts, zero, null, a very large number and rounding of 0.005. Rounding was a small trap. 1.005 with decimal2 gave 1.00 because of floating point, and I used a rounding based on integer cents for the currency format.

In the editor, each selected column has a small select for the format and one for the width. I labeled the selects, and the keyboard order goes by column.

Playwright checks that a report with a currency column shows the euro sign in the preview and in the downloaded PDF text. The PDF text check reads the file with a small parser.

Still open: formats for date columns, which still use the default one. I noted that and will ask Priya about how she wants dates in printed reports.

summary: Added a carrier comparison view to the costs page so managers can put up to three carriers side by side, and fixed a palette clash that made two carriers look identical.
body:
Jonas had asked for a way to compare carriers on the costs page without exporting to his spreadsheet, so today's session built a comparison view on top of the carrier table. A manager ticks up to three rows and a panel opens below the table with cost per shipment, cost per kilometer and the fuel surcharge share for each carrier, using the same period as the key number row.

The selection lives in the URL next to the period, the same way the table page and sort do now, so a comparison can be sent to someone as a link. I reused the multi-select logic from the carrier filter rather than writing a second one, and capped it at three because the stacked bar gets unreadable beyond that.

While testing with real data I found that two carriers got nearly the same blue in the dark theme when they were picked together, because the palette was assigned by position in the selection and not by carrier. I changed it to assign colors by a stable hash of the carrier id, so a carrier keeps its color across the table, the stacked bar and the comparison panel. This also fixed the legend showing a different color than the bar after hiding a series.

The API needed one new endpoint parameter, carrierIds, on the costs summary route. It validates that every id belongs to a carrier the user may see and returns 400 for more than three. I added Vitest cases for the limit, the empty selection and a carrier with no shipments in the period, which returns zeros and not a missing entry.

I checked the panel with screenshots in light and dark theme and with the keyboard only, since the accessibility pass last week showed how easily focus gets lost after such widgets. Focus now moves to the panel heading when it opens and back to the checkbox when it closes. Still open: the comparison does not yet follow the delivery time toggle for cost per delivered hour, and a Playwright test for the whole flow is not written. Next I will send Jonas a screenshot and ask whether three carriers is enough.

summary: Looked into a report of duplicated rows in the shipments CSV and found that shipments with two stops appeared twice because of a join, then fixed the export query.
body:
A dispatcher noticed that the export of the shipments table had more rows than the table showed: 1,312 against 1,248. I compared the ids and found 64 shipments that appeared twice in the file.

All of them had two stops. The export query joins the stops table to get the destination city, and the join returned one row per stop. The table query uses a lateral subquery that takes only the last stop, so it never had the problem. The two queries drifted apart after the export got its own copy of the select for the extra columns.

I changed the export to use the same lateral subquery for the destination. The count is now equal to the table for the same filters. The earlier work made the filter code shared, but the select part was still separate, so I moved the select into a shared builder as well, with a list of optional columns.

A test now compares the count of rows from the table endpoint with the count of the export for a fixture with two stops, and also checks that the row ids are unique.

I told the dispatcher that older exports may contain duplicates, and that the totals in them are too high for the shipments with two stops. They had used one in a cost sheet, so I offered to send a corrected file. The corrected export of a quarter still takes about 18 seconds, which is the slowness we already know about, and it did work in this case.

I deployed the fix this morning after the tests passed.

summary: Added a settings page section where users see their own recent logins from the login events, with a note about which devices they were, and tested it with Priya's wording.
body:
The login events table had one more use that I had noted: letting people see their own logins. It helps with the case of someone who thinks that another person used the account. This session built a small section in the settings page.

The endpoint /api/me/logins returns the last 20 successful and failed events of the current user, with time, a short device text and the result. The device text comes from the user agent, parsed into browser and system, like 'Safari on iPhone'. I used a small parser we already had for the admin list. The IP address is shown only as the first part, for example 192.168.x.x style, so that the page does not give out too much if someone looks over a shoulder.

Priya reviewed the wording. She changed 'wrong_password' into 'Wrong password entered' and 'locked' into 'Blocked for a short time after too many tries'. She also asked for a calm look, with no red warning unless there are several failures in a row. I made the text of the section neutral, and a hint appears only after three failures with a link to change the password.

The endpoint reads only the rows of the logged in user, taking the user id from the token and not from a parameter. There is a test that a request with another user's id in the query is ignored.

The list has a caption and works with the keyboard, per the earlier accessibility notes.

Open: the page cannot end a session from this list, because with the JWT login there is nothing to end on the server. That limitation is the same as with the logout, and I wrote it in the notes of the token plan.

summary: Added a note to the settings page recent logins list showing when the data starts, after users asked why older logins were missing.
body: Two dispatchers asked why their recent logins list showed only a few days. The login events table was only introduced recently, so nothing exists before that. I added a short line under the list saying that logins are shown from the start of the audit log and kept for 90 days. Priya reviewed the wording and shortened it to one sentence. I checked the line in the dark theme and at narrow width. No behavior of the login changed. Next is looking at how failed attempts should be shown to the user, which Jonas has not decided yet.

summary: Fixed the costs page period comparison showing infinity percent when the previous period had zero cost, by showing a dash instead.
body: Jonas sent a screenshot of the costs key numbers with a change of Infinity% for a new carrier. The cause was dividing by the previous period total, which was zero. I added a helper that returns null when the previous value is zero, and the key number component renders a dash with a tooltip saying there is no earlier data. The same helper is now used in the carrier table trend column, which had a similar problem with sorting last week. I added three Vitest cases: zero previous, zero current and both zero. The costs page was checked by hand with a range before the first shipment. Nothing else changed.

summary: Planned the scheduled report email redesign with Jonas: per-recipient time zones, a pause switch and a clear failure message, split into four steps.
body:
Jonas listed complaints about scheduled reports: they arrive at the server time zone, there is no way to pause one during holidays, and a failed report is silent. I went through the scheduler code in server/reports/schedule.ts to see what is possible. The schedule is stored as a cron string plus a report id, with no time zone column. Adding a time zone per schedule is a small migration, with a default of the Acme head office zone.

A pause switch needs a boolean and a check in the job loop. Silent failures are the larger part. Today the job logs an error and moves on. The plan is to store the last run status and error text on the schedule row, and show it in the list of schedules.

I proposed four steps. First the migration for time zone, paused and last status. Second the job changes. Third the UI in the schedule dialog. Fourth an email to the owner when a report fails twice in a row. Jonas agreed to the order and asked that the failure email be short and name the report. I wrote the steps into the notes file. Nothing was built yet. One open question is whether daylight saving changes should shift the local send time; I assumed yes, as users think in local time.

summary: Built step one and two of the scheduled report plan: schedule table gets time zone, paused flag and last status, and the job honors them.
body:
This follows the plan from earlier today. I wrote the migration adding time_zone, paused, last_run_at, last_status and last_error to report_schedules. The default time zone is the Acme head office zone, so existing schedules keep their current behavior for most users.

In the job loop I replaced the plain cron check with a function that computes the next run in the schedule's own time zone. I used the date library already in the project rather than adding a new one. The daylight saving case needed care. A report set for 02:30 does not exist on the spring change day, so the job runs it at the first valid time after.

Paused schedules are skipped and their next run is not advanced, so resuming does not send a flood. The status fields are updated at the end of each run, with the error message cut to 500 characters.

Tests: I added Vitest cases for a Berlin schedule across both daylight saving changes, for a paused schedule and for a failed run storing its error. All passed on the second try, after fixing an off by one hour mistake in the autumn case.

I ran the migration on the staging database copy and it took under a second. The existing load marker wait still works, since I left that part of the job untouched. Left: the dialog UI and the failure email. I also noticed the job loop reads all schedules every minute, which is fine for the current 40 schedules but worth remembering.

summary: Built the schedule dialog changes and the failure email for scheduled reports, and found the email repeated every run until the schedule was edited.
body:
The schedule dialog now has a time zone select, defaulting to the browser zone, and a pause switch. The list of schedules shows the last status as a small badge, with the error text in a tooltip.

For the failure email I added a function that runs when a schedule fails and the previous run also failed. The mail names the report, says when it failed and gives the short error. Priya looked at the template and asked for less text and a direct link to the schedule.

While testing on staging I broke a report on purpose by deleting a column it used. The first failure sent nothing, as designed. The second sent the email. The third also sent one, and the fourth. That was the bug: the check only asked whether the last two runs failed, so it fired on every run after that.

I added a notified_at field to the schedule. The email is sent only when the failure streak reaches two, and the streak count is stored in a new column that resets on success. After the change a broken report sent exactly one email over five runs.

I also fixed the dialog so that editing a schedule resets the streak, because the owner has presumably fixed something. A Vitest case covers the streak and one covers the reset.

The Playwright test for creating a schedule needed an update for the new time zone select. It now picks a zone explicitly. All tests pass locally.

Left for tomorrow: ask Jonas to try it with a real report, and write a release note for the dispatchers. I did not touch anything about the login in this work.

summary: Checked scheduled reports in production for a day after the release: time zones correct, two failures mailed once each, one real bug in a deleted saved filter.
body:
The scheduled report changes went out yesterday evening. This morning I went through the logs and the schedule list to see what happened in the first run window.

There are 41 schedules. All sent at their local times; I compared six of them by hand, including one set for a Berlin morning and one for a London morning. Both were on time.

Two schedules showed a failed status. The first was a report whose saved filter on a carrier had been deleted by a manager. The job threw an error when loading the filter. That is a real bug in how we handle deleted filters, not only in the schedule: opening that report in the builder shows an empty page.

The second failure was a timeout of the report query for a full year range. It succeeded on the next run, so it looks like a slow moment on the database. I noted it but did not change anything.

Both owners received one email each, and no repeats, so the streak fix works.

For the deleted filter, I made the report loader fall back to no filter and mark the block with a warning text saying that the saved filter no longer exists. In a scheduled run the mail then contains the report with a visible note, rather than failing. I think a visible note is better than silence, but I told Jonas it is a choice and he could prefer a failure.

I added tests for the loader with a missing filter id and a test for the warning text in the PDF output.

Jonas answered that the note is fine. I also wrote the short release note for the dispatchers, which he will forward.

Open item: the year range timeout. If it comes back, I will look at the query plan.

summary: Looked at the year range report query that timed out and found a missing index on shipments by delivery date and carrier, then added it.
body:
The timeout from the scheduled report last week came back for a second schedule, so I looked at the query. With EXPLAIN ANALYZE on staging, a full year grouped by carrier took 9.4 seconds. The plan showed a sequential scan on shipments with a filter on delivered_at, then a hash aggregate.

There was an index on delivered_at alone, but the planner ignored it because the date range covers about a third of the table. A composite index on carrier_id and delivered_at lets it use an index only scan for the columns the report needs, once I added the cost column with INCLUDE.

I created the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a migration, so writes were not blocked. On staging the same query went down to 1.8 seconds. I also checked the monthly range, which stayed around 80 ms.

The index adds about 90 MB. That is acceptable on the current plan. Shipment inserts from the nightly load were a little slower, about 4 percent in my test, which does not matter.

I deployed it this evening after the nightly load had finished. I will check the two schedules tomorrow. Nothing in the app code changed, only the migration.

summary: Confirmed the new shipments index fixed the slow year reports: both schedules ran in about two seconds, and noted the nightly load time was unchanged.
body:
After the index deployment last night I checked the report schedules this morning. Both of the year range reports that failed before finished, taking 2.1 and 2.4 seconds for the query. Their last status is ok, and the failure streak was reset by the success.

I also looked at the nightly data load duration in the logs. It ran 11 minutes, as it usually does, so the extra index does not slow it in a way that matters.

I looked at pg_stat_user_indexes to see if the index is being used by other queries. It already had a few hundred scans, mostly from the costs page, which groups by carrier as well. So the costs page likely got faster as well. I tried the costs overview with a one year range and it loaded in under a second, where it was around four seconds before.

I told Jonas that the costs page is quicker, since he had mentioned it felt slow for long ranges.

Nothing is left on this topic. A possible later step is to look at the other long range queries, but none has been reported.

summary: Started the accessibility pass on the report builder: keyboard reordering of blocks was impossible, so added move up and down buttons with announcements.
body:
The report builder lets users reorder blocks by drag and drop only. In the earlier keyboard pass, I noted this as a gap but fixed other items first. Today I started on it.

The first idea was to make the drag library keyboard capable. It has a keyboard sensor, but its announcements are in English only and the focus behavior was awkward with our block menu. I decided on a simpler solution: each block gets move up and move down buttons in its toolbar, with disabled states at the ends.

When a block moves, the focus stays on the button that was pressed, which means a user can press it repeatedly. An aria-live region announces the new position, for example Block 2 of 5. The labels use the existing translation file, so German is covered.

The buttons appear for everyone, which Priya liked, as it helps trackpad users with long reports as well. She asked for a smaller icon size, which I changed.

I tested with VoiceOver on a Mac. The announcements were read once each and focus did not jump. Tabbing through the toolbar now goes in a sensible order.

I added a Playwright test that moves a block down with the keyboard and checks the order in the saved report. It passed.

Left in the builder: the color pickers for chart blocks have no text labels, and the column width handles are mouse only. I wrote both into the accessibility notes.

summary: Fixed the report builder column width handles for keyboard users and added labels to the chart block color pickers, finishing the builder accessibility list.
body:
This completes the two builder items left from the last session.

The column width handles were plain divs with mouse handlers. I turned them into elements with role separator and made them focusable. Arrow keys now change the width in steps of 10 pixels, and shift with arrow steps of 50. The current width is exposed through aria-valuenow, and escape is not needed since changes apply directly.

There was one problem: the handle sat inside a table header cell that already had a sort button, and the arrow keys bubbled up to the table key handler for cell navigation. I stopped propagation in the handle only.

The color pickers of chart blocks showed a swatch with no name. I added an accessible name made of the series name and the word color, and the swatch now shows the hex value in a tooltip. Screen readers read Series Carrier A color, button.

I also checked the contrast of the swatch border in both themes. The dark theme border was too faint, 2.1 to 1, so I changed it to reach 3 to 1.

Tests: one Playwright test resizes a column by keyboard and checks the saved width. One Vitest case covers the clamp of minimum and maximum widths.

The builder list in the accessibility notes is done. What remains in those notes is the settings page and the invite dialog, which I will do after another session on a different topic.

summary: Answered Jonas's question about why some dispatchers see old data after midnight: the browser cached the shipments API for five minutes, and cache headers were adjusted.
body:
Jonas reported that a few dispatchers saw shipments from the previous evening in their table just after midnight. I looked at the response headers of the shipments endpoint. It sent Cache-Control max-age 300, which I had added months ago to lighten load during the morning peak.

That explains five minutes of stale data but not more. I asked the dispatchers through Jonas whether a reload fixed it. It did, which fits the cache. The browsers kept the response for the old day's default date range.

The real problem was that the cache key did not include the date. The URL for the default view had no date parameters, as the server chose today as the default. So after midnight the same URL meant a different range.

I changed the client to always send explicit from and to parameters, so the URL differs each day. I also lowered the max-age to 60 seconds for this endpoint.

I tested by changing the system clock in a browser profile across midnight. The request now goes out with new dates and the response is fresh.

Jonas confirmed no more reports in the next morning shift, which I will check again later.

summary: Fixed the date picker in the dashboard header so a range picked near midnight no longer shifts by a day for dispatchers in a different time zone than the server.
body:
Two dispatchers reported that the range they picked in the header showed one day less in the shipments table than in the picker. I reproduced it by setting the browser to a time zone far behind the server and picking a range at 23:30 local time. The picker returned local midnight Date objects, and the code turned them into strings with toISOString, which converts to UTC and moves the day.

The cause was in the helper src/lib/dateRange.ts. It built the query parameters from the Date objects through toISOString and cut the string at ten characters. For users east of UTC this moved the start one day back, and for users west of UTC the end moved one day forward. The costs page uses the same helper, so its period comparison was slightly wrong for those users as well. This is separate from the daylight saving bug fixed in the same file a few days ago.

I changed the helper to format the year, month and day from the local parts of the Date and to send plain day strings. The API treats them as whole days in the Acme time zone, as before. I also removed a second conversion in the URL state code that parsed the day strings with new Date and so reintroduced the shift on reload.

I added Vitest cases for four time zones with times at 00:10 and 23:50, plus a round trip through the URL. The tests failed before the change in three of the four zones and pass now. A Playwright test with the browser time zone set to a far-west zone picks a range and checks the row count against the API.

I checked the costs page by hand with the same ranges and the key numbers match the table totals now. Still open: the scheduled reports use the time zone of the schedule and not the viewer's, which is correct, but the report builder preview uses the browser zone. I noted that for a later session and did not change it today.

summary: Fixed the invite dialog accessibility: errors are now announced and tied to the email field, and focus returns to the invite button after closing.
body:
This was the first of two items left in the accessibility notes, the invite dialog on the settings page.

The validation error for a wrong email address appeared as red text under the field, but it was not linked to the input. I added aria-describedby and aria-invalid, and the message has role alert so it is read when it appears.

The dialog also lost focus on close. After pressing escape or the cancel button, focus went to the top of the page. I now store the element that opened the dialog and focus it again on close.

I also found that the role select inside the dialog had no visible label, only a placeholder. A real label was added, which Priya had suggested already.

One Playwright test types a wrong address, checks that the alert text exists and that the input has aria-invalid. A second test closes the dialog with escape and checks the active element.

Left: the settings page headings and landmark structure.

summary: Fixed the settings page structure for screen readers: one main landmark, proper heading levels and a skip link, closing the accessibility notes list.
body:
The settings page was the last item in the notes from the first keyboard pass. Its sections were styled divs with large text, not headings, so a screen reader user could not jump between them.

I changed the section titles to h2 elements with the same look, and the page title to h1. The recent logins section and the sessions area use h3 where they have subsections. I checked the heading outline with a browser extension and it now reads in order with no skipped levels.

There were two main elements, one from the layout and one in the settings component. I removed the inner one. I also added a skip to content link at the top of the layout, visible on focus, which helps on every page, not only settings.

The nav had no label, and there were two navs, the sidebar and the settings tabs. I gave them labels Main and Settings so they can be told apart in the landmark list.

I tested with VoiceOver and the rotor for headings and landmarks. Everything showed up as expected.

One Playwright test using the accessibility snapshot checks the heading order. I did not use an automated checker for contrast here, since the earlier pass covered it.

The accessibility notes list is now fully done. I wrote a short summary at the top of the file with what was fixed and what could be re-checked after big layout changes.

summary: Started a look at moving the mobile agency's driver endpoints to a versioned path, to avoid breaking their app when the dashboard API changes.
body:
The mobile agency asked, after the rate limit work, how they will learn about API changes. Today the driver app and the dashboard call the same unversioned routes, so a change for the dashboard can break the app, which updates much slower because of app store review.

I listed the endpoints that the driver app uses by looking at the access logs of the last two weeks, grouped by path and user agent. There are 11 of them. Five are shared with the dashboard, such as the shipment detail and the status update. Six are only used by the app.

The options I wrote down were three. First, a prefix like /v1 for all routes, copying the current behavior and only changing the prefix for new behavior. Second, versioning only the five shared routes. Third, doing nothing and agreeing on a notice period.

I think the first is best, though it is the most work, as the router needs a mount for both paths. The app would move to /v1 at their next release, and the old unversioned paths stay for the dashboard.

I asked about the effort for them. The agency answered that changing a base URL is one line in their config, so the cost is low on their side.

I also checked that the rate limit setup keys on the route group and not the full path, so adding a prefix will not reset the limits. It uses a group name, so that works.

The plan is to mount the existing router under both /api and /api/v1, then tell the agency. Nothing was changed in the code today. I will start the mount next, with a test that both paths return the same body for the shipment detail.

summary: Mounted the API router under a versioned /api/v1 path as well, with tests for parity, and told the mobile agency to switch their base URL.
body:
Following the plan from earlier, I made the changes for the versioned path.

In server/app.ts the router was mounted at /api. I moved the router creation into a function and mounted it twice, at /api and at /api/v1. Express makes this simple, but there was a catch: the auth middleware was applied inside the router setup using a shared instance. With two mounts the middleware list ran twice for some paths in my first attempt, because I applied it on the parent as well. I removed the parent application and kept it inside the function.

The rate limit keys use a group name, as I had checked, so they are shared between both paths. A driver using /api/v1 and a dashboard user on /api do not interfere, as the keys also include the token.

I wrote a Vitest and supertest suite that calls the five shared endpoints on both paths and compares status and body. For the shipment detail, the body contained a generated request id, which I removed before the comparison. All tests passed.

A small addition: a response header API-Version with the value 1 on the versioned path, so the agency can check in their logs which path they hit.

I documented the rule in the API notes: a change that breaks the response shape for the driver endpoints goes only on a new version prefix, and the old one stays for at least two months after a notice.

The deployment went out in the afternoon. I checked the logs and saw only the old path in use, as nobody has switched.

I sent the agency a message with the new base URL, the header and the notice rule. They will switch in their next release, in about two weeks.

One open point is the dashboard itself. It could move to /api/v1 later as well, which would let me drop the unversioned path, but I decided to leave it for now as there is no benefit yet.

Nothing about the login changed. The tokens work the same on both paths.

summary: Fixed the CSV export file name for reports that contained a slash in the report title, which made browsers save the file under the wrong name.
body:
A manager reported that a CSV export of the table block of a report named Q1/Q2 comparison was saved as Q2 comparison.csv, or on one browser with an odd name. The file name came from the report title, put directly in the Content-Disposition header.

I wrote a small function that makes the name safe: it replaces slashes, backslashes, colons and other path characters with a dash and trims spaces. It also cuts at 100 characters. For non ASCII characters like umlauts, I added the filename* parameter with UTF-8 encoding next to the plain one.

I tested with five titles, including one with an umlaut and a very long one. Chrome and Firefox saved all of them with the expected names.

This only touched the header. The export of large tables is still slow, as before, and I did not change that here.

summary: Looked at the onboarding feedback from Jonas's first users of invites and wrote a list of five small improvements for the first login experience.
body:
Jonas passed on comments from three new dispatchers who got invites this month. I went through them and tried the invite flow myself with a fresh test account on staging.

The comments were: the invite email subject looks like spam, the password rules are shown only after a failure, the first page after login is an empty shipments table with no hint, there is no way to resend an invite from the user list, and the dashboard does not say which date range it shows.

I checked each. The subject is the plain text Invitation, which I will change to name Acme and the dashboard. The password rules are indeed hidden until an error occurs. The empty table is real for a new user only when the default filter hides all shipments, as new users have no saved filters, but their carrier group is empty by default, so the table shows nothing.

That last point is the most important, and it needs a decision from Jonas: new users could start with all carriers.

The resend button needs a small API route and a button in the user list. The date range label is already in the date picker, so that comment points to the picker being too small.

I wrote the five items in a notes file in order of effort. Jonas will decide about the default carrier group. I did not start on any item yet.

If these grow into a proper first-run flow, it could become a larger piece of work, which I will plan with Priya before starting.

summary: Changed the invite email subject and added visible password rules at the registration step, the two quickest items from the first-login list.
body:
Jonas replied about the default carrier group: new users should see all carriers. I will do that next. Today I did the two quick items from the list.

The invite email subject now reads Your invitation to the Acme Logistics dashboard, and the sender name is the dashboard name instead of the plain system address. I sent test mails to two providers and neither put them in spam. The body text was also shortened by Priya's suggestion, with the button first.

For the password rules, the form now shows the list under the field from the start: at least 12 characters, no common passwords. Each rule gets a check mark as the user types. The rules were already enforced on the server, so I only moved the information forward and made the check marks use text as well as color.

I added a Vitest test for the rule checker and a Playwright test for the registration form.

summary: Made new users start with all carriers selected and added a resend button for invites in the user list, with a limit of one resend per hour.
body:
Two more items from the first-login list are done.

For the default carriers: a new user has an empty carrier group, so the shipments table filter excluded everything. I changed the filter logic so that no stored group means all carriers, instead of none. The code that read the group treated an empty list and a missing record the same. I split the two cases. An explicit empty group chosen by a manager stays empty, while a missing one means all.

I checked the places that used the group: the shipments table, the costs page and the report builder. The costs page had its own copy of the logic, which I replaced with the shared function. That removes a duplicate that could drift.

A test creates a user without a group and expects all carriers in the three places. Another test keeps an explicit empty group and expects none.

For the resend button, I added POST /users/:id/invite/resend, which creates a new invite token and sends the mail again. The old token is invalidated, so only one link works. A limit of one resend per hour per user avoids accidental repeats, answered with a clear message that says when it can be tried again.

The user list shows the button only for users who have not accepted yet, and also shows the date of the last invite as relative text.

I tried it on staging with a test address. The second click within the hour showed the message. After changing the stored send time by hand, a resend worked.

Left: the empty state for the table when a filter hides everything, and the date range label.

Nothing about the login was changed, although the invite token handling shares a helper with the password reset.

summary: Added an empty state to the shipments table that says which filters hide the data and offers a button to clear them.
body:
The remaining item from the first-login list was the empty table. Even with all carriers now the default, any user can filter their way to zero rows and see only a blank area.

I added an empty state component. When the table has no rows and no loading is in progress, it shows a short message, such as No shipments match these filters. Below it lists the active filters in plain words: the date range, the carriers, the status. A button clears everything except the date range.

If no filter is active and the table is still empty, it shows a different text: There are no shipments in this period, with a hint to widen the date range. That covers the new account case or a quiet holiday week.

Priya reviewed the wording and made the heading smaller. She also suggested an icon, but I left it out so as not to need alt text decisions.

The component is also used in the user list now, with its own text.

The paging code needed a fix. When the filters changed to a state with no rows, the page in the URL stayed on page three, so the table asked for a cursor that no longer existed. It showed the empty state but with an error in the console. I reset the cursor whenever filters change.

Tests: Vitest for the filter description and Playwright for clearing from the empty state.

summary: Made the date range label in the dashboard header larger and always visible, answering the last first-login comment, and checked it at narrow widths.
body:
The last comment from new dispatchers was that the dashboard does not say which date range it shows. The range is in the date picker button, but at narrow widths the label was cut to an icon.

I changed the header so the range text is always shown below the page title on small screens, and inside the button on wide ones. The format is 3 Mar to 9 Mar for ranges within a year, and with the year if they cross a year border. For presets, it shows the preset name followed by the dates, like Last 7 days, 3 to 9.

The text updates when the range changes, and is part of the live region that I added with the swap message, so changes are announced too.

I tested widths of 360, 768 and 1280 pixels. At 360 the title and the range took three lines in German, because of long words, so I reduced the title size at that width.

I checked both themes.

Playwright screenshots at the three widths were added to the visual test set. Two existing screenshots changed in the expected way and were updated.

With this, all five items from the list are done. I told Jonas and he will ask the dispatchers whether it helps. A real onboarding flow with tours and a checklist is a separate topic if Jonas wants it, and would be planned with Priya.

The code only touched the header and the date helpers. Nothing in the API changed.

summary: Investigated why the login events table grew faster than expected and added an index and a daily cleanup of events older than 90 days.
body:
The login events table was introduced a few weeks ago with a retention of 90 days, but retention was only a note, not code. I checked the size today to see what that means.

The table had 61,000 rows. With about 55 dispatchers logging in, I expected a few thousand. The reason was the mobile app: each driver app start calls the login endpoint when the stored token has expired or failed, and every attempt wrote a row. Failed attempts from the app, due to a bad network, also wrote rows.

The breakdown by user agent showed that the driver app made up about 80 percent of the rows. That is correct data, but it is noisy for the audit use. The settings page list of recent logins would show many entries for drivers. Dispatchers rarely look at it, so I did not change what is written.

Two things were done. The first is an index on user_id and created_at, because the settings page query filtered by user and sorted by time, and the plan showed a sort of all rows of the user. With the index the query on a driver account with 900 events went from 14 ms to under 1 ms.

The second is a cleanup job. It runs daily at night and deletes rows older than 90 days in batches of 5,000, so that it does not hold long locks. I wrote it to log the number deleted. Since nothing is older than 90 days yet, the first runs delete nothing, so I tested it on a staging copy with rows shifted back in time. It deleted 12,000 rows in four batches, and the log line was correct.

I also thought about whether failed attempts should have a shorter retention. Failed attempts are useful for spotting guessing, but 90 days is long. I wrote this as a question for Jonas, as it touches data policy at Acme.

The job is registered in the same scheduler file as the nightly load check, with its own lock so two instances do not run at once.

I wrote tests for the batch deletion with fake rows, and one for the lock.

Deployed in the evening. I will look at the job log tomorrow to confirm it ran.

summary: Confirmed the login events cleanup job ran overnight with zero deletions as expected, and Jonas chose 30 days retention for failed attempts.
body:
I checked the job log this afternoon. The cleanup ran at its scheduled time, took 40 ms, and logged zero rows deleted, which is right as nothing is older than 90 days yet. The lock was taken and released normally.

Jonas answered the question about failed attempts. He talked with the data protection contact at Acme, and they prefer a shorter time for failed attempts, so 30 days, and 90 days for successful ones. That also matches what is needed to spot guessing.

I changed the job to use two cutoffs, with the retention days in the config instead of code constants. The query for failed attempts uses an extra condition on the success flag. I added a partial index for failed rows, since the delete would otherwise scan the whole table.

On the staging copy I tested again with shifted rows. Failed rows older than 30 days and successful ones older than 90 were deleted, and the rest stayed. The counts in the log were separate for the two kinds.

I updated the note on the settings page about how long logins are shown, which says 90 days. It is still right for that list, since it only shows successful logins.

The change goes out with the next deploy.

summary: Added a first version of a costs export to the costs page as CSV, noting that big ranges are slow like the shipments export, without fixing that yet.
body:
Jonas asked for a way to download the carrier table of the costs page, as managers copy the numbers into their own spreadsheets today.

I reused the CSV code of the shipments export, with a column definition for the carrier table: carrier, shipments, total cost, cost per shipment, cost per kilometer and trend. The formatter that creates the date format once is part of the shared code, so the speedup from before applies here too.

The numbers in the file use the same rounding as the table on screen. I made the decimal separator follow the user's language, with a semicolon as the delimiter for German, since Excel there expects it. A byte order mark is added so umlauts in carrier names show correctly.

The export button sits next to the existing table actions and has a label that includes the table name, so a screen reader user knows which table it exports.

For the carrier table, the row count is small, at most about 60 carriers, so the export is quick. I also added the same button to the carrier comparison view, but there it exports the three chosen carriers by period.

I then tried the export of the underlying shipments for a year range, which Jonas also mentioned wanting. That uses the large shipments export, and it took over 40 seconds for 300,000 rows, ending in a timeout on Render for one of three tries. This is the known slow export of large tables. I did not change it here and told Jonas that the carrier table export is fine, but the full shipment export for long ranges stays slow for now.

Tests: Vitest on the column definitions and on the German format, and a Playwright test that downloads the carrier table file and checks the header line.

To do next time: look at the large export again, probably as its own piece of work.

summary: Checked the costs CSV export on a large range and measured how slow it gets, so the later fix has a baseline; nothing was changed yet.
body:
After the first costs export went out this afternoon, I ran it against the biggest range a manager could pick, twelve months across all carriers. It took about 41 seconds and the response used roughly 380 MB of memory on the Render instance at peak. The shipments export behaves the same way, since both build the whole file in memory before sending it.

I wrote the numbers into the notes file for the export so they can be compared later. Smaller ranges are fine: three months finished in under four seconds. I did not change the export code.

I also added a line in the costs page tooltip that says large ranges can take a while. Jonas has not complained yet, but the managers are the ones who will try the year range. Next I want to see whether the proxy timeout on Render is the real limit or only the memory.

summary: Found that the Render request timeout, not memory, cuts off the costs export at 100 seconds for the largest ranges, and wrote down the finding without a fix.
body:
I pushed the costs export with a synthetic range of three years to see where it breaks. The request died at 100 seconds with a 502 from the Render proxy, while memory was still below the instance limit. So both limits matter, but the timeout comes first for very large ranges.

I checked the query itself with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. The query takes about 2 seconds, so the time goes into building the rows in JavaScript and formatting the CSV text. That means a database index will not help here.

I added a log line with the row count and the duration of each export so I can see what real users do. No behavior change was made. The plan is to look at the logs after a week and then decide how to restructure the export.

summary: Fixed a small bug where the carrier comparison view on the costs page kept the old selection after the user changed the period.
body:
Priya noticed yesterday that when she changed the period on the costs page, the carrier comparison still showed the old three carriers with data from the previous period. The selection was stored in component state keyed only by carrier ids, and the data query was cached with the old range.

I added the period to the query key in the comparison hook, so changing it triggers a new fetch. The selected carriers stay selected, which is what Priya wanted.

I added a Vitest case for the hook that changes the period and checks that the fetch is called again. The test passed and the manual check in the browser looked right. Nothing else was touched.

summary: Looked into why logged-in dispatchers get logged out in the mobile app after a month, and traced it to the 30-day token expiry with no warning in the app.
body:
The mobile agency wrote that drivers are suddenly thrown to the login screen with no explanation. I looked at the tokens in the API logs for the affected users. All of them had accounts whose access token was issued exactly 30 days before the failures, so this is the normal expiry of our JWT access tokens.

The API returns 401 with the body {"error":"token_expired"}, but the mobile app treats every 401 the same and shows the login screen. I checked the app behavior from their test build notes and confirmed that.

I considered a few options. One is to extend the lifetime, which makes the stolen token problem worse. Another is a silent re-login in the app, which needs stored passwords and is a bad idea. A third is the refresh token design we discussed with the agency, which Jonas put on hold.

I did not change the lifetime. I added the error code token_expired to the API documentation we share with the agency, and asked them to show a proper message for that code. I also added a line to the 401 response with the expiry time, so the app can tell users when they will be logged out.

The next step is to ask Jonas again about the refresh design, now with real complaints from drivers. I wrote a short summary for him with the count of affected users: eleven in the last two weeks.

summary: Built the first part of dark theme for the dashboard: color tokens, the shipments table and the header, with charts still using light colors.
body:
Jonas asked for a dark theme because dispatchers work night shifts. I started by moving the hard-coded colors in the CSS into custom properties in a single tokens file, with a light and a dark set. About 140 color values were replaced; around 20 had no clear name and I grouped them by use.

The theme switch uses the prefers-color-scheme media query as a default and stores an explicit choice in local storage. The settings page got a select with three options: system, light, dark.

I converted the header, the sidebar, the shipments table and the date picker. The table zebra stripes needed a new contrast check, and I used 4.5:1 as the minimum for text. The disabled button state failed in dark mode and I made it lighter.

The ECharts charts are not converted yet. They still draw on a light background, which looks wrong in dark mode. Each chart has its own color array in the options, so I need a shared theme object registered with echarts.registerTheme.

I took screenshots with Playwright of the table page in both themes and put them in the review folder for Priya. She will look at the colors tomorrow. Open points: charts, the report builder preview, and the PDF output, which should always stay light.

summary: Registered shared light and dark ECharts themes so all dashboard charts follow the theme switch, after Priya approved the dark palette.
body:
Priya looked at the screenshots and wanted the dark background a bit less blue and the axis lines softer. I changed the two tokens and she accepted it.

For the charts I created a theme file with two ECharts themes built from the same tokens as the CSS. A small hook reads the current theme and passes the name to the chart component, which re-initializes the chart on change. Before, the charts only read colors once at mount.

I removed the per-chart color arrays except for the carrier palette, which keeps its meaning across themes. The legend text and tooltip backgrounds now come from the theme.

The report builder preview and the PDF output stay light on purpose. I added a test that checks the PDF render ignores the theme.

summary: Fixed a logout that did not log out: the dashboard cleared the token in memory but left it in local storage, so a reload logged the user back in.
body:
A manager reported that after clicking logout on a shared computer, the next person who opened the page saw her account. I reproduced it: the logout handler set the in-memory auth state to null, but the JWT stayed in local storage and was read again on load.

I changed the logout to remove the key from local storage first and then reset the state. I also added a storage event listener, so other open tabs log out too.

The token itself is still valid on the server until it expires, because the API has no way to revoke a JWT. Someone who copied it can keep using it. I noted that in the security notes file and told Jonas that real logout needs a server-side list or shorter lifetimes.

I wrote a Playwright test: log in, log out, reload, expect the login page. It passed after the fix and failed before. The shared computer case is solved for the browser, the stolen token case is not.

summary: Added the first version of the table filter bar for shipments with status, carrier and delay filters, and kept the filter state in the URL.
body:
Dispatchers asked for filters they can share as links, so I built the filter bar so that the URL is the source of truth. The query string has status, carrier and delayed parameters, and the table reads them through a small useFilters hook.

The status filter is a multi-select with the five shipment statuses. The carrier filter loads its options from the carriers endpoint and supports search, because Acme has about 60 carriers. The delay filter is a toggle for shipments more than 30 minutes late.

The API got matching parameters on GET /api/shipments. I used parameterized queries and an allow list for the status values. A carrier filter with many ids produced a long URL, so I capped it at 20 ids and show a message beyond that.

Pagination resets to page one when a filter changes. At first it did not, and a user on page 8 saw an empty table after filtering. I found that in manual testing and fixed it in the hook.

I wrote Vitest tests for the hook parsing, including bad values, and one Playwright test that sets a filter and reloads. Both pass.

Still missing: saved filters and a clear button next to each filter. The empty state added earlier already has a clear-all button, which works with the new URL state. I will ask Jonas which filters the dispatchers use most before adding more.

summary: Added a clear button on each table filter and a count badge of active filters, finishing the first filter bar iteration.
body:
This evening I added a small x button to each filter chip so that one filter can be removed without clearing all. It updates the URL by removing the single parameter.

The filter button also shows a badge with the number of active filters, which helps on narrow screens where the bar is collapsed. I checked the layout at 360 and 768 pixels.

The buttons have aria-labels that name the filter, for example Remove carrier filter. I tested with keyboard only and the focus moves to the next chip after a removal.

I added two Vitest cases and updated the Playwright test. Everything passed. The next thing for the table is saved filters, depending on what Jonas says.

summary: Sent Jonas the list of drivers affected by the 30-day token expiry and proposed shorter lifetimes with a refresh option, and he asked for a cost estimate.
body:
Over the last weeks the mobile app logout complaints piled up, so I prepared a one-page note for Jonas. It has the number of affected drivers, 23 in total now, and the reason: the access token lasts 30 days and the app does not handle expiry well.

I listed three options. First, keep 30 days and fix the app message only. Second, shorter tokens with a refresh token. Third, go back to sessions for the dashboard and keep tokens only for the app.

Jonas read it and wants an estimate of the work for the second option, for both the API and the dashboard. I said I would look at it after the filters work. He also asked what happens if a token is stolen; I answered that today it stays valid until expiry.

summary: Built saved filters for the shipments table: users can name a filter combination, reuse it from a menu, and share it with their team.
body:
Jonas said the dispatchers use the same four combinations every morning, so I implemented saved filters. A new table saved_filters stores owner id, name, the query string and a shared flag. The migration also has a unique index on owner and name.

The API has GET, POST and DELETE under /api/saved-filters. Shared filters are visible to every user of the same Acme account, but only the owner can delete them. I added tests for the permission cases, including a user trying to delete a shared filter of another person, which returns 403.

In the UI, the filter bar got a menu with the saved filters and a save button that opens a small dialog. The dialog asks for a name and has a checkbox for sharing. Applying a saved filter just sets the URL query, so the existing hook does the rest.

I had to decide what to do if a saved filter refers to a carrier that was deleted. The table shows the remaining filters and a notice that one carrier no longer exists. I remembered that the scheduled reports had a bug with a deleted saved filter some weeks ago, so I made sure the same case is handled here: the filter loads without error.

I tested name collisions: saving with an existing name asks whether to replace it. The Playwright test creates a filter, reloads, applies it and checks the rows.

One more thing: the menu loads on first open, not on page load, so the table is not slowed. The measure was 30 ms for 50 filters. The feature is done apart from renaming, which Jonas said can wait.

summary: Added a table density switch to the shipments table, with compact, normal and comfortable row heights that are remembered per user, after dispatchers asked to see more rows.
body:
Two dispatchers told Jonas that the shipments table shows too few rows on their small office monitors, so he asked for something quick. I added a density switch to the table toolbar with three options: compact at 28px rows, normal at 36px and comfortable at 44px. The choice is stored in the user settings row in Postgres through a new density column, so it follows the user to another computer.

The row height is set by one CSS variable on the table wrapper, which meant the cell padding and the font size could be changed in one place. The first try also shrank the font in compact mode, but the status badges became hard to read, so the font stays the same and only the padding changes. The sticky header and the virtual scrolling both read the row height, and I had to pass the value into the virtualizer, otherwise rows overlapped after a switch.

I added a Vitest test for the settings round trip and a Playwright test that switches the density and checks the number of visible rows at a 900px high window: 21, 17 and 14 rows. The dark theme work is not finished, and I checked the compact mode in the dark colors too, where the row borders looked too heavy, so I lightened them a little. Priya looked at screenshots of all three modes and asked for slightly more space around the checkboxes in compact mode, which I did. The saved filters from last week are not touched by this and still work. Left to do: the density setting is not yet applied to the costs page table, which uses another component, and I noted that for a later step.

summary: Looked at how the report builder handles very wide tables in PDF output and found columns shrink below readable size past nine columns.
body:
A manager made a report with twelve columns and said the PDF text was unreadable. I reproduced it with the same blocks: the layout scales the table to the page width, and at twelve columns the font went down to about 5 points.

I looked at three options: landscape orientation, splitting the columns across pages, or limiting columns. Landscape is the least work and gives about 40 percent more room. Splitting needs a repeated first column, which is more complex.

I added an orientation option to the PDF settings of the report, with landscape chosen automatically above eight columns. The font now stays at 7 points at twelve columns, which Priya called acceptable.

I wrote a snapshot test of the PDF layout metrics. The splitting option is noted as a possible later step.

summary: Investigated a mobile app complaint that the driver's token worked after the driver account was disabled, and confirmed that JWTs cannot be revoked today.
body:
The mobile agency reported that a former driver, whose account Jonas disabled yesterday, could still load shipments in the app. I checked the API: the disable flag is read only on login, not when an access token is verified.

The token verification middleware only checks the signature and the expiry. So a disabled user keeps access for up to 30 days.

A quick fix is to look up the user on every request and reject disabled ones. I tried that and it adds one indexed query per request, about 1.5 ms. That is acceptable for now, but it defeats part of the reason for stateless tokens.

I implemented the lookup in the middleware with a small in-process cache of 60 seconds, so the load stays low. A disabled user is now rejected within a minute.

I added tests: a valid token for an active user passes, a disabled user gets 401 with the code account_disabled, and the cache expires. I also checked that the dashboard shows a clear message for that code.

This is only a patch. The same problem exists for a plain logout, and I wrote that in the notes for the next talk with Jonas about token lifetimes. The mobile agency was told that disabled drivers will see account_disabled.

summary: Added an audit line for disabled accounts to the user list, showing who disabled whom and when, after the driver case showed there was no record.
body:
After the disabled driver case I wanted a record of who disabled the account, because Jonas could not remember if it was him or a dispatcher. I added columns disabled_by and disabled_at to the users table with a migration.

The disable endpoint fills them in, and enabling clears them but writes an entry to the existing login events table with the type account_enabled. The user list shows a small grey line under disabled users with the name of the person and the time.

Old disabled accounts have no data, so the line says Unknown for them. I did not backfill anything, since the information does not exist.

I wrote tests for the endpoint and for the list rendering. One test caught that the line showed Invalid Date when disabled_at was null, which I fixed. All tests pass.

summary: Added an audit line to the settings page for password changes, after the driver account case, with a test for the order of entries. The list is read only for managers.
body:
After the disabled driver case there was also the question of who changed a password and when, and the answer was that nobody could tell. I added a small table, password_changes, with the user id, the time, and whether the change came from the user or from an admin reset. The password is of course never stored, only the fact of the change.

The write happens in the same transaction as the password update, so the two cannot get out of step. The reset endpoint for admins writes the admin id as well, and the user list shows it next to the disable audit line that was added before. Managers see the list in the user detail view and dispatchers do not see it at all, which I checked with a test for each role.

I wrote tests for the order of the entries, newest first, and for the case where the user has no changes yet, which shows a short note instead of an empty box. One thing came up: older password changes have no record, so the list starts from the release, and I added a line that says so, like we did for the recent logins list. Jonas has not seen it yet, and I will show him the wording tomorrow.

summary: Answered Jonas about why the delay percentage on the dashboard differs from his spreadsheet: the dashboard counts delivered shipments only.
body:
Jonas compared the delay percentage of last week, 11.8 percent, with a number from his own spreadsheet, 9.4 percent, and asked which was right. I read the query: the dashboard divides late deliveries by delivered shipments, and the spreadsheet divides by all shipments including those still in transit.

Both are correct for their definition. The dashboard definition is the one agreed in the first version. I recalculated with his definition and got 9.4, which matched.

I added a tooltip on the metric card explaining the definition, and Jonas asked to keep the dashboard definition. No code logic changed.

summary: Estimated and sketched the move to short-lived tokens with refresh for the API, dashboard and mobile app, listing risks such as two tabs refreshing together.
body:
Jonas asked for the estimate, so I spent the morning on a written design. The idea is an access token of 15 minutes and a refresh token of 30 days, stored hashed in a new table, rotated at each use.

The API changes are a refresh endpoint, a table refresh_tokens with user id, hash, family id and expiry, and changes in the login response. I counted about three days for the API including tests.

The dashboard needs an interceptor that refreshes on a 401 and retries the request. The risk I see is that two tabs refresh at the same moment: with rotation, the second request would use an already used refresh token and look like theft. I would need a lock between tabs, for example with the Web Locks API, or a short grace period on the server.

The mobile app has the same risk when several requests fail at once. The agency must serialize refreshes in the app. I wrote this as a requirement in the shared document.

Another risk is reuse detection: when a used token appears again, the whole family is revoked. This is good for security but can log out honest users after a network failure where the app never got the new token. A small grace window might be needed.

Storage is a topic: local storage is readable by any script in the page. For the dashboard, I proposed keeping the access token in memory and the refresh token in an httpOnly cookie. The app uses its secure storage.

I estimated about eight working days in total with the agency's part. Jonas will decide after talking to the agency. I attached the sketch of the table and the flow as a text diagram.

summary: Jonas approved the refresh design; wrote the migration and the refresh endpoint code in a first pass and left the dashboard side untouched.
body:
Jonas came back with a yes after speaking with the agency, so I started on the API. First the migration: refresh_tokens with id, user_id, token_hash, family_id, expires_at, used_at and created_at, with an index on token_hash and one on family_id.

Then the endpoint POST /api/auth/refresh. It reads the token, hashes it with SHA-256, finds the row and checks expiry and used_at. If valid, it marks the row used, creates a new token in the same family and returns a new pair.

The case of a used token is not final yet. For now it revokes the family and returns 401 with the code refresh_reused. I left a TODO for a grace window, because I want to talk about the two-tab issue before choosing a number.

I wrote Vitest tests with a test database: a normal refresh, an expired token, an unknown token and a reused token. All four pass.

The login endpoint still returns the old 30 day token. I did not switch it, because the dashboard and the app have to change at the same time. The plan is a feature flag, so the old behavior stays until both clients are ready.

The next entries will cover the flag and the dashboard interceptor. The mobile agency got the endpoint contract in the shared document with example requests and error codes.

summary: Fixed the table pagination footer, which showed a wrong total after a filter was applied because it read the unfiltered count.
body:
Dispatchers saw 4,812 results in the footer while only 37 rows matched. The count query in the shipments endpoint ignored the filter parameters that were added recently, while the rows query used them.

I moved the where-clause construction into one function used by both queries. This makes it impossible for them to differ again.

I added a test that applies a carrier filter and compares the count with the number of rows over all pages. It failed before and passes now. I also checked the saved filter case, and the footer is right there too.

summary: Added the feature flag for refresh token login on the API and a config switch, without enabling it for any client yet.
body:
I added a setting AUTH_REFRESH_ENABLED to the API config, default off. When it is on, the login endpoint returns a 15 minute access token plus a refresh token. When it is off, the old 30 day token is returned and no refresh row is written.

The flag can also be turned on per client type, using a header the mobile app sends and a value for the dashboard. This allows a staged rollout, first the dashboard on a staging copy, then the app.

Tests cover both modes of the login response. I checked that the old tokens still pass verification in both modes, so nobody is logged out when the flag changes.

Nothing is enabled on Render yet. Next I will write the dashboard interceptor.

summary: Built the dashboard side of refresh login on staging: an interceptor that refreshes on 401 and a cross-tab lock, tested with two tabs.
body:
With the flag available, I changed the dashboard auth layer. The access token now lives in memory only, and the refresh token is set by the API as an httpOnly cookie on the path /api/auth.

The fetch wrapper of the dashboard catches a 401 with the code token_expired, calls the refresh endpoint once and retries the original request. Concurrent failing requests share one refresh promise, so a page with six charts only refreshes once.

For several tabs, I used the Web Locks API. A tab that wants to refresh takes a lock named auth-refresh, and before refreshing it checks whether another tab already did, using a BroadcastChannel message with the new access token. Tabs that waited just take the new token without calling the API.

I tested with Playwright by opening two pages in the same context and setting a token lifetime of 5 seconds on staging. Both pages made requests at the same time after expiry. The API logged one refresh call and no reuse alarm. Without the lock, I reproduced the reuse alarm in the old version of the code, which confirmed the risk from the design note.

After a reload, the page has no access token, so it calls refresh at startup using the cookie. This takes about 120 ms and the page shows a loading state for it. The logout endpoint now deletes the refresh family and clears the cookie.

Some issues remain. Safari private mode lacks the Web Locks in an older version, so I added a fallback with a random delay, which is not perfect. I wrote it down as a known weakness.

The flag is on for staging only. The app agency is testing their side this week. Production will wait for their confirmation.

summary: Reviewed the mobile agency's refresh implementation on staging and found they refreshed per request, causing reuse alarms in their test build.
body:
The agency sent a test build and logs from staging. Their app produced refresh_reused errors every few minutes for one test driver. I looked at the API logs and saw two refresh requests with the same token within 40 ms.

The cause was in their client: when a screen loaded with three requests, each got a 401 and each started its own refresh. The first succeeded and the second used the already rotated token.

I described the fix in the shared document: one refresh in flight, all other requests wait for its result and retry. They answered the same day that they had a queue in mind but not built.

I also looked at whether a short grace window on the server would help as a safety net. A window of 10 seconds in which the previous token is accepted once more and returns the same new pair is a common approach. The risk is a slightly larger theft window, but it is small. I decided to implement it as a config value, REFRESH_GRACE_SECONDS, default 10.

The code stores the id of the successor token on the used row, and within the window returns the successor's pair, which means the new refresh token has to be retrievable. Because only hashes are stored, I could not return the same token. So instead, in the window I issue another new token in the same family.

Tests: second use inside the window works, second use after 11 seconds revokes the family, third use inside the window works. All pass. I told the agency the grace window exists but that they should still fix their queue.

Production is still on the old tokens.

summary: Checked the staging logs after the agency's fixed build and saw no reuse alarms in a full day of test driver traffic.
body:
The agency delivered a new build with a single refresh queue. I let it run on staging for a day with three test drivers and the dashboard open in two browsers.
