The API log had 212 refresh calls, none with refresh_reused and none that needed the grace window. Average refresh time was 18 ms on the server.

One logout test worked as designed: after logout, the old refresh token returned 401 at once, and the access token expired within 15 minutes.

I wrote the result in the shared document and suggested a production rollout plan: dashboard first, the app a day later.

summary: Planned the production rollout of refresh token login with Jonas and wrote the checklist, including how to roll back by turning the flag off.
body:
I met Jonas to agree on the rollout. The order is the dashboard first on a quiet morning, then the app after the agency publishes their release, one day later.

The checklist has these items: run the refresh_tokens migration on production, check that the table exists, set AUTH_REFRESH_ENABLED for the dashboard client only, and watch the logs for refresh_reused and 401 rates for an hour.

For rollback, turning the flag off makes the login return the old 30 day token again. Users who already hold a refresh cookie are not harmed, because the old tokens still verify. I tested this on staging by switching the flag back and forth during a session.

I also added a cleanup job for expired refresh rows that runs nightly. Without it the table grows, so I set the delete to expires_at older than 7 days. The job was tested on staging data and removed the expected 140 rows.

Jonas asked what the users will notice. The answer is nothing, except that very long idle sessions end after 30 days of no use. He agreed to the plan, and the migration will run first thing next time I work on this.

summary: Dry-ran the refresh login rollout checklist on staging, including the flag rollback, and found one missing step: clearing stale cookies on the dashboard.
body:
Went through the production checklist from this morning on staging, step by step, with the flag turned on and then off again. The flag on path worked for the dashboard and for the agency's test build. The rollback path worked for the API: with the flag off, the refresh endpoint returned 404 and the old 30-day tokens were accepted again.

One gap showed up. A dashboard tab that had already received a short-lived token kept sending it after the rollback, and the API rejected it with 401 because the old verifier did not know the new signing key id. The user saw a blank page until a manual reload. I added a step to the checklist: on rollback, the dashboard clears its stored token on the first 401 that has the new key id and goes to the login page.

I also wrote the rollback timing into the checklist. The flag is read at request time, so it takes effect in about a minute after the config change on Render. Jonas does not need to do anything for the rollback; I will tell him when it happens.

Next is the real rollout, planned for the quiet hours of the dispatchers. I still need to code the clear-on-401 step before then.

summary: Added the clear-on-401 handling for tokens signed with the new key, so a rollback of the refresh flag no longer leaves a blank page in open dashboard tabs.
body:
This was the gap found in the staging dry run. The dashboard HTTP client now checks the 401 response: if the error code is key_unknown, it removes the stored token and sends the user to the login page with a short message.

I added a Vitest test for the client with a mocked 401 response and a second one for a normal expired token, which still goes through the refresh path. Both pass. A third test checks that two parallel requests failing with key_unknown only trigger one redirect.

I also ran the Playwright login flow on staging with the flag toggled halfway through. The tab ended on the login page, as intended. The change is small and sits behind the same flag, so it can go out with the rollout. Tomorrow I will deploy the API part and watch the logs.

summary: Prepared the production rollout of refresh token login for managers by deploying the API and dashboard build with the flag still off and checking the old token path.
body:
Deployed the API and the dashboard build to Render in the evening, when dispatcher traffic is low. The new login code is in the build, but the flag stayed off the whole time. I checked the health endpoint and the shipments page with a normal old token, and everything behaved as before. That was the main point of this step: the deploy itself must not change anything for users.

After that I went through the rollout checklist once more with the flag still off. I logged in with my own manager test account and confirmed that the login response is still the old one: a single long-lived token and no refresh cookie. Four managers were online, and none of them noticed anything. I did not turn the flag on for the manager role. I want one quiet look at the logs of the plain deploy first, so that any problem I see later can be tied to the flag and not to the build.

I watched the logs for about two hours. There were no new errors and no 401 responses with key_unknown, which is expected, since no token is signed with the new key yet. One tab that had been open since before the deploy kept working with its old token without trouble.

One thing I noticed while reading the code path again: the refresh call writes a new token row to Postgres on every refresh. On staging this took about 180 ms on average. That is fine for now, but it is the number to watch once dispatchers join. The query uses the index on the token family id, so I see no obvious quick win.

I have not enabled the flag for anyone, neither for managers nor for dispatchers nor for the mobile app. The plan with Jonas is to turn it on for managers tomorrow, after one more look at the logs. I wrote the deploy result and the staging latency numbers into the rollout checklist. If anything looks odd overnight, the rollback is still one config change, and the flag is off anyway.

summary: Planned the dispatcher step of the refresh login rollout with Jonas and wrote down what to check first, with the refresh flag still off for everyone.
body:
I looked at the staging logs from the last full day of test traffic, using the same view I had used for the agency's build, and found no reuse alarms. Average refresh time on staging was 165 ms, and the slowest was 410 ms, which happened during a Render deploy of another service. Managers are still on the old 30-day tokens, because the flag is off in production.

I told Jonas the result and we talked about the order of the rollout. He agreed that managers can go first and dispatchers after them, but only after one more check. Before deciding on a time, I looked at how many dispatchers keep several tabs open. The session analytics showed that about a third have two or more tabs. This is the case that the cross-tab lock handles, so I wrote a Playwright test with three tabs on the staging build and ran it a few times. All three tabs refreshed with one network call each time.

I did not turn anything on in production. Instead I wrote down what I want to see before the dispatcher step: the quiet time after the morning rush as the moment, a message to the dispatchers' team lead so nobody is surprised by a new login, and a way to see the alarms per user, not only in total. The last point needs a small query on the reuse alarm table, which I drafted but have not run.

I also thought about the sleeping browser case. A tab that wakes up late may send an old refresh token after another tab has rotated it, and then the whole token family is revoked and the user has to log in again. That is the designed behavior, but it means an alarm can hit real people. The grace window for rotation is zero seconds at the moment. I added a line to my notes to count these alarms per day once users are on, and to look at a short grace window then. The mobile app is still on the old 30-day tokens too.

summary: Read through the refresh token rotation code and proposed a ten second grace window for reused tokens, without changing any code yet.
body:
Went through the rotation code in the auth service to see how strict the reuse check is. It compares the presented token to the current one in the family row and revokes the family if they differ. A grace window would accept the previous token for a short time and return the same new token again, instead of creating a third one.

The reason I looked at it is the staging logs from the test driver traffic and the manager test accounts. They showed a few alarms where a tab woke from sleep and sent a refresh token that another tab had already rotated. With a zero grace window the API would treat that as theft and revoke the whole family, which logs the user out everywhere.

Ten seconds should cover the normal case of two tabs refreshing together. It does not cover a really sleeping tab, which wakes up after minutes. For that case the dashboard could retry once after a login redirect, but that is a worse experience than a plain new login, so I did not pursue it.

I wrote the proposal into the rollout notes, with the check I read and the two cases the window does and does not cover. It changes how strict the security is, so I will talk it over with Jonas before touching anything. No code changed today, and nothing about the rollout plan changed either.

summary: Jonas accepted the ten second grace window for refresh rotation, and I implemented it with a test for the reused token inside and outside the window.
body:
Jonas read the proposal and said ten seconds is fine, as long as a token used after that still revokes the family. I implemented it in the auth service: the family row now keeps the previous token hash and the time of the last rotation.

Within ten seconds, a request with the previous token gets the current token pair again, without a new rotation. After ten seconds it revokes the family and logs the alarm, as before.

I wrote three Vitest cases: reuse at 3 seconds returns the same pair, reuse at 12 seconds revokes, and a second reuse of the current token works normally. All pass. A migration added one nullable column for the previous hash.

The change is deployed to staging only. I will watch it for a day there with the agency's test traffic before production.

summary: Prepared the rotation grace window for production by reviewing staging results, writing the reuse alarm query and drafting the migration plan, without deploying.
body:
After a day of staging traffic without problems, I went through the grace window change once more and decided it was ready to be proposed for production, but I did not deploy it. The migration for the previous hash column ran on the staging copy in under a second, so I wrote down the exact steps and the order for the production run, with the flag rollback as the last line.

I wrote a small query for the reuse alarms per hour from the login events table, so that the working hours of a day can be compared before and after the change. For now it only gives the baseline. In the working hours of the last day there were three alarms, all from laptops waking up or tabs restored by the browser. I saved the query next to the checklist so that the same numbers can be pulled later.

I also measured the latency on staging: refresh averaged 168 ms. The extra read of the previous hash did not change that in a visible way, but staging has little traffic, so I want to measure again under real load before I trust the number.

I checked what happens to the cleanup job for old token families. It deletes rows by the last rotation time and is not affected by the new column, so no change is needed there.

One case will stay open even with the window. A tab that sleeps for hours still sends an old token and gets the family revoked. I looked at how often this might happen in the events table: one such case in the whole last day, from a user who came back after a lunch break with a closed laptop. That user has to log in again, which I think is an acceptable cost, and I will tell Jonas about it.

I updated the rollout checklist with the grace window and the alarm query. The remaining part is the mobile app. The agency's fixed build is on staging, and I need to agree on their release date with Jonas. I wrote an email draft for the agency with the token lifetimes, the refresh endpoint contract and the 10 second window, so that they can check their code against it. I have not sent it yet.

summary: Sent the agency the refresh contract and answered their questions about the grace window, the offline case and what the app should do after a revoked family.
body:
The agency answered the draft from last week with five questions. I replied in one message and added the answers to the API docs in the repo.

First, the grace window: the app should not rely on it. It exists for races, and the app must keep one refresh in flight at a time. Second, offline: if the phone is offline when the access token expires, the app should wait for the network and then refresh once, not retry in a loop.

Third, a revoked family: the API returns 401 with the code token_reuse. The app has to clear its tokens and show the login screen. The agency had asked whether it can silently log in again with the saved password, and I said no, the app does not store passwords and should not start.

Fourth, the lifetimes: access token 15 minutes, refresh token 30 days sliding. The drivers who open the app daily will almost never log in again. Those who stay away for a month will have to.

Fifth, the key id header. The app does not need to read it, but should not drop unknown headers in its HTTP layer.

I also pointed them to the staging endpoint with a test driver account and asked for a release date. They said the next store release is in about ten days. I told Jonas, who accepted that. Until then the drivers stay on 30-day tokens, so the old verifier has to stay in the API.

The docs update also lists the error codes: key_unknown, token_expired, token_reuse and refresh_invalid, each with the action the client should take.

summary: Fixed the chart legend overlap on the delivery times chart, which hid the last items when a dispatcher selected more than eight carriers.
body:
Jonas had forwarded a screenshot from a dispatcher: on the delivery times chart, with many carriers selected, the legend covered the lower part of the plot and the last carriers were not clickable.

I reproduced it with ten carriers on a narrow window. The legend was set to a fixed position at the bottom with type plain, so ECharts put all items in several rows over the grid.

The fix was to switch the legend to type scroll when there are more than eight items, and to compute the grid bottom from the number of legend rows. I kept the plain legend for eight or fewer items, because the scroll arrows are less clear for small lists and Priya had designed the plain one.

I added the change to the shared chart options helper, so the other two charts with a legend, costs by carrier and delay by region, get the same behavior. I checked each of them in light and dark theme.

A Vitest test covers the helper: nine items give a scroll legend and a larger bottom margin, six items give the plain one. The Playwright screenshot test for the delivery chart needed a new baseline, which I updated after looking at the images.

One detail remains: the legend text color in the dark theme for scroll arrows is a bit dark. I asked Priya what color she wants and will adjust it then.

summary: Wrote the plan for the report builder's scheduled reports idea after Jonas asked for weekly emails to managers, listing the parts and a rough size without starting.
body:
Jonas asked in a call whether managers could get the weekly delay report by email, without opening the dashboard. I wrote down what it needs.

Parts: a schedule model in Postgres with owner, report id, cron-like rule and recipients; a worker that runs due schedules; rendering of the report to PDF, which the report builder already does on request; the email sending; and a settings screen to manage schedules.

The PDF output is the biggest risk. It runs in a headless browser on the API service, and takes up to 20 seconds for large reports. Running that inside the web process would slow the API for the dispatchers, so the worker should be a separate Render service or at least a separate process.

The email sending needs a provider. We have nothing for that so far except the invite emails, which go through a simple SMTP account with a low daily limit. For weekly reports to maybe forty managers it is enough, but I would add a bounce log.

The time zone is another point: managers in two time zones want the report at eight in the morning local time. The schedule has to keep a time zone name, not an offset.

Size estimate: about six working days, including the settings screen. I put the plan in a document in the repo and sent the link to Jonas with two questions: who may create schedules for others, and whether the reports should link back to the dashboard. I did not start code. The refresh rollout is still the first priority.

summary: Looked into the slow shipments page for the largest client region and found the delay filter query scanned the whole table, then added a composite index that cut it from 2.4 to 0.2 seconds.
body:
A dispatcher reported that the shipments table takes several seconds to load when the delay filter is on and the region is the largest one. I took the request from the logs and ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on staging with a copy of the production data.

The query filters by region, status and a computed delay flag, and sorts by planned delivery time. The planner used the index on region and then filtered about 410,000 rows in memory. Total time was 2.4 seconds.

The delay is not a column. It is computed as actual minus planned delivery time greater than zero. I considered a generated column, but that would need a table rewrite on a big table, and I do not want to do that during the refresh rollout.

Instead I added a partial index on (region, planned_delivery_at) where status is delivered and actual_delivery_at is greater than planned_delivery_at. The delay filter in the API uses the same condition now, written the same way so the planner can match the index. The new plan is an index scan with 0.2 seconds in total.

I checked that the other filters did not get worse. Status only: unchanged, 40 ms. Carrier plus status: unchanged. The index adds about 90 MB, which is acceptable.

The filtered total for the pagination footer uses a count query. That one is now 0.15 seconds, also from the index.

I created the index with CONCURRENTLY on production in the late morning, and it took about four minutes without blocking writes. After that I loaded the page myself with the same filter: 0.3 seconds including the network.

I wrote the index and the reason into the migration notes, and added a test that the delay filter condition string in the API matches the one in the migration, because a small change in one place would silently disable the index.

summary: Prepared the first review of refresh login for dispatchers by reading the logs and planning what to check, without any switch to short-lived tokens having happened.
body:
I spent the evening preparing for the security review of the login change that Jonas and I agreed on, and looked at what we would need to measure once dispatchers use short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation. Nothing of this is live yet. Today's login is still the one with 30 day access tokens, and the laptop theft in support is still the reason the security review asked for a change.

I wrote down the numbers I want to see in the first week: the count of refresh calls per working day, the average and the 99th percentile of the response time, the number of reuse alarms, the forced logins that come from alarms, and the support messages about being logged out. For the first estimate I took the current request logs. Dispatchers make about 9,800 calls per working day to the shipments page, and a 15 minute token would mean roughly one refresh per active user every quarter hour. That seems small for the API, but I want to confirm it with a load test on staging before anything is enabled.

The weak point I worry about most is a lost response. The office in the north uses a mobile hotspot because of a line problem, and its users already show failed requests with network errors in the logs. If a refresh call reaches the server and the response gets lost, the client would repeat the call with an old token and the server would take it as a reuse. I thought about three options: a longer grace window, which lowers the security level; keeping the new token on the server until the client confirms it, which is a big change; or making the dashboard retry once after a short wait. I have not decided yet, and the third looks like the smallest one.

I added all of this to the plan document and sent it to Jonas, with a question about which dispatchers should be the first group. The Vitest test with a mocked network failure on the first refresh call is still to be written.

summary: Planned a retry for lost refresh responses and tested the idea on staging with throttling, without deploying anything to production.
body:
I wrote down the plan for the refresh retry for lost responses and tested it on staging with the browser's network throttling, using the setting that drops the response of the refresh call once. The dashboard stayed logged in and the second call returned the same pair, as the logs showed.

Nothing about this is deployed to production, and production still uses the long-lived tokens. The northern office has a late shift, so I looked at the logs of the last days to see how often calls from there fail on the network. Over the evening hours there were 14 requests from this office that ended with a network error, and the dashboard had no way to recover from them. That gives me a rough number to think about when the refresh design goes out, and I will check it again after the first review.

One detail from staging: the two calls came 2.1 seconds apart, and the server answered the same pair in both cases, as designed. I started adding a counter for retried refreshes to the login events table, so the number will be visible without searching logs. The migration is written but not applied.

I wrote the findings into the rollout notes, including the idea of confirming the new token server side, which I did not build. It would be needed if the rotation causes more trouble later.

The mobile app has the same weakness for lost responses. I added it to the list of points for the agency before their release, together with the suggestion of one retry with the same token.

summary: Read the login code and the 30-day token setup after the security review, and wrote down what a stolen token could do and what a logout really ends today.
body:
Looked at the logout flow and found that it does not really end anything that matters if a token is stolen. Started from a question I wrote down after the security review about the laptop theft in support: what does the logout button do, and what would a thief still be able to use? I read the logout handler in the API and the dashboard code that calls it. The handler returns 204 and does nothing on the server side. The dashboard then clears the token from its local storage and the cookie.

That works for the browser in question. The access token itself is a signed JWT with a 30-day life, and nothing on the server can revoke it. A copy taken from a log or a proxy keeps working for the whole time. I tried it on staging with curl: I logged out in the dashboard, then sent the old token to /api/shipments, and it answered 200. I repeated the call after a long gap using a token I had issued earlier with an adjusted expiry, and the behavior was the same until the expiry passed.

A second finding is about other devices. A user who logs out in the office keeps the laptop at home signed in, because every token is independent. There is no way to end all of them at once. Jonas has not asked for this, but the case of the stolen laptop shows that managers will want it.

I checked how many users hold more than one device and found that many dispatchers are signed in on two or three, so the problem is not rare. I did not change any code. I wrote the findings down with two options: shorter access tokens with a refresh token that the server can revoke and rotate, or a deny list for logged-out tokens. The first option is more work and needs the mobile agency to adapt their app, but it closes the gap for good, and I lean toward it. The second is cheap but the list will keep growing.

Next step is to bring the note to Jonas and the security reviewer and ask whether the larger change is worth the effort now.

summary: Answered Jonas's question why the costs page total differs from the invoice total, which came from the page showing costs by shipment date while invoices use the billing date.
body:
Jonas compared the costs page for one carrier with the carrier's invoice and found a difference of about 3,100 euros.

I checked the query behind the page. It sums the cost column by shipment date. The invoice from the carrier groups by billing date, which is often a few days after the delivery. Shipments from the last days of the month fall into the next invoice.

I ran the query once with the billing date and the totals matched the invoice to the cent for that carrier. So there was no error in the data, only a different definition of the period.

I told Jonas and suggested a switch on the costs page, date basis: shipment date or billing date. The billing date is already in the table, but it is empty for shipments not yet invoiced, and the page would need a note about that. He wants the switch, and it goes onto the list, not today's work.

For now I added a small text under the period selector saying that the costs are counted by shipment date. It is a two line change, and it avoids the same question from the managers next week.

summary: Added a revoke-all endpoint that deletes every refresh token family of a user, plus a button on the settings page labeled as signing out of all devices, with tests.
body:
Jonas agreed that a user must be able to end all sessions, so I built the smaller option from the logout review. The new endpoint POST /api/auth/revoke-all deletes every refresh family of the calling user in one statement and writes an audit line, like the one for password changes.

The settings page got a button with a confirmation dialog. After the call, the dashboard clears its own state and goes to the login page. I also made the user list for managers able to call the same action for another user, which is useful when a driver loses a phone. Only managers see it.

Tests in Vitest cover three cases: a user with three families ends with none, a user cannot revoke another user's families, and a manager can. A Playwright test logs in with two browser contexts, presses the button in one and checks that the second one is sent to login after its next refresh.

The second test showed the known limit again. The second context kept working until its access token ran out, so up to 15 minutes. I put this sentence under the button so no one is surprised: other devices are signed out within 15 minutes.

Nothing is deployed yet. I want one more look at the audit text with Priya and then release it to staging.

summary: Added the size check for report emails: PDFs above 5 MB are replaced by a download link, after a wide test report came out at 8 MB.
body:
The test run of the wide shipments report produced a PDF of 8.2 MB. Many mail servers reject attachments above 10 MB and some at 5, so I set the limit at 5 MB.

The worker now checks the size after rendering. Below the limit, the PDF is attached. Above it, the mail contains the link to the report in the dashboard and a link to a download of the same PDF. The download link is a signed URL that is valid for seven days, and it points to a file stored on the Render disk of the worker.

I wrote the signing with an HMAC over the run id and the expiry, and the API endpoint checks it before serving the file. Cleanup of old files is part of the existing nightly job, which now removes report files after seven days.

Tests: a signed link that is valid, one that is expired and one with a changed run id. All three give the expected status codes, 200, 410 and 403.

The disk of the worker is not shared with the API service on Render, so the download endpoint has to live in the worker. I will check how to expose it before enabling the feature for managers.

summary: Looked at the mobile agency's release candidate on staging, found it still refreshes twice after a lost response, and sent them the log lines as proof.
body:
The agency delivered a release candidate for the store. I tested it on staging with the test driver account, using the network conditioner on a phone to drop responses.

Normal operation was good: one refresh per expiry, no refresh per request, and the login screen after a token_reuse error. The lost response case was not good. The app retried at once, in under 200 ms, then a second time after a second. The first retry landed inside the window and got the same pair, but the app also kept the older pair in memory and used it for the second retry. That was 12 seconds later, outside the window, and the family was revoked.

I copied the three log lines with the token family id and the timing into a message to the agency and described what I think happens: the response of the first call arrives late and overwrites the new pair with the old one. They should keep only the latest pair and ignore a response if a newer refresh has finished.

They answered within the hour that they understood it and will send a new build tomorrow. I told Jonas that the store release may slip by a day or two.

summary: Prepared a test plan for the agency's fixed build against lost refresh responses and drafted the plan to end the old 30-day tokens, without approving the build yet.
body:
The agency's new build had not arrived yet, so I used the morning to prepare for it. I wrote down the test I will run on staging: drop the response of the refresh call once, twice, and three times in a row, on a phone with the network conditioner. For each case I noted what the app should do: retry once after a short wait, keep the session, show an offline message after repeated failures, and never revoke the token family on its own.

I also added a sleeping app case to the list: leave the phone locked for 20 minutes, longer than the access token life, then open the app and expect exactly one refresh and no errors. A third case is a family revoked by hand in the database, where the app should receive token_reuse and show the login screen.

I set up a filter on the API logs for the staging test, so that any reuse alarm during the test run is easy to spot. A clean run of about 40 minutes without an alarm is what I want to see before saying anything to the agency or Jonas.

Then I thought about the time after the release. The store review takes one to three days, and drivers update at their own pace, so some will stay on old versions for weeks. The API will have to accept both kinds of login for a long time: the old 30-day tokens for old app versions and the short-lived ones for new versions.

I started a plan to end the old tokens, with the steps: count the old tokens used per day, send a message to the agency when the count is small, and then remove the old verifier. There is no end date yet, and the plan is only a draft until the build is approved.

I added a counter to the login events table for tokens verified by the old verifier, tagged with the app version, so the numbers will be available when the time comes. It is not deployed yet, and I will test the migration on staging first.

summary: Deployed the worker for scheduled reports as a Render background service with the test address limit still on, and ran three schedules through it overnight-style at short intervals.
body:
I created the background worker service on Render from the same repository with the worker start command, the same environment variables as the API plus the SMTP settings, and a small disk for the report files.

After the first deploy, the service crashed at once with a missing headless browser binary. The build step for the API installs it, but the worker used a different build command. I added the browser install to the worker's build command and it started.

To test without waiting for a week, I created three schedules with a rule of every five minutes in a temporary test mode that only works with the limit address. Over 40 minutes the worker ran 24 times without a missed or double run, and every run wrote its row to report_runs. The average render took 15 seconds, the memory stayed at 380 MB.

The download endpoint for large files is served by the worker on its own URL, and the mail links point there. I tested one expired and one valid link from the mail.

Next steps are the removal of the test mode and a review of the mail text with Jonas. After that, the section on the settings page can be shown to the managers.

summary: Prepared the review of the planned refresh token login, drafted the open questions and a note to Jonas, and did not treat the change as done.
body:
Looked at the login work after the agency's build reached the staging check and wrote down what is known so far, before going back to other work. The new login with 15 minute access tokens and refresh token rotation is still a plan; nothing is switched on for users, and everyone, dashboard users and drivers, is still on the 30-day tokens and the current verifier.

Dashboard: I wrote down what the plan needs before the managers and dispatchers could be moved. The ten second grace window for the refresh and the client retry for lost responses are in the draft, and I listed the numbers I want from a test group first: refresh counts per client, failed refreshes and forced logins from reuse alarms. I want to see those for a full week on a test group before I say anything about them. No figures exist yet and I wrote none.

Mobile app: I counted the active drivers in the last week, 143 of them, and wrote down that all of them are on the old app and the old tokens. The agency's fixed build is not approved. I started a test plan for lost refresh responses against that build. I also drafted a counter for old token verifications, so that after a later rollout the number of old app versions still in use can be followed each week. It is not yet clear how fast drivers will update once a new version exists.

Security: the reason for the change is a stolen token that stays valid for 30 days. That stays true today for every client. I asked the agency whether an update notice in the old app could be shown through a remote config without a release, and they think so. We have not agreed on a start.

Weak spots I know of so far:
- Rotation with lost responses needs the client to retry within the grace window. The dashboard and the new app would both have to do this. A third client would need to know it, so I started a paragraph for the API docs.
- Every refresh would write a row to Postgres. With all drivers this will be several times more rows than now, and I still have to estimate the table growth and the cleanup job.
- Disabling an account: the access token would stay valid for up to 15 minutes, while the refresh token is revoked with the account. This is better than 30 days but not immediate. If Jonas needs an immediate logout, there would have to be a check against the user table on each request, which costs one query per request.

I began a short note to Jonas with the last point in plain words, since he asked earlier about the disabled driver case. I do not recommend extra work now. Next is the work on the scheduled reports and the costs page.

summary: Wrote Jonas a note on how long a disabled driver keeps access under the current 30-day tokens and what the options are for shortening it.
body:
After yesterday's review of the rollout I wrote the note for Jonas about the disabled driver case. Right now a disabled driver keeps working for up to 30 days, because the access token is only checked for its signature and expiry. Disabling the account in the manager screen does not touch a token that was already issued.

I described the two directions we could take. The first is the plan for short-lived access tokens with refresh token rotation. There the refresh token would be revoked at the moment the account is disabled, and the access token would run out within 15 minutes at the latest. This is not built yet, and I said so clearly in the note, so that he does not read it as the current behavior. The second option is to check the account status on every API request. That gives an immediate effect for the price of one more query per request, which I estimated at 1 to 2 ms with the user id index, but it ties each request to the database.

Jonas asked how often accounts are disabled for a security reason. I went through the audit lines added earlier: eleven disabled accounts in the last quarter, and nine of them were drivers who had left the company in the normal way. The other two were mistakes in the data. None was a security incident.

He said that a delay of up to 15 minutes would be fine for Acme, and that he will tell me if a case comes where it is not. I took that as the basis for the plan and did not write any code for the per-request check.

I drafted a short paragraph for the API docs about the expected limit, so that the agency and any future developer know it. I also noted that the checklist for disabling accounts needs a line about it. Both are only drafts for now, and nothing was changed in the app today.

summary: Fixed the table header on the shipments page: the sticky header lost its background in the dark theme, so rows showed through when a dispatcher scrolled.
body:
A dispatcher sent a screenshot in which rows of the shipments table ran through the column titles while scrolling. It only happened in the dark theme. I found the cause in the table styles: the sticky header used a transparent color token that was fine in the light theme, where the page was white anyway.

I gave the header an opaque surface token for both themes and added a thin bottom border using the existing divider color. The density switch needed a check as well, because the compact rows have less padding. The header stayed readable in all three heights.

I looked at the page at a narrow width too, since the filter bar wraps there and pushes the header down. The offset of the sticky position was hard coded at 56 pixels. I replaced it with a CSS variable that the filter bar sets from its own height, so the header no longer hides under the bar after wrapping.

A Playwright screenshot test for the dark theme at two widths was added, so this does not come back unnoticed. It passed locally. I shipped the change with the next regular deploy and told the dispatcher who reported it.

summary: Added the date basis switch to the costs page, shipment date or billing date, with a note for shipments that are not invoiced yet.
body:
Jonas had asked for this after the invoice question. The costs page now has a segmented control next to the period selector with two choices: shipment date, which is the default, and billing date.

The API endpoint for costs takes a new parameter, basis, with the values shipped and billed. With billed, the query filters and groups by billing_date and ignores rows where it is empty. To make this visible, the response includes the count and the sum of the shipments in the period that have no billing date yet, and the page shows it as a line under the chart, for example 212 shipments, 8,430 euros not yet invoiced.

I checked the numbers against the carrier invoice that Jonas had used. With billed, the sum matched to the cent, as in the earlier test. With shipped, it showed the old value.

The basis is kept in the URL, like the other filters, and also in the costs CSV export, whose file name now contains the basis. The export is still slow for big ranges, and I did not touch that.

I replaced the small explanation text that I added last time with a tooltip on the switch. The index for billing_date did not exist, and a query over a year took 1.8 seconds, so I added one with CONCURRENTLY. The same query now takes 0.2 seconds.

Tests: Vitest for the parameter handling and a Playwright check that switching the basis changes the total and the URL.

summary: Wrote the first tests for the scheduled report worker's retry of failed emails, and found that a failed send was marked as done and never tried again.
body:
After the overnight runs of the worker, I went through its logs and saw one schedule with a send error from the mail provider, a temporary 421 answer. The schedule was shown as sent in the table, though no mail had left. I wanted to understand this before the test address limit comes off.

The cause was in the worker's job function. It saved the status sent right after the report was rendered, and then called the mail provider. If the call threw an error, the status was already set. I reproduced this in a test with a fake mail client that fails once.

I changed the order. The job now saves the status sent only after the provider accepts the mail. On failure it saves failed with the error text and a next attempt time, and tries again after 5, then 20 minutes, up to three tries. After the third failure the schedule owner gets an in-app note.

Three tests were added: success on the first try, success on the second try, and three failures with the note. All pass, and the existing size check test still passes. I also reran two schedules on staging with the fake client set to fail once, and both mails arrived after the retry.

Still open: the worker could send a mail twice if it crashes between the provider call and the status write. I wrote this down and will add an id per send to the job next.

summary: Fixed the scheduled report worker so a failed email send is marked as failed and retried with backoff, instead of being recorded as done.
body:
Yesterday's tests showed that a failed send was marked as done. The cause was in worker/sendReport.ts: the catch block logged the error but then fell through to the line that sets status to 'sent'. I moved the status update into the success path and added a 'failed' status with an attempt counter.

The retry now waits 5 minutes, then 30 minutes, then 2 hours. After the third failure the schedule run is marked 'dead' and stays visible in the report history.

The tests from yesterday now pass. I added two more: one where the mail provider times out and one where it returns a 550 for a bad address. A 550 is not retried, because the address will not work later either.

I ran the worker against staging with the mail provider's sandbox set to fail every second call. Six runs ended with six delivered emails, four of them on the second attempt. The history page does not show the attempt count yet. That is the next small step.

summary: Added the attempt count and a failure reason to the report history list, so Jonas can see why a weekly email did not arrive.
body:
After the retry fix this morning I looked at what a manager or Jonas would see when an email fails. Until now the history list showed only the run time and a status word. I added two columns: attempts and the last error text, shortened to 80 characters with the full text in a tooltip.

The API route GET /api/report-schedules/:id/runs returns the new fields. The error text is stored as the provider returned it, which can contain the recipient address. Managers can see their own schedules only, so I left it unmasked, but I noted this for a later look.

The status badge has a new color for 'retrying'. Priya's palette has no orange that passes the contrast check in the dark theme, so I took the amber from the costs page for now and will ask her for the final one.

I checked the list on staging with a dead run, a retrying run and a sent run. All three looked right in both themes. One component test covers the badge.

summary: Turned off the test address limit for scheduled reports on staging and sent a real weekly report to Jonas to check layout and size in his mail client.
body:
The worker had so far sent only to a list of test addresses. I lifted the limit on staging, not on production, and made a schedule for Jonas with the weekly shipments report, set to run in a few minutes.

The email arrived on the first attempt. The PDF was 1.9 MB, below the 5 MB limit that replaces a file with a download link. The table fit the page in landscape, but the chart on page two was cut at the right edge. The cause was a fixed width of 1200 px in the print layout, while the page area is narrower.

I changed the print layout to use the page width and rendered again. The chart now fits, and the legend sits below it. Jonas looked at it on his phone and on his laptop and said both were readable.

Still open: the sender name shows the Render service address in one client, so I need to set a proper from-name. That is for tomorrow.

summary: Set a proper sender name and reply address for report emails and handled the unsubscribe question, so scheduled reports can go to real managers.
body:
The staging mail showed a sender that looked like a Render service name, and Jonas did not want managers to see that. I added two settings: REPORT_FROM_NAME and REPORT_FROM_ADDRESS. The name is 'Acme Dashboard Reports'. The address belongs to Acme's domain, which Jonas had their IT set up with the SPF and DKIM records.

I sent test mails to three providers that Acme managers use. Two landed in the inbox. One put the mail into spam. The headers showed DKIM passing but the SPF alignment failing, because the mail provider's return path was on its own domain. I asked Jonas to have Acme's IT add the provider's include to the SPF record.

We also talked about opting out. Jonas wants managers to be able to stop a weekly report without asking him. I added a link at the bottom of each email that opens a page in the dashboard, where the logged-in manager can pause that schedule. I did not use a one-click link without login, because it would be a token in a URL that anyone with the mail could use.

The page lists the schedule name, the frequency and a pause button. After a pause, the worker skips the schedule and the history shows 'paused by recipient'. There are tests for the pause route and for the worker skipping paused schedules.

Tomorrow I will recheck the spam case once the SPF change is in.

summary: Checked the spam case after Acme's IT changed the SPF record: the third provider now delivers report emails to the inbox.
body:
Acme's IT added the include to their SPF record late yesterday. I sent the same three test mails again. All three landed in the inbox, and the headers show SPF and DKIM both aligned.

I also looked at the DMARC policy of the Acme domain. It is set to none, so nothing is rejected for now, but Jonas should know that a stricter policy later will need these two records to stay correct. I wrote that in the notes file for the project.

The remaining checks were small. The from-name shows correctly in all three clients. The reply address is a mailbox that Jonas reads, and he said it is fine.

Next is the production switch for the worker's address limit. I will do it together with Jonas after he has chosen which managers get the first schedules.

summary: Fixed a bug in the pause page where a manager could open the schedule of another manager by changing the id in the address.
body:
While writing the production checklist I tried the pause page with the id of a schedule that belongs to someone else. The page loaded and showed the name and the frequency, and the pause button worked. That was my mistake in the route: it loaded the schedule by id and checked only that the user was logged in.

I changed the query to load by id and owner, or by id for an admin role. For other users the route now answers 404, not 403, so ids do not leak. I added a test with two users that tries both the read and the pause.

I checked the other schedule routes for the same pattern. The list route filtered by owner already. The delete route had the same flaw as the pause route, so I fixed it the same way and added a test.

No production data was affected, because the pause page and the worker were not live for clients yet. I will add an ownership test to the checklist for every new route that takes an id.

summary: Wrote the production checklist for scheduled reports: worker settings, address limit, first recipients and how to switch the worker off again.
body:
The checklist has seven steps. First the production environment variables for the sender and the mail provider key. Second a check that the worker and the API use the same database migration level. Third lifting the address limit for a list of managers that Jonas names. Fourth a first run with a schedule for Jonas himself.

The last steps cover watching. After the first real run I look at the history for failed and retrying runs and at the worker's memory in Render. To switch it off, I set SCHEDULES_ENABLED to false and the worker skips all runs but keeps the history.

I left a gap for the list of recipients. Jonas will send it today.

summary: Enabled scheduled reports in production for five managers and watched the first runs, which all arrived with sizes between 1 and 3 MB.
body:
Jonas sent five managers. I lifted the address limit for those five addresses, using an allow list in the settings, not a full removal. The worker had already been deployed, so only the config changed.

I made the five schedules together with Jonas from the report builder, all weekly, with times between 7 and 8 in the morning so that the reports are in the inbox when the managers start. Because it was not yet that time of day, I set one of them to run in ten minutes as a first test.

That run was fine. The email arrived, the PDF was 1.4 MB and the numbers matched the shipments page. The worker needed 9 seconds for the render, mostly the chart images.

I checked the Render metrics for the worker: memory 210 MB of 512 MB, with a short rise during the render. That leaves room.

The other four schedules will run tomorrow morning. I set an alert on my side to look at the history at 8. Jonas will tell the managers that the emails come from now on and how to pause them.

One point for later: reports for the largest region have more rows, and a wide table might hit the 5 MB limit. The link fallback handles that, but I want to see it once in production.

summary: Looked at the first morning of real scheduled reports: four of five arrived on time, and one was late because the worker restarted during the render.
body:
The history shows five runs. Four were sent between 7:00 and 7:03. The fifth, for the northern region, was marked retrying and went out at 7:35.

The cause was in the Render log: the worker was restarted at 7:01 during a routine instance move, in the middle of a render. The run stayed in status 'running' and nobody picked it up. Only the stale-run check I wrote for the retry caught it after 30 minutes, set it to failed and the retry sent it. So the retry path worked as designed, but 30 minutes is long for a morning report.

I shortened the heartbeat. The worker now writes a timestamp every 15 seconds to the run row, and a run without a heartbeat for 2 minutes counts as stale. I tested this by killing the worker process during a render on staging. The run was taken over after about 2 minutes and sent.

No manager complained, and Jonas had one thank-you message. The large-region report was 3.1 MB, so the link fallback has not been needed yet.

summary: Started the CSV export investigation: measured how long large shipment exports take and found the work is dominated by building the file in memory.
body:
Dispatchers complained to Jonas that exporting a full month of shipments from the largest region fails. I reproduced it on a copy of the data: 480,000 rows, 14 columns.

The export route loads all rows with one query, builds the full CSV as a string and then sends it. With 480,000 rows it took 74 seconds, and the Render proxy closes the request at 60 seconds, so the browser gets a 502. During the run the API process grew from 180 MB to about 1.1 GB, which is near the plan limit.

I tried a quick check to see where the time goes. The query itself takes 6 seconds. Building the string with many concatenations takes about 50 seconds, and the rest is quoting and date formatting per cell. So the database is not the main problem.

I wrote down three ideas: a faster string builder, a background job that produces the file and sends a link, or sending the rows as they come. I did not pick one yet, because the background job changes the flow for users and Jonas has to agree.

For now I told Jonas that exports above about 250,000 rows will fail, and that dispatchers can use a shorter date range as a workaround. He said that is acceptable for a few weeks.

summary: Reviewed the session handling of the dashboard under refresh login for the weak spot of tokens in local storage, and wrote down options without changing code.
body:
A question from Jonas started this: the agency doing his security check asked where the dashboard keeps its tokens. The access token lives in memory and the refresh token in local storage, which means any script injection on the page could read it.

I listed where user-supplied text is rendered. React escapes by default, and I found one use of dangerouslySetInnerHTML in the report builder's description field. That text comes from other managers, so it is a real input. I checked it: the text is passed through a sanitizer first, and a test with a script tag confirmed it is removed.

The options for the refresh token are an httpOnly cookie, which needs CSRF care on the refresh route, or leaving it in storage with a strict content security policy. Neither is simple, because the mobile app uses the same refresh route with the token in the body.

I wrote the options and the effects on the mobile app in the notes. A strict content security policy is the cheaper first step, so I proposed to try it in report-only mode first. Jonas will ask the agency whether this is enough for them.

summary: Added a content security policy in report-only mode to the dashboard and collected the first violations, mostly inline styles from ECharts and the font loader.
body:
I added the Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only header in the Express app, with default-src 'self', the API origin for connect-src, and a report endpoint that logs the violations to a table.

After a few hours of normal use by dispatchers I had 340 reports. Most came from three sources. The first is inline styles that ECharts sets on its containers, which style-src blocks. The second is the font loader, which pulls fonts from a CDN. The third is a browser extension injecting scripts, which I can ignore.

For the fonts I changed the build to bundle them from node_modules, so no CDN is needed. That removed about 120 reports. For the ECharts styles I allowed 'unsafe-inline' for style-src only. Scripts remain strict, and script injection is the risk that matters for tokens.

I also saw one report for the report builder's preview iframe, which loads a blob URL. I added blob: to frame-src.

After these changes I let it run for an hour on staging with all pages clicked through by a Playwright run. It gave 0 violations from our own code. I will keep the report-only mode for a week on production before it is enforced.

I also added a small page in the notes with the policy and why each source is there, for the next person who adds a library.

summary: Wrote a Playwright test that opens every main page with the content security policy enforced, so a new violation fails the build.
body:
The report-only mode only helps if someone reads the logs. I wanted a check in the build as well. The test starts the app with the policy in enforcing mode, visits the shipments page, the costs page, the report builder, the settings page and the schedule history, and collects console messages.

A violation shows up in the console as an error that starts with 'Refused to'. The test fails on any such message and prints it with the page name.

The first run failed on the report builder, because the date picker loads a small SVG as a data URL, which img-src did not allow. I added data: to img-src. After that all five pages passed.

I checked that the test really works by adding a script tag from an outside host to one page by hand. The test failed with the right message, and I removed the tag.

The suite takes 40 seconds longer in CI now, which is fine. I put it in its own file so it can be skipped locally.

summary: Enforced the content security policy on production after a week of clean report-only logs, with a quick rollback through one config switch.
body:
The week of report-only mode produced 52 reports on production. All of them came from browser extensions or from old cached bundles that still loaded the CDN fonts. None came from the current code.

I made the header mode a setting: CSP_MODE can be 'off', 'report' or 'enforce'. That gives a rollback without a deploy beyond a config change on Render, which takes about a minute to restart.

I discussed the timing with Jonas, and we chose the early evening, when few dispatchers are online. I set the mode to enforce at 17:10 and clicked through the pages myself with a production account. No errors in the console.

Then I watched the violation table for the first hour. Eleven reports came in. Nine were extensions. Two were from a dispatcher whose browser still had the old bundle open. After a reload they stopped.

One case worried me: the SSO callback page for managers. I tested the login with a manager test account, and it works, because the redirect happens through top-level navigation and not through an iframe or script.

The mobile app does not load web pages, so it is not affected by the header.

This closes the first step for the token storage question. I wrote the result for Jonas in two sentences that he can pass to the agency doing his security check: scripts are limited to our own origin, the one place with user HTML is sanitized and tested, and the refresh token still sits in local storage.

What remains is the cookie option. I will not start it until the agency says whether they need it.

summary: Decided with Jonas that exports above 250,000 rows are worth fixing now, since the dispatchers hit the failure twice this week, and chose to look at streaming first.
body:
Jonas wrote that two dispatchers could not export their monthly data again. The workaround of a shorter range annoys them because they then join files by hand.

I went through the three ideas from last week. A faster string builder would help but not remove the memory growth, since the whole file is still in memory. A background job with an emailed link works for every size, but needs file storage, cleanup and a new flow. Streaming would need only a change in the route, and the proxy would see bytes flowing instead of a silent wait.

I told Jonas that streaming is my first choice and the job is the fallback if the proxy still closes the connection. He agreed, and wants the dispatchers to keep one click.

Before writing code I checked what the database driver offers. The pg library can use a cursor, so rows can be read in batches of 2,000. I also checked that the Render proxy allows long responses as long as data keeps coming.

I did not change code today. The work is planned for one of the next sessions, with a test that compares the output of the old and new export for a small range.

summary: Answered Jonas's question whether managers can get the weekly reports in the Excel format; yes in principle, but it needs a library and a decision on formatting.
body:
Jonas asked because two managers copy the CSV into Excel and fix the column types every week. I looked at what the report builder produces today: a PDF for email and a CSV for tables.

A real xlsx file would keep dates as dates and costs as numbers. A library like exceljs can write it, and the size is small for report-sized tables. The costly part is deciding the styling: header color, column widths, number formats per currency.

I told Jonas that it is about two days of work, including a test with a sample. He said it is not urgent and put it behind the export fix. I noted it in the plan.

summary: Checked the memory of the API on Render after the report worker went live and found it stable at about 190 MB, so no plan upgrade is needed yet.
body:
I looked at the metrics for the last two weeks, since the worker and the larger exports both add load. The API's memory stays between 170 and 230 MB, with peaks only when someone exports a large table.

The worker is a separate service and uses 200 to 260 MB during renders. Both are inside their plans. The database connections are at 14 of 40.

I wrote the numbers in the notes so that the future export change can be compared with them. No action today.

summary: Looked into the 30-day login tokens that drivers and managers still use, and planned how to find out who depends on them before any change to the login.
body:
Pulled the token numbers for the last two weeks to see who presents 30-day tokens and for what. Everyone on the dashboard, dispatchers and managers, still logs in with them, and so do the drivers in the mobile app. The tokens are valid for a month, which is the problem the security review keeps coming back to: a stolen token would work for that whole time and we have no good way to cut it off short of a deny list.

To understand what a change to shorter-lived tokens would touch, I listed the 31 distinct devices that sent a token yesterday, grouped by app version, and sent the list to the agency. They want to know which app versions keep a token in storage and how they would handle a login that asks for a new token during use. A handful of old integration scripts also use a long-lived token, and one of them belongs to a dispatcher's own spreadsheet export, which Jonas will ask her about.

I did not change any code today. The idea I wrote down for discussion is a short token lifetime together with a refresh step, but only after the agency confirms that the app can cope with it. Next step is a log line that marks every token request with the client and its app version, so the count of who uses what needs no manual work.

summary: Investigated why large CSV exports fail and sketched how a cursor-based export could work, without changing the route yet.
body:
Spent the morning on the CSV export problem that the dispatchers hit twice this week. I did not change the route. I wanted to understand the failure first and decide what a fix would have to handle.

I measured the current export on a 480,000-row copy of the shipments table. The response starts only after the whole file is built in memory, which took 74 seconds, and the API memory climbed to 1.1 GB. That explains the gateway timeout on big tables and also why the export is risky for the small Render instance.

I read through the handler and the query layer to see what a cursor would need. The query is built in one place, so a cursor on the same query looks possible. I wrote down a few open questions for later. The column list is currently taken from the first row, which would break the header if the first batch came late or the table were empty. The field list from the query itself looks like a safer source. A client that closes the connection must also release the database connection, otherwise a cursor could keep running in the background.

I also ran the old export on a small range and looked at how it quotes a field that contains a line break. It does not follow the usual CSV rule, so any new output would differ there. I made a note to mention this to Jonas, because someone's spreadsheet macros might depend on the old behavior.

The last open point is what happens when something fails after the response has started. Once headers are sent there is no way to return a 500, so the file would just end. I need to think about how a cut file could be recognized. Nothing of this is written yet; the next step is a small branch-free experiment with a cursor on the test copy.

summary: Planned how to handle a failure in the middle of a large CSV export, so that a cut file cannot pass for a complete one.
body:
Spent the session thinking through what should happen when an export of many rows fails halfway, and wrote it down before touching the handler.

The problem is easy to state. Today the export builds the whole file in memory, so a database failure gives a clean error. If the rows are ever sent in pieces, a dropped database connection after 100,000 rows would leave the client with a status 200 and part of a file. A dispatcher could take that for the full data, which is worse than an error.

I listed three ways to signal a cut file. A trailer line at the end of the file would break the CSV format for tools that read it. A checksum header cannot be sent after the body without trailers, and I do not want to depend on those. The third option is to end the response with an abort, so the browser shows a failed download instead of a finished file. I am leaning toward the abort, because it needs no change to the file format and the browsers should treat it as a network failure.

I also noted that the cursor must be closed when a client cancels, and that the connection count should go back to normal soon after. A statement timeout of about 120 seconds on the export query looks sensible, so a stuck query cannot hold a connection for long.

Nothing is implemented yet. For tomorrow I prepared a short test plan: kill the database connection in the middle of a run on staging, check the result in Chrome and Firefox, and test a client that cancels. I will also ask Jonas whether the dispatchers need a visible message when a download fails.

summary: Planned the integration tests for the CSV export of large tables and worked out how to check the memory without buffering the response.
body:
Large exports are still slow and fail at the gateway timeout, so I spent the session working out how the tests for a fix should look, before any streaming code exists. The export today builds the whole file in memory, and I wanted the tests to be ready to show a difference.

The first test I sketched seeds 100,000 rows, including fields with commas, quotes, line breaks and umlauts. It would run the current export, parse the result with a CSV parser and compare each row with the seed. I wrote the seeding script and the comparison helper, and ran them against the existing handler. The output matched the seed, so the old behavior is a good baseline for any later change.

The second test is about memory. My plan is to run the export for 300,000 rows and check that the heap used grows by less than a fixed limit, which I set to 80 MB for now. In a trial run against the current handler the growth was 95 MB, and it also grew because the test collected the response in a buffer. I changed the test to count bytes and hash them as they arrive. With the old export the growth is still large, which is what I expect.

I also wrote down the abort case for later: a mocked cursor that throws after the third batch should leave the response destroyed and the connection released. It cannot pass yet, so I left it as a pending test.

The tests take about 12 seconds, which is acceptable in CI. One question remains for the review: the date columns use the server timezone, which is the same as before, so I left it alone.

summary: Investigated why the CSV export of the largest region is slow and measured how a cursor-based read could behave with different batch sizes, without changing the route.
body:
Looked again at the slow CSV export with fresh eyes. I ran the current export on staging for the largest region and wrote down what happens. 480,000 rows hit the gateway limit, and the memory of the API climbed steadily while the whole file was built in memory.

In a scratch script, away from the export route, I read the same table through a cursor and only counted rows, to see what a streamed read could cost. I tried batch sizes of 500, 2,000 and 10,000. The read times were 44, 39 and 38 seconds, so the larger size gains little and would use more memory. A batch of 2,000 looks like the sensible choice for the plan.

While planning the abort handling I noticed a trap to avoid: the sketch logged the batch counter where the row counter was meant, so after a failure it would say 240 where 480,000 was meant. I wrote that down as a case for the test plan. The route itself stays unchanged for now, and the notes list the open questions about cut files and the gateway timeout.

summary: Looked at an odd report from a dispatcher: a filtered table export ignored the carrier filter, which came from the export button using the saved filter, not the current one.
body:
A dispatcher said the export contained shipments from all carriers although she had filtered on two. I reproduced it: the export button read the filter state from the last saved view, not from the table's current state. A filter changed but not saved was lost.

The table keeps its filters in a hook, and the export button was written before that hook existed. It called an old helper that reads from local storage. I changed the button to take the filters as a prop from the table component, so there is one source.

I wrote a Playwright test: filter on two carriers, export, check that the downloaded file has rows of those two carriers only. It failed before the change and passes now.

I checked the report builder for the same helper, and it uses the same one for its table preview. I changed that as well. The preview matched the saved view only by accident before.

I told Jonas about this, since a few exports made in the last weeks might have contained too many rows. He said the dispatchers would have noticed because the totals would not match, and nobody else has reported it.

This is separate from the streaming work and I kept it in its own commit.

summary: Prepared the streamed export for release: updated the notes, checked the Render timeouts and wrote what to watch on the first day.
body:
The code is reviewed and the tests pass. Before the release I checked the proxy once more with a slow client, throttled to 1 MB per second. The 480,000-row file took several minutes and the connection stayed open, because data kept flowing.

I wrote the points to watch: the API memory on exports, the number of open database connections, and the count of aborted exports in the log. A rise in aborts would point to problems with the statement timeout.

I also updated the notes with the quoting change for line breaks, so that nobody is surprised by a changed file. The release is planned for tomorrow morning, when the dispatchers start slowly.

summary: Set up a small dashboard query that counts exports by size and duration, so the effect of the streaming change can be measured after the release.
body:
To compare before and after, I need numbers. The export route now writes a row into an export_log table at the end: user, row count, duration, bytes, and whether it was aborted. I added the migration and the insert.

For the history I used the old access logs from Render to get a rough picture of the last month. There were 31 exports above 100,000 rows, and 9 of them ended in a 502.

I wrote a query that groups by size class: below 50,000, up to 250,000 and above. It shows count, median duration and the number of aborts. It runs in 80 ms on the current table.

The log insert is wrapped so that a failure to write the row never fails the export. I tested this by dropping the table on staging for a moment. The export still worked and logged a warning.

I will run the query a week after the release and put the numbers in the journal.

summary: Prepared the streamed CSV export for release by checking the Render timeouts, writing the release notes and setting up the query that will measure export size and duration.
body:
Went through the streaming change for the CSV export one more time in the evening, and nothing was deployed. The release itself is planned for later, once the notes are final and the first day can be watched properly.

Read the Render settings for the API service and wrote down the limits that matter: the proxy timeout in front of the API is the one that cuts the large exports today, and the memory limit of the instance is well above what the streamed handler should need. The old in-memory build sits at about 195 MB when idle, so that is the number to compare against after the release.

Wrote the release notes. They say what changes (rows are read from a cursor in batches of 2,000 and written to the response as they arrive), what the user sees (the download starts right away instead of after a long wait) and what a cut file looks like when the stream fails in the middle. The rollback is a single revert of the release commit, and I put a line about that in the notes as well.

Added a small dashboard query that counts exports by size and duration, so the effect of the change can be measured and not guessed. I ran it against the exports of the last weeks to get a baseline. The exports above 250,000 rows are the ones that failed, and there are only a handful of them, so the comparison will rest on few data points.

What to watch on the first day, as written in the notes: API memory during large exports, any export that runs longer than the proxy limit, aborted connections in the logs, and whether the row count in the log matches the lines in the file. Next I want to ask Jonas which dispatcher usually runs the biggest exports, so that a real large one can be tried right after the release.

summary: Refresh token rotation design for the dashboard login written down after the stolen-token scare, with a short access token lifetime and a rotating refresh token stored hashed in Postgres.
body:
Spent the morning turning the idea of short-lived tokens into a written design before touching code. The problem is that the 30 day access tokens stay valid for a month if one leaks, and local storage makes a leak plausible.

Proposal: access token lives 15 minutes, refresh token lives 30 days and is single use. Every refresh issues a new pair and marks the old refresh token as used. The refresh tokens go into a new Postgres table, refresh_tokens, with columns user_id, token_hash, family_id, used_at, expires_at and created_at. Only the SHA-256 hash is stored, never the raw token.

The family_id is there for reuse detection. If a token that is already marked used comes back, the whole family is revoked, which forces a new login on that device. I noted that this could log out honest users when a network retry sends the same token twice, so the first version needs a short grace window of a few seconds. I did not decide the exact number yet.

The mobile app agency needs to know about this because their app stores the token. I drafted a short note for them describing the new /auth/refresh endpoint, the request body and the error codes 401 and 409. Nothing has been sent to Jonas or the agency yet.

Next step is the migration and the endpoint, then the client side interceptor in the React app. I also listed the tests I want: normal rotation, expired refresh token, reuse of a used token, and two parallel refreshes.

summary: Planned the refresh token table and the rotation endpoint for the dashboard login, and wrote down the open questions before touching any code.
body:
Sat down with the design note from the stolen-token scare and turned it into a concrete plan for the server side. The login still returns a single access token that lives 30 days, and nothing in the code was changed today.

The plan for the table: a refresh_tokens table with the hash of the token, a family_id, a used flag, an expiry and a created time, with an index on the hash and another on the family. Only the hash is stored, never the token itself. I sketched the migration on paper and checked the numbering of the existing migrations so the new one will follow the last one without a gap. I have not run anything against the local database yet.

The plan for the rotation: look the row up by hash with a row lock, refuse it if it is missing or expired, and if it was already used, revoke the whole family and answer 401 with a clear error code. Otherwise mark it used and issue a new one in the same family. I want all of that inside one transaction so a crash cannot leave a family half rotated. I wrote down the four test cases I intend to write first: a normal rotation, an expired token, a reused token, and a token that was never issued.

Open questions I listed for the next sessions. For the browser, an httpOnly cookie with a strict same-site setting and a narrow path looks right. The mobile app cannot use the cookie the same way, so I need to ask the agency whether they can take the token in the response body and store it in the secure storage of the phone. I also noted that two existing auth tests assume a 30 day access token and will need new expectations once the lifetime changes.

Things I know will come later and did not start: a short grace window for double submits, a logout that revokes the family, and the client side handling of a 401. The logout part is the one I care most about, because today logging out does not invalidate anything.

summary: Started planning the client side of short-lived tokens for the dashboard login, and wrote down what the shipments page does when four requests fire at once.
body:
Spent the session reading through src/api/client.ts and sketching how the React client should behave once the API hands out short-lived access tokens. Nothing of this is built or switched on yet. The server work for rotation is still in design, and the client has to match it.

The plan for the client is an axios response interceptor. On a 401 with the code token_expired it would call a refresh endpoint, keep the new access token in a module variable instead of local storage, and replay the original request once. A flag on the request config would stop an endless loop if the replay fails too. I wrote the plan as comments at the top of the file and a short list in the notes, with no code behind it.

I also wrote down the startup case. After a page reload the module variable is empty, so the app would need one silent refresh from the cookie before the first data call. Moving the token out of local storage would answer one of the open worries from the review, but only after this is built.

The case that worries me most is the shipments page. It fires four requests at once. If the token expires, all four will get a 401, and if each one calls refresh with the same token, the server will see three of them as reuse. With the revoke-everything rule in the design, that would log the user out in the middle of loading a page. So the client has to share a single pending refresh promise, and the server may need a short grace window as a second line of defense. I listed both as open questions to settle before writing code.

For testing I outlined a Playwright scenario. It would set a short token lifetime through an env variable, wait for expiry and then load the shipments page. I have not written it, because there is nothing yet to test against.
