Next step is to agree the error codes with the server side, so that token_expired is distinct from other 401s, and then start on the interceptor.

summary: Started on the parallel refresh problem in the client by sharing a single pending refresh promise, and wrote down what is still open for tabs.
body:
I started on the parallel refresh problem with a first sketch in the client: one pending refresh promise that every request waits on after a token_expired answer, cleared once it settles. The idea is that a page with four requests should refresh once instead of four times.

To see the problem first, I reloaded the shipments page with the token lifetime set to 5 seconds and watched the network tab. Four requests failed and four calls to /auth/refresh went out, and one of them failed because the old refresh token was already used.

I have not changed the client code yet. I wrote the Playwright test first, which waits for the token to expire, loads the page and counts calls to /auth/refresh, expecting exactly one. It fails now, as expected.

Two things are still open. If the refresh itself fails, the promise should reject and the user should go to the login page, and I will check that by hand once the promise is in. Two browser tabs share the same cookie, so they can refresh at the same moment, and a shared promise cannot help across tabs. That needs the server grace window or a tab lock, and I will look at it after the client part.

summary: Investigated the two-tab refresh race in the new rotation code and planned a server-side fix, without changing any behavior yet.
body:
Took on the two-tab problem today. Each tab holds the same refresh cookie, and when both notice an expired access token at nearly the same moment, the second request arrives with a token the first one just used. Under the current code that looks exactly like theft, so the whole family gets revoked and the user is logged out of every device.

I reproduced it locally with two browser windows and a short access token lifetime. It happened in about one try out of three, and always when both tabs were in the foreground and polling the shipments table. The server log shows the two refresh calls arriving a few milliseconds apart, so the timing is tight but real.

I considered a Web Locks lock in the browser, so only one tab refreshes at a time. It works in current browsers, but it does nothing for the mobile app or for a flaky network that sends one request twice. So I think the server needs to tolerate this case anyway, and the lock would only reduce the noise.

The plan I sketched in the design doc: refresh rows get a replaced_by column and a used_at timestamp. If a used token comes back within a short window of about ten seconds, the server would not revoke anything but would find the row that replaced it. Because we store only hashes, the existing refresh token cannot be recovered, so the server would have to create one more child row in the family and return that. Both tabs would end up with valid tokens, and the cookie set last would win. Outside the window the old rule stays: reuse revokes the family.

The drawback is that two valid children would exist briefly. I think that is acceptable, because the older one dies after one more rotation, and I wrote this down as an open point in the doc.

I have not changed any code yet. Next I will write the tests with a fake clock first, one for a reuse shortly after use and one for a reuse much later, and finish the logout work before touching the endpoint. A real two-tab check in staging is needed before anything of this goes further.

summary: Planned how logout should work with refresh token families and wrote down the limit of the short access token, without changing the logout endpoint yet.
body:
Spent the evening reading through POST /auth/logout and thinking about how it should behave once rotation is in place. Right now it only clears the cookie in the browser, so a copied token keeps working for its full life. That is the gap the security review pointed at, and I did not want the new refresh tokens to inherit it.

The plan is that logout reads the refresh cookie, finds its family and marks every row of that family as revoked, then clears the cookie. I sketched the query against the refresh_tokens table and checked that the family id column is indexed, so the update stays cheap. I have not changed the endpoint yet.

I also wrote a section in the design doc about what logout cannot do. The access token is a signed token that the API checks without a database lookup, so it stays valid until its 15 minutes end. I put that limit in the doc openly instead of leaving it for someone to discover. If Jonas wants an instant logout, we would need a list of revoked tokens that every request checks, and that costs a lookup per call.

Listed the tests I want to write next: logout revokes the family, and a refresh after logout returns 401. I will also do a manual check on the settings page, to see that it sends me to login after the next refresh.

summary: Planned the staging check of refresh token rotation with two tabs and the mobile test build, and wrote down what to test and which error codes to compare.
body:
Spent the afternoon preparing the staging check of the rotation branch rather than running it. The branch is not deployed anywhere yet, so the first job was to get the Render staging service ready to take it. I checked that the staging database has the refresh_tokens migration applied and that the environment variables for the access lifetime and the grace window are present. The access lifetime is still set to the long value there, so I wrote down the plan to lower it to 20 seconds, which makes a race between two tabs easy to provoke.

For the two-tab test I wrote a short script of steps. Both tabs stay open on the shipments page with auto refresh on, and I watch the cookie values and the server log for the refresh calls. The main thing I want to learn is whether a tab that loses the race can still present an old cookie after the grace window has closed. I have a suspicion that the browser may not have applied the Set-Cookie from a slower response before the next refresh reads the cookie. I made a note that if this happens, the client may need to wait for the cookie write before it clears its pending promise, and that a Web Locks lock around the refresh is another option. Nothing of this is changed in code yet.

For the mobile side, the agency told me they will send a test build. While waiting I read through my refresh endpoint and noticed that the status codes are not clearly separated. A used row and an expired row seem to share one branch. I do not know yet what their app does with a conflict status, so I wrote an error code table with a proposal: 401 with a separate code string for an expired refresh token, and a different one for a reused token. I will ask the agency how their retry logic treats each status before I send the table.

Open items: deploying the branch to staging, the two-tab run, the mobile build check, the status code tests, and the date for switching production.

summary: Started a Web Locks guard around the browser token refresh so tabs take turns, and wrote the first version of the soak test to reproduce the stale cookie logouts.
body:
Looked at the stale cookie logouts that showed up in the two-tab staging check and decided to try a Web Locks guard around the refresh call in src/api/client.ts. The plan is to wrap the call in navigator.locks.request with the lock name acme-refresh. Inside the lock the code would first re-read whether the access token is still expired, because another tab may have just refreshed it.

Sketched how the tabs would share the result: after each successful refresh the tab would post the new access token over a BroadcastChannel, and a waiting tab would take it and skip its own call. For browsers without Web Locks the idea is to keep the old behavior and rely on the server grace window. None of this was merged yet; the guard exists only as a rough draft on my machine and the client still refreshes the old way.

Wrote the soak test script first so there is a baseline. It opens three tabs, sets the access lifetime to 20 seconds and runs for 30 minutes. On the current client it logged out a tab about every eight minutes, and the server log showed token_reused events each time, which matches the bug reports from staging.

The mobile agency wrote back that the new 401 code fixes their retry loop, so that blocker is gone. Still open: finishing the guard, running the soak test against it, the cleanup job for old refresh token rows and the production switch plan.

summary: Planned the cleanup of refresh token rows by simulating token growth on staging and drafting a retention rule, without writing the job yet.
body:
Before choosing how long to keep refresh token rows, I wanted real numbers, so I wrote a script for staging that simulates 40 users with two devices each. With a 15 minute access token planned, the clients would refresh often, and every refresh would add a row. The simulation produced roughly 3,000 rows per day, which would reach a million rows in about a year if nothing ever deleted them. That is not urgent, but it is enough that I do not want to leave it open.

I drafted a retention rule on paper and checked it against what the rotation design needs. Rows whose expires_at is older than one day can go. Used rows must stay for about 7 days after use, because reuse detection needs the used row of a family to still exist when an old token shows up. Revoked families can also stay for 7 days, which helps with debugging.

I looked at how to delete without hurting the API. The idea is to delete in batches of about 5,000 with a short pause, using a CTE with LIMIT, so that no long lock is held. I filled a staging table with 500,000 synthetic rows to try the query plan. The first plan did a sequential scan on expires_at, so an index on that column is clearly needed. I have not added it to the migrations yet.

I also looked at the scheduler that already sends the invite reminders. It can run an hourly job, so I will put the cleanup there instead of adding a new mechanism. Nothing is written for the job itself yet, and no test exists for it.

What remains is the job, the test with rows of various ages, and a log line with the deleted count so growth is visible. I also started thinking about the production plan. The safest way seems to be to ship the server side first with the old 30 day tokens still accepted for a week, then cut over. I will write that up for Jonas once the numbers are settled.

summary: Set up a rollout plan for short-lived tokens with a one week overlap, so existing 30 day tokens keep working while the dashboard and the mobile app move to refresh tokens.
body:
Wrote the rollout plan and sent it to Jonas and the mobile agency.

Phase one: deploy the server with both token types accepted. Old tokens, which have no type claim, are accepted until a configurable cutoff. New logins get the 15 minute access token and a refresh token. The dashboard front end ships in the same release, so dispatchers get the new behavior on their next page load.

Phase two, after about a week: remove the acceptance of old tokens. Anyone still holding one logs in again. I will announce this to Jonas a few days ahead so the dispatchers are not surprised during a shift.

The mobile app is the difficult part, since the agency has to ship an app update and drivers update slowly. Because of that the cutoff for old tokens may need to be later for the mobile client. I added a claim check so the cutoff can be set separately for the client type mobile. The agency said their next release is in about two weeks.

I built the cutoff as two env variables, LEGACY_TOKEN_CUTOFF_WEB and LEGACY_TOKEN_CUTOFF_MOBILE, and a test for each combination. All pass.

I also added a small admin query that counts requests by token type per day, so we can see when old tokens stop showing up before turning them off.

Open question for Jonas: whether managers with SSO planned later are affected. They are not yet live, so no. I noted that SSO will need its own refresh handling.

Next is the release itself, planned for the day after tomorrow in the early morning when dispatch is quiet.

summary: Pre-release run of the full Playwright suite found three failures from the shorter token life, all in tests that waited longer than 15 minutes of simulated time, fixed by a clock helper.
body:
Before the release I ran the whole Playwright suite against staging with the real 15 minute token setting. Three tests failed.

The first two are the report builder tests, which open a long preview and then save. They took a simulated 20 minutes because they use a mocked clock, and the access token expired in the middle. The failing call was PUT /reports/:id returning 401. In real use the interceptor would refresh and replay, but the tests mock the network layer in a way that skips the interceptor. The third failure was the date picker test, which stubs fetch directly.

The fix was a helper in tests/support/auth.ts called loginWithLongToken. It signs a token with a one day life for the test user, and only works when the server runs with TEST_MODE. The three tests now use it. I would rather not weaken the real tokens for the suite, and this keeps production code untouched.

I also added a dedicated test of the real thing, with a short lifetime, that checks that the interceptor refreshes and replays a PUT with its body intact. That caught nothing, which is good, since the body is cloned before the replay.

After these changes the suite passed: 64 tests, about 7 minutes.

I checked the production environment variables on Render and added the two cutoff variables with a cutoff 7 days out for web and 30 days for mobile. The release is prepared. Rollback is simply a redeploy of the previous image, as the old tokens remain valid.

summary: Wrote the short announcement for dispatchers explaining that they may be asked to log in once after the update, and sent it to Jonas for forwarding.
body:
Jonas asked for something he could forward to the dispatchers, so I wrote a short text. It says the dashboard gets a security update tomorrow early, that nothing changes in daily use, and that people may see the login page once.

I kept it without technical words. The one thing worth saying is that the session now ends properly when you click log out, which several dispatchers had complained about on shared desks.

Jonas replied that he will send it this afternoon. He also asked whether managers would be affected differently, and I said no, they use the same login.

I will watch the logs in the morning after the release.

summary: Prepared the final pre-release checks for short-lived tokens with refresh rotation, and wrote down what to watch on the first morning after the release.
body:
Spent the morning going through the release checklist for the short-lived tokens with refresh rotation. Nothing is deployed yet. The plan is to ship once the staging results look clean and Jonas has forwarded the note to the dispatchers.

I compared the env variables on Render with staging one by one: the access token lifetime of 15 minutes, the refresh token lifetime, and the length of the grace window for two tabs refreshing at nearly the same moment. One value was still the old default in the production settings, so I wrote it on the list to fix before the release. I also ran the migration for the refresh token table against a copy of the production database. It took under a second, since the table is new and empty.

I then went through the log fields I want to follow after the release: the creation of refresh rows, the refresh call count per active user, the answer time, token_reused events, 500 errors, and how often the grace window is used. I made a small saved query for each, so I do not have to write them while the release is running.

One open question is the stale JavaScript in browsers. A user with an old cached file might still run the old login logic and see the login page twice. I want to look at the cache headers of index.html before the release, since it should not be cached for long. I put that on the list.

I also thought about the token types. After the release the old 30 day tokens will still be a large part of the requests, until they are renewed, so I prepared a count by token type to watch daily. The mobile app agency has not released their update yet, so mobile traffic will use old tokens only for now.

Things to do: fix the one env value, check the index.html cache headers, and make the daily old token count query. The cutoff of web legacy tokens will be planned for a week after the release.

summary: Traced the double login page for some users to a one hour cache on index.html and drafted a header change plus a reload banner, not yet deployed.
body:
Two users reported seeing the login page again the day after the release planning started. I had not shipped anything yet, so I looked at why their browsers behaved oddly in the staging check. The logs showed that their browsers loaded an old JavaScript bundle, which did not know about the planned refresh flow and kept using the old 30 day token until it hit a 401 and gave up. That told me the same thing would happen to many more users once the new login goes out.

I checked the response headers for the root document. It came with Cache-Control public, max-age 3600, which was the default of the static hosting setup. So after any release, browsers could keep the old index.html for up to an hour, and that file points to the old hashed bundle names.

I wrote down the fix for render.yaml but did not push it. The headers section would set Cache-Control no-cache for /index.html and for the root path, and public, max-age 31536000, immutable for /assets/*. Vite already puts a content hash in the asset file names, so the long cache is safe there. I tried the same headers on a local static server and checked with curl -I that both values came out as intended. The real host still has to be checked after the change goes live.

I also started a small version check in the client. It would fetch /version.json on focus and, when the build id differs, show a banner asking the user to reload. That is for tabs that stay open all week at the dispatch desks. The banner will use Priya's existing toast style, so no new design is needed.

Tests so far: one unit test of the version comparison. The banner itself I checked by hand by changing the build id locally.

Still to do is to review the config change, deploy it before the token release, and later watch the legacy token share, which was 48 percent today.

summary: Looked into why a dispatcher was logged out after lunch and planned a clearer login message for the reason, before the short-lived token change.
body:
Jonas asked why a dispatcher was logged out after lunch, and whether the 30 day tokens had stopped working. I looked at the logs for that user.

The 30 day token was fine, with 28 days left. The laptop had been asleep for two hours, and nothing was wrong with the token itself. The logout came from something else: the user had two profiles of the browser, and the two profiles shared one login that had been signed in twice. When the second profile came back, the server saw a session that no longer matched and ended it. The sleeping laptop only made the timing look suspicious, because the user came back from lunch and the page showed the login form.

The result looks like a bug to the user, even though the cause is not in the token life. I do not want to loosen any rule on the server for this, because the check is there for a reason. Instead I plan to make the login page say that the session ended for security reasons when the cause is a second sign-in, so the dispatcher knows to log in once and stay in one profile. I also want a log field with the reason, so the cases can be counted.

I explained this to Jonas in plain words. He accepted it and asked to be told if it happens more than a few times a week. I wrote down the wording of the message and will go through it with him before I add it to the page. This also fits the plan for the coming change to shorter tokens, since logouts will become more visible then and the message will help.

summary: Prepared a test plan for the mobile agency's upcoming build with the keychain refresh token storage and wrote down what to check against staging before the rotation goes live.
body:
The mobile agency told me their build with the new refresh flow is nearly ready, so I spent the session preparing to verify it. Rotation is not live yet, so everything runs against staging only.

I created two test driver accounts on staging and wrote a checklist of what the build has to do. Login must return both tokens, and the app must store the refresh token in the platform keychain instead of plain preferences. After 15 minutes the app should refresh on its own, and the staging log should show a new row in the same token family. Killing the app and restarting it should still work, because it loads the token from the keychain.

I also listed the failure cases. Airplane mode during a refresh should leave the app with the old pair and a retry when the network returns, and the grace window of 10 seconds should cover the case where the first request had actually arrived. An expired refresh token should give 401 with token_expired_refresh, and the app should go to its login screen.

One risk worried me. If the app has been in the background for a long time and then opens, it may send several requests at once with an expired access token, and each one may try to refresh. On a slow phone network, a request that arrives after the grace window would look like a reuse and revoke the family. I wrote the description of how the web client shares one refresh call between parallel requests, so I can send it to the agency if the test shows the problem.

I also considered a longer grace window for mobile clients. A longer window weakens the theft protection, so I decided against it and only noted it as an option.

The cutoff for legacy 30 day tokens on mobile stays as planned. I will check the usage ratio again after their release reaches the drivers.

summary: Checked the daily usage of 30 day tokens on web and drafted the client side of a planned change to short-lived tokens, without changing the server.
body:
The short-lived token release is due soon, so today I looked at the daily count of requests by token type before deciding anything. Tokens with the 30 day life are 2 percent of web requests, from 9 distinct users, and none of them has been active in the last two days. That looks safe enough, but I did not touch the server.

I wrote down what the change would need: the server would answer 401 with a token_legacy code for old web tokens, and the client would treat that as a signal to go to the login page without trying to refresh. I started a draft of the client side in the main checkout, without a branch, and added a Vitest case for the 401 handling. It is not merged and not enabled.

I also asked Jonas whether any dispatchers are known to leave tabs open for days, because those are the people most likely to see the login page once. He thinks a few do, so I will prepare a short note for them.

The mobile app stays as it is for now, since the agency's build with keychain storage for the refresh token is still to be tested against staging. I will decide on the web side after another look at the counts and the logs, and I will leave any removal of the old token code for a later cleanup.

summary: Chart legend scrolls now when a chart has many carriers, with muted page arrows and a fixed height, so long legends no longer push the plot area down.
body:
Dispatchers with 30 or more carriers in one chart had a legend that wrapped onto five or six rows and squeezed the plot area to almost nothing. I switched the ECharts legend to type 'scroll' in the shared chart options in src/charts/baseOptions.ts, so every chart inherits it. The legend is now one row high at the top, with page arrows at the right end.

The first attempt kept the legend at the bottom, but on narrow screens the arrows overlapped the x axis labels. Moving it to the top and reserving a fixed 32 px grid offset fixed that. Selection state is kept when paging, which I checked by hiding three carriers, paging forward and back, and seeing them still hidden.

The default arrow color was a dark grey that looked like a disabled button in the dark theme, so I set pageIconColor and pageIconInactiveColor from the theme tokens. The pageTextStyle uses the same muted token as the axis labels. Updated the two Vitest snapshot tests for the option objects and added one that checks the legend type is scroll when there are more than 8 series.

I took screenshots of the delivery cost chart and the shipments per carrier chart in light and dark theme and put them in the shared folder for Priya. Next step is her review of the screenshots. Still open: the legend on the small mobile web layout, which I have not tried yet.

summary: Priya approved the scrolling legend screenshots with one change: the page arrows should use the muted text color, which I applied.
body:
Priya reviewed the screenshots of the legend at three widths. She liked the scroll behavior and found the arrows too bright in the light theme, where they competed with the line colors.

I changed the arrow color to the muted text token and the inactive arrow to the disabled token, in both themes. The screenshot baselines were regenerated and committed.

She also asked that the legend font size match the axis labels, 12 pixels, instead of 13. That was a one line change in the shared options.

The suite passed afterwards.

summary: Started the multi-select carrier filter for the shipments table, with the filter state held in the URL so a filtered view can be shared between dispatchers.
body:
Jonas wants dispatchers to filter shipments by several carriers at once and send the link to a colleague. I started with the state handling, since the UI is simple once that is right.

The filter state now lives in the query string as carrier=a,b,c and is read with a small hook, useTableFilters. It validates the values against the list of carriers from the API, and drops unknown ones, so an old link cannot break the page.

The API endpoint /shipments accepts carrier as a repeated parameter. I changed the SQL to use carrier_id = ANY($1), with the array passed as a parameter, and checked that the existing index on carrier_id is used. The plan showed an index scan with 3 carriers on a test table of 200,000 rows, running in about 18 ms.

I have not built the dropdown yet. Tomorrow I will add the multi-select component with search, since some clients have more than 50 carriers.

One thing to decide with Priya is how the selected carriers should look in the table header, as chips or as a count.

summary: Finished the carrier multi-select with search and chips; it keeps the filter in the URL and resets pagination to the first page when the filter changes.
body:
Built the CarrierSelect component on top of the existing popover. It has a search field that filters the list as you type, checkboxes, and a clear button. For long lists the options are rendered in a virtualized list, since the largest client has 140 carriers and the plain list felt slow.

Priya answered that chips are better than a count for up to three carriers, and a count after that. I implemented it so, with a chip showing the carrier name and a small remove icon.

A bug appeared in testing: after choosing a carrier while on page 5, the table showed an empty page, because the page number stayed at 5 while the result had only two pages. The hook now sets the page to 1 whenever a filter changes. I also made the table fall back to the last valid page if the total shrinks for any other reason, for example new data.

Keyboard use: arrow keys move through the options, space toggles, escape closes. I checked it with a screen reader, and the checkbox labels are read properly. The count of selected carriers is announced through an aria-live region.

Tests: component tests for search and selection, and one Playwright test that selects two carriers, copies the URL, opens it in a new context, and sees the same rows. All pass.

I also checked the export button. The CSV export uses the same filter parameters, so exported files match the view. That works, but exports of the largest tables are still slow, and that stays on the list.

Not done: saving a filter as a named view, which Jonas mentioned for later.

summary: A dispatcher was logged out twice in one evening, and I traced the log lines to an office proxy and sketched a plan for a request id check, with no code written yet.
body:
One dispatcher reported being logged out twice in an evening, and Jonas forwarded the report. The server log showed two failed logins for the same user, and the second request arrived 14 seconds after the first. I could not tell yet whether the cause was in the client or the network.

I looked at the request details. The two requests had the same body but came from different source addresses, and the second one carried a header from a proxy used in the dispatcher's office. My theory is that the office proxy held the first request during a short network stall and delivered it late, after the client had already retried through another path.

This matters for the token change I have been planning. The short-lived token design would need a refresh step, and a late duplicate request like this one could look like a stolen token being replayed. I do not want to solve that by simply widening a grace window, because that would also widen the time an attacker has to replay a stolen token.

So I thought about the idea of the client sending an X-Request-Id on each refresh, a random value created once per attempt and reused on a retry. The server would keep the id with the record it creates, and a repeat with the same id would get the same answer instead of a logout. A different id would still count as reuse. An attacker with a stolen token would not know the id of the original request.

I sketched on paper a nullable request_id column with an index on it together with the token hash. I also wrote down the tests I want: same id after 60 seconds returns the stored result, different id after 60 seconds is treated as reuse, and no id behaves as before. None of this is written yet, and nothing is changed in the running login.

Tomorrow I will go through the plan again against the numbers from the token usage check, and I will tell Jonas what I found about the proxy and what the plan is.

summary: Planned the token lifetime change by checking how many requests still use the 30 day tokens and what a refresh token table might cost, with no code changes yet.
body:
Did the weekly review of the auth numbers using the admin queries, and used it to prepare the move away from long-lived tokens.

Legacy 30 day tokens are at 35 percent of mobile requests, down from 100 percent, since the agency's update reached part of the drivers. The mobile cutoff is still 30 days away, and at this rate I expect the share to fall below 10 percent by then. Web clients are almost clear of them.

The main open question is what a stolen token can do. Today it stays valid for the full 30 days, and the laptop theft in support showed that this is too long. I sketched the plan on paper: access tokens that live 15 minutes, and a refresh token that is replaced on every refresh, with the old one made invalid. Nothing of this is built, and the API still issues only the long tokens.

To size the storage, I wrote a small simulation of the refresh traffic. It gives about 3,000 new rows per day in a refresh table, so about 21,000 rows after a week, which Postgres handles without trouble. An hourly cleanup job would delete expired rows, and I estimated that each run would take well under two seconds.

I also listed the cases that could log users out by mistake: a proxy replaying a request, two tabs refreshing at once, and a user with two profiles open. Jonas asked about the double profile case earlier, so I noted that the login page should explain what happened. A short grace window for a repeated refresh looks necessary.

I wrote the numbers and the plan into the notes file in the repo so that the next review can compare them. No code changes today.

summary: Started the new-charts work by prototyping a delivery time distribution chart with ECharts, using binned data from a new API endpoint, and found the binning needs to happen in SQL.
body:
Created the branch new-charts and began with the chart that managers asked for: how delivery times are distributed, instead of only the average per day. The idea is a histogram with a marker for the median and for the 90th percentile.

First I tried the simple approach. The existing /shipments endpoint returns rows, and the client binned them with a small function. On a client with 180,000 shipments in the chosen range, the response was 38 MB and the browser needed more than four seconds to parse and bin it. That is too slow, and it would get worse.

So I wrote a new endpoint, /charts/delivery-distribution. It takes the date range and the carrier filter, and the SQL does the binning with width_bucket over the delivery duration in hours, with 24 bins up to a cap that depends on the 99th percentile, computed in the same query with percentile_cont. The response is 24 numbers plus the median and the p90, a few hundred bytes.

The query runs in about 140 ms on the test table of 500,000 shipments. The plan showed a sequential scan filtered by the date range, and an index on delivered_at and carrier_id brings it down to about 60 ms. I added that index in a migration and it built in 3 seconds locally. On production it will take a little longer, so I will create it with CONCURRENTLY.

On the chart side, I used a bar series with markLine for the median and p90. The tooltips show the bin range and the count and share in percent. The dark theme uses the shared palette, and the bars use the primary color with lower opacity for the tail beyond p90.

A first question for Priya is the way outliers are shown. I capped the last bin as 'longer than N hours', which she may or may not like.

Not done: the empty state when a range has no deliveries, loading skeletons, and tests. The chart is also not in the dashboard layout yet; it only renders on a test page.

summary: Added empty state, loading skeleton and tests to the delivery distribution chart, and Priya agreed that the last bin should read 'longer than N hours'.
body:
Continued on the new-charts branch with the parts that were missing from the prototype.

Priya looked at the chart in the evening and was fine with the capped last bin as long as the label is clear. It reads 'longer than 48 hours' now, with N from the cap, and the tooltip shows the number of shipments in it.

The empty state shows a short message and keeps the card height, so the layout does not jump. The skeleton is the same gray block used by the other charts. I also made the chart cancel its request when the filter changes quickly, using an AbortController, since two fast changes had shown the older answer after the newer one.

Tests: a Vitest test for the endpoint with a small fixture, checking that the bins add up to the total count and that the median is right. A component test for the empty state. Both pass.

The chart is not in the dashboard layout yet. That is next, together with the setting that lets managers choose the bin width.

summary: Built the on-time trend chart for the new charts set, with a daily percentage line and a target line, backed by one SQL aggregate instead of client-side grouping.
body:
The on-time trend chart is the second chart of the new-charts work, after the delivery distribution chart. It shows the share of shipments delivered within the promised window for each day, as a line with a dashed horizontal target line. I first tried to compute the percentage in the browser from raw shipment rows, but a 90 day range for a large carrier returned more than 60,000 rows and the chart froze for a second.

So I moved the aggregation into SQL. The new endpoint GET /api/charts/on-time-trend groups by day with date_trunc and uses a filtered count for the on-time shipments, so each day comes back as one row with total, on_time and the ratio. With the existing index on (carrier_id, delivered_at) the query took 22 ms for 90 days on the staging copy of production data. The endpoint accepts the same carrier and date parameters as the other charts, so the date picker works without changes.

Days without any delivery were a problem. A missing day looked like a drop to zero in the first version, which would have alarmed the dispatchers for no reason. I now return null for those days and set the ECharts series to connect nulls, so the line bridges the gap and the tooltip says 'no deliveries'.

The target is a constant of 95 percent for now. Jonas mentioned that different clients have different contracts, so I kept the value in one place on the server and left a note to make it configurable later. The tooltip shows the percentage, the count of on-time shipments and the total, because a day with 3 shipments should not look as solid as a day with 300.

I checked the chart in the light and the dark theme and the colors are readable in both. The empty and loading states are not done yet, and neither is the click behavior on a point. Next I will reuse the skeleton of the distribution chart for the loading state and write the tests for the endpoint, including a day with no data and a range that crosses a daylight saving change.

summary: Added empty and loading states to the on-time trend chart by reusing the skeleton from the distribution chart; tests pass.
body:
The on-time trend chart now shows the shared ChartSkeleton while loading and the shared empty state with the text 'No shipments in this range'. Both components came from the distribution chart work, so I only had to pass the height. I moved them into src/components/charts/ since two charts use them now.

I wrote Vitest tests for loading, empty, error and normal rendering, with ECharts mocked at the init call. One test caught a real problem: when the range changed while a request was in flight, the older response arrived last and overwrote the newer one. I added an abort controller per request, and the test now fires two requests in reverse order.

Nothing is split by carrier yet. That needs a decision on the legend, since the legend scroll work from last week handles many series but a line chart with 30 carriers is hardly readable anyway. I will ask Priya whether to show the top five plus 'other'.

summary: Wrote API tests for the on-time trend endpoint and fixed a bug where a daylight saving change in the range produced a duplicate day and a skipped one.
body:
The tests for the on-time trend endpoint came first this morning. I seeded a small Postgres test database with shipments for three carriers over 14 days, and wrote Vitest cases for a normal range, a single carrier, an empty range and a day with no deliveries. The first three passed at once. The case with a gap day passed too, and it returns null for the ratio as intended.

The daylight saving case failed. For a range that crossed the clock change in the spring, the result had two rows for one date and was missing the next date. The cause was that date_trunc ran on timestamptz in the database session time zone, while the endpoint built the list of expected days in UTC on the Node side and merged both lists by string.

The fix was to pass the client's time zone to the query and use date_trunc with AT TIME ZONE for the grouping. The Node side now takes the days from the query result and fills the gaps by stepping through calendar dates, not by adding 24 hours. Acme works in a single time zone, so I read it from the organisation settings and fall back to UTC when it is missing.

After the change the test passes, and so do the older ones. I also compared the output with a plain SQL count for one carrier over a month, and all 31 days matched. The endpoint now rejects ranges longer than 366 days with a 400 and a message, because a longer range only makes the chart unreadable and the query slower.

One more detail: the response used to include the ratio as a float with many decimals, which made the snapshot tests noisy. I round it to one decimal on the server and leave the raw counts in the response for the tooltip. The loading and empty states of the chart are next, and the point click after that.

summary: Wired the click on a trend chart point to open the shipments table filtered to that day and carrier, using the URL filter state from the carrier multi-select.
body:
A click on a point in the on-time chart now navigates to /shipments with the date range of that day and the carrier in the query string. This works because the carrier multi-select keeps its state in the URL. I only had to build the right URL and add a date param, which the table already understood from the date picker.

For the 'other' group the click opens the table with the carrier filter set to all carriers outside the top five. That made a long URL, about 400 characters with 25 ids. It works, but I added a note to look at a shorter form if the number of carriers grows.

The Playwright test seeds three days of shipments, clicks the second point and asserts that the table shows exactly the shipments of that day with the late ones marked. The first run was flaky because ECharts animates and the click landed before the point was in place. I turned animation off in the test mode of the chart config, which is a one-line change in the options builder.

I also checked keyboard use. A chart canvas cannot be tabbed into, so there is now a visually hidden table of the same data after the chart, which doubles as the accessible version. Jonas had not asked for it but the accessibility fixes are on the list anyway.

summary: Planned the refresh token rotation: wrote down the token lifetime, the reuse rule and the rollout steps for the mobile app, and checked the numbers of the current tokens.
body:
Ran the usual weekly queries against production. Tokens that live 30 days made up 18 percent of the mobile requests, down from 35 percent last week, so more drivers have updated the app. The agency says the rest are phones that have not opened the app for a long time.

The security review asked for shorter tokens after the laptop theft in support, because a stolen token stays valid for 30 days. I spent most of the session on a plan for that. The idea is an access token of about 15 minutes and a refresh token that is replaced at each refresh. I wrote down the open questions: how long the grace window should be for a poor network, what should happen when an old refresh token comes back, and whether one reuse should log out all the devices of the user or only one. I have not changed any code and nothing of this is running yet.

I also sketched the table that would hold the refresh tokens: a hash of the token, the user, a family id, the time of creation and the time of expiry. I estimated the size from the number of active users and the usual number of refreshes per day, and the result is small enough for Postgres with an index on the hash, so a lookup should stay fast. A cleanup job for expired rows will be needed from the start.

I will send the plan to Jonas and to the mobile app agency this week and ask them how much time they need to build the refresh in the app. Next check of the numbers is in a week.

summary: Added a carrier comparison bar chart to the new charts set, showing average delivery time per carrier with the sample size on each bar and sorting by either value.
body:
The next chart on the new-charts list is a horizontal bar chart comparing carriers by average delivery time. Jonas wants to use it in the monthly review with carriers, so it has to be fair: a carrier with 6 shipments should not look like a carrier with 6,000.

The endpoint /api/charts/carrier-times returns the mean and the median per carrier, plus the count. I show the median by default because a few shipments stuck for weeks dominate the mean. A switch lets the user pick the mean. The count appears in the label as 'Carrier name (n=812)', and carriers below 20 shipments are drawn in a lighter tone with a note in the tooltip.

Sorting works by value or by name. The chart height depends on the number of carriers, 28 px per bar with a minimum of 240 px, so 30 carriers do not squash into a small canvas. Inside a scrolling container this looked fine on a laptop.

SQL detail: the median uses percentile_cont(0.5) within group, which is slower than avg. On the staging data it takes about 210 ms for a 90 day range, which is acceptable for a chart but I do not want it on a page that loads several charts at once. I will look at caching the result for five minutes if the dashboard home gets it.

summary: Checked whether the carrier comparison chart should hide carriers with very few shipments, and decided to keep them but gray them out below a sample size of 20.
body:
Jonas looked at the carrier comparison chart and asked about a small carrier that appeared as the fastest, which looked suspicious. The carrier had only 4 shipments in the selected range, so its average was almost meaningless. I looked at the data and found six carriers out of 31 with fewer than 20 shipments in a typical 30 day range.

I considered hiding them, but a dispatcher who searches for a specific carrier would then think the data is missing. So I decided to keep every carrier in the chart and change how the small ones look. Bars with a sample size below 20 are drawn in a light gray with a hatched pattern, and the tooltip says 'small sample, n = 4'.

The threshold is a constant in the chart config for now. I tested it with the staging data and the chart still sorts correctly by either value, because the sort ignores the color. Sorting by average time puts the gray bars at the top sometimes, which is why I also added the option to sort by sample size. Priya will check the hatched pattern for contrast, since it must work in the dark theme too. I added two Vitest cases for the styling function and left the threshold configurable for later.

summary: Looked into why mobile users with a poor network get logged out and found that the cause is in the app's retry timing, which is a question for the agency before it is one for the server.
body:
The agency sent logs of three users who were logged out in the last days. The pattern was the same each time: the app sends a request for a new login token, the connection drops before the answer arrives, and the app tries again later. In the logs the retries came 40 to 90 seconds after the first call, because the app waits until the network is back.

The current login uses one long-lived token, and the security review asked to replace it with short-lived access tokens and a refresh token that changes with every refresh. I have only been thinking about this design so far, and nothing of it is built. The logs made me think about what such a design would do to these users. If a retry with an old refresh token counts as a reuse, then a user on a bad connection would be logged out on every device. I thought about a short grace window for exactly this case, and the logs show that ten seconds would not cover these retries.

I considered a window of two minutes and decided against it. The cost is clear: during that time a stolen token that was just used could be replayed and still receive a valid new pair, and that is the exact thing the change is meant to stop. A window that long would make the reuse alarm much less useful.

A better solution is on the client side. The app should keep its old token until the response with the new one has really arrived, and on a failed attempt it should retry with the same request id. For a lost response the server would have to keep the new pair for that request id, encrypted, for a short time. That is more state and more risk than I like, so I did not start on it.

For now nothing changes on the server. I wrote the finding down for the agency, with their logs, and asked them how often lost responses happen, so we can decide whether the extra logic is worth it. Jonas will hear about this in the weekly note without the technical detail.

summary: Added the on-time trend and carrier comparison charts to a new 'Performance' tab behind a feature flag, so Jonas can look at them before they replace anything.
body:
The new charts are collected on a Performance tab under the dashboard, switched by the flag newCharts, enabled for my account and Jonas's. The tab has a shared date range at the top that all three charts use, so the distribution, the trend and the carrier comparison always show the same period.

The range is kept in the URL like the table filters. I reused the hook from the shipments page, which saved a day of work and means a link to a view can be shared.

All three charts load in parallel. On the staging data the slowest is the carrier comparison at 210 ms, and the page is usable in under a second. I did not add caching.

Priya looked at the layout on a laptop and a large monitor. On the large one the charts got too wide, so I set a max width of 1400 px for the grid. Jonas gets the link tomorrow.

summary: Jonas reviewed the Performance tab and asked for the on-time target to be configurable per client contract; started with a settings field and a column on the organisation table.
body:
Jonas looked at the new tab this morning and liked it, with one request: the 95 percent target line is not the same for every contract. Some carriers are measured against 92. He wants to set it himself.

I added a nullable column on_time_target to the organisations table, with a migration that defaults to 95 so nothing changes for existing data. The settings page got a number field with validation between 50 and 100, only visible to managers. Dispatchers can see the target but not change it.

The API for the chart now returns the target with the data, and the chart takes the markLine value from there instead of the constant. I left the per-carrier targets out. That is more complicated, because the top five grouping would need a target for 'other', and Jonas confirmed that one target for the whole organisation is enough for now.

Tests: the settings validation, the permission check for dispatchers, and a chart test with a target of 92. All pass. I need to check one thing: the settings page is also used by the session and token code, and I did not want to change the form state handling there. I kept the new field in its own component.

summary: Late check of production after the target migration: it ran in 40 ms with no locks held, and the on-time chart shows the default line for all existing organisations.
body:
Deployed the migration for on_time_target in the evening, when the dispatchers are mostly offline. Adding a nullable column with a default is quick in Postgres of this version, and the migration took 40 ms. I watched the Render logs and the database connections for ten minutes; no errors and no blocked queries.

I opened the Performance tab as a manager account and saw the target line at 95. I then changed it to 92 on a test organisation and the line moved after a reload. A dispatcher account saw the value but had no input field.

The flag is still on only for two accounts. I will ask Jonas whether to open it to all managers after the weekend.

summary: Investigated a battery drain report from the mobile app that turned out to be a refresh loop after a long offline period, and planned a clearer error code for it.
body:
The mobile agency reported a battery drain complaint from one driver. I went through the log and found the app calling /auth/refresh every few seconds. The driver had been on holiday for five weeks, so the 30 day token was long expired, and the server answered 401 with the same code it uses for a bad access token. The app read that as 'refresh and try again' and went into a loop.

This is the same family of problem as the wrong error code found in the staging check a few weeks ago. Nothing is changed on the server yet. My plan is to return 401 with a separate code, refresh_expired, from /auth/refresh when the token is expired or revoked, and to keep the old code for access token problems. The app would then treat the new code as the end of the session and show the login screen.

I wrote down the three cases the tests must cover: expired, revoked and unknown token. All three should return the same status and the same code, so an attacker cannot tell them apart. I also want the response time to be the same within noise, which should hold if all three go through one lookup. I sketched the test cases but have not written the handler.

I sent the agency the proposed code name for their API notes. Their app already has a handler for unknown codes that goes to login, so they think the loop would stop even without an update. I asked them to check this against a staging build once the code exists. If the old app does stop, no hotfix is needed on their side.

Open point: a rate limit on /auth/refresh per token hash would stop any loop on the server side, whatever the client does. I put this on the list and will think about whether it conflicts with the grace window for clients on a poor network.

summary: Investigated the refresh loop from the mobile app and planned a rate limit for /auth/refresh, without building it yet.
body:
Following the 401 loop of the last entry, I looked at how the refresh endpoint behaves when a client hammers it. I wrote a small script that calls /auth/refresh in a tight loop with an expired token. Each call goes to Postgres to look up the token, so a client in a loop costs one query per attempt. The server held up in the test, but the load on the database was clearly higher than I like for a safety feature.

I wrote down a plan for a limiter. It would count per token hash and per IP, about 10 calls per minute each, in memory with a sliding window. The API runs as one instance on Render, so memory should be fine. If we ever run two instances, the counters would need to move to Postgres. I have not written any code for it yet.

The grace window case needs care. A second tab that refreshes within the grace window is a legal use, so it must not be punished. From the logs, two tabs and one retry stay far below 10 a minute, so the numbers look safe. I still want a test with four parallel requests that share one promise and make a single call.

I also read the web client code for refresh errors. Any failure on refresh sends the user to the login page, so a future 429 would log people out. That has to change first: the client should wait for a Retry-After header and try once more. Logging the user out because the server was busy would be a bad result.

The mobile client is not checked. I started a list of notes for the agency about the 429 case and the header.

One decision for now: no blocking of the IP for longer. A shared office IP of Acme would lock out all dispatchers at once.

summary: Started the table-v3 branch with a spike: replaced the shipments table with a virtualized grid and measured 50,000 rows scrolling smoothly in place of the old pagination.
body:
The first spike for the new table. The current shipments table uses pagination with 50 rows and renders everything per page. The managers want to scroll through large sets without clicking pages, and to pin columns.

I tried TanStack Table with TanStack Virtual in a branch, table-v3, since it keeps our own markup and styles, and does not bring a whole grid product with its own look. The spike renders only the visible rows, around 30, plus an overscan of 10. With 50,000 rows of fake data scrolling stayed at 60 frames per second in Chrome on my laptop, and memory was about 90 MB.

The old table's features have to be listed before a switch: sorting on the server, the carrier filter in the URL, column visibility, row selection for CSV export, and the status chips. In the spike only sorting and column visibility work, since the rest is bound to pagination in the old component.

The real question is the data loading. Virtual scrolling with server data needs either infinite loading in pages of 200 or a total count and range requests. I prefer range requests with offset and limit, with the total from a count query, but a count over the whole table is slow with filters. I will measure it next.

Nothing from the spike goes to main. The branch holds a route /shipments-v3 that only I use.

summary: Measured the count query behind the virtual table: with the carrier and date filters it takes 35 ms, but without any filter on the full table it takes 380 ms, so the total will be an estimate.
body:
The virtual table needs a total row count for the scrollbar. I ran the count on the staging copy with 400,000 shipments. With a carrier and date range it takes about 35 ms because the indexes help. With no filter it is a full count at 380 ms, and it is called each time a filter changes.

Two options: use the planner estimate from pg_class.reltuples for the unfiltered case, or cache the count. The estimate is off by a few percent but a scrollbar does not need to be exact. The table can show 'about 400,000' in that case and the exact number as soon as any filter is applied.

I chose the estimate for the unfiltered view, and an exact count for filtered views. The API returns total and a flag exact. The client shows the tilde sign when the flag is false.

The next step is infinite loading in blocks of 200 rows on the client. Tests for the endpoint cover both paths.

summary: Built range loading for the virtual table in table-v3: rows are fetched in blocks of 200 and cached by block index, and a sort or filter change drops the cache.
body:
The table-v3 grid now loads data in blocks. When the user scrolls to a row that is not loaded, the hook requests the block that contains it, plus the next one in the scroll direction. Blocks are kept in a Map by index. Rows not yet loaded are drawn as grey skeleton rows, so the scrollbar and the layout stay stable.

Changing a sort or a filter clears the Map and scrolls to the top. I first kept the old blocks while the new ones loaded, which looked smoother, but it showed rows that no longer matched the filter for a moment, and a dispatcher could click a wrong shipment. Clearing is the safe choice.

A problem came up with sorting by a column that is not unique, like the status. Rows with the same value can change order between two requests, so a row appeared twice at a block border. The API now adds the shipment id as a second sort key, always. This also fixed an old pagination duplicate that dispatchers had mentioned once.

Requests that are no longer needed are aborted when the user scrolls fast. With the abort, a fast scroll through 20,000 rows sent about 15 requests in place of 100. I tested it with the network throttled to slow 3G, and the skeleton rows were visible but the table stayed usable.

Still missing are row selection and the carrier filter. Selection needs a decision for 'select all', since the rows are not all loaded.

summary: Wrote the plan for row selection and CSV export in table-v3: select all becomes a filter-based selection on the server, because 50,000 rows cannot be held as ids in the browser.
body:
Today I did not write much code. I worked out how selection should work in the virtual table, since it also touches the CSV export, which is already slow for big sets.

The old table keeps selected ids in a Set, which is fine for 50 rows on a page. With virtual scrolling a user can press 'select all' for 50,000 rows. Loading all ids into the browser would defeat the purpose, and sending them back in a request is too big.

The plan has two modes. In the first, explicit mode, the client holds a Set of ids and the user clicks rows, with shift-click for a range inside the loaded blocks. In the second, filter mode, the client holds the current filter and sort, plus a Set of excluded ids. 'Select all' switches to that mode, and unchecking a row adds it to the exclusions. The header shows 'All 41,230 selected, 3 excluded'.

The export endpoint then takes either a list of ids or a filter plus exclusions. That is the same shape for both modes, so the server code has one path: it builds a where clause. The ids mode becomes id = any($1) and the filter mode uses the same filter builder as the table with an added id <> all($2).

I checked the current export code for the effect. It builds the whole CSV in memory, and for 40,000 rows it takes about 25 seconds and the Render request limit is 30 seconds. So large exports already fail now, and the new selection would make them more likely, since it is easier to select everything. That has to be solved, but I did not want to mix it into the table work. I put it on the list as its own item for the export code.

I wrote the plan into docs/table-v3.md, with the two modes and the API shape, and sent the short version to Jonas, since the 'select all' behaviour is visible to users. He agreed with the header text. Priya will check the look of the selection bar.

Next: implement the selection state as a reducer with tests, before touching the UI.

summary: Added a sticky header with a column menu to table-v3 and found the memory of the virtual list grew by 40 MB over a long scrolling session; the block cache needed a limit.
body:
Today's work on table-v3 started with the column menu that the managers asked for. The header of the virtual grid is now sticky and every column has a small menu to hide the column, sort by it, or reset the width. The hidden columns are stored in local storage next to the remembered widths from last week, under one key per user.

While testing the menu on the long list, I noticed in the browser memory profile that the tab grew steadily during scrolling. After scrolling through 50,000 rows several times, the heap was 40 MB larger than at the start and did not go down. This was not a leak of DOM nodes, since the number of rendered rows stayed constant at about 40. The cause was the block cache: blocks of 200 rows were cached by index and never dropped, unless the sort or filter changed.

I added a limit of 50 blocks, which is 10,000 rows, and removed the least recently used block when the limit is reached. The cache is a Map, and I move a key to the end on every read, so the first key is always the oldest. With the limit in place, the same scrolling session ended at 12 MB above the start, and the heap went down after a garbage collection.

The limit has a side effect: scrolling back to a block that was dropped fetches it again, and the user sees a blank row for a moment. On the local network the fetch takes about 30 ms, so it is not visible, but on a slow connection it could be. I added a placeholder row with a light skeleton for blocks that are loading, which also helps in the first load. I also prefetch one block in the direction of scrolling, which made the blanks mostly disappear in my test with network throttling set to slow 3G-like conditions.

Three new tests cover the cache limit, the order of removal and the reload of a dropped block. The existing Playwright tests still pass. Next is the memory check on the manager's older laptop, which Jonas offered to help with.

summary: Jonas asked whether table-v3 can ship before the export is fixed; I said yes if select all is hidden, and wrote down that large exports still time out at about 40,000 rows.
body:
Jonas asked this afternoon when the new table can go out, since the managers keep asking for scrolling. I gave him two options. The first is to wait for the export rework, which I cannot estimate well. The second is to release the table with 'select all' for export hidden, so that users can select explicit rows and export those, as today.

He chose the second option, with the note that the managers must be told that export of everything is not available in the new table yet. They can still use the old table at /shipments for that, which stays during the transition.

I wrote the known limit into the notes: exports of more than about 40,000 rows run into the 30 second request limit on Render and fail with a 502 after the wait. This is the case for the old table too, not only the new one. A fix needs the rows to stream, and not to be built in memory, but I have not started that.

The flag tableV3 will be on for managers first. Release is planned for next week after the filter work.

summary: Moved the carrier multi-select filter into table-v3 with its URL state intact, and fixed a bug where the filter change did not reset the scroll position of the virtual list.
body:
The carrier filter from a few weeks ago was bound to the old pagination, since it reset the page to one when the selection changed. In the virtual table there is no page, so I replaced that with the same reset the sort does: clear the block cache and scroll to the top.

The bug I found was that the cache was cleared but the scroll offset stayed. After filtering from 40,000 rows to 300, the virtual list kept an offset of 30,000 rows and showed an empty area with a scrollbar at the bottom. The fix is to call scrollToIndex(0) from the same effect that clears the cache, in that order. A test with a small container caught it.

The URL state still works as before. A shared link opens the table with the filter, sort and date range applied, and the hook reads them once at mount. I checked two things in the browser: the back button goes through the previous filters and does not leave the page, and a link with an unknown carrier id is ignored without an error.

The chips with search are the same component as before. I only had to change the height of the filter bar because the sticky selection bar needs to sit under it, and it overlapped by 4 px. Fixed.

summary: Dark theme and accessibility pass on table-v3: added grid roles, keyboard navigation with arrow keys, and fixed contrast on the selected row, which failed at 3.1 to 1.
body:
Before the release I went through the new table with the accessibility list. The first thing: a virtualized list built from divs has no table semantics, so a screen reader would read it as plain text. I added role=grid on the container, role=row on rows, role=gridcell on cells, and aria-rowcount with the total, so that the reader announces the right size even when only 30 rows are in the DOM. aria-rowindex is set on each row from its real index.

Keyboard use was missing. The arrow keys now move a focus cell by one, Home and End go to the start and end of the row, and Page Up and Down move by one screen. Space toggles the selection of the focused row and shift plus space extends the range, under the 1,000 limit. The focused row scrolls into view through the virtualizer. A test checks that after 100 arrow presses down the right row has the focus, which is where an off-by-one in the overscan showed up and was fixed.

Contrast: the selected row background in the dark theme was a blue with the text in a grey. I measured 3.1 to 1, below the 4.5 needed. Changed the background to a darker blue token and the text to the primary text color, now 7.2 to 1. In the light theme it was already fine at 5.8.

The focus ring was hidden by the overflow of the container, because it is drawn outside the cell. I switched to an inset outline of 2 px, and checked it in both themes.

One thing I did not solve: a screen reader still does not announce new rows when a block loads, which is probably right because we do not want chatter. I added a polite live region that says 'Loaded rows 201 to 400' only after a sort or filter change. I tried it with VoiceOver and it was understandable.

Priya looked at the focus ring and the selected row color and approved both. Remaining before the release: a Playwright run on the full suite and a note for the managers.

summary: Full Playwright run on table-v3 found two failing tests in the old table that shared a helper with the new one, which was fixed by splitting the selector helper.
body:
I ran the whole Playwright suite with the tableV3 flag on and off. With the flag off two old tests failed. They use a shared helper that finds table rows by a data-testid, and I had given the new rows the same testid. In the old table the helper then also counted the skeleton rows of the virtual list when both were rendered in the transition layout.

I split the helper into oldTableRows and gridRows, and renamed the testid of the new rows to grid-row. The suite then passed in both modes, 148 tests, in about 9 minutes on CI.

I also noticed a test that depends on the clock for token refresh, which uses the clock helper from the token release. It still works. No other changes were needed.

summary: Released table-v3 to managers behind the tableV3 flag, with the note that exporting all rows still has to use the old table; no errors in the first hour.
body:
The new table is on for the manager accounts. I sent Jonas the short text for them: scrolling instead of pages, pinned columns, selection of rows, and that 'export all' remains in the old table for now.

In the first hour the Render logs showed no errors. The block requests took 25 to 60 ms at the median. One manager's session loaded 12 blocks in a minute of scrolling, which is as expected.

I will check usage and the feedback in a few days. The export rework is the next big item.

summary: Feedback from two managers on the new table: they want the column widths remembered and a row count in the header; widths are easy and the count was already there, just too small.
body:
Two managers wrote to Jonas after using table-v3 for a couple of days. Both like the scrolling. They asked for the column widths to be remembered, and for a row count, which they thought was missing.

The count exists in the selection bar and as the aria value, but the text in the header was 11 px and grey, so they did not see it. I increased it to the normal text size and moved it next to the filters.

Widths are saved in local storage per user id and table name, after a debounce of 300 ms while dragging. A reset link in the column menu clears them. I put it in the settings of the table and not on the server, since it is a small thing and the server has enough to do with the sessions and tokens.

Tests cover saving, loading and the reset.

summary: Implemented remembered column widths for table-v3 in local storage per user, and enlarged the row count in the header after the managers' feedback.
body:
Two managers had asked for column widths to be remembered and a bigger row count, so I did both in one session. Widths are stored in local storage under a key made of the user id and the table name, so two users on one machine do not share them. The resize handler writes only on mouse release, because the first version wrote on every move and made the grid stutter.

A stored width is clamped between the minimum width of the column and 600 pixels. A saved value that no longer fits, for example after a column was renamed, is dropped instead of breaking the layout. The row count in the header went from the small gray text to the normal body size, with a thousands separator, and it says 'about' when the total is an estimate.

I added a 'reset columns' item to the column menu, which clears the stored widths. Vitest got four new tests: save, restore, clamp and reset. The Playwright run on the grid passed, apart from one flaky test of the sticky header that passed on a second run.

The widths are per browser only, not on the server. If the managers want them on every machine, that needs a column on the user settings table, and I noted it as a possible next step. I told Jonas the widths are on the tableV3 flag together with the rest of the grid.

summary: Checked the token numbers by hand after a manager reported being logged out twice in one morning, and found both were expired refresh tokens after a long meeting, not reuse alarms.
body:
A manager told Jonas that the dashboard had logged him out twice before lunch. I looked for his user id in the auth log. There were no reuse events for him at all.

Both logouts were refresh calls that arrived after the refresh token had expired. His laptop had been asleep for more than the idle limit, and the browser tab had no chance to refresh in between. That is the intended behavior, but the login page said nothing about why he was out.

I added a short message on the login page for the case where the server answers with the expired code: 'Your session ended because you were away for a while.' The code was already separate from the reuse code since the mobile 401 loop fix. The change is three lines in the login component and one test.

The weekly numbers are unchanged. I will mention the message to Jonas so he can pass it on to the managers.

summary: Started the costs overview for the new charts set, with a stacked bar of cost per carrier and month, and found the cost column mixes two currencies in a few old rows.
body:
The next chart for the new charts set is the cost overview that Jonas asked for. I began with a stacked bar chart with cost per carrier for each month, backed by one SQL aggregate like the on-time trend chart. The endpoint is GET /api/charts/cost-by-carrier with a date range.

While checking the numbers against a manual sum I found a gap of about 2 percent. The cause was 140 old shipments whose cost was stored in a different currency than the organisation default. The cost column has no currency next to it, so the sum silently added euros and pounds.

I did not guess a conversion. I listed the 140 rows by organisation and sent the list to Jonas to ask which currency each client contract uses. Until he answers, the endpoint excludes rows that do not match the organisation currency and returns their count in a field called skippedRows.

The chart shows a small note when skippedRows is above zero. I wrote API tests for the range, an empty range and the skipped rows. Tomorrow I will do the legend and the empty and loading states.

summary: Finished the cost chart states and legend, and Jonas answered that the 140 rows are all pounds from one client, so a currency column is next.
body:
Jonas answered quickly: all 140 rows belong to one client that was billed in pounds for the first months. That makes the fix simple. A currency column on the shipments table with a default of the organisation currency, and a one-time update for those rows.

I wrote the migration in two steps. First the nullable column was added, then the backfill ran in batches of 5,000, and last the not-null constraint with a default was set. On the production copy the backfill took 2 seconds. I will run it on production tomorrow morning when traffic is low.

The cost endpoint now groups by currency and the chart shows one stack per currency only if an organisation has more than one. For the usual case nothing changes. The skippedRows field stays for future bad data but should now be zero.

The legend uses the same component as the other charts in the set, with the click to hide a carrier. The empty state and the skeleton were reused from the on-time chart. Vitest passes. Left: run the migration on production and check the sums against the old report.

summary: Ran the currency migration on production and checked cost sums for three organisations against the old report; they match to the cent.
body:
I ran the three migration steps on production in the morning. The backfill took 2.4 seconds, no locks were held longer than a moment, and the app showed no errors. The 140 rows from the pound client now carry their own currency.

To check the result I compared the monthly cost sums of three organisations with the numbers of the old report page. All three matched to the cent. For the pound client the chart now shows a single stack in pounds, as Jonas wanted.

One detail came up: the CSV export of the shipments table does not have a currency column, so a manager reading an export of the pound client cannot tell the unit. I added the column to the export header and the row mapper. It is a small change, but the export format changed, so I told Jonas.

The skippedRows note stayed at zero for every organisation I tried. The cost chart is ready for the Performance tab flag.

summary: Fixed the token expiry handling in the web client so that a refresh failing with a network error no longer clears the stored session and logs the user out.
body:
A dispatcher reported that she was logged out whenever the train wifi dropped. In the client, any failed refresh call led to clearing the tokens, including a plain network error without any answer from the server. That is wrong, because the token may still be fine.

I separated the cases. A 401 with the expired or reuse code clears the session. A network error or a 5xx keeps the tokens and tries again after a short wait, with the wait growing from 2 to 30 seconds. While offline, requests wait for the refresh instead of failing at once.

I wrote tests with a mocked fetch for four cases: offline, 500, 401 expired and 401 reuse. The first two now keep the user in. I also tried the real thing in the browser by switching the network off in the dev tools for a minute; the tab recovered by itself.

The mobile app has its own client, so this change does not reach it. I will mention the same pattern to the agency.

summary: Added a language-neutral error code list for the auth API and sent it to the mobile app agency, so they can handle expired, reuse and rate-limited answers separately.
body:
After the 401 loop and the network fix I noticed that the auth error answers were never written down in one place. The web client knows them from the code, but the agency has only what we told them in chat. I wrote a short markdown file in the docs folder with every auth error.

The list has: token_expired, token_reused, token_revoked, refresh_rate_limited and invalid_credentials. For each one it gives the HTTP status, the meaning, and what a client should do. For example, token_expired means log in again, and refresh_rate_limited means wait for the Retry-After header.

I also wrote down what a client should not do: no repeated refresh calls on a network error without a pause, and no clearing of tokens on a 5xx answer. This is the same rule as in the web client now.

I sent the file to the agency contact and asked for a confirmation that their app maps each code. No reply yet. I will check the legacy token share next week to see whether their new version is rolling out.

summary: Checked why the Performance tab loads slowly for the largest client and found the on-time query scanned the whole shipments table because the date filter used a cast.
body:
Jonas said the Performance tab took about 6 seconds for the largest client. I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the on-time trend query. It did a sequential scan over all shipments, although there is an index on the delivery date.

The cause was a cast in the where clause: the delivery timestamp was cast to a date to compare with the range, so Postgres could not use the index. I changed the condition to compare the raw timestamp with a half-open range, start inclusive and end exclusive, computed in the organisation time zone.

The query went from 5.4 seconds to 90 ms on the production copy. The result is the same as before for the test data, including the daylight saving case from earlier. I added that case to the API tests as a guard.
