The cost and distribution endpoints had the same cast in one place each, so I fixed those too. The Performance tab now opens in under half a second for the big client.

summary: Planned the onboarding rework for new dispatchers: a short checklist after the first login, replacing the empty dashboard, with the steps agreed with Jonas and Priya.
body:
Jonas asked for a better first experience, because new dispatchers open the dashboard and see empty charts until data arrives. I met with him and Priya by chat and we agreed on the goal: a new user should do three things in the first ten minutes. They should set a time zone, invite a colleague and open a shipment.

I looked at what the data says. Of the last 40 invited users, 11 never opened a shipment and 17 never changed the default time zone. The time zone matters because the on-time charts depend on it, and a wrong zone gives wrong days.

The plan has four parts. First, a checklist card on the dashboard with three steps and a progress bar, which disappears when done or dismissed. Second, a time zone step that preselects the zone from the browser. Third, an invite step that reuses the existing invite dialog. Fourth, a sample shipment for accounts without data, so the table is not empty.

Priya will deliver the card design and the illustrations. I will build the state first. The progress is stored on the user, in a JSON column called onboarding_state with the keys for each step and a dismissed flag.

I considered computing the progress from existing data, for example 'has invited someone' from the invites table. I decided against it as the only source, because dismissing needs a stored flag anyway, and mixed sources are hard to test. The steps will check data once to complete themselves, then store the result.

Skipping must always be possible, since some users are invited only to read. The checklist will not block anything. I opened the onboarding branch and wrote the plan in the first commit message.

Open questions for Jonas: whether managers with SSO see the same checklist, and whether invited users from an existing organisation should skip the invite step. I will ask both tomorrow.

summary: Added the onboarding_state column and the API to read and update it, with a migration that ran in 30 ms and tests for the step transitions.
body:
The first code step of the onboarding branch is the state. The migration adds a JSON column onboarding_state to the users table with a default of an empty object. It ran on the production copy in 30 ms.

The API has two endpoints: GET /api/me/onboarding returns the steps with done flags, and PATCH /api/me/onboarding marks a step done or sets dismissed. The server accepts only the three known step names and answers 400 for others.

I put the step logic in one small module, so that the transitions are plain functions that are easy to test. A step cannot go from done back to open, and dismissing keeps the done flags. Vitest has nine tests for these rules.

Existing users get no checklist, because the migration marks them as dismissed through a second statement that sets the flag for all users created before today. Otherwise a manager from two years ago would suddenly see a welcome card.

summary: Built the onboarding checklist card with the time zone step, and fixed a bug where the zone picker preselected the browser zone but never saved it.
body:
Priya sent the card design in the morning, so I built the checklist component. It shows the title, a progress bar with the count of done steps, and three rows with an icon, a text and a button. The card sits at the top of the dashboard above the charts.

The time zone step was first. The picker reads the zone from Intl.DateTimeFormat in the browser and preselects it. The user confirms with a button, which calls the settings API and then marks the step done.

While testing I found that the zone shown in the picker was never saved if the user just pressed 'Done' on the step. The preselected value lived only in the component state, and the save call read the form value, which was still empty. I fixed it by initializing the form value together with the preselection.

A second small problem: the zone list had about 600 entries and the dropdown was slow on the old office laptops. I limited it to a search field with the first ten matches, and the most common zones for Acme at the top. Opening time went from 300 ms to 20 ms.

The card respects the dark theme. I used the theme tokens, not fixed colors, and checked the contrast of the progress bar with the checker, which gave 4.8 to 1.

I wrote component tests for the three states: all open, one done, and all done. The all-done state shows a short thank you message and the card hides itself on the next load. Keyboard use works with the tab order top to bottom.

For the open questions: Jonas said managers with SSO should see the same checklist, but without the invite step, because the invites come from the managers. That means the step list depends on the role. I will implement it tomorrow with a role filter in the step module.

summary: Made the onboarding steps depend on the role, so SSO managers see only the time zone and shipment steps, and users joining an existing organisation skip the invite step.
body:
Following Jonas's answer, the step module now takes the user role and the way the user was created. The invite step is left out for SSO managers. It is also left out for users who joined an existing organisation through an invite, because the person who invited them has done that already.

The progress bar counts only the steps that apply. A manager sees two steps, a dispatcher sees three. I changed the count text to read from the list, not from a fixed number three.

The tests grew from nine to fourteen. They cover the combinations of role and creation path. One test found a bug: the dismissed flag from the migration was read before the role filter, so a new SSO manager with an empty state was handled as 'all done' because the list of steps was empty by mistake. The order is now: filter, then count.

Still to do: the open shipment step and the sample shipment for empty accounts.

summary: Added the 'open a shipment' step and a sample shipment for accounts without data, marked clearly as an example and excluded from all sums and charts.
body:
Accounts with no data are the hardest case, because the step 'open a shipment' cannot be done on an empty table. I added a sample shipment that is shown only in the table when the organisation has no real shipments. It is not stored in the shipments table.

The sample is generated on the server in a separate endpoint and has a visible 'Example' badge. Its detail view looks like a real shipment, with a route, a status history and a cost, so the user can learn the layout. I made sure the charts and the CSV export never include it, because it does not exist in the database.

Opening the detail view of the sample, or of any real shipment, marks the step done. The check happens on the client when the detail route is opened and is sent through the existing PATCH endpoint.

I also considered a guided tour with highlighted areas. I left it out for now, because Priya prefers the plain card, and the tour libraries add 30 KB to the bundle. We can revisit it if the numbers show that the checklist is not enough.

Tests: the sample appears only for empty organisations, it vanishes when the first real shipment arrives, and the step completes on open. All green. Next is a review pass with Priya on the real screens.

summary: Reviewed the onboarding screens with Priya and changed the wording, the spacing of the card and the order of the steps; the invite step now comes last.
body:
Priya and I went through the checklist in the browser, in both themes and on a narrow window. She made a list of eight changes. Most were small: the card title now reads 'Get started' instead of 'Welcome to the dashboard', and the step texts start with a verb.

The bigger change is the order. She argued that the time zone should come first, then opening a shipment, and the invite last, because inviting a colleague asks the most from a new user. I agreed, since the time zone affects what the user sees at once.

Spacing and the progress bar were fixed in CSS. On a narrow window the buttons wrapped under the text and looked cramped, so they now take a full row below 480 pixels.

I also fixed a focus problem: after completing a step the focus stayed on the removed button and fell back to the page top. Now it moves to the next open step, which was a request from the accessibility checklist we use.

No logic changed, only order and presentation. The tests needed updates for the new order, and the snapshot of the card was renewed.

summary: Wrote the event tracking for onboarding steps, counting each step done and dismissals in the existing events table, so Jonas can see where new users stop.
body:
To know whether the checklist helps, Jonas wants numbers. The dashboard already has a small events table that records page views for the usage report. I added three event names: onboarding_step_done with the step name, onboarding_dismissed, and onboarding_completed.

The events are written on the server inside the PATCH endpoint, in the same transaction as the state change, so the counts cannot differ from the state. No personal data goes into the event beyond the user id, which the table already holds.

I wrote a query for a funnel: of the users created in a period, how many did each step and how many dismissed. Run on the test data it gives plausible numbers. I put the query in a script, not in the UI, because Jonas will only look at it now and then.

I noted for later that the numbers need two or three weeks before they say anything, since only new users are counted.

summary: The Playwright run for the onboarding branch failed in CI because the sample shipment depended on the clock; I made the sample use a fixed offset and fixed two other flaky tests.
body:
The full Playwright run in CI failed on three tests of the onboarding flow, although they passed locally. The first failure was the sample shipment: its detail view showed 'delivered 2 hours ago' computed from the current time, and the test compared the text with a fixed string.

I changed the sample generator to produce its timestamps from a reference time that the API can receive in test mode. In normal mode it uses the clock. The test now sends a fixed reference. This also removes a risk that the sample looked odd just after midnight.

The second failure was a race. The test clicked the time zone confirm button and checked the progress bar at once, but the bar updates after the PATCH call returns. I replaced the immediate check with a wait for the response, using the response wait of Playwright and not a sleep.

The third test failed only in CI. It created a user with an invite, and the invite email link was read from a local mail catcher. In CI the catcher starts a second later, so the first request got a refused connection. I added a readiness check to the CI script that polls the catcher port for up to 10 seconds.

After these three changes I ran the suite five times in a row in CI. Five green runs. It takes 6 minutes 20 seconds, nearly the same as before.

I also looked at why the suite is slow. Most of the time goes to logging in again in every test. Playwright can reuse a stored login state, which would cut maybe two minutes. This needs care now that tokens rotate, because a stored state contains a refresh token that is used once. A shared state across parallel workers could trigger the reuse alarm.

I decided to try one login state per worker, not one for all. I will test it tomorrow, with a note to check the reuse log after the run.

summary: Tried one stored login state per Playwright worker to speed up CI; it cut the run from 6:20 to 4:10 and caused no reuse events, but one test that logs out had to get its own user.
body:
Today I implemented the idea from last night: a global setup that logs in once for each worker and saves the browser state to a file named by the worker index. Each test file then starts with that state instead of the login form.

The first run showed the effect at once. The suite went from 6 minutes 20 seconds to 4 minutes 10 seconds. The login form tests stayed as they were, because they test the form itself and start without a state.

The worry was the refresh token rotation. A refresh token is used once, so if two workers shared one stored state, the second use would look like a reuse and log both out. With one state per worker there is no sharing. I checked the auth log after three CI runs and found no reuse events from the test users.

One test failed: the logout test. After the logout the server revokes the refresh token, and the next test of the same worker started with a state that no longer worked. The fix was to give that test its own fresh user and an own browser context, so the worker state is not touched.

Another problem showed up in a test that waits longer than the access token life of 15 minutes. It does not exist yet, but I wrote a comment in the setup file about it: the stored state contains an access token that will expire, and the client then refreshes with the stored refresh token. That works, but it rotates the token inside the test, and the file on disk is then out of date. For now each worker uses its state in memory after loading, which is fine for runs of a few minutes.

I also moved the helper that creates test users into the setup, so the users are created in parallel at the start. That saved 15 more seconds.

I updated the testing notes in the repository with the rule: one login state per worker, never share one, and tests that log out use their own user. I will merge the CI change into main separately from the onboarding branch, since it helps all work.

summary: Merged the faster Playwright setup into main and answered the agency's question on how long a mobile refresh token stays valid when the app is unused.
body:
I merged the CI change from yesterday into main with a short description. The first runs on main took 4 minutes 5 seconds and were green. The onboarding branch will pick it up when I merge main into it.

The agency replied to the error code list at last. They had one question: how long does a refresh token stay valid when the app is not used? The answer is 30 days from the last use, since each refresh issues a new token with a new 30 day life. After 30 days without any use the server answers token_expired, and the app has to ask for a password login.

They also asked whether a refresh token could be made to live longer for drivers, who may be on leave for a month. I said that this is a decision for Jonas, because it is a trade-off with security: a longer life means a stolen phone stays useful longer. I wrote the question to Jonas with both options and the current numbers: about 4 percent of mobile users came back after more than 30 days in the last quarter.

The agency confirmed that their new version maps all five error codes. They will ship it in the next release. When it is out, the legacy token share should fall further, and I will watch the weekly numbers for that.

I cleaned up the docs file. I added the validity rule and an example answer body for each error code, so that the agency does not need to ask again.

summary: Finished the onboarding branch work: reviewed all pieces, ran the funnel query on staging, fixed a double-count of completed events, and prepared the release behind a flag.
body:
Today I closed the main part of the onboarding branch. I merged main into it first, resolved one conflict in the settings route file, and ran the whole test suite. All unit tests and the Playwright run passed, in 4 minutes 12 seconds.

Then I went through the diff once more as a reviewer would. The branch has the state column, the two endpoints, the step module, the card, the sample shipment and the events. I found two small things: an unused import in the card and a missing index on the events table for the funnel query.

The funnel query ran on staging with fake users that I created with a script. It showed 'completed' counts that were too high. The reason was that onboarding_completed was written each time any step was marked done after all steps were finished, for example when a user pressed the time zone button again. The count of a user could then be two or three.

I fixed it by writing the completed event only in the transition from not completed to completed, and the step module now returns a flag for that transition. A test covers the second press. The counts on staging were right after the fix.

The index is on the event name and the creation time. The funnel query went from 400 ms to 12 ms on the staging table, which has 200,000 rows. Production has more, so the index will matter there.

I put the whole checklist behind a flag called onboarding, so we can switch it on for new users only and off again at once. The flag is read on the server, so that the API does not create state for users who should not have it. When the flag is off, the endpoints answer with an empty list.

I wrote the release note for Jonas. It says what new users will see, that existing users see nothing, and where he can look at the numbers. I attached screenshots in both themes.

A remaining item is the accessibility check with a screen reader. I tested with VoiceOver on the card: the progress bar is announced with its value, the steps are a list, and the buttons have clear labels. One problem: the done steps were announced as plain text without a state. I added visually hidden text 'done' and tested again.

Tomorrow I will release it to new users, and watch the logs for the first hour.

summary: Released the onboarding checklist to new users behind the flag in the evening; the first two accounts created got the card and no errors appeared.
body:
I switched the onboarding flag on for new accounts. The migration ran first, and the column existed already from the earlier step. It needed nothing more.

Two invited users logged in during the first hour. Both got the checklist, the time zone step preselected the right zone, and one of them completed it. The events table shows one step done and no errors in the log.

The response time of the dashboard page did not change, because the onboarding state is read in the same request as the user profile and adds one column. I looked at the p95 for the first hour: 180 ms, as before.

Jonas knows it is live. I will look at the funnel after a week.

summary: Started the scheduled reports work by writing a design for the email reports: a table of schedules, a job that runs every five minutes, and a report render that reuses the report builder.
body:
Jonas asked for reports that arrive by email every week or month, without anyone opening the dashboard. This session was only design and a first spike, since the report builder has to be understood first. I read through its code to see how a report is described. A report is a JSON definition with columns, filters, grouping and a chart type, and a render function turns it into a table or chart on the page.

For emails, the render needs to run on the server. Charts in ECharts can be rendered on the server to SVG, and I tried it in a small script. It works, but many mail clients do not show SVG. So the email will carry a PNG made from the SVG, and a link to the live report.

The plan has these parts. A schedules table with the report id, the owner, a cron-like rule limited to daily, weekly and monthly, the time zone, the recipients and the last run time. A job runner that starts every five minutes and takes the schedules that are due. A render step. A send step with the mail provider we already use for invites.

I thought about how to avoid sending twice. The job takes a schedule with a row lock and sets next_run_at before it renders, in the same transaction. If the render fails, the failure is stored and the next run is set to a retry time, so that a failing report does not block others or spam.

The access question matters: the report runs with the rights of its owner at the time of sending. If the owner loses access to a client, the schedule must stop and tell the owner. I wrote that as a rule in the design.

For the spike I rendered one existing report to PNG on the server with the node canvas package. The image took 400 ms for a chart with 90 points. Memory looked fine. Installing the canvas package on Render needs system libraries, so I checked the build log of a test deploy, and it builds.

The question for Jonas is the number of recipients. I proposed a limit of ten per schedule at the start. A second question is whether recipients must be dashboard users. Allowing any address makes it easy to send data outside the company, so I suggested allowing only users of the same organisation first.

The design is written in the docs folder, with the table definition. I will start on the schedule table and the API next.

summary: Built the schedules table and CRUD API for scheduled reports, with validation of recipients against organisation users and a limit of ten recipients.
body:
Jonas agreed to both limits: at most ten recipients, and only users of the same organisation. He also wants the owner to receive a copy by default. I built the first step of the scheduled reports feature.

The migration creates a report_schedules table. It holds the report id, the owner id, the frequency (daily, weekly or monthly), the day and hour, the time zone, the recipient user ids as an array, next_run_at, last_run_at and last_error. There is an index on next_run_at for the job query.

The API has the usual four routes under /api/reports/:id/schedules. Creating one validates the frequency, the hour from 0 to 23, the zone name against the zone list, and the recipients. A recipient who is not in the organisation gets a 422 with the list of bad ids.

The next_run_at is computed in one function from the rule and the zone. This function took most of the thinking, since weekly and monthly rules cross daylight saving changes. For a monthly rule on the 31st, months with fewer days use the last day. I wrote 18 tests, including a daylight saving change in spring and one in autumn, where an hour does not exist and one hour exists twice.

The daylight saving cases found a bug at once: for a schedule at 02:30 on the day when the clocks jump forward, my first version produced a time one hour late on the next day. It now moves the run to the first valid time after the gap, on the same day.

An owner can only create schedules for reports that they can see. I reused the check of the report API, not a new one. A user with a read-only role can see reports, but not schedule them, which Jonas confirmed.

The response of the list route includes the next run time in the zone of the schedule and in UTC, so the UI can show both. I did not build the UI yet.

Tests pass, 31 new ones in total. The runner job comes next, and I will start with the locking query.

summary: Wrote the scheduler job for reports, using a row lock with skip locked so two instances cannot run the same schedule, and tested it with two parallel runners.
body:
The job runs every five minutes and picks the due schedules. The core is one query: select the schedules with next_run_at in the past, order by next_run_at, limit 20, for update skip locked. Inside the same transaction the job sets the next run time, then commits, and only then renders and sends.

I chose to commit before the rendering on purpose. A report with a heavy query must not hold a database lock. The cost is that a crash between the commit and the send loses one run. I accepted this for now and stored a pending flag, so that a run can be seen as lost and shown to the owner.

To test the locking I started two runner processes against a test database with 50 due schedules. Each schedule ran exactly once, and the two runners shared the work, 27 and 23. Without skip locked in a trial run the second runner waited and then ran several schedules twice.

On failure the job writes the message to last_error and moves the next run to 30 minutes later, with at most three tries. After three failures the schedule is paused and the owner gets a short mail. I wrote tests with a render function that throws.

The job is started by a small timer in the API process for now, because Render has only one instance of the API. If we add a second instance, the lock protects us. I wrote this in the design file.

The render and send steps are still stubs that log. Next is the real render with the PNG.

summary: Connected the render and send steps for scheduled reports: the server builds the report as a PNG and a table, and sends the email; found that large reports are slow and capped them at 5,000 rows.
body:
Today the stubs got replaced. The render step loads the report definition, runs it with the rights of the owner, and produces two things: a PNG of the chart, and an HTML table of the first rows. The email shows the chart, the table, and a link to the live report.

The query runs through the same code as the page, so the numbers in the email equal what the user sees. I wrote a test that renders a report and compares the sums in the table with the API result. They match.

For the PNG I used the server rendering of ECharts with the canvas package. With a chart of 90 points it takes 400 ms. A chart with 3,000 points took 2.8 seconds, so I limited the chart to 500 points by sampling the series at even steps. The email says 'chart shows a sample' in that case.

The table is the problem. A report with 60,000 rows made the render take 40 seconds and the process memory went up by 300 MB, because the code builds the whole HTML in memory. An email of that size makes no sense anyway. I capped the table in the email at 5,000 rows, and the mail states how many rows are left and links to the live report.

This is the same problem as the slow CSV export of large tables: the code collects all the rows first. Managers also ask for an attachment as a CSV. I decided not to attach the CSV for now, because the export of large tables times out at about 40,000 rows. For small reports below 5,000 rows I attach it, built by the same export code.

The send step uses the mail provider with the existing templates for layout. Each recipient gets a separate message, so that nobody sees the addresses of the others, and there is an unsubscribe link that removes the user from that schedule. The link carries a signed token and no login is needed.

I tested with three real mailboxes. Gmail and the Outlook web client showed the PNG, the table and the link properly. The dark mode of one client inverted the PNG background, so I gave the image a white background of its own.

The job now measures the run time per schedule and stores it in last_duration_ms. In a test with 20 due schedules the whole job took 14 seconds, mostly because the reports run one after another. That is fine for the current load.

Still open: the UI for schedules on the report page, and the pause of a schedule when the owner loses access.

summary: Built the schedule dialog on the report page, with frequency, time, zone and recipients, and added the pause of schedules when the owner loses access to the report.
body:
The last parts of the first version of scheduled reports are the UI and the access rule. I started with the dialog. A button 'Schedule' on the report page opens it. The form has the frequency, the day for weekly or monthly, the hour, the time zone, which is preselected from the user settings, and a recipient picker with the organisation users.

The picker shows chips like the carrier filter does, and it stops at ten recipients with a clear message. The owner is added by default, and the owner chip can be removed. Below the form the dialog shows 'Next run: in 3 days, at 08:00 your time', computed by the API, so the client does not repeat the date logic.

Validation errors from the API appear next to the fields. A 422 for a bad recipient marks the chip in red. I tested this by sending a user id of another organisation through a changed request, and the field showed the error.

The list of schedules for a report is a small table in the same dialog, with the next run, the last run, the last error, and pause and delete buttons. A paused schedule shows its reason, for example 'paused after 3 failed runs'.

Now the access rule. Before each run the job checks that the owner still has the right to see the report and the data behind it. If not, the schedule is paused with the reason 'owner lost access' and the owner gets a mail, as in the design. There is a test where I remove the role of a user between two runs, and the second run is skipped and paused.

I also noticed the job did not handle deleted users. When a user is deleted, the schedules of that user stay in the table. I added a cascade on the owner id, and for recipients the job removes ids that no longer exist before sending. The migration for the cascade ran in 25 ms.

Accessibility: the dialog traps the focus, closes with Escape, and returns the focus to the button. The frequency choice is a radio group with labels, and the time field is a native select. A screen reader pass on the dialog read all fields in a good order.

Playwright tests: create a schedule, see it in the list, pause it, delete it. They pass with the worker login state. In total the CI run is 4 minutes 30 seconds now.

I did not release the feature yet. I put it behind a flag called scheduledReports and asked Jonas for two managers who can try it for a week. The first real report is due the day after tomorrow morning. I will check the job log then.

summary: Tested the scheduled report email in Gmail and Outlook and fixed the inline PNG, which Outlook showed as an attachment only.
body: I sent test reports to a Gmail and an Outlook account from staging. Gmail showed the chart fine, but Outlook listed the PNG as an attachment and left a blank box in the body. The cause was that the image was attached without a Content-ID, so the HTML could not reference it. I added a cid reference in the template and set the content disposition to inline. The table part, which is plain HTML, rendered well in both clients. A second send showed the chart inline in Outlook too. Left to do: the dark mode of mail clients, which inverts the chart background.

summary: Added a time zone and daylight saving test suite for the report scheduler after a schedule at 02:30 ran twice in a simulated clock change.
body: While reading the scheduler I suspected that local times that do not exist or happen twice around a clock change would misfire. I wrote tests with a fake clock for Europe/Berlin and America/Chicago. The 02:30 schedule on the spring change day was skipped, and on the autumn change it ran twice. The fix computes next_run_at in UTC from the zone each time and stores the last run, so a run is never repeated within the same hour. Non-existent times now move to the first valid minute after the gap. Eleven new tests cover this and all pass. I also checked that the schedule dialog shows the next run in the zone of the schedule. Nothing was changed in production yet.

summary: Scheduled reports are released behind a flag to Jonas's own organisation, with a failure log table so that bounced mails can be seen.
body: I added a report_runs table with status, row count, duration and error text, written by the scheduler for each run. The settings page of a schedule now shows the last five runs. Failed sends retry up to three times with a growing delay, then the schedule shows an error state. I enabled the flag for the Acme head office organisation only. Jonas created two schedules himself, a weekly cost report and a daily late shipments table. Both arrived at the planned time. One recipient bounced because of a typo, and the run list showed the bounce text clearly. Render logs showed the job taking 1.2 s on average. The five minute tick works, and memory stays flat. Next step is to watch it for a few days before opening it to all managers. One open issue is that the report owner is not told about a paused schedule. I noted that as the next small task. I also removed an old debug log line that printed recipients, since it is personal data. The release note for Jonas lists the 5,000 row cap and the ten recipient limit.

summary: The owner of a paused schedule now gets an email, and the pause rules were made consistent for deleted users and for role changes.
body:
Until now a schedule paused silently when its owner lost access to the report. Jonas asked that the owner or an organisation admin is told. I wrote a small notice email with the report name, the reason and a link to the schedule list. The reasons are: owner removed, owner lost access to the report, report deleted. Each reason has its own text.

While testing I found that a role change from manager to dispatcher did not trigger the pause check at all, because the check ran only on report sharing changes. I moved the check into a function that runs on both events and in the nightly consistency job. The function returns the list of schedules to pause and the reason, which made it easy to test.

Another problem was that a deleted user's schedules were still active and sent mail to old recipients. They are now paused and flagged for the admin. The tests cover six cases and use the fixture organisations. I ran the nightly job on staging and it paused three old test schedules as expected.

One question remains: should an admin be able to take over a paused schedule? Jonas thinks yes. I wrote it down as the next item, with a button on the schedule list that changes the owner. The notice uses the same sender as the reports, so spam filters treat it the same way. I checked the text with Priya's wording guide and shortened two sentences.

summary: Built the take-over button for paused schedules, so an admin can become the owner and resume them with one click.
body:
The schedule list now shows a Take over button to admins for paused schedules. The API call sets the owner to the admin, checks that the admin can see the report, and clears the pause flag. If the admin cannot see the report, the call returns an error with a clear message. I added a confirmation dialog that lists the recipients, since taking over means sending mail in the admin's name. The audit entry records the old and new owner.

Tests cover the success case, the no access case and a non-admin calling the endpoint. The last one returns 403. Playwright got one new test for the full flow with a paused fixture schedule. It first failed because the dialog animation was still running, and I waited for the dialog role instead of a timeout. Staging works. I also fixed a layout bug where the button wrapped on narrow screens. The design was approved by Priya in chat. Release is behind the same flag as the rest.

summary: Looked into why the session of a long open dashboard tab ended during a meeting; the refresh timer is paused when the browser throttles background tabs.
body:
A manager at Acme reported that after a long meeting with the dashboard open in the background, the next click sent them to the login page. I checked the logs for the user: the refresh token was still valid, but no refresh call had happened for 25 minutes, and the access token had expired. The client refreshes on a setTimeout shortly before expiry. Browsers throttle timers in background tabs, and in some cases the laptop slept, so the timer fired late or never.

I reproduced it in Chrome by sleeping the tab with the devtools throttle and changing the system clock. After a wake-up the first API call got a 401 and the client logged out directly. That is wrong, because the refresh token was fine.

The fix has two parts. On a 401 the client now tries one refresh and repeats the call once. A visibilitychange listener checks the expiry when the tab becomes visible and refreshes at once if needed. Both paths share the single-flight refresh promise, so two tabs of the same browser do not fire two refreshes in the same tab.

I added unit tests with fake timers for the wake-up case and the failed refresh case. The manager's case is covered. A cross-tab race still exists in theory, since local storage is shared; I will look at it in a separate entry. For now the log shows no reuse alarms for that user.

summary: Fixed the cross-tab refresh race with a lock in local storage plus the Web Locks API, after reproducing a reuse alarm with two tabs waking up together.
body:
Following the wake-up fix of this morning I wanted to close the cross-tab case. Two tabs of one browser wake up at the same moment, both see an expired access token and both call the refresh endpoint with the same refresh token. The server rotates on the first call, and the second call arrives with a used token. That looks like a reuse and triggers the alarm.

I reproduced it in Playwright with two pages in one context. I froze the clock, advanced it past the expiry and triggered the visibility event in both pages. In 7 of 10 runs the server logged a reuse and revoked the family. That matched the complaints.

The fix uses navigator.locks.request with a fixed name around the refresh. Inside the lock, the code first reads the stored tokens again. If another tab already refreshed, it uses the new access token and does not call the server. Browsers without Web Locks fall back to a lock key in local storage with a timeout of five seconds.

I also added a grace window on the server of ten seconds, where the previous refresh token returns the same new pair instead of a reuse error. I chose a short window because a longer one weakens the rotation. The grace window needs the pair stored for a moment, so I keep the hash of the last issued pair in the token row.

The test now runs 50 times with two and with three tabs and gave zero reuse events. Unit tests cover the server grace window, including the case after eleven seconds, which must still count as reuse.

I checked that a real stolen token replay still triggers the alarm: an old token used after the window revokes the family. The mobile app is not affected, since it has one process, but the grace window helps if it retries after a network drop. I told nobody at the agency yet, because the error codes did not change. I will mention it in the next message to them. Left to do: watch the reuse events for a week and compare with the earlier numbers.

summary: Wrote the report builder v2 plan: saved filters as named presets, multiple charts per report, and a shared layout grid.
body: Jonas wants managers to put several charts and a table in one report. I sketched the changes with the current builder in mind. A report becomes a list of blocks, each with a type, a query and a size on a 12-column grid. Old reports migrate to one block each. Saved filters become presets that a report can reference, instead of copying the filter. The scheduled report render needs to loop over the blocks, so I checked that the render code takes a block and not a report. It mostly does. The plan has four steps: the data model and migration, the block editor, the preset UI, and the render. I estimated about two weeks and shared the plan with Jonas and Priya.

summary: Added the report blocks table and a migration that turns every old report into a report with one block, checked on a copy of production.
body: I created report_blocks with report_id, position, type, config JSON and the grid size. The migration reads each old report and inserts one block with the same chart type and filter. I ran it on a restore of the production backup. 412 reports became 412 blocks and the migration took 180 ms. A check query compared the old and new config for each report and found no differences. The report API returns the blocks, and for a short time also the old fields, so the current client keeps working. I wrote tests for ordering and for deleting a report with blocks, which cascades. The next step is the block editor in the UI.

summary: Built the block editor of report builder v2 with add, remove and drag to reorder, and fixed ECharts not resizing inside the grid.
body:
The editor shows the blocks as cards on the 12-column grid. You can add a chart or a table block, remove a block, and drag to reorder with keyboard support through up and down buttons. Each block has its own settings drawer that reuses the old chart form.

The charts first stayed at their old size after a resize of the card. ECharts needs resize called after the container changes. I wrapped the chart in a ResizeObserver hook and debounced it to one frame. That fixed the bug in the grid and in the drawer preview.

I also found that reordering sent one request per block. It now sends one request with the new order list. The tests cover the reorder call and the keyboard path. Playwright has one new test that adds two blocks and reloads the page. Not done yet: presets and the layout of blocks on small screens, where they should stack in one column.

summary: Added filter presets to report builder v2, so a report can point to a named preset and changes to the preset reach all reports using it.
body: A preset has a name, the filter JSON and the organisation. In the builder, the filter bar got a Preset dropdown and a Save as preset action. A block stores either its own filter or a preset id. I decided that editing a preset shows a warning with the number of reports that use it. Deleting a used preset is blocked. The API has CRUD calls and a usage count query. Tests cover the usage count and the blocked delete. I tried it with Jonas's weekly report and it worked. The render for scheduled reports still reads the old filter field and needs the same change tomorrow.

summary: Switched the scheduled report render to the block model and presets, and a three-block report now arrives as one email.
body: The render function now loops over the blocks and resolves the preset for each one. Charts come out as PNGs in the order of the blocks, and a table block becomes an HTML table capped at 5,000 rows, as before. I kept one browser page for the whole report to avoid starting it three times. The run for a three-block report took 4.1 s against 1.3 s for the old one block report. That is fine for the five minute tick. The email layout puts the blocks one under the other. A test with a snapshot of the HTML covers it. A report whose preset was deleted shows a short error block and the run is marked as partial. I sent one to Jonas for review.

summary: Reviewed the access of sessions after a manager asked why an old laptop was still logged in, and found the 30-day refresh lifetime matches what was agreed.
body:
A manager at Acme wrote that a colleague's old laptop was still logged in weeks after they had handed it back. Jonas asked me whether this is a bug.

I looked at the token table for that user. The laptop held a refresh token family created 19 days earlier, rotated every few days when the browser was opened. Since the refresh token lives 30 days and slides on each rotation, an active browser stays logged in. It is as designed, but the user has no way to see or end it.

I checked what a logout does. It revokes the family of the current browser, nothing else. So there is no way to log out the other devices, and the logout does not touch the access token, which lives for 15 minutes. For the access token we use the deny list in Postgres, which has about 38,000 rows now, because each logout adds a row until it expires.

I wrote up three options for Jonas:
- a button to revoke all families of the user, simple to build,
- a list of devices with a revoke for each, which needs a device name per family,
- a shorter absolute lifetime for refresh tokens, for example 14 days, which logs out people who use the dashboard rarely.

I measured how many users would be hit by 14 days: 11 of 160 active users had a gap longer than 14 days in the last quarter, which is small. Still, the choice belongs to Jonas.

I also noticed that the deny list is only cleaned by a manual script. I wrote a small job that deletes rows past their expiry, and ran it once on staging; it removed 31,000 rows and took 2 s. I did not run it on production yet. Next step: Jonas decides, and I build the revoke all button either way, since it is needed for lost laptops.

summary: Built the log out of all devices action for the refresh token setup, revoking every family of a user and adding the current token to the deny list.
body: Jonas chose the simple option: one button on the settings page that ends all logins of the user. The API call marks all refresh token families of the user as revoked. The tokens in use right now are covered by the deny list for their remaining 15 minutes, so I add the current access token id. Other access tokens of that user are not known, so I store a revoked_before time per user. The auth check compares the token issue time with this value. That avoids one deny row per token. The button has a confirmation and logs the user out of the current browser as well. Tests cover the revoked_before check and a family revoke. I ran the cleanup job on production and it removed 36,000 old deny rows.

summary: Fixed a bug in report builder v2 where the grid sizes of blocks were lost on duplicate, and added a duplicate-report test.
body: Priya noticed that a duplicated report had all blocks at the default width. The duplicate call copied type and config but not the grid size column that I added later. I fixed the copy and wrote a test that duplicates a report with three differently sized blocks and compares them. While there I also found that preset references were copied as the filter JSON, which loses the link. The copy now keeps the preset id. Both cases pass. I checked the old reports on staging and they still duplicate correctly.

summary: Looked into slow CSV export of the shipments table: a 400,000 row export takes over a minute and sometimes gets cut off by the proxy, so I measured where the time goes.
body:
Two dispatchers reported that the CSV export of all shipments for a long date range fails with a gateway timeout. Jonas asked whether we can make it work this week. I took the largest organisation and ran the export code locally against a copy of the data.

For 400,000 rows the export took 74 s. I split it into steps with timers. The query took 6 s, the mapping of rows to objects 9 s, building the CSV string 31 s, and sending the response the rest. Memory rose to 1.4 GB at the peak, which is also a risk on the small Render instance.

The string building is slow because the code joins values with quoting checks per cell and appends to one big string. I tried a faster quote function and got from 31 s to 19 s. That helps, but does not remove the memory peak.

The proxy on Render cuts requests with no bytes for 30 seconds, which explains the timeout, since nothing is sent until the file is complete. So even a faster build would only move the limit to larger exports.

I wrote down the options. Raising the proxy limit is not possible on our plan. A background job that creates the file and mails a link works, but it is a bigger piece of work. Sending the rows as they are produced would solve the timeout and the memory together, but I have not tried it, and the export code is shared with the report render, so changes need care.

For now I only shipped the faster quote function, with a test for quotes, commas and line breaks in cells. I also added a message in the export dialog when the row count is above 200,000, telling people to narrow the date range. Next step is a decision with Jonas about the bigger change.

summary: Upgraded Vite and its plugins to the next major version and fixed three build errors; the dev start time dropped from 4.8 s to 2.1 s.
body:
I upgraded Vite, the React plugin and Vitest together on a branch of main. The first build failed with three errors. One was a removed config option for the CJS build, which I deleted. The second was an import of a JSON file with a named export that the new version rejects, so I changed it to a default import. The third was a plugin for SVG imports that had no release for the new version; I replaced it with the query suffix feature that Vite has built in.

After that the production build worked. The bundle was 3 percent smaller, 1.12 MB against 1.16 MB before. The dev server start went from 4.8 s to 2.1 s on my machine.

Vitest needed a changed setting for the jsdom environment, and two tests that relied on the old module mocking order failed. I fixed them by moving the mock calls to the top of the file. All 640 unit tests pass.

Playwright ran against the preview build and found one failure: the font preload path of the dark theme changed because of a different asset hashing. I updated the link tag in index.html.

I checked the Render build, which uses Node 18. The new Vite needs 18 or newer, so it is fine, and the build took 52 s instead of 61 s. I deployed to staging and looked at the charts, the report builder and the table by hand. One thing remains: a warning about a deprecated Sass API in the console, which I will leave for a later upgrade. I merged after a green CI run.

summary: Upgraded React to the next minor version with the new compiler checks turned on in lint only, and fixed 14 warnings about effects with missing dependencies.
body:
After the Vite upgrade I moved React to the latest minor release. The upgrade itself caused no failures in the unit tests or in Playwright. I then turned on the stricter lint rule set for hooks in warning mode and counted 14 findings.

Most were effects with missing dependencies. In nine cases the effect really depended on a function that was recreated at each render, so adding it would have caused loops. I wrapped those functions with useCallback or moved them out of the component.

Two findings pointed to real bugs. In the date picker, an effect used an old value of the range and did not update the label after a preset click. In the report builder, a block drawer kept the first filter after switching to another block. Both are fixed and each got a test.

Three findings were set to ignore with a comment, since the effect should run once on mount, for example the chart init. I wrote the reason in each comment.

I also removed a library for class names that the new code does not need, as a small tidy up. The bundle changed by less than 1 kB. Strict mode double effects found nothing new. Next I want to look at the slow render of the shipments table when the filter changes, but that belongs to another session. I merged after CI.

summary: Started the costs page: a table and chart of cost per shipment, per carrier and per route, with the currency column from last time and a sum row per currency.
body:
Jonas wants a page where managers see what the deliveries cost, grouped by carrier, route and month. The data is there since the cost chart work in the new charts set, and the currency column now exists. I started with the API and the page shell.

The endpoint takes a date range, a grouping and optional carrier filters, and returns rows with the sum per currency. I decided not to convert currencies, since there is no rate source and Jonas said the clients mostly use one currency. The page shows one sum row per currency instead.

The SQL groups by the chosen field and the currency. I checked it against the old cost report for three organisations. The sums match. The explain plan showed a sequential scan on shipments for the largest client, 1.9 s. An index on organisation, delivered date and currency brought it down to 140 ms. The migration to create the index ran in 4 s on production with the concurrent option.

On the front end I built a header with the date picker and grouping select, the table with sortable columns, and a bar chart with ECharts above it. The chart takes the top ten groups and puts the rest into an Other bar. Colours come from the existing palette, and the legend follows the pattern from the chart legend fix of last year.

The empty state, the loading skeleton and the error state were done. The number format uses the user's locale and the currency code. For pounds and euros it shows the symbols.

Things I noticed: a few shipments have a null cost for cancelled jobs, which are counted as zero in the average. I excluded them from averages and show their count in a note. Open work: export of the cost table, permissions so that dispatchers do not see costs, and tests. The permission part needs a question to Jonas about which roles may see the page.

summary: Jonas confirmed that only managers and admins may see the costs page, so I added the role check to the API and hid the menu entry for dispatchers.
body: I asked Jonas which roles see costs. His answer was short: managers and admins only, never dispatchers. I added the check in the API middleware for the cost endpoint and returned 403 for others. The menu hides the entry for dispatchers, and a direct visit to the URL shows a plain no access page. SSO managers have the manager role, so they see it. Tests cover all three roles and the direct call with a dispatcher session. I also checked that the cost column is not returned by the shipments table API to dispatchers; it was not, which is good. Next is the export of the cost table.

summary: Added CSV export to the costs page for the visible grouped table, which is small, and confirmed that the large shipment export is still slow.
body: The costs table has at most a few hundred grouped rows, so I reused the existing export function for it. It finishes in under 200 ms. I added the currency column and the sum rows to the file and checked the quoting with a carrier name that has a comma. Excel opened the file fine with the BOM. I also tried the shipments export for the largest organisation again to see if the faster quote function from before is enough: 300,000 rows still took 52 s and the gateway cut one run. So that problem is open. Jonas knows and has no deadline yet. I noted it for the list of next work.

summary: Accessibility pass on the costs page and the report builder blocks with a screen reader, fixing the chart text alternative, focus order and the drag handle labels.
body:
Priya asked for an accessibility check on the two newest pages. I used VoiceOver and the axe checks in Playwright.

On the costs page the chart had no text alternative. I added an aria-label with a summary of the top three groups, and a visually hidden table with the data below the chart, which is also what the table already shows. The sort buttons in the table headers had no state; I added aria-sort.

In the report builder the drag handles were announced as buttons with no name. They now have labels such as Move block 2 up. The new up and down buttons announce the position after a move, using a live region. The focus went back to the page top after removing a block, so I move it to the next block or the add button.

Axe found two contrast problems in the dark theme: the muted text in the block cards had a ratio of 3.8 to 1, and I raised it to 4.6. The date picker popup lost focus on Escape, which I fixed too.

I added axe checks for both pages into the Playwright suite, so a regression fails CI. The run time rose by about 6 seconds. Priya will look at the result on her laptop tomorrow. Still open is the chart colour pair for red and green on the on-time chart, where colour is the only signal.

summary: Fixed the on-time chart so that late and on-time are also told apart by pattern and label, not only by red and green.
body: This was the open item of the accessibility pass. On the on-time chart, late and on-time deliveries differ only by colour, which fails for people with red-green colour blindness. I changed the colours to a blue and an orange that work in simulation, and added a diagonal pattern to the late series with ECharts decal. The legend shows the pattern too. The tooltip says late or on time in words. I checked with a colour blindness simulator in the browser devtools for three types, and the series were clear in each. The dark theme needed different tones, since the orange was too bright, so I picked a darker one and checked contrast against the background at 4.9 to 1. The bar labels on top of the stack show percent, which also helps. Priya saw the screenshots and agreed. I had to update two visual snapshots in Playwright. One more place uses the same pair, the small status dots in the shipments table, and I gave them an icon shape in addition to colour. Tests pass. I will tell Jonas in the next release note, since managers who print the charts in black and white will see a difference.

summary: Wrote and ran the cleanup of expired refresh token rows and the now-empty deny list, and measured that the tokens table shrank from 2.3 million to 190,000 rows.
body:
The refresh token table had grown with every rotation, since old rows were only marked as used. With 160 active users and rotation at every access token expiry, it reached 2.3 million rows. Queries on the table slowed down, and the auth check for the reuse alarm needed 40 ms on average.

I wrote a cleanup job that deletes rows whose family is expired or revoked and which are older than seven days. I keep seven days so that reuse detection still works for recent tokens and the grace window of ten seconds is far inside it. The job deletes in batches of 5,000 rows and sleeps briefly between batches, to keep locks short.

I first ran it on a restore of production. It took 3 minutes and removed 2.1 million rows. The table size went from 640 MB to 58 MB after a vacuum. Then I ran it on production at a quiet time in the evening. It took 4 minutes and nobody was logged out; I checked the login errors in the log for the hour after, and there were none.

The auth check dropped to 6 ms. I also added an index on family_id that was missing, which was the main reason for the slow lookup. The index was created concurrently.

The job now runs nightly through the same scheduler that sends reports, with the same row lock so two instances cannot run it together. I added a log line with the count of deleted rows, and an alert if the count is zero for three nights, which would mean that the job is broken. The deny list of access tokens gets cleaned in the same job. Remaining: the deny list is still needed for logout, and I wonder how long we will keep this design. Jonas has not asked yet. I wrote two tests for the batch deletion and the seven day rule.

summary: Looked at what happens to scheduled reports when the report grows beyond the 5,000 row cap and added a visible note in the email and a link to the full table.
body:
Since the scheduled reports were released, one manager asked why her table in the email had exactly 5,000 rows and ended without a word. The cap was set for speed, but the email gave no sign that rows were missing. That is a bad surprise for a report that people trust.

I changed the render so that it counts the total rows with a separate count query first. If the total is above the cap, the table block ends with a line: Showing 5,000 of 38,214 rows, with a link to the report page with the same filter applied. The link uses the preset id or the filter in the URL, as the table-v3 URL state does. The report is opened after login, so no data is exposed in the mail.

The count query adds about 80 ms for the largest organisation. I checked that it uses the same filter code as the data query, because two different filter paths would give wrong numbers. They share one function now, and a test compares the count with the length of the unlimited result for a small fixture.

For the chart blocks the cap does not apply, since charts aggregate in the database. I confirmed that by a run with the 38,000 row report, which created the chart in 1.4 s.

I also thought about attaching a CSV for large reports. It would run into the same memory problem as the export of the large tables, so I did not do it. The note and the link are the first step. I sent a test mail to Jonas and he found the note clear. The wording was shortened after Priya's comment. Next I will check how the mail looks on a phone, since many managers read reports there.

summary: Added a per-schedule failure counter so a scheduled report that bounces three times in a row pauses itself instead of mailing a dead address every day.
body:
Following the failure log table from last week, I looked at what happens when a recipient address keeps bouncing. Until now the scheduler tried again at every run and the log only grew.

I added a consecutive_failures column to report_schedules with a migration and a default of 0. The scheduler job increments it when the send step fails and resets it to 0 on a success. At three failures in a row the schedule is set to paused with the reason 'delivery_failed', which reuses the pause flow from two weeks ago.

The owner gets the same pause email as for the other reasons, with the bounced address named in the text. I changed the email template so that the reason line is chosen from a small map, not from an if chain.

Tests: four new Vitest cases for the counter, one for the reset after a success, and one that checks a paused schedule is skipped by the skip locked query. All pass, and the existing scheduler suite is unchanged.

Open question for Jonas: whether three is the right number. For now it is a constant in scheduler/config.ts. A temporary soft bounce from a full mailbox could pause a schedule too early, so I may later separate soft and hard bounces. The take-over button already resumes the schedule and resets the counter.

summary: Settings page session check: found that the access token lifetime shown to users said 30 days, which was stale, and rewrote the text to match the refresh setup.
body:
Priya noticed while reviewing the settings page that the security section still says 'You stay logged in for 30 days'. That was true for the old long-lived tokens but no longer describes what happens.

I checked the real behaviour in the code first. The access token lives 15 minutes, the refresh token slides, and the hard limit is 30 days from the login. So the sentence was partly right by accident, but it hid that being idle ends nothing and that a log out of all devices ends everything at once.

I wrote new text with Priya: 'You stay logged in on this device for up to 30 days. Use Log out of all devices if you lose a laptop or phone.' The button now sits directly under the text instead of in a separate card.

I also changed the Playwright test for the settings page, which matched the old sentence by text. It now looks for the button by role. While there I fixed the card heading level, which jumped from h1 to h3.

Nothing else changed in the API. Jonas will see the text at the next release.

summary: Profiled the 400,000 row shipments export in detail: building the CSV string takes 60 percent of the time and peak memory reaches 1.4 GB, so the export is memory bound, not query bound.
body:
Continuing from the measurements of two weeks ago, I wanted to know why the large export is slow and also why the Render instance sometimes restarts during one. I ran the export locally against a copy of production data with the Node inspector attached.

The query itself, run in psql with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, returns all 400,000 rows in about 6 seconds. The driver then builds an array of row objects, and the export code maps every row to a string and joins them into one big string. That step takes around 38 seconds and the heap peaks at 1.4 GB, with long garbage collection pauses.

Then the response is written in one piece, so the proxy sees no bytes for over a minute. That explains the cut-offs. It also explains why smaller exports are fine: under 50,000 rows the memory stays low.

I tried two cheap improvements: reducing the columns to the ones visible in the table, and using a faster escape function. Together they bring the time from 71 s down to 52 s, which is still too slow and still all in memory.

I did not change the production code yet. I wrote the numbers into the issue for Jonas, and told him that large exports stay slow for now. A real fix has to change how the data goes out, and I will think about that after the reports work is calmer.

summary: Answered Jonas's question whether managers can see scheduled reports of other managers: they cannot, only admins can list all schedules of the organisation.
body:
Jonas asked by message whether a manager can see which scheduled reports the other managers set up. I checked the API and the UI to be sure rather than answer from memory.

The schedules list endpoint filters by owner_id unless the role is admin. A manager therefore sees only their own schedules, and a dispatcher cannot create any. The report page shows the schedule dialog only for the owner or an admin.

I wrote a short answer for him and added that if he wants a shared view, the admin list page could get a read-only mode for managers. I did not build it. He will decide after seeing how many schedules exist in his organisation, which is currently 11.

summary: Built the admin page that lists all scheduled reports with owner, next run, last status and a pause toggle, because support questions about reports needed database queries before.
body:
After the questions from Jonas's team about who gets which report, I built an admin overview. Until now I answered those by running SQL by hand.

The new page is under Settings, Scheduled reports, visible to admins only. It is a table with report name, owner, frequency, next run in the zone of the schedule, last status and the number of recipients. The API endpoint GET /api/admin/schedules uses the same query as the owner list but without the owner filter, and it is paginated by 50.

The next run is calculated on the server with the same function the scheduler uses, so the page cannot disagree with what will happen. That function was exported from scheduler/time.ts for this.

Each row has a pause toggle. Pausing from here sets the reason 'admin' and sends no email to the owner for now; I noted that as a decision to confirm. Resuming resets the failure counter.

I also added filters for status (active, paused, failing) using the table filter component from the shipments table, which needed one small change to accept custom option lists. Tests: API tests for the role check, a component test for the toggle, and a Playwright test that pauses a schedule and checks the badge.

Open: the failing filter counts schedules with at least one failure, not three, and the label should say so. I will fix the wording tomorrow.

summary: Replaced the in-memory report PNG render with a small worker pool of two headless renders, cutting the scheduled report batch at the busy hour from 9 minutes to under 3.
body:
The scheduler runs every five minutes, but at the full hour several schedules fall due at once, and the logs showed the batch needing almost 9 minutes at the busiest hour. The next tick then started while the first was still working. The row lock kept it safe, but the emails arrived late.

I measured first. Rendering one report as a PNG takes about 4 s, mostly the start of the headless page and the ECharts init. The table and the email send are quick. The render was done one report after another in a single process.

I changed the render module to keep a pool of two long-lived render pages. A report takes a free page, loads its blocks, waits for the chart finished event, takes the screenshot and gives the page back. Pages are recycled after 50 renders to stop slow memory growth.

Why two: the Render instance has limited memory. With three pages the process went over 700 MB in my local test, with two it stayed near 480 MB.

Results on a test set of 30 schedules due at the same time: before 8 min 50 s, after 2 min 40 s. Memory peak was acceptable and no render timed out.

I also added a timeout of 45 s per report. A report that exceeds it counts as a failure for the counter and the page is thrown away and recreated, since a hung page could otherwise block the pool.

One bug on the way: the first render after a recycle was blank because the font was not yet loaded. I now wait for document.fonts.ready before the screenshot.

Tests cover the pool with a fake page that hangs. Next step is to watch the real batch times for a few days.

summary: Checked the first real batch with the render pool: the busy hour took 2 min 20 s and no report was late, so the pool size of two stays.
body:
I looked at the scheduler logs for the first real busy hour after the pool change. 24 schedules were due and the batch finished in 2 min 20 s, which matches the local test.

Memory on the Render instance peaked at 520 MB, below the plan limit, and there were no restarts. One render hit the 45 s timeout; it was a report with six blocks and a slow filter preset. The page was recreated as designed and the schedule was retried at the next tick, and sent fine.

That slow preset query is worth a look. It scans the shipments table without using the carrier index, because the preset stores the carrier list as text. I opened a note for it but did not start.

I left the pool at two. No further change today.

summary: Fixed the preset query that scanned all shipments for a carrier list by storing carrier ids instead of names, bringing the slow report preview from 31 s to 1.2 s.
body:
This is the slow preset from the render timeout earlier today. The preset stored its carrier filter as an array of carrier names, and the query compared lower(carrier_name) with the list, which cannot use the index on carrier_id. On the production copy EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan over 3.1 million shipments.

First I tried a functional index on lower(carrier_name). It worked, with the preview at 4 s, but it meant another index on a big table and renaming a carrier would still break old presets silently.

So I chose the cleaner fix: presets now store carrier ids. The migration reads every preset, maps the names to ids through the carriers table, and writes the new array. Names that no longer match any carrier are listed in the migration output instead of being dropped without notice. There were 3 such presets, all from carriers that were merged last year. I mapped them by hand to the merged carrier.

The filter builder in the UI already had the id available in its select component, so the change there was one line: it keeps the id in the value instead of the label. The query builder on the API side now uses carrier_id = ANY($1).

Results on the production copy: the preview of the worst preset went from 31 s to 1.2 s, and the scheduled render of the same report from 33 s to 5 s.

Tests: the migration was run on a copy and then rolled back and forward again. I added Vitest cases for the query builder with ids, and a Playwright test that saves a preset, renames the carrier and checks that the preset still filters.

I dropped the functional index test branch locally. Deployed late in the evening because the migration is quick, about 3 seconds.

summary: Wrote the session review for the managers' SSO accounts: SSO users have no password, so the log out of all devices flow needed a second path that does not ask for one.
body:
Marta from nobody at Acme asked, no: Jonas forwarded a question from one manager who logs in through SSO and could not use Log out of all devices, because the dialog asks to confirm the password.

I checked the code. The confirm step calls POST /api/auth/verify-password, which fails for accounts created through SSO because they have an empty password hash. The button therefore ended in an error toast saying only 'Something went wrong'.

Options I weighed: ask the identity provider again for a fresh login, or skip the confirmation for SSO users. The first is the safer one, because the action is meant for a lost device, but it needs a redirect and a return. The second is simple but lets an open browser do the action unprompted.

I built the first in a light form: for SSO users the dialog says 'Confirm with your company login', starts the SSO flow with prompt=login and a return path, and on return a one-time marker with a 5 minute life allows the action. The marker is stored in the refresh token family row, not in the browser.

I also fixed the error toast so it shows the real reason when the confirmation fails.

Tested with the test identity provider we use for SSO: log in, press the button, get redirected, come back, and all other families are revoked while the current one stays. Also tested that the marker expires after 5 minutes and cannot be used twice.

Open: the password path for normal users is unchanged. I want Jonas to try it with the real manager account before I call this done.

summary: Started the plan for the session list on the settings page: show each active login with device, last use and place, with a revoke button per row, built on the refresh token families.
body:
Jonas wants managers to see where they are logged in, not only to press the all-or-nothing button. This is the plan and the first measurements, no UI yet.

Data: each refresh token family is one login on one device. The table has created_at, last_used_at, the user agent string and the IP at creation. What is missing is a readable device name and a rough place. I do not want to add a paid geo service for this. A small offline lookup of country and city from the IP is enough, and I will check the licence of the free database file before using it.

Device name: the user agent is parsed on the server with a small library into 'Chrome on macOS' or 'Acme driver app on Android'. I tested it on 200 real user agents from the table and 11 came out as 'Unknown', mostly old mobile app builds. That is acceptable, and I will add a rule for the app.

API sketch:
- GET /api/auth/sessions returns the families of the current user, with a flag for the current one
- DELETE /api/auth/sessions/:id revokes one family and adds its current token to the deny list
- the current family cannot be revoked here, since that is the normal logout

I checked the cost. The families query joins with the tokens table to find last use; with the cleaned table of 190,000 rows it runs in 4 ms for a user with many families, so no new index is needed.

Priya will draw the list. I asked for the row to have a clear 'This device' badge and for a confirm-less revoke with an undo notice, though undo is not possible after a revoke, so a confirm dialog is probably better. I told her that.

Next: add the user agent parser, the endpoints and tests, then the UI when Priya's draft is ready.

summary: Built the sessions API: list and revoke per device, with a user agent parser and a rule that names the Acme driver app, tested for ownership so nobody can revoke another user's login.
body:
The plan from this morning is now code on the API side.

I added the parser as a small module, sessions/device.ts, that turns a user agent into a browser and OS label. It has a rule for the driver app, whose user agent starts with AcmeDriver, which brings the unknown share on the 200 samples from 11 down to 3.

GET /api/auth/sessions returns for each family: id, device label, created, last used, a coarse country from the offline lookup and a current flag. The lookup file is loaded once at start and takes 38 MB of memory, which I accepted for now. Private and missing IPs return null and the UI will show nothing for them.

DELETE /api/auth/sessions/:id looks the family up with both id and the user id of the request. A family of another user answers 404, not 403, so that ids cannot be probed. Revoking the current family answers 400 with a message to use the normal logout. For other families, the family is marked revoked and its newest token goes to the deny list in one transaction.

Tests, 14 new ones:
- listing returns only own families
- another user's id gives 404 and changes nothing
- revoked family tokens are rejected at the next refresh
- the current flag is correct with two families
- the parser cases, including the driver app

One thing I noticed: the reuse alarm treats a refresh with a revoked family as theft and logs a warning. Revoking by hand should not look like theft in the logs, so I added a reason field and the alarm only fires for reason 'reuse'.

No UI yet. I am waiting for Priya's sketch, and the endpoints are behind the same auth middleware as the rest.

summary: Built the session list UI on the settings page from Priya's design, with device rows, a This device badge, a confirm dialog for revoke, and empty and error states.
body:
Priya sent the design this morning and I built it in the afternoon. It lives in the security section of the settings page, above the log out of all devices button.

Each row shows an icon for the device type, the device label, the country and the last used time in relative words such as '3 hours ago', with the exact time in a tooltip. The current device has a green 'This device' badge and no revoke button. Other rows have a Revoke button that opens a confirm dialog naming the device.

I used the existing dialog component, so focus is trapped and Escape closes it. After the revoke succeeds, the row is removed from the list with the react-query cache updated directly, not by refetching, and a status message is announced for screen readers, which I checked with VoiceOver given the accessibility pass of last week.

States I handled:
- loading: three skeleton rows
- empty: cannot really happen since the current device is always there, but a safe text exists
- error: an inline message with a retry button
- revoke failure: the dialog stays open with the error text

A difference to the design: Priya drew the last used time in grey on grey, which fails contrast. I used the darker grey of the table secondary text and showed her; she agreed.

The dark theme needed one fix. The badge green was too bright on the dark background, so I took the theme token for success text.

Tests: component tests for the rows and the dialog, and a Playwright test with two browser contexts for the same user. The first revokes the second, and the second gets sent to the login page at its next request. The second context needed a forced refresh in the test since access tokens are valid for up to 15 minutes, which I want to mention to Jonas: a revoked device may keep working for that time.

I did not change that lifetime. It is a known consequence of the short tokens.

summary: Wrote down the 15 minute gap after a per-device revoke and tried a cheap check against the deny list on every request; it adds 1.8 ms and closes the gap.
body:
The Playwright test this afternoon showed the gap clearly: after revoking another device, its access token still works until it expires, up to 15 minutes. For a lost laptop that is not great.

The log out of all devices action already adds the current token to the deny list, but the middleware only checks the list on the refresh endpoint, not on every API call. That was a design choice from when we introduced rotation, to avoid a database read per request.

I measured what a check on every request costs. The deny list is a Postgres table with an index on the token id, and after the cleanup it has few rows. With the check in the middleware, a request to the shipments endpoint went from 41 ms to 42.8 ms on average over 2,000 requests locally, so about 1.8 ms.

I tried it on a branch of the middleware: the access token carries a jti, and the middleware looks it up. A revoked device now gets a 401 on its next call. The test passes without a forced refresh.
