I did not merge it. The cost is small but it moves the system back towards a per-request lookup, and the deny list must then stay in good shape, with cleanup of expired rows running reliably. I want to talk to Jonas about whether the 15 minute gap is acceptable for his managers or not.

For now I left the branch unmerged with a note in the repo's docs folder.

summary: Jonas decided the 15 minute gap is not acceptable for lost devices, so the per-request deny list check was merged and the cleanup job now logs its row counts.
body:
I wrote to Jonas about the gap and the 1.8 ms. His answer was short: a lost phone with access to cost data for 15 minutes is not something he wants to explain to Acme, so the check goes in.

I merged the middleware change. Before that I added two things. The first is a cleanup that removes deny list rows whose token has expired, since they can never matter again; the existing job covers that, and I made it log the number of rows removed. The second is a check in the health endpoint that fails when the deny list has more than 100,000 rows, as an early sign that the cleanup stopped.

I ran the whole Vitest suite and the Playwright suite, both green. The revoke test no longer needs a forced refresh.

Deployed. Watching the response time chart on Render for the rest of the day.

summary: Reviewed the dashboard bundle after the Vite upgrade: the ECharts import was pulling the full library, and switching to the modular import cut the main chunk from 1.9 MB to 1.1 MB.
body:
Since Vite got faster in the dev start, I wanted to look at the production bundle too. I ran the visualizer plugin and the picture was clear: ECharts took more than half of the main chunk.

Cause: three older files used import * as echarts from 'echarts', which brings every chart type, every component and every renderer. The newer charts used the modular form, but the shared chart wrapper did the wildcard import, so everything came along.

The change:
- the wrapper now imports from echarts/core and registers only what the dashboard uses: bar, line, pie, scatter, the grid, tooltip, legend, dataZoom, markLine and the canvas renderer
- the three old files use the wrapper
- I added a small test that renders every chart type of the app once, to catch a missing registration, since ECharts then fails only at runtime with 'Component grid is used but not imported'

That test found two missing registrations at once: the visualMap component for the heat chart on the routes page and the title component in the report builder. I added both.

Numbers from the build output:
- main chunk before 1.9 MB, after 1.1 MB (gzip 610 KB to 340 KB)
- the costs page and the report builder now split into their own chunks through route level lazy loading, 180 KB and 240 KB

On a throttled connection in the browser dev tools, the first load of the login page goes from 7.2 s to 4.1 s. Dispatchers on weaker office connections should notice that.

I checked that the print layout of reports still works, since it uses the SVG renderer in one place. It does, so I registered the SVG renderer too, which costs 30 KB.

One warning remains in the build about a chunk over 500 KB, which is the main one. Splitting the shipments table code is a possible next step but the table-v3 work will change it anyway, so I will wait.

All tests pass and I deployed in the afternoon.

summary: Looked into a bug report that the scheduled report shows yesterday's numbers at 06:00: the render uses the zone of the server for relative dates instead of the zone of the schedule.
body:
A dispatcher manager said the 06:00 morning report 'for today' showed numbers that looked like yesterday's. I reproduced it with the simulated clock from the daylight saving suite.

The report filter 'today' is stored as a relative range. The scheduler converts it to absolute times when rendering, but it used the server's zone, which is UTC, not the zone stored on the schedule, which is Europe/Berlin for this one. At 06:00 Berlin it is 04:00 or 05:00 UTC, which is still the same day in UTC, so 'today' was right by UTC but the shipments of the Berlin night were counted differently, and 'yesterday' ranges were shifted by an hour or two.

In the case reported, the range 'last 24 hours' was fine, but 'today' began at 00:00 UTC, which is 01:00 or 02:00 Berlin, so the first shipments of the day were missing.

Fix: the range resolver takes a zone argument, and the scheduler passes the schedule zone. The preview in the report builder uses the browser zone, so it was right all along, which is why nobody saw the difference there.

I added tests with three zones, including one with a half hour offset, and the two daylight saving days. All previous scheduler tests stayed green.

I also re-rendered the affected report for the manager and sent it by hand with a short note. I will mention the fix to Jonas at the next call.

summary: Planned the new-charts follow-up: a delivery time distribution chart and a carrier comparison chart, with decisions on binning, outliers and what the dispatchers actually asked for.
body:
Jonas collected wishes from the dispatchers in a list, and two of them came up repeatedly: how long deliveries really take, and how carriers compare. This entry is the plan and a first data check, before any chart code.

Delivery time distribution. A histogram of hours from pickup to delivery. I looked at the data: the median is 26 hours, but the tail is long, with 2 percent of shipments over 200 hours, mostly cross-border cases and a few with wrong timestamps. Linear bins would squash everything into the first bar. My plan is bins of 4 hours up to 72, then 24 hour bins, and one last bin for 'over a week'. The binning is done in SQL with width_bucket, not in the browser, to keep the payload small.

Carrier comparison. A box-like chart per carrier, with median, the quartiles and the 90th percentile. ECharts has a boxplot series, but it expects the raw values per category. Sending 3 million values is out of the question, so I will compute percentile_cont per carrier in Postgres and build the box data on the server.

Open decisions for Jonas:
- should cancelled shipments count? I propose no, and a note under the chart
- should the comparison use the same date range as the page filter? yes, I think
- minimum shipments per carrier to appear: I suggest 30, otherwise the box is noise

I tested the percentile query on the production copy for a quarter of data. It takes 2.3 s without an index change, which is acceptable for a page chart but I would like a cache of a few minutes since the same query runs for every viewer.

Priya should get a say on colours. The chart legend rework from earlier fixed the way colours are chosen per series, and the box chart should use one colour per carrier consistently with the other pages.

Order of work: the SQL and endpoints first, with tests for the edge cases (empty range, one shipment, all same value), then the histogram, then the box chart. Branch new-charts is the one to use for it.

summary: Wrote the SQL and endpoint for the delivery time histogram, with width_bucket bins, an overflow bin and tests for empty ranges and null delivery times.
body:
First code step of the new charts plan. The endpoint GET /api/charts/delivery-time takes the date range and optional carrier ids and returns bins as label, from, to and count.

The query uses width_bucket for the 4 hour bins up to 72 hours, a second expression for the 24 hour bins up to a week, and a final bin for the rest. I put the bin edges in one constant so the chart and the tests share them. Cancelled shipments and rows with a null or negative duration are excluded, and the number of excluded wrong timestamps is returned in a separate field so the UI can note it.

On the production copy for a quarter the query takes 0.9 s. Tests cover an empty range, a single shipment, a shipment exactly on an edge, and negative durations. The edge case first landed in the wrong bin, since width_bucket puts the upper bound in the next bucket, and I fixed the expectation after checking the intended meaning of from inclusive, to exclusive.

summary: Built the delivery time histogram chart on the analytics page with ECharts, a median line, a note on excluded shipments and a table alternative for screen readers.
body:
The chart component takes the bins from yesterday's endpoint and draws a bar series. The bars use the primary series colour and the last bin, 'over a week', is drawn with a hatch pattern so it is read as a catch-all and not as a normal bar.

The median is shown as a markLine with a label of 'Median 26 h'. The median value comes from the same endpoint, where I added it with percentile_cont, which costs almost nothing on top of the query.

Under the chart, a small line says how many shipments were left out because of missing or wrong timestamps. Jonas will want to know that number, since 1.1 percent is higher than he might expect.

For accessibility I followed the pattern of the costs page: a text alternative that states the median and the biggest bin, and a visually hidden table with the bins and counts that can be reached with the keyboard.

The tooltip shows the range in words, such as '8 to 12 hours', and the share of all shipments as a percentage. I tested the dark theme and the legend placement on a narrow screen. The labels of the x axis rotate on narrow screens, which is ugly, so I show every second label there.

A Vitest test renders the component with fixture bins, and one Playwright screenshot test was added with the existing tolerance settings.

summary: Added the percentile query and endpoint for the carrier comparison box chart, with a 30 shipment minimum and a five minute server cache.
body:
This is the server part of the second new chart. GET /api/charts/carrier-comparison returns, for each carrier with at least 30 delivered shipments in the range: the minimum, the first quartile, the median, the third quartile, the 90th percentile and the count.

I used percentile_cont with a within group clause and grouped by carrier_id. Whiskers are the 10th and 90th percentile, not the min and max, so a single wrong timestamp does not stretch a box over the whole axis. That was the decision from the plan and I wrote it in the response description.

The cache is a small in-process map keyed by the range and the carrier filter, with a five minute life. With two API instances each has its own cache, which is fine for this. A test checks that a second call within the time does not run the query, using a spy on the database layer.

On a quarter of production data the first call takes 2.1 s and the cached one 3 ms. I checked the number of carriers: 19 appear and 7 are hidden because of the minimum, which the response lists in an 'omitted' field so the UI can say so.

Tests also cover a carrier with exactly 30 shipments and one with 29.

summary: Built the carrier comparison box chart, fixed a sort order that changed with every filter, and agreed with Jonas that cancelled shipments are left out with a note.
body:
The box chart uses the ECharts boxplot series with data from the endpoint of this morning. Each carrier gets its consistent colour from the shared palette function, so a carrier looks the same here as on the costs page.

The first version sorted carriers by the median, which made the chart jump around when the filter changed, because a small change in the range reorders the boxes. Dispatchers compare the same carriers repeatedly, so I changed it to alphabetical by default and added a switch to sort by median.

Jonas answered the open questions from the plan: cancelled shipments stay out, with a note under the chart, the chart follows the page date range, and 30 is a fine minimum. I added the note, and a second note that lists the omitted carriers by count, such as '7 carriers with fewer than 30 shipments are not shown'. The names are available in a tooltip on that note.

On narrow screens the carrier names were cut, so the chart switches to horizontal boxes below a certain width. That needed the axis types swapped, and I wrote a helper for it rather than duplicating options.

Accessibility again: the text alternative names the carrier with the lowest and the highest median, and the hidden table has all values. I read it with VoiceOver and the order was right.

One bug: with a single carrier selected, the box was drawn with zero height when all values were equal in a test fixture. I made the minimum visible height two pixels.

Tests pass. I asked Priya for a visual review, and I will merge the branch when she has looked.

summary: Handled Priya's review of the new charts and a performance problem in the box chart on slow laptops, then merged the delivery time and carrier comparison charts to main.
body:
Priya reviewed both charts in the morning and sent six points. Four were small: the median label overlapped the tallest bar, the box colours were too close for two carriers in the dark theme, the axis titles were missing units, and the tooltip text used a different tone than other pages. I fixed them one by one.

The fifth point was that the histogram bars should not touch, which I did with a barGap and a category gap of 12 percent. The sixth was the empty state: a range with no shipments showed an empty frame. It now shows a short message and a hint to widen the date range.

On the dark theme I changed two carrier colours in the palette, checking the contrast between neighbouring boxes with a script that compares all pairs and reports those under a ratio of 1.5. Three pairs were under it before, and none afterwards. Because the palette is shared, the change also reaches the costs page, where I checked the legend and found it fine.

Then the performance problem. A dispatcher with an older laptop said the analytics page froze for about a second when the date range changed. I profiled with CPU throttling at 4x. Both charts re-initialised ECharts on every data update, because the component created a new options object and used notMerge. Resizes also fired the observer several times.

Fixes:
- keep the chart instance, call setOption with the new data only
- debounce the resize observer to 100 ms
- skip the animation on the first draw when the data is large

The freeze dropped from about 1000 ms to 180 ms in the throttled test.

I ran the complete test suites, which passed, rebased the new-charts branch on main since the bundle change had touched the chart wrapper, resolved one conflict in the registration list, and merged. The two new charts are deployed behind no flag, since they only add things to the analytics page.

Next: Jonas wants to see real use for a week before deciding on more charts. The branch can be deleted.

summary: Cleaned up after the charts merge: deleted the branch, added the two endpoints to the API docs, and noted that the carrier comparison cache is per instance.
body:
Small housekeeping after the merge of the new charts.

I deleted the new-charts branch locally and on the remote, and checked that no open pull request still pointed at it. The API docs in the repo now describe the two endpoints, with parameters, the response fields and the omitted carriers field, plus an example for each.

I also wrote a short note in the docs about the cache of the carrier comparison: it is in memory per instance with five minutes of life, so two instances can show slightly different numbers for a short time after new shipments come in. If that becomes an issue, the cache can move to Postgres or a shared store.

The release notes for Jonas list the two charts, the faster first load, and the fix for the freeze on older laptops.

summary: Planned the table-v3 rewrite of the shipments table: virtualized rows, server-side sort and filter, and column state kept in the URL, before touching any code.
body:
The old shipments table renders every loaded row into the DOM and gets sluggish above about 5,000 rows. I wrote a plan for table-v3 that replaces it with a virtualized body, so only the visible rows exist in the DOM. Sorting and filtering move to the server, because sorting 400,000 rows in the browser is not an option.

The plan lists what has to survive: the saved filters, the column picker, the CSV export button and the keyboard navigation that Priya asked for last time. Column order, widths and sort are stored in the URL query string so that a dispatcher can send a link to a colleague. I looked at two virtualization libraries and picked TanStack Virtual because it does not force its own markup, which keeps the accessibility roles under our control.

Open questions are noted for Jonas: whether dispatchers need row selection across pages, and whether the export should respect the current sort. No code yet; the branch table-v3 is created from main and only holds the plan file. Next step is the paged endpoint with a cursor.

summary: Built the cursor-paged shipments endpoint for table-v3 with server-side sort on five columns, and found that sorting by delivery time needed a composite index to stay under 100 ms.
body:
The new endpoint is GET /api/shipments/page. It takes a cursor, a page size of up to 200, a sort column and direction, and the same filter parameters as the old list. The cursor encodes the sort value plus the shipment id as tie breaker, so paging stays stable when many rows share a value.

Sorting is allowed on five columns: created time, delivery time, carrier, status and cost. The column name is checked against a fixed map and never put into the SQL directly. I wrote the query builder in server/shipments/page.ts with the keyset condition built per direction.

On the staging copy with 400,000 shipments the first page sorted by created time took 12 ms. Sorting by delivery time took 340 ms, because Postgres sorted the whole filtered set. EXPLAIN showed a sequential scan with a sort node. I added an index on (org_id, delivery_minutes, id) and the time fell to 9 ms.

Carrier and status sorts were fine already because of the existing indexes. Cost sort needed an index too, so I added (org_id, cost_cents, id). Each new index costs a little on insert; the shipments import writes about 2,000 rows per run, and I measured no visible change.

Tests cover the first page, the last page, an empty result, a tie on the sort value and a descending sort with nulls. Nulls sort last in both directions, which I wrote into the API docs. The old endpoint stays until the new table replaces it. Next is the virtualized body in the front end.

summary: Wired the virtualized table body to the paged endpoint; scrolling 400,000 rows now stays smooth, but the scrollbar height lies because the total is only an estimate.
body:
I built the new table body with TanStack Virtual and a fetch hook that loads pages as the user scrolls near the end of what is loaded. Rows are 40 pixels high, and about 25 DOM rows exist at any time. Memory in the browser stays flat at around 90 MB while scrolling, where the old table passed 600 MB at 100,000 rows.

The scrollbar is a problem. The cursor approach does not give an exact total cheaply, and a count query on the filtered set takes 200 to 400 ms. I used the planner estimate for the scrollbar and replace it with the exact count when the count query returns, which makes the thumb jump once. Priya may not like that; I will show her.

Sticky header and column resizing work. Keyboard navigation does not yet: arrow keys move the focus out of the rendered window and the focused row is unmounted. I noted that the focused row index has to be kept and the row scrolled into view before moving focus.

Filtering resets the cursor and scrolls to the top, which was the expected behavior. One bug found late in the evening: switching the sort fast fired two requests and the older answer sometimes arrived last and replaced the newer one. I added an abort controller per query key and the problem went away in a manual test of 50 quick switches. A Playwright test for it is still to be written.

summary: Fixed keyboard navigation in the virtual table so focus follows the row index, and wrote Playwright tests for sort race, arrow keys and Home/End.
body:
The focus problem came from keeping focus on a DOM node that virtualization removes. The table now keeps the active row index in state, and the container has role grid with aria-activedescendant pointing at the row id. Arrow up and down change the index and scroll the row into view if needed.

Home and End jump to the first and last loaded row. Page up and down move by the visible count. Ctrl+End would need the last page, which we may not have loaded, so it loads the last page by cursor from the reverse sort and then moves the index. That works but takes one extra request.

Playwright tests added:
- fast sort switching ends on the newest query result
- arrow keys after scrolling 500 rows keep the active row visible
- Home and End behave as described
- a filter change resets the active row

All four pass in Chromium and in Firefox. I tried a screen reader pass with VoiceOver and it reads row number and column header, but announces the full row twice on every move. That is probably the activedescendant combined with a live region I left in; I will remove the live region next time and check again.

summary: Removed the duplicate screen reader announcement in the new table and replaced the jumping scrollbar with a stable estimate, which Priya approved after trying it.
body:
The double announcement came from the live region that announced the sort state on every render. I limited it to changes of the sort or filter and the row announcements are now said once in VoiceOver. I also checked with NVDA on the Windows laptop of the agency test device, and it reads the same.

For the scrollbar I showed Priya two options. One keeps the thumb jump when the exact count arrives, the other hides the thumb size claim by showing a text like 400,000 shipments next to the table and using a fixed estimate. She preferred a stable thumb with the count shown in the table footer. So the scroll height is now computed from the first count we get, and later counts only change it when the difference is above 5 percent.

The footer shows the filtered count and the number of loaded rows. While the count query runs it shows a small skeleton instead of a number.

I also fixed the column resize handle, which had no label for assistive tech; it is a separator with an aria-label of the column name now. The remaining items for table-v3 are saved filters, the column picker and the export button. I made a list in the branch notes and ordered them by risk: saved filters first, since they touch the URL state.

summary: Ported saved filters to the new table, which exposed that the old format stored column names that table-v3 renamed, so I wrote a migration with a fallback for unknown keys.
body:
Saved filters are stored per user as JSON in the saved_filters table. The old table wrote keys like carrierName and statusText. In table-v3 the filter model uses carrierId and status codes, which is also what the paged endpoint expects. Loading an old saved filter therefore gave an empty result with no error.

I wrote a migration, db/migrations/0147_saved_filters_v3.sql, that rewrites the keys. Carrier names are mapped to ids by a join on the carriers table. Some names no longer matched, because carriers had been renamed. Of 312 saved filters in production, 296 mapped cleanly, 11 had a carrier name that no longer existed and 5 had a status text we no longer use.

For those 16 I did not drop the filter. The migration keeps the mappable parts and writes the unmappable part into an ignored_keys field. The UI shows a small banner reading that part of this saved filter could not be applied, with the list of what was dropped. That seemed better than silently showing a different result.

I ran the migration on a staging copy and compared counts for ten filters before and after; the row counts were the same except for the filters with dropped parts. I also added a unit test for the mapping function with renamed carriers.

The filter bar of the new table uses the same component as before, so the front end change was small: the model type and the serialization into the URL. One detail: the URL now holds the filter as a compact encoded string, which can get long. With 12 filter conditions the URL was about 900 characters, which is still fine for browsers and for Render's proxy.

Next is the column picker, then the export button, then a pass with Jonas on real dispatcher workflows.

summary: Built the column picker and per-user column state for table-v3, and found that hiding a column that is also the sort column left the table sorted by something invisible.
body:
The column picker is a popover with a checkbox list and drag handles for order, which reuses the sortable list from the report builder. The state is stored in the URL, and also saved per user in the preferences table so that a new tab starts with the last used setup. The URL wins when both exist.

A bug appeared in testing: if the user hides the column that the table is sorted by, the sort stays active and the rows look randomly ordered. Options were to block hiding, to reset the sort, or to keep the sort and show it. I chose to keep the sort and show a chip above the table that says sorted by delivery time (hidden) with a button to clear it. That does not change the data under the user's hands.

Other details:
- at least three columns have to stay visible, because an empty table is useless
- the id column cannot be hidden, since the row actions need it
- reset to default is one button
- the picker is keyboard operable and the order can be changed with Alt plus arrows, which I tested with a screen reader

I wrote tests for hiding the sort column and for the URL versus preference priority. A third test checks that a stale preference with a column that no longer exists is ignored rather than throwing, which happened once in my manual test after renaming a column key.

The branch now has paging, virtual rows, sort, filters and columns. The export button is the last big piece. The current export calls the old endpoint and would ignore the new sort, so I need to look at that carefully, and the large export is still slow, which I will not try to fix here.

summary: Connected the export button in table-v3 to the existing CSV endpoint with the current filters and sort, and left the slow large export as it is.
body:
The button in the new table passes the filter model and the sort to the existing export endpoint, so the file matches what the user sees. Before, the export took only filters; I added the sort parameter and checked that the order of rows in the file follows it. For up to about 20,000 rows it finishes in a few seconds.

For 400,000 rows it still builds the file in memory and takes well over a minute, and on staging it hit the proxy timeout once. I did not touch that, since it belongs to a separate piece of work. The button now shows a hint above 100,000 rows that the export may take a while. A test checks that sort and filters reach the endpoint.

summary: Reviewed the whole table-v3 branch against the old table with Jonas's dispatcher checklist and found five gaps, of which the row selection across pages was the biggest.
body:
Jonas sent a checklist of what dispatchers do in the table every day, and I went through it on the branch with the staging data. Of 14 items, nine worked the same or better, and five had gaps.

The gaps:
1. Row selection across pages: the old table selected loaded rows only, but dispatchers use select all and then bulk assign a carrier. With virtual paging, select all means all rows of the filter, not just the loaded ones.
2. The status colors were slightly different from the old table, since I used the new design tokens.
3. Copying a cell value with Ctrl+C did nothing, because the cells are not selectable text in the grid.
4. The footer count flickered when filters changed quickly.
5. Print view printed only the visible 25 rows.

I fixed 2 and 4 on the spot. The color difference was just a token mapping, and the flicker came from showing the skeleton for every count request; it now appears only if the count takes more than 300 ms.

For selection I wrote a design. The selection state holds either a set of ids or a mode of all matching with a set of excluded ids. Bulk actions send the filter plus the excluded ids to the server, which resolves them. This avoids sending 400,000 ids. The bulk assign endpoint needs a change to accept the filter form, and I checked that it has a cap and a confirmation: the dialog shows the number of affected shipments, and above 1,000 it asks the user to type the number.

For 3, I made the focused cell copyable with Ctrl+C by writing to the clipboard from the key handler. For 5, print is harder. I proposed to Jonas that the print button prints up to 500 rows of the current sort with a note, since nobody prints 400,000 rows. He agreed in a short reply and said that dispatchers print about 50 rows at most.

So the remaining work is the selection model, the bulk endpoint change and the print limit. I estimated two sessions for it.

summary: Implemented the select-all-matching model for table-v3 with an excluded-ids set, and extended the bulk assign endpoint to take a filter instead of a list of ids.
body:
The selection state is now a small reducer with two modes. In ids mode it holds the selected ids. In all mode it holds the filter snapshot and the excluded ids. Clicking the header checkbox selects the loaded rows; a banner then offers to select all 400,000 matching shipments, like mail clients do.

The bulk assign endpoint accepts either ids or a filter plus excluded ids. On the server I resolve the filter with the same query builder that the page endpoint uses, so the two cannot drift apart. The update runs in one statement with a limit check: more than 5,000 rows needs a confirm flag set by the dialog.

Tests:
- ids mode behaves like before
- all mode with three exclusions updates the right count
- a filter that matches nothing returns zero without error
- another organisation's shipments are never touched, checked with two orgs in the fixture

The last test matters most, because the filter form is a new way into the data. The query always adds org_id from the session, never from the request body.

One edge case: if shipments change between the dialog and the confirm, the count shown can differ from the count updated. The response now returns the real count, and the toast reports it. That was acceptable to me for this use.

summary: Added the print limit and a final pass on the table-v3 branch, then ran the full Playwright suite against it: 63 pass, two flaky tests traced to a missing wait for the count.
body:
The print button now prints up to 500 rows in the current sort, with a line at the top that says how many rows exist in total and that only the first 500 are shown. I used a print stylesheet that hides the toolbar and the selection column. A manual print to PDF of a 500 row page took under a second.

Then I ran the whole Playwright suite on the branch. 63 tests passed and two failed. Both failures were in the filter tests and both were about the footer count: they asserted the number right after applying the filter, before the count request returned. In the earlier skeleton version the number was there at once, so the tests had worked by luck. I changed them to wait for the count element to have a numeric text, using the web-first assertion instead of a fixed pause.

I ran the suite three times in a row after that and it was green each time. The unit tests also pass, 412 in total.

A list of what is left before merging: an accessibility check by Priya, a test on the slow laptop, and a decision on when to remove the old table code. I suggested removing the old table one release after the merge, so there is a way back. Jonas wants to try the branch on staging for a week with two dispatchers first, so I deployed the branch to the staging service and sent him the link.

summary: Two dispatchers' staging feedback on table-v3 showed the date column sorted as text for rows imported from the old CSV loader, which I fixed with a data cleanup and a stricter column type.
body:
Jonas passed on feedback from the two dispatchers. One of them noticed that sorting by delivery date put some rows in a strange order: dates like 9.3. came after 31.1. The paged endpoint was sorting correctly, so I looked at the data. About 1,900 older rows had delivery_date stored in a text column variant that came from an early CSV loader, while the newer rows used a proper timestamp column. The query coalesced the two.

The coalesce expression broke the index use and also sorted text for the old rows. I wrote a one-time cleanup that parsed the text values into the timestamp column. Of 1,912 rows, 1,897 parsed with the expected day-month-year format, and 15 had values like n/a or empty. Those I left as null and wrote their ids to a file for Jonas to check against his records.

After the cleanup I removed the text column from the query and added a not-null-free check constraint that forbids the old column from being written again. The migration is db/migrations/0151_drop_text_delivery_date.sql; I kept the old column for now and will drop it after a few weeks, in case Jonas finds a record that needs it.

The sort by delivery date now takes 8 ms again, from 60 ms with the coalesce. The other feedback was small: one dispatcher wanted the footer count to stay when scrolling, which it already does, so I think the footer was covered by the browser bar on a small laptop. I added bottom padding on that screen size.

summary: Looked at why some managers were logged out right after opening the new table in two tabs and found the refresh race is back for the new page's parallel requests.
body:
A manager reported being logged out when opening the table in a second tab. In the logs I saw two refresh calls within 30 ms from different tabs, and the second one used a refresh token that the first had just rotated, which the reuse alarm treated as theft.

The tabs coordinate through a lock in the browser, but the new table's count and page requests started before the lock check on first load, since they ran from a hook that mounted early. I moved the token check into the shared fetch wrapper so every request waits for the same refresh promise. A Playwright test with two pages sharing a context now passes.

I also widened the server's grace window for a just-rotated token from 2 to 10 seconds, which Jonas had agreed to earlier for such cases. The reuse alarm still fires after that. The lock fix is the real cure; the grace window only protects against slow networks.

summary: Priya's accessibility review of table-v3 found three issues: low contrast on the hidden-sort chip, a missing caption, and focus lost after the bulk dialog closed.
body:
Priya went through the staging table with a keyboard and a screen reader and sent a short list. The chip that says sorted by a hidden column used a grey on light grey that measured 3.1 to 1, below the 4.5 needed, so I darkened the text token and now it measures 7.2.

The grid had no accessible name. I added a caption that reads shipments table with the filtered count, and tied it to the grid with aria-labelledby.

The third issue was real: after the bulk assign dialog closed, focus went to the body, so a keyboard user had to tab from the top of the page through the whole toolbar. The dialog now returns focus to the bulk actions button, which is the element that opened it. I wrote a Playwright check for that. Priya will review again after these fixes.

summary: Tested table-v3 on the slow laptop with six times CPU throttling and found the cell renderer re-creating formatters on every row, which I memoized to bring scroll frames from 28 ms to 11 ms.
body:
I used the browser profiler with the CPU throttled six times to imitate the old dispatcher laptops. Scrolling showed frames of around 28 ms, with a lot of time in Intl.NumberFormat and Intl.DateTimeFormat constructors. Each cell created its own formatter on render.

I moved the formatters into module-level caches keyed by locale and currency, so they are created once. Row components are wrapped in memo with a comparison on the row id and the visible column keys, which stopped re-renders of unchanged rows while a new page loaded.

After that the throttled frames were about 11 ms during fast scrolling and the long task warnings disappeared. Without throttling the numbers were 4 ms.

I also checked memory after scrolling through 400,000 rows: it stayed at 95 MB, because loaded pages beyond 40 are dropped from the cache and refetched when the user scrolls back. That is a decision worth noting: scrolling back far causes a short skeleton, which I accepted.

summary: Merged table-v3 into main after a week on staging with two dispatchers, with the old table kept behind a flag for one release and a short rollback note.
body:
Jonas reported that the two dispatchers had used the staging table for a week without a blocker. The remaining requests were small and already fixed. Priya confirmed her accessibility items after the fixes.

Before merging I rebased the branch on main, which had moved by 14 commits. There was one conflict, in the filter bar component, where main had a label change and the branch had the new filter model. I resolved it by keeping the branch logic and the new label. After the rebase the unit tests passed, 418 of them, and the Playwright suite was green.

The merge brought:
- the paged endpoint with the new indexes
- the virtualized table with keyboard navigation
- migrated saved filters
- column picker and state in the URL
- select all matching with the bulk endpoint
- print limit of 500 rows

The old table is still in the code behind a flag called legacy_table, which is off by default but can be turned on per organisation in the admin page. Plan: remove it after one release if nobody uses the flag.

The migrations ran on production during the deploy in about 20 seconds, the index creation being the slowest part, since I created the indexes concurrently. I watched the error rate for an hour and it stayed at the usual level. Response time of the table page endpoint in production was 15 ms median.

A rollback note is in the docs: turn on the flag, and the old endpoint still works, since I did not remove it. The indexes can stay either way.

One follow-up remains: the large CSV export is still slow and builds in memory. It stays on the list.

summary: Deleted the table-v3 branch, wrote the user-facing notes of the new table for Jonas, and recorded that the legacy_table flag has not been used by any organisation.
body:
After a day on production with no problems I deleted the table-v3 branch locally and on the remote. The merge commit is the reference if someone needs the history.

I wrote a short note for Jonas to forward to the dispatchers: what changed, the select all banner, the hidden sort chip and the print limit. I kept it to one page, with two screenshots from Priya's design.

I queried the flag table and no organisation has legacy_table on. I added a reminder to remove the old table component and endpoint after the next release. The API docs now describe the paged endpoint and mark the old list endpoint as deprecated.

summary: Dispatchers asked for a way to pin a few columns on the left in the new table, and I weighed sticky columns against the virtual grid, built a first version and measured it.
body:
Jonas passed on a request from the dispatchers who work on wide tables: they lose the shipment number and carrier when they scroll to the cost columns. They want to pin columns on the left.

With a virtualized grid, sticky columns are doable with CSS position sticky on the cells, as long as every row uses the same grid template. Our rows already do. The difficulty is the left offset: each pinned cell needs the sum of the widths of the pinned columns before it. I compute these offsets once per column state and set them as CSS variables on the table container, not per cell.

The column picker got a pin toggle per column, with a limit of three pinned columns. More than three would leave too little room on a laptop, since the pinned width could exceed the viewport. The limit also applies if the window is narrow: if pinned columns take more than 60 percent of the width, the pin is ignored and a note appears.

I had to deal with these details:
- the header cells need a higher z-index than the body cells and sticky both ways
- the pinned columns get a shadow on their right edge only when the table is scrolled, which I detect by the scroll position
- the keyboard focus ring must not be hidden by the sticky cell next to it, so scroll padding is set to the pinned width
- the pin state is stored in the URL and in the preferences like the other column state

I measured frame times with the throttling again: 12 ms during fast scroll, only one ms more than without pinning, so the CSS approach costs almost nothing.

One bug I did not fix yet: when a pinned column is resized, the offsets of the next pinned column lag by one frame. It is visible as a small flicker. A test and a fix come next, probably by updating the variables in the same event handler as the width.

I also asked Jonas whether pinning should be saved per user or per saved filter; he said per user is enough.

summary: Fixed the one-frame lag of pinned column offsets by setting the CSS variables in the resize handler itself, and added tests for pin limits and the narrow window rule.
body:
The flicker came from computing offsets in an effect after the width state changed, so the browser painted once with old offsets. I moved the calculation into the resize pointer handler and write the CSS variables directly on the container before React renders, then let the state catch up. The flicker is gone in a screen recording at 60 frames per second that I stepped through frame by frame.

Tests added:
- pinning a fourth column is refused with a message
- unpinning restores the original column order
- with a 700 pixel window and three pinned columns, the pin is ignored and the note appears
- the pinned state survives a reload through the URL

The narrow window test needed a viewport resize in Playwright, and the note has role status so that it is announced.

I also checked the dark theme: the shadow on the pinned edge was too faint on dark backgrounds, so I used a separate token with a lighter shadow color there.

Priya looked at the screenshots and wanted the pin icon to be filled when active instead of just colored, so that it does not rely on color alone. I changed that. Remaining: update the docs and tell Jonas it is ready for the dispatchers to try.

summary: Removed the legacy table component and the old shipments list endpoint after confirming that no organisation used the flag and no request hit the old route in the logs.
body:
The reminder from the merge said to remove the old table one release later. I checked two things first: the legacy_table flag was off for every organisation, and the access logs of the past two weeks showed no request to the old list route except from my own tests.

The mobile app agency uses the API too, so I checked with them in the shared channel whether the app used the old list endpoint. They answered that the driver app uses its own endpoint for the driver's shipments, not the dashboard list, so it was safe.

I deleted the old table component, its styles, the flag and its admin toggle, the old endpoint and its tests. The diff removed about 1,800 lines and added 40. Bundle size of the main chunk went down by 38 KB.

The saved filter migration code stays, since it is a record of how the data was moved. I ran the test suite and the Playwright suite, both green, and deployed. I watched the logs for an hour and saw no 404 on the removed route.

summary: Deleted a stale test fixture directory, tightened the table cell tests, and found that a removed legacy route was still linked from the help page, which now points to the new table.
body:
After the legacy table removal, I did a cleanup pass on what it had left behind. The first step was a search through the repository for imports of the old component names, and it found nothing in the source. It did find a fixtures directory with 14 JSON files that only the deleted tests had used, so I removed it. That cut the test folder by about 2 MB and made the Vitest run a little quicker.

The second find was in the help page. One of the help texts still linked to the old shipments list route with an anchor for the old column menu. The link returned a 404 inside the app, so a dispatcher who clicked it would have seen a blank page. I rewrote the text to describe the column picker and the pinned columns of the new table, and I pointed the link to the settings section where the column state is stored.

Third, I tightened the cell tests of the new table. Two of them waited a fixed 200 ms for the formatter, which is exactly the kind of wait that made the earlier Playwright runs flaky. I replaced both with a wait for the rendered text and ran the suite five times in a row. All five runs passed without a single retry.

I also checked the server logs for the old route again and saw no requests at all in the last week. Nothing else refers to it, so the removal is complete. What is left is a short note for Jonas that the help page changed, since he proofreads the texts the dispatchers see. I will send that tomorrow together with the onboarding questions.

summary: Planned the onboarding rework for new Acme users after Jonas showed that a third of invited users never finish their first login, and wrote down steps, metrics and open questions.
body:
Jonas shared numbers from the invite emails of the last quarter: about a third of invited users never completed the first login. He asked whether the dashboard could do more to guide new users. This entry is the plan, with no code yet.

I first looked at what we know. The invite link goes to a page where the user sets a password, then lands on the login page and has to type the same email and password again. For managers with SSO the path is different and works well, so the problem concerns dispatchers and drivers' office staff. In the logs, 41 percent of the expired-invite cases came from links opened after the seven day expiry, and the rest dropped at the set password step.

Proposed steps:
1. Log the user in directly after they set the password, so they do not see the login page again.
2. Let an expired invite request a new one by itself, with a rate limit, instead of asking an admin.
3. Show a short first-run guide of three steps: filters, the table and the report builder, with a skip button.
4. Send one reminder email after three days to invites that are still open.

I wrote down how the first step could work with the current login: the set password endpoint would issue the same kind of token the login endpoint issues, with the same expiry and the same storage on the client, so the new user is signed in like after a normal login. I checked that the invite token is single use and invalidated in the same transaction, so a reused link cannot create a second login.

For measuring I proposed an events table with invite sent, link opened, password set and first page seen, so that we can compare before and after. Jonas should decide whether storing these events is fine for the client; I think so, as they contain no personal data beyond the user id.

Open questions: should the guide be shown again on demand, and should admins be able to customize the reminder text? I asked Priya for a design of the guide and the expired invite page. The work goes on the onboarding branch, which I created from main with this plan as the first commit.

summary: Wrote the onboarding rework's first step: an invite email landing page that explains the login and sets the password in one screen, replacing the bare form.
body:
Jonas showed yesterday that a third of invited users never finish their first login, so I started the onboarding branch with the first thing they see. The old invite link opened the plain login form, and users who had no password yet did not know what to do. The new landing page greets the user by organisation name, shows who invited them, and asks for a password in the same screen.

I added a route /invite/:token in the React app and an endpoint GET /api/invites/:token that returns the organisation name, the inviter's name and the email, or 404 for an unknown token. A used or expired token returns 410, and the page shows a short message with a link to ask for a new invite. Before this the page just showed a generic error.

The password form has a strength hint, a show-password toggle and an inline error for the two rules we have: ten characters minimum and not the email itself. Submitting calls the existing accept-invite endpoint, which I left unchanged. After success the user is logged in and sent to the dashboard rather than to the login form, which removes one step where people dropped out.

I wrote Vitest tests for the page states: loading, valid, expired, used, and server error. A Playwright test walks through an invite from the email link to the first dashboard view using the seeded test mailbox. Both pass locally.

One open point is the email text itself, which still says 'activate your account' and does not match the page. I left it for the next entry since Priya wants to review the wording. I also noted that the invite token lives 7 days, and Jonas should confirm whether that is right for Acme, because some invites are sent before a new dispatcher starts.

summary: Rewrote the invite email with Priya's wording draft and added a plain-text part, after finding the old email was HTML only and landed in spam for one Acme domain.
body:
The invite email was the next piece of the onboarding work. The old one said 'activate your account', had a small grey button and no plain-text version. Jonas had mentioned that two invited managers never saw it, so I checked the headers of a test send and found that the HTML-only mail scored badly with the spam filter of one Acme mail domain.

I rewrote the template with Priya's draft text: who invited you, what the dashboard is for, one big button, and the link as plain text below it. I added a plain-text part generated from the same template, so both stay in step. The subject now names the inviter instead of the product.

I sent test mails to three mailboxes, including a mailbox at the Acme domain Jonas gave me. All arrived in the inbox. The button renders correctly in the two clients I could check, but I could not test the oldest desktop client Acme uses.

I also added a line saying the link is valid for 7 days and who to ask for a new one. The template test now checks that both parts contain the link.

Left for later: a reminder email for invites that were not opened after three days. I wrote it down as a step in the onboarding plan and did not start it.

summary: Added a first-login checklist to the dashboard with three steps, stored per user, and found that the invite flow created users without a settings row, which broke the checklist.
body:
After the invite page and the email, I built the part new users see after their first login: a small checklist card with three steps, 'pick your depot', 'save a filter' and 'open a report'. Each step is marked done by the app when the user does the thing, so nobody has to tick boxes.

The state lives in a new table onboarding_progress with user_id, step and done_at. A GET /api/onboarding returns the steps and a PUT marks one done. I kept it small on purpose, because the plan has open questions about what else belongs there.

While testing with a freshly invited user the card crashed. The cause was that users created through the invite flow had no row in user_settings, which the depot step reads for the default depot. Users created by hand in the seed had one, so I had not seen it before. I fixed it in two places: the accept-invite endpoint now creates the settings row, and a migration adds missing rows for existing users.

The migration touched 41 users. I checked that none of them had a default depot set by mistake.

The card has a dismiss button, and a dismissed card stays gone. I wrote tests for the endpoint, for the dismiss case and for the invite path. The card has not been shown to Priya yet.

Next steps are the copy and the look of the card, then a metric so that we can tell whether the completion rate of the first login really improves.

summary: Added event logging for the onboarding funnel: invite sent, opened, password set, first dashboard view, so the third-never-finish number can be measured again after the rework.
body:
Jonas's number of one third came from a manual query, and I wanted the funnel to be measurable without that. I added a small onboarding_events table with user_id, event and created_at, and wrote events at four points: invite sent, invite page opened, password set, first dashboard view.

The page-opened event is written by the GET endpoint for the invite, so it counts reloads. I deduplicated by token in the query rather than in the write, which keeps the write path simple.

I wrote one SQL view that gives the counts per step for the last 30 days, and ran it on the existing data. It only has the data from now on, so the baseline still has to come from Jonas's old query. I saved that query in the repo next to the view.

No user-facing change. Tests cover the event writes.

summary: Fixed the checklist card copy after Priya's feedback and made the card collapse after all three steps are done instead of staying as a row of green ticks.
body:
Priya went through the checklist card and found the wording too technical: 'save a filter' became 'save your first view of the shipments'. I changed all three labels and added a one-line hint under each.

She also pointed out that a card full of ticks that never goes away looks like clutter. When all steps are done the card now collapses to a single line, 'You are all set', and disappears on the next visit.

I updated the component tests for the collapsed state. The spacing was adjusted to her sizes from the design file. The dark theme needed one colour fix for the tick icon, which was nearly invisible on the dark background.

Nothing else changed. The reminder email is still open.

summary: Built the reminder email for invites unopened after three days, with a daily job, a cap of one reminder per invite, and a fix for a time zone slip in the due query.
body:
This was the reminder step of the onboarding plan. Invites that nobody opened for three days get one reminder, and no more than one. The job runs once a day at 08:00 server time, finds the due invites and sends the mail.

I added a reminded_at column to invites so that the cap is enforced in the data and not by the job's memory. The due query selects invites with no opened_at, no reminded_at, a creation older than three days and a token that is not expired yet. An invite that would expire within a day is still reminded, because that is when the reminder matters most.

The first test run found a bug: invites created late in the evening were reminded a day early. The query compared a date cast in the session time zone with a timestamp stored in UTC. I changed it to compare timestamps with an interval and added a test that freezes the clock at 23:30.

The reminder text is short, names the inviter again and repeats the link. I reused the template layout from the invite mail, with the plain-text part.

I ran the job against a copy of the staging data in dry-run mode. It found 9 invites, which matched a count by hand. The job logs the ids it would send to.

The job is registered in the scheduler on Render but disabled by a flag until Jonas has read the text. I wrote that in the notes.

summary: Looked into why invited managers with SSO got stuck on the new invite page, and found the page offered a password form to users whose organisation requires SSO.
body:
Jonas passed on a report from one manager at Acme whose organisation uses SSO: the invite page asked her for a password, and after setting one she still could not log in with it, because the SSO organisation blocks password login.

The invite endpoint did not know about the login method of the organisation. I added a field sso_required to the response of GET /api/invites/:token. The page now shows a single button, 'Continue with your company login', and no password form for those organisations.

The accept-invite endpoint also had to refuse a password for such an organisation, otherwise a direct call would still create a useless password. It returns 403 with a clear message now.

The SSO redirect keeps the invite token in the state parameter, so the user returns to the invite and is marked as accepted. I tested the round trip with the test identity provider we use for SSO work. The checklist appears afterwards as for other users.

The manager who reported it was fixed by hand by marking her invite as accepted. I added tests for both organisation types. I did not check the case of an SSO user invited to two organisations, which stays an open point.

summary: Made it possible for one email to accept invites into several organisations by adding a memberships table, and left the permission checks and the organisation switcher for the next step.
body:
Handled the two-organisations case for invites. The open point from the SSO fix turned out to be real: a regional manager at Acme belongs to two organisations, and the second invite failed with a unique constraint on users.email.

I looked at three options. One was a user per organisation, which would double the accounts and the logins. The second was a membership table linking one user to many organisations. The third was to refuse the second invite and make support merge by hand. Jonas said the membership approach is what he expects, since managers do sit in several depots, so I went with that.

The schema already had organisation_id on users, so I added memberships with user_id, organisation_id and role, and copied the existing rows into it with a migration. users.organisation_id stays for now as the last used organisation, and nothing reads it for permissions in the new code.

Accept-invite now looks for an existing user by email. If there is one, it adds a membership and asks for no new password. The user sees a 'You were added to Acme North' message after logging in.

I did not touch the permission checks in the API yet. They still use the single organisation of the user, so a user in two organisations sees only the last used one. An organisation switcher is the next step.

I wrote migration tests on a copy of staging with 41 users and checked the counts of memberships. Tests for the invite with an existing email pass. The login code was not changed, and I left the token handling alone while working on this.

summary: Planned the organisation switcher for users with two memberships and worked out where the active organisation should live, without building it yet.
body:
With memberships in place, the API needs to know which organisation a user is working in. I spent the session on a plan for that and did not write the switcher itself.

I read through the permission middleware and listed every place that assumes one organisation per user. There are eleven routes, mostly the shipment list, the costs queries and the CSV export. For now the active organisation has to be carried with the request, so I sketched a version where the client sends an organisation id with each call and the middleware checks it against the user's memberships. A user who names an organisation they do not belong to would get a 403. I wrote this down as the test case to build first.

I also sketched the header: a small dropdown that appears only for users with more than one membership, and nothing new for single-organisation users. I sent the rough layout to Priya and asked whether the dropdown should show the depot count next to each name.

While reading the code I noticed a likely problem. The saved filters are stored per user, so someone with two organisations will see filters that point to the other organisation's depots. I have not changed anything yet. The plan is to add an organisation id to the filters table in a migration and keep the existing filters in the user's first organisation. I wrote that down for the next session, along with the open question of where the active value should be kept.

summary: Reviewed the onboarding branch against the plan with Jonas: invite page, checklist, reminders and memberships are done, and two items, a help tour and the metric review, were cut.
body:
Went through the onboarding plan from the start of the branch with Jonas, step by step, using the staging site.

Done and checked: the invite landing page, the new invite email, the checklist card, the event logging, the reminder job, the SSO invite fix and the multiple organisations with the switcher. He liked the single screen for the password.

Two items were cut. The guided tour of the dashboard with tooltips would add a library and a lot of copy, and Jonas thought the checklist is enough for now. A weekly funnel email to him was replaced by the SQL view, which he can open when he wants.

He asked for one change: the reminder should be sent in the morning of the user's working day, not at 08:00 server time. I noted it and will use the depot time zone, which the settings page already stores.

Open before the merge: enable the reminder flag, the time zone change, and one more run of the Playwright suite on staging.

summary: Made the reminder job send at 08:00 in each invitee's depot time zone and found that invites for users without a depot had no zone, so they now fall back to the organisation zone.
body:
Jonas asked in the review that reminders arrive in the morning of the invited person, so I changed the daily job to an hourly one that sends only to those for whom it is currently 08:00.

The zone comes from the depot of the invite. The first problem was that an invite has no depot until the user picks one in the checklist. For those users the job used nothing and skipped them for ever. I added a fallback chain: depot zone, then organisation zone, then Europe/Berlin as the default, which is where most of Acme is.

The hourly job needs to be safe against running twice. The reminded_at column handles that, and I also set it inside the same transaction as the send queue insert, so a crash between them does not send twice.

Tests use a frozen clock for three zones and check that nobody is reminded twice over 24 simulated hourly runs. A test with a zone name that is not valid falls back to the default and logs a warning.

I noticed that the time zone list of the settings page contains some zones the database does not know. I did not change that, but wrote it in the notes.

The job runs in dry-run mode on staging. It listed 6 invites over a day, which matched the count of unopened invites older than three days. The flag is still off. I want one more look at the email text with Jonas before turning it on.

On the side I deleted the unused daily job entry from the scheduler config.

summary: Ran the full Playwright suite for the onboarding branch and fixed three failures: a stale invite fixture, a race on the checklist card, and a missing wait in the organisation switcher test.
body:
Before the merge I ran the full Playwright suite against the onboarding branch on staging. 71 tests passed and 3 failed.

The first failure was the invite fixture. The seed created invites with a token that expired after 7 days, and the fixture had been made a week ago. I changed the seed to create the token at the start of the run.

The second failure was a race on the checklist card: the test clicked the saved-view step before the card had loaded from the API, and the card re-rendered afterwards. The fix was a wait for the response and not a sleep. This was a test problem, not an app bug, though the card does flicker for a moment, so I gave it a skeleton of the same height.

The third was in the organisation switcher test. It read the table before the new organisation's data arrived and saw the old rows. I added a wait for the shipments request after the switch.

After the changes all 74 pass. I ran the suite three times to look for flakiness and it was green each time.

I also ran the Vitest tests, which were green, and a type check with no errors. The branch is ready except for the reminder flag.

Notes for the merge: the migration for memberships runs first, then the settings backfill. I wrote the order down in the rollback note, and the rollback for memberships is to drop the table, as users.organisation_id was kept.

summary: Merged the onboarding branch to main and enabled the reminder flag after Jonas approved the email text, with the funnel view as the first thing to check next week.
body:
Jonas read the reminder text and approved it with one word changed. I merged the onboarding branch into main and deployed. The migrations ran in the order of the rollback note, and the check afterwards showed 41 users with a settings row and a membership each.

The reminder flag is on. The first hourly run sent nothing, as expected, since the due invites are reminded only at 08:00 of their zone.

I deleted the onboarding branch. The funnel view now has no baseline except Jonas's old number, and I told him to look at it in a week. The remaining idea of a help tour stays out of scope.

summary: Looked at the funnel view after a week: invites finishing the first login rose from about two thirds to 81 percent, with most of the remaining drop-off at the invite page itself.
body:
A week after the onboarding merge I read the funnel view with the first real numbers. Of 58 invites sent in the period, 47 reached the first dashboard view, which is 81 percent. Jonas's baseline was about 67 percent, so the one third who never finished is now one in five.

The drop-off by step is more interesting than the total. Of the 11 who did not finish, 7 never opened the invite page, 3 opened it and left without setting a password, and one set a password and never opened the dashboard. The reminder mail was sent to 6 of the 7 unopened ones, and 2 of them did come back afterwards.

The 3 who left on the page are the ones I looked at in detail. Two of them came from the same Acme depot and opened the link on a phone. The page works on a phone, but the password strength hint overlapped the submit button on a narrow screen of 360 pixels. That is a bug on our side and I reproduced it with the device emulation.

I fixed the overlap by letting the hint wrap and moving it above the button. I added a Playwright test with a 360 pixel viewport that checks the button is not covered. It failed before the fix and passes now.

For the 7 who never opened the invite I cannot do much in the app. One of them has a mailbox on the domain that had the spam problem, and I asked Jonas to check with Acme whether the sender address can be allowed on their side.

I wrote the numbers and the reading of them into the notes of the project, so that the next comparison has a baseline. The next look is planned for a month from now. No other change was made in this session.

summary: Started the report builder v2 plan with a review of what users do in v1: most reports reuse one of four layouts, and the biggest complaint is that groupings cannot be nested.
body:
The next large topic is the report builder v2. Before planning I wanted facts about how v1 is used, so I ran queries on the saved reports and talked with Jonas about what the managers say.

There are 212 saved reports from 38 users. When I grouped them by their structure, four layouts cover 171 of them: shipments per carrier, cost per depot, delivery time per week and late shipments per customer. The others are one-offs or small variations. This suggests that templates would help more than a more flexible builder.

Jonas's list of complaints from managers is short but consistent. First, groups cannot be nested, for example depot and then carrier. Second, a filter on the report cannot be changed without editing the report. Third, the totals row sums things that should not be summed, such as an average delivery time. The third one is a bug, and I confirmed it: the totals row adds up every numeric column.

I also looked at the code. The report definition is a JSON blob with columns, one group-by and filters, and the renderer builds one SQL query out of it. Nested groups need a change in the query builder: a GROUP BY with several columns and a rollup for the subtotals. Postgres supports ROLLUP, so this is feasible without a rewrite.

The plan I wrote has four steps. Step one is to fix the totals row by giving each column an aggregate type: sum, average, min, max or none. Step two is nested groups with subtotals. Step three is parameters, so that a saved report can be opened with a different date range or depot. Step four is the templates for the four common layouts.

Open questions: whether subtotals should be collapsible in the table and in the exported CSV, and whether report definitions need a version field. I think they do, since old saved reports must keep working, and I proposed a version number with an upgrade function on load.

I sent Jonas the plan with the numbers and asked him to rank the steps. The totals bug goes first in any case, because it gives wrong numbers to managers today. No code was written in this session.

The scheduled reports use the same definitions, which makes the version field more important, since a scheduled run could break at 06:00 with nobody watching.

summary: Fixed the wrong totals row in the report builder by adding an aggregate type per column, with a version field and an upgrade function for the old saved definitions.
body:
Jonas ranked the totals bug first, so I started with it. The totals row of a report summed every numeric column, which gave nonsense for averages: a total 'average delivery time' of 5,400 minutes was one example he had found.

I added an aggregate field to each column in the report definition, with the values sum, avg, min, max and none. The totals row now applies the aggregate of the column. For avg it is a weighted average, which needs the row count, so the query returns the count of shipments per group as a hidden column. A plain average of group averages would be wrong, and I wrote a test with unequal group sizes to show the difference.

The old definitions have no aggregate field, so I added version: 2 to the format and an upgrade function that runs on load. It sets the aggregate by the column type: sum for counts and costs, avg for durations, and none for the rest. Definitions without a version are treated as version 1. I ran the upgrade over all 212 saved reports in a script and compared the totals before and after. 19 reports changed their totals, all in duration columns, and Jonas wanted the list of them.

The scheduled reports load definitions through the same function, so they get the fix without more work. I ran one scheduled report in the staging environment and the email had the right totals.

I did not save the upgraded definition back to the database. The upgrade happens in memory at each load, and the saved JSON is only written when a user edits the report. This keeps a rollback trivial.

Tests: 12 new Vitest tests for the aggregates and the upgrade, with the weighted average case, empty reports and a column without an aggregate. The builder UI got a dropdown per column to choose the aggregate. It defaults to the value from the upgrade.

I sent Jonas the list of 19 reports whose totals changed and a one-line explanation he can pass on to the managers. The next step is nested groups.

summary: Built nested grouping with subtotals in the report query builder using ROLLUP, and found that sorting inside groups broke when a group label was null.
body:
The second step of the report builder v2 was nested groups, for example depot and then carrier. I changed the definition to accept a list of group-by columns instead of one, and the version-2 upgrade wraps the old single value into a list.

The query builder now emits GROUP BY ROLLUP(a, b) when subtotals are on, and plain GROUP BY a, b when they are off. A GROUPING() call tells the renderer which rows are subtotals and which is the grand total, so I do not have to guess from null values. The result rows get a level field: 0 for detail, 1 for a subtotal of the first group and 2 for the grand total.

The problem came with sorting. I sort the detail rows inside each group by a chosen column, and ORDER BY with ROLLUP put subtotals in the wrong place when a group label was null. Shipments without a carrier have a null carrier, and the subtotal row for them is also null in that column. The first version mixed the two. I fixed this by coalescing the label to a text value in a subquery and ordering by the GROUPING value first, then the label, then the chosen sort.

I added tests with null carriers, with one group only, with three levels and with the totals off. The expected rows are written by hand in the test and not generated by the code under test.

The table in the UI shows the subtotal rows in bold with a light background. In the dark theme I had to pick a different background so that the text keeps its contrast. Priya will look at the colours later.

The CSV export of a report with subtotals writes the level as a column, so that a spreadsheet user can filter on it. Large reports are still slow to export, as before, and I did not look into that here. A report of 300,000 rows with two groups ran in 2.4 seconds on staging for the query itself.

Performance of the rollup is acceptable, but it needs the same index as the plain group-by. Collapsing of subtotal groups in the table is not done yet. That is the open question about collapsible groups from the plan, and I will ask Jonas.

summary: Added collapsible subtotal groups to the report table after Jonas said managers want to see only the subtotals first, and kept the collapse state out of the saved definition.
body:
Jonas answered the question about collapsing: managers want to open a report and see the subtotals first, then expand what they care about. I built that for the report table.

Each subtotal row got an arrow button that hides or shows the detail rows below it. The renderer already had the level field from the rollup, so the grouping of rows is simple. By default a report with nested groups opens with the detail rows collapsed.

I kept the collapse state in the component and in the URL as a short list of open group keys, not in the saved definition. A report is a definition, and who opened which group is a view state. This also means that a link can be shared with a group opened.

The buttons need to work with the keyboard and a screen reader, so they have aria-expanded and the row has an aria-controls reference. Priya had asked for this after the accessibility pass of the table.

The CSV export always contains all rows, whether collapsed or not, and I wrote that in the help text of the export button. A test checks it.

One bug: toggling a group scrolled the table back to the top because the row keys changed with the index. I switched to keys from the group values.

summary: Reviewed Priya's colour changes for subtotal rows and the aggregate dropdown in the report builder and adjusted contrast in the dark theme to the AA ratio.
body:
Priya looked at the report builder with the subtotals and gave feedback on three things. The bold subtotal rows were fine in the light theme, but in the dark theme the background was too close to the page and the grand total row did not stand out.

I changed the dark theme colours to her values and checked the contrast with the browser tool: 5.1 to 1 for the subtotal text and 7 to 1 for the grand total. Both pass AA.

She also wanted the aggregate dropdown to show a short label instead of 'avg', so I used 'Average' and 'Sum' with the short form in the tooltip only. The Vitest snapshot was updated.

Nothing else was found. Parameters for reports are the next step.

summary: Implemented report parameters so that a saved report opens with a different date range or depot, and made scheduled reports keep their own fixed parameters.
body:
The third step of the plan was parameters. A report can now declare parameters in its definition, for example date_range and depot, and the filter bar above the report shows them. The user changes a value and the report reruns without being saved again.

In the definition a parameter has a name, a type, a default and a target, which is the filter it feeds. I kept the types to date_range, single depot and carrier list, since these were what managers asked for. The renderer replaces the filter values before the query is built, and the values are validated on the server against the type, so nobody can inject something through the URL.

The values live in the URL as query parameters, so a link opens the report with them. If a value is missing, the default of the definition is used.

The scheduled reports needed a decision. A schedule should not follow whatever somebody typed in the URL, so each schedule stores its own parameter values at creation. If it has none, the defaults apply. I added a parameters column to the schedules table and the migration sets it to an empty object for the existing ones.

The relative date default, for example last 7 days, is evaluated in the zone of the schedule. This is the fix from the 06:00 bug of before, and I added a test that renders one report in two zones.

I wrote 9 Vitest tests, including invalid types, a parameter that targets a missing filter and defaults. A Playwright test opens a report with a depot parameter from a link and checks the rows.

The version number stays at 2, since parameters are optional and old definitions do not have them. The next step is the templates.

summary: Added the four report templates and a template picker to the builder, and found that the cost per depot template silently ignored depots without a cost center.
body:
Last step of the report builder v2 plan: templates for the four layouts that cover most saved reports. The templates are definitions in code with a name, a description and a preview, and the picker opens when a user creates a new report.

The four are shipments per carrier, cost per depot, delivery time per week and late shipments per customer. Each one uses the aggregates, the nested groups where it makes sense and one or two parameters. For example delivery time per week has a date range parameter and an average duration column.

I checked each template against the real saved reports by running the template on staging and comparing it with the existing report of the same kind. Three matched. The cost per depot template had fewer rows: it joined the cost centers table with an inner join, so depots without a cost center vanished. I changed it to a left join and the depots show with a cost of zero and a marker 'no cost center'.

That also means that the existing saved reports of this kind are likely missing those depots. I counted: 6 saved reports use the inner join. I did not change them, but sent the list to Jonas so he can tell the owners.

The picker has a 'blank report' choice as before. Choosing a template copies the definition, so changing it later does not affect the template.

Tests: one for each template that checks the generated SQL runs on the seed data and returns rows. The picker has a Playwright test.
