The report builder v2 plan is complete with this step, apart from the question of the slow CSV export of large reports, which belongs to the export topic.

summary: Wrote a long-form review of the report builder v2 as shipped: what changed, the numbers from the first two weeks, three follow-ups, and the questions that Jonas still has to answer.
body:
With the templates done I made a review of the whole report builder v2, to have one place where the result is described.

What changed: columns have an aggregate type, so the totals row is correct. Groups can be nested with subtotals through ROLLUP and the subtotals can be collapsed. Reports have parameters, and scheduled reports keep their own. There are four templates. The definition has a version field with an upgrade function on load, and no saved report was rewritten.

The numbers from the first two weeks: 31 new reports were created, of which 22 started from a template. The average time to create a report is not measured, but Jonas says that two managers who used to ask him to build reports now do it themselves. 14 reports use nested groups. Nobody has reported a wrong total since the fix.

Three follow-ups remain. First, the 6 cost reports with the inner join still miss depots. Second, a parameter of type carrier list does not show the carriers of the active organisation only, but all, which is a leak of names between organisations through the dropdown. It does not leak data, but the names are visible. I fixed this at once by filtering the options by the active organisation, and added a test.

The third follow-up is the CSV export of big reports. A report with 300,000 rows still builds the file in memory and takes so long that on staging the request ran into the 30 second limit of the proxy twice. I looked at the problem only enough to confirm it is the same as for the tables, and I did not change anything. It stays on the list as a separate topic.

Questions for Jonas: should templates be editable by an admin of the organisation, so that Acme can have its own? Should parameters be shown in the scheduled email so that the reader knows which depot the numbers are for? I think yes for the second one, and I will add a line to the email if he agrees.

I also noticed that the upgrade function has a branch for version 1 that is never hit in new code, but I kept it because of the saved reports. Removing it would need a one-time rewrite of the saved definitions, and I see no reason to do it now.

The review is stored in the project notes, with the list of the 19 changed reports from the totals fix and the 6 cost reports.

summary: Added the parameter line to scheduled report emails after Jonas agreed, so a reader sees which depot and date range the numbers are for.
body:
Jonas answered the questions of the review. Templates stay as they are for now. He wants the parameter line in the scheduled emails, since one manager received two reports for different depots and could not tell them apart.

The email now has a line under the title, for example 'Depot: Hamburg, Last 7 days (Mon to Sun)'. I wrote the date range as real dates from the render zone, which is the zone of the schedule, and not as the relative phrase only, because an email is read later than it is sent.

The line is built from the parameters of the schedule and the labels of the definition. A report without parameters shows no line. I added the line to the plain-text part too.

Tests render the email for a report with two parameters, one without, and one with a depot that has a long name that wraps. The snapshot for the HTML part was updated. I sent myself a test mail from staging and checked it in two clients.

The 6 cost reports with the missing depots have been passed on to their owners by Jonas.

summary: Looked at the slow CSV export of a large report again without fixing it: measured memory and time at 100,000, 300,000 and 600,000 rows, to size the problem for later.
body:
The export keeps coming up, so I measured it properly instead of guessing. I ran the report export on staging with three sizes and watched the time and the memory of the API process.

At 100,000 rows the export took 6 seconds and the process grew by about 180 MB. At 300,000 rows it took 21 seconds and 520 MB. At 600,000 rows it ran into the 30 second proxy limit and returned a 504, while the process went above 1 GB before the request ended. The Render instance has 2 GB, so two parallel big exports could kill the process.

The time is not in the query. The SQL for 600,000 rows ran in 3.1 seconds. The rest is spent building the row objects, formatting each cell, and joining one big string before sending it. That is why memory grows linearly with the rows.

I wrote the numbers into the notes with the three sizes and the observation about the string. The obvious direction is to send the rows as they come from the database, but I have not tried it, and I want to plan it together with the table export, which uses the same code.

For now managers with big reports are told to narrow the date range. Jonas knows that this is a workaround and asked for a fix soon.

No code was changed in this session apart from a log line that records the number of rows and the duration of each export, so that we can see how often this happens. The first day of data will show whether it is rare or common.

summary: Planned the new-charts work with Jonas: which four charts come first, how ECharts options are shared, and what the dispatchers actually look at each morning.
body:
Jonas and I went through the current dashboard to decide what the new charts branch should deliver. The managers use three views every day: deliveries per depot, late shipments by hour, and cost per kilometre. The dispatchers mostly use the table, and only glance at one chart.

We agreed on four charts for the first round: a stacked bar of delivery status per depot, a heatmap of late shipments by weekday and hour of day, a cost per kilometre line with a target band, and a small sparkline for the shipments page header. The heatmap was Jonas's idea after a manager asked why Mondays feel worse.

The current charts each build their own ECharts option object, and about 60 percent of the code is the same: axis style, tooltip, legend position, colours from the theme. I proposed a small set of option builders in src/charts/base that take data and a few settings and return a complete option. The legend work from last year would move into the base so all charts behave the same.

One question was data volume. The heatmap needs 168 cells per depot, which is trivial, but the line chart over a full year of daily points for 40 depots is about 14,600 points. ECharts handles that, but I want to try its sampling option before building anything custom.

Priya will deliver the colour scale for the heatmap, and it must work in the dark theme and for colour blind users. I asked for a sequential scale with a clear lightness change, not a rainbow. She said she would have a draft in a few days.

The API side needs two new endpoints: late shipments grouped by weekday and hour, and cost per kilometre by day. Both are aggregate queries on the shipments table. I checked the existing indexes and the grouping by hour of the delivery timestamp has none, so I will measure before adding one.

I created the new-charts branch and wrote the plan in docs/new-charts.md with the four charts, the order, and the open questions. The order is: base builders, status bar, cost line, heatmap, sparkline. Next is the base builder module and moving the legend into it.

summary: Created the shared chart option builders and moved the legend code into them; the two existing charts now use the base with no visible change.
body:
I added src/charts/base with a function for the common option: grid, axis style, tooltip and legend, all taking colours from the theme object. The legend behaviour from last year, such as click to isolate a series and the scroll mode for long lists, now lives in one place.

I switched the existing deliveries bar chart and the delivery time chart to the base. Both rendered the same as before in a pixel comparison of screenshots, apart from a tooltip padding difference of 2 pixels that I fixed in the base.

The unit tests check that the base returns the right legend type for more than eight series. A small snapshot test for each chart option would have been too brittle, so I kept to a few focused tests. Next is the stacked status bar chart.

summary: Built the stacked delivery status chart per depot and found that depots with no late shipments dropped out of the series, leaving gaps in the legend and the colours.
body:
The new status chart shows on time, late, failed and returned shipments per depot as stacked bars. I added the endpoint GET /api/charts/status-by-depot, which groups the shipments of the chosen date range.

The first version looked wrong for some depots. When a depot had no late shipments, the query returned no row for that status, and the chart built its series from the rows it received. The series order changed between depots and the colours moved: late turned from red to the colour of failed.

The fix is on the client. The builder now takes a fixed list of statuses with their colours and fills zeros for missing combinations. I also moved the status colours into the theme so the dark theme can adjust them.

Second problem: with 40 depots the category labels overlapped. I switched to a horizontal bar for more than 12 depots and sorted by total, which reads much better. A dataZoom slider was an alternative, but Jonas said managers will not drag a slider.

I added tests for the zero filling and for the switch to horizontal. The empty state shows a message when the date range has no shipments, instead of an empty frame.

A quick check with the production sized data in staging showed 180 ms for the query on a 90 day range, which is fine. Next is the cost per kilometre line.

summary: Added the cost per kilometre line chart with a target band, and fixed division by zero for depot days with no distance driven.
body:
The cost chart plots daily cost divided by kilometres for the selected depots, with a shaded band for the target range that Jonas set per depot. The endpoint is GET /api/charts/cost-per-km.

First bug: days with zero kilometres, such as Sundays at small depots, produced Infinity in SQL as an error. Postgres raised division by zero and the endpoint answered 500. I used NULLIF on the distance and the chart now shows a gap in the line for these days, with connectNulls off, so it is honest about missing data.

The target band uses ECharts markArea. It was hard to read in the dark theme because the band colour was too close to the grid lines, so I made the band a low opacity version of the accent colour.

I tried the sampling option for the full year view. With lttb sampling the line stays smooth and the shape of peaks is kept. The tooltip still shows the real values of the hovered point.

Tests cover the null handling and the band rendering. Priya's heatmap scale has not arrived yet, so that chart waits.

summary: Wrote the late shipments heatmap with Priya's colour scale, and measured the query that groups by hour and weekday at 240 ms before an index and 40 ms after.
body:
Priya sent the sequential scale: six steps from pale yellow to deep blue-violet, with a separate dark theme version. I checked it with a colour blindness simulator for deuteranopia and protanopia, and the steps are still distinguishable by lightness.

The endpoint GET /api/charts/late-heatmap groups late shipments by day of week and hour of the planned delivery time. On the staging copy with 2.1 million shipments, the query took 240 ms for a 90 day range. The plan showed a sequential scan filtered on status and date.

I added a partial index on planned_at for rows with status late. The same query now takes 40 ms. The migration builds the index concurrently, so it does not lock the table. I tested the migration on staging first.

On the client, the heatmap uses the ECharts visualMap in piecewise mode with the six steps, so the legend shows ranges instead of a gradient. Cells show the count in the tooltip and the share of all shipments in that hour.

One detail: the hour is in the depot time zone, not UTC. The first version grouped in UTC and moved the late peak by an hour for the depots in the east. The query now uses the depot zone from the depots table.

Tests cover the time zone grouping with a fixture of three depots. The sparkline for the page header is the last chart of the plan.

summary: Built the shipments page sparkline from the existing summary endpoint, so it needs no new query, and kept its size under 3 KB of extra code.
body:
The sparkline shows deliveries per day over the last 14 days in the page header of the shipments page. I looked at whether it needed a new endpoint, but the summary endpoint that the header cards use already returns the daily counts, so I reused it.

I used a minimal ECharts setup with no axes, no tooltip and a thin line. The component imports only the line chart and the canvas renderer, and the build report shows about 3 KB of added code since ECharts core was already in the bundle.

The line colour follows the trend: accent colour when the last day is above the 14 day average, muted otherwise. Priya did not like green and red for this, as it adds a judgement that dispatchers may not agree with.

There is a test for the empty case and one for a single day of data. With this, all four planned charts are in place and the remaining work is polishing and a review with Jonas.

summary: Looked at why every login of the mobile drivers hit the dashboard API twice, and found the app calls the profile endpoint before and after the token refresh.
body:
The API logs showed a pattern in the mobile app traffic: each app start made two calls to /api/me within a second, and the first one often answered 401. I looked at the logs of one driver over a morning to be sure.

The cause is on the app side. The app sends the call with the stored access token, and when it gets a 401 because the token is expired, it refreshes and sends the call again. Since the access tokens live a short time now, this happens on most starts after the driver has put the phone away for a while. It is expected behaviour, not a bug, but the first call is wasted.

I wrote to the mobile app agency with the numbers: about 38 percent of app starts hit the 401 first. The suggestion was to read the expiry from the token and refresh before the call if it is close. They replied the same afternoon that this is simple for them and they will include it in the next release.

On our side I checked that the 401 response has the code token_expired in the body, so the app can tell an expired token from an invalid one. It does. I also added a line about this in the API notes for the agency.

No code change in the dashboard for this. I wanted the finding written down because it will show up again as noise in the logs and in the 401 rate of the monitoring.

Nothing else changed today. I will check the 401 rate after their release.

summary: Reviewed the four new charts with Jonas on staging: he approved the status bar and the cost line, wanted the heatmap labels in plain words, and asked for a PNG download.
body:
We went through the charts on the staging site with Jonas, using real data of last month. The status bar and the cost line were approved without changes.

For the heatmap he did not understand the legend ranges at first. The wording was counts like 0-4 and 5-9. He wanted words such as few, some and many late shipments, with the numbers in the tooltip. I will change the legend labels.

He also asked for a way to download a chart as an image for his slide decks. ECharts has saveAsImage in its toolbox, so that is cheap, but the image needs a white background in the dark theme. I noted it as a small follow-up.

The sparkline got a comment that it is too small to notice. We left it as is and will see if anyone asks.

summary: Added the chart image download and the plain word heatmap legend, and found that exporting in the dark theme produced black text on a transparent background.
body:
I started with the heatmap legend. The piecewise ranges now have labels few, some, many and very many, and the numeric range is part of the tooltip. The thresholds are computed from the data's maximum so the words keep their meaning across depots, rounded to numbers that are easy to read.

For the image download I enabled the ECharts toolbox with saveAsImage on the four charts. The first test in the dark theme gave an image with a transparent background and light text, which is invisible when pasted on a white slide. The text was fine on screen only because the page background is dark.

I changed the export to set a background colour and to use the light theme colours for text and axes during export. ECharts has no hook for switching theme for the export only, so I used the getDataURL call with its own backgroundColor and rebuilt a temporary instance of the chart with the light theme in a hidden element. The code is in src/charts/exportImage.ts.

The temporary instance matters for the size too. It renders at the pixel ratio 2, so the pasted image looks sharp on a projector. A 900 by 400 chart gives a 1800 by 800 PNG of about 60 KB.

I tested it by hand in three browsers and wrote a Playwright test that clicks the download button and checks that a file with the PNG header arrives and is larger than 10 KB. The image content is not compared pixel by pixel because anti-aliasing differs between machines.

One more finding: the hidden instance must be disposed after the export, or each click leaks a canvas. I confirmed with the memory profile of ten exports in a row that memory stays flat after the dispose call was added.

I also made the file name from the chart title and the date range, for example status-by-depot-last-30-days.png, so Jonas does not end up with a folder of chart.png files.

The branch is now feature complete according to the plan. What remains is the accessibility pass for the charts, where screen readers get a text summary, and a final regression check of the old charts.

summary: Added text summaries and ARIA labels for the new charts, and a visually hidden data table as fallback, after a keyboard and screen reader check.
body:
ECharts has an aria option that generates a description of the chart. I enabled it for the four new charts and wrote the labels in plain language, such as the title of the chart and the main message, for example the depot with the most late shipments.

The generated description alone was too long for the heatmap with its 168 cells. For that chart I wrote a short summary by hand from the data: the busiest late hour and the weekday with the most late shipments. The full numbers are in a visually hidden table below the chart that screen readers can read row by row.

I tested with VoiceOver in Safari. The summary is read when the focus enters the chart region, and the table is reachable with the table commands. The toolbox buttons were not reachable by keyboard before. I gave the download button a real button element with a label, instead of relying on the ECharts toolbox icon.

A test with axe on the dashboard page reported two issues, both low contrast on the muted axis labels in the light theme. I raised the label colour to the AA ratio.

The hidden table adds some DOM for large depot counts: 40 depots by 4 statuses is 160 cells, which is fine.

Next is the merge of new-charts into main after a regression check.

summary: Ran the regression check of all charts before merging new-charts, and found that the old delivery time chart lost its zoom after the base builder change.
body:
I opened every chart of the dashboard on staging and compared it with production. Most were identical. The delivery time chart had lost its dataZoom slider, so users could not narrow the range.

The cause was that the base builder merges options with a shallow copy, and the chart's own dataZoom array was replaced by the empty default. I changed the merge to concatenate arrays for dataZoom and series, and to override for everything else.

I added a test that builds the delivery time chart and expects a dataZoom entry. I also wrote a small script that renders each chart option to JSON and diffs against the version on main, to catch anything else of this kind. It found one more: the tooltip formatter of the cost per kilometre chart was dropped in an earlier step because of the same merge. That is fixed too.

The Playwright suite passes. Bundle size grew by 21 KB gzip, mostly the heatmap and visualMap modules, and I accepted this.

I will merge when Jonas has seen the final heatmap legend.

summary: Merged new-charts into main after Jonas approved the heatmap legend and turned on the charts for all organisations at once, with no feature flag.
body:
Jonas looked at the heatmap legend with the words and approved it. He asked if the charts could be limited to a few organisations first. I explained that the new charts replace nothing: the old charts stay on their pages, and the new ones are added in a separate tab called Insights. A flag would only hide a tab.

I merged the branch into main and deployed to Render. The deploy took four minutes. After it, I opened the Insights tab with a manager account and a dispatcher account and checked all four charts.

The migration with the partial index ran during the deploy in 6 seconds on production. I checked the query times in the logs after an hour: the heatmap endpoint answers in 55 ms on average on production data.

I deleted the branch locally and on the remote.

summary: Checked the logs the day after the charts release: no errors, the heatmap is the most opened chart, and the mobile 401 rate is unchanged until the app release.
body:
I went through the error log and the request counts of the Insights endpoints. No 500 errors in the day, and the slowest response was 310 ms for the cost per kilometre over a full year of all depots.

Usage: 22 managers opened Insights, the heatmap got the most views, then the status bar. The image download was used 9 times.

The 401 rate of the mobile app is still about 38 percent of app starts, as expected. The agency's release with the early refresh is not out yet. I will look again after it.

Nothing needed fixing today.

summary: Fixed a session-less edge in the dark theme toggle where the saved choice was lost on a new device, by storing the theme on the user settings row.
body:
Jonas reported that a manager who changed to the dark theme on the office computer found the light theme again on the laptop. The theme was only kept in local storage of the browser.

I added a theme column to the user settings table with the values light, dark and system, with system as default. The settings API returns it, and the app reads it after login. The local storage value is still used for the first paint, to avoid a flash of the wrong theme before the settings load, and it is updated from the server value.

The migration adds the column with a default so no backfill was needed. The case of a user who has local storage set to dark but nothing on the server: on first load after the deploy, the client sends its local choice to the server once.

I wrote tests for the settings endpoint and for the sync on first load. The flash on first paint was checked by throttling the CPU in the browser and watching the first frames.

One gap: the mobile app does not use this setting, so no change for the agency. Done for now.

summary: Wrote a long review of the new charts three weeks after release: usage numbers, what dispatchers ignore, what managers use, and a ranked list of follow-ups for Jonas to decide.
body:
I collected the numbers from the request logs and the event table for the three weeks since the Insights tab went live. The aim was to give Jonas something to decide on, not just a report.

Usage: 31 of the 44 manager accounts opened Insights at least once, and 19 came back in more than one week. Among dispatchers, 6 of 58 opened it. That fits what Jonas said before, that dispatchers live in the table.

By chart: the heatmap had 41 percent of all chart views, the status bar 27 percent, the cost line 24 percent, and the sparkline cannot be measured, because it is part of the page. The image download was used 63 times by 11 users. Date range changes were frequent: most users change the range right after opening, so the default of 30 days is probably not what they want. The most common choice is the last 90 days.

Performance: median endpoint time was 70 ms, the 95th percentile was 340 ms, and the worst was the cost line over a year for all depots at 900 ms once during a deploy. No timeouts.

Problems found in the period: one report of a heatmap with all cells in the lightest colour. It was a depot with only 3 late shipments in the range, where the scale from the maximum made every cell look the same. I changed the lowest piece to start at one, so single events are visible.

What dispatchers ignore: the chart tab itself. A suggestion is a small late shipments by hour chart inside the shipments page, where they already are. I did not build it.

Follow-ups, ranked by what I think matters:
1. Change the default range to 90 days, a one-line change.
2. Add a depot compare mode to the cost line, since managers compare depots by eye.
3. A late shipments chart on the shipments page for dispatchers.
4. Save a chart view, so a manager can reopen with the same depots and range.
5. Scheduled chart images in the report emails, which would connect to the scheduled reports.

Questions for Jonas: whether dispatchers should get the chart at all, whether the cost line should be limited to managers because of the cost data, and whether item 5 is worth the work. For the second question I noted that the cost line currently shows cost to anyone who can open Insights, and I think it should check the manager role as the costs page does.

I wrote the whole review in docs/charts-review.md and sent Jonas the link. I changed the default range to 90 days in the same session since it is trivial and nobody would object.

summary: Restricted the cost per kilometre chart to managers, matching the costs page, after finding that dispatchers could call the endpoint directly.
body:
Jonas answered the review questions and confirmed that dispatchers should not see cost data. The tab hid the chart in the interface for dispatchers only by accident, because no dispatcher had opened it, but the endpoint had no role check.

I tested with a dispatcher token and a curl call to /api/charts/cost-per-km. It answered 200 with data. That was my miss in the original work. The costs page endpoints use a requireRole('manager') middleware, and I had not copied it to the chart route.

I added the middleware and a test that a dispatcher gets 403 and a manager gets 200. I also searched the other new endpoints: status-by-depot and late-heatmap contain no cost data and are fine for both roles.

On the client, the cost chart is hidden for dispatchers and the tab layout adjusts. I checked the logs for earlier calls to the endpoint by dispatcher accounts: none, so no data was seen.

I told Jonas about the gap and that it is closed. I will do a check of all routes for the role middleware as a small audit later.

summary: Audited every API route for its role check and found two more that lacked one: the depot list export and the scheduled report preview.
body:
After the cost chart gap I wrote a script that loads the Express router, lists every route with its middleware names, and prints the ones without requireAuth or requireRole. The aim was to see all unprotected routes at once instead of reading the files.

The output had 71 routes. 58 had both authentication and a role rule. 9 were intentionally public: health check, login, the invite landing page endpoints, password reset and the SSO callback. That left four routes to look at.

Two were fine on a closer look: they check the role inside the handler, and I moved this into the middleware so the script sees it. The other two were real gaps:
- GET /api/depots/export returned the depot list with cost center codes to any logged in user, including dispatchers.
- POST /api/reports/schedule/preview rendered a scheduled report for a given definition id without checking that the report belonged to the caller's organisation.

The second one is more serious, because with another organisation's report id a user could see its numbers. I checked the logs for the past months: the preview endpoint was called 212 times, and all calls were for report ids of the caller's own organisation. So nothing leaked in practice.

I fixed both. The depot export now requires the manager role, and the preview loads the report with the organisation filter and answers 404 if it is not found. I wrote tests for both, including the cross organisation case with two fixture organisations.

The audit script now runs in CI and fails if a route has no auth middleware and is not in an explicit allow list of public routes. The list is in tests/publicRoutes.ts, so adding a public route needs a visible decision.

I told Jonas the summary: two gaps, no data seen by the wrong people in the logs, both closed. He asked if the mobile app calls any of the changed routes. It does not.

One thing I did not do is check the session handling of the active organisation for the new check; that works through the existing middleware, so I left it.

summary: Started the slow large-table work by profiling the shipments table with 50,000 rows, finding the cost is in cell rendering, not in the data fetch.
body:
The dispatchers with the biggest depots complained that the shipments table freezes when they remove all filters. I took a production sized copy and made a profile with the browser tools, to see where the time goes before changing anything.

With 50,000 rows loaded by the paged endpoint, 500 at a time, the network part is small: each page takes 120 ms. The freeze comes from rendering. After the pages arrive, React renders all rows into the DOM, around 50,000 times 14 cells, which is 700,000 nodes. Scripting took 4.8 seconds and layout another 2.1 seconds in the profile.

The table-v3 work last year already improved the cell components, but rows are still not virtualised in the all-filters-off case. The new table renders only the rows of the current page by default and the dispatchers switched on the show all option, which loads everything.

I considered three options:
1. Remove show all and limit to pages. Simple, but dispatchers asked for it for searching with the browser's find.
2. Virtualise rows with a windowing library. The best for the experience, but it breaks the browser's find and the pinned column logic would need a check.
3. Keep show all but cap it at 5,000 rows with a message to narrow the filter.

I measured a quick prototype of option 2 with a window of 40 rows plus overscan of 10. Scripting dropped to 180 ms and layout to 25 ms for the same 50,000 rows. Scrolling was smooth at 60 frames per second in the profile.

The cost of option 2 is the find in page. The dispatchers use that to look for a shipment number. A search field in the table that filters by the shipment number would give them the same, and the table already has the column filter. I will ask Jonas whether they would accept this.

I also noticed that the row selection state is stored in an array and checked with includes for each row, which is O(n squared) for large selections. Changing it to a Set is a cheap fix that I will do either way.

No code was committed today except the profile script in scripts/profile-table.ts, which fills the table with synthetic rows of a chosen size so that the numbers can be repeated. Next I will talk to Jonas and then decide between options 2 and 3.

summary: Jonas accepted virtual rows for the show-all mode if the table gets a shipment number search, so I changed the selection to a Set and started the windowing.
body:
Jonas asked two dispatchers about the browser's find. Both said they only use it for the shipment number, and a search box that jumps to the shipment would do. He accepted virtualised rows on that condition.

First the cheap fix: the selected row ids moved from an array to a Set. Selecting all 50,000 rows took 2.3 seconds before because of the includes call per row, and now takes 40 ms. The select all checkbox and the bulk actions use the same Set, so I updated them and their tests.

Then I started the windowing. The virtualisation applies only in show all mode, while the paged mode stays as it is, so the common case does not change. I wrote a useRowWindow hook that takes the scroll position, the row height and the container height and returns the first and last row to render. The row height is fixed at 40 pixels for this mode, as variable heights would complicate it.

The pinned columns use sticky positioning, which works inside the scrolling container with the windowed rows, but the spacer elements above and below the window must span the full width, or the pinned cells jump. I got this right on the second try.

The search box and the final measurements come next.

summary: Added the shipment number search to the windowed table, which scrolls to the matching row and highlights it, and checked it with 50,000 rows.
body:
The search box sits above the table in show all mode. When the user types a shipment number and presses enter, the table finds the index in the loaded rows, scrolls so that the row is in the middle of the window and gives it a highlight that fades after two seconds.

The lookup uses a Map from shipment number to row index, built once when the rows are loaded, so it is instant. With no match the box shows a small not found message instead of nothing.

I checked with 50,000 synthetic rows: the jump takes under 20 ms and the window renders 50 rows. A Playwright test types a number, presses enter and expects the highlighted row to be visible.

The keyboard focus moves to the row after the jump, so that arrow keys work from there.

summary: Measured the windowed table against the old show-all mode with three data sizes and wrote the numbers down, then fixed a flicker of blank rows on fast scrolling.
body:
With the search done, I ran the profile script for 5,000, 20,000 and 50,000 rows, with the old full render and the windowed mode, three runs each on the same laptop.

Scripting plus layout time to first usable table:
- 5,000 rows: 620 ms full render, 90 ms windowed.
- 20,000 rows: 2.4 seconds full, 110 ms windowed.
- 50,000 rows: 6.9 seconds full, 150 ms windowed.

Memory in the browser tab after load was 1.1 GB for 50,000 rows with the full render and 210 MB windowed. The remaining 210 MB is mostly the row data itself, so a lighter row object could help later, but it is no problem now.

The windowed mode has a flaw I saw while scrolling fast with the scrollbar: for a moment blank rows show, because the window is computed on scroll events and the render comes a frame later. Overscan of 10 rows is too small for a fast drag. I raised the overscan to 25 and switched the scroll handler to use requestAnimationFrame so that the window is computed once per frame, and not on every event.

With the new overscan, the blank flash did not appear in my test of dragging the scrollbar from top to bottom in half a second. The cost of the extra rows is small, 15 more rows of 14 cells.

There was also a problem with the sticky header in Safari, where it flickered when the window changed. Adding will-change: transform to the header stopped it. I only saw it in Safari 17, so I wrote the reason in a comment next to the line.

A second check was the keyboard: tab order inside the windowed table. Rows that are not rendered cannot receive focus, so tabbing from the last rendered row to the next would skip many rows. I made the table a single tab stop with arrow key navigation, like a grid role, for this mode. The screen reader reads the row count and position through aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex, so users know the table is long.

The unit tests cover the window calculation at the start, the end and with fewer rows than the window. The Playwright suite passes.

I wrote the numbers in docs/large-table.md for Jonas and the next person who touches the table.

summary: Deployed the windowed show-all table and watched the first dispatchers use it; one reported that the column sort resets the scroll position, which I fixed.
body:
I deployed the windowed table to production in the morning. It applies to show all mode only, and the paged mode is unchanged.

After lunch one dispatcher at the biggest depot wrote to Jonas that sorting a column in show all mode jumps back to the top. That is by design in the sense that the order changed, but she was looking at a particular shipment and lost it.

I changed the sort to keep the row of the first visible shipment in view if it is still in the list, scrolling to its new position. For a big list this is a lookup in the Map, so it is cheap. If the user has a selected row, that one is kept in view instead, as it is the better anchor.

I added a test for both cases and deployed. She confirmed it feels right.

I also checked the browser error reports of the day, and there were none from the table. One slow case: opening show all with no filters on a laptop with 4 GB of memory took 3 seconds to load the data, which is the network and parsing, not the rendering.

summary: Looked into a manager's report that he seemed to be logged in twice from his phone, and traced the cause to a login call that the mobile app sent again after a timeout.
body:
A manager told Jonas that something looked odd with his login: he had seen his phone twice in a list of devices and asked whether someone else was logged in. I looked up his data in Postgres and found two login records created 300 ms apart, with the same user agent and the same address, so nobody else was logged in.

The cause was in the mobile app's login call. It timed out on a slow network, and the app sent the request again, while the server had already handled the first one and created a record. The client only got the answer of the second call, so the first record stayed behind.

I did not want to merge records in the server by guessing, so for now I only wrote down a small safe plan: a login request that carries the same device id header within ten seconds, for the same user, should reuse the existing record instead of creating a new one. The device id header is already sent by the app, so the agency does not need to change anything.

I sketched the tests I want to add: a repeat within the window, and a second login after a minute, which should create a new record. I deleted the stray record of the manager by hand and told Jonas it was a harmless duplicate. The server change itself is still to be done, and I have not touched the login code yet.

summary: Wrote a plan for performance of the report table with 100,000 rows, comparing a server side window and the client virtualisation, and listed what each would break.
body:
The report builder shows its result in a table too, and the reports of the larger depots now reach 100,000 rows or more, as I saw when measuring the CSV export. The client virtualisation of the shipments table does not carry over directly, because the report rows are computed by a ROLLUP query with subtotal groups that can be collapsed.

I looked at what the report table does today. The server returns the whole result as JSON in one response. For 100,000 rows with 12 columns this is about 28 MB uncompressed and 3 MB gzip. The response takes 4 seconds on production and the browser spends another 3 seconds parsing and rendering. The collapse state is applied in the client by hiding rows.

Option A: reuse the row window hook. The collapsed groups make the row list a derived array, which I would compute before windowing: visible rows only. This is simple and keeps all work on the client. It does not fix the 28 MB response.

Option B: server side paging with a cursor over the ordered result. It fixes the response size, but subtotals and the grand total would need their own queries or a window function, and the collapse of a group means fetching different pages. This is a large piece of work.

Option C: send only the subtotal rows first and fetch the detail rows of a group when it is expanded. This matches how Jonas said managers use the report, as they look at the subtotals first. The detail request would reuse the same query with the group key as a filter.

I prefer C with A for the detail rows of a very large group. The first load becomes small, usually a few hundred subtotal rows, and large groups are windowed. The changes:
1. The query builder gets a mode that returns only rows with a grouping level above zero.
2. A new endpoint returns the detail rows for one group key, with the saved parameters.
3. The client keeps expanded groups in its state and fetches on expand.
4. The export is not affected, as it reads from the query, not from the table.

Risks: sorting inside groups happens in SQL, and the detail endpoint must use the same order. The null group label bug of before shows what happens when the two differ. Reports without grouping have no subtotals and stay on the current path with option A only.

Questions for Jonas: whether reports without grouping above 100,000 rows are common, and whether the collapse state should be remembered between sessions, which I kept out of the saved definition before. I wrote everything in docs/report-table-plan.md. I did not start the work because the CSV export is the more pressing complaint and should be handled first.

summary: Looked at the dispatcher complaint that the date picker forgets the last range after reload, and stored the range per user instead of per browser tab.
body:
A dispatcher told Jonas that she sets the date range every morning, since the picker starts at the default after each reload. The picker kept its value only in React state and in the URL query when she used a link.

I added a last used range to the user settings: the preset name when it is a preset like last 7 days, or the two dates when it is a custom range. A preset is stored by name so that last 7 days stays last 7 days tomorrow, not the fixed dates of today.

The order of what wins on load is: the URL query, then the stored setting, then the default. A shared link therefore still shows exactly the range of the sender.

The settings write is debounced by one second so that clicking through the picker does not send a request on every click. Tests cover the three cases of the order and the preset storage.

The Insights charts use their own range with the 90 day default I set before. I left them alone, as managers change the range there anyway. Jonas can say if the same memory is wanted for them.

summary: Built a first server-side window for the 100,000 row report table, sorting and paging in SQL, and it opened in 380 ms but broke the totals row.
body:
After the plan of this morning I tried the server-side window first, because it is the smaller change to the table component. The endpoint /api/reports/:id/rows now takes offset, limit and sort, and returns the rows plus a total count.

With 100,000 rows the first window of 200 rows came back in 380 ms, against several seconds for the full fetch. Sorting by cost used an ORDER BY on the report query, which is fine for the depot reports but slow for the cost per depot template, where the sort column is computed in a CTE. That one took 1.4 s per window.

The totals row broke. It summed the rows that the client had in memory, so with a window it showed the sum of 200 rows. I added a second query for the totals, but it doubles the load on the database for each scroll that changes the sort.

Count(*) over the report query was also slow, about 600 ms for the large report. I tried caching the count for 60 seconds per report and parameters, which helps but means the total can be slightly off.

The selection from the shipments table cannot be reused here, because rows outside the window have no state. Select all would need a server-side meaning.

Nothing is merged; the work lives in an uncommitted state on my local checkout. Next I want to try the client virtualisation on the same report to compare the two with real numbers. Open question for Jonas is whether the totals may come from a cached query.

summary: Tried client virtualisation on the 100,000 row report table: scrolling is smooth, but the initial JSON of 38 MB makes the first view take 6 seconds.
body:
I reused the windowing from the shipments table for the report table and loaded all rows into the client. Scrolling stayed at 60 frames per second, and the totals row was correct because all the data is there.

The cost moved to the load. The response for 100,000 rows was 38 MB of JSON, 4.2 MB gzipped, and parsing took about 1.1 s on my laptop. The first view appeared after roughly 6 seconds on the Render staging box.

On the older dispatcher laptops with 8 GB of memory the tab used 900 MB. That is too much for a page people keep open all day.

So the two approaches fail in opposite places: the server window is quick to open but has the totals and count problem, and the client approach has a slow open and memory use. A mix looks sensible: the server sends the totals and the first window, and the client fetches further windows as the user scrolls.

I wrote the numbers into the plan document and did not start the mixed version yet. Jonas should see the table with the totals from the cache before I decide.

summary: Investigated why the session cleanup job leaves thousands of expired rows in Postgres and planned a fix, without changing anything yet.
body:
A look at the sessions table while working on the settings page showed about 12,000 rows that are long expired. The cleanup job runs every night and logs that it deleted rows, so I read the query to see why so many were left.

It deletes where created_at is older than 30 days, but sessions that are renewed on use get a later expires_at. The rows left over are mostly sessions of users who never came back after a short visit with the old 1-day lifetime, created more than a month ago, and a few that had been touched. I counted them by hand with a select and the numbers matched the log.

The same condition can also hit the wrong rows. A session created 31 days ago and used yesterday matches created_at older than 30 days, so the job would delete it and log that dispatcher out in the middle of a shift. That may explain a complaint from last week that I had put down to a browser clearing cookies. I asked the dispatcher which browser he uses and when it happened, and I will compare that with the job's run log.

I have not changed the job yet. My plan is to switch the condition to expires_at less than now and to delete in batches of 1,000 rows so the table is not locked, and to write a test with three rows: expired, old but renewed, and fresh. For now I left a note in the task list and went back to the settings page.

summary: Wrote a design for the mixed report table: the server sends totals and the first window, the client loads further windows, with notes on what breaks.
body:
Following the two experiments of yesterday, I wrote down the mixed design before building it. The response of the first request holds the totals, the row count, and the first 500 rows. Later windows are fetched in chunks of 500 as the scroll position approaches the end of what is loaded.

The totals come from one SQL query per report and parameter set. I will cache it for 60 seconds, keyed by report id and the parameters, so scrolling does not trigger it again. A sort change needs no new totals, which saves the doubled load I saw.

The chunks must be stable. With offset paging, a shipment that is updated between two requests can shift rows and show one twice. I propose keyset paging on the sort column plus the id, which avoids the shift but makes jumping to the middle of the table harder.

The jump is needed for the scrollbar. My idea is to give the scrollbar the full height from the row count, and to load the window that matches the position, using offset only for jumps and keyset when scrolling down in order.

What would break: the select all checkbox, the in-page search that works on loaded rows, and the CSV export button, which today takes the loaded rows. The export is a separate problem and the server must build it itself anyway; large exports are still slow and I do not touch that here.

The open questions for Jonas are these: may the totals be up to a minute old, is search over all rows needed, and should select all mean all rows or the visible ones. I also listed a test plan: 1,000, 50,000 and 100,000 rows, a slow network, and an update during scrolling.

I will build the first version with offset paging only, to get something to show, and check the keyset idea if the shift shows up in practice.

summary: Asked Jonas the three table questions: totals may be a minute old, search only needs loaded rows for now, and select all means the visible rows.
body:
I sent the three questions of the design to Jonas and went through them with him on a call of about 20 minutes.

For the totals he said a minute of delay is fine for the reports, but not on the shipments page, which is live data. That page keeps its own table and is not affected, since its windowing works on the client.

For the search he first wanted everything, then agreed that a search over the loaded rows with a note "searching 2,000 of 100,000 rows" is acceptable until we see that people need more. Priya should check the wording of the note.

For select all he wanted the visible rows only, because the managers use the selection to mark a few rows for a comment, not to act on the whole report. A button "select all 100,000 rows" as in mail programs is not needed.

He also asked how long the work takes. I said about one week for the first usable version, then a week of testing with the managers who open the largest reports.

The decisions are written in the plan document. That removes the three hardest parts of the design and I can start with the endpoint tomorrow.

One more thing came up: the cost per depot report is used by one manager in particular who has 160,000 rows over a long date range. I will use his report as the test case.

summary: Built the chunked rows endpoint for the report table with cached totals, and measured 90 ms per 500 row chunk on a 160,000 row report.
body:
I implemented GET /api/reports/:id/window in the Express API. It takes the offset, the limit up to 1,000, the sort column and direction, and the report parameters. The response has the rows and, for the first request, the totals and the row count.

The totals use a small in-process cache with a 60 second lifetime, keyed by report id and the parameter hash. The API runs as a single Render instance, so a process cache is enough; I noted that this has to change if we add a second instance.

I measured the endpoint on the 160,000 row report of the manager. The first request with totals took 720 ms, mostly the count and the sum. Later chunks took 90 ms for 500 rows when the sort column is indexed, and 310 ms when sorted by the computed cost column.

For the computed sort I tried a materialised sub-select with the cost column, but the plan was not better. An index on the expression helped a bit, down to 180 ms, and I left it out for now because it slows down the nightly import of shipments.

I also checked the role checks, after the audit of a few weeks ago. The new route uses the same report access check as the old rows route, and I wrote a test with a dispatcher who is not allowed to see the cost report; it gets a 403.

Tests: six new Vitest tests for the paging, the limit cap, the sort whitelist and the totals cache. The sort column comes from a whitelist, not from the query string, to avoid injection.

The client does not use it yet. That is next, together with the scrollbar height from the row count.

summary: Connected the report table to the chunked endpoint: the scrollbar shows the full height, and chunks load as needed, with blank placeholder rows while loading.
body:
The report table now uses the window endpoint. The scrollbar has the full height from the row count, and the rows that are not loaded yet are placeholder rows with a grey bar.

A small hook keeps a map from chunk index to rows. When the visible range changes, it asks for the chunks that are missing, with a debounce of 80 ms, so a fast drag of the scrollbar does not send fifty requests. Requests for chunks that are no longer visible are cancelled with an AbortController.

On the 160,000 row report the first view appears after 0.9 s. Scrolling to the middle by dragging loads the chunk in about 150 ms, which feels immediate on staging. Memory use of the tab stays around 180 MB.

Two problems remain. A sort change clears the chunk map and the scroll jumps to the top, which is what users expect, but the placeholder rows flash. I will keep the old rows until the first new chunk arrives.

The second is the select all checkbox. It selects the loaded rows only at the moment, which does not match what Jonas decided, the visible rows. I have to change the selection logic to use the visible range.

summary: Fixed the sort flash and the select all behaviour in the report table, and found that the totals cache returned stale numbers after a parameter change.
body:
I kept the old rows visible until the first chunk of the new sort arrives, which removes the flash. The scroll still resets to the top on a sort change.

Select all now selects the rows in the visible range, as Jonas decided. The selection is a Set of shipment ids as in the shipments table, so I could reuse the code. A test with a 50,000 row report checks that the set has about 30 entries, not 50,000.

While testing I changed the depot parameter of a saved report and saw the old totals for up to a minute. The cache key used the report id and the date range, but not the depot, because the parameters were passed as two fields and I hashed only the first.

I changed the key to a hash of the whole sorted parameter object, and added a test that two different depots give two different cache entries. Before the fix, a manager could have seen the numbers of the wrong depot for a minute, but only on the totals row, not in the rows.

I checked the logs of staging: this happened twice in my own testing, and nobody else used it yet, so no real users were affected.

The cache also needs to be dropped when the nightly import runs, otherwise the totals lag behind the rows by a minute at the worst moment. I added a call to clear it at the end of the import.

Next is the search note and a test on a slow network.

summary: Added the search over loaded rows to the report table with the note about how many rows are searched, wording agreed with Priya.
body:
The report table got the search box of the shipments table. It searches the rows that are loaded in the chunk map and highlights the match, scrolling to it as before.

Because only some rows are loaded, a note appears below the box: "Searching 2,000 of 160,000 rows. Scroll to load more." Priya changed the wording a little, because "load" sounded technical for the dispatchers. It now says "Searching the rows you have already seen" with the numbers in smaller type.

The count of loaded rows updates as chunks arrive, so the note changes while scrolling. I throttled it to one update per half second, since it flickered.

If there is no match, the message says that and offers a link "Search all rows", which is not working yet. I left the link out of the first release and put the idea into the follow-up list: a server-side search by shipment number, which is indexed, would cover the main use.

The test checks the search with three loaded chunks and a match in a chunk that is not loaded, which must give the "no match" message with the right numbers.

I also checked the keyboard use: the box is reachable with Tab, and the screen reader reads the note, using aria-live set to polite.

Still to do are the slow network test and the real update during scrolling.

summary: Tested the report table on a throttled network and with data changing during scrolling, and found that offset paging shows one row twice after an insert.
body:
I ran the table with Chrome throttled to a slow 3G profile on the 160,000 row report. The first view took 4.8 s, which is long but it shows the totals and the placeholder rows early, so it does not look frozen. The chunk requests took 1 to 2 s each; with the debounce, dragging the scrollbar only loaded the chunk where it stopped.

Then the update test. I scrolled to the chunk at row 2,000 and, in a second terminal, inserted 20 shipments that belong in the earlier part of the sort order. The next chunk started with rows that I had already seen at the end of the previous one, so the same 20 shipments showed twice.

This is the shift that I expected from offset paging. With the nightly import it will not happen during the day, but Acme also creates shipments by hand, and a dispatcher scrolling a report of today would see it.

I looked at keyset paging as a fix. It needs the last sort value and id of the previous chunk, which the client has when scrolling down in order. For a jump by the scrollbar there is no previous chunk, so offset is used and a shift of a few rows is acceptable.

I wrote the keyset variant for the sort by date and by id, which are the common sorts. For the others the endpoint falls back to offset. This keeps the code smaller than a full solution.

With keyset, my insert test showed no duplicates when scrolling down in order. Scrolling up still uses offset and can show a shift.

Tests: two new ones for the keyset query, one with equal sort values to check that the id breaks the tie. That case failed first because I compared with greater than only; it needs a tuple comparison.

I have not merged. Tomorrow I want to run it with the manager's report and ask him to try it.

summary: Investigated why the "Log out of all devices" idea for the settings page was missing and planned how a logout option and its wording could look, using the login as it works today.
body:
While testing the report table on staging I looked at the settings page and noticed there is no way for a user to end their login on other devices. The only option is the normal logout button, which ends the current login and sends the user to the login screen. That is fine for one device, but Jonas had mentioned that dispatchers share workstations and sometimes forget to log out.

I checked how the login works now. The access token lives 30 days and is checked on every request, and the refresh token rotates. There is a deny list in Postgres for logged-out tokens, and it only covers single tokens. A logout of all devices would mean adding every token of the user to that list, and the app does not keep a list of the tokens a user has issued. So the button is not a small change.

I wrote down a plan with two options. The first one, "Log out of all other devices", would keep the current login and the user would stay on the page. The second one, the full version, would log out everywhere and show the message "You were logged out on all devices" on the login screen, so the user does not think the page crashed.

I sketched what each option would need: a way to find all the tokens of one user, and a test with three logins for one user that checks that the current one stays and the other two are refused. I have not written any code yet.

I also sent Priya the two button labels and the message and asked her to check the wording against her copy. Nothing is changed in main for now, and I will decide how to build it after her answer.

summary: Reviewed the chunked report table with Jonas on staging, took his two change requests, and wrote down the remaining edge cases before the table goes to the managers.
body:
Sat down with Jonas on staging and went through the chunked report table with a 160,000 row report. He scrolled to the bottom first, then used the search, then changed the depot parameter while chunks were loading. The first view opened in about 400 ms and he said it felt like the old small tables.

He asked for two changes. The placeholder rows should say 'Loading rows' in plain words for screen readers, and the totals row should show a small note when the cached totals are older than a minute. I agreed to both. The wording of the note is still open, and I will take it to Priya.

While he clicked around I noted four edge cases:
- A parameter change during a chunk request can bring back rows of the old parameters. The request needs a parameter key that is checked on arrival.
- Select all only covers the visible rows, which is what Jonas agreed to, but the button label still says 'Select all'.
- The search over loaded rows finds nothing for a row that has not been loaded yet, and the note about how many rows are searched is easy to miss on a narrow screen.
- Offset paging can still show a row twice after an insert. This is known and has no fix yet.

I fixed the first one right away. Each chunk response now carries the parameter key, and the client drops a response whose key does not match the current one. I reproduced it before the fix by changing the depot with a throttled network, and after the fix the stale rows no longer appear. I added a Vitest case for it.

The label of the select button, the totals note and the screen reader text are next. After that I will repeat the throttled network test. Jonas wants to show the table to two managers before anything is merged into main.

One side note from the session: the login on staging looked odd when the page was open in two tabs, because the settings page listed it twice. That is a different issue and I left it alone for now.

summary: Finished the find-by-number search for the report table, which jumps to the right chunk in about 200 ms, and fixed the reset of column widths.
body:
The find endpoint is done. It looks up the shipment in the report, checks that it matches the report parameters, and counts the rows before it in the current sort. The result is the position, and the client loads the chunk that contains it.

The client search box now does two things. It first searches the loaded rows, which is instant. If there is no match and the text looks like a shipment number, it calls the endpoint. The note no longer says that only some rows are searched, which was confusing; it only appears if the text is not a number.

On the 160,000 row report the jump took about 200 ms with the date sort, and 1.1 s with the computed cost sort. For that second case I show a small spinner in the box. The shipment must also belong to the user's allowed depots, and a test checks that a dispatcher of another depot gets a 404 and not the position.

The column width reset came from storing widths in component state that was recreated by the sort change. I moved it to the saved table settings of the user, which the shipments table already uses. Now widths survive a sort, a reload and a new device.

I added three Vitest tests and one Playwright test: open a big report, search a number in the middle, check that the right row is highlighted. The Playwright test takes 12 s with the fixture of 100,000 rows, which I accept.

The branch is ready for a second look by the manager and then a merge, planned for the end of the week.

summary: Jonas asked whether a partner page on another subdomain could reuse the dashboard login; I looked at the login cookie and advised against sharing it for now.
body:
Jonas asked in the morning if a partner page on another subdomain could reuse the dashboard login. At this point the dashboard login is a JWT access token, so I looked at how the token is stored and sent. In the browser it sits in local storage and goes out in a header, which means another subdomain would not see it at all, and local storage is not shared between origins.

The tokens could be moved into a cookie with the Domain attribute set to the parent domain, but then every subdomain would receive the login token, including any that run code we do not control. I advised against that for the partner page. A token that lives for 30 days and cannot be revoked quickly makes this riskier.

The cleaner way would be a separate login for the partner page, or an SSO flow like the one we built for the managers. Both need work and a decision on who may see what.

I wrote this to Jonas in three short points and asked for the use case before we plan anything. No code change was made.

summary: Merged the chunked report table into main after the manager confirmed the search and the speed, and watched the first hour of logs.
body:
The manager tried the search of shipment numbers on staging again and found every number he tried, so I merged table-v3 into main and deployed.

Before the merge I ran the whole Vitest suite, 412 tests, and the Playwright suite, which took 9 minutes. One Playwright test of the old report table failed because it counted all rows in the DOM; with the windowing the DOM holds only about 40 rows. I changed it to check the row count in the header.

After the deploy I watched the logs for an hour. The window endpoint was called about 340 times, with a median of 85 ms and a slowest call of 1.3 s, which was a computed cost sort on a big report. No errors and no 403 other than my own test.

The totals cache hit rate was 71 percent, so scrolling does not load the database much.

The CSV export of a large report is still the old code and still slow. It uses the loaded rows no longer, but it builds the file in memory on the server. That is the next topic after this one, and I did not touch it here.

I wrote a note for Jonas about what is live and the known limits: scrolling up can show a small shift after changes, and sorting by the computed cost is slower.

One dispatcher already asked how to see the page of a row; I explained that the header shows the position as the row number.

summary: Investigated why the nightly job that clears old login data is not yet in place and planned how the login could later be cleaned up, after a slow night with the mobile agency's test run.
body:
Looked at the nightly cleanup job for old login data and found that it took 41 minutes on a bad night, which is long for a job that should run for seconds. Today the login still uses JWT tokens, so there is no sessions table to tidy up. The slow job is the one that removes entries from the deny list for logged-out tokens, and I spent the session on that.

I went through the logs. The deny list had about 190,000 expired entries, because a script test by the mobile agency created many tokens with a short lifetime and logged them out during their test run. The job deletes rows in batches of 1,000 with a pause of 1 s. Each batch took 0.4 s, so most of the 41 minutes was spent waiting.

The pause was put there to protect live queries. I measured the login endpoint while the cleanup ran, and its latency did not change: 12 ms before and 13 ms during. So the pause looks too careful. I wrote down a plan to try larger batches with a much shorter pause, and to time each batch so that the size can be halved when a batch takes more than 1 s and grow again when batches are fast. I have not changed the job yet.

There is an index on expires_at already. I checked the query plan on a copy of the database with 200,000 expired rows, and the index is used, so the delete itself is not the problem, only the waiting.

I asked the mobile agency to tell me before they run big token tests, because they fill the table. They answered that they would use a test user and log out the tokens afterwards.

I also noted that the job should log the number of deleted rows together with the total duration, so that the next odd night is visible without reading the lines. That goes on the list for the next session.

summary: Fixed the contrast of the placeholder rows in the dark theme after Priya noticed they were almost invisible.
body:
Priya looked at the new report table in the dark theme and said the grey placeholder bars were barely visible, with a contrast of about 1.3 to 1. They are not text, but a user should still see that rows are loading.

I changed the colour to use the theme's muted border colour at a higher opacity, which gives about 3 to 1 against the table background. I also checked the light theme and it stayed the same.

The animation of the bars is now off when the user prefers reduced motion. I took a screenshot in both themes for Priya and she approved.

summary: Profiled the slow CSV export of a 160,000 row report after the table work and sized three possible fixes without implementing any of them.
body:
Now that the table is done, I came back to the CSV export. A manager reported that the export of the 160,000 row cost report ends with a timeout error from Render after 30 seconds.

I reproduced it on staging. The export route reads all rows from Postgres with one query, builds the rows as objects, turns them into one big string, and sends the string. At 160,000 rows, the memory of the Node process rose to about 1.1 GB, and the request ran for 41 seconds, so the proxy cut the connection.

Time was spread like this: the query took 3.5 s, creating the objects 6 s, the string building 9 s, and the rest was garbage collection and the send. The process was also slow for other requests during that time, since the event loop was busy. A login request took 2.4 s while an export was running.

I wrote down three possible fixes:
1. Raise the proxy timeout and the memory. This is cheap, but does not solve the blocked loop and only moves the limit.
2. Build the file in a background job and send the manager an email with a link. It works for any size but changes how people use the export.
3. Send the rows to the client as they are read, in chunks, so nothing is held in memory. It keeps the button as it is, but needs care with errors in the middle of a download.

I did not build any of them. The reasons are the open choice for the user experience, which is Jonas' decision, and that the mobile agency also uses a smaller export.

I also found that the export uses the filters of the page but not the sort, so the file has a different order than the table. That is a bug of its own and I put it on the list.

The message to Jonas contains the three options with the effect for the user, and my recommendation to look at option 3 first, but I left it open. A reproduction script is in the repository as scripts/export-large.ts, so I can measure again after any change.

summary: Fixed the CSV export so that it keeps the sort order of the table, which it ignored before, and added a test with a shuffled fixture.
body:
The export bug I found yesterday was simple. The table sends the sort column and direction to the rows endpoint, but the export button only sent the filters, so the file came in database order.

I added the sort parameters to the export request, using the same whitelist as the window endpoint, so a made-up column name gives a 400. The query uses the same ORDER BY builder, which I moved into a shared function.

The test uses a fixture of 200 shipments in a shuffled insert order and checks that the file rows follow the sort by cost, descending, and then by date with the id as tie breaker.

The size problem of large exports is not changed by this. The 160,000 row report still times out, and I left it as it is until Jonas decides how the export should work.

The fix went to main in the afternoon without a feature flag, since the change only makes the file match what the user sees.

summary: Started the onboarding rework with a plan and a click-through of the current first-run flow, which has seven steps and loses about a third of new users at the invite step.
body:
Jonas wants the first run of a new user to be shorter, so I started the onboarding branch with a look at what exists. I created the branch onboarding and walked through the flow as a new dispatcher on staging, then as a new manager.

The flow has seven steps: accept the invite, set a password, confirm the email, choose a depot, pick the default date range, a tour of the shipments page, and a prompt for the notification settings. The manager flow adds a step for the SSO choice.

I pulled the numbers from the events table for the last 90 days. Of 214 invited users, 143 finished the flow, so a third did not. The biggest drop is at the invite step: 38 of the people who got an invite never opened the page with the password form. It could be mail that went to spam, or invites that expired after 7 days.

The second drop is at the depot choice, 14 people, and from the interviews with Jonas this is a step where users are not sure which depot to pick when they work at two.

The tour has the lowest finish rate of the optional parts, but it does no harm, since people can leave it.

Plan for the next weeks:
- Join the email confirmation with the invite, since a user who opens the invite link has already proven the address, so one step less.
- Preselect the depot if the invite carries it, which the inviting manager can set.
- Allow more than one depot in the choice.
- Make the tour optional and move it into a help button.
- Remind people with a mail after 3 days, if the invite is not used.

I also noticed that the invite link carries a token that is valid for 7 days. I did not yet look at what happens after the password is set and the user is logged in for the first time, so I put a check of that part on the list before I change the order of the steps.

I shared the plan with Jonas and asked about the reminder mail, since it is new behaviour that Acme might not want. Priya will look at the screens when I have the first version, and she asked to see the current flow in screenshots, which I made from the walk-through.

summary: Planned how to fold the email confirmation into the invite step of the onboarding branch to cut the first-run flow from seven steps to six, and checked the code it touches.
body:
I started the onboarding branch by reading the current first-run flow closely. Today the user opens the invite, sets a password, and then gets a second mail to confirm the address. That second mail is where many people drop out, so it is the first thing I want to remove.

The invite link already goes to the address, so opening it proves control of the mailbox. My plan is to set email_confirmed_at in the same transaction that stores the password, and then drop the second mail from the flow. I have not changed any code for this yet, I only wrote down which handlers and templates are involved. The confirmation mail stays for the case that a user changes the address in the settings later, since that does need a proof, and I sketched a test for both paths.

While reading the invite code I noticed a small risk: the invite token is single use, but it is marked as used in a separate step after the password is saved, so two tabs could in theory both use it. I have not reproduced it yet. I plan to write a test with two parallel requests and then move the marking into the same transaction, so that one request gets a 410.

On staging the flow still has seven steps. I clicked through it as a dispatcher and as a manager with SSO to have a baseline for later. Next I will build the join itself, and after that come the depot choice, for which I will ask Jonas about the field in the invite form.

summary: Added depot selection to the invite form and made the new user's depot step skip itself when the invite already names depots, with a multi depot choice otherwise.
body:
The invite form on the settings page has an optional depot field now, a multi select that lists the depots of the inviting manager. The chosen depots are stored with the invite in a new column depot_ids, an integer array.

When the new user opens the link, the depot step is skipped if the invite has at least one depot. The user is placed in these depots and the default view uses the first. If the invite has none, the step appears as before, but with checkboxes instead of a single choice, so a person who works at two depots can pick both.

I wrote a migration for the column with an empty array as default, so old invites still work. I ran it on a copy of the production data first, which took under a second for 214 rows.

There was one catch. A manager can invite only to depots they are allowed to see, and the form filters the list, but the endpoint did not check it, so a crafted request could name another depot. After the role audit of the weeks before, I did not want to leave this, and added a check that every depot id is in the manager's allowed set. A test sends a foreign depot and expects a 403.

The user store also needed a change: the first depot is the default, but the settings page assumed one depot and showed only the first. I fixed that so it lists all depots of the user.

Playwright test: invite with two depots, open the link, set the password, and land on the shipments page with both depots in the filter. It passes in 14 s.

Priya looked at the new checkbox screen and asked for the depot names to be sorted and the text under the title to say "You can pick more than one". I changed both.

I deployed the branch to staging only. The invite reminder mail is next, and I need an answer from Jonas about it before I build that.

One open point is that old users who never finished the flow stay as they are; I did not touch them.

summary: Built the reminder mail for unused invites after Jonas agreed to one reminder after three days, and tested it with a clock that I can move forward.
body:
Jonas answered that one reminder is fine but not more, and that the text should come from the inviting manager's name, so it does not look like spam. I built it on the onboarding branch.

A small job runs every hour, in the same scheduler that sends the scheduled reports. It selects invites that are older than 72 hours, not used, not expired, and without reminder_sent_at. For each of them it sends one mail and sets the column in the same step.

The mail says "Anna invited you to the Acme dashboard" with the manager's name in place of Anna, shows the link again, and names the days left until the invite expires. The link is the same token as before and not a new one, so the expiry stays at 7 days.

The order of the work matters. If the mail is sent first and the update fails, the user gets two reminders; if the update comes first and the mail fails, the user gets none. I chose to mark first, within a transaction that rolls back if the send throws, and the send happens before the commit. A crash between send and commit can still cause a second mail, which I accept, since it is rare and harmless.

For tests the job takes a clock function, so Vitest can move the time. There are five cases: younger than 72 hours, exactly after, already reminded, used, and expired. All pass.

On staging I created three invites and set their dates back in the database. The job sent three mails in the next run, and nothing in the one after. The mails arrived in the test mailbox with the right names and the days left.

There was one problem with the layout in a dark mail client: the button had a white text on a light background, since the style was set only for light. I gave it an explicit background colour. Priya checked it in two clients.
