I also added a line to the events table when a reminder is sent, so we can compare the finish rate of reminded and not reminded invites in a few weeks. This is the number Jonas will want to see.

Still to do on the branch: the tour moved behind a help button, and a final click-through with Priya before the merge.

summary: Checked the onboarding flow on a phone after the reminder mail work and found the new password step overflows on narrow screens, which I fixed with a layout change.
body:
After yesterday's reminder mail I opened the invite link from the mail on a phone, because many invited dispatchers read mail there. The password step worked, but on a 360 px wide screen the hint list under the password field pushed the submit button below the fold, and the keyboard covered it completely.

I changed the hint list into a single line that shows only the rule not yet met, and moved the button into a sticky footer of the form. In the depot step, the multi depot checkboxes had a tap target of about 24 px, so I raised it to 44 px by making the whole row clickable.

I checked the flow in the browser device mode with three widths (360, 390 and 768 px) and added a Playwright test with a small viewport that runs the invite link through to the last step. The test passed after the fix and failed before it, as intended.

Open: the welcome screen at the end still has a large illustration that Priya wants to shrink on mobile. I left it and sent her a screenshot. Next I want to look at what happens when an invite link is opened a second time after the password is set.

summary: Handled opening an invite link twice in the onboarding flow: the second visit now shows a clear message and a login link instead of a raw error, and the reminder mail respects it.
body:
I followed up on the open question from this afternoon: what happens when a user opens the invite link again after setting the password. Before the change, the second visit returned a plain 410 from the API, and the page showed the text "Request failed". Two of the users in the early onboarding numbers probably hit exactly this, since they open the mail on the phone and again on the desktop.

The invite token is single use, and that stays. What changed is the answer. The endpoint now tells apart three cases: the token is unknown, the token is expired, and the token was already used. For the used case, the API returns a 409 with a code, and the page shows "This invite was already used. Log in with your email and password" with a button to the login page. For the expired case, the page offers a button that asks for a new invite from the Acme admin, which sends a mail to Jonas's team address that is already configured.

I checked that the three cases do not leak anything: an unknown token and a used token must not reveal the email address of the invite. The used case shows no address at all, and the login page does not prefill it.

The reminder mail needed a fix too. The job that sends the reminder after three days selected invites with no password set, but it did not skip invites that had been revoked by an admin, so a revoked invite could still get a reminder. I added the revoked check to the query and a test with the movable clock for it.

I wrote tests for all three link states in Vitest on the API side, and one Playwright test that opens the link twice. All passed, and the full suite took about four minutes.

Still open: the expired invite request goes to a mail address without a rate limit, so someone could press the button many times. I will add a limit of one request per hour per invite next. I also noted that Priya should look at the wording of the three messages, since I wrote them myself.

summary: Started table-v3 virtualized rows for the shipments table; scrolling 20k rows went from about 900 ms per frame to under 16 ms in a first spike.
body:
Began the virtualization work on the shipments table in the table-v3 branch. The old table rendered every row, and with 20k shipments the browser froze on scroll. I added a windowed renderer with a fixed row height of 44px and an overscan of 8 rows.

In the first spike, the frame time while scrolling dropped from about 900 ms to under 16 ms. Sticky headers still broke because the header was inside the scroll container, so I moved it into its own grid row. Column widths drifted between header and body, which I solved by sharing one CSS grid template.

Not done yet: row selection with shift-click, and expandable rows, which need variable heights. Next I will check the keyboard focus behavior with Priya's spec.

summary: Variable-height expandable rows broke the table-v3 virtual scroller; settled on measuring heights lazily and caching them by shipment id.
body:
Expandable rows in table-v3 showed the shipment's stops and notes, and the fixed 44px assumption failed as soon as one was opened. Rows below jumped and the scrollbar length changed.

I tried recomputing all offsets on every toggle, which was too slow at 20k rows. The fix was to keep a height cache keyed by shipment id and a prefix-sum array that is updated from the changed index only. Unmeasured rows use an estimate of 44px.

The Vitest tests for the offset math pass. A Playwright test that opens three rows and scrolls still flickers once on the first render, so I will look at that tomorrow.

summary: Wrote the table-v3 Playwright scenarios for scroll, expand and selection, and found that the flicker came from measuring rows after paint.
body:
Spent the evening on end-to-end coverage for the new table. Three scenarios: scroll to the bottom and back, expand rows and keep the position, and select a range with shift-click.

The flicker from the afternoon was real. Rows were measured in a useEffect, so the first paint used the estimate and the second used the real height. Switching to useLayoutEffect for the measurement removed the visible jump.

Shift-click selection failed at first because the anchor row could be out of the rendered window. I now store the anchor as a shipment id instead of a DOM index. After that all three scenarios passed locally.

One remaining problem is that the tests are slow in CI, about 90 seconds for the table alone, because the seed creates 20k rows through the API. I will insert them with a SQL script instead.

I also noted that the sort header still resets the scroll position. That is a small fix for tomorrow.

Priya's keyboard spec is the other open item. Arrow keys should move focus between rows, and with a virtual window the focused row may not exist in the DOM, so I will scroll it into view first.

summary: Seeded the Playwright database with a SQL script instead of the API, cutting the table-v3 end-to-end run from 90 seconds to 21.
body: Replaced the API-based seeding with a single INSERT ... SELECT using generate_series in a setup script. It creates 20k shipments with random statuses, carriers and delivery times. The table suite now takes 21 seconds in CI. I also fixed the sort header so it keeps the scroll offset when the sort changes. The seed is deterministic through a fixed random seed, so screenshots stay stable.

summary: Keyboard navigation in the table-v3 grid works with arrow keys, Home and End, even when the focused row is outside the rendered window.
body:
Implemented Priya's keyboard spec for the new table. The grid has one tab stop, and arrow keys move an active row index held in state, not in the DOM.

When the active index leaves the rendered window, the scroller scrolls it into view first and then focuses the row after the next layout. Home and End jump to the first and last row, and Page Down moves by the visible row count.

I added aria-rowindex and aria-rowcount so screen readers know the true size of the list, as the DOM only holds about 30 rows. A quick check with VoiceOver announced the position correctly.

Open point: the expand button inside a row is a second focus target. For now Enter on the row toggles it, and I will ask Priya whether that is fine.

summary: Looked into why refresh calls from the table-v3 page sometimes returned 401 and logged the user out; two tabs rotating the refresh token at once caused it.
body:
While testing the new table with two tabs open, one tab was logged out after a few minutes. The API log showed two POST /auth/refresh calls within 40 ms carrying the same refresh token. The first one rotated it, and the second one was treated as a reuse and revoked the whole family.

This is the known race, and the table work just made it visible because the page polls more often. A reuse alarm that kills the family is correct for theft, but wrong for two tabs of the same browser.

I wrote a failing integration test that fires two refreshes at once. For the fix I considered three options:
- a grace window of a few seconds in which the previous token is still accepted once more;
- a lock across tabs in the client using the Web Locks API;
- both.

I chose both. The server keeps the previous token valid for 10 seconds and returns the same new pair, and the client takes a navigator.locks lock named auth-refresh so that only one tab refreshes and the others wait and re-read storage.

The test passes. The mobile app has no tabs, so only the server window matters there. I will tell Jonas that unexpected logouts should drop, but that the 10 seconds is a trade-off against replay protection.

Still to do: the metrics for how often the grace window is used, to see if it is too wide.

summary: Added the grace-window counter for refresh tokens and merged the Web Locks refresh into main; table-v3 rebased on top of it.
body:
Added a counter to the auth route that logs each time the 10 second grace window is used. After a morning on staging it fired 14 times, all from the same two tabs of my own browser, so the window seems to work as intended.

The client refresh lock was extracted into src/auth/refreshLock.ts. It falls back to a plain in-memory promise when navigator.locks is missing, which matters for older Safari. Unit tests cover both paths.

I merged this into main and rebased table-v3, which had a conflict in the api client file because both touched the 401 handler. I kept the lock version and re-applied the table polling interval change by hand.

After the rebase all Vitest and Playwright suites passed. Next is the filter bar for the new table.

summary: Built the filter bar for table-v3 with status, carrier and date range chips that sync to the URL, so dispatchers can share a filtered view.
body:
The old table kept filters in component state, so a reload lost them. In table-v3 the filters are stored in the query string and parsed by one small helper with a schema, which ignores unknown keys.

The chips show an active filter and clear it with one click. The carrier list has about 60 entries, so I used a searchable multiselect instead of a plain dropdown.

The date range reuses the existing date picker. Its timezone handling surprised me: it returned local midnight, while the API expects UTC day bounds. I convert at the boundary and added a test for a user in a UTC+2 zone.

The API query got an index on (carrier_id, delivered_at) because the carrier plus date filter took 600 ms on the staging data. It now takes about 40 ms.

Priya wants the chips a little less heavy, so a styling pass is pending.

summary: Wrote a plan for the onboarding flow for new Acme users after Jonas described the dispatcher first-login problems, and set up the onboarding branch.
body:
Jonas had a call with two new dispatchers who could not find where to invite colleagues or set their default depot. I wrote down what a first-time user needs to do in the first ten minutes, and the flow I would build.

Steps: set a password, pick a depot, choose the default view of the dashboard, and an optional invite of two colleagues. A progress bar at the top shows where they are, and each step can be skipped, except the password.

Technical plan:
- a new onboarding_state column on users with a JSON object of finished steps;
- a route /welcome that the app redirects to while the state is incomplete;
- a small step component API so Priya can add or reorder steps without code changes in the router.

I created the onboarding branch from main and added the empty route and the redirect guard behind a feature flag. The guard must not trap users who are already active, so existing users get the state set to complete in the migration.

Questions for Jonas: does the manager role with SSO skip the password step, and should the invite step be visible to dispatchers? I assumed yes to the first and no to the second until he answers.

I also checked the existing invite email, which links to the old settings page. It needs a new link target, noted for later. The migration is written but not yet run on staging.

summary: Jonas confirmed that SSO managers skip the password step and dispatchers cannot invite, so the onboarding step list is final for the first version.
body:
Jonas answered in the morning. Managers who come through SSO skip the password step, since they have none. Dispatchers do not see the invite step; only managers invite.

I changed the step definitions so each step has a visible(user) predicate. The progress bar counts only the visible steps, so a manager sees 3 steps and a dispatcher sees 3 as well, with different ones.

The migration ran on staging. It marked 212 existing users as complete and left 3 test accounts incomplete, which is what I wanted for manual tests.

The redirect guard has one edge case: a user who opens a deep link, such as a shipment URL from an email, gets sent to /welcome and loses the target. I store the original path in sessionStorage and return to it afterwards.

summary: Built the password and depot steps of the onboarding flow, with a password strength hint and a depot picker that remembers the choice for filters.
body:
Today's work in the onboarding branch was the first two real steps.

Password step: two fields, a strength hint, and the same rules as the settings page, at least 10 characters and not in the top common list. I moved the rule code into a shared module so both places use it. The API route sets the password and marks the step done in one transaction.

Depot step: a searchable list from /api/depots. The choice is saved as the user's default depot, and the shipments table and the charts use it as an initial filter. Before, every dispatcher had to set it on each visit.

I hit a bug where the depot step showed before the password step for users who had been invited by the old flow, as their state object was missing a key. The step order is now computed from the definitions, not from the stored keys.

Tests:
- Vitest for the visibility predicates and the order;
- Playwright for a complete run as a new dispatcher;
- a Playwright check that an SSO manager never sees the password step.

All three pass. The SSO test uses the mocked identity provider that we built earlier.

One thing I do not like is the full-page reload after the password is set. The access token is replaced on that call, and the client only reads it at start. I will make the client accept the new token from the response in the next session.

Priya sent mockups for the default-view step. I will start on it after the token handling.

summary: Fixed the client to pick up the new access token after the password step without a reload, and found a stale refresh token left in local storage.
body:
The onboarding password step returned a new token pair, but the API client kept using the old one until a reload. I added a setTokens function in the auth module that updates the in-memory copy and storage together, and the step calls it with the response.

While testing I found that the old refresh token stayed in local storage under a legacy key from the first JWT version. It was harmless, as the server rejects it, but it is a leftover that could be read by any script on the page. The module now removes the legacy key on start.

That made me look at what else we keep in local storage. Currently:
- the access token;
- the refresh token;
- the theme choice;
- the table column widths.

The two tokens are the sensitive ones. Moving them into httpOnly cookies would be the clean way, but the mobile app and the current API design rely on the bearer header. I wrote this down as a point for the next security review and did not change it today.

With the token fix, the onboarding flow no longer reloads. The Playwright run is 4 seconds faster.

I also tested the refresh lock from last week while the onboarding flow was open in two tabs. Both tabs stayed logged in for twenty minutes with a 5 minute token life.

The default-view step is next. It needs a preview of the three layouts, and Priya's images are ready.

summary: Added the default-view and invite steps to onboarding; managers can invite two colleagues, and the invite email now links to the welcome flow.
body:
Two steps finished in the onboarding branch.

Default view: three cards with a preview image from Priya, for the table first, the charts first or the map first. The selection is saved in the user's settings and the home route reads it. The images are 40 KB each as WebP.

Invite step: only managers see it. It takes up to two email addresses and uses the existing invite endpoint. I limited it to two to keep the step short; the full invite page in settings stays for more. Invalid emails are shown inline and do not block skipping.

The invite email used to link to the settings page, which a new user cannot use before logging in. The link now points to /welcome with the invite token, which sets the password in the first step. The old link still works for 30 days, so mails already sent do not break.

I found a bug in the invite endpoint: inviting an address that already exists returned a 500 because of a unique constraint. It now returns 409 with a clear message, and the step shows 'already has an account'.

Tests added:
- invite of a new address;
- invite of an existing address;
- skipping the step;
- the email link as a Playwright test using the mail catcher.

The full onboarding run now has 9 Playwright checks and takes 38 seconds.

What is missing: a progress save when the user closes the tab in the middle of the flow, and the copy texts, which Jonas wants to review. I will send him a staging link tomorrow.

summary: Jonas reviewed the onboarding copy on staging and asked for shorter texts and a welcome back message; changes made in one pass.
body:
Jonas went through the flow on staging with a fresh test account. He found the texts too long and asked to remove the sentence about data protection from step one, as it is in the footer already.

I shortened every step description to one line and changed the step titles to plain verbs, such as Set your password and Pick your depot. All strings are now in one file, so Jonas can edit them in a pull request without touching components.

He also asked what happens if a user leaves in the middle. The state is saved after each step, so they return to the first unfinished one. I added a small message, Welcome back, 2 steps left, to show that.

He liked the default-view cards. Priya will adjust the card corners next week.

summary: Explained to Jonas why the table and chart pages do a refresh call every 4 minutes, and checked that the rate is low enough for the API.
body:
Jonas saw in the logs a regular POST /auth/refresh per user and asked if something was looping. It is not a loop: access tokens live 5 minutes and the client refreshes about a minute before expiry, so roughly once per 4 minutes for an open dashboard.

I counted on staging: with 40 users open, that is 10 refresh calls per minute, each about 6 ms in the API and one row write in Postgres for the rotation. No concern at the current size.

I noted for the future that the rotation writes a row each time, and that the table of old refresh tokens needs a cleanup. Today it holds about 180k rows.

summary: The refresh token table grew to 180k rows with no cleanup; added a nightly delete of expired and rotated tokens and an index on the expiry column.
body:
Following up on the refresh question, I looked at the table of refresh tokens. It had about 180k rows, nearly all of them rotated or expired, and the lookup by hash was starting to take 15 ms instead of 1 ms.

Changes:
- an index on expires_at, so the cleanup query does not scan the table;
- a nightly job that deletes rows that are expired or were rotated more than 1 day ago;
- the 1 day is kept because the reuse detection needs the recent rotated tokens to recognize a replay.

The first run on staging deleted 176k rows in about 3 seconds. I ran the delete in batches of 5000 so that it does not hold a long lock.

I also checked the deny list for logged-out access tokens, which has the same growth problem. It has 60k rows, with entries that are useless once the token has expired anyway. I did not change it today, but it gets the same kind of cleanup next, keyed on the token expiry.

On the point that every logout writes to that list and every request reads it, I measured the extra query: 0.8 ms on average. It is fine for now, but it is one more thing to keep alive.

The job is registered in the same scheduler file as the report mails, and I added a log line with the number of deleted rows. Unit test for the batch loop included.

Next: the same job for the deny list, and then back to the onboarding progress save.

summary: Added expiry-based cleanup for the access token deny list and a test that a token on the list stays rejected until it would have expired anyway.
body:
The deny list held logged-out access tokens with their original expiry, but nothing removed rows after that time. I wrote a job that deletes rows whose expires_at is more than a minute in the past.

The subtle point was the test. A token must stay rejected for the whole of its remaining life, so the cleanup must never remove an entry that could still be valid. I added a test with a clock stub: an entry one second before expiry stays, and one a minute after it goes.

The first staging run deleted 58k of 60k rows. The remaining 2k belong to tokens still alive, as expected.

I also found that the logout of a mobile app token wrote its entry with the refresh token's expiry rather than the access token's. That made the rows live much longer than needed. It is fixed, with a comment in the code explaining the difference.

The deny list stays a growing piece of state we have to keep clean, and it adds a read to each authenticated request.

summary: Onboarding now saves progress when the user closes the tab mid-step, so the form fields of the current step are restored on return.
body: Until now only finished steps were stored. I added a draft object per step, saved to sessionStorage on change with a short debounce, and cleared when the step completes. Passwords are never stored, only the depot, the view and the email fields. I tested closing and reopening the tab in Playwright, and the invite fields came back. One small bug was that a restored depot id of a removed depot crashed the picker, so unknown ids are now ignored.

summary: Merged the onboarding branch into main after a final check on staging; 212 existing users are unaffected and three new test accounts completed the flow.
body:
The last review of the onboarding branch covered the migration, the guard and the feature flag. I ran the full test suite and then three new accounts on staging: a dispatcher, a manager with SSO and a manager with a password.

All three finished in under two minutes. The SSO manager saw no password step, and the dispatcher saw no invite step.

Before merging I checked that the redirect guard exempts the logout route, the API routes and the static assets. It missed the health check path used by Render, which would have returned a redirect and made the deploy look unhealthy. It is now excluded and there is a test for it.

I merged the branch, turned the flag on for new users only, and left it off for existing ones, as they are marked complete anyway. The deploy went through without problems.

I will watch the completion rate for a week. If many users skip the depot step, the default will need a rethink.

summary: Priya's polish items for onboarding done, and the first numbers show 9 of 11 new users finished all steps, with two skipping the invite step.
body:
Small design fixes from Priya: card corner radius, the spacing of the progress bar and a darker text color for the helper lines, which failed the contrast check at 3.9:1. It is 6.2:1 now.

I also looked at the first week of data from the completion events. Eleven new users started the flow. Nine finished every visible step, one stopped after the password, and one stopped at the depot step.

Two managers skipped the invite step. That is allowed, but I will tell Jonas, as he hoped they would invite colleagues.

The depot picker took 1.2 seconds to open for one user, because the list was loaded on opening. It is now prefetched when the step mounts.

Another small point: the welcome back message says 2 steps left even when it is 1. It uses a plural helper now.

The event table is small, but I added an index on the user id anyway for the report Jonas might want.

The branch is merged, so these changes went straight into main. I am done with onboarding unless the numbers get worse.

summary: Large table-v3 grids lagged when sorting 50k rows on the client; moved the sort to the API with keyset paging, and the response is about 70 ms.
body:
A manager at Acme loaded the full shipment history, about 50k rows, and sorting by delivery time froze the tab for over a second. Virtualization solved rendering, but the sort still ran in JavaScript over the whole array.

I moved sorting and paging to the API. The endpoint now accepts a sort key and a cursor, and uses keyset paging on (sort column, id), so deep pages do not get slower the way OFFSET does.

The client fetches pages of 500 rows and fills the virtual list as the user scrolls. A skeleton row is shown for pages not yet loaded.

Results on staging with 50k rows:
- first page: about 70 ms;
- sort change: about 70 ms plus one render;
- memory in the browser: from 140 MB to 38 MB.

I needed composite indexes for the three sortable columns that were not indexed yet. The migration took 4 seconds.

Select all now means all matching rows on the server, not the loaded ones, so the bulk actions send the filter instead of a list of ids. I wrote this behavior into the table's README.

The CSV export of the full table still builds everything in memory and is slow for big selections. I did not touch it.

summary: Went through the table-v3 branch against the old table feature by feature and wrote down 6 gaps before it can replace the old table.
Column drag-reorder and cell copy are in table-v3; reorder uses pointer events, so it works on touch screens in the dispatch office too.
body:
Implemented column reordering with pointer events, not the HTML drag API, as the latter does not work well on the touch screens that two Acme depots use. A column header can be dragged, a ghost follows the pointer, and a line shows the drop position.

The order is saved in the same settings object as the widths. A reset option in the column menu goes back to the default.

The keyboard alternative is Alt+Left and Alt+Right on a focused header, which Priya's accessibility checklist asks for. Screen readers announce Column moved to position 3.

Cell copy: Ctrl+C on the active cell copies its text, and a context menu offers Copy cell and Copy row as tab-separated text. For the row copy, the virtual list only knows loaded rows, so it fetches the row by id when needed.

I wrote tests for the reorder math and one Playwright test for the drag. Touch input was checked by hand on a tablet.

Two items are left: the print view and the review by Jonas.

summary: Jonas said dispatchers rarely print the table, so print stays at 1000 rows with a note; table-v3 is ready for a staging review.
body:
Jonas answered the print question: only a few managers print, and only short lists. So the print view renders the current filtered result up to 1000 rows and shows a note, Showing first 1000 of N rows, when there are more. It uses a plain static table inside a print stylesheet, hidden on screen.

I tested printing to PDF with 1000 rows, and it gives 22 pages with the header repeated on each. The status colors are kept through print-color-adjust.

With this, the list of six gaps is closed. I ran the full suite: 143 Vitest tests and 31 Playwright checks pass.

The branch is deployed to staging for Jonas to review.

summary: Switched the dashboard to table-v3 behind a flag for 10 percent of users; the first day showed one bug with column widths and no error spikes.
body:
I enabled the new table for 10 percent of users, chosen by a hash of the user id, with a header in the settings page where Jonas can switch himself on or off. The old table stays in the code until the rollout is complete.

First observations after a morning:
- no rise in client errors in the log;
- the median time to first rows is 310 ms, against 540 ms before;
- two users used the print view.

One bug was reported by a dispatcher: the column widths were reset on each login. The cause was that the settings were written to local storage only, and the new login flow clears storage on logout, which is intended for tokens. I moved the table settings to the user's settings on the server, with local storage as a cache, so they survive the logout.

This also touched the logout code. The clear of local storage removed everything, including the theme. It now removes only auth keys, which is a cleaner rule anyway.

I wrote a test that logs out and in and checks that the widths and the theme remain.

The settings endpoint got a size limit of 16 KB for the JSON, as a safeguard.

Plan for the rollout: 10 percent for three days, then 50 percent, then everyone. At each step I check the error log and ask Jonas for feedback. The CSV export on the new table is the same as before, and one dispatcher noted that a big export timed out again. That is known and is on the list after the rollout.

Priya wants to review the final look on the real data next week.

summary: Fixed the column width bug from the table-v3 flag rollout: saved widths were stored by index, so reordered columns got the wrong widths.
body:
The one bug from the first day of the 10 percent rollout was a column width problem. Dispatchers who had dragged columns around saw widths that belonged to other columns. The cause was that widths were saved in local storage by column index, not by column id. After a reorder the index pointed at a different column.

I changed the storage to key by column id and added a small migration that drops old index-based entries. A Vitest case covers reorder followed by reload. I also checked the flagged users in the logs and saw no further errors. The rollout stays at 10 percent until tomorrow.

summary: Wrote a Playwright check and a fix for table-v3 losing selection when a filter chip changes, and compared memory use with the old table over a long session.
body:
A dispatcher reported through Jonas that selected rows vanished when she changed a filter chip. I reproduced it in a Playwright scenario: select three rows, add the carrier chip, and the selection was empty even though two of the rows were still visible. The selection state lived in the virtual scroller and was reset whenever the data array identity changed.

I moved the selection into a set of shipment ids kept above the scroller. Rows now read their selected state from that set. When the filter removes a selected shipment, it stays in the set but is not counted in the toolbar. The toolbar now says 'n selected, m hidden by filters'.

The scenario now passes in 24 seconds with the seeded database. I added a second scenario for select, scroll far down, scroll back, and the selection must still be there. That one passed at once.

Then I looked at memory. I let the old table and table-v3 run for 40 minutes each with the 4 minute refresh calls and a 20k row dataset, using the Chrome performance tab. The old table grew to about 410 MB. Table-v3 stayed near 190 MB and did not climb.

One oddity: the height cache by shipment id never shrinks. For 20k rows it is small, about 300 KB, so I left it and wrote a note in the code. If the dataset ever reaches millions of rows, a bound will be needed. No other change was needed today. Tomorrow I will check the flagged users' feedback and decide whether to go to 25 percent.

summary: Added error tracking tags for the table-v3 flag so errors can be split by old and new table; the first evening showed no difference in error rate.
body:
To judge the rollout properly I needed errors split by table version. The client error reporter had no field for the flag, so every error looked the same. I added a tag 'table' with the value 'v2' or 'v3' to the reporter context, set once when the flag is read at startup.

The API logs got the same field through a request header, X-Table-Version. It is only informational and the server ignores it for logic. I added it to the access log format on Render and checked that the log search can filter on it.

For the evening I compared the two groups. The v3 group had about 10 percent of the sessions and 9 percent of the client errors. Most errors in both groups were the same canceled requests when a user navigates away. I filtered those out of the report since they are not real failures.

There was one real v3 error: a ResizeObserver loop warning that fires in the scroller on some window sizes. It is harmless and the old table had a similar one. I silenced it in the reporter but left a comment.

I also wrote down the numbers that will tell us whether to widen the rollout: error share, API 4xx and 5xx rate on the shipments endpoint, and median scroll frame time from the performance marks. Tomorrow I will fill that table in with a full day of data.

summary: Widened the table-v3 rollout to 50 percent after three clean days, and fixed a sticky header offset that showed up on the dark theme.
body:
After three days at 10 and then 25 percent, the error share of v3 stayed in line with its traffic, so I raised the flag to 50 percent. The 4xx and 5xx rate on the shipments endpoint did not move. The median frame time for scrolling in v3 users is 11 ms.

With more users came more reports. One was visual: in the dark theme the sticky header of the table was 2 pixels too high, so a thin line of the first row showed through. The header used a hardcoded top offset that matched the light theme border. The dark theme has a different border width from the theme work last year.

I replaced the offset with a CSS variable for the border width that both themes define. The header now uses calc with that variable. I checked both themes at 100, 125 and 150 percent zoom, since fractional pixels were part of the problem.

Another report said the row expand animation stutters on an older office laptop. I profiled it on the slowest machine I could get at through Jonas's contact. The cost was layout thrash because the expand measured the height after each animation step. I now measure once at the start and animate with a transform.

I added both fixes to the Playwright run, which includes a screenshot comparison for the dark header. The run time is still about 22 seconds.

Tomorrow I will check with Priya on the row spacing, since she said it looks slightly tight in v3 compared to the mockups.

summary: Went through the 6 gaps list against table-v3: the last two, saved column sets and the CSV export of the visible columns, are done, and the old table can be retired.
body:
Late session to close the gap list from a week ago. Four gaps were done earlier. Two were left: saved column sets per user, and exporting only the visible columns to CSV.

Saved column sets: the old table kept the visible columns in local storage. For v3 I stored them in the user settings row in Postgres, so they follow the user to another machine. The API has a new field on the settings endpoint, columns, an ordered list of column ids with a visible flag. Unknown ids are ignored, so removing a column later does not break old settings. I wrote a migration that copies the local storage values on first load of v3 and then deletes them.

CSV export of visible columns: the export button used a fixed list of columns on the server. It now sends the column ids, in order, as a query parameter. The server checks them against an allow list so that no one can request internal fields. Header labels come from the same column definition as the table, so they match.

I should say that large exports are still slow. A 50k row export takes about 40 seconds and sometimes hits the Render request timeout, because the server builds the whole file in memory. This is not part of the table work and I did not touch it. I wrote it into the notes as a separate topic for later.

Tests: Vitest cases for the allow list and the migration, and one Playwright scenario for reordering, hiding a column and exporting a small file, checking the header line.

With that, all 6 gaps are closed. I wrote the result in the plan file and told Jonas that table-v3 can replace the old table once the rollout has reached everybody. The old table code stays for one more release.

Tomorrow: the 100 percent step of the rollout, if the numbers hold.

summary: Rolled table-v3 out to all users; one report of a blank table for a user with an old settings value was traced to a bad saved column set.
body:
I set the flag to 100 percent in the morning after the numbers held at 50 percent for two days. The error share stayed flat.

By noon one dispatcher reported a blank table. I found her settings row: the columns field held an empty list. This came from the migration of local storage values. Her old local storage value was an empty array from a long ago bug in the old table, and the migration copied it as is.

The fix has two parts. The migration now ignores empty lists. The table also treats an empty visible list as no setting and falls back to the default columns. I repaired her row by hand and checked with a query that two other rows had the same problem. I fixed them too.

I added a Vitest case for the empty list. The old table code is still in the repository behind the flag, and I will remove it later.

Session handling had one small point: her access token expired during the debug call and the refresh worked, so nothing to do there.

Next: remove the flag and the old table code after a week without problems.

summary: Removed the old table component and the flag branches after table-v3 ran for everyone, and deleted about 1,900 lines of code.
body:
The rollout has been at 100 percent for a day without reports, and Jonas agreed that we do not need a fallback. I removed the old shipments table component, its styles, and the flag checks around it. The cleanup deleted about 1,900 lines and 11 files.

Two other pages imported a helper from the old table folder, the cell formatter for durations and money. I moved it to a shared formatters folder and updated the imports. A Vitest run found one missed import in the costs page tests.

I also deleted the unused local storage keys from the settings code, and left a one-time cleanup that removes them from browsers. The bundle size of the main chunk fell by 38 KB gzipped.

The type check and the full Playwright run both pass. Run time of the end-to-end suite is 21 seconds for the table part, as before.

I merged the branch into main. The next task is the cost of rendering the charts on the dashboard home page, which Priya mentioned feels slow.

summary: Profiled the slow dashboard home page: five ECharts instances re-rendered on every refresh tick, and batching them cut the cost from 480 ms to 120 ms.
body:
Priya said the home page feels heavy, mostly right after the 4 minute background refresh. I profiled it with the Chrome performance tab on the office laptop class of machine and a normal data size.

The page has five charts. Each one had its own query hook, and when the refresh tick came, each hook set state separately. That caused five renders in a row and each chart called setOption with a full new option object, so ECharts rebuilt everything. The total scripting time per tick was 480 ms, with a visible freeze.

I made three changes. First, one shared query for the home page returns the data for all five charts, so the state changes once. Second, the chart components compare the new data with the old data by a cheap hash of the series and skip setOption if nothing changed. In most ticks only one or two charts really change. Third, I switched setOption to the notMerge false mode with lazyUpdate, so ECharts updates only changed parts.

The scripting cost per tick fell to 120 ms. The freeze is not visible any more. The first paint of the page did not change much, about 900 ms on the slow machine, since that is mostly the bundle and the first query.

I also looked at the API side. The combined endpoint runs the five queries in parallel in Postgres, and the response takes about 160 ms. That is fine and I made no change.

One issue appeared: the hash of the series skipped an update when only the axis labels changed because the timezone setting changed. I included the axis labels in the hash. A Vitest case covers it.

I also lazy loaded the two charts below the fold with an intersection observer. This saved another 60 ms on first load.

I sent Priya a screen recording of the before and after in the performance tab. She will check the feel on her own machine.

Next step: the legend click on the home page charts resets the zoom, which is a separate bug that Jonas reported.

summary: Fixed the chart legend click that reset the zoom: the option update after the click replaced the dataZoom state with its defaults.
body:
Jonas had reported that when he clicks a legend item to hide a carrier, the chart zooms out again. I reproduced it on the delivery times chart.

The cause was in the change from last week. After a legend click, our handler stored the selected series in state and passed a new option object. The option contained a dataZoom block with start and end set to the defaults, so ECharts replaced the current zoom.

I changed the option builder to leave dataZoom out of updates. It is only set at the first render. The current zoom is read from the chart through getOption when we have to rebuild, and the range is kept in a ref.

I also found the same issue in the costs chart. It uses the same builder, so the fix covered it.

I wrote a Playwright scenario that zooms, clicks the legend, and checks the zoom range through the chart instance exposed in test mode. It fails on the old code and passes now.

The branch is new-charts, since the work belongs to the chart rework. Next I want to look at the tooltip, which clips at the right edge on narrow screens.

summary: Built the first version of the shipment status stacked bar chart for new-charts, with the colors from Priya's palette and an accessible data table fallback.
body:
Priya delivered the palette and the mockup for a stacked bar chart that shows shipments per day split by status: delivered, in transit, delayed, failed. I built it in the new-charts branch.

The API gets a new endpoint, shipments per day by status, with a date range and optional carrier and depot filters. The SQL groups by the delivery date truncated to the day in the user's timezone, and uses a filter count per status. For 90 days and about 30k shipments it takes 35 ms. I added an index on the shipment date and depot since the first plan showed a sequential scan.

On the client, the chart uses ECharts with stacked bars and the four colors from the palette. I checked contrast of the labels. The failed color on the dark theme was below 4.5 to 1 against the background, so Priya gave me a lighter variant, and I put it into the dark theme tokens.

The tooltip shows the day and the four counts plus the total. Clicking a bar sets the date range chip of the filter bar to that day, so a dispatcher can go from the chart to the table. That works through the URL state, the same one the filter bar uses.

For accessibility I added a visually hidden table with the same data and an aria label on the chart. A toggle below the chart lets people switch to the table view. The screen reader test with VoiceOver reads the table correctly, with headers.

Three tests are in: a Vitest unit test of the data mapper, an API test for the timezone grouping around midnight, and a Playwright test of the click to the table. The timezone test found an off-by-one for users east of UTC, which I fixed by passing the timezone name and not the offset.

Open points: empty days show no bar and the axis skips them, so I need to fill the gaps with zeros. Also the mobile width of the legend needs work.

Next session: gap filling and the narrow layout.

summary: Wrote the first stacked bar chart variant for new-charts: shipment status per day, but the legend toggles and the 31-day range needed a rework of the series build.
body:
Today's session continued the new-charts work with the shipment status stacked bar chart, now on the real API instead of the fixture data. The endpoint /api/shipments/status-by-day returns one row per day and status, and the client pivots it into one ECharts series per status. With 31 days and six statuses the pivot ran on every refresh tick, so I moved it into a memoized selector keyed by the response etag.

The first version also had a bug: days with no shipments in a status were missing from the series, which shifted the stacks to the left. The fix is to fill the gaps with zeros on the server, using generate_series in the query, and the bars line up now. Legend toggling works and keeps the dataZoom state, which matters after last week's fix of the legend click.

Open points: the 90 day range makes bars too thin, so I will try weekly buckets above 60 days. Priya still has to confirm the color order of the statuses, because failed and cancelled look too similar on the dark theme. Next is the accessible data table fallback for this chart.

summary: Answered Jonas's question why the cost per delivery chart differs from the finance export: the chart excludes failed deliveries, the export does not.
body:
Jonas asked why the average cost per delivery on the dashboard shows 14.20 while the finance sheet he got says 15.05. I compared the two queries.

The chart query divides the total cost by the count of delivered shipments, and leaves out failed ones. The finance export divides by all shipments that had a cost booked, including failed and returned ones, which still cost money. The difference explains the whole gap. I checked it with the same range for last month and got 15.05 when I included failed ones.

I did not change any numbers, since both are right for their purpose. But the label of the chart said only 'cost per delivery', which is misleading. I changed the label to 'cost per delivered shipment' and added an info tooltip with the rule.

I wrote the explanation in a short message for Jonas. He wants a second line in the chart for cost per attempted shipment, which would match finance. I put it on the list for the new-charts branch as a small task.

summary: Added the second line for cost per attempted shipment to the cost chart, so the dashboard now matches the finance sheet for any range.
body:
As agreed with Jonas, the cost chart now has two lines: cost per delivered shipment and cost per attempted shipment. The second one matches the finance sheet.

The API endpoint returns both numbers per day. I computed them in one query with two filtered sums, so it is a single pass. For a 90 day range it is 40 ms. The earlier unit test of the mapper was extended with a day that has only failed shipments, where the first value is null and not a division by zero. The chart shows a gap in the line for null, and does not draw a zero.

The colors come from Priya's palette. The two lines needed to be distinguishable without color too, so the second one is dashed. The legend shows the dash style.

I compared the sum for last month with the finance sheet again, and it matches to the cent.

One more thing that came up: the tooltip showed 14.2 and not 14.20. I switched to the shared money formatter, which I had moved out of the old table folder last week. It gives two decimals and the euro sign.

I added a Playwright check for both legend entries and the dashed style through the chart option. All tests pass and I pushed the branch. Jonas will look at it on staging tomorrow.

summary: Jonas reviewed the cost chart on staging and approved it, with one request to default the range to 30 days instead of 90.
body:
Jonas looked at the staging build of new-charts in the morning. He liked the two cost lines and the explanation tooltip, and confirmed the numbers against the finance sheet again.

His one request was that the default range of the cost chart be 30 days. With 90 days the lines are too flat for the daily decisions managers make. I changed the default and kept the picker with the 7, 30 and 90 day presets. The choice is remembered per user in the settings, the same mechanism as the columns of the table.

While I was in the settings code I noticed that the settings endpoint reads the user from the access token on each call. That is fine at the moment. I only noted that the refresh every 4 minutes means a changed setting can be read with a token that is a few minutes old, but the settings come from Postgres, not from the token, so nothing is stale.

I updated the Vitest tests for the default range and the stored preference. One test needed a fixed clock since the range is computed from the current day.

The branch is ready to merge after Priya checks the last mockup details. Remaining items on the branch: the tooltip clipping on narrow screens, and a pass on the on-hover highlight of the stacked bars.

summary: Fixed tooltip clipping at the right edge of the charts by confining the tooltip to the chart container and flipping it on narrow screens.
body:
The tooltip of the status and cost charts was cut off at the right edge when the cursor was near the last day, mostly on screens under 900 px. I worked on it in new-charts.

ECharts has a confine option for tooltips, which keeps them inside the chart's DOM element. I set it to true. That fixed the right edge but made the tooltip overlap the cursor point on the last bars, which hid the bar the user is looking at.

So I added a position function. It takes the cursor position, the tooltip size and the container size, and puts the tooltip left of the cursor if there is no room on the right. It also puts it above if there is no room below. The function is small, about 15 lines, and I put it in a shared chart helper file so all charts use it.

I tested at widths of 360, 600, 900 and 1280 px, with the cursor at the left, middle and right. A Playwright test at 600 px hovers the last bar and checks that the tooltip bounding box is inside the chart bounding box and does not contain the cursor point.

The touch case needed attention too. On touch screens in the dispatch office there is no hover, and the tooltip opens on tap. With the position function the tooltip stayed under the finger. I added a vertical offset of 24 px for touch, detected with the pointer media query.

The hover highlight on stacked bars was the other open item. The emphasis style dimmed the other segments but the dimming was too strong on the dark theme. I set the blur opacity to 0.5 and the focus mode to series. Priya looked at it over a screenshot and agreed.

All the tests pass. I asked Priya for a last visual review before merging the branch.

summary: Priya's last review of new-charts brought five small visual fixes; the branch is merged into main and the old chart config helpers are deleted.
body:
Priya sent her review in the evening with five points: the axis label color in the dark theme, the gap between bars, the legend font size, the title alignment, and the missing unit on the cost axis.

Axis labels: the dark theme used the muted text token, which was too faint. I switched to the secondary text token, which has enough contrast. Bar gap: set to 30 percent, as in the mockup. Legend font: 12 px to 13 px. Title alignment: left aligned with the card padding. Cost axis unit: the euro sign in the axis label formatter.

I went through the charts again at 100 and 150 percent zoom in both themes and made a set of screenshots for Priya. She approved them.

Then I merged new-charts into main. There were two conflicts, both in the shared chart helper file, since the legend fix of last week was done directly in main. I resolved them by keeping both changes and re-ran the whole test suite: 214 Vitest tests and the Playwright suite, with no failures.

After the merge I deleted the old chart config helpers that only the replaced charts used, about 400 lines. I also searched the code for leftover imports and found none.

I deployed to Render and watched the first 20 minutes of logs. No new errors showed up. The bundle size grew by 14 KB gzipped because of the new charts and helpers.

The branch is closed. Open topics from this work: nothing big, only the idea of a delivery time distribution chart that Jonas mentioned for later.

summary: Looked into a logout report from a manager and found the SSO callback set a token with a shorter life than the normal login, so it expired in the middle of a session.
body:
A manager told Jonas that she gets logged out about every 15 minutes when she signs in through SSO, while the dispatchers do not. I looked at the SSO callback code.

The normal login issues an access token with the short life and a refresh token, and the client schedules the refresh. The SSO callback issued the access token correctly, but it returned the refresh token only in the redirect fragment, and the client code read it from a different place. So the client never stored the refresh token for SSO users. When the access token expired after 15 minutes, there was nothing to refresh with, and the user was sent to the login.

The onboarding work earlier had changed the client to pick up new tokens after the password step. SSO managers skip that step, so that path did not run for them. That is why the problem was not seen in testing: the SSO test accounts were used for short sessions.

I fixed the client to read the refresh token from the fragment, store it the same way as the normal login, and then clear the fragment from the URL so the token does not stay in the browser history. I added a Playwright test for the SSO flow with a mock identity provider that waits past the token life, using a short test lifetime of 5 seconds, and checks that the session continues.

I also searched for other places that wrote tokens to storage and found three. All use the same helper function now.

I asked Jonas to have the manager sign in again. I will check the logs tomorrow for 401s from SSO users.

summary: Confirmed in the logs that SSO users no longer get 401 after 15 minutes; the fix of yesterday works for all five managers who signed in.
body:
I checked the API logs for the managers who use SSO. Five of them signed in since the fix. Each shows normal refresh calls about every 14 minutes and no 401 on the refresh endpoint.

The manager who had reported the problem used the dashboard for two hours and was not logged out. I wrote that to Jonas.

I also looked at the count of refresh calls in total, to make sure the fix did not add load. It is within a few percent of before. The query on the refresh token table takes under 2 ms, and the nightly cleanup of last week keeps the table small.

Nothing else needed doing. I closed the item in the notes.

summary: Planned the delivery time distribution chart Jonas asked for: a histogram with percentile markers, based on the shipment durations in Postgres.
body:
Jonas wants to see how long deliveries really take, not only the average. I wrote a plan for a distribution chart before building anything.

Data: the duration from pickup to delivery per shipment, in hours. For 30 days the dataset is about 10k rows. The histogram can be computed in Postgres with width_bucket, so the client gets 24 buckets and not raw rows. The percentiles p50, p90 and p95 come from percentile_cont in the same query.

Chart: bars for the buckets with vertical lines for the percentiles, drawn with ECharts markLine. The labels show the values in hours and minutes. The filters of the filter bar apply: carrier, depot, date range.

Decisions for Jonas: should failed deliveries be excluded? I proposed yes, since they have no real duration, and to show their count in a note below the chart. Should the bucket width adapt to the data? I proposed fixed 2-hour buckets with a last bucket for 48 hours and more, which is simple to read and compare over time.

Risks: the percentile query might be slow on large ranges. A test with 1 year of data, about 120k rows, gave 90 ms in a quick experiment, which is acceptable. An index on the delivery time column may still help, and I will check the plan.

Accessibility: the same table fallback as in the status chart, with the buckets and counts.

Steps: the API endpoint with tests, the chart component, the filter integration, the review with Priya. I estimate two sessions. I sent the open questions to Jonas and will start when he answers.

summary: Built the delivery time distribution endpoint and chart; with Jonas's answers the failed deliveries are excluded and a 48 hours plus bucket closes the range.
body:
Jonas confirmed both proposals: exclude failed deliveries with a note, and fixed 2 hour buckets with an open last bucket. I built the endpoint first.

The SQL computes the duration in hours as the delivered time minus the pickup time. It buckets with width_bucket into 24 buckets, and the last one collects everything from 48 hours. A second CTE computes p50, p90 and p95 with percentile_cont. The response has the buckets as an array of count and range, the three percentiles, and the number of excluded failed shipments. For a 30 day range the query takes 22 ms. For one year, 85 ms. The query plan used the date index, so no new index was needed.

Tests: a Vitest test of the mapper, and an API test with a seeded set where I know the answers. The seeded set has 10 deliveries with known durations, one failed one and one with a duration of exactly 48 hours. The exact boundary landed in the last bucket, as intended. The test also found that shipments without a pickup time gave null durations, which broke the percentile. I excluded them as well and counted them in the note.

The chart is a bar series with the three percentile markLines. The label formatter shows 'p90 31 h 20 min'. The lines are dashed in three shades from the palette. The note below says how many shipments are excluded and why.

The filters work through the same query parameters as the status chart, so I reused the hook. Changing the carrier chip updates the chart in about 150 ms.

The accessible table is there, and the toggle too. VoiceOver reads the bucket ranges well.

One point left: the percentile lines overlap when p90 and p95 are close, so the labels collide. I will need a label offset logic. Tomorrow I will do that and show it to Priya.

summary: Fixed colliding percentile labels in the distribution chart by staggering their vertical position, and got Priya's approval of the layout.
body:
When the p90 and p95 values were close, their labels were drawn on top of each other. I fixed that in the chart option builder.

The builder now checks the distance between neighbouring percentile lines in pixels, estimated from the plot width and the axis range. If two lines are closer than 90 px, the later label moves down by one line height. With three close lines they stack in three levels. The label position is set through the markLine label offset.

I tested it with three data sets: a wide distribution where the lines are far apart, a tight one where p90 and p95 are within one bucket, and a degenerate one where all three are equal because there are few shipments. The last case shows a single line with a merged label 'p50 = p90 = p95 12 h'. That merge needed a small special case, and a Vitest case now covers it.

Priya looked at screenshots of the three cases at 600 and 1280 px and approved the layout. She asked for the median line to be drawn a bit stronger, so I made it 2 px and the other two 1 px.

A Playwright test loads the chart with the tight seed and checks that the label boxes do not intersect, using their bounding boxes through the chart instance in test mode. It passes.

I merged this into main as part of the charts work and deployed. The chart is available to managers now. Jonas wants to watch how they use it for a week.

summary: Wrote down for the notes what the dashboard's background refresh and token handling look like now, after a question from the mobile app agency about call frequency.
body:
The mobile app agency asked how often their app should call the refresh endpoint, since they saw 401 responses at the start of some sessions. I looked at how the dashboard does it and wrote the answer.

The web client refreshes every 4 minutes while the page is active, and also on a 401 once. The access token lives 15 minutes, so there is margin. The refresh token rotates on each use, and there is a grace window for the case of two parallel calls, which came from the two tabs problem. The mobile app should serialize its own refresh calls, because a second call with the old refresh token inside the grace window is accepted once, and after that it counts as reuse.

Their 401s at session start were likely from the app using an access token that expired while the app was in the background. I advised refreshing before the first call after resume if the token is within 2 minutes of expiry.

I sent them the short description with the exact numbers and the error codes of the refresh endpoint.

summary: Merged a small fix for the settings page: the saved default range of the charts was not applied to the distribution chart after a reload.
body:
A manager noticed that the distribution chart ignored the default range he had chosen in the settings and always showed 30 days after a reload. The cost chart did it right.

The cause was simple. The new chart hook read the range from the URL state only and did not fall back to the user setting, which the cost chart does through a shared helper. I changed the distribution hook to use the same helper, with the order: URL, then user setting, then the 30 day default.

I added a Vitest case for the three levels of fallback and ran the suite. All tests pass. I deployed it and asked the manager to check on his side.

summary: Checked the dashboard's polling interval against the mobile agency's call numbers and found the web refresh tick is only a quarter of their traffic, so no change is needed.
body:
The agency asked about call frequency, so I counted requests per user in the API logs for one weekday-sized sample of traffic, split by client type. The web dashboard polls every 60 seconds while a tab is visible and stops when it is hidden. The mobile app polls every 15 seconds while the driver screen is open.

Over the sample the web dashboard produced about 24 percent of all calls. The mobile app produced the rest, mostly the shipment list endpoint. Postgres was not under pressure at that load, and the p95 of the list endpoint stayed at about 90 ms.

I also checked that hidden tabs really stop polling. They do, through the visibilitychange handler in the refresh hook. One tab left open on a second screen in the dispatch office still polls normally, which is expected.

I wrote the numbers into the notes for the agency and suggested they poll every 30 seconds and back off when the response is unchanged. We have no reason to rate limit them yet. Next I will add an ETag to the list endpoint, which would make their unchanged polls nearly free.

summary: Added ETag support to the shipment list endpoint so unchanged polls return 304 and skip the query result serialization; mobile traffic cost drops by about half.
body:
After the call frequency check I implemented ETags on GET /api/shipments. The server computes a hash from the max updated_at and the row count for the filtered set, which is a cheap query with the existing index on (account_id, updated_at). If If-None-Match matches, the API answers 304 with no body.

First attempt hashed the full JSON body. That saved bandwidth but not database time, so I replaced it with the cheap version-style hash. One edge case surfaced: deleting a shipment lowers the row count but can leave max updated_at unchanged. The count in the hash handles that, but a delete plus an insert in the same moment would give the same hash. I added a small trigger-free fix by touching a per-account version column on delete.

I tested with curl and with a Vitest integration test that sends the ETag back and expects 304, then edits a shipment and expects 200. The web dashboard needed no change because the browser handles conditional requests itself. Measured over an hour on staging with a script imitating the mobile polling, the mean response time for unchanged polls fell from 38 ms to 9 ms.

I sent the agency the header details. They said they will adopt If-None-Match in their next build. Remaining: the same ETag logic for the costs endpoint, which has a different filter set.

summary: Added a percentile marker toggle spec and checked the distribution chart against 1.2 million shipment durations; the p95 matches a manual query within one minute.
body:
Jonas asked whether the numbers in the new distribution chart can be trusted, so I checked them against raw data. I wrote a standalone SQL query that takes every delivered shipment of the last 90 days and computes p50, p90 and p95 with percentile_cont. Then I compared the result with what the endpoint returns for the same range. The p50 and p90 were identical to the minute, and the p95 differed by under one minute.

The small difference came from rounding: the endpoint rounds durations to whole minutes before bucketing, while my query used the exact interval. I decided to leave it, because the chart axis is in hours and nobody reads minutes there. I noted the rounding in a code comment in the distribution query so it does not look like a bug later.

I also tried the endpoint on the largest account, with about 1.2 million shipments in the range. The query took 340 ms with the existing index on delivered_at, which is fine for a page that refreshes rarely. For a one-year range it took 1.1 seconds, so I added a limit of 400 days to the range parameter and a clear error message above it.

Failed deliveries are excluded as Jonas decided, and I added a test with three failed shipments that proves they do not change the percentiles. The test lives next to the endpoint tests and runs in Vitest in about 2 seconds. Still open is the note under the chart that explains how to read the percentile lines; I will write it next, together with the toggle for the markers.

summary: Added the explanatory note under the distribution chart and the percentile marker toggle, with the choice saved in the user's settings.
body:
Both small requests from Jonas are done. The note under the chart reads that the last bucket contains all deliveries of 48 hours or longer and that failed deliveries are excluded. It uses the same muted text style as the cost chart footnote.

The toggle sits in the chart header and hides the markPoint and markLine entries for the percentiles by calling setOption with only those series pieces. I made sure not to replace the whole option, remembering the legend zoom bug from a few days ago. The state is stored in the user settings table under chart_prefs, so it survives a reload.

One snag: users with no chart_prefs row got undefined and the toggle rendered off. I defaulted it to on in the settings reader and added a test for the missing row.

The unit tests pass and the Playwright check for the chart toggles through the switch and reads the aria-pressed state. Next is the bucket export.

summary: Dispatcher got logged out while a long report was open; the access token expired after 15 minutes and the refresh ran only on the next API call, which came too late.
body:
A dispatcher reported that she was sent to the login page while she was reading a report that had been open for almost an hour. I looked at the request logs for her user and saw a 401 on the report data call, then no refresh attempt before the redirect. The cause was that the client refreshed the access token only after a call failed, and the failed call was a background load that did not retry.

I changed the API client so that it checks the token expiry before each call and refreshes if fewer than 60 seconds remain. A 401 still triggers one refresh and one replay of the call, as before. That covers both the early and the late case.

I wrote a Vitest test with a fake clock that moves 14 minutes ahead and then makes a call, and it passes now. It failed before the change, as expected. I also tried it by hand in the browser with a token of 2 minutes life on the dev server, and the report stayed open for 10 minutes without a redirect. I will watch the 401 count in the logs for the next days; before the change it was about 20 a day, mostly from idle tabs.

summary: Looked at the nightly session-less login logs after a dispatcher said she was asked to sign in twice in one morning; the refresh tokens of her two tabs raced.
body:
The dispatcher keeps the dashboard in two browser tabs. In the logs I found two refresh calls within 80 ms of each other from the same user, one with the rotated token and one with the previous one. The second call was treated as reuse and the family was revoked, so she was logged out.

This is the known two-tab race. A short grace window on the old token would fix it but weakens the reuse check. I noted the options: a lock across tabs with the Web Locks API, or the grace window of a few seconds. I prefer the Web Locks API because it needs no server change. I did not build it yet.

summary: Fixed the two-tab refresh race by taking a Web Locks lock around the token refresh, so only one tab calls the API and the other reads the new token.
body:
The client refresh function now runs inside navigator.locks.request('token-refresh', ...). Inside the lock the code first re-reads the stored token expiry. If another tab has already refreshed, it skips the call and uses the fresh token.

Before the change I reproduced the problem with a Playwright test that opens two pages in one context, sets the access token to expire in 2 seconds and fires an API call in both at the same moment. It failed in 7 of 10 runs with a 401 and a forced logout. After the change it passed 30 of 30 runs.

Browsers without Web Locks are rare in the client list, but I added a fallback that uses a localStorage flag with a timeout of 5 seconds. The fallback is less exact, and I wrote this in a code comment. I also added a log line when the fallback is used, so we can see whether it ever happens.

The server is unchanged, and the reuse detection stays strict. I deployed to staging and tested with two tabs and a throttled network. Next I will watch the reuse alarm counts for a few days on production. The mobile app is not affected, since it has one process only. Jonas will tell the dispatcher that the fix is out.

summary: Wrote the plan for the report builder's scheduled email feature after Jonas asked for weekly reports to managers, with three open questions on time zones and recipients.
body:
Jonas wants managers to receive a weekly summary by email, built from reports they already saved. I sketched the parts needed: a schedules table, a worker that runs due schedules, a render step that produces a PDF or CSV, and an email sender.

The schedules table would hold report_id, cron-like fields reduced to weekday and hour, a time zone, recipients and last_run_at. I would run the worker as a small loop inside the API process at first, with a Postgres advisory lock so that two instances never run the same schedule. A separate worker can come later if needed.

Open questions for Jonas: which time zone counts when managers sit in different places, whether recipients can be outside Acme, and whether a failed run should notify the owner. I suggested the schedule owner's time zone, Acme addresses only at first, and an email to the owner on failure.

For rendering, the existing CSV export would work for tables, but charts need an image. I have not decided between a headless browser and server-side ECharts rendering. Server-side ECharts with SVG is lighter, so I will try it first. A spike for that is the next step.

summary: Spiked server-side ECharts rendering to SVG for the email reports; it works for the bar and line charts in about 60 ms each, but fonts needed care.
body:
I made a small script that calls echarts.init with ssr: true and renderToSVGString for the cost chart and the status bar chart. Output is a valid SVG with the same colors as the dashboard.

The first result had missing text because no font was available in the render environment on Render. Setting a font family the base image has fixed the labels. Email clients mostly do not show SVG, so the image must become PNG. I tried resvg and it converted the SVG in about 25 ms with good quality.

The dataZoom and the tooltip parts have no meaning in a static image, so I strip them in the option before render. Accessibility fallback: the email gets the numbers as a small table below the picture.

Verdict: no headless browser is needed. I will build the real render module next, behind a small interface so the chart types can be added one by one.

summary: Wrote the scheduler's time zone handling for the weekly report emails: schedules store the zone name, and the worker computes the next run with the zone's daylight saving rules.
body:
After the first real email reached Jonas, I worked on the open question of time zones. The schedule stores a weekday, an hour and an IANA zone name such as Europe/Berlin, and never a fixed offset. A fixed offset would send the report an hour off twice a year.

The worker computes the next run time from these three values with the date library the project already uses. I wrote it as a pure function, nextRun(schedule, now), so it can be tested without waiting. The tests cover a normal week, a schedule at 02:30 on the night when clocks go forward, which does not exist, and one on the night when clocks go back, which exists twice. For the missing hour the run moves to 03:00, and for the doubled hour it runs only once.

I also checked what happens if the worker is down at the planned time. It now looks for schedules whose next run is in the past by less than 6 hours and sends them late, and older ones are skipped with a log line. Jonas had no opinion, so I took 6 hours as the limit because a report that arrives at the wrong part of the day is not useful.

The tests are 11 cases and run in under a second. One question is still open: whether managers should see the sending time in their own zone in the form, or in the zone of the schedule. I will ask Jonas and Priya, since it is mostly a design choice.

summary: Connected the report render module and the mail provider to the schedule worker; the first real weekly email reached Jonas with a chart image and table.
body:
The render module takes a saved report definition, runs its queries as the schedule owner, and returns HTML with inline PNG images and a table fallback. Charts use the SSR path from the spike, tables are cut to the first 50 rows with a link to the full report.

I first built queries with the owner's current permissions, and this is deliberate: if a manager loses access to a site, the scheduled report must not leak it. A test covers this with two accounts.

The mail is sent through the provider's HTTP API. The first send to Jonas arrived with the picture, but the dark theme colors made the chart nearly unreadable on a white email. The renderer now always uses the light palette from Priya.

A second problem was subject lines with umlauts, which came out wrong until I set the encoding. Each email contains an unsubscribe link that disables only that schedule. The link carries a signed token valid for 30 days that is not a login token, so it cannot be used to enter the dashboard.

Remaining: the UI to create schedules in the report builder and a rate limit on the number of schedules per user.

summary: Added the schedule form to the report builder with weekday, hour, time zone and recipients, plus a limit of 5 schedules per user.
body:
The form appears in the report menu under Schedule. It validates recipients against the Acme domain list on the client and again on the API. The time zone defaults to the browser's zone and can be changed.

The limit of 5 was my guess; Jonas can change it in a config constant. The API answers 409 with a clear message when the limit is hit, and the form shows it under the button.

I wrote a Playwright test that creates a schedule, checks the row in the list, edits the hour and deletes it. Priya will look at the layout of the form in the next review. A small bug found in testing: the hour select showed 24 h values but the saved value was off by one for the time zone change, fixed by storing the hour in local time of the schedule zone.

summary: Monitored the reuse alarm after the two-tab fix and saw no false logouts in three days, while one real alarm came from an old mobile app build.
body:
I checked the alarm log for the refresh token reuse events since the lock fix went out. Before the fix there were about 6 events per day from web users. Since then there are none from the web client.

One event came from the mobile app: an old build sends its refresh call twice when the app returns from the background with a bad connection. This is not our bug. I wrote to the agency with the request ids and the timestamps, and asked whether they can serialize the refresh in their app as we did in the web client.

Until they fix it, the user is logged out in this case and has to sign in again. A grace window would hide it, but I do not want to weaken the check for everyone. I will look at the log again at the end of the week.

summary: Found why the CSV export of the full shipments table times out for large accounts: it builds the whole file in memory and the request hits the 30 second limit at about 400k rows.
body:
Jonas passed on a complaint from a manager whose export of a year of shipments failed. I reproduced it on staging with a seeded account of 600k rows. The request ran 30 seconds and the proxy cut it with a 504.

Profiling showed three costs. The query is fast, about 2 seconds. The big part is the loop that maps every row into strings and joins them into one array, which took 11 seconds and pushed the Node heap to over 900 MB. The last part is the response write.

The heap size is also a risk for the other users on the same instance, since Render restarted the service once during my test because of memory.

I looked at the options. One is to raise the timeout, which only moves the limit and keeps the memory problem. A second is to make the export a background job that emails a link, which changes the experience a lot. A third is to produce the file in smaller pieces. I did not choose yet, but I want to avoid a big redesign now.
