For the moment I added a warning in the export dialog when the estimated row count is above 200k, and a count query to show the estimate. I wrote down the measurements in the notes: 100k rows take 4 seconds and 120 MB, 400k rows take 24 seconds and 520 MB.

This needs a decision with Jonas, and I will bring the three options to him.

summary: Jonas chose to keep the export as a direct download and asked for a quick mitigation, so the dialog now offers a date range split for big exports.
body:
I presented the three options. Jonas does not want emails with links for exports, because the managers want the file at once. He accepted that very large exports may take more work later, but asked for something now.

The mitigation is in the export dialog: when the estimate is above 200k rows, the dialog suggests splitting by quarter and can download several files one after another. Each file stays below 150k rows and finishes in about 6 seconds.

The split uses the same endpoint with from and to parameters, so the API did not change. I added a test for the quarter boundaries, including a year change, and the progress text for 4 files.

This is only a workaround. The memory use per request is still high, and a stronger fix is still to be done. I put it on the list for the coming weeks.

summary: Fixed an accessibility problem in the schedule form: the recipient chips could not be removed with the keyboard and had no label for screen readers.
body:
While testing the form with the keyboard I found that the little x on each recipient chip was a span with a click handler. It could not be focused and a screen reader just read the address.

I changed it to a button with aria-label 'Remove recipient name@acme.example'. Backspace in the empty input now removes the last chip and announces it in a live region. The focus returns to the input after a removal.

I ran axe in the Playwright test for the form and it reported no violations. The contrast of the muted help text was borderline at 4.4 to 1, so I darkened it slightly to pass 4.5.

summary: Priya reviewed the schedule form and asked for a preview of the email; I added a send-test-now button that mails the report to the owner only.
body:
Priya found that users cannot tell what the weekly mail will look like. Instead of building an in-app preview, I added Send test now to the form. It runs the same render path and sends the mail to the owner's address only, marked with Test in the subject.

A test send counts against a limit of 10 per hour per user, so nobody can use it to send spam. The API returns 429 above the limit.

Priya also asked for a friendlier empty state in the schedule list, and for the weekday names to show in the user's language. Both are done.

Two managers will try the feature next week with real reports. I want their comments on the table length before I change the 50 rows cut.

summary: Looked into a session cookie question from the notes: web clients still use short-lived access tokens, and a user who is deactivated keeps access until the token ends.
body:
Jonas asked what happens when he deactivates a user who is working at the moment. I checked the flow. The access token lives 15 minutes and the refresh call checks the active flag, so the user is cut off within 15 minutes at the latest.

For an immediate cut there is the deny list in Postgres, but it only holds logged-out tokens, not deactivated users. I could add a check of the active flag on every request, at the cost of one lookup, which the user table cache would absorb.

I did not change anything yet. I told Jonas that 15 minutes is the current worst case and asked whether that is acceptable. He wants to think about it.

summary: Jonas decided that 15 minutes is too long for deactivated users, so the auth middleware now checks the active flag with a 30 second cache.
body:
Jonas replied that a fired dispatcher should lose access nearly at once. I added the check to the auth middleware: after verifying the token, it looks up the user's active flag in a small in-memory cache with a 30 second life.

Deactivating a user clears the cache entry on the same instance. With more than one instance, the worst case stays at 30 seconds, which Jonas accepts.

A Vitest test deactivates a user and expects 401 on the next call after the cache is cleared. Another test checks that the lookup happens at most once per 30 seconds for a busy user.

The lookup cost is below 1 ms on average. Still, this is one more thing the token check depends on, and it does not feel clean. It is a reminder that token logout needs state on the server anyway.

summary: Checked what the nightly session-less login logs say about deactivated users after the 30 second cache change; the cache works and no active user was blocked by mistake.
body:
Since the auth middleware started to check the active flag with a 30 second cache, I wanted proof that it does not block the wrong people. I read the logs of the last days and counted the requests that were rejected because of an inactive user. There were 14, all from two accounts that Jonas had deactivated on purpose, and none from an account that was active.

Then I tested the delay itself. I deactivated a test user on staging and made a call every 5 seconds with its token. The calls worked for 24 seconds and then returned 401, which fits the 30 second cache. Before the change the same user stayed in for the full 15 minutes of the token.

I also looked at the load. The cache is in memory per API instance, so each instance asks Postgres at most once per user every 30 seconds. At the current traffic that is about 40 extra small queries per minute, which is not visible in the database graphs. Reactivating a user has the same delay, and I wrote that into the admin page text so nobody is surprised.

One gap remains: with two API instances the cache of one instance can be up to 30 seconds behind the other, which is still inside the limit Jonas chose. I did not add a shared cache. I added a Vitest test with a fake clock that checks the expiry of cache entries. I will leave the topic here unless the logs show something new.

summary: Wrote the first version of the costs page plan: a monthly cost table by site and carrier, a trend line, and a comparison with the previous period, based on Jonas's sketch.
body:
Jonas sent a spreadsheet sketch of what the finance people want to see. I turned it into a plan with three blocks.

Block one is a table by site and carrier with columns for shipments, total cost, cost per delivery and cost per attempted shipment, matching the two lines of the cost chart. Block two is a trend line per month for the last 12 months. Block three is a comparison against the previous period with the difference in percent, colored by direction, with a text sign for color blind users.

The data comes from the costs table in Postgres. I checked it for the 12 months and found some rows with null carrier, about 0.8 percent, from old imports. I will show them as Unknown instead of dropping them, so the totals still match the finance sheet.

For the API I propose one endpoint with a group_by parameter and a period parameter, and a cache of one minute. I estimated the page at about three days of work including tests.

Questions for Jonas: whether the currency is always euro, and whether managers see only their own sites. He said euro only and yes for sites, using the same permission as the shipments.

summary: Built the costs API endpoint with grouping by site, carrier and month, and checked that totals equal the finance sheet for the last quarter to the cent.
body:
The endpoint GET /api/costs takes group_by, from and to, and returns rows with shipments, total, per delivered and per attempted. It uses one SQL query with GROUPING SETS only for the totals row, and plain GROUP BY otherwise.

Permissions apply through the same site filter as the shipments endpoint, so a manager with two sites sees two sites. I wrote a test with three accounts.

I compared the quarter with Jonas's finance sheet. The first run was off by 212.40 euro. The cause was a timezone problem: shipments just after midnight were counted in UTC on my side and local time in the sheet. After using the account's time zone for the date boundaries the total matched exactly, and the per-carrier lines matched as well.

Null carriers show as Unknown, 0.8 percent of rows. Performance for a full year grouped by month and site is 140 ms with the existing index on shipped_at, and I added a composite index on (site_id, shipped_at) that brought it to 60 ms.

The response is cached for a minute by account and parameters. Cache keys include the permission set, so a change of sites does not show old data.

Next is the table component and the trend chart. I will reuse table-v3 for the grid and the ECharts config helpers.

summary: Built the costs page table with table-v3 and a fixed total row; sorting works by every column.
body:
The grid shows site, carrier, shipments, total and the two per-unit costs. The total row is pinned at the bottom so it stays visible when scrolling. Numbers are right aligned and formatted by the user's locale.

Sorting uses the client, because the response has at most a few hundred rows. A Playwright test sorts by total and checks the order.

summary: Added the monthly trend line and the previous period comparison to the costs page, with arrows and signs so the direction does not depend on color.
body:
The trend chart shows 12 months with two lines, cost per delivery and per attempted shipment, using Priya's palette. The tooltip shows both values and the month name.

The comparison block asks the API for the same length of time before the chosen range. A change of plus 3.2 percent shows as an up arrow with the text plus 3.2 percent, and costs going up are shown in the warning color, because for costs up is bad. Priya had asked for this, and I added an aria-label to say increased or decreased.

A problem came with ranges that have no data in the previous period. The first version divided by zero and showed Infinity. It now shows a dash and the label No previous data.

I also fixed the default range to 30 days, as Jonas asked for the cost chart before. The range from the settings page applies here too, after last week's fix for the distribution chart.

The page is behind no flag, but only managers see the menu entry. I checked a dispatcher account and the page answers 403 as expected.

Tests: three Vitest tests for the comparison math and one Playwright test of the page load. Priya will do a visual review.

summary: Priya reviewed the costs page and asked for four spacing and label changes; all four are done and the page is ready for Jonas to check on staging.
body:
Priya's review was short. She wanted more space between the comparison block and the trend chart, shorter column headers on narrow screens, the unit euro in the header instead of in every cell, and the Unknown carrier row in a muted style.

All four changes were small. The header unit change meant the CSV export of the table needed the unit in its header too, so I updated that and the test.

The page is deployed to staging. I asked Jonas to check the numbers with someone from finance before it goes to the managers.

summary: Started the refresh token families: each login now creates a family, and rotating a token inside it lets the server tell a normal refresh from a stolen, replayed token.
body:
Jonas asked for a way to see and end single logins without ending all of them, so the first step is a family table in Postgres. A family row holds the user id, a device label taken from the user agent, a created time and a last used time. Every login creates one family, and each refresh token carries the family id and a counter.

On refresh the server checks that the counter matches the last one it issued. If it does, it issues the next token and counts up. If an older counter shows up, the whole family is marked revoked, because that means a token was copied. I wrote the migration and the repository functions, plus six Vitest cases for rotation, replay and an unknown family id.

The endpoints and the settings page list are not built yet. Next is the list of families for the current user, with a revoke action. The existing refresh code still works for old tokens until the migration has run on staging, and I left a note in the auth module about removing that path later.

summary: Wrote the settings page device list design and its first API, and checked how the numbers compare with the family table on staging before wiring the revoke button.
body:
This session prepared the device list that sits on top of the refresh families. Jonas wants users to see where they are logged in, and Priya sketched a simple table with a device label, a last used time and a revoke button. I started with what the data can say, because the family table only has a user agent string and a last used time.

The user agent parser turned most strings into labels like Chrome on macOS or the mobile app, with an app version. Out of the 118 active users on staging data copied last week, a few had strings that gave only Unknown device. For those I show the browser name if there is one, and otherwise the creation time as a fallback label. Priya agreed that this is acceptable for a first version.

The list endpoint returns the families of the current user, newest use first, and marks the one that belongs to the request. That marker matters, because the user must not revoke the session they are using without a warning. The query uses the index on user id and runs in about 2 ms on staging.

I wrote the response type once in a shared file so that the web client and the API test use the same shape. The Vitest cases cover a user with no families, a user with three, and a revoked family that must not appear. A fourth case checks that one user can never see the families of another user, and it passed on the first run.

The last used time is only written when a refresh happens, so for a quiet device it can be up to 15 minutes old. I wrote this into the endpoint comment and will put a short note under the table later. Writing it on every API call would add a database write to each request, which I did not want.

The revoke action is not connected yet. It needs to set the revoked flag on the family and refuse its next refresh. What it cannot do is end the current access token of that device before it expires. That is a known limit of short tokens, and I will show Jonas the effect in a demo so that he decides if the window is acceptable.

Next step is the families endpoint for revoking and the table in the settings page, built with the shared table component.

summary: Built the families endpoints and the settings page list; revoking a device works, but the access token of the revoked device stays valid until it ends, as planned.
body:
I built the work planned yesterday. The endpoint GET /api/auth/families joins the refresh token families with the newest token row to get the last used time. The user agent is parsed with the ua-parser-js package into 'Chrome on macOS' style names. Mobile builds that send no usable string show as 'Mobile app'.

DELETE /api/auth/families/:id checks that the family belongs to the caller and sets revoked_at. The refresh endpoint now rejects tokens of revoked families with a 401 and a code family_revoked, which the client treats like a normal logout. I also made the reuse alarm skip revoked families, because a user who revokes a device and then uses it would otherwise raise a false alarm.

On the settings page there is a table with device, last active and a revoke button, and the current device is marked with a text label, not only a color. A confirm dialog shows before revoking. The button 'Log out other devices' calls a bulk endpoint in one transaction.

Tests: five Vitest cases for the endpoints, including a user trying to revoke a family of another user (404), and one Playwright test that logs in with two browser contexts, revokes one from the other and checks that the refresh of the first fails. All pass. The 15 minute window is still there. When I tested by hand, the revoked browser kept loading data until its token ended. I wrote this into the pull request text so Jonas can decide whether the window is acceptable.

summary: Jonas accepted the 15 minute window for revoked devices after seeing the demo, and asked only for a clearer note in the settings page.
body:
I showed Jonas the device list on staging, including the revoke of a second browser. He tried it and saw the second browser keep working for a while. He said that for lost laptops the window is fine because the data on screen is not new anyway, and the next refresh fails.

He asked that the page says this plainly. I added a short line under the list: 'A revoked device loses access within 15 minutes.' Priya reviewed the wording and asked for a smaller grey text with enough contrast, which I did.

I also fixed a small thing I found while testing: the list showed the family twice when a refresh happened in the same second as the list request, because the join returned two token rows. I took the newest row with a lateral subquery instead. A Vitest case covers it now. Merged to main after the checks passed.

summary: Started the onboarding flow for new dashboard users: a three step checklist after the first login, planned with Priya's sketch and built as far as the step container and progress state.
body:
Jonas wants new users, especially managers invited by SSO, to see what to do first. Priya sent a sketch with three steps: pick the default date range, choose the sites to follow, and create a first saved report. I worked on the branch onboarding.

The progress is stored in a new table onboarding_progress with user_id, step and completed_at, so it survives a new browser. I added the migration and a small API: GET /api/onboarding returns the steps with their state, and POST /api/onboarding/:step/complete marks one done. A user can also skip the whole flow, which sets a dismissed flag.

On the front end I built a Stepper component with a progress bar that also has text like 'Step 2 of 3', and each step is a card with a heading and a short text. The focus moves to the heading of the next step when one is completed, which I checked with the keyboard. For now the steps only contain placeholder content.

The flow shows when a user has no completed steps and has not dismissed it. One question remains: invited users who already had accounts before this feature would see it too. I think we should mark all existing users as dismissed in the migration, and I did that in a second migration step. Next is the real content of step 1 and 2.

summary: Filled the first two onboarding steps with the real default range picker and the site selector, reusing the settings components so the choices are saved the same way.
body:
I reused the date range control and the site multi select from the settings page inside the onboarding cards. Both write to the same user settings endpoint, so nothing new is stored in a second place. Completing a step happens when the user presses Next, not on every change.

A bug appeared: the site selector loaded all 140 sites of a large account into the card, which was too tall. I limited the list height and added a search box. For accounts with only one site, step 2 is skipped automatically and marked done.

The Vitest tests cover the skip rule. I will do step 3 next.

summary: Built onboarding step 3 where a user creates a first saved report from a template, and checked the whole flow with a Playwright run for a fresh user.
body:
Step 3 offers three templates from the report builder: weekly shipments, delivery times and costs by site. Choosing one creates a saved report with the user's default range and sites from the earlier steps and completes the step.

The Playwright test creates a new user, logs in, goes through all three steps and checks that the flow does not show again after a reload. It also tests the skip button. Both pass in about 20 seconds.

One thing left is the final screen. Right now the flow just disappears, and Priya wants a short 'You are ready' card with a link to the new report. I will add it tomorrow.

summary: Reviewed the mobile app agency's refresh handling after a burst of failed refreshes and found their app retries a revoked token every few seconds, which our server counts as replays.
body:
The agency wrote that some drivers were logged out of the app without having done anything. I looked at the server logs of the last two days around the reuse alarm. There were 14 families revoked by replay, and 11 of them belonged to the mobile app.

The pattern was the same each time. The app sent a refresh, the response was lost on a bad mobile connection, and the app sent the same refresh token again. Our server saw an old counter and treated it as a stolen token, so the family was revoked and the driver had to log in again.

This is a real weakness of strict rotation. The web client does not hit it much, because its network is stable and the lock keeps tabs from racing. For the app it happens in tunnels and in poor coverage, so the alarm is correct by its rules but harsh for the user.

I looked at a grace period. If the old token is presented again within 20 seconds and the family has not moved on, the server returns the same new token pair it gave before instead of revoking. That needs the last issued pair, or at least its hash, to be kept on the family row for a short time.

I sketched the change and tested it by hand with two refresh calls in a row. The second call returned the same new token and the family stayed active. A call after 30 seconds with the old token still revoked the family, as it should.

I have not merged this. A grace period weakens the replay check a little, so Jonas should know, and the agency should get a note that their app must also handle the 401 correctly. I wrote both points into a short message for Jonas and listed the decision as open.

The next step is Jonas's answer, then the migration for the extra column and Vitest cases for the 20 second window.

summary: Looked at a mobile agency question about a 401 with code family_revoked and explained that the app must treat it as a logout and not retry.
body:
The agency wrote that their app got a 401 on refresh after a user revoked a device in the web settings, and the app then retried three times. That is the new family_revoked response from the device list work. I explained in the answer that this code is final: the family is gone, so the app should clear its stored tokens and show the login screen.

I checked the logs. Between the release and now, 14 refresh calls with this code came from the app, most of them in bursts of three, so it matches their retry. No other kind of error is involved.

I added a line about the code to the API notes with the exact JSON body. The agency said they will fix the retry in their next build. Nothing to change on our side.

summary: Found that onboarding progress was lost for SSO managers because their user rows are created on first login after the migration marked everyone dismissed; fixed by tying dismissal to a created time.
body:
A manager who logged in with SSO for the first time did not see the onboarding flow, which Jonas noticed in a demo. I reproduced it with a test SSO account. The user row was created at the first login, but the flag showed dismissed.

The reason was in my migration. I had marked all existing users as dismissed, and I wrote it as a default on the column, not as an update of the existing rows. So new rows also got true. This is why the flow only worked for users created by invite, where the code set the value explicitly.

The fix has three parts. The column default is false again. A new migration sets dismissed to true only for users whose created time is before the onboarding release. The SSO user creation does not touch the flag.

I wrote a Vitest case that creates a user through the SSO callback and asks the onboarding endpoint. It would have failed before. I also ran a query on staging to find users affected: 6 SSO users had been created since the release, and I reset their flag by hand.

I will watch for new SSO users next week.

summary: Reviewed the slow shipment table with 200k rows for the table-v3 work: scrolling janked because row height was measured per row, and a fixed height estimate with measuring on demand fixed it.
body:
Part of the new table in the branch table-v3 is virtual scrolling for large result sets. Jonas reported that scrolling in a dispatcher's view of 200k rows was jerky. I profiled it in Chrome and saw layout work on every scroll frame: each row measured its height after render.

The cause was the cells with long address text, which wrap. The virtualizer could not know their height, so it asked the DOM. I changed the table to use a fixed estimate of 40 px per row, and only rows with wrapped text measure themselves once and cache the value. The address column also got a max of two lines with an ellipsis and a title with the full text.

After the change the frame times in the profile dropped from about 45 ms to 9 ms during a fast scroll. The scrollbar thumb also stopped jumping, because the total height is now stable.

I checked the keyboard behavior. Arrow navigation and Page Down still move the focus and scroll the row into view. One regression showed up: when a row is taller than the estimate, scrolling up by arrow keys skipped by a few pixels. I added a scroll margin to fix it.

Tests: a Playwright test scrolls to the end of 50k generated rows and checks that the last row is visible and the first is not in the DOM. The count of rendered rows stays below 80. It passes.

One point stays open. The column resize still triggers a full re-measure of the cached heights, which takes about 150 ms with 200k rows. It is acceptable for now and I wrote it in the branch notes.

summary: Added saved column layouts to the new table: users can hide, reorder and resize columns and the choice is stored in their settings per table.
body:
This step of table-v3 adds the layout memory that Jonas asked for after the dispatchers complained that they hide the same four columns every morning. A layout is an array of column ids with a visible flag and a width.

I added a JSON column table_layouts to the user settings, keyed by table name, and the settings endpoint validates the shape with zod. Unknown column ids are dropped on read, so a column that is removed later does not break the page. New columns are appended at the end and visible.

On the front end there is a column menu with checkboxes and drag handles. Drag and drop is also possible with the keyboard: space picks up the item, arrows move it, space drops it, and a live region announces the new position. Priya checked the menu and asked for a reset button, which restores the default layout.

The resizing saves after the pointer is released and with a debounce of 500 ms, not on each move. Before that, I saw 60 requests during one drag, which was silly.

Tests: a Vitest suite for the layout merge function with six cases, including renamed and missing columns, and a Playwright test that hides a column, reloads and checks the column is still hidden.

A corner case came up: the shipments table and the costs table both use the table component but have different column sets. Because the layouts are keyed by table name, they do not collide. I added a test for it.

The next step is the sticky first column on narrow screens, which Priya wants.

summary: Debugged why the cleanup of expired refresh families deleted too many rows and logged out users who were still active; the job compared the wrong timestamp and is fixed with a test.
body:
A dispatcher wrote that she was logged out in the middle of the day although she had used the dashboard all morning. Two more reports came in within an hour, so I looked at the nightly cleanup job for the refresh token families.

The job deletes families that have not been used for 60 days. Its query compared created_at with the limit, not last_used_at. A family created more than 60 days ago was therefore deleted even when it was used yesterday. The next refresh then failed with an unknown family, and the client showed the login page. This had been running for three weeks, but only since the first families passed 60 days, which is why the reports started now.

I counted the damage on the logs. The job deleted 212 families in the last run, and 171 of them had a last use within the last 3 days. These users had to sign in again, and no data was lost.

The fix changes the query to use last_used_at, with created_at as a fallback when a family was never used. I wrote a Vitest case with three families: old and unused, old and recently used, new. Only the first is deleted. The test failed on the old code, as it should.

I also added a log line with the number of deleted families and the oldest last_used_at among them, so that a wrong run is visible in the logs at once. A guard stops the job if it would delete more than 20 percent of all families, and logs an error. Jonas asked that the support is told, so I wrote a short text for him to send to the affected users. The next run is tonight and I will read the log tomorrow morning.

summary: Checked the cleanup job log after the night run: it deleted 9 families, all unused for more than 60 days, and the guard did not trigger.
body:
The log shows the corrected job ran at 03:00 and deleted 9 families. I checked each last_used_at in the backup of the table and all of them were older than 60 days. No support message about forced logins came in this morning.

The new log line also works and prints the oldest last use. I will look at it again after the weekend. The guard threshold of 20 percent is far away at this size, about 0.1 percent.

summary: Added a sticky first column to the new table for narrow screens, so the shipment number stays visible during horizontal scroll, with a shadow that appears only while scrolled.
body:
Priya asked for the first column of the table in table-v3 to stay in place when the table is scrolled horizontally, which matters on the dispatchers' small laptops. I used position sticky with left 0 on the first cell of each row and the header.

Two problems came up. The background of the sticky cells was transparent, so the other columns showed through. I gave them the row background, including the hover and selected states and the dark theme colors. Second, the virtualizer positions rows with transforms, and sticky inside a transformed parent does not work. I moved the horizontal scroll to the container that holds both header and rows and kept the transforms only vertical.

The shadow on the right edge of the sticky column appears when scrollLeft is more than zero. I used a scroll listener with requestAnimationFrame and a class toggle. It respects reduced motion since there is no animation.

A Playwright test scrolls right in a narrow viewport and checks that the first cell stays at the left edge. It passes in Chromium and Firefox.

summary: Wrote the plan for the 'log out of all devices' feature for the web client and weighed a user level token version against revoking all families one by one.
body:
Jonas asked for a real 'log out everywhere' button, after the lost laptop case earlier. We already have the bulk revoke of other devices, but he wants one that also ends the current session and works quickly.

I looked at two ways. Option one revokes all families of the user in one update, which is what the bulk button does. The access tokens stay valid until they end, up to 15 minutes. Option two adds a token_version integer on the user, written into every access token and checked in the middleware. Increasing it makes all existing access tokens invalid at once.

Option two closes the gap, but the middleware already loads the user for the active flag with a 30 second cache, so the version check costs nothing extra. The window would be at most 30 seconds. The downside is that each token carries one more claim and the mobile app tokens are affected too, which is intended.

I recommend option two together with the family revoke. Questions for Jonas: should a password change also increase the version? I think yes. Should the mobile app be logged out as well? He said earlier that it should. I wrote the migration and the middleware change as a plan, with tests listed, and did not code yet.

The effort is about one day including the UI text and the confirm dialog.

summary: Jonas approved the token version plan and added that a password change should log out all other devices too, so both go into one build.
body:
I sent the plan to Jonas and he answered within the hour. He agreed with the user level token version and the 30 second window. He also confirmed that a password change should increase the version, and that the device doing the change stays logged in by getting a new token.

I scheduled the build for the afternoon. The notes now say that the migration adds token_version with default 0 and that existing tokens without the claim count as version 0.

summary: Built the token version check and the log out everywhere button; increasing the version ends all access tokens within 30 seconds, and a password change uses the same path.
body:
The migration adds users.token_version integer not null default 0. Access tokens now carry a tv claim, and the auth middleware compares it with the cached user row. A token without the claim is read as 0, so tokens issued before the release keep working until the version changes.

The new endpoint POST /api/auth/logout-all increments the version in one update, revokes all families of the user and returns a fresh token pair for the calling device only if the body asks to keep the current session. The settings page has the button 'Log out of all devices' with two choices in the confirm dialog: keep this device or log out here as well.

The password change endpoint calls the same function with keep-current true. I tested by hand with two browsers: after the change, the second browser got a 401 at its next call, which came after the cache ran out, about 25 seconds later.

The user cache needed one fix. It is per process, and the API runs two instances on Render, so the instance that did not handle the request kept the old version for up to 30 seconds. This is inside the accepted window, but I wrote it down so nobody expects instant effect.

Tests: Vitest for the middleware with a stale version, for the logout-all endpoint with both choices, and for the password change. A Playwright test runs the two browser case with the cache time set to 1 second in the test config. All pass.

The mobile agency gets a note: a 401 with code token_version_changed means the stored refresh token is also dead, and the app should show the login. I added that code to the API notes.

summary: Fixed the report builder preview, which showed an empty chart when a saved report used a site that was later removed from the account.
body:
A manager reported that opening an old saved report showed an empty chart without any message. I reproduced it: the report filter contained a site id that had been deleted from the account, and the API returned a 400 for the unknown site. The preview code swallowed the error.

The API now ignores unknown site ids in report filters and returns a list of ignored ids in the response. The report page shows a short notice: '1 site no longer exists and was left out.' The report itself is not changed, so the user can save the cleaned filter if they want.

I also made the preview show the error text when a request fails for any reason, instead of an empty chart. Two Vitest cases cover the ignored ids and the empty list. Checked on staging with the manager's report.

summary: Checked the mail provider's bounce reports for the weekly emails: 3 of 41 recipients bounce, so scheduled reports now pause for an address after two hard bounces.
body:
Jonas forwarded a note that a few managers never got their weekly report. I read the provider's event log for the last four runs. Of 41 recipients, 3 addresses produced hard bounces every week, two with typos and one for a person who had left Acme.

The worker kept sending to them, which is bad for the sender reputation. I added a table mail_suppressions and a webhook endpoint that stores hard bounce events. After two hard bounces for the same address, the worker skips it and writes a line to the schedule's run log.

In the schedule form the recipient chip of a suppressed address gets a warning icon and the text 'Not delivered, check the address', which is not only a color. The owner can clear the suppression by editing the address.

I tested the webhook with the provider's sample payloads, including a bad signature, which returns 401. Three Vitest cases and one form test were added. Jonas will fix the three addresses with the managers.

summary: Upgraded Vite to the next minor version and fixed one broken import alias in the Vitest config; build time dropped from 41 to 33 seconds.
body:
I updated Vite and the React plugin after the release notes showed only small changes. The build passed, but Vitest failed in 12 files because the alias for the shared folder was resolved differently. I changed the config to use the absolute path from import.meta.url.

After that all 418 unit tests and the 36 Playwright tests passed. The production build went from 41 to 33 seconds on Render. The bundle size changed by less than 1 percent.

I checked the dev server with the login flow and the ECharts pages by hand, since the charts are lazy loaded. Nothing broke. Merged to main.

summary: Answered Jonas's question about how many users have more than one active device: 31 of 118 active users have two or more refresh families, mostly a laptop plus the mobile app.
body:
Jonas wanted to know whether the device list is worth the effort. I ran a query on the families table for families that are not revoked and were used within 30 days. Of 118 active users, 31 have two or more families. Most of these are a laptop and a phone, and 5 users have four or more, which is probably old browsers.

I also counted the use of the new list since release: 22 visits to the page section and 7 revokes, one of them the log out everywhere button. The numbers are small but real. I sent him the query and the table of counts. He said he is happy to leave it as it is.

summary: Started the accessibility pass for the onboarding flow and the device list: found 6 issues with a screen reader and fixed the 4 in the flow, leaving two in the device table for later.
body:
I ran through the new onboarding flow and the device list with VoiceOver and the axe checks in Playwright. The axe run reported two violations, and the manual pass found four more.

In the onboarding flow: the progress bar had no accessible name, the skip button was announced only as 'button', the step cards had two headings of the same level, and the focus was lost after the last step when the card was removed. I gave the progress bar an aria-label with the step count, renamed the skip button to 'Skip the introduction', fixed the heading levels and moved the focus to the closing card.

In the device list: the revoke buttons were all announced as 'Revoke', so I added the device name to the label, for example 'Revoke Chrome on macOS'. The second issue is the confirm dialog, which does not return the focus to the revoke button after cancel. I did not fix that yet because the dialog component is shared with other pages, and a change there needs a check of all of them.

After the fixes axe reports no violations in the flow. The Playwright test now includes the axe check for the onboarding pages, so a regression fails the build.

Left for later: the focus return in the shared dialog, and the table headers of the device list, which should use scope attributes. Priya will test the flow with her own screen reader setup next week.

summary: Fixed the two remaining screen reader issues in the device table: row headers were missing and the revoke button had no name that said which device it ends.
body:
The accessibility pass from this morning left two issues in the device list on the settings page. First, the table had no row headers, so a screen reader read only 'cell' for each device name. The device name cell is now a th with scope row. Second, every revoke button was just announced as 'Revoke', which made a list of six identical buttons.

Each button now has an aria-label such as 'Revoke Chrome on Windows, last used yesterday'. The label is built from the same fields as the visible row, so the two cannot drift apart. I also made sure that after a revoke the focus moves to the table caption, not to the top of the page, and that a status message says 'Device revoked' in a live region.

I tested with VoiceOver and with the axe run in Playwright, which now reports 0 issues on the settings page. The old count was 2 serious ones. Left to do: a check of the keyboard order when the list has more than 10 devices and paging appears. That goes into the next accessibility pass.

summary: Wrote a Playwright check for the device list and the onboarding flow that runs axe on each step, so the accessibility fixes of this morning cannot silently break again.
body:
After the fixes of the morning I wanted a guard. The new spec file e2e/a11y.spec.ts opens the settings page with a user who has three devices, runs axe, and fails on any serious or critical issue. A second test walks through the three onboarding steps for a fresh user and runs axe after each one.

The first run failed on step 2, because the site selector dropdown had a low contrast placeholder color in the dark theme. The ratio was 3.8 to 1 and the limit is 4.5. I changed the token to a lighter gray and the check passes now.

The tests add about 14 seconds to the Playwright run, which is now 3 minutes and 10 seconds in CI. I kept them in the main suite, not in a nightly job, since the cost is small. Next I want to add the report builder to the same check, but it has a known issue with the chart legend that needs its own fix.

summary: Traced duplicate 'family_revoked' logouts to two browser tabs sending the same refresh token at the same moment, and added a short grace window so the second request gets the new token.
body:
Support noted that a few users were logged out right after opening the dashboard in a second tab. In the server log I found pairs of refresh calls with the same token, about 40 ms apart, from one family. The first one rotated the token. The second one arrived with the old token and was counted as a replay, so the whole family was revoked.

The cause is that both tabs wake up from a stored expiry time and refresh at once. The family check was strict: any use of a rotated token is a theft. For a real attack that is right, but two tabs of one browser are a normal case.

I added a grace window of 10 seconds. If a rotated token is used again inside the window, and it is the direct predecessor of the current token, the server answers with the current pair again and does not revoke. The old token is still treated as a replay after the window, or if it is older than the predecessor.

There is a unit test with two parallel requests, one with a replay after 11 seconds, and one with a predecessor of the predecessor. All three behave as planned. I also logged a counter 'refresh_grace_used' to see how often it happens on staging.

On the client side, a tab lock with the Web Locks API would remove most of these races. I wrote that as the next step, because the server fix alone does not stop two tabs from doing double work. The grace window stays as the safety net. I told no one outside yet, because I want one day of counter data first.

The mobile app agency does not share a browser, so they are not affected by this change.

summary: Added the Web Locks tab coordination for token refresh and checked on staging: the grace counter fell from 17 uses in a day to 2 after the change.
body:
The client now takes a lock named 'auth-refresh' before it refreshes the access token. A tab that waits for the lock first checks whether another tab has already stored a fresh token in local storage; if so it uses that and skips the call. The code is in src/auth/refreshLock.ts, about 45 lines.

For browsers without the Web Locks API there is a fallback with a localStorage flag and a 5 second timeout. It is not perfect, but the server grace window covers the rest. I tested the fallback by disabling navigator.locks in a Playwright test with two pages sharing one context.

On staging, the counter from the grace window change showed 17 uses in the last day before the lock. After deploying the lock to staging, a day of normal use by the team gave 2 uses. Both came from the fallback path in an old Safari.

I also checked that a tab that was in the background for an hour comes back correctly. It takes the lock, refreshes, and the other tabs pick up the token from storage via the storage event. No extra 401 was seen.

Done for this topic. The production deploy goes with the next release. I will look at the counter again after a few days there.

summary: Planned the new-charts style for the delivery time charts: a shared ECharts theme object, with tokens from Priya's design, so light and dark themes stop having separate chart code.
body:
The delivery time charts were each built with their own color and font settings, which is why the dark theme work left a few charts with unreadable axis labels. Priya sent a small palette sheet: eight series colors that keep contrast on both backgrounds, a text color, a grid line color, and tooltip styles.

My plan is one module, src/charts/theme.ts, that exports a function getChartTheme(mode) and registers it with echarts.registerTheme. Each chart then only passes the theme name and its data options. I listed all chart components: there are 9. Four of them set colors by hand, and three set fonts by hand. Those get cleaned up first.

There are also two things that the theme cannot cover. The heat map needs a continuous scale, so it takes its own visualMap colors. The pie chart on the costs page needs patterns for color blind users, which Priya wants as a second step.

I also thought about the legend. The legend position differs between charts, and that has caused bugs before. The plan sets one default (top, left aligned) and allows an override per chart.

Order of work: first the theme module and the line chart as a test, then bars, then the rest. I made a branch new-charts for it. Each chart gets a Vitest snapshot of its option object, so a change to colors is visible in review.

Jonas does not need to decide anything here. I will show Priya the first chart in the dark theme when it is done, within a few days.

summary: Built the shared chart theme module and moved the delivery time line chart to it; the dark theme labels are readable now and the chart code shrank by 40 lines.
body:
I wrote src/charts/theme.ts with the eight series colors, text, grid and tooltip tokens for light and dark. The line chart for delivery times now calls echarts.init with the theme name and only sets its series and axes. The chart component lost about 40 lines of color and font settings.

The theme switch used to rebuild the chart option. Now the component disposes and re-inits the chart on a mode change, which is simpler and fine for the data sizes we have. A Vitest snapshot covers the option object. Priya will see the dark version tomorrow.

summary: Moved the bar charts and the cost trend chart to the shared theme and found that tooltips ignored the dark mode because they were rendered as HTML with fixed inline colors.
body:
Five more charts moved to the theme module today: the three bar charts, the cost trend line and the on-time rate gauge. Each lost its local color settings and got a snapshot test of its option.

While checking the dark theme I found that tooltips still showed white boxes with dark text on the bar charts. The cause was a tooltip formatter that returned an HTML string with inline style attributes, color #333 and background white. The theme tooltip settings do not reach those, because the formatter output wins.

I changed the formatter into a small helper, formatTooltip, which builds the markup with CSS classes. The classes get their colors from the CSS variables of the dashboard theme, so they follow light and dark without any chart code. Three charts used the same inline pattern, so one helper replaced three copies.

There was a second problem: the tooltip of the stacked bar chart listed the series in reverse order compared to the legend. That was in the old code as well. I sorted the entries by the series index so they match the legend order.

The tests found one regression. The snapshot of the cost trend chart changed because the area fill opacity was 0.3 in the theme and 0.15 before. I kept 0.15 as an override in that chart.

Visual check: I made screenshots of all moved charts in both themes with a Playwright script and looked at them side by side. They are consistent. Two things remain: the heat map with its own scale, and the pie chart patterns that Priya wants. Those two are for the next sessions on this branch.

summary: Built the heat map on the shared theme with its own continuous color scale, tested on both themes, and fixed an unreadable label on the darkest cells.
body:
The heat map shows deliveries by hour of day and weekday for each site. It cannot use the eight series colors, because it needs a continuous scale from low to high. I added a second export to the theme module, getHeatScale(mode), that returns a list of seven colors for the visualMap.

For light mode the scale goes from a pale blue to a dark blue. For dark mode it starts at a dark slate and ends at a bright cyan, so that more is always brighter against the background. Priya's palette sheet had no value for this, so I derived the ends from her primary color and sent her the result for review.

The cells show their number as a label. On the darkest cells of the light scale the label was dark gray, and the contrast was only 2.1 to 1. I now choose the label color per cell by the luminance of the cell color: white above a threshold of darkness, near black otherwise. A small function in the same file does that, with a test for the two ends of the scale.

The visualMap itself had its own text color, set to black. It is now taken from the theme, so the legend of the scale is readable in the dark mode.

Another detail was the empty cells. A site with no deliveries in an hour showed as the lowest color, which looks the same as a very small number. I changed it so that a zero is a distinct neutral cell with a dashed outline. A tooltip says 'no deliveries'.

I checked the chart with 3 data sets: one normal, one with a single busy hour, and one all zeros. The all zero case used to crash the scale because min and max were equal. It now sets max to 1 in that case.

The snapshot tests pass, and the screenshot comparison shows no change on the other charts. Open: the pie patterns, which I will do next after Priya's answer.

summary: Added pattern fills to the cost pie chart so the slices differ without color, using ECharts decal patterns, and checked them with a simulated color blind view.
body:
Priya asked that the pie chart on the costs page should not rely on color alone. ECharts has a decal option for this, and I turned it on for the pie with a set of six patterns: stripes in two angles, dots, small crosses, a wave and plain.

The decals use the series color for their lines, so they work in both themes. In the dark mode the pattern lines were too faint, so the theme now sets the decal color to a slightly lighter shade of each slice color.

I looked at the chart through the color vision simulation in the browser dev tools, for deuteranopia and for grayscale. All slices could be told apart. With more than six slices, the patterns repeat, and the chart groups everything after the fifth carrier into 'Other', which was already the case.

The legend shows the same patterns next to the names, which ECharts does by default once the decal is on. I checked that the click to hide a slice still works.

The bar charts have the same question for stacked series. I made a note to try decals there too, but I think the stacks are readable because of the order and the labels. I will ask Priya.

Tests: the option snapshot of the pie changed as expected, and I updated it. One test that counts the series colors needed the new decal field, which I fixed.

summary: Priya reviewed the themed charts in both modes and asked for three changes: thinner grid lines, a smaller legend font and consistent axis name spacing; all three are done.
body:
I sent Priya the screenshots of all nine charts in light and dark. She was happy with the colors and the heat map scale, and the pie patterns got a thumbs up.

Her three changes were: the grid lines are too strong and should be lighter, the legend font should go from 14 to 12 pixels, and the axis names have different distances to the axis in different charts.

The grid line color token now has a lower opacity, 0.35 in the light theme and 0.25 in the dark one. The legend font size is in the theme, so it changed in all charts at once. For the axis names I found that four charts set nameGap by hand, with values from 20 to 40. I removed those and set one default of 28 in the theme.

The long axis names on the delivery time chart now got cut off on narrow screens, so I let that chart use a rotate of 0 and a shorter name 'Hours'. The unit is in the tooltip anyway.

I ran the Playwright screenshot script again and the snapshots of the option objects were updated in one commit, so the review can see exactly the three values. Priya will take a last look when the branch is merged on staging.

summary: Merged new-charts to main after a full test run and a staging check; the chart bundle got 18 KB smaller because the per-chart ECharts imports are now shared.
body:
Today I finished the branch. First I rebased new-charts on main, which had two commits from the refresh work. There was one conflict in the package lock file, which I solved by regenerating it.

The full test run passed: 412 Vitest tests and the Playwright suite in 3 minutes 20 seconds. The option snapshots for the nine charts are all in the repository now, which will make later style changes easy to review.

While moving the charts I had also changed the ECharts imports. Before, each chart component imported what it needed from 'echarts/components', and some imported the whole 'echarts' package by mistake. Now the theme module registers the shared pieces once with echarts.use, and the charts only import the chart types. The production bundle for the dashboard chunk went from 612 KB to 594 KB, so 18 KB less, and the heat map chunk is loaded lazily as before.

On staging I checked every page with charts, in both themes, with the real data of the last quarter. Two things showed up. On the costs page the legend overlapped the chart on a 1024 pixel wide window. I set the grid top to leave room for two legend rows, and it was fine. On the shipment page the line chart tooltip showed a number with 6 decimals; the formatter was passing the raw value. I used the same number formatter as the table.

I asked Priya for the last look, and she approved with one remark about the pie chart title weight, which I changed in the theme to 600.

The branch is merged and deployed to staging. The production deploy goes with the next release. I deleted the local branch. A note for later: the report builder charts use their own option builder and are not on the theme yet. That would be a good small task for the report builder work.

I also updated the README section on charts with a short description of the theme module and how to add a new chart: copy a chart component, pick a theme name, write the snapshot test.

summary: Moved the report builder preview charts to the shared theme, so saved reports look the same as the dashboard in dark mode.
body:
This was the small task noted after the merge of new-charts. The report builder had its own function, buildPreviewOption, that created the ECharts options with a fixed palette and white background. In dark mode the preview was a bright box.

I replaced the palette and text settings with the theme name and kept only the data parts. The PDF export of reports uses the light theme on purpose, so I pass the mode explicitly there and do not follow the user setting.

Two snapshot tests changed and I updated them. I also checked a saved report with 7 series: the colors repeat after 8, as in the dashboard. Nothing else was needed. The preview of the scheduled report email image still uses the old code path, which I will check separately.

summary: Found why the scheduled report email images ignored the new chart theme: they are rendered by a server job with its own ECharts setup, which now calls the same theme module.
body:
After the preview fix I looked at the email images of scheduled reports. They were still using the old blue palette. The images are made by a Node job that renders ECharts to SVG on the server, and it had a copy of the old color list in jobs/renderChart.ts.

The theme module only used browser things in one place, a check of the CSS variable for the tooltip. I split the file so that the token part has no DOM access, and the server job imports only that part. The job registers the light theme and renders with it.

I rendered the same report before and after and compared the images. Colors now match the dashboard, and the legend text is 12 pixels like in the app. The SVG size got slightly smaller, 31 KB instead of 36 KB, as the grid lines are thinner.

One problem: the fonts. The server has no Inter font, so the text falls back to a default sans. That was the case before as well. For email it is acceptable, as the mail client converts the image anyway. I noted it for Priya in case she wants to bundle a font.

A test now renders a sample option on the server and checks that the SVG contains the first theme color. The weekly job ran fine in the dry run for 5 reports.

summary: Reviewed the mobile agency's report of users logged out after the app was in the background overnight and found their refresh used an access token that the server had already rotated away.
body:
The agency sent logs of three drivers who were asked to log in again every morning. In each log, the app woke up, sent a refresh with the token it had stored, and received 401 with code family_revoked.

On our side I looked up the three families. Each had a replay event the evening before. The sequence was: the app refreshed at 21:10, got a new pair and began to save it, then the operating system suspended the app before the write was finished. In the morning the app still had the old refresh token and sent it. For the server that is a replay of a rotated token, outside the 10 second grace window.

So the server did what it was designed to do, but the case is not a theft. The cause is on the app side: it should store the new token before it uses the response, and it should do the write atomically. The agency said they save the access token first and the refresh token after.

I wrote them a short note with the order of operations: write both tokens in one secure storage call, or write the refresh token first. I also suggested that on family_revoked the app shows the login screen once and does not retry, which they already do after our talk last week.

For our server I thought about a longer grace window for the mobile client. I do not want that, because a window of hours would weaken the replay detection a lot. A narrower option would be to keep the predecessor valid until the successor is first used. That is a real design, and many systems do it, but it needs a state field 'successor_used_at' and a migration.

I put the option in the notes for Jonas and the agency. For now the agency fixes the storage order, and I will count how many of the revoked families in the next week have this pattern. If it stays above a few per week, we build the successor rule.

summary: Counted the family_revoked events of the last week: 11 of 14 follow the suspended-app pattern, so the successor-used rule is worth building if the agency's fix does not help.
body:
I wrote a query on the auth event table that finds revoked families where the replayed token was the direct predecessor of the current one and the last rotation was more than 10 seconds earlier. Over the last 7 days there were 14 revoked families, and 11 of them match this pattern, all from the mobile app user agent.

The other 3 were from web browsers, and two of those were users who had a very old tab open after the lock change. The third one looks like a real replay from a different IP address, and I flagged that account to Jonas for a password reset.

The agency released a build with the changed storage order two days ago, but only about a fifth of the drivers have updated. I will repeat the query next week and compare only the updated builds.

summary: Started the new onboarding tips for managers: a short tour of the costs page that shows once, built on the onboarding step container and stored with the same dismissal time field.
body:
Jonas asked for a way to show new managers what the costs page offers, as they mostly come from the SSO and skip the settings. Priya's sketch has three small tooltips that point at the site filter, the trend line and the previous period comparison.

I reused the step container of the onboarding flow and the dismissal field that I changed some days ago to be tied to a created time. A manager who is created after the tour was released sees it once. Older users do not, unless they choose 'Show tour' in the help menu.

The tooltips are positioned with a small library that we already use for popovers, and they follow the elements when the page resizes. On narrow screens the tour changes to a bottom sheet with next and back buttons. I took care that the focus moves into the tooltip and returns to the page element when the tour ends, and that Escape ends the tour. The screen reader reads each step as a dialog with a label.

The tour state is stored in the user settings: a field tours.costs with the step reached and the dismissed time. If someone closes the browser in the middle of the tour, the tour continues at the same step at the next visit.

Tests: Vitest tests for the state machine with 6 cases, and a Playwright test for a new manager that goes through all three steps. One flaky point: the trend line tooltip points at a chart element that is not there until the data is loaded. The tour now waits for the element with a 5 second timeout and skips the step if it does not appear.

Axe finds no issue on the tour. What is left: the German text from Priya, and the help menu entry that restarts the tour. I will do them when I have the texts.

summary: Built the session-less login log report that Jonas asked for: a weekly table of logins by user, device type and failure reason, with a CSV download that is slow for the full quarter.
body:
Jonas wants to see once a week how many people log in, from which device type, and why logins fail, so that he can answer questions of the Acme IT without asking me. The data is in the auth event table that we already keep for the refresh families.

I wrote an endpoint /api/admin/login-report with a date range and grouping by week. For each week it returns the number of successful logins, the number of distinct users, the split between web and mobile by user agent, and the failures by reason: wrong password, inactive user, SSO error, and family_revoked.

The page is a table with a small stacked bar chart on the shared chart theme. Only the admin role can open it. A user with a manager role gets 403, and there is a test for that.

The numbers need care. A refresh is not a login, so I count only events of type login and sso_login. The first draft counted refreshes as well and gave 40 times too many logins. I compared the result with a manual count in SQL for one week: 1,284 logins in both.

For the failure reasons I had to map the old event codes. Before the families existed, the event had a single reason text. A small mapping table in the code handles both, and unknown reasons are shown as 'other'. In the last quarter that is 2% of events.

The CSV download calls the same query with no limit. For one month it takes 2 seconds, but for a whole quarter it takes about 25 seconds and the request is close to the Render timeout of 30 seconds. The export builds the whole file in memory first, as the other exports do. I did not change it now, and I added a warning in the UI for ranges over 60 days.

The long exports are a known weak point of all CSV exports. I noted it in the list for later, since the table exports of the shipments have the same problem for big accounts.

Jonas will check the page with Acme IT on staging. Next I want an index on the event table for type and created time, because the query uses a sequential scan now. It takes 0.4 seconds, so it can wait.

summary: Checked the login report against the raw auth events for one site and found two failure reasons counted as one, so the report now separates a wrong password from a locked account.
body:
Jonas noticed that the weekly login report showed 212 failures for the Hamburg depot, which looked too high for 14 dispatchers. I compared the report with the raw auth events table for that site and one week, using a plain SQL query grouped by the failure code.

The report grouped by a label, and the label for 'bad_password' and for 'account_locked' was the same text, 'Login failed'. The lock comes after five wrong passwords in ten minutes, so each locked user produced one wrong password failure and then several lock failures for every further try. That inflated the count and hid the real picture.

I changed the report query to group by the failure code and gave the two codes their own labels: 'Wrong password' and 'Account locked'. The info text that Jonas asked for last week now also says that repeated tries by a locked account are counted once per hour and not once per try. For that I added a small distinct step on user, device and hour for the lock failures.

After the change the Hamburg week shows 61 wrong passwords, 9 locked accounts and 4 inactive-user failures. The sum is 74, against 212 before. I checked two other sites the same way and the numbers match the raw events to the row.

I added a Vitest case with a fixture of one user who fails six times, and it expects one wrong password count of five and one lock entry. The CSV download uses the same query, so it is correct too, but the full quarter is still slow. That stays on the list for later.

Next step is to show Jonas the new table and ask whether Acme IT wants the lock count as a separate chart.

summary: Jonas looked at the login report with Acme IT and wants the failures split by site, plus a note that an inactive-user failure is expected after offboarding.
body:
The review with Acme IT went well. They liked the weekly view. They asked for two changes: show failed logins by site, so they can see if one depot has a problem with passwords, and add a short explanation next to the inactive user failures.

The site is not stored on the event, but the user has a home site, so I join through the user table. For users deleted since then the site shows as 'unknown'. That is only a few rows.

The explanation says that an inactive user failure is expected for people who left the company and still try the app, and that it is only a problem if it is a current employee. I wrote it as a small info text under the chart.

I will build both tomorrow. Jonas also asked about the retention, and he said 400 days is fine, so I can turn the cleanup job on after the site change.

summary: Added the site split and the info text to the login report and turned on the 400 day cleanup of auth events after a dry run that would delete 62,000 rows.
body:
The login report has a site filter and a site column now. The join goes from event to user to site, with a left join so that deleted users do not drop out. Events without a site show as 'unknown'. The query is still fast, 45 ms for a quarter, because the index on type and time does most of the work.

The info text about inactive user failures is under the chart, in plain words from Jonas's wording. I added a test that the text is only shown when there are such failures in the range.

For the cleanup, I ran the batched delete in dry run mode on staging data. It counted 62,000 rows older than 400 days out of 910k. That is what I expected, since most of the history came from the first months of the refresh tokens.

I turned the job on for the night run at 03:00 with batches of 5,000 rows and a pause of 200 ms between them. It logs the count per night. The first real run on staging deleted the 62,000 rows in about 40 seconds without a visible effect on the other queries.

A guard stops the job if a batch would delete more than 20% of the table in one night, to avoid a mistake with a wrong timestamp like the one in the family cleanup last week. The guard has a test that sets the cutoff to the future and checks that nothing is deleted.

On production the job will start with the next release. I will check the log the day after.

summary: Wrote the plan for the onboarding checklist's progress reminder email after Jonas noticed 38 of 118 users never finish step 3, and weighed an in-app nudge against an email.
body:
Jonas looked at the numbers for the onboarding flow and saw that 38 of the 118 active users never finish step 3, the first saved report. Most of them finished steps 1 and 2. He asked if we can remind them.

I first checked the data. Of the 38, 21 logged in more than once after the flow started, so they are active users who did not want the report. 17 logged in only once. That is a difference: the first group may not need reports, and the second group might just have forgotten the dashboard.

I wrote down two options. The first is an in-app nudge: a small card on the shipments page that says 'Create your first report' with a button to step 3, shown at most three times and hidden when the user dismisses it. It is cheap, reaches those who return, and uses the dismissal fields we have.

The second is an email after 3 days, sent to those who have not finished step 3. It reaches those who logged in once and did not come back. But it needs a template, an opt out and a check with the mail provider, and some Acme users have strict mail filters.

My suggestion was to build the in-app card first, measure for two weeks, and then decide on the email only for the 17. The card needs about a day of work. The email would need two or three days, plus a consent question for Acme.

I also checked what other recurring mails exist: the scheduled reports and the invites. A reminder would be the first mail that is not requested by the user, so Jonas should decide whether it is allowed under the contract with Acme.

Priya made a small mock of the card. It uses the same style as the tour tooltips, so the two features look alike. She wants the card to be quiet, not red, and to disappear forever once the first report exists.

I waited for Jonas's answer before any code. He agreed with the in-app card first and said he would ask Acme about the email.

summary: Built the in-app nudge card for the first report, shown up to three times and gone once a report exists; it is in the main checkout and tested for fresh and old users.
body:
The card is a component, FirstReportNudge, placed above the shipments table. It is shown when the user finished step 2 but has no saved report and has seen the card fewer than three times.

The view count is stored in the user settings next to the tour state. It counts one view per session, not per page load, which I did with sessionStorage so a reload does not use up a view. Dismissing the card sets the dismissed time and hides it for good.

Once a report exists, the card does not render at all. The check uses the report count that the shipments page already loads, so there is no new API call.

Priya's style is used: a light gray background, an outlined button and no red. The card has a heading level that fits under the page title, and the dismiss button is labeled 'Dismiss this tip'. Axe found nothing.

Tests: three Vitest cases for the show rules, and a Playwright run with a fresh user who sees the card, reloads and still has views left, and then creates a report and sees the card gone. A user who joined before the onboarding existed gets the same card, which is what Jonas wants, since they are the most likely to never have made a report.

I added a counter event for shown and clicked, so we can measure after two weeks.

summary: Debugged a 'log out of all devices' bug where the web client stayed logged in for up to 30 seconds and showed stale data; the version check now clears the client state at the first 401.
body:
A tester reported that after pressing 'Log out of all devices' in one browser, a second browser kept working and even showed data for a while. The design says an increase of the token version ends all access tokens within 30 seconds, so some delay is expected. But the tester said the second browser also kept sending requests after the 401 and showed an error banner, not a login page.

I reproduced it with two Playwright contexts. After the version bump, the second context got 401 with code token_version on the next call. The client interceptor treats a 401 by trying a refresh. The refresh also failed, because the families were revoked, with family_revoked. Then the code path for that case threw an error inside the interceptor and left the UI in a half logged out state: the user object was still in the store, and the page showed the error banner.

The cause was that the family_revoked branch only cleared the token storage but did not reset the store or redirect, since it had been written for the mobile app's case and copied. The web path for the plain expired refresh did redirect, so the bug only shows with revoked families.

The fix is one function, forceLogout(reason), used by all failure cases: it clears storage, resets the user store, closes any open websocket-like polling, and redirects to the login page with a message. The message differs: 'You were logged out on another device' for family_revoked and token_version, and 'Your session expired' otherwise.

I also made sure that parallel requests that fail at once call forceLogout only once, with a simple flag, otherwise the redirect was triggered five times and the message flashed.

A new Playwright test covers the two context case: log out everywhere in one, wait for the next poll in the other and check that the login page with the right message appears within 40 seconds. It takes some seconds, so the test sets the cache timeout short through an environment flag.

The 30 second delay itself stays, as Jonas accepted it. The message at least tells the user what happened. I also updated the note on the settings page to say that other devices may stay active for up to 30 seconds.

summary: Looked at the slow shipment CSV export for an account with 180k rows: the request takes about 38 seconds and Render cuts it, so large exports fail for the biggest Acme depot.
body:
A dispatcher at the biggest depot wrote to Jonas that the CSV export of all shipments of the last year never finishes; the browser shows a network error. I tried the same export on staging with a copy of that account's data, 180k rows.

The request took about 38 seconds before the proxy closed it at 30 seconds. The server log shows the query itself takes 2.4 seconds. The rest is spent in the code that builds the file: it loads all rows into an array, maps each row to a formatted object, and joins the lines into one string. The memory went up to about 900 MB during the export, which also made other requests slower, and I saw one restart of the instance due to memory on staging.

Three reasons add up: the whole result is held in memory, the date and number formatting runs for every cell with a new Intl object each time, and the string is concatenated at the end.

The cheap fix is to create the formatters once, and I measured that: the time went from 38 to 27 seconds. That is under the limit, but only barely, and a bigger account will fail again. The memory use stayed the same.

The real fix is to send the rows as they come, but that needs a change in the API and in the client download, so I did not start it today. For now I added a limit message: exports over 100k rows show a hint to narrow the date range. Jonas agreed to this as a stopgap and told the dispatcher to export by quarter.

I wrote the formatter change as a small commit, with a test that compares the output of the old and the new code for 1,000 rows, byte for byte. The commit is on main and deployed to staging.

I wrote the streaming idea down with the details I know: use a database cursor with batches of 2,000 rows, write each batch to the response, and set the headers for a download without a content length. I will plan it with Jonas after the next release.

summary: Checked the production counters after two weeks of the in-app nudge card: 14 of 38 users created a first report after seeing it, and no one dismissed it more than once.
body:
The nudge card was deployed to production about two weeks ago, so I looked at the shown and clicked events. The card was shown to 36 of the 38 users who had not finished step 3; the other two have not logged in since.

Of those 36, 14 created a first report after seeing the card, and 9 of them clicked the button directly. The other 5 made a report through the normal menu. 22 users did not create one. Of those, 11 dismissed the card, and 11 let it run out after three views.

That is a rate of about 39 percent, which is better than I expected, since most of these users had ignored the step in the flow before. The users who logged in only once are still the weak group: only 2 of the 17 have come back at all, so the card cannot reach them.

For them, an email would be the only way. I asked Jonas again whether Acme allows it. He said the contract does not forbid it, but the Acme IT lead wants to see the text first. I will draft a short text with an opt out link and send it to Jonas for them.

I did not build any email code yet. The numbers say it would reach 15 people at most, so the effort is small, but so is the gain. I put it as an optional item at the end of the list.

summary: Reviewed the first two weeks of the new nudge card and the onboarding tips together: step 3 completion rose from 80 of 118 users to 92, and the tips are shown once as designed.
body:
Pulled the counters for the onboarding checklist after the nudge card and the manager tour had both been live for two weeks. Step 3 had been finished by 80 of 118 users before; it is 92 now. The in-app card accounts for most of the change, and the costs page tour for managers did not move step 3 at all, which is expected because it targets a different step.

The tour is shown once per manager and the dismissal time field is written correctly in all 22 cases I checked in Postgres. Two managers saw it twice because they used a second browser; the field is stored per user, so this means the client cached an old value. I looked at the cache key in the onboarding step container and it ignores the user id after a logout and login on the same machine.
