Fixed the key so it includes the user id and added a Vitest case that logs in as two users in a row. The case failed before the change and passes now.

I also wrote the numbers into a short note for Jonas. He asked earlier whether the email reminder is still needed. My view is that it is not needed for now, because 26 users still missing step 3 are mostly inactive accounts that Acme plans to offboard. I put the email plan on hold rather than dropping it.

Next is a look at whether the nudge card should also appear for the second report, but I will wait for Jonas to say if he wants that.

summary: Started on the slow large CSV exports: profiled the 180k row shipment export and found 31 of 38 seconds go into building the string in memory, before any byte is sent.
body:
Reproduced the failing export on staging with a copy of the biggest Acme depot, 180k shipment rows. The request still takes about 38 seconds and Render cuts the connection, as seen last week. This time I measured where the time goes instead of guessing.

I added timing logs around the three phases in the export route. The Postgres query takes 4 seconds. Mapping the rows to objects with the column formatters takes 3 seconds. Building the whole CSV as one string and escaping the fields takes 31 seconds, and memory of the Node process climbs to about 900 MB during it. The last number is the worrying one, since the Render instance has little headroom and two exports at once would probably kill it.

The escaping function is slow in itself: it runs three regular expressions on every field, including numbers. A quick test that skips the regular expressions for numeric columns cut the string phase from 31 to 19 seconds. That helps, but it does not fix the memory use, and it will not hold for a depot of 500k rows.

I decided not to ship the escaping change alone. It would only move the limit a little, and the user would think the export is fixed. For now I wrote up the three numbers in the ticket and told Jonas that the biggest depot will keep failing until the export is changed in a larger way.

I also checked who exports large tables. In the last month 9 exports passed 100k rows, 6 of them from the same two dispatchers. I will ask Jonas whether those two could split by month as a workaround until the real change.

Nothing was merged in this session; the timing logs are on a local branch only.

summary: Jonas accepted the monthly split as a workaround for the two dispatchers with huge exports; I added a hint with the row count to the export dialog.
body: Jonas answered the question from yesterday: the two dispatchers can split their exports by month for now. To make that easy I added a line to the export dialog that shows the row count of the current filter and warns above 100k rows. The warning links to the date picker so the range can be shortened. The text was checked with Jonas and says that large exports may fail, without promising a date. Tested the dialog with 0, 1, 99,999 and 180k rows. The count comes from the same filter query as the table, so it needs no extra request.

summary: Investigated why the login report undercounts logins of a removed site, found the join on the current site list, and planned the fix.
body:
Acme IT noticed that the login report for last quarter showed fewer logins than the raw auth events for one site. I looked into the report query and found the cause: it joins the events to the current list of sites, so events of a site that was removed from the account drop out of the result.

I ran the raw count against the report on a copy of the data: 4,118 raw events against 3,962 in the report. The difference is exactly the events of the removed site. I have not changed the query yet. The plan is to use the site id stored on the event and a left join for the display name, with a fallback label 'removed site', so the totals should match the raw events afterwards.

This looks like the same kind of problem as the report builder preview two months ago, where a removed site gave an empty chart. I went through the other report queries for the same join pattern and found it in the scheduled report for managers as well. I wrote down both places and drafted a test that removes a site and expects its rows to stay in the result. It fails on the current code, as it should.

I will tell Jonas that last quarter's numbers will change slightly once the fix is in, and why, before anyone sees the new totals.

summary: Wrote the plan for a streamed CSV export: query with a Postgres cursor, write rows to the response as they come, and keep the old path for small exports until it is proven.
body:
Planned the real fix for the slow exports, after the profiling of yesterday. The goal is that the memory use stays flat and the first byte reaches the browser quickly, so Render does not cut the request.

The plan has four steps. First, read the rows with a cursor in batches of 2,000 instead of loading all of them. Second, format and escape each batch and write it to the response stream, with attention to backpressure so a slow client does not fill memory. Third, send the headers and the BOM at once, so the download starts at the beginning. Fourth, keep the old in-memory path behind a flag for small exports, and remove it later when the new one has run for some weeks.

Risks: the date and number formatters are written for objects, not for streams, so they need a small check. An error in the middle of a stream cannot change the status code any more; the plan is to end the file with a clear marker row and log the error. I also need to test that Render does not buffer the response.

I did not start the code yet. This plan goes to the ticket so Jonas can see that the work is a larger change.

summary: Fixed a table filter bug where choosing 'all statuses' after a single status kept the old filter in the URL, so reloading the page showed the wrong rows.
body:
A dispatcher reported that after selecting one shipment status and then going back to 'all statuses', a page reload brought the single status back. I reproduced it in the main checkout.

The filter state is mirrored into the query string. When the user picks 'all', the code set the value to an empty array but the URL writer skipped empty arrays instead of removing the parameter. So the old parameter stayed in the URL and the next load read it.

I changed the writer to delete the parameter when the value is empty and wrote a Vitest case for the three filters that use arrays: status, depot and carrier. I also added a Playwright step that selects, clears and reloads.

The fix is small. I checked the saved reports too, because they store filters in a similar way, and they were not affected, since they save the filter object and not the URL.

summary: Profiled the slow CSV export again and sketched how a cursor-based reader could work, without writing the reader yet.
body:
Started on the plan from this morning for the large CSV exports. First I looked at where the time goes. With the 180k row copy of the shipment table, the query itself returns in about 5 seconds, and most of the rest of the old export time is spent building the whole file as one string in memory. Process memory climbs to about 900 MB during that step, which explains why the dispatchers with huge exports see timeouts.

I then looked at how a cursor could replace the query-everything approach. The pg-cursor package is already a dependency of pg, so no new package is needed. One thing I noted is that a cursor keeps its connection checked out for the whole export, so a few long exports could starve the pool. My idea is a limit of three parallel exports, and a fourth request would get a clear 429 message asking the user to try again soon. I have not written any of this yet, only a short note in the plan file.

I also wrote down the questions that still need an answer before coding: how to flush batches so a proxy does not hold them back, how the response writer should react when the client drops the connection, and what the file should look like if the query fails halfway. I will ask Jonas about the last one, since it depends on whether anybody imports these files automatically.

Next step is a small spike of the reader with a Vitest case that checks the cursor is closed when the consumer stops early.

summary: Profiled the slow CSV export further and wrote down the plan for a streaming writer, including how a failure in the middle of a file should look, without building the writer yet.
body:
Went back to the large CSV export after the profiling from earlier. The 180k row export still spends almost all of its time building the whole string in memory before the first byte goes out, so a gateway timeout is only a matter of a few more rows.

I sketched the writer on paper first. It would take batches from a cursor reader, format each row with the existing column formatters, escape the fields, and write to the Express response. When write returns false it has to wait for the drain event, so a slow client cannot make the memory grow. I have not written any of this code yet. The cursor reader itself is also still to do, so there is nothing to connect.

I did look at the escaping function, because it is cheap to improve on its own. It runs a regular expression for every field, even for numeric columns that can never contain a quote or a comma. A plain check for numeric columns and one test for the rest should save a good part of the formatting time. I measured the escaping in isolation on a copy of the data and the saving is clear, but I have not changed the production function yet.

The open problem I thought about most is an error after the headers are sent. A broken cursor, for example, could no longer produce a 500, so the browser would get a short file and a user might take it for a complete one. Options I wrote down: a final row with a marker like '# export failed', a trailer that browsers ignore, or a count check on the client. The marker row is simple and visible in a spreadsheet, so it is my favorite for now. Its downside is that it makes the file invalid for automatic import, so I want to ask Jonas whether any Acme system imports these files.

The plan is to put the new path behind a flag called EXPORT_STREAMING and keep the old path as the default, so small exports do not change. Nothing exists yet, and nothing is switched on.

summary: Asked Jonas whether anything reads the exported CSV files automatically, to decide how a failed streaming export should end.
body: Before going further with the streaming export I needed to know what happens when an error hits after the headers are already sent. The response is then a half-finished file with a normal status, and I did not want to pick a failure marker without knowing who opens the files. I asked Jonas whether any system at Acme imports the CSV files automatically. He checked with Acme and said all files are opened by people in a spreadsheet. A visible last line is therefore an acceptable option for the failure case. I wrote down the idea of a final line reading '# export failed, please try again', plus logging of the account id and the filter. I also listed the test I want: a Vitest case that breaks the cursor after the third batch and checks the end of the output. Nothing is changed in the writer yet. Next I will look at how the writer handles errors, then run a staging test behind the flag.

summary: Planned how to test the streaming CSV export on staging and went through the open questions about proxy buffering, compression and concurrent exports before any deploy.
body:
I did not deploy anything today. The cursor reader and the streaming response writer exist only on the branch and in local tests, so I spent the time working out how to check them on staging later.

The main worry is that something between the app and the client buffers the data. Render sits in front of the app, and the compression middleware collects data until it reaches a threshold. If either of them holds back small chunks, the first byte may not go out early and the gateway timeout would still hit. I wrote a short test script with curl and a timer on the output that prints the size and arrival time of every piece. It ran against a local server with compression on, and the pieces came in a few large blocks, which showed the problem could be real. I have not tried any fix yet. Two ideas are on my list: flushing after every batch, and checking whether the compression stream needs its own flush. I want to keep compression, because CSV text compresses very well, probably several times smaller on the wire.

I also wrote down the cases for the staging run: one export of 180k rows through the public URL, then two and four exports at the same time. The limit on concurrent exports should answer the fourth one with a 429. I will watch the memory of the staging instance during these runs.

Open points: a test with a client that is slow on purpose, to see that backpressure holds and the cursor closes, and the question of what the dispatchers see in the browser while the download runs. If the export dialog closes at once, the browser's download bar may be the only sign of progress. I will ask Priya whether a small hint in the dialog would be enough.

Next I will finish the error-in-the-middle handling, so the plan for staging is complete.

summary: Ran a deliberately slow client against the streaming CSV export on staging to check memory and cursor cleanup, and planned what to check next before any production decision.
body:
Used curl with a rate limit of 50 KB per second against the staging export of 180k rows. The server memory stayed around 90 MB for the whole time, so the drain handling seems to work as intended. After about two minutes I killed curl. The log showed the close event, the cursor was closed right away, and the pool had all its connections back.

I also checked that the export count limit went down again after the dropped connection, and it did. This was only one slow client, so I still want to try a few at the same time and one that drops in the middle of the first batch.

The export is not on for any production account yet. I want to wait a few days and look at the logs of staging first, and I will decide after that whether a trial with one depot makes sense. The marker row for a failed export still needs a test with a real error in the middle.

summary: Looked at the session cleanup job before the move back to server-side sessions, found a full scan on a 40,000-row table, and planned the index fix and a limit on how often the session is touched.
body:
Before the move back to server-side sessions, I prepared a test copy of the session setup and ran the nightly cleanup job against it. The job deletes sessions that expired or that were revoked more than a week ago. On the test copy, filled with rows shaped like the production data from the JWT period, it would remove between 2,100 and 2,500 rows each night, which fits the number of active users and devices.

The duration was the surprise. The delete takes about 9 seconds, and the session table has only about 40,000 rows. The explain output showed a sequential scan, because the condition uses a coalesce of two columns, expires_at and revoked_at, and no index can serve that.

I wrote a small migration but have not run it anywhere except locally: a partial index on expires_at for rows that are not revoked, and a second partial index on revoked_at for revoked rows. The delete would run as two statements, one for each index. Locally the whole job dropped from 9 seconds to 40 milliseconds.

I am being careful with the migration, since the session table will be read on every request. Creating an index takes a lock that blocks writes, so the plan is to use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and run it outside a transaction. I wrote that down as a step in the rollout notes and will try it on staging first.

The second finding is about the lookup on every request. The session read by id is on the primary key, so it is fast; I measured 0.3 ms at the median. But the touch that extends the session on each request is a write. For the dashboard, which makes many calls when a page loads, that is many writes of the same row. I counted 14 writes for one page load of the main dashboard.

The idea is to extend the session at most once per minute. The session middleware has an option for this, and I tested it locally. With it, the same page load causes one write. The effect for users is that the session may end up to a minute earlier than before, which should not matter for a 30 minute idle limit. I will ask Jonas to confirm that before anything goes further.

summary: Prepared the per-account flag for the streaming CSV export and added logging, so a trial with one depot can follow.
body:
The staging logs of several days stayed clean, so today I prepared the step from the global flag to a per-account flag. Nothing is switched on in production yet. The streaming path is still only active on staging, and every production account stays on the old path.

The flag now reads a list of account ids from the settings table instead of one global value. I wrote a small test that checks three cases: an account on the list gets the streaming handler, an account not on the list gets the old handler, and an empty list means nobody streams. The test passes locally.

I also added a log line at the start and at the end of each streamed export with the row count, the duration and the peak memory. On staging I ran the 180k row table twice to look at the output. It finished in 15 and 16 seconds, and the peak memory stayed flat. A third run with a narrow date range of 4k rows took under a second.

I looked at which depot to choose for the trial. The biggest depot has the table with 180k shipment rows, which is the best case for the test, because it is the one that suffers most from the slow exports. I wrote the plan down for Jonas: one depot first, a day of watching the logs, then a decision. I asked him to tell the depot's dispatchers that downloads may look a bit different.

One thing I noticed on staging is that the browser shows no total size for a streamed download, so the progress bar can only move without a real percentage. That is normal for a stream. I will think about a small message in the export dialog, and I will tell Jonas before the trial starts so it does not surprise anyone.

Next I will check the flag list once more and then plan the trial with Jonas.

summary: Built the session list on the settings page further: each row shows device type, last use and city, and the current session is marked and cannot be revoked from its own row.
body:
Worked on the session list of the settings page. The first version, from last week, showed only the session ids and the creation time, which nobody can read. The goal today was a list a dispatcher understands.

Each row now has the device type, which is read from the user agent at login and stored in a new column device_label ('Chrome on Mac', 'Driver app on Android'). It shows the last use as a relative time, and an approximate place from the IP. For the place I used the lookup table that already serves the login report, so no new service is needed. If the IP is private or unknown, the row shows nothing instead of a wrong place.

The current session is marked 'This device'. Its revoke button is replaced by the normal logout, because ending your own session from the list sends the user to a login page with no explanation. I tested that a second tab of the same session also shows the mark.

The revoke action calls the existing endpoint that sets revoked_at. I added a check on the server that a user can only revoke their own sessions; a manager cannot revoke the sessions of a dispatcher from this list. There was no check before, because the list used to show the own sessions only, but the endpoint took any id. A Vitest case now tries to revoke a foreign id and expects a 404.

The accessibility lessons from the device table of last month are applied here too: row headers exist, and the revoke button has a name that says which device it ends, for example 'Revoke session Chrome on Mac'. I ran the axe check from the Playwright suite on the page and it found nothing.

Open: the list is not paged. Users have at most 6 sessions at the moment, so it is fine for now. Also Priya has not seen the page. I sent her a screenshot and asked for a look at the spacing and the icons.

The next step is the 'log out of all other devices' button, which should keep the current session.

summary: Added 'log out of all other devices' to the session list and found that the mobile app sessions were revoked too, which is intended, but the app showed no message afterwards.
body:
Built the button that revokes every session of the user except the current one. On the server it is one update with the condition that the id is not the current id, and it returns the number of revoked sessions. The button shows that number in a short confirmation.

Testing with a laptop session and a phone session through the mobile app test build, the laptop revoke worked. The app session was ended, as it should be. The app got a 401 on its next call and then showed a blank loading screen, with no way back to the login.

That is the agency's part, so I did not fix it. I wrote them a short note with the exact response, the 401 body with the code session_revoked, and asked them to show the login screen on this code. Before the move to sessions the app had its own handling for the refresh token failing, and the new code is simply not known to it.

On the web side the same 401 is already handled by the version check from last month, which clears the client state at the first 401. I verified it with two browsers.

I added the Vitest and Playwright cases. The Playwright case logs in with two contexts, revokes from the first and expects the second to show the login page after its next click.

One more detail: the 'other devices' button is hidden if the user has only one session, so nobody presses a button that does nothing.

Waiting for the agency's answer about the blank screen.

summary: Prepared the streaming CSV export for a wider rollout by reviewing the trial depot's logs, checking edge cases and drafting the dialog text, without switching it on for all accounts.
body:
The trial depot had now run for about a week with 17 streamed exports and no failure. I went through the logs again, looking for marker rows and for the 429 limit. Neither had happened. I did not change the flag today. The streaming export is still on for that one depot only, and I wrote down what has to be true before it goes to everyone.

To get a number for the effect on normal users, I compared the export logs of the trial depot with those of the other accounts on the old path. The median export of about 20k rows takes 6 seconds on the old path and 2 seconds on the streaming path. Memory peaks on the Render instance are the other thing I looked at: one big export on the old path can push it above 800 MB, and the streamed exports of the trial stayed below 250 MB. These are numbers from one depot, so I treat them as a first indication and not as proof.

I thought about how to roll it out. My plan is to turn the flag on for all accounts only after one more check of the logs, and to keep the old path behind the flag for two more weeks, in case a problem shows up that the trial did not cover, for example an odd character in a carrier name. The escaping function is tested in Vitest with quotes, newlines, a semicolon and Unicode, and I added a line with an emoji, which passed.

The export dialog got a draft text: 'Large files start downloading at once and may take up to a minute.' I showed it to Jonas and he liked it. It will only appear once a wider rollout happens.

I also looked at the limit of three parallel exports. With 118 users that seems plenty, and the log shows at most two at the same time so far, so I left the limit as it is.

One thing to follow up: the scheduled report job sends CSV attachments by email and uses the old in-memory function. Those files are small, under 5k rows, so it is not urgent. I put a note in the backlog.

The case that began this work, a dispatcher from the big depot with an export of about 181k rows, is still the one I want to test on the new path before I call anything finished. I will ask Jonas to have them try it once the flag is wider.

summary: Answered Jonas's question how long users stay logged in now: the median session lasts 11 days, and 9 of 118 users have a session older than 30 days.
body:
Jonas asked whether the sessions end by themselves, since Acme IT wants to know the rules. I looked at the session table in production.

The idle limit is 30 days of no use, and the touch happens at most once per minute since the change of last week. The median age of an active session is 11 days. The oldest active one is 52 days old, a manager who opens the dashboard every morning.

Nine users have a session older than 30 days. All nine use the dashboard at least weekly, so the idle limit never hit them. Acme IT asked for an absolute limit as well. I proposed 90 days, after which the user must log in again, and said the mobile app would need to handle the login screen on the expiry.

I wrote the answer in plain words for Jonas, with the three numbers and the proposal. No code change yet; he will discuss the 90 days with Acme IT.

While looking at the data I noticed 31 sessions of the driver app with no last-use update for more than 20 days. They belong to drivers who left. The cleanup job removes them when the idle limit passes, so nothing needs doing.

summary: Built the absolute 90 day session limit that Acme IT agreed to, with a clear 401 code session_expired so the web client and the mobile app can show the login page.
body:
Jonas came back with a yes from Acme IT for the absolute limit of 90 days. I added a created_at check in the session lookup: a session older than 90 days counts as expired, whatever its last use.

The response uses the code session_expired instead of the generic unauthorized, so clients can tell the reason. On the web, the client state clearing at the first 401 already exists, and I added a message on the login page: 'Your session ended after 90 days. Please sign in again.' The message is shown only for this code, and not for a normal logout.

The cleanup job needed an addition. It must also delete sessions older than 90 days, plus the usual grace of a week. I added a third statement, using an index on created_at. That index is new and was created concurrently on staging in under a second.

Tests: a Vitest case with a session of 91 days that has a fresh last use, expecting session_expired; one of 89 days that passes; and a Playwright case for the message text. I changed the clock in the tests with fake timers.

The agency has still not answered about the blank screen after revocation, so I sent them the second code in the same note, so both codes are handled together.

In production, 3 users have sessions between 90 and 100 days at the moment, which means the three of them will see the login page after the deploy. I told Jonas so that he can warn them. The deploy is planned for tomorrow morning, so that Acme's dispatchers are not caught at the start of their shift.

summary: Deployed the 90 day session limit; three managers were sent to the login page as expected, and the message text showed correctly for all of them.
body:
Deployed in the quiet hour before the dispatchers begin. After the deploy I looked at the auth events: exactly three session_expired responses, all from the managers I knew about. Each of them logged in again within a few minutes.

The message on the login page showed, I checked it in the logs by the event of the page view with the expiry reason. Nobody reported a problem to Jonas.

The cleanup job ran at night as usual. It took 60 milliseconds for all three statements and removed 2,380 rows.

I also checked the mobile app by logs: its calls with the expired sessions got the new code, and the agency's app still shows the blank screen for it. I sent a reminder to the agency, with the log lines. It affects only three drivers so far, but the number will grow with time.

Nothing else is open on this topic except the agency.

summary: Investigated why one scheduled report of 60k rows pushed the mail job to 700 MB and wrote down a plan for the fix, without changing the job yet.
body:
The backlog note from last week turned out to matter earlier than I thought. A manager had made a scheduled report of all shipments for a quarter, which came to 60k rows, much more than the 5k I had assumed. The mail job built the CSV in memory with the old function and its memory rose to 700 MB for a short time. The job survived, but only just.

I spent the session finding out what exactly happens. I ran the real report on staging with a memory profile attached and saw that the rows are first collected into one array, then joined into one big string, and then the mail library copies the attachment into a buffer again. So the data exists three times at the peak. The export route has the same shape for large tables, and large exports are still slow there, but I did not touch it.

The plan is to give the job a reader that goes through the rows with a cursor and writes them into a temporary file, then to attach the file from the disk so the mail library does not hold the data. The temporary file must be deleted after sending, also on an error, so I will use a finally block. For the writer I need to check how much of it is tied to the response object, because it may have to take any writable stream. I wrote these points into the backlog note with the numbers from the profile.

I also thought about a size limit: if a scheduled report would produce more than 200k rows, the mail could carry a link to the dashboard instead of an attachment, because many mail providers refuse large attachments. I asked Jonas about the text of such a mail and sent him a first draft. He has not answered yet.

For tests I listed two cases to write: the cleanup of the temporary file on an error, and the 200k limit with a mocked row count. The bounce handling from before stays as it is. All staging mails during the profile run went only to the test address.

summary: Did the first accessibility pass of the session list and the new login messages; found 5 issues with a screen reader and fixed all of them, including a live region for the revoke confirmation.
body:
Went through the settings page with the session list using VoiceOver on Mac and NVDA on a Windows test machine, as I did for the device table last month. The automated axe check was clean, but the screen reader tests found five issues.

First, the confirmation after 'log out of all other devices' was shown as a text that appeared visually, but the screen reader said nothing. I added a polite live region and the text now reads 'Logged out of 2 other devices'.

Second, after revoking a single session, the row disappeared and the keyboard focus fell to the top of the page. The focus now moves to the heading of the list, which is focusable with tabindex minus one, and the list heading announces the new count.

Third, the relative time 'last used 3 days ago' was rendered with a time element but the title attribute carried the exact time, and the screen reader read both. I removed the title and put the exact time in a visually hidden span only for the first use.

Fourth, the mark 'This device' was a colored badge only. The text was there, but with low contrast in the dark theme, 3.1 to 1. I took the color token from Priya's design for secondary text, which gives 5.2 to 1.

Fifth, the login page message about the 90 day expiry was inserted after the page loaded, so it was not read. It has role status now and is in the page from the start, with the content set before the focus goes to the form.

I wrote Playwright steps for the first, second and fifth: checks for the live region content and for the focus target after the revoke. The contrast is covered by axe already in the dark theme project of the config; I confirmed that it fails with the old color by reverting for a moment.

Priya looked at the badge color and was fine with it, since it follows her tokens. She also asked to keep the icons of the device types decorative, with an empty alt, and that is how they are.

All fixes are in the main checkout and the whole test suite passed, 412 Vitest cases and 38 Playwright cases.

What is left: the mobile app is not part of this, and the agency does its own checks. I will mention the live region idea to them as a suggestion for their revoke message.

summary: Planned the report builder v2 filter groups: reports will allow 'and' and 'or' groups of conditions, stored as a small tree, with a migration for the saved reports of today.
body:
Jonas wants managers to build reports like 'status delayed and (depot A or depot B)'. The report builder today only joins all filters with 'and'. I wrote the plan for v2 before touching code.

The data model: a filter tree where a node is either a condition (field, operator, value) or a group (mode 'and' or 'or', children). Saved reports now store a flat array. A migration wraps each flat array in a root group with mode 'and', so all 214 saved reports keep their results. I will check this with a script that runs every saved report before and after, and compares the row counts on a copy of production.

The SQL side: a function turns the tree into a parameterized where clause. Field names come from a fixed list of allowed columns, never from the input, and values go as parameters. The depth is limited to 3 levels and the number of conditions to 20, so that nobody builds a query that takes minutes. Both limits are checked on the server and in the form.

The UI: the first idea was nested boxes with drag and drop. I think that is too much for the dispatchers. The plan is an indented list with an 'add condition' and an 'add group' button, and a toggle 'all of / any of' on the group head. It is simpler to make accessible too, and I want to avoid a repeat of the screen reader work with drag handles.

The preview chart and the table use the same filter, so they get it from the same function. The scheduled reports also read the saved filter, and the job must use the new tree reader. I listed the three places where the filter is read: the preview, the scheduled job and the CSV export, which takes the filter of the table.

Testing plan: Vitest cases for the tree to SQL function with 12 shapes including empty groups, which should be ignored, and a group with one child. Playwright for building a group in the UI with the keyboard.

Open questions for Jonas: should 'not' exist? I would leave it out for now, because 'is not' operators on fields cover most cases. And should managers see the depth limit as an error or should the UI simply not offer the button? I prefer the second.

I will start with the migration and the tree to SQL function, because they are the risky part, and leave the UI for later.

summary: Wrote the filter tree to SQL function and the migration for saved reports; all 214 saved reports return the same row counts before and after on a production copy.
body:
Began with the risky parts of the plan from this morning. The function buildWhere takes the tree and returns a text and a list of parameters. A condition becomes 'column operator $n'. A group joins its children with AND or OR and puts parentheses around the result. Empty groups are dropped, and a group with a single child returns the child without parentheses.

The allowed fields are in one map from the field name to the column and the type. The operators allowed depend on the type: text fields have equals, not equals and contains; numbers and dates have comparison operators. An unknown field or operator throws an error that the API turns into a 400. Depth above 3 or more than 20 conditions also gives a 400.

I wrote 14 Vitest cases. Besides the shapes in the plan I added one with a value that looks like SQL, a quote and a semicolon, and checked that it appears only in the parameters list. Another case builds a tree with the maximum depth and one level more.

The migration changes the saved reports table. It wraps the old flat array into a root group in a JSON column, and keeps the old column for a few weeks as a backup. The migration is written to be run twice without harm, by testing whether the value already has a mode key.

Then the comparison script. It loads every saved report from a copy of production, runs the old query code, then the migrated tree with the new code, and compares the counts. All 214 matched. Four reports were saved with a removed site; they return zero rows in both versions, so the preview fix of last quarter is not touched.

I did not look at the scheduled job or the export yet. They still read the old column and would work only because it is kept. Both come next.

summary: Moved the scheduled report job and the table export to the filter tree reader and built the first version of the group editor with keyboard controls.
body:
Two things were left from the plan. The scheduled job and the CSV export both read the old flat column. I switched both to the tree, using the same buildWhere function. The job needed one more change: it had its own copy of the filter code from the time before the report builder was shared, and I deleted that copy. A Vitest case runs a saved report through the job and the preview and expects the same rows.

Then the editor. It is an indented list. A group has a head with a select 'all of' or 'any of', then its children, then two buttons: 'Add condition' and 'Add group'. Each condition has field, operator and value controls, and a remove button whose name says which condition it removes, as I learned from the device table. The add group button is not shown at the depth limit, as planned.

Focus management was the part that took time. After adding a condition the focus goes to the field select of the new row, and after a removal it goes to the previous row, or to the group head if none is left. I used the same live region approach as in the session list to announce 'Condition added, 3 conditions'.

I built a Playwright case that makes the example from Jonas, delayed and (depot A or depot B), by keyboard only, and checks that the preview shows the right count. It passed on the third try, after I fixed an issue with the value select being replaced while the operator was changing.

The visual design is plain for now. Priya will look at it, and I sent her screenshots in both themes. The indentation uses a left border, and I know that the dark theme version is a little weak.

Not done: the 'not' question, still waiting for Jonas, and the removal of the old column, which needs a few weeks of calm. The next step is a staging test with two managers who use the report builder a lot.

summary: Finished the keyboard controls of the filter group editor in report builder v2 and fixed focus loss when a condition is removed, so the editor works without a mouse.
body:
The first version of the group editor from this morning could add and nest groups, but removing a condition threw the focus to the top of the page. I traced it to the key prop, which used the array index, so React remounted the neighbouring rows after a delete. The conditions have stable ids in the tree now, and the key uses them.

After a delete, the focus moves to the next condition, or to the previous one if the last was removed, or to the 'add condition' button if the group is empty. I added arrow key movement between rows and Alt+Down to nest a condition into a new group. Escape closes an open operator dropdown without leaving the editor.

I wrote 9 Vitest tests for the reducer that edits the tree, including deleting the only child of a nested group, which should remove the empty group. One of them failed first: an empty 'or' group stayed in the tree and the SQL function produced 'WHERE ()'. The reducer prunes empty groups now.

I also ran the editor with a screen reader for a few minutes. The group has a label like 'Group 2, match any of', but the nesting level is not announced yet. That is left for the accessibility pass. Next is the preview count that shows how many rows a report matches while the user edits.

summary: Added a live row count preview to the report builder v2 editor; it uses a debounced count query with a 3 second limit so a heavy filter tree cannot stall the database.
body:
Jonas asked in the morning that dispatchers see how many shipments a report matches before they save it. I built a count endpoint that takes the filter tree, runs it through the tree to SQL function and returns the count only.

The first version ran on every keystroke and the staging database showed 40 queries in a few seconds when I typed in a value field. I added a 400 ms debounce on the client and cancel the previous request with an AbortController. On the server the query runs with statement_timeout set to 3 seconds in its own transaction. If it times out, the editor shows 'more than we can count quickly' and not an error.

I tested the timeout with a tree of six 'or' groups on text columns with LIKE '%...%', which takes about 11 seconds on the production copy. It stops at 3 seconds and the connection returns to the pool without a leak, which I checked by reading pg_stat_activity afterwards.

The count respects the same account scoping as the table, which I checked with two test accounts. A dispatcher of one depot cannot see counts of another depot's shipments. I added a Playwright test for this.

Still open: the count says 0 while loading, which looks like a real result. I want a skeleton or a dash there. I wrote it into the list for tomorrow.

summary: Reviewed report builder v2 against a production copy and found two saved reports whose 'or' behaviour changed because of an old negated condition.
body:
Before showing v2 to Jonas I ran every one of the 214 saved reports through the old reader and the new tree reader and compared not only row counts but also the sorted list of shipment ids. 212 matched. Two reports returned more rows in v2.

Both had a condition 'status is not delivered' combined with a second condition on the same column. The old format stored the conditions as a flat list joined by 'and', but for a negated condition on the same column the old SQL builder turned the whole group into an 'or' by accident. That was a bug, but users had saved those reports with the behaviour they saw, so the numbers in their reports would change.

I looked at what the two owners meant. One report is called 'Open, not delivered, not cancelled' and clearly wanted 'and'. The other, a manager's weekly summary, has a name that fits the accidental 'or'. I did not change either automatically. The migration now keeps the old behaviour for these two by writing an explicit 'or' group, and adds a flag in a migration log table so I can tell Jonas which reports were touched.

I wrote this up for Jonas in short form: two reports, their names, the old result and what v2 gives. He will ask the owners. I also added a test with both cases to the migration tests so the quirk does not return.

Other checks went well. The group depth limit of 4 holds, and a tree with 40 conditions still builds SQL in under 2 ms. Exports of large v2 reports are still slow, since they build the whole file in memory like the other exports, but that is a separate problem and I left it alone for now.

Next I want to look at the editor with Priya's mockups, since she had comments about the group borders.

summary: Applied Priya's feedback to the filter group editor: lighter group borders, an indent per level and a clearer 'match all / any' toggle.
body:
Priya sent notes on the group editor. The nested borders looked heavy at depth 3, so I replaced the full border with a left bar of 3 px and an indent of 16 px per level. The colour comes from the theme tokens, so the dark theme works without extra rules.

The 'match all / any' control was a select element and people did not find it. It is a two-button toggle now with the text 'all of these' and 'any of these' next to the group. The toggle is a real radio group, so the keyboard and the screen reader behave as before.

I checked the contrast of the left bars in both themes. The dark theme bar was at 2.6 to 1, below the 3 to 1 needed for graphics, so I lightened it. Priya will look at the result tomorrow.

summary: Found that report builder v2 allowed saving a report with an empty group, which then matched all shipments; save is blocked now with a message that points at the group.
body:
A test with a half built tree showed that a saved report with one empty group matched every shipment. The SQL function treated an empty group as 'no condition', which is right for the old reports but a trap for a user who just forgot to fill a group.

I split the two cases. The reader still accepts empty groups, because the migration of old reports must not break, but the editor validates before saving. An empty group or a condition without a value gets an error state and the save button explains the problem: 'Group 2 has no conditions'. The message links to the group and moves focus there.

The validation runs on the server too, since the scheduled report job and the API could save reports without the editor. I added a 422 with a list of paths into the tree, like groups[1].conditions[0]. Seven new tests cover empty groups, missing values, an unknown column and a tree deeper than 4.

One case was less clear: a condition 'value is empty' has no value on purpose. I marked these operators in a small table, so validation knows which operators need a value. The editor hides the value field for them.

I deployed it to staging. Tomorrow I show it to Jonas together with the two changed reports.

summary: Walked Jonas through report builder v2 on staging; he accepted the groups, chose 'and' for one of the two changed reports and asked for report copies with one click.
body:
The session with Jonas took about 40 minutes. He built a report with an 'or' group for two depots and an 'and' condition on the delivery delay and understood the editor without explanation. He liked the live count, but asked why it showed a dash for a second after each change. I explained that it is the loading state, and he said it was fine.

For the two reports with the old accidental behaviour he asked the owners by phone. The owner of 'Open, not delivered, not cancelled' wants 'and', so I changed that tree to an 'and' group and the row count dropped from 3,140 to 1,902, which matches what the owner expected. The manager's weekly summary stays with 'or'.

He asked for a 'copy report' action because dispatchers make a report for each depot that differs by one condition. I think this is small: copy the tree, add 'copy' to the name and open the editor. Another request was to show who created a report in the list. That needs a join to users and a decision about deleted users, so I did not promise a date.

I also noticed that the report list is slow with 214 reports and a count column; the count for each report is calculated on load. That is a separate problem. I noted it and will measure before changing anything.

Next steps: copy action, then a look at the list loading time.

summary: Added a copy action to the report list and measured that the list takes 2.4 seconds because it counts rows for each report; counts will be cached for 10 minutes.
body:
The copy action was quick. It duplicates the saved tree, sets the name to 'Name (copy)', assigns the current user as owner and opens the editor. Reports shared with a depot are copied as private, so a user cannot create a shared report by accident. Three tests cover this.

Then I measured the list. With 214 reports the page needs 2.4 seconds on staging, and 2.1 of them are the 214 count queries running one after another. Most users have 5 to 15 reports, but the managers see all of them.

I first tried running the counts in parallel with a limit of 5, which brought it to 0.9 seconds but put load on the pool. A cache is better because the counts do not need to be exact. The counts are saved in a column with the time they were taken and are reused for 10 minutes. A stale count shows a small 'about' before the number.

The report list now loads in 180 ms from the cache. A refresh button recalculates a single report. The cache is also cleared when a report's tree changes, which I checked with a test.

summary: Upgraded Vite and its React plugin to the next major version; the build works, but the dev server broke on a proxy setting for the API and one ECharts import path.
body:
I started the Vite upgrade on a separate commit so I could revert it cleanly. The package changes were small: vite, @vitejs/plugin-react and vitest to matching versions. The first build already passed, and the bundle came out 4 percent smaller.

The dev server did not work. Every call to /api returned a 502. The proxy target was written as 'localhost:3000', and the new version resolves localhost to the IPv6 address first, while the Express server listens only on IPv4. Changing the target to http://127.0.0.1:3000 fixed it. I also made Express listen on both, so the same problem does not appear on another machine.

The second problem was an import of 'echarts/lib/chart/bar' in the old chart wrapper. The new resolution rules reject this deep path because ECharts defines an exports map. I changed the imports to the documented 'echarts/charts' and 'echarts/components' entries and registered only the charts we use. This also removed one unused chart type from the bundle.

Vitest ran 612 tests: 610 passed, and two failed on a snapshot of the CSS class order, which now differs. I checked that the snapshots were only different in order and updated them. Playwright passed on all three browsers.

I built the production bundle and compared the sizes: the main chunk went from 412 KB to 396 KB gzipped. The source maps are produced as before, and I verified that Render's build command needs no change.

I left the upgrade on staging and want to watch the console for a day before it goes to production. Tomorrow I check the lazy loaded routes with a slow network setting.

summary: Fixed the dev server problems after the Vite upgrade and prepared a staging deploy of the new build, which is not in production yet.
body:
The Vite upgrade from earlier had left two problems: the dev server failed on a proxy setting for the API, and one ECharts import path no longer resolved. I rewrote the proxy block in the Vite config to the new option format, and the API calls from the dev server work again.

The ECharts import now uses the package's own entry point instead of the deep path, and the charts render in the dev server and in the production build. I ran the Vitest suite and the Playwright smoke tests against the new build, and all of them passed.

I deployed the build to staging in the evening and opened the dashboard, the report builder and the settings page with the session list. On a throttled fast 3G profile the first load went from 3.9 to 3.8 seconds, and the largest chart appeared about 120 ms earlier. I will let staging run for a day and read the browser error reports before I decide on production.

summary: Answered Jonas's question on whether the session list shows logins from the mobile app: yes, with device type 'app', but the city is empty because the app sends no IP-forwarding header.
body:
Jonas saw rows in the session list without a city and asked if it was a bug. The rows are the mobile app sessions. The city comes from the IP address of the request, and Render passes the client address in X-Forwarded-For. The app's requests do carry it, but our lookup used the socket address for requests that have the app header, which is a leftover of the old token code.

I checked the middleware and found the condition. Fixing it is a one line change, but the agency should know that the city will then show where the phone's mobile network exits, which is not always the true city. I will tell Jonas to mention this to them, and I did not change the code yet.

summary: Fixed the city lookup for mobile app sessions to use the forwarded address, and added a note in the session list that the place of a phone is approximate.
body:
After Jonas confirmed that an approximate city is better than an empty field, I changed the middleware. The client IP is now taken from the forwarded header for all requests, the same way for web and app, and the old branch for the app header is deleted.

The trust setting matters here. Express only reads X-Forwarded-For correctly when 'trust proxy' is set to the number of proxies. On Render it is 1. I wrote a test with three headers, including one with a fake address added by the client in front of the real one, and the middleware takes the right one.

Existing sessions have no city saved because it is looked up at login. I wrote a small script that fills the city from the last IP address saved on the session row. It touched 41 app sessions, and 6 had no IP address at all and stayed empty. The script ran in a transaction and I checked the counts before and after.

The session list shows 'about' before the city for the app sessions, and a tooltip says that the place of a phone can be inexact. Priya reviewed the wording by message and shortened it.

I also added the country as a fallback when the city is not found. That happens for 12 percent of the lookups in the test data, mostly mobile networks.

The mobile agency has not been contacted by me; Jonas will tell them. Nothing in the app needs to change on their side.

summary: Wrote the plan for the costs page drill-down: from a monthly total to the cost per depot and then to single shipments, using one summary query per level.
body:
Jonas wants managers to click a bar on the costs page and see what is behind it. I wrote the plan before building anything, since the costs page is the one with the heaviest queries.

There are three levels. The first is the cost per month, which exists. The second is the cost per depot for a month, and the third is the list of shipments of one depot in that month with their cost parts: fuel, tolls and waiting time. Each click should load only its own level.

For the queries I looked at the current one. It sums the cost parts over the whole shipments table with a group by month and takes 600 ms on the production copy. The second level filters by month and groups by depot, so the existing index on delivery date should help. I checked with EXPLAIN and it uses an index scan, about 45 ms for a month with 30k shipments.

The third level can be big, so it uses the same table component with server side paging and not the whole list. Export of this level can use the streaming writer as is.

Things to decide: how the back button works, and how a deep link looks. My proposal is to keep the selection in the URL as ?month=...&depot=..., so a manager can send a link. That fits how the table filters already work.

The risks are the permissions: a depot manager must only see his own depot at level two. The existing account scoping should apply, but I will write a test for it first.

I will start with the API for level two tomorrow, and ask Priya for the look of the drill-down breadcrumbs.

summary: Built the API for the costs page depot level with account scoping, and a test that a depot manager gets only his own depot's row.
body:
I added GET /api/costs/depots?month=... which returns one row per depot with fuel, tolls, waiting time and the total. The query reuses the scoping helper of the shipments routes, so it adds the depot filter for depot managers and none for the Acme managers.

The test came first. A depot manager of the north depot asks for a month and must get exactly one row, while a head manager gets all 7 depots. It passed after I wired the helper in. A second test sends a depot id of another depot in the query; the server ignores it for depot managers and returns their own row, not an error.

The query takes 45 ms on the production copy for a busy month. I added a short cache header of 60 seconds, private, since the data changes only when shipments are completed.

The response has the total at the end as a separate field, so the client does not have to add the numbers and risk rounding differences. Costs are stored in cents as integers, and I kept that in the API.

Next is the shipment level and the chart click.

summary: Connected the cost chart clicks to the depot level and the shipment level, with the selection in the URL so the back button and shared links work.
body:
The monthly bar chart now reacts to a click: it sets ?month= in the URL and the depot table appears below it. A click on a depot row sets &depot= and shows the shipments of that depot with the cost parts.

I used the existing URL state hook from the table filters, which meant that back and forward work without extra code. A reload gives the same view. I tested with a link opened in a new tab as another user: a depot manager who opens a link for another depot sees his own depot, as designed.

ECharts needed a small fix. The click event gives the series data, and the month was in a label that is formatted for display. I now keep the month key in the data item and read that.

The third level reuses the table component with server side paging, 50 rows per page. Sorting by the cost columns works, and I confirmed that the sort order goes to the server and not just the visible page.

A breadcrumb shows 'Costs / May / North depot' in the design from Priya, but of course with the month name in the user's language. I did not add the export button to level three yet.

Two things I found: the chart does not mark the selected bar, and on a narrow screen the breadcrumb wraps badly. Both are in the list for tomorrow's polish.

summary: Polished the cost drill-down: the selected bar is highlighted, the breadcrumb wraps on small screens and level three has a CSV export button.
body:
The selected month now has a darker colour in the bar chart, using the ECharts emphasis state set from the URL. On narrow screens the breadcrumb shows only the last two parts with an ellipsis for the first.

Level three got the export button. It passes the month and depot to the existing export route, which builds the whole file in memory before sending it. I tested with a month of 28k shipments and the file took a few seconds to start downloading, which is fine for a single month at one depot. For a whole year the same button would probably be slow, since large exports are already known to be slow, so I added a note to the list to look at that later and did not change the route.

I ran the Playwright test for the whole path from chart to shipment list and it passed on all three browsers.

summary: Dispatchers reported the cost drill-down rounds the totals differently than the table; the cause was a client side division by 100 before summing, now done once at the end.
body:
One dispatcher noticed that the sum of the shipment rows on level three was 0.02 lower than the depot total on level two. The API values are exact cents, but the table component formatted each cost with a division and a rounding to two decimals, and the footer summed the rounded values.

I changed the footer to sum the integer cents and divide once when displaying. A test with 50 rows of 0.005-like values, such as 1,333 and 667 cents, shows the correct total now. The other tables that show money use the same formatter, and I checked them; only this footer summed rounded numbers.

summary: Started the accessibility pass for the report builder v2 and the cost drill-down: found 11 issues with a screen reader and keyboard, fixed 8 and listed 3 for a design decision.
body:
I went through both new features with a screen reader and the keyboard only, since they are the newest and have the most custom controls.

In the report builder, the group nesting was not announced. I added aria-level style text through a visually hidden prefix: 'Group, level 2, match any of'. Moving between conditions with the arrow keys now announces 'Condition 3 of 5'. The delete button had only an icon and no name; it says 'Remove condition 3' now.

The live count had no announcement at all. A polite live region says '1,902 shipments match' after the debounce, and not on every keystroke. I took care that it does not repeat the same text, which some readers read again.

On the cost page, the ECharts bars are not reachable by keyboard. ECharts has an aria module that generates a description, which I turned on, but a click on a bar is still only possible with a mouse. I added a table view toggle that shows the same numbers as a table, where the rows are buttons. That is the same drill-down by keyboard and it also helps people who like numbers.

The breadcrumb used a nav element without a label. It has aria-label 'Costs path', and the last item has aria-current.

The contrast check found two failures: the gray text of the 'about' hint at 3.9 to 1 and the disabled save button text. I darkened the hint. The disabled button is exempt by the rules, but I made it a bit clearer anyway.

The three open issues need decisions: whether the chart should be hidden from the screen reader when the table view exists, how to handle zoom at 400 percent in the editor where the groups get very narrow, and whether the toggle should be remembered per user. I will ask Priya about the first two.

I wrote 6 new Playwright checks with axe for these pages, which found nothing more. The pass is not done: the settings page and the login messages were done earlier, the report list is still to check.

summary: Finished the accessibility pass with Priya's decisions: the chart stays visible to screen readers with a pointer to the table view, and the editor stacks its groups at 400 percent zoom.
body:
Priya answered the open points of the accessibility list. For the chart she prefers that it stays reachable for screen readers, since the description is useful, but it should say that a table view exists. The aria description now ends with 'A table view with the same numbers is available above the chart.' She also wanted the toggle remembered, so the choice is saved in local storage per browser and not on the server.

For 400 percent zoom, the group editor lost its width because of the indent per level. At a narrow viewport I now reduce the indent to 8 px and let the condition fields stack vertically, operator below column and value below operator. I tested at 320 CSS pixels wide, which is what 400 percent on a normal laptop screen gives, and no horizontal scrolling is needed for the editor itself.

Then the report list, which I had not checked. The list is a table with a row menu. The menu button had the name 'More', which does not say for which report. It says 'More actions for Weekly summary' now. The sort buttons in the headers did not announce the direction, so I added aria-sort. The copy action I built a few days ago announces 'Report copied' in the live region and moves focus to the new report's name.

Axe found one more issue there: two links with the same name 'Open' pointing to different reports. They include the report name in a hidden text now.

I ran the whole set of checks again. 11 issues from last week are closed and the second pass found 4 more, all fixed. Axe finds nothing on the pages: login, dashboard, tables, report builder, report list, costs, settings.

I also tried the pages with Windows high contrast mode through the browser emulation. The left bars of the groups disappeared, because they are drawn with background colour. I changed them to a border-left, which stays visible in forced colours mode.

I wrote a short note in the repo docs listing the checks to repeat for new features: keyboard only, a screen reader, 400 percent zoom, forced colours and axe.

summary: Investigated a slow login report: the session-based query took 7 seconds for a year of data, and a composite index on site and login time brought it to 300 ms.
body:
A manager complained that the login report for the whole last year needed a long time. I ran the query on the production copy. It took about 7 seconds, and most of it was in the aggregation of auth events by site and day.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan over about 1.1 million rows. The existing index was only on the event time, and the query also filtered by event type and joined on the site at the time of login, which I fixed some weeks ago. Postgres chose the scan because the time range covered most of the table.

I considered three options. A materialized view with daily counts would be the fastest, but needs a refresh and I want the report to show today's logins. A summary table written by the cleanup job would have the same issue. The simplest was a better index first, and to see if that is enough.

I created an index on (event_type, site_id, created_at) and a partial one only for successful logins, as the report counts those. The partial index is about a third of the size. With it the planner uses an index only scan, and the query takes 300 ms for a year and 40 ms for a month.

Creating an index on the live table can lock writes, so I used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which took 38 seconds on production, and no login failed in that time; I watched the error rate. I also dropped an older single column index that nothing used any more, which I checked in pg_stat_user_indexes, where it had zero scans for two months.

The cleanup of auth events after 400 days keeps the table at a stable size, so this index will not grow without a limit. Writes of auth events are a little slower with the extra index, but at about 900 events per day that does not matter.

I told the manager that the report is faster, and she opened it with the full year and was fine. Next I will see if the other reports on the page use the same index.

summary: Fixed scheduled report emails sending twice when two Render instances ran the job during a deploy, by taking a Postgres advisory lock per report run.
body:
Jonas forwarded a mail from a dispatcher who got the same scheduled report twice in the morning, and the sent-mail log confirmed 6 duplicates out of 41 reports. All six went out within a minute of a deploy. During a deploy Render runs the old and the new instance side by side, and both ran the scheduler tick and found the same reports due.

The job only checked a last_sent_at column before sending and wrote it after the mail was handed over. That left a window of a few seconds in which both instances saw the report as due. The slow reports, with 40k rows or more, had the widest window, which fits the pattern.

The fix is a claim step. Before building a report, the job runs a transactional update that sets claimed_at and claimed_by on the row only if it is null or older than 15 minutes, and it continues only when exactly one row was changed. I first tried pg_try_advisory_lock on the report id. It works, but the lock is tied to a connection, and the pool made it hard to reason about, so I dropped that idea. The claim is released by writing last_sent_at, and a crashed instance leaves a claim that expires on its own.

I wrote a Vitest test that starts two job runners against the same test database with 20 due reports and asserts that each report produces exactly one mail record. It failed 9 times in 10 before the change and passed 50 runs in a row after it. I also ran the check against a copy of the production schedule table, and the claim query takes under 2 ms with the existing index on next_run_at.

Not done yet: the deploy of today must be watched, and I want to look at the mail log after the next release to confirm no duplicates. The login rate limiter has the same two-instance weakness, and I will look at it next.

summary: Checked the sent-mail log after the lock change: 41 scheduled reports went out in the morning, each exactly once, including the deploy of the afternoon.
body:
I compared the schedule list with the sent log for the last two days. 41 reports were due and 41 mails were sent, none twice. One deploy happened at lunch time, while two schedules were due within the same minute, and the new lock handled it: the log shows 'skipped, locked' once for the old instance.

No row stayed in 'running' longer than 20 seconds. The longest report took 14 seconds, the one with 60k rows. I consider the problem closed and will look again after a week.

summary: Replaced the in-memory rate limiter of the login route with one backed by Postgres, because two Render instances during a deploy each allowed 10 attempts instead of 10 in total.
body:
While reading the deploy overlap of the mail job I thought of the other places where state lives in the process. The login rate limiter is one. It counts failed attempts per email and per IP in memory, which is fine with one instance, but during a deploy two instances run and each has its own count.

I checked how much it mattered by a test with a script doing 18 wrong passwords against two instances behind a simple round robin. Both counted 9 and let everything pass, where the limit is 10 per 15 minutes. Not a big hole, but not what Acme IT was told.

I wrote the limiter on a table login_attempts with the key, the count and the window start. An attempt does an upsert, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, that either increases the count or resets the window if it has expired. This is one query on the login path, and since logins are few, the extra 2 ms are fine.

I took care of the failure case. If the database call fails, the limiter lets the request through and logs a warning, because the login needs the database anyway for the session. A failed limiter should not be a second reason for a login failure.

The cleanup job for old sessions now also deletes attempt rows older than a day. I added this to the same nightly run in a second statement, and it uses an index on the window start.

Tests: 6 new ones for the upsert, the window reset, the per-IP key, the per-email key, success clearing the email count and the failure fallback. With the same 18 attempt script against two instances, the 11th attempt got the 429 response as intended.

One consideration was the forwarded IP: the key uses the same trusted client address as the city lookup, so the limiter cannot be bypassed with a fake header.

Deployed in the evening. I watched the login errors for an hour and saw 3 wrong passwords and no 429 for real users.

summary: Reviewed the week of login rate limit logs: 2 users hit the limit, both with a password manager that filled an old password, and the message now tells them to wait and how long.
body:
I looked at the login attempts table and the logs since the Postgres limiter went live. 214 failed attempts in total, almost all single mistakes. Two users reached the limit of 10 in 15 minutes.

Both were dispatchers on a shared desk computer where a password manager filled in an old password after the reset of last month and retried the login on its own. They saw only 'Too many attempts', with no idea what to do, and one of them called Jonas.

I changed the 429 response to include a Retry-After header and a field with the seconds left. The login page shows 'Too many attempts. Try again in 9 minutes.' and a link to the password reset. The text is in a live region so a screen reader announces it, and I used the checks from last week's pass.

The mobile app also receives the 429. I told Jonas that the field retry_after_seconds is new and optional; the app shows its own text now and keeps working without it. He will pass the information on to the agency.

I also thought about the per-email key. An attacker could lock out a real user by failing on purpose. The lock lasts 15 minutes and the reset link works, which Acme IT accepts for now. I wrote it in the notes as a known trade-off and not as a bug.

The two dispatchers got the information about the old stored password from Jonas, and their desk computer was fixed. No further limit hits since then.

Next I will build the small admin view that Jonas asked for, where he can see locked emails and clear a lock for a user who is stuck.

summary: Planned the cleanup job for old session rows: expired and revoked sessions are deleted in batches at night, with a 30 day grace period so support can still look at recent ones.
body:
The sessions table grew to 412k rows in under a month, mostly from the mobile app, which opens a new session on each cold start. Nothing deletes them yet. Today I wrote the plan before touching code.

Rules agreed with myself: a row is deletable when it is expired, or revoked, and its last activity is older than 30 days. The grace period exists because support sometimes asks why a user was logged out, and the row is the only evidence. Deletes run in batches of 5000 ordered by id, with a short pause between batches, so the job never holds a long lock.

I checked the numbers on a production copy. With the rule above, 318k of the 412k rows are deletable. The query to find them used a sequential scan and took 1.9 seconds, so I added a partial index on last_activity for rows that are expired or revoked. The scan went down to 40 ms.

Where the job runs was the open question. Two Render instances run during a deploy, and the scheduled report fix of last week took an advisory lock for this reason. The cleanup will use the same pattern with its own lock key, so a second instance just skips the run.

I also thought about the 90 day absolute limit from a few days ago. Sessions past that limit count as expired, so they fall under the same rule and need no extra case.

Not decided yet: whether to log the number of deleted rows per run to the existing job log table or only to stdout. I lean toward the table, because Jonas asked once how many sessions Acme has per month and this would answer it. Next step is the job itself with a test on a small fixture set.

summary: Started the session cleanup job: a nightly batch delete of expired and revoked session rows, after the sessions table grew to several hundred thousand rows with nobody pruning it.
body:
The sessions table has never been cleaned since the move back to server-side sessions, and it has grown to about 410k rows. Most of them are expired or revoked. They slow down the session list query a little and make the nightly backup larger. Today was spent on the design and a first version of the job, and nothing is deployed yet.

The rule is simple. A row is deleted when it is expired or revoked and the end happened more than 30 days ago. The grace period is there so that support can still look at recent sessions when a user writes in about a strange logout. Active sessions are never touched, whatever their age, because the absolute 90 day limit already ends them by itself.

The delete runs in batches of 5000 rows. Each batch selects the ids with a limit and deletes by id, with a short pause of 200 ms between batches. One big DELETE would hold locks for too long and could block logins during the run. I tested the batch size on a production copy: 5000 rows took about 90 ms, 50000 took over a second, so I kept the small size.

The job runs at 03:10 and takes the same Postgres advisory lock that the scheduled report job uses, with its own key. That way two Render instances during a deploy cannot both run it. It also logs how many rows it deleted, how many batches it needed and the total run time.

I added a dry run mode that only counts the rows that would go. On the production copy it reports 321k rows, which matches my own count from a manual query. I also wrote a test that creates sessions in all states, runs the job and checks that only the old expired and revoked ones are gone.

Still open: an index on the end time of sessions, since the selection now scans, and a decision on whether the session list should hide revoked rows earlier. Next is the deploy with a watch on the first run.

summary: Deployed the session cleanup job and watched the first run: it removed 321k old rows, the table is a quarter of its size, and no login got slower.
body:
The job went to production this afternoon, and I started the first run by hand instead of waiting for the night.

It deleted 321,455 rows in 47 seconds. The sessions table went from 412k rows to about 96k. The login p95 on the monitoring page stayed at 120 ms during the run.

The table is still large on disk, because Postgres does not give the space back after the deletes. Autovacuum will mark it reusable, which is enough for now. A VACUUM FULL would lock the table, so I did not do it.

I added a line to the runbook explaining the rule and the grace period, so that anyone asking why an old session is gone finds the answer. Tomorrow I will check the log of the first scheduled night run.

summary: Built the 'log out of all devices' endpoint: it revokes every session of the user except, optionally, the current one, and returns how many were revoked.
body:
Jonas asked for a way for users to end all their sessions after losing a phone. With sessions as rows this is one update statement.

The new route POST /api/sessions/revoke-all takes a flag keep_current. It sets revoked_at on all active sessions of the user, and when the flag is set it leaves the one of the request. The response has the count.

The mobile app gets a 401 with code session_revoked on its next call, the same as for a single revoke, so the agency needs no change.

Tests: another user's sessions are untouched, the current session survives with the flag, and a second call returns 0. I also checked that the rate limiter counts this route, since it is a cheap way to hammer the database otherwise.

The button on the settings page comes next.

summary: Added the 'log out of all devices' button to the settings page with a confirmation dialog and a live region that announces how many sessions were ended.
body:
The settings page now has a button under the session list. It opens a dialog asking whether to keep the current device, with that as the default choice.

After the call the list reloads and a live region says, for example, '3 sessions were ended'. I took the pattern from the revoke confirmation of the accessibility pass, so a screen reader user gets the same behavior.

I tried it with the keyboard only: focus moves into the dialog, escape closes it and focus returns to the button. With a screen reader the dialog title is read first, which was the point of the test.

Priya looked at the wording and wanted 'Sign out everywhere' instead of my 'Revoke all'. Changed. Her second note, a warning color for the confirm button, is done too.

Playwright test added: log in on two browser contexts, use the button in one, and see the other one sent to the login page on its next request.

summary: Investigated why some users still saw a revoked session in the list for a minute: the list response was cached by the browser, so the fix is a no-store header on the sessions routes.
body:
A dispatcher wrote that after ending a session on his phone, the old entry stayed in the list on his desktop. I could reproduce it.

First guess was the 10 minute count cache from the report list. That was wrong, the session list does not use it. Second guess was the database replica, but we have none.

The network tab showed the answer: GET /api/sessions had no Cache-Control header, and Chrome applied heuristic caching because of the Last-Modified header that Express adds for the static-like response from our etag middleware. The entry stayed for about 60 seconds.
