The fix is Cache-Control: no-store on all routes under /api/sessions and /api/auth, set in one middleware. I also removed the etag for these routes.

A test checks the header on both route groups. After the deploy I repeated the steps of the dispatcher and the entry vanished at once.

I looked for other routes that return personal data without the header. The costs summaries and the shipments list do, but they are not sensitive in the same way, and caching them helps speed. I left them and wrote a note in the backlog.

Small lesson: the earlier logout bugs in the JWT time were about tokens, this one is just plain HTTP caching.

summary: Checked the first week of nightly cleanup runs: about 9k rows deleted per night, run time under 5 seconds and the table size is flat.
body:
I read the job log table for the seven runs since the deploy. The counts are between 8.4k and 10.1k deleted rows per night, and the run time is 3 to 5 seconds.

The sessions table holds about 105k rows, which matches the active users plus the 30 day grace period. Disk use of the table stopped growing, since the freed space is reused.

One night the run took 19 seconds. It overlapped with the scheduled report job at 03:30, and the report job held more load. I moved the cleanup to 04:10.

Nothing else to fix. I will check again after the 90 day limit has had its first full cycle of expiries.

summary: Planned the reports history page: every scheduled run gets a row with status, row count and mail recipients, so Jonas can answer 'did my report go out' without asking me.
body:
Jonas asked twice in the last weeks whether a specific scheduled report was sent. Right now I answer from the sent-mail log, which only I can read.

The plan is a table report_runs with report_id, started_at, finished_at, status (ok, failed, skipped), row_count, byte_size and an error text. The scheduled job writes the row at the start and updates it at the end. The advisory lock from the double-send fix already marks the place where a run begins, so the code change is small.

The page is a list per report in the report builder, newest first, with a filter for failed runs. Recipients are not stored per run but read from the report at display time, which is wrong if the list changed later. To be correct, I will store a copy of the recipient addresses on each run.

Privacy question: addresses are personal data, so I will delete run rows after 12 months with the same job pattern as the session cleanup.

I sized it: 41 reports, mostly daily, so about 15k rows per year. No index trouble.

Order of work: migration, writing from the job, API with account scoping, then the page. A skipped run is also written, with the reason, for the case that the lock is taken by another instance. That one may be noisy during deploys, so I will only record it when the lock holder is a different run of the same report, not on every skip.

summary: Wrote the report_runs migration and made the scheduled job write a row per run, including failed runs with the error text cut to 500 characters.
body:
The migration creates report_runs with an index on report_id and started_at descending. The job inserts a row after taking the lock and updates it in a finally block, so a crash in the middle still leaves a status of failed.

A hard process kill is not covered by the finally block. For that case I added a sweep at the start of each job run: rows with status running and started more than one hour ago become failed with the text 'interrupted'.

I ran the job on staging against the 41 reports. All 41 rows appeared with ok and row counts that match the table exports. One report with a deliberately broken filter produced a failed row with the SQL error message.

The recipient copy is stored as a text array. Tests cover the ok path, the failed path and the sweep. API and page follow.

summary: Added the API for report run history with account scoping; a manager sees only runs of reports of his own account.
body:
The route GET /api/reports/:id/runs returns the last 50 runs with a cursor for more. It checks that the report belongs to the account of the user, the same helper as the report copy action uses.

I wrote a test with two accounts: the second one gets a 404, not a 403, so the existence of a report id is not revealed. Another test checks the order and the cursor.

The failed filter is a query parameter, status=failed. The error text is only returned to users with the manager role, since it can contain table names.

The page comes next.

summary: Built the run history list in the report builder: a table with status badge, rows, size and time, plus a filter for failed runs only.
body:
The history is a tab on the report detail view. Each row shows the start time, a status badge with text and icon so it does not rely on color alone, the row count and the size in a readable unit.

The failed filter is a checkbox that updates the URL, like the cost drill-down does. Loading more uses a button instead of infinite scroll, which is easier with a keyboard.

For a failed row the error text is shown in an expandable region for managers. Dispatchers see only 'failed'.

I checked the page with the screen reader quickly: the table has a caption and the badges are read correctly. Priya will review the look tomorrow.

summary: Applied Priya's notes to the run history tab: calmer badges, relative times with the exact time in a tooltip, and an empty state that explains the schedule.
body:
Priya found the badges too loud when many runs are ok. They are now plain text with a small icon, and only failed runs get a colored background.

Times show as '2 hours ago' with the exact local time in the title and in a visually hidden span, so screen readers get the exact value too.

The empty state used to say 'No data'. It now says that the report has not run yet and shows the next planned run from the schedule.

I took one note and did not do it: a chart of run times. With at most a daily run it would show little.

summary: Found that the run history showed a skipped run for every deploy because both instances tried the lock; skips are now written only when another run of the same report holds it.
body:
Looking at staging after a deploy I saw 41 skipped rows, one per report. They came from the old instance and the new instance both reaching the job at the same time.

That was the noise I had feared in the plan. The fix checks the report_runs table: if there is a running row for this report that started in the last hour, the skip is recorded. Otherwise the instance that lost the lock just returns.

In practice this means a skip row only appears when a run is really slow and the next schedule hits it. I forced this case on staging with a sleep in the job, and exactly one skipped row appeared.

The tests include the deploy case with two simultaneous starts. The history is now quiet and shows only what matters. Deployed to production at the end of the session.

Next I want to add the 12 month cleanup of old run rows.

summary: Reviewed the whole session system with a security checklist and found three gaps: no limit of sessions per user, a long-lived remember cookie flag and an unlogged revoke-all.
body:
Eight months after the move back to sessions it was time for a review. I went through the code from login to cleanup with a list: cookie flags, fixation, revoke, expiry, logging and abuse.

Good: the cookie is HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Lax, the session id is renewed at login, the 90 day limit works, and the rate limiter is shared between instances.

Gap 1: there is no limit on the number of active sessions per user. A script could log in 10,000 times with a valid password and fill the table. The rate limit slows it but does not stop it over days. Proposal: keep the 20 newest sessions, revoke older ones at login. The mobile app agency should know, because a driver with many reinstalls could hit it, but 20 is far above normal use. The biggest user today has 9.

Gap 2: the remember flag from the first version still sets a cookie max-age of 90 days on shared computers even when the box was not ticked, in one code path of the SSO login. I confirmed it with a test using the SSO callback. Fix: that path must set a session cookie without max-age when remember is false.

Gap 3: revoke-all writes no audit line. A single revoke is logged with user, session and IP, but the new endpoint of last week is not. Support could not tell who ended the sessions.

I wrote tickets for the three with a small test for each. I did the audit line at once, three lines of code, and the test checks the log entry.

I also looked at things that are fine and need no change: password reset ends all sessions, a password change does too, and SSO logout from the identity provider is not supported by design, which Jonas knows.

Order: gap 2 first because it is a real exposure, then gap 1. I will tell Jonas the cap of 20 before it goes live.

summary: Fixed the SSO login path that set a 90 day cookie even when 'remember me' was off; it now issues a browser-session cookie as intended.
body:
The test from the review reproduced it: after the SSO callback without remember, the Set-Cookie header carried Max-Age of 7776000 seconds.

The cause was a helper that defaulted the remember value to true when the callback state did not contain the flag. The state is built before the redirect to the identity provider, and the flag was only added for the password form.

Now the flag is stored in the state for both flows and the default is false. The test checks that the header has no Max-Age without the flag and has it with the flag.

Existing sessions of managers are not changed, since the cookie lives in their browsers. The absolute 90 day limit still applies on the server side, so the exposure was bounded.

Deployed.

summary: Implemented the cap of 20 active sessions per user: at login the oldest ones beyond the cap are revoked with the reason 'cap'.
body:
After the login creates a session, one update revokes all but the 20 most recently active sessions of that user. The reason field is set to cap so the list and the logs can show why.

A test creates 25 sessions and checks that 20 stay active and the 5 oldest are revoked. A second test checks that the current session is never among the revoked ones.

I told Jonas about the cap in a short message. He had no objection. The mobile app agency gets the same 401 session_revoked as for any revoke.

The settings list shows 'ended because of too many sessions' for such rows.

summary: Answered Jonas on how long Acme sessions really last: most are under 3 days of activity, and only 6 percent reach the 90 day limit.
body:
Jonas wanted to know if the 90 day limit annoys people. I queried the sessions of the last quarter.

The median session had activity over 2.6 days. The 90th percentile was 41 days, and 6 percent of sessions ended by hitting the absolute limit. Most of those belong to dispatchers who keep a browser open on a wall screen.

For the wall screens the forced login every 90 days is a small chore, once a quarter. Acme IT agreed to the limit, so I recommended no change. If it becomes a complaint, a dedicated read-only display account could be the answer, but that is a design topic for later.

I sent Jonas the three numbers and the query so that he can ask again himself.

summary: Planned and started the CSV export of large tables from the table view: measured that a 400k row export takes 38 seconds and that the browser waits on one request.
body:
Dispatchers export big shipment ranges from the table view, and managers complained that it is slow and sometimes ends with a gateway timeout. Before changing anything I measured.

A range with 400k rows took 38 seconds to the first byte on production. The timeout of the Render proxy is 100 seconds, so ranges of about 1 million rows fail. The server builds the whole file in memory before it sends it, with a peak of 1.1 GB, which also risks the instance.

I looked at the code path. The route reads all rows with one query, maps them to CSV lines in an array and joins them. The mapping itself is cheap, 4 seconds for 400k rows. Most time is the query with a join on depots, which takes 21 seconds, and then the string joining and the response.

Ideas I wrote down: a streaming response with a database cursor, a background export with a download link by mail, and a limit of rows with a message. The mail option is what the scheduled reports already do, but dispatchers want the file at once.

For now I only collected data and did not choose. The scheduled reports use another writer which was fixed for memory some weeks ago, and I want to see whether the table export can share it.

I also found that the date filter of the table is applied after the join, which makes the query read more than needed. An index on shipments(delivered_at) exists, but the planner does not use it because of a cast. Fixing the cast brought the query from 21 to 9 seconds on the copy. That is a good small step.

I made that change and ran the shipments tests, all green. The total for 400k rows is now 26 seconds. It is not enough, but it helps. Deployed the query fix only.

Next: compare the two export paths and decide about the larger change.

summary: Compared the table export path with the scheduled report writer and wrote down why they should not be merged yet: filters, column choice and permissions differ.
body:
Following up on the export measurements, I read both implementations side by side.

The scheduled report writer takes a filter tree, a fixed column list and a user context from the saved report. The table export takes the current table state: filters of the table, the visible columns in the visible order, the sort and the language of the user. It also formats dates and numbers in the user locale, while reports use a fixed format.

Permissions are applied in different places. Reports apply the account scope in the SQL function from the filter tree. The table applies it in the route before the query. Merging means choosing one of them, and a mistake would leak rows of another account. I do not want to take that risk in the middle of other changes.

So the conclusion: keep two paths for now, and improve the table export by itself.

I tried a quick experiment on a branch-free local copy: reading the rows with a cursor, 1000 at a time, and counting lines without building the file. Memory stayed under 120 MB, but I did not write a response yet. This only proves that reading is not the problem.

There are other things to settle first. Excel users expect a BOM at the start of the file for umlauts. The current export has it, so any new path must keep it. The line ending is CRLF, also expected by Acme.

I listed the acceptance points: same bytes as now for a small range, BOM and CRLF kept, memory flat, scope tests pass, and abort of the download stops the query.

I shared the list with Jonas to see if anything is missing. He added that the file name should contain the range, which it does today.

Nothing was deployed in this session. The next session starts on the real change.

summary: Built a cursor based reader for the table export that pages through rows with keyset pagination, as the first step toward fixing slow large exports; not wired in yet.
body:
The 400k row export measured earlier takes 38 seconds because the route builds the whole file in memory and the browser waits on one request. Today I only built the reader, and left the route alone. It is a new module, src/server/export/cursorReader.ts, that fetches rows in pages of 5,000 using keyset pagination on (shipped_at, id) instead of OFFSET, because OFFSET got slower with each page in a quick test on a production copy.

The reader takes the same filter tree that report builder v2 uses, so the filters of the table view and the saved reports go through the existing tree to SQL function. It also applies the account scoping, and a test checks that a depot manager gets only the rows of his own depot. I considered a Postgres server side cursor, but with the connection pool of two Render instances it would hold a connection for the whole export, so keyset pages are the safer choice.

I wrote 9 Vitest tests: empty result, exactly one page, a page boundary that falls inside a group of rows with the same timestamp, and a filter that matches nothing. The tie case found a real bug in my first version, which skipped rows when two shipments had the same shipped_at, and adding id to the key fixed it. On a copy with 1.2 million rows the reader walks the whole table in 19 seconds, and memory stays flat at about 60 MB.

Not done yet: the formatting. The old path writes a BOM, CRLF line ends and locale formatted numbers, and the reader returns raw rows only. Next step is to feed the rows into a writer that keeps those exactly, and to compare the bytes with the old export before anything uses the new reader.

summary: Planned the cursor based table export and wrote a comparison script that checks the old export output for 12 sample ranges, without changing the real route.
body:
Large table exports are still slow, so I spent the session preparing the fix instead of changing the route. The real export route has not been touched and still has only the old path, which builds the whole file in memory.

First I wrote down what the new export has to keep: the BOM at the start, CRLF at the end of each line, and the locale formatting of numbers and dates for both languages. The header line also goes through the formatter in the old path, so a header with a comma is quoted. I noted this because it is easy to miss.

Then I wrote a comparison script that is meant to run two implementations for 12 ranges, from 3 rows to 80k rows, with different column sets and both languages, and diff the output byte by byte. For now it runs the old path twice, to check that the script itself is stable. The 12 ranges give identical files, so the baseline is clean. It also covers a filter that matches nothing, where the file should have only the header line.

I looked at the scope test of the table export too. A depot manager gets only the rows of his depot. The test runs against the current path only, so I listed what it needs to be parametrized for a second path, so that the same cases can run against both without being rewritten.

I also thought about aborts. If the user closes the browser tab in the middle of a long export, the server must stop reading and must not leave a database cursor open. I sketched a test for this that closes the request after the first chunk and checks the open cursors in Postgres. It is not written yet.

Next I will build the cursor based reader with keyset pagination as a separate module and not connect it to the route. A feature flag read from the environment will come when the reader passes the comparison script.

summary: Planned how to test the CSV export of large tables on staging and measured how the current in-memory export behaves, before any cursor-based change exists.
body:
I wrote down a plan for the large table exports and took baseline numbers on staging with the current export path, which builds the whole file in memory. A 400k row range took 38 seconds, which matches what I saw on the table view earlier. An 800k row range took well over a minute, and the instance memory climbed to more than 600 MB before the response started.

A run with 1.2 million rows was cut by the proxy at 100 seconds, and nothing had been sent by then. That is expected with this path, because the first byte only goes out after the file is complete. What I do not know yet is whether the proxy limit counts the time without data or the total request time. I need to read the Render documentation on this, since so far I am only guessing.

The answer matters for the plan. If the limit is on the total time, then even a faster export will fail above a certain size, and a clear message for very large ranges may be enough. The largest export in the logs of last quarter was 1.3 million rows, and dispatchers rarely go above a few hundred thousand.

I listed the open points: the proxy limit, how to keep the BOM, CRLF and locale formatting identical to the old file, and how to compare the bytes of a new export against the old one on a set of sample ranges. I did not change any code today. The export route is untouched, and no flag exists yet.

summary: Found why the large export run failed on staging at 2 million rows, and prepared a smaller chunk size and a row limit, with the cursor export still off in production.
body:
I read the Render docs and tested with a long running local mock: the proxy closes a connection when no byte arrives for 100 seconds, and a long response that keeps sending is fine. So the idle timeout counts the time between bytes, not the total time of the response. My staging failure at 2 million rows was something else.

Looking at the logs of that run, the cursor read was fine, but the formatter for the cost column was slow on a certain block of rows with very long decimal text, and a gap of more than 100 seconds opened between two chunks. I could not reproduce the gap on a second run. Most likely the instance was busy with the scheduled job at that time.

To be safe I added a heartbeat idea to my notes, then dropped it: nothing can be added to a CSV without breaking it. Instead I made the chunk size smaller, 500 rows, so bytes flow more often. This is only in the staging build for now.

I also wrote a hard limit of 2.5 million rows, with a message in the table view saying that the range is too large and which filters to use. The check is a count query with a 3 second limit, like the one in the report builder preview.

I ran the 2 million range on staging three times, and all finished, at about 120 seconds each.

The cursor flag is still off in production, and exports there use the old path. Next I want to run the large ranges on staging at a busy moment of the scheduled job, to see whether the gap comes back, and then decide when to switch the flag on and watch the logs and the memory graph.

The cleanup of old report run rows is still to do, and I will take it up after that.

summary: Prepared the check of the CSV export of large tables by measuring the old path and planning a cursor based reader, without changing the export yet.
body:
I read the export log and the memory graph for the day to get a baseline before touching the export. There were 23 table exports, between 40 rows and 640k rows. The largest one ran for 78 seconds on the old path and only just got through the gateway, so the long runs are close to the limit.

The memory peak of the instance was more than a gigabyte, and it came from the old path, which builds the whole file in memory before it sends the first byte. The browser waits on one request the whole time, and a user who cancelled a download after a few seconds still left the server building the file to the end.

I asked one dispatcher to open a recent export in Excel so that I know what must stay the same. Umlauts are right, and the columns are in the order of the table. The byte order mark, the CRLF line ends and the locale formatting all have to survive any change, so I saved twelve sample ranges of the current output as reference files.

I plan to write a reader that pages through the rows with keyset pagination and to compare its output byte by byte with those reference files. Nothing is wired into the export route yet, and the old path stays as it is. If the comparison is clean, the next step is to try it on staging with the largest ranges.

summary: Prepared the cursor based table export for a trial on staging and wrote the 12 month retention job for report run rows, without deploying either.
body:
The cursor based export reader from the last days is not live yet, so I spent the first part of the session on how it should be checked before anyone relies on it. I ran the comparison script against 12 sample ranges on staging and the output matched the old export byte for byte in 11 of them. The twelfth differed in the order of rows with equal timestamps, so I added the shipment id as a second sort key in the keyset pagination. After that all 12 ranges matched.

I also measured the old in-memory path again with a table of 1.1 million rows. It needs a lot of memory and takes longer than the gateway allows, which is the known problem. I wrote the numbers down so that I can compare them later. The route itself is unchanged, and the cursor reader is still not wired in. I listed the open questions for the switch: the chunk size, a row limit, and how to fall back to the old path if something fails. Nothing is decided yet, and I want Jonas to know that big exports will stay slow for now.

The second part was the retention for report_runs from the plan, and I wrote this job today. It is a small job built the same way as the session cleanup: advisory lock, batches of 5000, and a count in the job log. The rule deletes rows with started_at older than 12 months.

There are only 9 months of rows today, so the first run would delete nothing. I tested with a fixture that has rows of 13 months, and the test checks that only these are removed and the recent ones stay.

I planned the schedule for 04:30 on Sundays, after the session cleanup, so the two do not overlap. I started a line for the runbook next to the one for sessions, including the reason, which is the recipient addresses stored in the rows. Nothing is deployed yet. Open topics for the next weeks are the accessibility check of the run history page and the first look at the costs page for the new fiscal year.

summary: Wrote down what the session system looks like after the cleanup, the cap and the revoke-all work, so the next person to touch the login starts from one page.
body:
The login has changed three times and the notes were scattered over old entries. I wrote one page in docs/auth.md that describes the current state. Sessions are rows in Postgres with an id, user id, created and last seen time, a revoke reason and an expiry.

The cookie holds only the session id. It is httpOnly and secure, and it is a browser-session cookie unless 'remember me' is on, in which case it lives 90 days. The SSO path now follows the same rule.

The page lists the nightly cleanup: expired and revoked rows are deleted after a 30 day grace period. It also lists the cap of 20 active sessions per user, with the reason 'cap', and the revoke-all endpoint with its count.

I added a short section on what to check when a user says they were logged out: first the revoke reason in the row, then the cleanup log, then the cap. I also listed the rate limit on the login route, which lives in Postgres since the deploy problem.

Nothing in the code changed. The next topic is the report builder, where Jonas wants a copy function for reports.

summary: Added a 'duplicate report' action to the report builder after Jonas asked for it, copying filters, columns and the schedule but not the recipients.
body:
Jonas said that his managers build almost the same report for each region and start from nothing every time. I added a duplicate action in the report list menu. It calls POST /api/reports/:id/duplicate and returns the new report.

The copy takes the filters, the column choice, the grouping and the chart type. The name gets ' (copy)' appended. The schedule is copied but set to paused, so a copy cannot send mail by accident.

I left out the recipients on purpose. A copy that mails the same people twice would be annoying, and the first thing a manager does is change the audience anyway. The dialog says this in one line.

The account scoping is the same as for the other report routes: the endpoint loads the report with the account of the session and returns 404 otherwise. I wrote a Vitest case that tries to duplicate a report of another account and expects a 404.

The copy runs in one transaction, because a report has rows in two tables, reports and report_columns. A failure in the second insert used to leave an empty report in my first draft, and the test with a forced error caught it.

Playwright got one new test: open the menu, duplicate, check the new name and the paused badge. It passed on the second run; the first failed because the menu animation was still running, so the test now waits for the menu item to be visible and stable.

To do: Priya should look at the position of the action in the menu.

summary: Applied Priya's review of the duplicate action: moved it below 'edit', added a toast with an undo, and fixed the focus after the dialog closes.
body:
Priya looked at the duplicate action this afternoon and had three notes. The action sat above 'edit' and looked like the main action, so I moved it below. Delete stays last, separated by a line.

She wanted feedback that does not interrupt the work. The dialog after the copy is gone; a toast says 'Report copied, schedule paused' and has an undo button. Undo deletes the new report with the existing delete route, which is allowed because it has never run.

The third note was about keyboard use. After the menu closed, the focus went to the body of the page. I made the focus go to the name of the new row in the list, and the live region announces the copy for screen readers.

I checked with VoiceOver on the Mac. The list announces 'Report copied, schedule paused' once, not twice as in the first try, where both the toast and the region spoke. The toast now has aria-hidden and only the region speaks.

The toast timeout is 8 seconds, longer than the usual 4, because undo needs time to be found. Priya agreed.

I updated the Playwright test to click undo and check that the row disappears. It is stable over 10 runs in a loop.

The duplicate action is finished from my side. Jonas gets it with the next deploy.

summary: Traced a slow reports list to an N+1 query that counted runs per report, and replaced it with one grouped query; the list went from 1.9 s to 140 ms for Acme's largest account.
body:
A manager told Jonas that the reports list takes a long time to open. I reproduced it with the largest account, which has 212 reports. The page needed 1.9 seconds for the API call alone.

The query log showed the cause. The list handler loaded the reports, and then for each report it ran one query for the last run and one for the run count. That is 425 queries for a single page, since the run history page added the report_runs table.

I replaced both with one query. It uses a lateral join for the last run and a grouped count over report_runs for the same set of report ids. The result is mapped by report id in the handler.

I first tried a window function over the whole table, but the planner scanned all of report_runs. The grouped count restricted by report id with ANY($1) uses the index on report_id.

I checked that the index exists in the migration of last week, and it does. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows an index scan and 11 ms for the aggregate.

Result: 3 queries instead of 425, and the API call takes 140 ms for the same account. The smaller accounts went from about 200 ms to 40 ms.

I added a test that counts queries with a simple wrapper around the pool and fails if the list uses more than 4 for 50 reports. This should stop the problem from coming back.

The response format did not change, so the frontend is untouched. I deployed after the tests passed and watched the response times for an hour; they stayed under 200 ms for the whole hour.

The run count was always the total of all runs, but the page shows only 12 months since the cleanup. I noted this for Jonas; the counts may drop a bit and that is correct.

summary: Confirmed after the deploy that the reports list stays fast: the 95th percentile over the night was 170 ms and no new slow queries showed up.
body:
I looked at the Render logs and the slow query log of Postgres for the night after the grouped query change. The 95th percentile of the reports list was 170 ms, the slowest single call 310 ms.

No query of the list route appeared in the slow log, whose threshold is 200 ms. The only entries were the known nightly session cleanup, which takes under 5 seconds.

I also checked that the count of runs shown matches the database for three accounts by hand. They matched.

Nothing more to do for this topic. I closed the note in the todo file.

summary: Planned the accessibility pass over the charts: keyboard access to data points, a table alternative per chart, and colour contrast of the series in the light and dark theme.
body:
An Acme manager uses a screen reader and told Jonas that the charts are silent. I went through the charts page and wrote down what is missing.

First, the ECharts canvas has no text at all. ECharts has an aria option that generates a description, and I want to switch it on with a custom label per chart that says what is shown and for which range.

Second, the data points cannot be reached by keyboard. A simple and robust way is a button 'show as table' under each chart that opens the same data in an accessible table. I prefer this to a custom keyboard model on the canvas, which would take weeks.

Third, contrast. I measured the series colours against the background. Three of eight colours in the dark theme are below 3:1, which is the limit for graphics. Priya has to choose new values, so I sent her the list of the three.

Fourth, the legend items must be real buttons with a pressed state. Today they are divs with a click handler.

Order of work: the aria descriptions first, since they are cheap, then the legend buttons, then the table alternative, and the colours when Priya answers.

I estimate three sessions. The table alternative can reuse the table component of the shipments page, which saves most of the work.

summary: Turned on ECharts aria descriptions with a label per chart and made the legend items real toggle buttons with aria-pressed, verified with VoiceOver.
body:
I started with the cheap parts of the plan. Each chart component now passes an ariaLabel prop to a small wrapper, which sets the ECharts option aria.enabled and aria.label.description. The text is built from the title, the range and the unit, for example 'Delivery times per day, last 30 days, in hours'.

ECharts adds the series data to the description if I allow it, but for 30 days and 8 series the text was far too long. I limited it to the general label and left the data for the table alternative.

The legend was the larger change. The old legend was a row of divs. I replaced it with buttons that have aria-pressed, a visible focus ring and the same click action as before. Space and Enter both work now, which comes for free with a button.

The dark theme made the focus ring invisible on two legend colours, so the ring uses an outline offset with the text colour of the theme instead of the series colour.

With VoiceOver, the chart is announced as an image with the description, and the legend reads like 'Late deliveries, toggle button, pressed'. That is what I wanted.

I updated the snapshot tests for the legend; there were 6 changed snapshots, all expected. Playwright has one new test that tabs to a legend button and toggles a series with the keyboard.

Next: the 'show as table' button for each chart. Priya has not yet answered about the colours.

summary: Built the 'show as table' alternative for all charts by reusing the shipments table component, with the chart data and totals in an accessible table and a CSV download of that table.
body:
This was the main part of the accessibility pass. Each chart now has a button 'Show as table' under it that swaps the canvas for a table of the same data. The button has aria-expanded and the table gets focus when it opens.

The charts build their series in different shapes, so I added an adapter per chart type. It turns the series into rows and columns: the first column is the category or the day, and there is one column per series. Line charts, bar charts and the pie chart each needed one adapter, and a stacked bar needed a total column on top.

The table is the shared table component from the shipments page, with sorting turned off and a caption that repeats the chart title. Reusing it gave me the header scope attributes and the row navigation without extra work.

Units were a problem. The chart shows hours but the raw data is minutes. The adapter now formats values with the same formatter as the tooltip, so the table and the chart agree. I checked three charts by comparing numbers by hand.

I also added a small download link that exports the visible table as CSV. It goes through the client side writer used for small tables, since the data is at most a few hundred rows. The large table export is a different path and is untouched.

One bug: when the user switched the date range while the table was open, the table kept the old rows. The adapter output was memoized by chart id only. I added the range to the key and the table follows the picker now.

Vitest has 9 new tests for the adapters, including an empty series, which shows 'No data in this range' in the table.

In Playwright I added a test that opens the table, checks the row count and presses Escape to return to the chart with the focus on the button.

Open: the colours for the dark theme. I asked Priya again.

summary: Priya sent three new dark theme series colours that pass 3:1 contrast, and I replaced them in the theme file and checked every chart by eye and by measurement.
body:
Priya answered with replacements for the three weak colours in the dark theme: a brighter orange, a lighter purple and a softer yellow. I put them into theme/dark.ts.

I measured them against the chart background with the contrast script I used before. The new values give 3.4:1, 3.9:1 and 7.8:1, so all are above the limit.

Then I looked at all eight charts in the dark theme. The orange was now too close to the red of 'late' on the stacked chart, so Priya suggested a pattern on the red series. I did not do this yet and only noted it.

The light theme was not changed, since its colours passed already. The visual snapshots of the dark theme changed in 7 places, which I accepted after looking at each one.

The red and orange case goes on the list for the next pass.

summary: Answered Jonas's question whether managers can see who logged out other devices: yes for the new log, no for the time before it, because revoke-all was not logged earlier.
body:
Jonas asked on behalf of an Acme manager whether the dashboard can show that a user ended all his sessions, because a dispatcher claimed he never did it. I looked at what we have.

The security review of some days ago found that revoke-all was not logged. Since the fix, every call writes a row to the audit_log table with the user, the time, the number of revoked sessions and whether the current session was kept. So for the time since that fix, the answer is yes.

For earlier calls there is only an indirect trace: the sessions have a revoke reason, and the reason 'revoke_all' exists. I counted these for the account in question. There are 4 sessions with this reason, all revoked within the same second, three weeks ago, which fits one click.

That is not a proof of who clicked, since the action needs a valid session of the user, but it shows that it was done from an account session and not by an admin tool. Admin revocation uses the reason 'admin'.

I wrote this down for Jonas in plain words, with the one timestamp and the IP address of the session that did it. The IP matched the office of the dispatcher, according to Jonas.

I did not build a page for this, since it is a rare question. If it comes up again, a small read-only audit view for managers could be worth it. I added it to the ideas list.

The audit log has no cleanup yet. At the current rate it grows by about 300 rows a day, so there is no hurry, but I noted that it needs a retention rule like the report runs.

summary: Added a retention rule for audit_log rows and a nightly batch delete, keeping 18 months so that questions like the revoke-all one can still be answered.
body:
After the question from Jonas, I looked at the audit_log table. It has 41k rows and grows by about 300 a day, so there is no space problem, but a table without a rule tends to be forgotten.

I chose 18 months of retention. The reason is that managers ask about things that happened in the last year, and a rule that is longer than the yearly review of Acme avoids a gap. Jonas agreed when I asked him.

The job reuses the batch delete helper of the session cleanup. It deletes in batches of 5000 rows by id order with a short pause between batches, so it does not hold locks for long.

The helper had a small flaw. It stopped when a batch deleted fewer rows than the batch size, but with a concurrent insert it could end early without any harm; the problem was the opposite. If the delete returned zero rows because of a lock timeout, it logged success. I made it distinguish an error from an empty batch.

The table needed an index on created_at for the delete to be cheap. I added it in a migration with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which Render's deploy handles fine as long as the migration is not wrapped in a transaction. The migration tool needed the no-transaction flag for that file.

I ran the job against a copy of the production data with the retention set to 1 month, to see it work. It deleted 36k rows in 4 batches in about 2 seconds.

In production the first run will find nothing to delete, since the oldest row is 6 months old. So there is nothing to watch for now.

I added a log line with the count per run, the same format as the session cleanup, so that one search shows both jobs. A Vitest case checks that rows younger than the limit are never touched.

The job is scheduled at 03:20, after the session cleanup at 03:00, so they do not compete. Done for now.

summary: Fixed the scheduled report emails that showed times in UTC for managers in other time zones by storing a time zone per account and formatting dates in the job with it.
body:
A manager in Acme's Lisbon office wrote that the daily report arrived at the right hour but the tables inside showed times one hour off. I reproduced it by running the job for the account with a fixed clock.

The cause was in the report writer. It formatted timestamps with the default of the server, which is UTC on Render, while the dashboard in the browser uses the local zone of the user. The two views therefore disagreed in summer time of the Lisbon office, and in the winter they matched, which is why nobody noticed for so long.

The account had no time zone setting. I added a column time_zone with the default 'Europe/Berlin', since most Acme sites are in Germany, and a select field on the account settings page that lists the IANA zones.

The report writer now takes the zone from the account and formats all timestamps with Intl.DateTimeFormat. The schedule hour itself also uses the zone. That was a second bug: a report scheduled for 07:00 ran at 07:00 UTC for everyone.

Changing the schedule logic was the risky part. For existing reports I computed the next run in the new zone and compared it with the old one. For Berlin accounts the next run moves by one or two hours, so that would have sent the morning reports at the wrong time after the deploy.

To avoid this, the migration converts the stored hour from UTC into the account zone, so that reports keep running at the same moment in real time. A managers' 07:00 report, which really ran at 08:00 Berlin time, now shows as 08:00 in the zone Berlin. I told Jonas about this, because it shows people that their reports ran at other hours than they set.

Daylight saving was tested with fixed dates in Vitest: a report at 02:30 on the night when the clock jumps runs once at the next valid time, and on the night when the clock goes back it runs only once, not twice. The advisory lock helps here too.

The CSV and the xlsx attachments use the same formatter now, so the attached files match the table in the mail.

I deployed late in the evening, so that no report was due for hours. The next morning's run is the check. Open: the audit log view might also need the zone.

summary: Checked the morning scheduled reports after the time zone change: 44 reports went out, all at the hour their owners see in the dashboard, and the Lisbon table times were right.
body:
I compared the report_runs rows of this morning with the schedules in the settings. 44 reports ran, each once, and every start time was within 20 seconds of the hour shown in the dashboard for the account zone.

For the Lisbon account I opened the mail and checked the timestamps against the shipments table in the browser. They agreed for ten rows I picked.

Two owners of reports had asked why their report now says 08:00 and not 07:00. I answered with the explanation of the migration. Jonas will say the same in his weekly mail.

No failed runs, no skipped runs. The topic is closed.

One small thing: the account settings page does not tell that the zone also affects the schedule. I added a help text below the select.

summary: Reviewed the time zone work from the report side and found that the 'last run' column in the run history still showed server time, so it now uses the account zone too.
body:
After the time zone change for scheduled report emails, I went through the report builder looking for other places that format times. The run history tab showed relative times with an exact time in a tooltip, and that tooltip was still rendered in the browser zone of the viewer. For a manager in Lisbon looking at a report owned by an account in Berlin, the tooltip and the email disagreed by an hour.

I changed the tooltip to format with the account time zone and added the zone abbreviation, so '08:00 CET' is visible next to the time. The relative text ('2 hours ago') was already correct because it does not depend on a zone. I added two Vitest cases that render the same run with two different account zones, one of them across a daylight saving change. The audit_log list on the settings page still uses the browser zone, and I left it that way on purpose, because those entries describe what the user did on their own device. I noted the decision in the code comment of the formatter so it is not mistaken for a leftover.

The next step is to ask Jonas whether he wants the zone shown in the report list as well.

summary: Wrote a script that checks every pair of series colours in both themes for colour difference, and it found two more close pairs on the costs page that I fixed with adjusted shades.
body:
After the decal fix, I did not want to find such pairs by eye again. I wrote scripts/check-palette.ts, which loads the two theme files and computes the CIEDE2000 difference for every pair of series colours of a palette.

The limit is 20 for pairs that appear in the same chart. Below that, two colours are too close to be told apart reliably in a small legend. The script prints the pairs under the limit and exits with an error code, so it can run in CI.

The first run found the known pair, red and orange in the dark theme, at 14. With the decal that one is allowed. I added an explicit allow list with a comment for each entry, so exceptions are visible and not silent.

It found two more pairs that I had not noticed. On the costs page, the 'fuel' and 'tolls' series have a difference of 17 in the light theme, and 'fuel' and 'maintenance' have 18 in the dark theme.

I changed the shade of 'tolls' in the light theme to a darker teal and 'maintenance' in the dark theme to a lighter blue. The new differences are 26 and 23.

I sent the two changes to Priya as a screenshot before I merged anything, since she owns the palette. She liked the teal and asked for a slightly warmer blue, which I applied; the difference is still 22.

The pairs depend on which series appear together. The script knows only the palette order, not the charts. A pair that never appears in one chart is reported anyway, which creates false alarms. For now the palette has 8 colours and all appear together in the biggest chart, so the simple rule is fine.

The CI step runs in about 1 second. I added it to the workflow after the unit tests and checked that it fails when I change one colour to a duplicate.

I also wrote a short note in the contributing file: new colours must pass the script, and exceptions need a reason.

The visual snapshots for the costs page changed in both themes, 4 files in all. I looked at each and accepted them.

Nothing is left for the palette. The next topic is the keyboard focus order on the filters of the tables.

summary: Reviewed the focus order of the table filters and found that the filter popover traps no focus and lets tab leave it open, so I added a focus trap and an Escape handler.
body:
I went through the shipments table with the keyboard only. The filter row works until a popover opens, for example the status filter with its checkboxes.

Three problems showed up. When the popover opens, the focus stays on the button, so the next tab goes to the table and not to the first checkbox. When the user tabs out of the popover, it stays open and covers the header. And Escape does nothing.

I used the small focus trap helper that the settings dialogs already use, so no new dependency. On open it moves the focus to the first control, tab and shift-tab cycle inside, and Escape closes the popover and returns the focus to the button that opened it.

A popover is not strictly a modal, so some people argue that it should not trap focus. I decided that a trap is the easier model for a filter with several controls and an apply button, as long as Escape always leaves it.

The date range filter was different. It uses the date picker from the first version, which handles its own keys. Its popover needed only the Escape and the return of the focus. I tested the arrow keys inside the calendar, and they work.

The 'apply' button used to close the popover without moving the focus, so the focus got lost. It now goes back to the filter button, and the live region announces how many rows match.

Playwright tests: open the status filter by Enter, tick two boxes with Space, press Escape and check that the focus is on the button and the table is unchanged. A second test applies and checks the announced count.

I ran the tests in Chromium and WebKit. WebKit failed once because buttons there do not take focus on click, and my test relied on a click for the first step. The test uses the keyboard now, which is the point anyway.

The next step is to look at the column header menus.

summary: Fixed the column header menus of the table: arrow keys now move between items, the menu opens with Enter or Space, and the sort state is announced with aria-sort on the header cell.
body:
The column header menus were the last keyboard gap of the shipments table. A click on a header opens a small menu with sort ascending, sort descending, hide column and pin column. With the keyboard, the header was not even focusable.

I made the header cell contain a button that opens the menu. Enter and Space open it, and the focus goes to the first item. Arrow up and down move between items and wrap around, Home and End jump to the ends, and Escape closes the menu and returns the focus.

I used role=menu and role=menuitem for the list, which tells screen readers to expect arrow key navigation. A common mistake is to use the menu role for something that is not a menu, but this is an action list, so it is right here.

The sort state was missing. The header th now has aria-sort with ascending, descending or none, which makes VoiceOver say 'sorted ascending' when the cell is read. I tested with two columns sorted one after the other and the first one resets to none, as expected.

There was a bug in the pin action. After pinning with the keyboard, the table re-rendered the header and the focus was lost, because the cells have keys that include the pin state. I changed the key to the column id alone, and the focus stays on the button.

The type-ahead feature of the menu, where a letter jumps to an item starting with it, I left out. There are only four items.

The dark theme again hid the focus ring on the header button, which sits on a grey background. I used the same outline rule as in the legend, with an offset.

Tests: Vitest checks the key handling of the menu with testing-library user-event, for 9 cases including wrap around and Escape. Playwright opens a menu, sorts by the keyboard and checks aria-sort. All passed on the first run, except the WebKit one, which needed the same keyboard fix as before.

I ran axe on the page afterwards. It reported no violations for the table, and one for the colour of the placeholder text in the search field, which has a contrast of 3.9:1. I raised the placeholder colour a bit and axe is clean.

That finishes the table part of the accessibility list. Left are the settings page forms and the error messages of the invite dialog.

summary: Wrote Playwright tests for the table keyboard behaviour added in the last days: filter popover focus trap, Escape handling and the header menus with arrow keys and aria-sort.
body:
The accessibility fixes of the table filters and column header menus had only been checked by hand, so I covered them with Playwright tests before they could regress. The first test opens the filter popover with the keyboard, presses Tab more times than there are controls and asserts that focus stays inside, then presses Escape and asserts that the popover closes and focus returns to the filter button.

The second test opens a column header menu with Enter and with Space, moves with the arrow keys, and checks that Home and End jump to the first and last item. A third test sorts a column and reads the aria-sort attribute on the header cell, which should go from none to ascending to descending. While writing these I found that the menu did not close when Tab was pressed from the last item, and fixed it in the same session. All new tests run in about 14 seconds on CI together with the existing table specs. I did not add a screen reader test, since Playwright cannot drive VoiceOver, and the manual check stays on the release checklist.

summary: Investigated why the session list on the settings page showed the wrong device names for the mobile app and fixed the parsing so the agency's app shows as 'Acme Driver' with its version.
body:
A manager looked at his session list and saw 'Unknown browser on Linux' next to a session that he said was from a driver's phone. It turned out that the sessions of the driver app are listed in the same table, since the agency's app uses the same API.

I looked at the user agent string that the app sends. It is 'AcmeDriver/2.4.1 (Android 13; Pixel 6) okhttp/4.12'. My device parser is built for browsers, matches names like Chrome and Safari, and found none here, so it fell through to the default.

It matched 'Linux' because Android user agents of some libraries contain the word. That explains the wrong system.

I added a first rule to the parser for the AcmeDriver prefix. It returns the label 'Acme Driver 2.4.1' and the system 'Android 13' or 'iOS 17', from the text in the brackets. The device model is left out of the label but kept in the tooltip.

The parser is a small pure function, so I extended its test file. There are now 14 cases, three of them new: the Android app, the iOS app and a malformed string with no version, which falls back to 'Acme Driver'.

Then I checked the data. There are 58 sessions of the app among the active ones, and 3 variants of the user agent, including an old one without brackets from version 1.x. The old format falls back to the plain name.

The display of the 'current session' marker worked already, because it compares session ids, not names.

Next, I looked at whether a manager should see the driver app sessions of other people at all. The list is for the own user only, so a manager sees only his own. A manager who has a driver app login himself is rare, but the case exists, like this one.

While I was there, I noticed that the location column uses an IP lookup, which for mobile networks gives the location of the carrier gateway, often a city far away. The manager had asked about this too. I added a small hint 'approximate' in the tooltip and shortened the label to the country when the accuracy is the city and the network is mobile. This is not exact, but it avoids the claim that a driver is in a wrong city.

I asked the agency by mail whether the user agent format will stay stable. They said yes and that the next version adds a build number, which my regexp ignores.

The change is deployed and the manager's list shows the right label. I did not touch the revoke logic.

summary: Added a revoke button per row in the session list so a user can end one other session, backed by a route that checks the session belongs to the user and logs the action.
body:
Until now the settings page had only 'log out of all devices'. The manager from the last topic wanted to end a single session, for example the driver app on a lost phone, without losing the others.

The new route is DELETE /api/sessions/:id. It loads the session by id and user id from the cookie session, and returns 404 when the row belongs to somebody else, so the route does not reveal whether an id exists.

The revoke sets revoked_at and the reason 'user'. Ending the current session through this route is refused with a 400 and a message that points to the logout button, because two ways to log out would make the audit rows confusing.

The action writes an audit_log row, with the session id and the label of the device, in the same transaction as the revoke. This follows from the gap I found in the security review, where revoke-all had no log.

In the list, each row, except the current one, has a button 'End session'. A click opens no dialog, since the action is easy to repeat by logging in again, but the row gets a short undo-less toast: 'Session ended: Acme Driver 2.4.1'. The live region announces the same text.

The list response is no-store since the earlier caching fix, so the row disappears after the refetch. I used an optimistic removal first, and it showed a flicker when the request failed, so the row now stays until the server answers and shows a spinner on the button.

The app of the agency needs to handle this as well. When its session is revoked, the next API call returns 401 and the app sends the driver to the login screen. I tested with a copy of the app request in a script. The agency confirmed that their app does this.

Tests: Vitest covers the route, with the own session, a session of another user, the current session and an unknown id. Playwright logs in with two browser contexts, ends the second from the first and checks that the second gets the login page on the next click.

I noticed that the rate limit of the login route does not apply to this route. An attacker with a valid session could revoke only his own sessions, so there is nothing to protect. I left it.

Deployed. Next: show the reason of a revoked session in the list for 30 days, since support can see it in the database but users cannot.

summary: Showed recently ended sessions in a collapsed section of the session list with the reason in plain words, using the 30 day grace period that the cleanup job already keeps.
body:
Users who find themselves logged out ask why, and the answer is in the revoked rows: 'user', 'revoke_all', 'cap', 'admin' or expired. The cleanup keeps these rows for 30 days, so the data exists. I decided to show it.

The sessions route got a query parameter, include=ended. Without it the response is unchanged, so the agency app and old clients see no difference. With it, the API returns also rows that ended in the last 30 days, with ended_at and the reason.

The frontend shows a collapsed section below the list, titled 'Recently ended sessions' with the count in the title. It is a disclosure button with aria-expanded, so the list is not read to screen reader users unless they open it.

The reasons are translated to sentences: 'You ended this session', 'You logged out of all devices', 'Ended because you had more than 20 sessions', 'Ended by an administrator', 'Expired'. The cap text is the one that helps most, since people did not understand why an old laptop session vanished.

The admin reason raised a question. Should a user see that an administrator ended his session? I asked Jonas, and he said yes, as long as it does not show the name of the admin. The text does not.

Expired sessions are many, since every session expires at some point. They would fill the section. I show only the last 10 ended sessions and a line 'Older sessions are removed after 30 days'.

The device label uses the same parser as the active list, so the Acme Driver label from the earlier fix appears here too.

There was a bug in my query. The route filtered by user id and ended_at, but the index on sessions covers user id and revoked_at, so the plan used a sequential scan on a user's rows. For one user it is small, but I still added the ended_at ordering to an existing composite index in a migration, and the plan uses the index now.

Tests: the route returns ended rows only with the parameter, never rows of other users and never rows older than 30 days. A component test opens the section and checks the texts for the five reasons.

Priya checked the section in the design. She asked for a lighter text colour for the ended rows and an icon for each reason. I did the colour and left the icons, since they are decoration and add work for the descriptions.

Deployed in the afternoon. I watched the logs for 500 errors from the route for an hour and there were none.

Open: the German texts for the reasons exist only as English in the first version, and the dashboard has a German locale. I put them into the next session.

summary: Added the German texts for the session list and the audit messages, found three strings still hardcoded in English, and added a test that fails when a key is missing in one language.
body:
The dashboard has two locales, German and English, and most Acme users read German. The session features of the last days were written with English strings only, so a German user would have seen a mix.

I listed the new strings: the reasons of ended sessions, the section title, the toast of the revoke, the button texts and the hint 'approximate' for the location. There were 19 keys in all.

I wrote the German texts and read them against the existing wording of the settings page, so the terms agree. For example the page says 'Sitzung' for session, and 'Geräte' for devices, so 'Von allen Geräten abmelden' matches the earlier button. The cap reason became 'Beendet, weil mehr als 20 Sitzungen aktiv waren'.

Plurals need care. The title 'Recently ended sessions' has a count. The i18n library uses ICU message format, so I wrote the one and other forms for both languages and checked the cases 0, 1 and 2.

While searching for hardcoded text, I found three strings that never went through the translation function: the 'Report copied, schedule paused' toast of the duplicate action, the text 'No data in this range' of the chart table, and the 'required' word for screen readers in the forms. All three were from the last weeks.

I moved them to keys. The screen reader text matters most, because a German user with VoiceOver in German would hear the English word read with a German accent.

To stop this from happening again, I wrote a test that loads both message files and compares the key sets. It fails with a list of the keys that are missing on one side. A second test scans the source for JSX text nodes that look like English sentences, with a short allow list. The second one is crude and gave 6 false alarms for brand names, which went into the list.

The key test found two more missing English keys of an old feature, the onboarding hint texts, which existed in German only. I added them with English wording.

I switched the browser to German and walked through the session page, the reports list and a chart with the table. Everything is German now, apart from the names of the Acme Driver app and the user agent strings, which are data.

Priya looked at the text lengths. The German ending text for the cap is long and wraps to two lines in the narrow mobile layout. It is acceptable, and the row grows in height without a layout break.

The check is in CI and takes about a second. A pull request that adds only an English key now fails with a clear message.

With this the session list and the accessibility work are complete. I will ask Jonas what he wants next for reports.

summary: Planned the next stage of scheduled reports after talking to Jonas: a pause-until date, a 'send now' button and a warning when a report has had no data for a week.
body:
Jonas gave me his wishes for the scheduled reports, after the history page and the time zone fix made them more visible to his managers. I wrote them down in order of value and cost.

First, a 'send now' button in the report list. Managers want to check a new schedule without waiting for the next morning. It would run the same job code for one report with the lock, and write a row in report_runs with the trigger 'manual'. The cost is small, since the job is a function of the report id.

Second, a pause until a date, for holidays. Today a manager has to pause and remember to resume, and Jonas said that three reports stayed paused for months. A column paused_until, checked by the job, handles it. The list shows 'paused until' in the account zone.

Third, a warning for reports that send empty tables. Some filters match nothing after a client changes names, and the manager gets a mail with an empty table every day. The idea is that after 7 runs with zero rows, the owner sees a hint in the list and one mail that says the report has been empty for a week. The mail should be sent once, not daily, so it needs a flag on the report.

I discussed whether the empty report should pause itself. Jonas said no, since some reports are empty on purpose, for example late deliveries in a good week. A hint is enough.

Fourth, an idea I put at the end: recipients that are not users, for example a customer address. It raises questions on privacy and on unsubscribing, so it needs an extra talk and probably a legal look on the Acme side.

Order of work: send now, then paused until, then the empty hint. Each is about a session. The send now button needs a rate limit, since a click per second would send mail to every recipient, so I plan one manual run per report per minute, using the same Postgres based limiter as the login.

Also for the plan: the new texts must go into both languages from the start, with the key test running, and the controls need keyboard and screen reader support as the earlier work. I will use the list of the accessibility pass as a checklist.

Jonas will confirm the wording of the empty hint mail, which goes to managers under his company's name. I start with the send now button next.

summary: Added the pause-until date to scheduled reports: a nullable column, a date picker in the schedule dialog, and the job skips paused reports and resumes on its own.
body: First step of the plan from earlier today with Jonas. I added a nullable paused_until column to scheduled_reports with a migration, and the scheduler query now skips rows where paused_until is later than the current time in the account zone. The schedule dialog got a date picker that reuses the existing date picker component, with a clear button to resume at once. A paused report shows a 'Paused until' label in the reports list, and its schedule is kept, so nothing has to be set up again afterwards. I wrote three Vitest cases for the job: a paused report is skipped, a report whose pause ended runs at its next slot, and a pause date in the past is treated as no pause. The German texts are added and the missing key test passes. 'Send now' and the no-data warning are still open and come next.

summary: Built the 'send now' button for scheduled reports: it queues one run through the normal job path, is rate limited per report, and shows up in run history as a manual run.
body:
This is the second step of the scheduled reports plan, after the pause-until date this morning. The first idea was a separate code path that renders and mails the report directly from the route. I dropped it after reading the scheduler job, because it would have duplicated the filter, column and time zone handling that we fixed a few days ago. Instead the route POST /api/reports/:id/send-now inserts a run row with trigger set to 'manual' and hands it to the same worker function that the schedule uses.

The route checks that the report belongs to the user's account and that the user may see its data, with the same permission check as the report page. A manual run ignores paused_until, since someone pressing the button clearly wants the mail. It still goes to the saved recipients and does not change the next scheduled slot.

I added a limit of one manual run per report per five minutes. A second press inside that window returns 429 with a message that the UI shows as a toast with the minutes left. Without it, a double click sent two mails to every recipient in my first local test.

In the run history, the new trigger column shows 'Manual' or 'Scheduled', and for manual runs it also shows the name of the user who pressed the button. The 'last run' column keeps using the account time zone. The action is written to audit_log with the report id and the user, so that the retention rule from last week covers it.

In the reports list, the button sits in the row menu below 'duplicate', as Priya's layout has it, and it is disabled while a run is queued. After the press, the row shows 'Sending' until the run row changes to done or failed. I used polling every three seconds for this, because the list has no live updates elsewhere.

Tests: four Vitest cases for the route covering permission, the rate limit, the paused report and the trigger value, and one Playwright test that presses the button and waits for the run to appear in the history. All pass. The German texts are added. Next is the warning for reports that had no data for a week.

summary: Added a cleanup job that deletes expired session rows from Postgres every night, since the sessions table had grown to about 380k rows after the move from JWT.
body:
The sessions table kept every row since the login moved back to server-side sessions, and nothing removed expired ones. A count showed about 380k rows, most of them past their expiry. Lookups were still fast because of the index on the session id, but the table size was already a concern on the small Render database.

I wrote a job in server/jobs/sessionCleanup.ts that runs at 03:10 and deletes rows where expires_at is older than one hour. It deletes in batches of 5,000 so it does not hold a long lock. The first run removed 361k rows in about 40 seconds.

The job is started from the API process with a simple interval and a Postgres advisory lock. The lock matters because Render may run two instances for a short time during a deploy, and both would otherwise delete at once. I tested the lock by starting two processes in a terminal; the second one logged 'cleanup already running' and exited.

I added a Vitest test that inserts expired and valid sessions and checks that only the expired ones are removed. A second test checks that the batch loop ends when fewer rows than the batch size are found. Both pass.

I also added an index on expires_at, because the delete had to scan the whole table. After the index, the same delete on a copy of the data took 9 seconds instead of 40.

What is left: the job logs the number of rows it removed, but nothing alerts if it fails. I will look at that after the session list work. Jonas does not need to know about this; it is housekeeping.

summary: Wrote the plan for a 'log out of all devices' button: one endpoint that deletes all session rows of a user, with the current session optionally kept.
body:
Jonas asked this morning whether managers can end all their sessions after losing a laptop. With sessions in Postgres this is easy, which is one of the reasons for the move last quarter. I wrote down the plan before changing code.

The endpoint will be POST /api/auth/logout-all. It deletes every row in sessions for the user id. A body flag keep_current=true keeps the session of the request, so the button on the settings page does not log the person out of the page they are looking at.

Open questions I settled with the user. First, the mobile app uses the same sessions, so drivers lose their login too; the user said this is fine and the app agency already handles a 401 by showing the login screen. Second, we should write an audit line with the user id, the time and the number of rows removed. We use the existing audit_log table.

I also checked the session middleware. It reads the row on every request, so a deleted row means a 401 on the next request, with no delay. There is no cache in between, which I confirmed by reading the store code.

I started the implementation: the SQL, the route and two tests. One test checks that other sessions of the same user are gone, the other that sessions of other users stay. Both pass locally.

The front end button and the confirm dialog are next. Priya will be asked for the wording of the dialog.

summary: Shipped 'log out of all devices' with a confirm dialog on the settings page; the dialog text from Priya says that drivers using the app are signed out too.
body:
The endpoint from earlier this week is now connected to the settings page. A new section 'Security' has a button 'Log out of all devices'. A click opens a confirm dialog, and after the confirm the call is made with keep_current=true.

Priya sent the wording this morning. The dialog says that every browser and every app signed in with this account will need to log in again. She wanted a short sentence and the destructive button in the red of the theme. I used the existing danger button variant and checked both the light and the dark theme.

While testing I found a bug. After the call the session list on the page, which I had not built yet, is not a problem, but the toast said 'Signed out of 0 devices' when only the current session existed. The count came from rows removed, which was 0 as the current one is kept. I changed the message to 'No other sessions were active' in that case, and to 'Signed out of N other devices' otherwise.

I wrote a Playwright test. It logs in through two browser contexts, presses the button in the first, and checks that a reload in the second context shows the login page while the first stays logged in. It takes about 6 seconds and passes.

One thing I checked on purpose: the CSRF token. The route is protected by the same middleware as the other POST routes, and a call without the header returns 403. I added that case to the Vitest tests.

I deployed to Render at about 17:20 and tried it on production with my own test account. It worked, and the audit_log line was there.

Next is the session list, so people can see what they are ending. That needs a user agent and a last seen time on the sessions rows.

summary: Added user_agent, ip and last_seen_at columns to sessions with a migration, as the base for the session list.
body:
The session list needs more than an id and an expiry. I wrote migration 0047 that adds user_agent, ip and last_seen_at to the sessions table. Existing rows get last_seen_at set to their created_at.

The middleware now fills user_agent and ip on login. To update last_seen_at on every request would be a write per request, so I only update it when the old value is more than five minutes old. A quick local test with 200 requests produced 1 write.

I left out a geo lookup of the ip on purpose. The user thinks it is more than we need, and the ip is only shown as text.

summary: Built the session list on the settings page, showing browser, system, last seen time and a button to end single sessions.
body:
The list reads GET /api/auth/sessions and shows one row per session of the user. The user agent string is parsed with the ua-parser-js package into 'Chrome on macOS' or similar. The current session is marked with a badge.

Each row has an 'End session' button that calls DELETE /api/auth/sessions/:id. The route checks that the row belongs to the user, otherwise it returns 404, not 403, so ids of others are not confirmed. A test covers this.

The mobile app sessions show up as 'Unknown' because the agency's app sends a user agent like 'okhttp/4.12'. I mapped okhttp and CFNetwork to 'Acme driver app'. I asked the user whether the agency can send a proper name; they will write to them.

The last seen time is shown as relative text, for example '3 hours ago', using Intl.RelativeTimeFormat. The table is a plain list, not the big table component, as it has at most ten rows.

Still to do: an empty state and the mobile layout, which overflows under 360 px width.

summary: Traced slow scheduled report emails to the report query running once per recipient; one run per report now cuts the nightly batch from 14 minutes to 3.
body:
Jonas said the morning reports were arriving late, some after nine. I looked at the scheduler logs for the last week. The batch starts at 06:00 and the last email was sent at about 06:14, which is too long for 60 or so reports.

The cause was in server/reports/scheduler.ts. For every schedule, the code loops over recipients and calls renderReport for each one. The query and the chart rendering are the same for all recipients of a schedule, so this was repeated work. Some schedules have 8 recipients.

I changed it to render once per schedule and attach the same PDF to every email. Only the greeting line differs by person, and it lives in the email template, not in the PDF.

I measured with a copy of production data. Before: 14 minutes 20 seconds. After: 3 minutes 5 seconds. The number of database queries in the batch fell from about 1,900 to 260.

One risk: reports with a filter that depends on the viewer, such as 'only my depot'. I checked the code and found that scheduled reports store a fixed filter, so the viewer is not used. The report builder v2 has an option 'run as recipient' on the roadmap, and I left a comment in the scheduler where that would need the old loop.

I added a test with three recipients that counts the calls to renderReport and expects one. The existing tests still pass.

The remaining time is mostly the PDF rendering with headless Chromium, about 2 seconds per report. I did not touch it. I will deploy this tonight so that tomorrow's run is the first real check.

summary: Deployed the scheduler change and added a log line with total batch time so that the next morning's run can be checked quickly.
body:
I added one log line at the end of the batch: the number of schedules, the number of emails and the total time in seconds. Before that, the time had to be calculated from the first and last email lines.

The deploy to Render went through at 13:20. I started a manual run for one test schedule with three recipients, and all three mails arrived with the same PDF.

I also made the batch continue if one schedule fails. Before, an exception in one render stopped the loop for all schedules after it. Now the error is logged with the schedule id and the loop goes on. A test makes one render throw and checks that the other two are sent.

Tomorrow I will read the batch line and tell Jonas the result.

summary: The first morning run after the scheduler fix finished in 2 minutes 50 seconds, and all 61 reports arrived before 06:03.
body:
