I read the batch log line this morning: 61 schedules, 238 emails, 170 seconds. The first mail went out at 06:00 and the last at 06:02, so nobody should see a late report anymore.

I sent Jonas a short message with the result. He answered that two managers had complained about late reports last week, and he will tell them.

While in the logs I saw 4 bounces from addresses at an old Acme domain. They are not new, but they fill the log. I made a list for Jonas of the addresses so he can remove them from the schedules, rather than deleting them myself.

I also noticed that the PDF attachments are about 1.8 MB each for the big shipment reports, because of the chart images at 2x scale. Most mail clients cope with that, but it is near the limit of some. I wrote it in the todo list as something to check later and did not change the scale.

Nothing else to do on this topic. The change is finished.

summary: Checked the first nightly session cleanup in production: 212k expired rows deleted, the sessions table is down to about 168k rows, and login latency did not change.
body:
The cleanup job from the last entries ran for the first time at 03:00 last night, so this morning I checked the logs and the table. It deleted 212,430 expired session rows in 41 seconds, in batches of 5,000 rows to avoid a long lock on the table. Before the run the table held about 380k rows, and afterwards it held about 168k.

I also compared login latency from the request logs for the hour of the run and for the same hour the evening before. The median was 48 ms in both, and the 95th percentile moved from 130 ms to 134 ms, which is noise. The batched delete used the index on expires_at, and EXPLAIN showed an index scan, not a sequential scan.

The remaining 168k rows are mostly sessions that are still valid under the sliding window of 14 days. Many of them belong to the driver app, which opens a new session after each restart and never ends the old one. That explains why the table stays larger than the number of active people would suggest.

I added a log line with the number of deleted rows and the run time, so a run that suddenly deletes nothing is easy to spot. I did not add an alert, because one quiet night can be normal at the weekend. Next I will look at whether the app should reuse its session on restart, and that question goes to the mobile app agency. The session list for the settings page needs a few more columns first, so that work comes before this one.

summary: Question from the user: why do sessions expire after 14 days of inactivity? Answer: it was copied from the old cookie setting, and a sliding window of 14 days stays.
body:
The user asked while reviewing the settings page why a session ends after 14 days and whether that is a deliberate rule. I looked up the history in the repo and in my earlier entries.

The 14 days came from the first version of the login, where the cookie had a maxAge of 14 days. When we moved to JWT, the tokens got 30 days, and later short-lived tokens with refresh. When the login moved back to sessions, I reused the 14 days from the first version, without an explicit decision from Jonas.

The current behavior is a sliding window. Each request that is more than five minutes after the last one pushes expires_at to 14 days from now. So an active user never gets logged out, and a person who is away for two weeks does.

I listed the options for the user.
- Keep 14 days sliding. Simple, and fits dispatchers who log in every day.
- Shorten to 8 hours for dispatchers, matching a shift. Safer on shared desktops in depots, but more logins.
- Add an absolute maximum of 90 days, so that a session cannot live forever.

The user decided to keep the sliding 14 days and to add the absolute maximum of 90 days. The reason was that Jonas had mentioned a shared PC in one depot.

I have not implemented it yet. It needs a created_at check in the middleware next to the expires_at check, which is two lines, plus a test with a session that is 91 days old but was used yesterday.

I will do that in the next session and mention it in the settings page text.

summary: Implemented the 90 day absolute session limit: the middleware now rejects sessions older than that, even if they were used yesterday.
body:
The change is in server/auth/sessionMiddleware.ts. After loading the row, it now checks both expires_at and created_at. If created_at is older than 90 days, the row is deleted and the request gets a 401 with the code session_too_old.

The front end already redirects to the login on any 401, but I made it show a short message for this code: 'For your safety, please log in again.' Before, the user saw only the login page, which looked like a bug to people who had been using the dashboard daily.

The constant lives in config/auth.ts as MAX_SESSION_AGE_DAYS, so the number is in one place. The cleanup job also uses it, so rows older than the limit are removed at night, not only when someone tries to use them.

Tests: a session created 91 days ago with last use yesterday gets 401; one created 89 days ago is fine; and the cleanup deletes the first but not the second. All pass.

I looked at how many real sessions this would hit. A query on production showed 9 sessions older than 90 days, out of about 410. Seven belong to the same two managers, so they will see the message once.

I warned Jonas by message, so the two managers are not surprised. He said that is fine.

The settings page text now says that sessions end after 14 days without use, or after 90 days in any case. I asked Priya to look at the wording, because it is a bit long for the small text style.

Deployed at 19:20. Nothing else open on this topic.

summary: Upgraded React to the next minor version and fixed two warnings from the strict mode about effects that subscribed twice in the shipments table.
body:
The upgrade itself was quick. I changed the versions in package.json, ran the install, and the build and the Vitest suite passed at the first try. 212 tests, no failures.

In the dev server the console had new warnings, though. Two components subscribed to a window resize event inside an effect and did not remove the listener in the cleanup function. Under strict mode, effects run twice in development, which made the problem visible. In production it meant a leaked listener each time the table was mounted.

The two components were ShipmentsTable and the chart container in components/charts/Container.tsx. In both I returned a cleanup function that calls removeEventListener with the same function reference. In the chart container the handler was created inline, so I moved it into a useCallback.

To confirm the leak, I used the Chrome performance tools. I switched between the shipments page and the settings page 20 times. Before the fix, the listener count rose by 20 for each component. After the fix, it stayed at one.

The Playwright suite also passed, 48 tests in about 4 minutes. I looked at the dark theme screenshots, which we compare by eye and not by pixels, and saw no change.

I did not upgrade Vite in the same step, to keep the changes apart. That is for the next days.

summary: Upgraded Vite to the next major version; the build broke on a CommonJS-only chart helper, fixed by an alias, and the bundle is 11% smaller.
body:
After the React upgrade, I took Vite. The release notes list a new default for the build target and a changed handling of the CSS minifier. I read them before starting, and I created a branch of the work in the main checkout to compare builds.

The first build failed with 'require is not defined' coming from a helper package we use for the ECharts theme loader. The package ships only CommonJS. The old Vite version pre-bundled it automatically in dev, and the new one handles it differently in the production build.

I tried to add it to optimizeDeps.include, which fixed the dev server but not the build. In the end I added build.commonjsOptions.include for that package in vite.config.ts, and the build passed. I wrote a comment above it with the package name and the reason, so it can be removed if the package gets an ES build.

The second problem was small. The plugin for React was one version behind and printed a peer warning. I raised it and the warning went away.

Build sizes, measured with the rollup visualizer:
- before: 1.92 MB total, 612 KB gzipped
- after: 1.71 MB total, 548 KB gzipped

The 11% gain comes mostly from the new chunk splitting; ECharts is now in its own chunk and loads only on pages with charts. The settings page loads about 300 KB less.

The cold start of the dev server went from 3.1 seconds to 1.8 seconds on my laptop.

I ran the unit tests and the whole Playwright suite. One Playwright test failed, the CSV export download test, because the downloaded file name changed. This was not Vite; the test was waiting on the old name from an earlier change. I fixed the expectation.

I deployed to Render at 14:10 after the checks and watched the first minutes of the logs. No errors. The user will look at the pages tomorrow with the real data.

summary: Started the costs page: a table of cost per shipment and a monthly chart, with the data from a new /api/costs endpoint that sums the cost lines in Postgres.
body:
Jonas wants managers to see what the deliveries cost, split by depot and by carrier. This is the first session on the costs page, and I started with the API, because the shape of the data decides the front end.

The shipments table has a cost_lines child table with fuel, toll, labor and other. The new endpoint GET /api/costs takes from, to, group_by (depot, carrier or month) and returns the sums per group. The SQL is a single query with a GROUP BY and a join. I wrote it by hand, not with the query builder, because the builder produced an extra subquery that was slower.

I tested the speed with the production-sized data in staging: 1.2 million cost lines. A year of data grouped by month takes 180 ms, grouped by carrier 240 ms. Without an index on cost_lines.shipment_id it took 2.4 seconds, so I added it in migration 0049.

Money is stored as integer cents. The API returns cents and the currency, and the front end formats it. I wrote this down in the endpoint comment, because an earlier bug in the report builder came from mixing float euros and cents.

On the front end I made the page route /costs, a summary row with three numbers (total, per shipment, change against the previous period) and an ECharts bar chart per month. The date picker is the same one as everywhere, with the keyboard fixes from last week.

The table under the chart is not finished. It shows depot, carrier, shipments, total and cost per shipment, and sorting works on the server. The filters for depot and carrier are still missing.

Permissions: only managers see the page, not dispatchers. I added a role check in the route and in the menu. A test confirms that a dispatcher gets 403 from the endpoint.

Open question for Jonas: should the period comparison use the same number of days before, or the same period a year earlier? I used the days before for now and put the question in the message.

Next: the filters, the CSV export of this table and the empty state.

summary: Jonas answered that the costs comparison should be against the previous period of equal length, so the current behavior of the costs page stays.
body:
Jonas replied to the question from this morning. He wants the change against the previous period of the same length, as in the summary row today. A year-over-year view may come later, he said, once there is enough history in the new cost lines.

I wrote his answer in the comment of the function that computes the previous period, so that the next person sees it was a decision.

I also added the depot and carrier filters as dropdowns above the table. They send the ids to the endpoint, which adds them to the WHERE clause with parameters. A test with an injection-like string in the carrier filter confirms that it is treated as a value.

The empty state shows 'No costs in this period' with a link to reset the dates. The CSV export for this table is next.

summary: Added CSV export to the costs table; it works for a normal year but a three-year export of all depots still takes about 50 seconds and sometimes times out.
body:
The costs table now has an Export button next to the filters, using the same export code as the shipments table. It sends the current filters to the server, which builds the file and returns it.

For a typical case this is fine. A year of costs for one depot gives 18,000 rows and returns in about 2 seconds. A year for all depots gives 140,000 rows in about 11 seconds.

The long case is the problem. A three-year export for all depots has about 420,000 rows. It took 48 seconds on staging, and twice out of five tries Render closed the request at the 60 second limit, and the browser showed a failed download. The memory of the API process also rose by about 300 MB during the export, because the file is built fully in memory before sending.

This is the same weakness that the shipments export has, which the managers have mentioned. I did not try to fix it now. The code is shared, so the fix should be done once for both tables, and it needs care with the encoding and the headers.

As a stopgap, I added a warning in the dialog when the estimated row count is above 200,000: 'Large exports can fail. Try a shorter period.' The estimate comes from a count query that takes 40 ms.

I added this item to the todo list with the measurements, so the later work starts with numbers. I also told Jonas that very large exports are unreliable for now, and he said that the managers can live with it as long as the warning is shown.

The rest of the costs page is done except for the final review with Priya on the chart colors.

summary: Priya reviewed the costs page and asked for a colorblind-safe palette; the chart now uses one with distinct lightness steps and patterns for the stacked bars.
body:
Priya looked at the costs page yesterday evening and sent comments early this morning. Her main point was that the four cost types, fuel, toll, labor and other, used colors that look the same under red-green color blindness.

I replaced the palette with one from her suggestion, which differs in lightness as well as hue. For the stacked bar chart I also turned on the ECharts decal pattern, so each cost type has a stripe or dot pattern in addition to the color. The legend shows the same patterns.

The dark theme needed its own variant, since the light colors were too bright on the dark background. I made two palettes in the theme file and the chart picks one by the active theme.

I checked the result with a color blindness simulator in the browser tools, for deuteranopia and protanopia. The four types can be told apart in both.

Her second comment was about the number format. Large sums showed as 1234567.89 in the tooltip, and she wanted thousands separators and the currency symbol. The tooltip now uses the same formatter as the table.

Third, the summary row at a width under 600 px wrapped badly. I changed the three numbers to stack in a column on small screens.

The tests for the page pass, and I updated two screenshots that we keep for reference. Priya will take a final look when it is deployed.

summary: Found why 'log out of all devices' left a driver app logged in: the app caches the last good response and only checks the session at the next restart.
body:
A report from the mobile app agency reached the user: a driver pressed 'log out of all devices' on the dashboard, and the driver app on his phone still showed the shipments list for hours. The agency asked whether our logout was broken.

I tested it first on the server side. After the call the session rows are gone, and every API request with the old cookie gets a 401. I checked that with curl against staging, using the cookie value of a test session. So the server did what it should.

Then I read the agency's description again. The app shows the last good response from a local cache when the network is slow, and it only refreshes the list in the background. The 401 from the background request is swallowed by their code, so the screen stays unchanged until the app restarts. They confirmed this when the user asked.

So this is a bug in the app, not in the API. Still, there is something we can do on our side. I made the 401 response body more explicit: {"error":"session_ended","reason":"logout_all"} or reason 'expired' or 'ended_by_user'. The agency can use that to clear their cache on a session_ended error.

To be able to give the reason, I needed to know why a row is missing. Until now a deleted row looks like a row that never existed. I added a small table of ended sessions, ended_sessions, with the session id hash, the reason and the time, which the cleanup job removes after 7 days. The middleware looks it up only when no session row is found, so a normal request costs nothing extra.

I wrote tests for the three reasons and for an unknown cookie, which gets the plain 401 as before.

The documentation of the API, a markdown file in docs/, has a new section for this response. The user will send it to the agency with a short explanation.

After their change in the app, the case should end. Until then, drivers should know that restarting the app finishes the logout.

summary: Wrote the first version of the scheduled report 'recipient view' option so a report can run once per person with that person's depot filter, using the old loop only when needed.
body:
This is the feature that I had left a comment for in the scheduler after the speed fix. Jonas asked for it: a weekly cost report should show every depot manager only their own depot, from one schedule.

The design keeps the speed gain. A schedule gets a new boolean, per_recipient. When it is false, which is the default and the case for all 61 existing schedules, the render happens once, as now. When it is true, the scheduler groups the recipients by their effective filter and renders once per distinct filter, not once per person.

The effective filter is the schedule filter combined with the recipient's depot ids from the users table. Two managers of the same depot get the same PDF. A manager with no depot restriction gets the full report. I wrote a function effectiveFilter(schedule, user) and a key function that turns it into a stable string for grouping.

Database: migration 0051 adds per_recipient with default false.

The report builder UI has a checkbox 'Personalize by depot' in the schedule dialog. It is shown only when the report has no fixed depot filter, because the combination would be confusing. A short help text explains it. I tested the dialog with the keyboard and with the screen reader labels.

Tests, in four groups:
- one schedule, per_recipient false: one render
- three recipients with two distinct depots: two renders
- a recipient without a depot: full report
- a recipient whose depot was deleted: the email is skipped and a warning is logged

The last case needed a decision. Sending the full report to someone whose depot is gone would leak data, and sending nothing silently would hide the problem. I chose to skip and log, and to show the skipped count on the schedule page next to the last run.

I ran a trial on staging with a copy of one real schedule and five test recipients in three depots. Three PDFs were rendered, and each mail had the right one; I opened all five to check the totals.

The security side was the part I checked most. The depot filter is applied in the SQL query, not by hiding rows in the PDF, so the data of other depots never reaches the renderer.

What is left: a review by the user, the note for managers on how to use it, and a look at the file size, since three PDFs per schedule is more mail volume.

summary: The user reviewed the per-recipient reports and asked for a preview of who gets which PDF; I added a dry-run button listing recipients with their depot filter.
body:
The user read the code yesterday evening and liked the grouping, but asked how a manager building a schedule can be sure who gets what. A wrong depot assignment in the users table would send a wrong report, and nobody would see it before the mail is out.

I added a dry-run. The schedule dialog has a button 'Preview recipients'. It calls POST /api/schedules/preview with the draft and returns a list: recipient email, the effective depot ids, and the group number, so one can see that two people share a PDF. Nothing is rendered or sent.

The response also marks recipients who would be skipped, with the reason 'depot missing', in a warning color and with text, not only color.

The endpoint uses the same effectiveFilter function as the real run, so the preview cannot differ from what happens. I made that explicit with a test that runs both on the same data and compares the groups.

The permission is the same as for editing the schedule. A dispatcher gets 403.

I deployed the whole feature at 18:00. I wrote the short note for managers and sent it to Jonas, who will forward it. The first personalized schedule will be created by him, and I will check the log of its first run.

summary: The first personalized weekly cost report went out to 6 depot managers; 5 got their depot PDF and one was skipped because the depot of that user was missing.
body:
Jonas created the schedule yesterday evening, and it ran at its time this morning. I read the log of the run: 1 schedule, 6 recipients, 5 distinct filters, 5 PDFs, 5 emails, 1 skipped, total 21 seconds.

The skipped person is a manager who moved from one depot to a regional role, and his depot list in the user record was empty because the depot was removed. The schedule page showed 'skipped 1' as designed, and Jonas saw it right away. He is going to assign the region, which means the user has to get a multi-depot setting. That is a task in the user admin, not in the reports.

I opened two of the PDFs and compared the totals with the costs page filtered on the same depot. They matched to the cent.

The mail volume was fine. The largest PDF was 1.4 MB.

One small thing: the greeting in the mail said 'Hello,' without the name for these emails, because the template reads the name from the schedule's first recipient. I changed it to use the name of each recipient, which was an easy fix in the template, and a test checks it.

The feature is finished. If the multi-depot setting for users gets built, the effective filter already handles several ids.

summary: Fixed an accessibility problem in the shipments table: sortable column headers are real buttons with aria-sort now, and the row count is announced after filtering.
body:
The next item of the accessibility list was the shipments table. A screen reader user could not tell which columns were sortable, since the headers were plain cells with a click handler on a span.

I changed each sortable header to contain a button. The th element carries aria-sort with ascending, descending or none, and the button label reads like 'Sort by delivery time'. The click still toggles the sort, and Enter and Space work as with any button. The visible arrow icon is hidden from the reader with aria-hidden, since the state is already said by aria-sort.

The second problem was that after a filter was changed, the table content changed silently. I added a visually hidden live region with polite announcements, 'Showing 42 of 1,310 shipments'. It updates after the data arrives, with a debounce of 500 ms so typing in the search field does not produce a sentence per letter.

The third change was the focus outline. A global style removed it for the header buttons. I put back a visible two pixel outline with the theme's accent color and checked the contrast in both themes. It is above 3:1 against the background in both.

I tested with VoiceOver and with keyboard only. The tab order is the filters, then the headers, then the rows, and the paging controls last, which is the order on the screen.

Playwright tests: one checks that aria-sort changes after a click, another that the live region text contains the new count after a filter. Both pass, and the full suite of 52 tests is green.

Not done: the row selection checkboxes need labels with the shipment id, and the sticky header overlaps focused rows when scrolling with the keyboard. I wrote both into the list for the next session.

summary: Fixed the two remaining table accessibility items: row checkboxes have labels with the shipment id, and the sticky header no longer hides the focused row.
body:
I continued with the two items left over from yesterday's work on the shipments table.

The row checkboxes had no accessible name, so a screen reader said only 'checkbox'. Each one now has an aria-label such as 'Select shipment AC-20417', built from the shipment reference. The checkbox in the header says 'Select all shipments on this page', and when the page changes the state is reset, which was an existing behavior.

The sticky header problem happened when a user tabbed through the rows in a long table. The browser scrolls the focused element into view, but the header covers the top 44 px, so the focused row sat behind it. The fix was the CSS property scroll-margin-top on the rows, set to the header height plus a few pixels. The header height is a CSS variable, so the value follows if the header changes.

I checked that it works in Chromium, Firefox and Safari. Safari needed the same property on the cells, not only the row, so I set it on both.

I also looked at the zoom case, since an accessibility reviewer will try 200% browser zoom. At that level the table scrolls sideways inside its container and the first column, the shipment reference, stays sticky. Focus handling was fine there. At 400% the filters wrap into one column, which is acceptable.

A Playwright test tabs down ten rows and checks that the focused row's top edge is below the bottom edge of the header. It passes. The count of tests is now 53.

With this, the list from the accessibility check has only the dark theme contrast of the date range highlight left, which waits for Priya's color. I wrote her a message with a screenshot and two proposed values.

summary: Added a keyboard-focus ring and skip link to the dashboard layout, finishing the accessibility pass that began with the shipments table
body:
After the table fixes of this morning, I went through the layout shell. There was no skip link, so keyboard users had to tab through the whole sidebar on every page. I added a 'Skip to content' link that appears on focus and jumps to the main region.

The focus ring was also a problem. A global rule had set outline: none on buttons, probably from the first version. I removed it and added a 2px ring with a color that passes 3:1 contrast on both the light and the dark theme. The dark theme needed its own value, because the light one vanished against the sidebar.

I ran axe through Playwright on five pages: shipments, costs, reports, settings and the session list. Before the change it reported 9 issues, afterwards 2. Both left are color contrast on the grey helper text in the date picker.

The date picker is a shared component and Priya owns its colors, so I did not change them. I wrote the two findings into a note for her with the selectors and the measured ratios (3.8:1 and 4.1:1). Next step is to add the axe run to the Playwright suite so that new issues fail the build. I started the spec file but left it unfinished because the settings page needs a logged-in fixture, which comes next.

summary: Added an axe accessibility check to the Playwright suite with a logged-in fixture, so new violations on five pages fail CI
body:
Finished the spec I started yesterday. The settings and costs pages need a session, so I wrote a fixture that creates a user and a session row directly in Postgres and sets the cookie in the browser context. That is much faster than going through the login form for each test.

The spec visits five pages and runs axe with the wcag2a and wcag2aa tags. It fails on any violation with impact serious or critical. The two known contrast issues of the date picker are allowed through a list with a comment that names the open note to Priya. Without the list the build would be red from the first run.

The first run in CI failed for an odd reason: the fixture user was left over from the previous run, and the unique email constraint rejected the insert. I added a cleanup in the fixture teardown and a random suffix on the email.

The whole suite now takes 4 minutes 10 seconds instead of 3 minutes 40. The extra 30 seconds come from the page loads and are acceptable. I will ask Priya next week whether she can give new colors for the helper text. After that the list can be emptied.

summary: Jonas asked for a manager view that shows costs per depot, so I planned a depot breakdown on the costs page using the existing /api/costs endpoint
body:
Jonas wrote that the managers want to see which depot costs most without exporting the table. I looked at what the costs page has today. It has a per-shipment table and a monthly chart, and the endpoint sums cost lines in Postgres by month only.

The plan is a new optional parameter groupBy=depot on /api/costs. The query would join cost lines with shipments to get the depot id and group by depot and month. I ran an EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a draft of it for the last twelve months. It took 380 ms and used a sequential scan on the cost lines, because there is no index on the shipment id there.

An index on cost_lines(shipment_id) should bring it down. I tested it on a copy of the production database and the same query dropped to 90 ms. The index build took 11 seconds on the copy, so the migration is safe to run during the day.

For the display I want a horizontal bar chart of depots, sorted by total, with the same palette that Priya approved for the stacked bars. Clicking a bar filters the table below to that depot.

Open questions for Jonas: should depots with no cost in the period appear with zero, and is the sort by total or by name? I sent both questions. I will start with the migration and the endpoint, and the chart after his answer.

summary: Implemented groupBy=depot in /api/costs with the new shipment_id index; the query runs in about 90 ms and returns zero rows for idle depots
body:
Jonas answered quickly: idle depots should show with zero, and the sort is by total, highest first. That matches what I had guessed for the sort.

I wrote the migration for the index on cost_lines(shipment_id) and ran it on staging first. It took 4 seconds there. Then I extended the costs route. When groupBy is depot, the query starts from the depots table and left-joins the cost lines in the chosen period, so that idle depots appear with a total of 0.

I added validation: groupBy accepts only month or depot, anything else gets a 400 with a message. Before this the parameter did not exist, so no old client is affected.

Tests: three Vitest tests for the route with a small fixture of 3 depots, one of them without costs. They check the totals, the zero row and the order. A fourth test checks the 400 for a bad value. All pass.

The previous period comparison, which Jonas confirmed some time ago, also works with the depot grouping, because the endpoint runs the same query twice with the shifted range. I did not change that logic. In production I will check the timing after the deploy, since staging has much less data. The chart component is next.

summary: Built the depot bar chart on the costs page; clicking a bar filters the cost table to that depot
body:
I added the horizontal bar chart with ECharts above the cost table. It reads the depot totals from the new groupBy=depot call and sorts by total. The colors come from the colorblind-safe palette, and a single color is used for all bars, since depots are not a category with meaning here.

Clicking a bar sets a depot filter in the page state and the table reloads for that depot. A second click on the same bar clears it. The active bar gets a darker outline so it is visible without color.

For screen readers the chart has a visually hidden table with the depot names and totals. I checked the page with the axe spec and it still passes.

On production the endpoint answered in 110 ms for twelve months of data. Jonas looked at it and was happy. One thing remains: the depot names are long for two depots and get cut at the axis, so I will look at label wrapping tomorrow.

summary: Found that the session middleware ran one Postgres query per request to update last_seen_at and cut that to at most one write per five minutes per session
body:
While looking at database load for the costs endpoint I noticed in the Render metrics that Postgres had many small UPDATE statements. The slow query log showed that almost all of them were UPDATE sessions SET last_seen_at on the session row. The column was added about a month ago for the session list, and the middleware writes it on every authenticated request.

A dashboard page makes between 6 and 15 API calls, so one page load meant that many writes to the same row. I counted on a normal weekday morning of production logs: roughly 41,000 updates per hour at the peak. That is not dangerous yet, but each write creates a dead tuple, and the sessions table is already large.

The fix is to write only when the stored value is older than five minutes. The middleware already loads the session row for the check, so it can compare the timestamps without an extra query. The session list shows 'last seen' in minutes at best, so five minutes of imprecision does not hurt anybody.

The sliding 14 day expiry uses the same timestamp. Five minutes more or less does not matter there either, but I checked the code to be sure that the expiry check reads the stored value and not a value from memory. It does.

I wrote a test with a fake clock: the first request writes, a request after two minutes does not, a request after six minutes does. I also made sure that a session without any last_seen_at value, from before the migration, is written at once.

I deployed the change in the evening and let it run. The first look at the metrics shows the update rate already falling by a large factor. I will check the numbers again tomorrow morning when the load is higher, and compare to the figures from today.

summary: Morning numbers confirm the last_seen_at throttle: session updates fell from about 41k to 3k per hour at peak, and the session list still looks right
body:
I compared the Postgres metrics of this morning's peak with those of the day before. Session updates were about 3,000 per hour, against about 41,000 before the change. Overall write IOPS dropped visibly and the table's dead tuple count grew much more slowly.

I also checked that the session list on the settings page still behaves. I logged in on two browsers, used one of them for a few minutes and looked at the list from the other. The 'last seen' value for the active browser was at most five minutes old, which is what I expected. Ending a single session still works.

One concern was the nightly cleanup job, which deletes by expiry. It does not read last_seen_at in a way that depends on exact values, so nothing changes there. I read the job once more to be certain.

The costs page was also slow in the evening of the previous day for one user. I looked into it because the timing was close to my deploy. It turned out that the user had a three-year range selected and the table query without a limit was the cause. That is not related to sessions. The table is paginated on the client but the server returns all rows. I noted it as an item for later, since the same problem exists in the CSV export of large tables.

I did not change the pagination yet. It touches the table component and the endpoint, and deserves its own plan. For now I wrote down the observation with the numbers: 120k rows returned for three years of all depots, 9 MB of JSON, about 6 seconds in the browser.

The next step is to decide with the user whether server pagination goes first or the export problem.

summary: Planned server-side pagination for the costs table: cursor by shipment id and date, a total count query, and a limit of 100 rows per page
body:
The user decided that pagination for the costs table comes before the export work, because the page is used daily and the export only now and then. I wrote the plan today and will implement it step by step.

Current state: /api/costs/rows returns every row in the range. For three years of all depots that is about 120k rows and 9 MB of JSON. The browser then paginates the array. The page takes about 6 seconds to show anything.

Plan for the endpoint:
- limit parameter, default 100, maximum 500
- cursor parameter, an opaque string made of the shipment date and id of the last row
- ordering by date descending and id descending, which gives a stable order
- a separate count endpoint, so the first page does not wait for the count

I considered offset pagination because it is simpler and the table has page numbers. The problem is that offset 100000 forces Postgres to read and drop that many rows. I tested it on a production copy: offset 100000 took 640 ms and a cursor query at the same position took 8 ms. So the cursor wins, and page numbers will be replaced by next and previous buttons plus the total.

The sort by other columns is a complication. The table lets users sort by cost, depot and so on. A cursor on date does not work for these. For the first version I will limit server sorting to date and cost. For cost the cursor holds cost and id. The other columns will be sorted only within the loaded page, and the header will say so in its aria label.

An index on cost_lines or shipments by date and id is needed for the date order. I checked and shipments already has one on (shipped_at, id).

The client side needs a hook that holds the pages already seen, so that 'previous' does not hit the server again. I will use a small array of cursors.

Testing: Vitest tests for the cursor encoding and the boundary cases, such as equal dates and the last page, and one Playwright test that walks three pages and back.

I expect two sessions of work. The export is not part of this plan.

summary: Implemented the cursor pagination in the /api/costs/rows endpoint with date and cost ordering; the first page of three years now returns in about 40 ms
body:
I wrote the cursor encoding as base64 of a small JSON object with the sort value and the id. The route decodes it, validates the types and uses a row comparison in SQL, so the query is WHERE (shipped_at, id) < ($1, $2) with the order matching.

For the cost ordering the same idea works with (cost, id). I added a test for rows with equal costs, which was the case most likely to break, and it caught an off-by-one in my first version that skipped a row at the page border. The comparison was correct but I had fetched limit rows instead of limit plus one to detect a next page.

A bad cursor returns a 400 and not a 500. The first page of three years of all depots takes about 40 ms now. The count endpoint takes about 300 ms and runs in parallel on the client later.

summary: Replaced the page numbers of the costs table with next and previous buttons backed by the cursor API, plus an async total count
body:
The table component now uses a hook that fetches a page, keeps the list of cursors it has seen, and offers next and previous. Previous uses the stored cursor, so it needs no extra logic on the server.

The total count is fetched in a second request. While it loads the footer shows 'Loading total', and afterwards 'Rows 1 to 100 of 119,874'. I made sure the announcement for screen readers says the same, using the polite live region that I added for the filter counts.

Changing the filters or the date range resets the cursors. I first forgot the sort change, which left the old cursors in place and gave wrong rows in a manual test. A Vitest test for the hook now covers filter, range and sort changes.

The sort on the other columns works only within the page. I changed the header buttons for those columns so that the aria label says 'sorts this page only', and added a small text hint in the footer. Priya has not seen it, so I will ask her whether the wording is clear.

The Playwright test walks three pages forward and one back and checks that the first row of each page differs and that going back shows the same first row as before. It passes locally. CI run is green.

One leftover: the CSV export of the costs table used the old endpoint that returned everything, so I checked that it still works. It does, and it is as slow as before, about 50 seconds for the large case. I did not touch it because the plan keeps the export separate.

I will deploy tomorrow morning when the dispatchers are not yet online.

summary: Deployed the paginated costs table; the page for three years of data now shows its first rows in under half a second instead of about six seconds
body:
I deployed early in the morning. The first load of the costs page for three years of all depots now takes about 450 ms to show rows, and the total count appears after about 700 ms. Before it was around 6 seconds with 9 MB of JSON, and now a page is about 80 KB.

I watched the server logs for errors for an hour. There was one 400 for a cursor, which came from a browser tab that had been open since before the deploy and sent an old style request with page numbers. The reload fixed it. I did not add compatibility for that.

Jonas tried the page and said it feels much faster. He asked where the page numbers went. I explained that jumping to page 50 is replaced by the date filter and the sorting, and he accepted that for now but wants to see if the managers complain.

Priya looked at the footer hint for the sorting and suggested shorter text: 'Sorted within this page'. I changed the visible hint and the aria label.

Database load fell as well, because the big unlimited query no longer runs. One more thing came up: the shipments table has the same structure, with all rows loaded, but it has filters that keep it small for most users, so I left it.

The next piece would be the export, but the user wants to wait until the next planning talk with Jonas.

summary: Investigated a report from a dispatcher who was logged out in the middle of work, and found that the 90 day absolute limit had hit a session that was used daily
body:
A dispatcher wrote to Jonas that the dashboard suddenly sent her to the login page while she was entering a filter. She had not been idle. Jonas passed it on.

I looked up her user in the sessions table. The latest session row for her was created just a minute before her report, which fits a fresh login after the logout. The old row was already deleted by the cleanup job, but the middleware logs a line when it rejects a session, and the log of that moment showed reason=absolute_limit. So the 90 day rule from a few weeks ago had ended a session that was in daily use. That is how the rule is designed, but nobody told the users.

The cases will repeat: every user who logged in right after the migration from JWT reaches 90 days at about the same time. Many of them are dispatchers, so a wave of logouts is likely in the next days. I counted sessions that are older than 80 days and still active: 37.

Two things can reduce the surprise. First, a warning banner before the end, which needs the session to expose its remaining time. Second, a message on the login page that says why the user came back. I chose the second for the moment because it is small. The middleware now redirects to /login?reason=expired_absolute, and the login page shows 'For your security you have to sign in again every 90 days'.

I also added reason=idle for the sliding window, with a different text. Both texts need a check from Priya. I put them into the translation file so that she can change them without code.

Tests: the middleware test now asserts the redirect reason for both cases. The login page has a test for each message, including an unknown reason, which shows nothing.

I told Jonas about the 37 sessions, so that he can warn the dispatchers by mail if he wants. The banner is on the list for later, and I will ask whether it is worth it.

summary: Added a banner that warns a user seven days before the 90 day session limit, using a remaining_days field from /api/me
body:
Jonas decided that the warning banner is worth it, because he does not want dispatchers losing a half-filled form. I implemented it in two parts.

On the server, /api/me now returns sessionExpiresAt, which is the creation time plus 90 days. The value is computed from the session row, and the client does not need to know the rule. I made the limit a constant in one file so that the middleware and the endpoint cannot disagree. They used two separate literals before, so I fixed that too.

On the client, a banner component shows when fewer than seven days remain: 'Your session ends in 5 days. Sign in again at a good moment to keep working without interruption.' It has a link to log out and a close button that hides it for the rest of the browser session. It uses role status, so it is polite for screen readers.

The drivers' app uses the same endpoint but ignores unknown fields, so adding one is safe. I confirmed by reading the agency's last API note, which says their client uses a lenient parser.

Tests: a Vitest test for the days calculation including the border at exactly seven days and one for a session that has already expired, which shows nothing because the request would not pass. A Playwright test sets the session creation time back by 85 days in the database and checks that the banner appears.

Priya has not seen the visual yet. I used the existing info style of the alerts. I will show it to her on the next review and ask about the wording.

The 37 sessions from earlier will get the banner at once after the deploy. I deployed in the evening. A first check shows 29 users with the banner, which is plausible, since some of the 37 had already logged out.

summary: Priya reviewed the session banner and the login messages, and asked for the warning to say the exact day count and use the alert color with better contrast
body:
Priya went through the banner and the two login messages this morning. Her notes were short and useful.

First, the banner color. The info blue passed contrast, but the text on it was small and she wanted a stronger visual for something that can cost a user their work. She asked for the warning color of the design system, with an icon that does not depend on color. I changed it and checked the contrast: 7.2:1 for the text.

Second, the count. 'in 5 days' is fine, but on the last day it should say 'today' instead of 'in 0 days'. I had not tested that case. A session ending in less than a day showed 'in 0 days', which was ugly. I added the cases for today and tomorrow, with a test for each.

Third, the login messages. She shortened the 90 day text to 'You were signed out for security reasons. Please sign in again.' and kept the idle text as it was. I updated the translation file and the tests that check the text.

She also pointed to the close button, which was too small for touch. It is 32 pixels now, with a bigger hit area. I deployed all of it before noon.

One question she asked was whether the banner could offer 'extend session'. That would defeat the point of an absolute limit, so I explained why not. She agreed. A later idea is a login that returns the user to the same page and keeps the filters. That needs the app to save the filter state, and I wrote it as a possible item without a plan.

summary: Fixed return-to-page after login: the login page now sends users back to the URL they were on, with a check that blocks redirects to other sites
body:
Following the idea from the review, I made the login remember where the user was. When the middleware redirects to /login it adds a next parameter with the path and query of the requested page. After a successful login the client navigates there.

The security side matters here. A next parameter is a classic open redirect. I accept only values that start with a single slash and do not start with two slashes or a backslash, and I parse the value with the URL class against a fixed base to confirm the origin did not change. Anything else falls back to the shipments page.

The filters of the dashboard live in the query string, so the date range and the depot filter come back with the user. The shipments table and the costs table both read their filters from there. The report builder keeps its draft in component state, so it is not restored. I noted that as a limit.

Tests: a Vitest table of 12 values for the next check, among them //evil.example, /\evil.example, https://evil.example, a path with encoded newlines and a normal path with a query. All except the normal one fall back. A Playwright test logs in with next set to the costs page with a depot filter and checks that the filter is still set.

The SSO login for managers goes through a callback, so I checked that the next value survives it. At first it did not, because the callback handler built its own redirect. I stored the next value in a short-lived cookie before the SSO call and read it in the callback, with the same check. It works in staging with the test identity provider.

I deployed it in the afternoon. The report builder draft is the only gap, and I will bring it up with the user.

summary: Looked at autosaving the report builder draft so that a forced login does not lose it, and decided on localStorage with a per-user key
body:
The return-to-page change leaves the report builder draft out, since the draft lives only in React state. A user in the middle of building a report who is logged out would still lose everything.

I considered three options. Saving drafts on the server needs a table and endpoints, which is a lot for this. Session storage dies with the tab but survives the redirect, which would be enough for the login case. Local storage survives everything, but a draft would be visible to the next person on a shared computer, and dispatchers do share computers.

I chose session storage with a key that includes the user id, and the draft is removed at logout. That covers the forced login case and avoids the shared computer problem.

The save runs with a debounce of one second after each change. The draft is small, about 2 KB of JSON for a normal report. On load the builder checks for a draft and asks 'Restore your unsaved report?'.

I have not implemented it yet. The first task tomorrow is to find all the state that belongs in the draft, because the recipient view option from some weeks ago added fields.

summary: Implemented autosave of the report builder draft in session storage, with a restore prompt and cleanup at logout
body:
I moved the builder state into one reducer object so that saving is a single call. The fields are the name, the query settings, the schedule, the recipient view option and the recipient list.

The save hook is debounced by one second and writes under the key reportDraft:userId. On mount the builder reads the key, validates the shape with a small schema and shows the restore prompt. A draft with an unknown shape is dropped silently, which protects against old drafts after later changes.

Logout removes the key, and so does a successful save of the report. I tested the logout path by hand and with a Vitest test on the logout function. A Playwright test builds half a report, expires the session in the database, reloads, logs in and restores the draft.

summary: Fixed the draft restore for the recipient view option, which came back switched off because the saved boolean was read as a string
body:
In a manual check the restore worked for everything except one field. The recipient view toggle always came back off, even if it had been on. The cause was that the toggle's state was stored as the string 'true' from an older form handler, and the restore code compared it with the boolean true.

I fixed the form handler so that it stores a real boolean. The schema check at restore now coerces the two literal strings 'true' and 'false' to booleans, which also helps drafts that were saved before the fix.

I added a test for the old shape and the new shape. The Playwright test now toggles the option before expiring the session and checks it afterwards. Both pass and I deployed the fix.

summary: Started the shipments table pagination work: measured the shipments query, found it filters before limiting, and planned to reuse the cursor code from the costs table
body:
The costs table is paginated on the server and fast, and the shipments table still loads the whole filtered result. For most users filters keep it small, but I wanted real numbers before deciding. I ran the shipments query for different filters on a production copy.

With a one-week range, the result is about 2,300 rows and 60 ms. With a one-year range for all depots it is about 118k rows and 5.5 seconds, and 8 MB of JSON. Managers do use the one-year range for the charts, and the table below the charts shares the filter, so they pay for it even if they never look at the table.

That is the real reason to paginate. The cursor code of the costs rows is a single module with encode, decode and the SQL helper. It takes the sort columns as an argument, so it can serve shipments if the ordering is declared. The shipments table sorts by shipped_at, status, depot and delivery time. Server-side sorting can support shipped_at and delivery time, and the others stay within the page, as on the costs page.

The delivery time column is calculated: it is the difference between two timestamps. A cursor on it needs the expression in the order clause and in the row comparison. I tested the query with the expression and the planner did a sort of all matching rows, 900 ms for the year range. That is acceptable, but not great. A generated column with an index would be better. A generated stored column on a table of this size needs a table rewrite, which takes locks, so I would do it in a quiet window.

I decided on the first step: support shipped_at ordering on the server and leave the delivery time sort within the page, with the same hint as on the costs page. The generated column goes into the notes for later.

The export of shipments also uses the table query. I checked it: the export has a separate code path that builds a file from all rows. It stays as it is.

I wrote the list of work for the next sessions: the endpoint change, the shared hook, the table component change, the tests, and the deployment. The shared hook is the main thing, since the costs table hook has costs-specific pieces that need to be taken out first.

Nothing is committed yet except the notes, which I put in the docs folder.

summary: Extracted a generic useCursorPages hook from the costs table and moved the cursor SQL helper into a shared module, with the costs tests passing unchanged
body:
This was a refactor with no change in behavior, to prepare the shipments table. The costs hook had the cursor list, the reset on filter changes, the count request and the announcements, all tied to costs types.

I made useCursorPages generic over the row type. It takes a fetchPage function, a fetchCount function and a resetKey that is a stable string of the filters and the sort. When the resetKey changes, the state is cleared. This replaced the explicit reset calls that I had to remember for each filter before, and it fixes the kind of bug I hit with the sort change earlier.

On the server I moved the cursor helper into server/lib/cursor.ts. It exports encodeCursor, decodeCursor and a function that builds the WHERE and ORDER BY pieces from a list of column definitions with a direction. The costs route now calls it with its two orderings.

Two details were annoying. The row comparison for descending order on two columns is (a, b) < ($1, $2), and for ascending order it is the other direction. My first helper handled only descending. I added a direction per ordering and a test for ascending order with equal values. The second was NULL values: cost can be null for lines without a price, and a row comparison with null yields null, so those rows vanish from pages. In the costs data nulls are rare but exist. I changed the cost expression to coalesce(cost, 0) both in the order and in the comparison, and added a test with a null row.

The null case was a genuine bug in the costs table: it dropped rows with no price at the page borders. I looked at the production data and found 14 such lines among the 120k, so users have probably never noticed. The fix is in this commit and I will mention it when deploying.

All the tests of the costs table passed without change, apart from the added ones. The Playwright walk through three pages also passed. The Vitest count is 212 tests now.

The shipments endpoint is the next step. I did not start it today.

summary: Added cursor pagination to /api/shipments with shipped_at ordering and a count endpoint, reusing the shared cursor module
body:
I changed the shipments route so that it accepts limit and cursor like the costs rows. The default limit is 100 and the maximum is 500. The order is shipped_at descending with the id as a tie breaker, which uses the existing index on (shipped_at, id).

The filters of the table are status, depot, date range and a free text search on the shipment number. They were already built as a list of SQL conditions with parameters, so the cursor condition is appended to that list. I took care that the parameter numbering stays right, because the old code numbered them by position. A test with all filters and a cursor set at once covers this.

The count endpoint reuses the same filter builder without the cursor and returns a number. For the one-year range for all depots it takes about 260 ms.

Numbers after the change on the production copy: the first page for the year range takes 35 ms against 5.5 seconds before, and the page is about 70 KB.

One case worried me. The free text search uses ILIKE with a leading wildcard, which cannot use an index. With the year range and a search term the query takes about 700 ms, because it scans the matching range. That was the same before the pagination, so it is not a regression. A trigram index would help and goes on the list.

Tests: I added 9 Vitest tests for the route, among them the combination of filters with a cursor, the last page, an empty result and a bad cursor. They pass.

The client side still uses the old call, so the endpoint answers with the old shape when no limit is passed, to avoid breaking the current table until the client switches. The drivers' app does not call this endpoint, I checked the agency's documentation to be sure.

The table component comes next.

summary: Switched the shipments table to the shared pagination hook and finished the work with tests; the deployment is planned for tomorrow early morning
body:
The shipments table now uses useCursorPages with the new endpoint. The resetKey is built from the filters, the search term and the sort. The footer shows next, previous and the total, as in the costs table, so users see the same pattern on both pages.

The header buttons for sorting by status, depot and delivery time are marked 'Sorted within this page', as agreed with Priya for the costs table. Sorting by shipped_at goes to the server. The aria-sort attributes and the announcement of the row count that I made last week still work: after filtering, the live region says how many rows were found, and I kept it tied to the count request, so it announces the total and not the 100 of the page.

Two problems came up while testing. First, the row selection with the checkboxes kept selected ids across pages, which is useful, but the 'select all' box then meant only the page. I changed its label to 'Select all rows on this page' and wrote the same in the aria label. Second, the sticky header fix from some days ago assumed that the table scrolls inside its container. With 100 rows it still does, so nothing changed, but I tested it by keyboard again.

The charts above the table use their own aggregate endpoints, so they are independent of the pagination. I checked that changing the date range still updates both.

Playwright: a new test walks pages of the shipments table, applies a status filter, checks that the first row changes and that the total matches the count of the filter. An axe run on the shipments page is part of the suite and passes.

The CI run is green with 224 Vitest tests and 41 Playwright tests. The suite takes 4 minutes 30 seconds.

I will deploy early tomorrow, before the dispatchers start. After that, the remaining items are the trigram index for the search, the generated column for the delivery time and the export of large tables, which is still slow.

summary: Deployed the paginated shipments table early in the morning; first rows for a large depot now appear in about 0.4 seconds instead of five seconds.
body:
The deployment ran at the planned early slot and went through without a rollback. I watched the logs on Render for the first hour. The new /api/shipments cursor endpoint answered the first page in 35 to 60 ms, and the count endpoint took about 300 ms for the largest depot, which is fine because the table shows the count asynchronously.

I compared the page against the old one with the same filters. Before, a dispatcher at the biggest depot waited about five seconds for the first rows; now it is under half a second. Sorting by shipped_at works in both directions.

One thing I noticed: the filter by status resets the cursor, as intended, but the browser back button restored the old cursor and showed an empty page for a moment. I wrote it down as a small follow-up. Nothing else looked wrong, and the session list and login were not touched by the change.

Next I will ask Jonas to try it with a real dispatcher and tell me if sorting by other columns is missed.

summary: Checked the new shipments pagination on production after the early deploy and found that the status filter count query was the slowest part, so it now runs after the first rows render.
body:
I started the afternoon by looking at the numbers from the morning deploy of the paginated shipments table. The first rows for a large depot arrive in about 0.4 seconds, which matches the test copy. The slowest remaining piece was the count endpoint when a status filter is active.

I pulled the slow query log for the last few hours and found that the count with a status filter and a depot filter took between 600 and 900 ms for the biggest depots. The query planner used the new shipped_at index but still had to filter every row for the status. I looked at the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and saw a bitmap heap scan with about 180k rows removed by filter.

The table does not wait for the count, because the hook from last week fetches it asynchronously. So dispatchers see rows at once and the total shows up a moment later. Even so, a count that takes nearly a second wastes database time during the busy morning hours, and the dashboard asks for it every time a filter changes.

I considered a composite index on depot_id, status and shipped_at. That would make the count fast, but the table already has several indexes and the writes from the mobile app go through the same table. I did not want to add another one without measuring the write cost. So I left the index idea open and wrote it down for later.

Instead I changed the client so that the count request is debounced by 300 ms and cancelled when the filter changes again. Before, a dispatcher clicking through three statuses fired three counts and all three ran to the end on the server. With an AbortController on the fetch and a check of the closed connection in the handler, the abandoned counts stop early.

I also made the count endpoint return an approximate number, marked with a flag, when the estimate from the planner is above 50000 rows and no filter is set. For the unfiltered view the exact number does not matter to anyone, and the label shows 'about 120,000'. With a filter set the count stays exact.

I added two Vitest cases for the debounce and one API test for the approximate flag. All shipments tests pass, and the costs table tests, which share the hook, pass unchanged. In a local run against the test copy, clicking through four statuses in a row now causes one count on the server instead of four.

Next I want to watch the slow query log tomorrow and then decide about the composite index. I will also ask Jonas whether an approximate total is acceptable in the unfiltered view; I expect yes, but the label wording is his decision.

summary: Wrote the plan to check the shipments table with screen reader and keyboard use after pagination, since the next and previous buttons replaced the page numbers and the old row count announcement.
body:
After the count work I turned to a gap that I noticed while reading the table code: the accessibility pass of the weeks before the costs work was done with the old page numbers, and the shipments table now uses the shared pagination hook with next and previous buttons. I wanted to be sure that none of the earlier fixes got lost in the switch. This entry is a plan and a first check, not a finished change.

I listed what the earlier work promised. Sortable column headers are buttons with aria-sort. The row count is announced after filtering. Row checkboxes have labels with the shipment id. The sticky header does not hide the focused row. The axe check in Playwright covers five pages with a logged-in fixture.

Then I ran the axe suite locally against the new table. It passes, with no new violations. But axe cannot tell whether an announcement happens, so I checked by hand with VoiceOver. The row count announcement works after a filter change, but after pressing next the focus stays on the button, which is now at the bottom of a new page, and nothing says that the rows changed.

That is a real problem for a keyboard user. They press next, and they hear nothing, and the old rows are gone. I decided on a small live region that says 'Rows 101 to 200 loaded' after each page, and the focus should stay on the button so that a second press works at once. Moving the focus to the first row would be surprising when someone wants to press next several times.

I also found that the disabled previous button on the first page is removed from the tab order, which is correct, but it has no explanation. I plan to use aria-disabled with a visible disabled style instead, so that a screen reader still finds it and reads that it is unavailable.

The async total count has the same issue. When the total arrives late, the text 'of 120,000' changes without notice. I think it should not be announced, because it would interrupt the page message, so it stays outside the live region.

The plan is: add the page live region, change the previous button to aria-disabled, add a Playwright test that presses next and checks the live region text, and ask Priya to look at the disabled style. I did not change any code yet except a failing Playwright test that shows the missing announcement. It fails as expected, and the work starts tomorrow.

summary: Implemented null-safe cursors for the shipments sort by delivery time; undelivered shipments are no longer skipped across page boundaries.
body:
The shared cursor helper compared the sort key with a plain greater-than, which is never true for null. That would silently drop all undelivered rows after the first page boundary inside them.

I changed the helper so that the cursor holds the key and a flag saying whether the key was null. For ascending order with nulls last, the condition is now: key greater than the cursor key, or key is null, or (same key and id greater). When the cursor itself is in the null block, it only compares the id.

I wrote tests against a Postgres test database with 250 rows, 90 of them with null delivered_at, and a page size of 20. Walking all pages in both directions returns every row exactly once. Before the change, the same test lost 70 rows.

The costs endpoint uses the helper too, but its sort columns are never null, so its tests stayed green. I left the indexes migration for tomorrow.

summary: Ran the two new shipments indexes concurrently on production; the weight sort fell from about 700 ms to 25 ms, and the delivery time sort to 30 ms.
body:
I ran the migration late in the evening when traffic is lowest. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY took about four minutes for the weight index and five for the delivered_at index. I watched pg_stat_activity during the build and saw no long locks and no slow queries from the dashboard.

Afterwards I re-ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on both queries for the biggest depot. Both use an index scan now. First page by weight: 25 ms. First page by delivery time with nulls last: 30 ms. The next-page queries in the middle of the data were the same.

I also checked the table size. The two indexes together added about 190 MB, which is acceptable on the current Render plan. The write path for new shipments got slightly slower, but the insert benchmark showed less than 1 ms difference.

The sort controls for the two columns are enabled in the table header now, and I deployed the URL cursor fix together with the null-safe cursor. A smoke test with the Playwright suite passed on production. What is left is to tell Jonas and ask whether dispatchers want other columns.

summary: Jonas confirmed the faster shipments table works for dispatchers and asked for the status filter to be remembered between visits.
body:
Jonas talked to two dispatchers at the biggest depot today. They said the table opens fast and the new sort by delivery time is what they wanted. One of them noticed that the page after a long scroll is quick too.

His new request is that the status filter is remembered, because every morning they set it to 'in transit' first. I looked at what already exists. The report builder draft is stored per user in session storage, but a filter preference should survive a browser restart, so it needs a different place.

I decided to save it in the user's settings row in Postgres, as a small JSON field, and read it through /api/me so the table starts with it. That also works on a second computer. The URL params still win over the saved filter, so shared links keep working.

I wrote the plan and the field name, default_filters, in the notes. Implementation is for tomorrow.

summary: Added default_filters to user settings and /api/me, and the shipments table now starts with the saved status filter unless the URL says otherwise.
body:
I added a migration with a default_filters JSONB column, not null, default empty object, on the user settings table. PATCH /api/settings accepts it with a schema check that only allows the known filter keys, status and depot, with values from the existing enums.

/api/me now returns default_filters. The shipments page reads it once after login and uses it as the initial filter when the URL has no filter params. If the URL has any filter, the saved one is ignored completely; mixing them was confusing in a first try.

The filter bar got a small 'save as my default' button and a 'reset' link. After saving, a toast confirms it. I used the same toast component as the settings page.

Tests: a Vitest test for the schema check that rejects an unknown status, and a Playwright test that saves a filter, logs out, logs in and sees the same filter on the table. Both pass. The session middleware needed no change, since the value is read from the database and not from the session.

I asked Priya for a look at the button position, since it sits close to the export button.

summary: Priya liked the save-as-default button but asked to move it into the filter menu, so it no longer sits next to the CSV export button.
body:
Priya reviewed the screenshots this afternoon. Her point was that two buttons with similar weight next to each other make people hit the wrong one, and the export is a heavier action.

I moved 'save as my default' and 'reset' into the filter dropdown, below the filter fields, as a text button and a link. The dropdown shows a small dot on the filter icon when a saved default is active. Priya approved the new version in the review thread. The change is deployed together with the default filters.

summary: Investigated why the costs page CSV export for three years and all depots still takes about 50 seconds, and found the file is built fully in memory before sending.
body:
The export is slow and sometimes times out, as noted when I added it to the costs table. Today I wanted to see where the time goes before changing anything.

I ran the export for three years of all depots on a copy of the production data, with timing around each step. The query itself takes about 6 seconds. Building the row objects takes about 9 seconds. Turning them into a CSV string takes about 14 seconds, and the rest is writing the response. The server memory peaked at about 900 MB for one export, which on the small Render instance is close to the limit.

Two causes are clear. First, the whole result is loaded into an array before anything is sent. Second, the CSV code concatenates strings per cell, which is slow for 1.3 million cells.

The load balancer on Render closes a request that sends nothing for 30 seconds, so the long exports fail when the query and the build take longer than that. A cheap trick like a higher timeout would not fix the memory use.

I have not changed the code. Options for later are to run the export as a background job and mail a link, or to change the way the file is built. I wrote both down with their costs and will talk to the user about which one fits Acme.

summary: Wrote down two export options for the user: a background job with an emailed link, or a faster in-process build; no code changed yet.
body:
After the measurements I wrote a short comparison so the user can decide.

Option A, background job: the export runs in a worker, the file is stored, and the user gets an email with a link that expires. It works for any size, but needs a storage place, a table for job state, a cleanup job, and the user waits for an email instead of getting a download. That is about three to four days of work.

Option B, a better in-process build: reduce the memory and the string work, and send the file sooner. It is smaller, maybe one day, and the user gets the download right in the browser as now. I do not know yet whether it is enough for the biggest exports.

I also checked how often the big exports happen. The logs show 11 exports over one year of data in the last month, and 2 of the three-year exports, both by the same manager. So the problem is rare.

My recommendation is to try B first and keep A as a later step if B does not get the biggest export under the timeout. The user can answer when they have time.

summary: The user chose to try the smaller export change first and asked me to keep the session cleanup job in mind, since it runs at night near the export times.
body:
The user read the options and agreed with the order: the smaller in-process approach first, a background job only if it fails for the biggest case. They also pointed out that Acme managers usually export in the morning, so it should not be an issue with the nightly jobs.

I checked the nightly jobs anyway. The session cleanup deletes expired rows from the sessions table at 03:00 and takes about 8 seconds. The scheduled reports go out at 06:00 and 07:00. None of them overlap with morning exports at 08:00 or later.

I did a quick look at which part of the export code is easy to change without touching the API. The route /api/costs/export calls a function that returns an array, so the change can stay inside that function and its caller.

I noted the plan: measure again with a smaller memory profile and then decide. I did not start the code today.

summary: Reviewed the first draft of the scheduled report email layout with the user and fixed the PDF links that broke in the plain text part of the mail, plus a long depot name that overflowed the header.
body:
The user asked me this evening to look at the layout of the scheduled report emails, because two managers had told Jonas that the mails looked odd on their phones. I opened the rendered output for the weekly cost report and checked it in the HTML part and in the plain text part. Both were generated from the same template data, but they had drifted apart.

In the plain text part the link to the report page was printed twice, once as the label and once as the address, and the PDF link had lost its query string. The cause was a helper that stripped everything after the question mark, written long ago for tracking parameters. It also removed the recipient parameter that the personalized reports use. I fixed the helper to remove only the tracking parameters and keep the rest.

The second problem was the header. A depot with a very long name, 'Nordhafen Umschlag und Kühllager', pushed the title out of the mail width in a narrow client. I set a max width, allowed wrapping, and reduced the title size by two points for names over 28 characters. I checked it in a narrow viewport and in the desktop preview.

I also noticed that the dry-run list of recipients, which I built a few weeks ago, does not show the mail layout, only the recipient and the depot filter. I did not change that, but it would be useful to send a test mail to the user's own address. I wrote this as an idea and did not start it.

The rendering tests got two new cases: one for the query string in the plain text part and one for the long depot name. Both fail on the old code and pass now. The whole scheduled report suite passes, 41 tests.

The user looked at the result in a mail client on a phone and was happy with the header. They asked for a smaller logo, which I reduced from 160 to 120 pixels. Priya has not seen the new header, so I will send her a screenshot tomorrow. What remains is the test mail idea and the check with the managers who complained, once the next weekly run has gone out.

summary: Added the duplicate-report button and remembered column order to the report builder, with tests for both.
body:
I did the two other small items from the list.

Duplicate report: a button in the report list creates a copy with the name 'Copy of ...', the same columns, filters and schedule disabled. I disabled the schedule on purpose, because a copy with the same recipients would send mails twice. The recipient view option is copied too, and I checked that the draft restore bug of before does not touch it, since the copy is read from the database and not from storage.

Column order: the builder lets users drag columns, but the order was lost when the report was saved and opened again. The order is now stored as an array of column keys in the report JSON. Old reports without it use the default order. Unknown keys in the array are dropped, so a removed column cannot break a saved report.

Tests: a Vitest test for loading an old report without the order, and a Playwright test that drags a column, saves, reloads and compares the header order.

I also ran the axe check from the Playwright suite on the report builder page, and the drag handles needed an aria-label. Added: 'Move column, name of column'. The axe check passes.

summary: Added a test mail button to the scheduled report settings that sends one rendered report to the user's own address, so layout changes can be checked before the weekly run.
body:
