This was the small idea from yesterday's mail layout review. On the scheduled report page there is now a 'Send test mail to me' button next to the dry-run button. It renders the report for the current user, with that user's depot filter when the recipient view option is on, and sends it to the address of the logged-in user only.

The endpoint is POST /api/reports/:id/test-mail. It reuses the same render function as the weekly job, so the test mail cannot differ from the real one. I made it refuse any other address in the request, because I did not want a way to send mail to arbitrary people from the dashboard.

I added a rate limit of five test mails per hour per user, since the PDF rendering takes about two seconds and uses memory. The button shows a message when the limit is reached. The subject line starts with 'Test:' so nobody mistakes it for a real report.

Three API tests cover the normal case, the rate limit and a user without a depot. The last case sends the report without a depot filter and adds a note at the top of the mail that no depot was found, which is the same situation that skipped one manager in the first personalized run. I sent a test mail to myself in the staging setup and the layout was right in the HTML and the plain text part.

summary: Added a scheduled-report failure digest: when a weekly report skips a recipient, the owner now gets one summary mail listing who was skipped and why, instead of silent gaps.
body:
After the first personalized cost report went out and one depot manager was skipped because the user had no depot, the skip was only visible in the server log. Nobody at Acme would have noticed unless that manager complained. Today I made skips visible.

The scheduler now collects a list of skipped recipients during a run, each with a reason code: missing_depot, inactive_user, empty_result and render_error. After the last recipient is processed, one digest mail goes to the report owner. It lists the skipped people, the reason in plain words, and a link to the report settings page where the problem can be fixed. If nothing was skipped, no digest is sent, so the mail only appears when it matters.

I reused the layout of the test mail so the digest looks like the other report mails, including the plain text part, which I checked first this time after the broken links of last week. The reason codes are also stored in a new column on the report_runs table, so the settings page can later show the history of a run. The migration only adds a nullable json column and ran without trouble on the staging copy.

Tests: four Vitest cases, one for each reason, plus one that confirms no digest is sent for a clean run. I also replayed the run from the first personalized report against staging data, and the digest listed exactly the one user without a depot.

Open points: the empty_result case may be too noisy for depots that are idle on purpose, so I left it listed but marked as informational. I will ask Jonas whether he wants those hidden. The nightly session cleanup job is unaffected, since the digest runs right after the report, not at night. Next, I want to show the run history on the settings page.

summary: Started the export memory work: replaced per-cell string concatenation in the CSV writer and measured, but the peak memory is still about 800 MB because rows are collected first.
body:
Following the user's choice I started with the cheap part of the export. The CSV writer built each line by concatenating cells with plus and escaping with several regex passes. I replaced it with a single function that checks whether a cell needs quotes, using one test for comma, quote and newline, and joins the cells of a row with an array join.

I measured on the same copy of data as before, the three-year export of all depots. The CSV build step fell from about 14 seconds to 5 seconds. The total time went from about 50 to 40 seconds. That is better, but the time to the first byte is still about 35 seconds, since the response starts only when everything is ready.

The memory peak did not change much: about 800 MB against 900 MB before. The cause is as expected, the query result is held as an array of objects, and then the whole CSV string is held as well.

So this step helps with the speed but not with the timeout, and the load balancer would still close the request at 30 seconds without data. I added a test that compares the output of the old and new writer on 5,000 rows with quotes, commas, newlines and unicode, and it is identical.

I did not deploy this yet. The faster writer is a good base for the next step, which would be to send rows as they come from the database. I will think about how to do that with the pg driver, and where the route's error handling has to change, since headers are already sent after the first chunk.

summary: Wrote the plan for the next export step: read rows with a Postgres cursor in batches and write them out as they come, with error handling after the first chunk.
body:
I read through how the pg driver can read big results in parts. A cursor with batches of 2,000 rows keeps the memory small, since only one batch is in memory at a time.

The tricky part is errors. Once the first chunk is sent, the status code 200 is fixed, so a database error in the middle can only close the connection. The client would then get a cut file. I plan to log it with the export id and to end the response with an error so the browser shows a failed download.

I wrote down the steps and will test them on the copy of the data.

summary: Profiled the table-v3-era column resizing code that slows the shipments table on 200 visible rows, and cut re-renders from 200 per drag to about 8.
body:
A dispatcher told Jonas that dragging the column width in the shipments table feels sticky. I measured it with the React profiler on a page with 200 rows.

Every mouse move updated the width in the state of the table component, which re-rendered all rows and all cells. One drag event took about 45 ms on my machine, and about 90 ms with a slower CPU throttle, so the drag felt jumpy.

I changed it so that during the drag the width is applied through a CSS variable on the table element, set in a requestAnimationFrame callback, with no React state update. On mouse up the final width is saved in state once, and into local storage for the per-user layout, as before.

Result: the commit count per drag fell from about 200 to 8, and a drag event takes about 4 ms. With the throttled CPU it is 11 ms.

The sticky header still lined up with the cells in the Playwright screenshot test. I checked the keyboard resize too, which the accessibility pass added: arrow keys on the resize handle change the width in steps of 10 pixels, and they go through the same final state update. The test for it passes.

One limitation: the CSS variable approach needs the cells to use the width from the variable, and the old code used inline widths on each cell. I changed the cell style to read the variable with a fallback to the saved width. I deployed it together with the previous changes.

summary: Answered a question from Jonas about why a manager saw a 'session expired' message in the morning: the cleanup job was not at fault, the user had used 'log out of all devices' on a phone.
body:
Jonas asked why a manager at Acme was shown 'session expired' at 08:00 and had to log in again, and whether the nightly cleanup deleted a live session.

I looked up the user in the sessions table and the audit log. The cleanup job only deletes rows whose expiry is in the past, and the row of this user was not among the deleted ones, since its deletion came from the log out of all devices action at 07:52. That action was taken from a phone, and it removes every session row of the user, including the one on the office computer.

So it worked as designed. The message on the login page, however, said only 'session expired', which does not tell the user what happened. I suggested that the session table keeps a reason for deletion in the audit log, and that the next login page can say 'you were logged out on another device'.

I wrote this as a small task and told Jonas the answer. He was fine with the explanation.

summary: Prepared the streaming CSV export by reading the current handler, measuring where the memory goes, and sketching the cursor-based design before changing any route code.
body:
I worked in a branch of my own checkout and used the plan from this morning as a checklist. First I read the export route again from the top. It runs the query, collects all rows into an array, builds the whole CSV string and sends it with a Content-Length header. That explains the peak memory of about 800 MB on the three-year export of all depots, and it also explains why nothing reaches the load balancer until the very end.

Then I wrote down what a streaming version would need. The route would have to open a Postgres cursor and read the rows in batches, perhaps 2,000 at a time. The headers would have to go out before the first batch. The writer would have to wait for the drain event when the write buffer is full. I also noticed that the Content-Length header cannot stay, because the size is not known in advance, so the response would have to be chunked. I only noted this down and did not touch the route yet.

The hardest question is what happens when the database fails after some chunks were already sent. The status code is gone by then, so the only honest signal is to close the connection with an error so the browser shows a failed download. I want the log line to carry the export id and the number of rows sent. I wrote this as a short list of test cases next to the plan.

For the tests I set up a fixture of 20,000 rows and a small script that runs the current writer on it and saves the output. The later streamed version can be compared against that file byte by byte. I also made a list of the checks that still have to be done later: a slow client at about 100 kB per second, several exports at once, and a run on a copy of production data.

I did not run any timing yet. Before anything goes to production, the user should read the change.

summary: Profiled the CSV export memory use, wrote down what a streaming approach would need to handle, and checked how exports compete with the API for database connections.
body:
Following the export memory work from earlier, I looked at what is still open before any change to the export route. The streaming route does not exist yet. The handler still collects all rows first, so I worked from the current code and from measurements.

Memory: I ran the three-year export of all depots on a test copy and watched the process. The peak is still about 800 MB, as before. Replacing the string concatenation in the CSV writer helped a little, but the rows are all held in memory until the file is built, so this will not shrink without reading in batches.

Slow client: I used curl with a rate limit of 100 kB per second on the same export. The file is about 60 MB, so the download takes around 10 minutes. The server builds the whole file first, then sends it, so the slow client does not change memory much, but it keeps the response open for the whole time. I noted that a cursor-based approach would keep a database cursor open for that long, which needs thought.

Connections: the API pool has 10 connections. Today an export holds a connection only while it reads rows, but a cursor would hold it for the whole download. I did a rough calculation: five exports at once would leave the dashboard with five connections. I did not build anything for this. In my notes I listed two options to discuss: a separate small pool for exports, and a per-user limit on parallel exports with a clear error message.

I also noted that a statement timeout for the export connection would be useful, so a stuck query cannot hold a connection forever.

Nothing was changed in the export route and nothing was deployed. Next I will write the plan with these open points and show it to the user.

summary: Wrote a status note on the export work: the plan for a streaming CSV route with a cursor, what is prepared, and what still has to be measured before anything is changed in production.
body:
Wrote a long note on where the export work stands after a long day, so that the next steps are clear. Nothing of the streaming change is finished or released. It is a plan with some first measurements.

What exists so far: a faster CSV writer on a branch, which cut the build step from 14 seconds to about 5 on the test copy. Per-cell string concatenation is gone. The peak memory is still about 800 MB, because the route still collects all rows before writing the file, and that is the real cause of the gateway timeout on large exports.

What is planned: a new route that reads rows with a Postgres cursor in batches of 2,000 rows and writes them out as they arrive. The plan includes a separate pool for exports with 3 connections, a limit of 2 exports at once per user, and a statement timeout of 120 seconds. I sketched the tests I want: byte-for-byte equality with the old output, an error in the middle of a stream, and a slow client.

Open questions: the test copy is smaller than production for the last months, so I cannot yet say how long the three-year export of all depots will take. My guess is somewhere between 20 and 30 seconds, but I have no real number, and I want to measure on production data in a quiet moment before trusting it.

Risks I wrote down: a user who closes the browser in the middle could leave a cursor open until the socket close is noticed, so the close event must release the connection. I will test that with curl and Ctrl-C. The statement timeout would cut an export of an unusually large range and leave an incomplete file. The log should have the row count for that case. A visible message in the last line of the file only makes sense if the user wants it, since extra lines break spreadsheets.

The costs table export and the shipments table export share the route, so both would profit. Report PDFs have their own path and are not affected.

Next: the user reads the plan and the writer branch, then I implement the cursor route, run the tests, and check the large case on production data. The old buffered code stays until all of that is done.

summary: Read through the export plan with the user and wrote down what the CSV export needs before any streaming code exists: a separate Postgres pool and a clear rule for errors after the first chunk.
body:
The user went through the export handler this morning and the plan for the next step, and had two comments: the export uses the main pool, and it was unclear what should happen when an error comes after the first chunk. Nothing is changed in the handler yet. It still builds the whole file in memory, so large exports are still slow and the longest ones still hit the gateway timeout.

I measured the pool problem first. With the current setup, five parallel exports held five of the ten main pool connections, and the dashboard queries waited. I ran the five-exports test against a staging copy and the shipments table response time roughly doubled while the exports ran. So the plan now says that exports get their own pool in a new file, db/exportPool.ts, with a maximum of 4 connections and a 10 second connection timeout, and that the export route takes its client from there. I wrote this down but did not add the pool yet.

For the error case, I wrote down that once a first chunk is sent the status is already 200, so the route must not write an error page into the CSV. The plan is to destroy the response and log the failure with the export id, so the client sees a broken download instead of a file that looks complete but is cut off. The user agreed with that rule.

Still open: the timeout case has to be checked on production-sized data before anything is merged, and the session cleanup job should run at a different time than the usual export hours. I looked at the cleanup schedule and it overlaps with the morning exports, which I will move next.

summary: Moved the nightly session cleanup job away from the export hours and made it delete old sessions in batches of 5000, so it no longer holds long locks
body:
The user asked me earlier to keep the session cleanup job in mind, because it runs at 02:00 and some managers start large exports around then. I looked at the job in jobs/cleanupSessions.ts. It ran a single DELETE for every session row that had expired more than a day ago.

On a copy of production the table held about 410,000 session rows, and the single delete took 14 seconds and held row locks for the whole time. That is too long next to a streamed export that uses a cursor on the same database.

I changed the job to delete in batches of 5000 using a subquery with LIMIT and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, with a 200 ms pause between batches. The same cleanup now takes about 19 seconds in total, but no single statement runs longer than 150 ms.

I also moved the schedule to 04:30, when almost no dispatchers are online and the weekly report emails have already gone out. The schedule is read from an environment variable now, SESSION_CLEANUP_CRON, with the new value as the default.

Tests: a new Vitest case inserts 12,000 expired and 300 active sessions, runs the job, and checks that only the expired ones are gone and that the batches ran three times. The existing cleanup tests pass unchanged.

One thing I noticed and left alone: there is no index on expires_at for the sessions table. The batch query is fast enough on the copy, so I wrote it down as a possible follow-up rather than adding an index on production now.

summary: Ran the CSV export against production-sized data in staging and found that the shipments export with a delivery time sort can stay silent for longer than the 60 second proxy idle timeout.
body:
The plan for today was to find out whether the export work really fixes the timeout case on production data. At this point the export still builds its file in memory in the main checkout, so I ran it in a staging copy with the full three-year costs data for all depots, about 3.1 million rows, and watched what happened.

The result was bad, as expected. The export did not finish before the gateway cut it off, and memory of the API process climbed past 1.5 GB before the process was restarted. This confirms that the problem is not only the size of the file but also the way it is built.

I then looked at the shipments export with the status filter and a delivery time sort, because Jonas mentioned that one manager had trouble with it. Its query needs a sort over a large set before any row is returned, and on the staging copy the first row took 71 seconds. Render's proxy closes a connection that has sent no bytes for 60 seconds, so even a streaming approach would show the user a failed download unless something is sent early. I wrote that down as a risk for the plan, but I did not change any code for it today.

I looked at three ways to deal with the slow first row on paper. First, send the CSV header line immediately, before the query runs, which should reset the idle timer and costs nothing. Second, add a covering index for that sort, which the two indexes from last week partly do already. Third, a background job that mails a link, which is the heavier option the user did not choose.

I checked the query plan for the delivery time sort with explain. The new index is used when the status filter covers more than a third of the rows, but not for small filters, which is fine because those are fast anyway. For the large filters the sort is still the slow part.

What is left: write up the findings for the user and agree on the approach before I touch the export handler. I also want to add a log line with the time to first row, so that a slow export shows up in the logs before a user complains.

summary: Added a plan and a first measurement script for the slow CSV exports, and wrote down what the numbers were in the staging run, without changing how the file is built.
body:
I started with measuring, because we still do not know how often the export is slow or why. I added structured logging to the export route. Each export now logs the export id, the user id, the row count, the milliseconds until the first byte of the response, and the total milliseconds when it finishes or fails.

I kept the user's email out of the log line on purpose, only the id, because the logs go to Render's log stream.

I ran six exports on staging to see typical values. Costs, one year, one depot: first byte 90 ms, total 1.2 seconds, 41,000 rows. Costs, three years, all depots: the file is built fully in memory first, so nothing is sent for 24 seconds, and the process used a lot of memory for 3.1 million rows. Shipments, delivery time sort, wide filter: nothing for 71 seconds, total 80 seconds.

The last two are over the 30 second gateway timeout, so the dispatchers would see a failed download. The numbers show that the problem is the whole file being built before any byte goes out. I wrote down a plan for the next step: read the rows from a Postgres cursor and write them to the response as they come, with a separate small connection pool for exports. I did not start that yet, the plan is only in the notes for the review with the user.

I also added a warning log when an export takes longer than 20 seconds, so it is easy to search for.

A small cleanup: the export code had two copies of the CSV escaping function, one in the writer and one in an old test helper. I removed the copy in the helper and imported the real one.

All Vitest tests pass and the lint is clean. I did not change the pool settings.

summary: Fixed a flaky Playwright test for the export button that clicked before the filter menu had closed
body:
The export button test failed twice in the last CI runs with an error that the element was covered by another element. The cause was the filter menu, which closes with a 150 ms animation after Priya's move of the save-as-default button into it.

The test clicked the export button right after choosing a filter. I changed it to wait until the menu is hidden before clicking, using the locator's hidden state instead of a fixed timeout.

I ran the test 30 times in a loop and it passed each time. No application code changed.

summary: Answered the user's question about whether exports respect the saved default filters: they do not, the export uses the filters in the URL only, and that is now written down
body:
The user asked whether the CSV export from the shipments table uses the default status filter that was added last week. I read the export route and the table component to check.

The table starts with the saved default filter when the URL has none. The export button builds its request from the current table state, so when the table shows the default filter, the export contains that filter too. But a direct call to the export endpoint without parameters, such as the one in the scheduled reports, has no filters and exports everything.

That difference is correct, since the scheduled reports have their own filter settings. I confirmed with a test call and a click in the browser that both paths behave as described.

I did not change the code. I added two sentences to the export section of the README so that the next reader does not have to look it up. The user was happy with that answer and did not ask for a change.

summary: Wrote a unit test that proves the session list on the settings page hides sessions that were ended by log out of all devices
body:
While looking at the cleanup job earlier I noticed that the session list test only covered active sessions. The list on the settings page should not show sessions that the user ended with log out of all devices, even though the rows stay in the table until the cleanup runs.

I wrote a Vitest test that creates three sessions, calls the log out of all devices endpoint from one of them, and then reads the list. It expects the list to be empty for the other two and to contain only the current session if the endpoint keeps it.

The endpoint ends all sessions including the current one, so the test expects an unauthorized response on the list call afterwards, which it got. The query already filters on revoked_at, so the code needed no change.

The test is in tests/sessions.list.test.ts and runs in about 300 ms.

summary: Prepared the streamed CSV export branch for review: renamed the export pool, reran the tests and measured memory with five parallel exports, with nothing merged or deployed yet.
body:
The user finished a first pass over the streaming export branch and had one remaining comment about naming, where exportPool should say what it is for. I renamed it to exportDbPool and updated the three imports.

I reran the whole Vitest suite and the Playwright export tests on the branch. Everything passed. I also ran the five-exports test once more with the separate pool: memory stayed under 200 MB and the shipments table kept its normal speed while the exports ran.

The branch is not merged. I told the user that the review is done on their side but that I want one more run against a copy of production-sized data before anything goes out. The pool and the early header flush are both in the branch and behave as expected in staging.

I looked at the new log lines on the staging run. They show the id, the row count and the timings, and no email, which is what I wanted to confirm before they can reach production logs.

The old in-memory export code is still in place. In the branch it sits behind a flag, EXPORT_STREAMING, and I plan to set it to on by default only at deploy time, so that the user can switch it off in Render without a deploy if something goes wrong.

Next step is to do the production-sized run, ask the user for a final okay, and then decide when to merge and deploy. Removing the flag and the old path comes only after the streamed export has run in production for a while.

summary: Planned how to check the CSV export for slow first rows before it ships, after reading the export code and a staging EXPLAIN of a slow sort
body:
The streamed export branch is not merged yet, so I used the day to prepare for the deploy and to look for cases where the first row arrives late. Large exports still run through the old in-memory builder in production, which is why they hit the 30 second gateway timeout. The plan is to stream from a cursor and flush the header early so the connection stays alive.

The risk I wanted to understand is a query that is slow to produce its first row, because a cursor does not help when the database has to sort many rows first. I took a shipments export sorted by weight, filtered to a single depot with a three-year range, and ran EXPLAIN on a staging copy. The planner used the depot index and then sorted about 900,000 rows. Forcing the weight index made it fast, but that is not something I want to put in the export code, so I left it out.

I also noticed that the table statistics on staging looked stale after the last large import, which may explain the plan choice. I wrote down the query, the plan and the timing in the branch notes so they can be compared once streaming is in place. I added time-to-first-row logging to my to-do list for the export route, so the numbers exist from the first day.

I noted that autovacuum thresholds for the shipments table are the default, and the table grows quickly. A lower analyze scale factor for that table is a possible follow-up, and I plan to ask the user whether to change it before the deploy.

summary: Set a lower autovacuum analyze threshold on the shipments table so the planner statistics stay fresh after large imports
body:
The user agreed to the follow-up from the morning. The shipments table receives big batches from the depots' nightly imports, and with the default scale factor of 0.1 the analyze can lag by tens of thousands of rows.

I wrote a migration, 0047_shipments_autovacuum.sql, that sets autovacuum_analyze_scale_factor to 0.02 for the shipments table only. The costs table grows slower, so I left it alone.

I ran the migration on staging first and checked pg_stat_user_tables. The last_autoanalyze time moved up after the next import simulation of 60,000 rows, where before it had not triggered.

Then I ran it on production in a quiet period. The setting change takes a very short lock and finished in a few milliseconds.

I repeated the weight-sorted export with the single depot and the three-year range, and the first row came after 0.6 seconds.

I added a line to the ops notes of the repo describing the setting and why it exists. No application code changed.

Next I will look at the logs again tomorrow to see if any export has a first row over 20 seconds.

summary: Planned and began the accessibility check of the paginated shipments table with keyboard and screen reader, and fixed the first three problems found
body:
The plan written earlier called for checking the shipments table after the pagination change, so I started that this evening. I used keyboard navigation in the browser and VoiceOver on the Mac.

First finding: the next and previous buttons did not announce what they do. They had only an arrow icon and no accessible name. I added aria-labels, Next page of shipments and Previous page of shipments.

Second finding: the old table announced the row count when the page changed, and the new one said nothing. I added a visually hidden live region with role status that says, for example, Showing 50 shipments. It updates after each page load. The total from the count endpoint comes later, so the text first says the number of rows and then adds the total when it arrives.

Third finding: after clicking Next, focus stayed on the button, which was fine, but when the button became disabled at the last page, focus was lost to the body. I changed the code to move focus to the table caption in that case, with tabindex minus one.

I also checked the filter menu with the keyboard. Escape closes it and returns focus to the trigger, which works. The save-as-default button inside the menu is reachable with Tab.

What I did not finish: the column header sort buttons announce the sort direction only by an icon. I wrote that down as the next item, together with a check of color contrast in the dark theme for the disabled pagination buttons.

Tests: I added Playwright checks for the aria-labels and the live region text. They run against the paginated table with seeded data of 120 shipments. Unit tests for the hook did not change.

The work is in the main checkout and not deployed yet. I will continue with the sort headers tomorrow.

summary: Finished the table accessibility items: sort headers now expose aria-sort, and the disabled pagination buttons pass contrast in the dark theme after a color change
body:
This evening I continued with the two items left over from the check of the shipments table.

The sort headers were buttons with only an arrow icon. I added aria-sort to the th elements with values ascending, descending or none, and the button's accessible name now says Sort by delivery time. With VoiceOver the header reads as Delivery time, sorted ascending, button.

I also found that the null-safe delivery time sort from last week shows undelivered shipments last, and nothing tells a screen reader user that. I added a short hint to the live region when that sort is active: Undelivered shipments are listed last.

For the contrast, I measured the disabled pagination buttons in the dark theme. The text had a ratio of 2.6 to 1 against the background, below the 4.5 needed for text. Disabled controls are formally exempt, but Priya had asked for them to stay readable, so I raised the color from gray 600 to gray 400 in the dark theme variables, which gives 4.9.

Priya's palette file is the source for these colors. I only changed the one token, dark.text.disabled, and left a comment with the ratio.

I ran axe through Playwright on the table page in both themes. It found no serious or critical issues. It reported one moderate issue, a landmark region without a label, in the page layout. I gave the nav a label, and the report is clean now.

Tests added: a check of aria-sort after clicking a header twice, and the axe run for the shipments page. The whole Playwright suite takes 4 minutes 10 seconds now.

The changes are in the main checkout, committed in three commits. I did not deploy because there is a change of the dark token that Priya should see first. I will send her screenshots.

summary: Priya approved the stronger disabled button color for the dark theme, and I prepared the accessibility changes for deploy and planned how to check the CSV export timeout later.
body:
Priya looked at the screenshots of the dark theme and said the lighter disabled color is fine, as long as the buttons still look inactive. They do, since the cursor and the missing hover effect still show it. She asked me to keep the old gray for the light theme, which I had not changed.

I prepared the accessibility changes for the deploy just before lunch. I ran the unit tests and the Playwright keyboard tests for the paginated shipments table again, and they passed. I wrote down the deploy steps on Render, which should take about three minutes plus the health check, and I will ship them after Jonas has seen the final screenshots.

Afterwards I read the export logs of the last two days to see how large exports behave today. Large exports are still slow. The current handler builds the whole file in memory, and the biggest ones come close to the 30 second gateway timeout. There were 41 exports, and the longest took 27 seconds, a costs export for all depots. Two exports were aborted, both with the client closing the connection after a few seconds. That is a user cancelling the download, and the route logs them as aborted, not as failed, which is what I intended.

A small item from the logs: one export request came with a date range of twelve years, and the API accepted it. It finished, but only just, and it shows that there is no upper limit on the range. I did not add a limit, because Jonas has not asked for one. I made a note to think about whether streaming the rows from a cursor would be a better answer than a limit.

I wrote the note for the user: the accessibility pass is ready to ship. The export timeout is still open, and I will look at it as the next task from this block, starting with a test table of about a million rows.

summary: Jonas asked whether the weekly scheduled reports can also carry a CSV attachment, and I outlined what that needs and what the open questions are, without writing code.
body:
Jonas wrote to the user that some dispatchers want the weekly report mail to carry a CSV file in addition to the PDF link. The user passed the question to me to check what it would take.

The scheduled report job renders the report as HTML and PDF today and sends a mail through the existing mail service. The CSV export today builds the whole file in memory and sends it as the response of the export request. It is a single function that returns one big string, and it is tied to the request, because it reads the filters and the user from the request object. Large exports are slow, and some of them hit the gateway timeout, which is a known problem that is still open. For a mail job that runs at night this matters less, because nobody waits for the first byte, but the memory use of a large file in the job process is something to watch.

I read the code to see how to reuse it. The simplest way is to pull the part that builds the rows and the CSV text out of the request handler, so that the job can call it with a user and a filter and get a buffer. That is a small refactoring and I would do it first. I did not start it.

The open questions are size and mail limits. A report for one depot and one week is small, usually under 2 MB. But a report with all depots and a long range could be over 25 MB, which many mail servers reject. I suggest an attachment only below 5 MB, and above it a mail with the download link, which the PDF link already does.

A second question is who may receive it. The recipients of a report may include people who can see fewer depots than the report owner. The CSV must be built with the permissions of the recipient, as the PDF link does after login, or only sent to recipients with the same access. I looked at the code and the PDF is rendered with the owner's permissions, so it has the same problem in the mail body, but the PDF link requires a login for the details.

I wrote this down as a short plan with three steps: extract the row builder from the request handler, size rule, permission rule. I did not write code. The user will ask Jonas about the size rule and the permission question.

summary: Planned how to check the CSV export for large tables and read the export code, without changing anything.
body:
I looked at the CSV export today, because large exports are still slow and Jonas's team has complained again. Nothing was changed in the code, and the export works as before.

In routes/export.ts the handler calls buildCsvInMemory in lib/csv.ts, which is about 70 lines. It loads all rows from the query into an array, joins them into one string and sends the whole file at the end. I read it to see where the time goes. For a table of a few thousand rows it is fine, but for the big shipment tables nothing goes out until the whole file is built, so the gateway waits and eventually gives up with its 30 second limit. The memory use also grows with the row count, which I could see in the Render metrics during a test export.

I searched for every use of buildCsvInMemory and found two test files that import it. They check the output format, so whatever I change later, those tests must keep covering the exact format, including the quotes and the byte order mark. I wrote down the cases a fixture file should include: commas and quotes inside fields, empty values and non-ASCII depot names.

I also ran an export of a mid-sized table on staging and timed it, to have a baseline for later. The query itself returned quickly, so the delay is in building the file and not in Postgres.

Next I want to think about how to send rows as they are read instead of at the end, and how to test it with a very large table. That is only a plan for now, and I have not started any of it. The CSV attachment idea from Jonas for the scheduled reports is separate and still waits for his answers.

summary: Looked into why the session list on the settings page shows the same phone twice and fixed it by updating the existing session row for a device instead of adding a new one on each login
body:
A manager told Jonas that the session list shows his phone three times, with the same browser name. The user asked me to find out why.

I looked at the sessions table for that manager on production, read only. There were three active rows with the same user agent string and the same IP range, created on three different days. He did not log out in between, because the mobile browser forgets the cookie when the app is closed, so each visit created a new row.

The login code always inserts a new session. There is no device concept, so the list cannot tell whether two rows are the same phone.

I considered adding a device id cookie that lives for a year, and reusing the row if the cookie matches. That is a bigger change with a privacy side and I did not want to do it without the user's decision.

The smaller change I made: at login, if the same user has an active session with the same user agent and the same /24 network and it was last seen more than a day ago, that row is ended and replaced. So the list shows only the newest one. The old one is marked revoked with the reason replaced_on_login, which is shown nowhere but helps in later debugging.

I wrote tests for four cases: same agent and network replaced, different agent kept, different network kept, and a session seen in the last day kept, because it may be a second tab or a real second device in the same office.

The last case means that two identical laptops in one office within a day still show twice. That is acceptable.

I ran the tests, and they pass. I deployed after the user's quick look at the diff.

After the deploy I checked that login time did not change; the extra query takes about 2 ms using the existing user_id index. For the manager's three rows, they will collapse at his next login. Nothing is deleted by hand.

summary: Started the costs page work for the chart that compares cost per kilometer by depot, with the query and a first version of the chart component
body:
Jonas asked last week for a chart on the costs page that shows the cost per kilometer for each depot, so that managers can see which depots are expensive. I started with the query.

The costs table has the cost amount and the shipments table has the distance. I joined them by shipment id and grouped by depot and by month. On a staging copy with three years of data the query took 1.9 seconds, which is too slow for a page load.

I added a materialized view, depot_month_costs, that holds the sums of cost and distance for each depot and month. It has about 1,800 rows. A refresh takes 6 seconds and I scheduled it after the nightly import.

The chart reads from the view and divides in the API, so a month with zero distance gives null and not a division error. The API route is /api/costs/per-km.

The component uses ECharts with one line per depot. With 24 depots the legend is crowded, so I reused the legend scroll type from the chart legend work of last year.

It works on staging data. The tooltips still show raw numbers without the currency format, and the colors repeat after 10 depots. Both are on the list for the next session.

summary: Finished the cost per kilometer chart with currency tooltips, a color rule for many depots, and a depot selector that defaults to the five most expensive
body:
I continued from the first version this morning. The tooltips now use the same currency formatter as the costs table, so they show 1.84 EUR and not 1.8401234.

For the color problem, 24 lines with repeating colors are hard to read anyway. I made the chart start with the five depots with the highest average cost per kilometer, and a multi-select lets the user add others. Selected depots get a color from a fixed palette of 12 that Priya defined, and I assign them in the order of selection so the same depot keeps its color while the selection changes.

The selection is stored in the URL as a depots parameter, so a link shares the same view. This follows the pattern of the table filters.

I checked the empty state: when a depot has no data in the range, its line is simply absent, and the tooltip does not show it. A depot with only one month of data shows a single dot, since a line needs two points. I turned on symbols for that case.

Tests: a Vitest test for the API division with zero distance, and a Playwright test that selects a depot and checks the URL. Both pass.

I asked the user to show it to Jonas. A remaining item is the accessibility text of the chart. Other charts have a table view alternative and this one needs the same.

summary: Added the table alternative and a text summary for the cost per kilometer chart so screen reader users get the same data
body:
The other charts on the dashboard offer a Show as table toggle, and the new per-kilometer chart had none. I added it using the same ChartTableToggle component.

The table has a row per month and a column per selected depot, with values in the currency format. With five depots it fits the screen, and with more it scrolls horizontally with a sticky first column.

I also wrote a text summary above the chart that is read by screen readers: it names the most and the least expensive depot in the range and the change from the first to the last month for the selected depots. The text comes from a small function with unit tests for the cases of one depot, a tie, and no data.

The axe check through Playwright reports no serious issues for the costs page. I did not deploy yet, since Jonas has not seen the chart.

summary: Jonas saw the cost per kilometer chart and asked to exclude cancelled shipments and to show the overall average as a dashed line
body:
The user passed on Jonas's feedback after he looked at the staging version. He liked the chart, and had two requests.

First, cancelled shipments should not count. They have a cost entry for the booking but no distance, and so they raise the cost per kilometer. I checked the data and about 2.4 percent of shipments are cancelled. I added a status filter to the view definition and refreshed it. The averages dropped by about 3 percent.

Second, a dashed line for the overall average of all depots. I added a series with a dashed style and gray color, computed in the API as total cost over total distance for each month, not an average of averages. I noted that in a code comment.

Both changes pass the tests. The deploy is planned for tomorrow morning.

summary: Deployed the cost per kilometer chart and found the materialized view refresh collided with the nightly import lock, so the refresh now runs concurrently
body:
I deployed the chart this morning, and then looked at the first nightly run on staging, which had happened before. The refresh of depot_month_costs ran at the same time as the import and waited for 40 seconds on a lock held by the import transaction. Meanwhile the costs page read the view and was blocked too, because a normal refresh takes an exclusive lock.

On production this would have meant a costs page that hangs during the refresh. The fix is REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY, which needs a unique index on the view. I added a unique index on depot id and month in a migration.

I tested the concurrent refresh on staging while running a loop of reads on the view. No read waited longer than 20 ms, and the refresh took 9 seconds, a bit slower than the plain one.

I changed the scheduled job to call the concurrent form, and to start 10 minutes after the import's usual end, not at a fixed time. It reads the import's finished marker row, and if it is missing it waits and retries up to 5 times.

The migration ran on production with no problems. I triggered one refresh by hand and watched the pages: no slowdown.

I also checked the first production load of the chart: the API answered in 40 ms and the chart rendered in about 300 ms with 5 depots, and in 450 ms with all 24.

I told the user it is live. One loose end is that the refresh job has no alert when it fails. I will add a log line at error level and look at how the failure digest for scheduled reports works, since that could be reused.

summary: Added error logging and a failure digest mail for the materialized view refresh job, reusing the digest code of the scheduled reports
body:
The refresh job for the costs view could fail silently, and the page would then show old numbers without anyone noticing. I added two things.

First, the job catches errors and logs them at error level with the job name and the message. It also stores the time of the last successful refresh in a small table, job_status.

Second, the costs page shows a small gray note, Data as of, with the time of the last refresh. This was something Jonas asked about earlier for other pages too, since managers sometimes wonder how fresh the numbers are. If the last success is older than 36 hours, the note turns amber.

For the alert, I reused the digest mail function of the scheduled reports from last week. It takes a list of items and an owner address and sends one mail. I generalized it a little so the items can be of any kind, and kept the report digest tests unchanged. The refresh failure sends a mail to the address in the ADMIN_ALERT_EMAIL setting, at most once per 12 hours.

I tested by making the view name wrong on staging: the log line appeared, the mail arrived once, and a second failure within the hour did not send another one. After fixing the name, the next run succeeded and the amber note went away.

Tests: three Vitest tests for the throttle logic, with a fake clock.

Deployed in the evening. The amber threshold is a constant and the user can change it if 36 hours is too long or too short.

summary: Read through the logs of the past days: the view refresh and the session cleanup are healthy, and large CSV exports are still slow and a risk before the costs page grows.
body:
A routine check of the logs this morning. The materialized view refresh ran every night without a collision with the import lock, and the Data as of note on the costs page shows the current morning.

The session cleanup job ran at 04:30 as configured, in 7 batches, with the slowest statement at 120 ms. The number of session rows dropped from about 410,000 to 96,000 after the first runs, because it had a backlog.

Exports looked less good. There were 63 in the last week and none failed, but the long ones are slow. The longest time to first row was 3.4 seconds for a table of a moderate size, and the bigger tables take much longer because the handler still builds the whole file in memory before it sends anything. I checked the memory graph on Render and saw a spike during the biggest export, though nothing crashed.

I did not look into the database connections used by exports yet, since nothing pointed to a problem there.

I wrote a note in the backlog: test an export of more than 200,000 rows against the 30 second gateway timeout on a staging copy, to see where it breaks, and think about how the handler could send rows sooner. I changed nothing in the export code today.

summary: Implemented the CSV attachment for weekly reports under 5 MB, built with the recipient's own permissions, after Jonas confirmed both rules
body:
Jonas answered the two questions through the user: attachments only below 5 MB, with a link above it, and the CSV must not contain depots that the recipient cannot see. I implemented that today.

The scheduled report job loops over recipients. For each one it now loads the recipient's depot permissions, and builds the CSV with them through the streaming writer, writing to a temporary file in os.tmpdir. The file name contains the report id and a random suffix, and the file is deleted in a finally block.

The size rule: after the file is written, I check its size. Under 5 MB it is attached to the mail. At or above, the mail contains the download link text and no attachment. The link goes to the existing export route, which asks for a login and applies the permissions of the logged in user.

The permission part needed a change in the query builder. The export route took permissions from the request session, but the job has no session. I extracted a function that takes a user id and returns the allowed depot ids, and the route and the job both call it now. The route tests passed unchanged after this, which was a good sign.

In the mail service I added attachment support to the send function. The plain text part now says that a CSV file is attached or that it is too large, so the plain text readers are not confused, which I remembered from the broken PDF links in the text part.

I tested with three recipients of a staging report: an owner with all depots, a dispatcher with one depot, and a manager with two. The three files had 41,200, 3,900, and 7,100 rows, and the dispatcher's file contained only his depot. I compared by loading each file and counting distinct depot names.

A test with a fake 6 MB result checked that the attachment is dropped and the link text is used.

The temp file cleanup was checked by making the mail send throw: the file was gone afterwards.

Adding the test mail button of last week, I made it include the CSV too, so the user can check the layout and the file.

The tests pass. I will deploy before the next weekly run and watch the first run.

summary: Deployed the CSV attachments for scheduled reports and checked the first run: 14 mails went out, 11 with a CSV and 3 with the link text because of size
body:
I deployed the change early this morning, before the weekly run. The run happened later and I read the log afterwards.

There were 14 report mails to 9 recipients. Eleven mails carried a CSV attachment, with sizes from 38 KB to 3.9 MB. Three mails were over 5 MB and had the link text instead, all from the same all-depots report for the owner and two managers.

No recipient was skipped, so the failure digest did not fire. The temp directory was empty after the run.

I checked one of the large mails in a mail client. The plain text and the HTML part both say that the file is too large to attach and give the link. It reads well.

One observation: the all-depots report took 3.5 minutes in total, mostly because the CSV is built once for each recipient. For recipients with identical permissions the file is the same. I could cache by the sorted depot id list within a run. That would cut the run time a lot for large recipient lists.

I did not build the cache yet, as the run time is not a problem now. I wrote it into the notes as an idea, and I told the user that the attachment feature is live and working.

summary: Checked the second day of scheduled report mails with CSV attachments: no bounces, but one recipient's mail client showed the file name garbled because of an umlaut.
body:
I went through the mail provider's log for the second run of weekly reports after the CSV attachment deploy. 16 mails went out, 13 with a CSV and 3 with the link text because the file was over 5 MB. None bounced.

One dispatcher wrote to Jonas that the attachment name looked like 'Lieferungen_=3FK...'. The depot name in the file name contained an umlaut, and the header was not encoded in the RFC 2231 way.

I changed the file name builder to produce ASCII only, with the depot name transliterated, for example 'ae' for the a-umlaut. A unit test covers three depot names with special characters. The change is small and goes out with the next deploy. I did not touch the content of the CSV, which is UTF-8 with a BOM and opens fine in Excel.

summary: Planned and started the report builder v2 feature for saved column sets, so Acme users can keep their own column choice for tables and exports.
body:
Jonas asked last week that managers can save which columns they see in the shipments table and in the reports. Today I wrote down what that needs before touching code.

The data model is one new table, saved_column_sets, with user_id, name, a JSON list of column keys and an is_default flag. There is a unique index on user_id and name. The API gets three routes: list, save and delete. Each checks that the set belongs to the session user.

I first checked how the table component stores its visible columns now. It keeps them in component state and in the URL, which means a page reload from a bookmark works but a new login starts from the default again. That is the gap Jonas sees.

The plan has a rule for conflicts: URL columns win over the saved default, in the same way as filters in exports, which only use the URL. I wrote that down so nobody is surprised later.

I wrote the migration and the three routes with Vitest tests for ownership and for the unique name case. The tests pass. The frontend is not started yet.

One open question is whether scheduled reports should use the saved set of the owner. I left it out of this step and put the question in the notes for Jonas. The next step is a small dropdown above the table that lists the sets, with a save button and a default star.

summary: Built the column set dropdown above the shipments table, with save, rename and default star, wired to the new routes.
body:
The frontend part of the saved column sets is in place. A dropdown above the shipments table lists the user's sets, and choosing one updates the visible columns and the URL.

Save opens a small inline field for the name. If the name exists, the API answers 409 and the field shows 'name already used' instead of a generic error. Rename uses the same field. The star marks the default set, and setting a new default clears the old one in one transaction.

I had a bug first: after choosing a set, the table kept the old column widths, because the width state was keyed by the column index and not the key. Keying it by the column key fixed it, and the resizing code from the last weeks was not affected.

The dropdown is keyboard reachable and has labels, since the accessibility check of the table is still fresh. I did not run a screen reader on it yet.

A Playwright test saves a set, reloads and checks that the columns are restored. It passed in three runs. What remains is the empty state text and Priya's look at the spacing.

summary: Priya reviewed the column set dropdown and asked for a clearer default star and smaller spacing; both changed, and the screen reader check found one missing label.
body:
Priya looked at the dropdown in the staging copy this evening. She liked the structure but found the star too faint in the dark theme and the row spacing too loose compared with the filter bar.

I made the star filled when it is the default and outlined otherwise, with a text 'default' in the accessible name. In the dark theme I used the same color token as the disabled button fix, which keeps the contrast over 4.5. The spacing now uses the same 8 px step as the filter bar.

Then I ran VoiceOver over the dropdown. The delete button read only 'button' because the icon had no label. I added aria-label with the set name, for example 'Delete column set Depot overview'. Everything else read well.

I also wrote the empty state: 'No saved column sets yet. Choose columns and press Save.' Priya approved the text.

The branch is ready for a normal deploy tomorrow. I want to check one thing first: what happens when a saved set contains a column that was removed later. Right now the table ignores unknown keys, and I added a test for that.

summary: Deployed saved column sets and checked the first real use: three managers saved sets within the first hours and no errors appeared in the logs.
body:
The saved column sets went to production this afternoon. I watched the API logs and the database for the first hours.

Three managers created sets, one of them with a default. There was one 409 for a duplicate name, which is the expected answer. No 500 errors appeared.

I checked the query plan of the list route. It uses the unique index and takes well under a millisecond.

Jonas asked in the evening whether the sets can be shared between users. That is a different feature with permission questions, so I only noted it. For now each set stays private to its owner.

summary: Investigated why some users were asked to log in again after a deploy and found the session cookie max age was reset on every response, not only on activity.
body:
Jonas passed on a complaint from two dispatchers: after the deploy of saved column sets they had to log in again, even though they used the dashboard that morning. I started with the session rows in Postgres.

Their old session rows were gone, but the cleanup job had not deleted them. It logs the number of deleted rows per batch, and the numbers for the night were normal, about 400 rows.

So I looked at the session middleware. The rolling option was on, which means the cookie expiry is renewed on each response. That is intended. But the expiry column in Postgres was only updated when the session data changed, and the touch call was throttled to once per hour by a setting I had added months ago to reduce writes.

The deploy itself was not the cause. The cause was a combination: the cookie lived on, the row expiry did not. After 24 hours without a data change, the row expired while the browser still sent the cookie. The server then found no row and asked for a login.

I reproduced it in a test with a fake clock. A session that was active every hour but never changed data expired exactly at the row expiry time. The test failed as expected before the fix.

The fix is to touch the row when the remaining lifetime is under half of the max age, not once per hour. That keeps writes low and keeps the row and the cookie in step. For a 24 hour session this means at most one write per 12 hours per user.

I also added a log line when a cookie arrives with no matching row, with the age of the cookie. That shows how often it happens in future.

The test now passes. I did not deploy yet because the session code is sensitive and I want the user to read the diff first. I wrote the summary for the user with the reproduction steps and the number of affected sessions, which I estimated at about 30 per day from the log lines.

summary: The user reviewed the session touch fix and asked for a metric on how many cookies arrive with no row; added a counter and deployed.
body:
The user read the diff of the session touch change and agreed with the half-lifetime rule. They asked for a simple counter for cookies with no matching row, so the effect of the fix can be seen and not only guessed.

I added a counter in the existing metrics module and logged it once per hour as a number, as the other metrics are logged. It separates 'expired row' from 'unknown id', because an unknown id can also come from a forged cookie.

I ran the session tests and the Playwright login tests. All passed. I deployed in the evening.

The first hour after the deploy showed 2 expired-row cases, which were sessions that started before the fix. I will look at the numbers again tomorrow.

The expected result is that these cases drop to nearly zero after one day.

summary: Sketched the plan for sharing saved column sets within a depot and listed the permission questions that Jonas has to answer first.
body:
Jonas asked for shared column sets, so I wrote a plan before any code. The main point is that sharing touches permissions, and the dashboard already has depot-based access for dispatchers and company-wide access for managers.

The simplest model is a visibility field on the set with three values: private, depot and company. A depot set would be visible to users of the same depot. A company set could only be created by managers.

The questions for Jonas are these:
- Can a dispatcher edit a depot set made by a colleague, or only copy it?
- What happens to a shared set when its owner leaves and the account is deactivated?
- Should a shared set be able to be the default for other users, or only a suggestion?

My proposal is: copy only, the set moves to the depot's oldest manager on deactivation, and shared sets are suggestions only. That keeps surprises low.

Technically the change adds a column and an index on visibility and depot_id, and the list route becomes a union of own and visible sets. I estimated half a day for the backend and one day for the frontend with tests.

I did not start the code. The session fix goes first, and the answers from Jonas decide the rest.

I also wrote down a risk. A shared set that includes a column that a dispatcher may not see, such as cost columns, must not reveal that column. The table should apply the permission check after the set, never before. A test for this is the first one I will write.

summary: Looked at the counter after one day: cookies with no row dropped from about 30 to 1 per day, and then started the work on the page for scheduled report history.
body:
The first thing this morning was the new counter. In the last 24 hours there was one expired-row case and none with unknown ids. Before the fix the estimate was about 30 per day, so the half-lifetime touch rule works.

Jonas answered the questions about shared sets: copy only, suggestions only, and the owner change on deactivation is fine. He added that company sets are not needed now. I noted that and will build depot sets first.

Then I started a smaller item he asked for: a page that shows the history of scheduled report runs. Today the managers only see the mails. They want to see when a report ran, how many recipients got it, and whether the CSV was attached or the link text was used.

The scheduled reports job already writes a row per run into report_runs, but only with the start time and a status. I added columns: recipients_count, csv_attached_count and link_only_count. The job fills them after sending.

The API route returns the last 50 runs of a report with the counts. It checks that the user owns the report or is a manager of the depot.

I wrote the migration so that old rows get null counts, and the page shows a dash for them instead of zero. A zero would be wrong, since the old runs did send mails.

Tests cover the permission check and the null case. They pass.

The page itself is not built yet. I planned a plain table with a status badge and a text for the attachment case, using the same table component as the shipments page, so keyboard and screen reader behaviour is the same.

summary: Built the report run history table with status badges and attachment counts, including a text alternative to the badge colors.
body:
The page for the run history of scheduled reports now exists under the report's detail view. It shows time, status, recipients, how many got a CSV and how many only a link.

The status badge has the colors green, amber and red, but each also has a word: sent, partly sent, failed. That keeps it readable without color, which matters after the accessibility work on the shipments table.

The times are shown in the user's time zone, as in the rest of the dashboard. I reused the formatting helper and did not write a new one.

One problem came up: the run rows were sorted by id in the query, and ids from the retry of a failed run were out of order. I sorted by started_at descending with the id as a tie breaker. A test with two runs at the same second covers it.

The list loads 50 rows with one query and a limit. I added an index on report_id and started_at to keep it fast, and checked with EXPLAIN that the index is used.

What I did not do is paging. 50 runs of a weekly report are about a year, which is enough for now. If daily reports appear, this will have to change.

Playwright test: open a report, see at least one run, check that a null count shows a dash. It passed.

summary: Answered Jonas's question why a weekly report went out with the link text only: the CSV was 5.4 MB, just over the limit.
body:
Jonas asked why the report of the north depot arrived without a CSV attachment this week. I looked at the run history page, which now shows this kind of case directly.

The run had 6 recipients, 0 with CSV and 6 link only. The CSV for that depot was 5.4 MB, and the rule is under 5 MB. The depot had a busy week with more shipments than usual.

So the system worked as agreed. I told Jonas the number and that the link in the mail gives the full file. He asked whether the limit could be 8 MB. I said that depends on the mail providers of the recipients, and that I would check which limits their servers state before changing it.

summary: Checked the attachment size limits of the recipients' mail domains and found that 8 MB is risky for one of them, so the 5 MB limit stays.
body:
I looked at the bounce history and the domains of the recipients of scheduled reports. Most are on two large mail providers, whose limits are well above 8 MB. One smaller domain, used by two depots, answered a test mail with a size limit of 7 MB for the whole message.

A CSV attachment grows by about a third when it is encoded for mail. So an 8 MB file would become about 10.7 MB and would be rejected there.

Even 5 MB becomes about 6.7 MB, which is under that limit but not by much.

I wrote this to Jonas with the numbers and suggested keeping 5 MB. As an option for later, the report could be zipped, since CSV compresses to about a fifth. That would fit much larger files, but some mail filters block zip files from unknown senders, so I did not build it.

Jonas agreed to keep the limit. I put the reasoning into the notes next to the limit constant in the code, so that nobody raises it without checking the domain.

summary: Started the depot-shared column sets: added the visibility column, the union query, and the first test that a shared set never reveals cost columns to dispatchers.
body:
With Jonas's answers in hand, I built the backend of depot-shared column sets. The first step was the migration: a visibility column with the values private and depot, a depot_id column, and an index on both.

The list route now returns own sets plus depot sets of the user's depot. Each entry carries an owner name and a flag that says whether the user may edit it. Only the owner may edit, as agreed.

Before anything else I wrote the permission test I had planned. A manager creates a depot set that includes the cost per kilometer column. A dispatcher of the same depot loads the set. The test expects that the set arrives, but that the cost column is filtered out of the column list. It failed at first, since the route returned the stored list as it was.

The fix filters the column keys against the permissions of the requesting user in the route and not in the table. That means the frontend never receives a key it must not show. I added the same filter to the export route, because an export uses the columns of the URL, and a crafted URL with a cost column should not work for a dispatcher either. I checked that, and found that the export route already filters, so the new test there only confirms it.

A second test covers the copy action. Copying a depot set creates a private set of the user with the filtered columns only.

The deactivation rule from Jonas, moving the set to the depot's oldest manager, is implemented as a step in the user deactivation function. I tested it with a depot that has two managers, and with a depot that has none, where the set becomes private to nobody and is deleted. I flagged this edge case in the notes.

All Vitest tests pass. The frontend part comes next.

summary: Added the shared sets section to the column dropdown, with a copy button and a clear label of the owner, and checked it with the keyboard.
body:
The dropdown above the shipments table now has two groups: 'My sets' and 'Depot sets'. Each depot set shows the owner's name in a smaller text, and the copy button replaces the edit and delete buttons for sets the user does not own.

The groups use proper group labels, so a screen reader announces 'Depot sets' when the focus enters the group. I walked through it with the keyboard: arrow keys move through all entries, and the copy button is reachable with tab.

A small problem was that long owner names pushed the buttons out of the dropdown. I truncated the name with an ellipsis and put the full name into the title and the accessible description.

When the user copies a set, the copy appears under 'My sets' with the name 'Copy of ...' and the name field opens for renaming at once. This took a bit of focus handling, because the new row is rendered after the API answer.

I added a Playwright test with two users in the same depot. The first creates a depot set, the second sees it and copies it. It passed.

Still to do: Priya should see the groups, and I want to test with 40 sets to check how the dropdown scrolls.

summary: Tested the column dropdown with 40 sets and added a max height with scrolling so it no longer runs off the screen.
body:
I generated 40 sets in a test account and opened the dropdown. It grew taller than the window on a laptop screen, and the lower entries were not reachable.

I set a max height of 60 percent of the viewport with vertical scrolling, and the group headers stay sticky while scrolling. Keyboard focus scrolls the active entry into view.

I checked it in the dark theme as well, where the sticky header background had no color and let entries show through. It uses the theme surface token now.

The Playwright test for the scrolling is a simple check that the last entry can be reached by keyboard.

summary: Deployed depot-shared column sets after Priya's review and found in the logs that the list route was slower for depots with many sets, so I added a limit and an index.
body:
Priya reviewed the two groups in the dropdown and asked for a thin divider between them and a lighter color for the owner name. Both were small changes, and she approved after the second look.

I deployed in the late afternoon. The first requests worked as expected, and managers started creating depot sets quickly.

After about an hour I checked the route timings in the logs. The list route had a median of 12 ms, but a few requests took 150 ms. They all belonged to the biggest depot, where users had saved many sets.

I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the union query with the data of that depot. The part for depot sets used the index on visibility, which is not selective, and filtered by depot_id afterwards. The index I created had the columns in the wrong order for this query.

I created a new index with depot_id first and visibility second, and dropped the old one after checking that nothing else used it. The query time for the biggest depot went from 140 ms to about 3 ms in staging with a copy of the data.

I also added a limit of 100 sets per depot in the response, with an order by name. A depot with more than 100 shared sets would be a sign of a problem anyway, and the limit protects the dropdown. The response includes a flag if the limit was reached, and the frontend shows a short note.

The migration for the index ran without locking problems, since I used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY. I deployed it in the evening and looked at the timings again: the slow requests are gone, with the highest at 9 ms.

Jonas was told that the feature is live. Open items are a cleanup of sets from deactivated users after 90 days, which I noted but did not build, and a short help text for the dropdown.

summary: Wrote the help text for the column sets dropdown and a short section for the Acme user guide, with screenshots in both themes.
body:
Jonas asked for a short explanation so the managers know what private and depot sets mean. I wrote a help text of three sentences that appears behind a question mark button in the dropdown.

The text explains that private sets are only visible to the owner, depot sets are visible to the colleagues in the depot, and that colleagues can copy but not change a set. It is a popover with proper focus handling, and Escape closes it.

For the user guide I wrote a section with the steps: choose columns, press Save, choose the visibility, set a default. I took screenshots in the light and dark theme, and cropped them to the dropdown.

Priya looked at the wording and changed 'visibility' to 'who can see this', which is clearer for dispatchers.

I also checked the German texts. The dashboard is used in German by most dispatchers, and I translated the popover and the buttons. One label, 'Depot sets', became 'Sets des Depots'.

The tests that check labels were updated for the new texts. Everything passed.

summary: Built the cleanup of column sets of deactivated users after 90 days and hooked it into the existing nightly job runner, with a dry run mode.
body:
The open item from the deploy was the cleanup of shared sets whose owners are gone. Last week's rule moves depot sets to a manager on deactivation, but private sets of deactivated users stay in the table forever.

I wrote a job that deletes private sets of users who were deactivated more than 90 days ago. It runs in the same job runner as the session cleanup, but at a different hour, so the two do not compete. I put it at 05:15, after the session cleanup at 04:30 has finished.

The job works in batches of 500 and logs the number of deleted rows per batch, in the same format as the session cleanup. That makes the logs easy to read together.

I added a dry run mode with an environment variable. In dry run, the job only logs how many rows it would delete. I ran it against a copy of the production data and it reported 37 sets from 9 users.

A test creates a deactivated user with an old and a recent deactivation date, and checks that only the old one's sets are deleted. Another test checks that depot sets already moved to a manager are never touched.

I did not enable the real mode yet. The plan is to run the dry run for a week, compare the numbers and then switch it on.

One thing I noticed while reading the user deactivation code: it does not end the sessions of the user in the same transaction. It does it afterwards, in a second call. If the second call fails, the user stays logged in. I added it to my list as a separate item, because it concerns the login and should be looked at with the user.

summary: Fixed the deactivation so that ending the user's sessions happens in the same transaction as the deactivation, with a test that forces the second step to fail.
body:
I looked at the item from the cleanup work. Deactivating a user set the flag first and then deleted the session rows in a second call. If that call failed, the user kept a valid session for up to 24 hours.

Since sessions are rows in Postgres, both steps can share one transaction. I moved the delete of the session rows into the deactivation function, inside the same transaction as the flag change.

The test makes the session delete throw an error and checks that the flag is not set afterwards. Before the change, the flag stayed set and the test failed.

I also checked the 'log out of all devices' function, which already used one transaction. Both now use the same helper to delete a user's sessions.

All tests passed. The change is small, but I will ask the user to look at it tomorrow because it affects who can log in.

summary: The user reviewed the deactivation change, then I investigated a report that the date picker lost the selected range after a browser back, and fixed it by moving the range into the URL.
body:
The user read the deactivation diff in the morning and approved it without changes. I deployed it before ten.

The next item came from a dispatcher through Jonas: after choosing a date range and opening a shipment, pressing the browser's back button showed the default range again. The shipments list was then wrong for what they had been looking at.

I reproduced it in the browser. The date picker kept its range in React state of the page component. On back, the page mounted again and used the default.

The filters of the table were already in the URL, as the export depends on that. The date range was the one filter that was not. I had assumed it was, since the export used it, but the export read it from a separate query parameter set only at the moment of export.

So the fix was to write the range into the URL when it changes, with from and to as ISO dates, and to read it from the URL on mount. The export now reads the same parameters, which removes the special case.

I used replace instead of push for the history entry while the user clicks through presets, so that the back button is not filled with every intermediate range. A custom range from the calendar uses push once, when the user confirms.

Invalid values in the URL are a risk. I added a parse step: if from or to is not a valid date, or from is after to, the default range is used and the URL is corrected. A test covers four bad inputs.

I updated the Playwright test: choose a range, open a shipment, go back, expect the same range in the picker. It passed in five runs.

Bookmarks with the old URLs have no range and still work, using the default.

One side effect is good: links copied between dispatchers now include the range, so they see the same table. I told Jonas, who liked that.

Next I will check the charts page, which has its own picker and probably the same problem.
