summary: Added a reactivation guard and a restore path for column sets after a manager asked why a returning colleague's saved sets were gone, and tested the cleanup edge cases.
body:
A manager at Acme asked Jonas why a colleague who came back after a long leave had no saved column sets. The cause was the cleanup job from the last weeks: the colleague had been deactivated for more than 90 days, so the job had removed the sets before the account was reactivated. That was the intended rule, but nobody at Acme had known it, so the surprise was understandable.

I first checked the production numbers. Of the 31 sets deleted in the first real run, 6 belonged to users who had been deactivated for a long time and 25 to accounts that had left Acme. I found no case where a set of an active user was removed, which confirmed that the reactivation check from the dry run works.

Then I looked at what could be done for the returning colleague. The sets are hard deleted, so I could not bring them back from the table. I asked the user whether to keep a soft delete. We agreed on a smaller step: the deletion now writes the set name and its column list into a small archive table, which is kept for another 180 days. A new admin route restores the archived sets of one user when the account is reactivated, and it skips any set whose name is already taken.

I wrote tests for four cases: restore after reactivation, a name that collides with a new set, a user with no archived sets, and an archive entry that has expired. The collision case adds the suffix "(restored)" to the name instead of failing. The first version of the test for expired entries was wrong because it relied on the clock of the test database, so I changed it to set the timestamps by hand.

I also added one line to the deactivation dialog on the settings page: "Saved column sets are deleted 90 days after deactivation." Priya has not seen the wording yet, so I left it for her review. The archive and the restore route are not deployed yet. Next I will deploy them after the user's review and tell Jonas how a restore is done for the colleague who asked.

summary: Looked at the first week of the dry run of the column set cleanup and found it would also delete sets of users who were reactivated, so added a check for the reactivation case.
body:
The dry run of the cleanup job has run for some nights now, and I compared the numbers in the logs with a query on the database. The job reports it would delete 37 sets, which matches the first count.

While checking which users are behind the sets, I found three that look strange. They were deactivated more than 90 days ago, but their accounts are active now. They were reactivated by Jonas when employees came back from leave.

The job selected by the deactivated_at column, which stays set after a reactivation. The reactivation function sets the active flag but does not clear the date. So the job would have deleted private sets of active users.

I fixed this in two places. The job now requires that the active flag is false as well as the old date. And the reactivation function clears deactivated_at, so the data stays consistent. For existing rows I wrote a migration that clears the date for users that are active now.

A test covers the case: a user deactivated 100 days ago and reactivated yesterday keeps the sets. It failed before the change.

I ran the dry run again on a copy of production data. The count dropped from 37 to 31 sets, and the users behind them are all really inactive.

The lesson is that the dry run was worth it. A real run would have deleted the sets of three active people, and restoring them would have meant going to a backup.

I will let the dry run go on for a few more nights and then ask the user to review the numbers before the real mode is turned on.

A smaller thing I noticed: the user list in the settings page shows a deactivated date for active users in the same way, which was confusing as well. With the migration it shows nothing for them now.

I also added the active flag check to the session cleanup tests, to make sure that job does not have a similar assumption. It does not, since it only looks at session expiry.

summary: Turned on the real mode of the column set cleanup after the user checked the dry run numbers, and the first run deleted 31 sets as predicted.
body:
The user looked at the dry run logs of the last nights and the query result, and agreed that the 31 sets belong to inactive users. We switched the environment variable to the real mode this morning.

I watched the first run at 05:15 in the logs of the job. It deleted 31 sets in one batch and finished in 40 ms. The number is the same as the dry run, which is what I wanted to see.

No errors appeared, and the session cleanup before it was not affected. I kept the dry run flag in the code, as a safety for later changes.

summary: Upgraded ECharts to the latest minor version and fixed a legend overflow change that broke the layout of the cost per kilometer chart on narrow screens.
body:
I upgraded ECharts to the newest minor version this afternoon, since the release notes mention fixes for large datasets and for the tooltip position.

The unit tests passed at once, but the visual check showed a problem. On narrow screens, the legend of the cost per kilometer chart now wrapped differently and overlapped the plot area. With five depots selected it covered the top of the lines.

The cause was a changed default for legend overflow handling. Before, the legend scrolled in one row, and now it wraps if the width is small. The chart has a fixed grid top margin, so wrapped rows ran into the plot.

I set the legend type to scroll explicitly, which restores the old behaviour, and the grid top margin stays as before. I also checked the charts page, where the legends are on the right side, and they were not affected.

I took screenshots of all charts in both themes at three widths and compared them to the screenshots from before the upgrade. Apart from the cost chart, there were no differences larger than a pixel of anti-aliasing.

The dashed average line for the cost chart still shows correctly, and the tooltips with currency formatting work.

The text summary and the table alternative for screen readers are separate from ECharts, and I checked that they still match the chart data.

I ran the whole Playwright suite, which passed, and deployed in the evening with a note in the notes of the release about the legend setting. The build size grew by 4 KB, which is fine.

summary: Checked the ECharts upgrade on the other charts after the legend fix and found the delivery time chart tooltip overlapping the legend on narrow screens, now fixed.
body:
After the cost per kilometer fix of this morning I opened every chart page at 360, 768 and 1280 px width. Only the delivery time chart had a problem: the tooltip now overlapped the legend because the new minor version changed the default confine behavior.

I set confine: true on the tooltip in the shared chart options file, so all charts get it. The cost chart and the shipments per depot chart looked the same as before. I also compared the dark theme, where the legend text color had not changed.

The Playwright screenshot tests for the three pages needed new baselines, since anti-aliasing differs slightly. I checked the diffs by eye before accepting them. Nothing else is open for the upgrade.

summary: Looked at the overnight logs after the ECharts upgrade: no client errors, and the session cleanup and view refresh ran normally.
body:
I read the logs of the night before starting work. The session cleanup ran at 04:30 and finished in under two minutes. The materialized view refresh ran concurrently without lock waits.

The client error reporting showed no new chart exceptions since the upgrade was deployed. One 401 burst appeared around 03:10, from a single IP, which looked like an old bookmarked session cookie being retried. The counter for cookies with no row stayed at 1.

Nothing to fix. I noted the 401 burst only so it can be compared if it comes back.

summary: Planned and built the first step of a scheduled report pause feature, so managers can stop a weekly report during holidays without deleting it.
body:
Jonas had asked twice that managers should be able to pause a scheduled report instead of deleting it and recreating it later. I wrote down what a pause means before coding: no mail is sent, the schedule and recipients stay, and the run history shows a skipped entry.

I added a paused_until nullable timestamp column to scheduled_reports with a migration. The scheduler query now skips rows where paused_until is in the future. A paused report with no end date is stored with a far future value, which I did not like, so I used a separate paused boolean as well.

The report run history table gets a new status skipped, with a badge and a text label, since the badges must not rely on color alone. I extended the status enum and the badge component.

Tests: a paused report is not picked up, a report whose pause ended is picked up, and a skipped run is written to the history exactly once per schedule slot. The last test caught a bug where the scheduler wrote a skipped entry on every poll, about every minute. I fixed it with a unique key on report id and slot time.

The UI is not done. The route to set and clear the pause works and is tested, but the button on the report list page comes next. I also still need to ask Jonas whether recipients should be told when a pause ends.

summary: Added the pause button and a date choice to the scheduled report list and checked it with the keyboard and a screen reader.
body:
The list page for scheduled reports got a pause menu per row: pause until a date, pause with no end date, and resume. It uses the same dropdown component as the column sets, so the keyboard behavior was already tested.

A paused row shows a text label Paused until followed by the date in the user's format, and the row has reduced contrast only as an extra hint. The screen reader announced the label correctly after I added aria-live to the row status.

The date input rejects dates in the past and dates more than one year ahead. I chose one year because a longer pause is more likely a forgotten report.

One problem: after resuming, the next run time column still showed the old value until a reload. I invalidated the list query after the mutation and it updated.

Open question for Jonas: should the owner get a mail when a pause ends? I did not build it.

summary: Reviewed the pause feature with Priya, who asked for a clearer label and a confirmation text, and deployed it after both changes.
body:
Priya looked at the pause menu on her phone and on desktop. She found the label Paused until too quiet next to the report name and asked for a small pill with an icon plus text. I changed it and kept the text in the pill so it works without the icon.

She also asked that resuming a report show a short confirmation, since nothing visible happened before except the label disappearing. I added a toast with the next run time.

The screen reader check found that the toast was announced twice. The cause was that both the toast container and the toast itself had role status, so I removed it from the container.

I ran the Vitest and Playwright suites, then deployed. In the first hour two reports were paused by managers and the scheduler logs showed the skipped entries once each. No errors.

summary: Jonas answered that owners want a mail when a pause ends, so I built the reminder with a rule not to send it for pauses shorter than three days.
body:
Jonas replied that a manager had already forgotten a paused report for two months, so a reminder is wanted. He also said a mail for a two day pause is noise.

I added a job that runs with the nightly job runner and finds reports whose paused_until ended in the last 24 hours and whose pause lasted at least three days. It sends a short mail through the existing digest code, with a link to the report page and a resume now note.

A reminder_sent_at column keeps the job from sending twice if it runs again. Pauses with no end date never get a reminder, because there is no end.

Tests cover the three day rule, the double run, and a user who was deactivated in the meantime, who gets no mail. The deactivated case matters because of the cleanup work of last week.

I ran the job against the staging data in dry run mode and it listed 2 reports. Real mode goes on with the next deploy.

summary: Deployed the pause reminder and confirmed the first run sent two mails with correct links and no duplicates.
body:
The reminder job went out with this morning's deploy. At the nightly run it found two reports whose pause had ended, both with pauses over three days.

I checked the sent mails in the mail provider log. Both were delivered, the links led to the right report page, and the reminder_sent_at column was set. The second job run in the logs found nothing, so there was no duplicate.

One of the recipients had a name with an umlaut, and the subject displayed correctly, which was the problem of the file name before. I had set the encoding explicitly this time.

I also added the reminder count to the failure digest summary so a silent failure would show up. Nothing else is open on pausing.

summary: Investigated a report that the settings page session list showed the same device twice and found that a refresh of the login created a second row.
body:
A manager wrote that her laptop appeared twice in the list of sessions on the settings page. I looked at the sessions table and found two rows with the same user agent and IP, created 4 seconds apart.

The cause was the SSO callback. When the browser followed the redirect and the page also called the session endpoint at once, both requests found no session and each created one. The session cookie of the second request won, so the first row was orphaned until the cleanup.

I reproduced it with a Playwright test that fires two requests in parallel after the callback. The fix is to create the session only in the callback and make the session endpoint read only. I also made the callback use an upsert keyed on a one time login id.

The orphaned rows are harmless and the cleanup will remove them. I wrote a one time query to count them: 17 in the last month. I did not delete them by hand.

summary: Fixed the duplicate session rows after the SSO callback and added a regression test, then the user reviewed and asked for a log line on the rare case.
body:
The fix from this morning is in: the session endpoint no longer creates sessions, and the SSO callback does it once with a one time login id in the state.

The parallel test now passes, and it failed before the change, which I checked by reverting the fix. I also ran the full login tests for password login, SSO login and log out of all devices.

The user reviewed the change. He asked what happens if the session endpoint is called with no cookie, since the frontend relied on it to create one in one old flow. I searched the code and found that flow was only the invite acceptance page. I changed that page to call the login route explicitly.

He also asked for a log line at info level when the callback finds an existing login id, because that means a double request happened. I added it with the user id and no other data.

I deployed in the afternoon. The log line appeared twice within an hour, so the double request happens in real use, and the fix did its work.

summary: Answered the user's question how many sessions a typical manager has: the median is 2 and the highest is 14, which is fine for the list page.
body:
The user asked whether the session list on the settings page needs paging. I queried the sessions table for active rows per user.

The median is 2, the 95th percentile is 5, and the highest is 14. That one belongs to a dispatcher who uses several shared desk computers and never logs out.

A list of 14 rows renders without trouble, but I noted that the list on a phone needs the cards layout, which it already has. No paging is needed now.

I suggested that the idle sessions older than 30 days are already removed by the cleanup, so the number should not grow. The user agreed to leave it.

summary: Wrote the plan for an export of the shipments table with the user's saved column set, and listed what blocks it because large exports are still slow.
body:
Managers asked that the CSV export use the column set that is currently selected. I wrote down the plan.

The export route takes a column set id, checks that the user may see it, and uses its columns in the same order. Cost columns stay hidden for dispatchers, as in the table.

The blocker is that large exports still build the whole file in memory and time out above roughly 200,000 rows. A change of columns does not make this worse, but promising the feature to managers with big depots would disappoint them.

I listed two ways to handle it: limit the feature for now, or solve the timeout first. I will ask the user which one he prefers tomorrow.

summary: Built the saved column set option for the CSV export, with permissions checks and tests, and left the large export timeout as a known limit.
body:
The user chose to build the feature now and treat the timeout separately. The export dialog now has a column set choice, with the current set as the default.

The export route accepts a columnSetId. It loads the set with the same union query used by the dropdown, so own sets and depot-shared sets are both allowed. A set from another depot returns 404, not 403, so ids are not revealed.

The columns are filtered against what the user's role may see. A shared set made by a manager with cost columns gives a dispatcher a file without them. The test from the shared sets work already covered the table, so I added the same case for the export.

Headers use the labels of the table, in the language of the user. The old export used database field names, which some managers had complained about. This is a visible change, so I added a note in the dialog.

I tried an export of 50,000 rows with 12 columns and it took 6 seconds. With 250,000 rows it hit the 30 second limit again. That is the known problem and I did not touch it.

I wrote a Playwright test that selects a set, exports, and compares the first line of the CSV with the set's labels. It passed.

Still to do: the dialog text for the timeout, and a check with Priya about the wording of the note.

summary: Priya reviewed the export dialog and changed the wording of the note about new column headers, and I added a visible warning for exports over 100,000 rows.
body:
Priya found the note about new headers too technical. She rewrote it as: The file now uses the same column names as the table. I used her text in German and English.

She also pointed out that the dialog gives no hint that a large export can fail. I added a count of rows that would be exported, from a cheap count query, and a warning text above 100,000 rows saying that the export may take a long time and may fail, with a suggestion to narrow the date range.

The count query uses the same filters as the table. For the largest depot it took 40 ms, so the dialog opens without delay.

The warning text is connected with aria-describedby to the export button, so screen reader users hear it before they start. I checked it with VoiceOver.

The tests pass. I will deploy after the user has looked at it.

summary: Deployed the export with column sets and the large export warning, and saw the first three exports run without errors.
body:
After the user approved the wording I deployed both changes together. The logs showed three exports in the first hour, all with a column set, between 2,000 and 18,000 rows. All finished in under 3 seconds.

One manager exported with a set that had been renamed minutes earlier, and the file used the new labels, as expected, since the labels come from the column definitions, not the set name.

The warning for large exports was shown once, to a manager with 130,000 rows. She narrowed the date range and exported 40,000 rows. That is what I hoped for.

I added a line to the user guide about the column set in the export. The slow export for very large tables is still open.

summary: Looked at the report builder v2 backlog with the user and sorted it into what stays small and what needs Jonas, and started with sorting inside saved sets.
body:
The user and I went through the backlog of the report builder v2. We found six items: sort order inside a column set, a set for a single chart, duplicate set names, export of the set definition, a set for a report mail, and a limit of sets per user.

We agreed that the sort order is small and useful, since managers always sort by delivery time after loading their set. The chart set and the report mail set need decisions of Jonas, so I wrote the questions for him.

I started with the sort order. The set table gets a sort_column and sort_direction. I used a check constraint that the sort column must be part of the set, which avoids a set that sorts by a hidden column.

The migration is simple and nullable, so old sets stay unchanged. The route validates the pair and the table applies it when a set is selected, unless the user has already clicked a header in this session.

Tests cover the constraint and the route. The frontend part follows.

summary: Finished the sort order for column sets in the table, including the rule that a manual header click wins, and tested it with the keyboard.
body:
The dropdown now shows the sort in the set's save dialog: a select for the column and a direction toggle. The default is no sort.

When a set is chosen, the table applies the sort once. If the user then clicks a header, that click wins and stays until a different set is chosen. I stored this in the URL state, like the date range, so a browser back keeps it.

The header sort buttons have aria-sort, and I checked that the attribute changes when a set applies its sort. It did.

One bug: removing a column from a set that sorted by it left a broken sort. The route now clears the sort when the column is removed and the dialog shows a message.

I ran the suites and everything passed. Deploy waits for the evening so that the quiet hours are used.

summary: Wrote a short note on what the report builder v2 work so far changed and which report builder items are still open, after the pause feature and the mobile cookie check.
body:
Today's session was a small housekeeping step between two larger pieces of work. The aim was to write down in one place what report builder v2 has delivered and what is still open, so that the next talk with Jonas does not start from memory. I went through the journal of the last weeks and through the open tickets in the repository.

Delivered so far: saved column sets with rename and default star, depot-shared sets, the visibility rule that keeps cost columns away from dispatchers, the CSV attachment for scheduled reports, the report run history table, and the pause for scheduled reports with its reminder mail. The cleanup of column sets of deactivated users also runs in real mode now, and the first run deleted 31 sets as predicted by the dry run.

Open items are fewer than I expected. Sorting inside saved sets is the next small step. Chart sets are wanted later, as Jonas said, so I did not plan them. Mail sets for scheduled reports were also still on the list, and I marked them as the next real piece of work.

I also noted the known limits. Large exports are still slow, and I wrote down that this is a separate topic from the column sets, so that nobody reads the slow exports as a bug of the new feature. The 5 MB limit for attachments stays, because one recipient domain is risky at 8 MB.

The note is a plain text file in the docs folder of the repository, about one screen long, with three short lists: done, open and needs Jonas. No code changed today and nothing was deployed. Next I will start with sorting inside saved sets, since it needs no answer from anyone.

summary: Investigated why the cookie with no row counter went up to 9 in one night and found that a mobile app user kept sending an old token-style header.
body:
When I opened the metrics this evening the counter for cookies with no row showed 9 for the last night, after being at 1 for days. I wanted to know whether the deploy had caused it.

First I compared the time of the events with deploys: they were between 01:00 and 03:00, with no deploy near. So the code change was unlikely.

Then I grouped the log lines by user agent. All 9 came from one user agent of the mobile app, and from two IP addresses. The requests carried a cookie value that looked like the old format, from the time when sessions were stored in memory, before the move to Postgres.

The app webview must have kept an old cookie jar. The cookie had no row because those sessions did not exist anymore, so the requests got a 401 and the app repeated the call about once every ten minutes.

I looked at the mobile app's behavior with the 401: it does not clear its cookie, and retries. That is a problem on their side. The API response is correct.

Still, I thought a simple server side help is possible. When a session cookie has no row, the response now includes a Set-Cookie that expires the cookie. Browsers then drop it, and the webview probably does too.

I wrote the change and a test that a request with an unknown cookie gets the expiring Set-Cookie header, and a valid cookie does not. I also confirmed that this does not affect the SSO callback.

I deployed it and will check the counter tomorrow. I also wrote a short note for the mobile agency, so they can clear the cookie jar on 401 if it does not work.

summary: The counter dropped back to 1 after the expiring cookie change, so the note to the mobile agency is only informational.
body:
I checked the counter this morning. Since the deploy it recorded one event, from a browser, not from the mobile app.

The two IP addresses of last night did not appear again, so the webview dropped the cookie on the first 401, as hoped.

I sent the note to the agency anyway, in a short version: their app keeps sending a stale cookie after a 401, and clearing it on a 401 would be cleaner. No reply is needed.

Nothing else is open.

summary: Jonas answered the column set questions: chart sets are wanted later, mail sets now, and a limit of 30 sets per user is fine.
body:
Jonas replied to my list. A set for a single chart is not important for now, he said, and he wants it only if managers ask. A set for a report mail is wanted, since managers keep different columns for the attached CSV.

He accepted a limit of 30 sets per user. He said nobody he knows has more than ten.

I planned the mail set: a scheduled report gets an optional column set id, the CSV attachment uses it, and the permissions of the recipient still decide which columns appear. That rule was agreed earlier for attachments, so it stays.

The limit is the easy part. It needs a count check in the create route and a clear message in the dropdown.

I will start with the limit today and the mail set tomorrow.

summary: Added the limit of 30 column sets per user with a clear message in the dropdown, and checked that existing users are not over it.
body:
First I counted existing sets per user: the highest is 17, so nobody is above the new limit.

The create and copy routes now count the user's sets in the same transaction and return 409 with a code set_limit_reached when it is 30. Two parallel creates at 29 could still pass the check, so I used a row lock on the user's row for the count. A test with parallel requests confirms that only one succeeds.

The dropdown shows the message Limit of 30 sets reached, delete one to save a new one, and the save button is disabled with an explanation linked by aria-describedby.

Copying a shared set counts as creating, so a user at the limit sees the message on the copy button too.

Tests pass. I will deploy together with the mail set.

summary: Built the column set choice for scheduled reports so the CSV attachment of a weekly mail uses the chosen set, still limited by each recipient's permissions.
body:
The scheduled_reports table got a nullable column_set_id with a foreign key that sets it to null when the set is deleted. The report form has a new select that lists the owner's sets and the depot-shared sets.

The attachment builder loads the set and intersects its columns with what the recipient may see, as agreed before. A recipient who is a dispatcher gets no cost columns, even when the owner is a manager and chose a set with costs.

If the set is deleted, the report falls back to the default columns, and the run history shows a note. I added the note text to the history table.

I tested three cases: owner set, shared set, and deleted set. The deleted set test showed that my first version crashed with a null set, which I fixed.

The attachment size rule of 5 MB is unchanged, and fewer columns can make more reports fit under it, which is a side benefit.

summary: Deployed the set limit and the report column sets, then the user reviewed and asked to show the columns used in the run history details.
body:
I deployed both changes this morning. The logs showed no errors, and the migration for scheduled_reports ran in under a second.

The user reviewed the change and liked the permission intersection, but he asked a question: when a manager sees a report mail with fewer columns than her set, how does she know why? He suggested putting the used columns in the run history details.

I added a details row in the history table that lists the columns that went into the attachment, and a line saying that some columns were left out because of the recipient's permissions, when that is the case. It does not say which columns, so cost columns are not revealed in the history to someone who may not see them.

I wrote tests that the history for a dispatcher never contains the names of cost columns. The test fails if a cost label appears in the response.

The details row is collapsed by default and uses a disclosure button, which I checked with the keyboard.

The first scheduled mail with a column set ran at noon. It had 8 columns, and the attachment size was 1.2 MB.

I will check the second run tomorrow.

summary: Checked the first report mails with column sets: 9 went out with the chosen columns and one fell back to default because its set had been deleted.
body:
I looked at the run history after the evening batch. Nine reports used a column set, and the attachments had the expected columns.

One report had lost its set, deleted by the owner after choosing it, and fell back to the default columns with the note in the history. That is the designed behavior, but it shows that an owner might not know. I wrote this down as a possible improvement: warn when deleting a set that is used by a report.

The sizes were smaller than before: 3 of the reports that sent the link text last week now fit under 5 MB.

No bounces, and the file names showed correctly.

summary: Added a warning when deleting a column set that scheduled reports use, listing the report names, after the fallback seen in last night's run.
body:
The delete button of a set now first asks the server which scheduled reports use it. A new route returns the report names the user may see, and the dialog lists them with the text that these reports will use the default columns afterwards.

I took care that the list contains only reports the user owns or is allowed to view. A shared set may be used by reports of other people, so those show only a count, such as 2 more reports of other users.

The user can still delete. I did not want to block deletes, because sets would become impossible to remove. The dialog has Delete anyway and Cancel, with focus on Cancel.

Tests: set with no reports, set with own report, set with reports of others, and the count. The last one first leaked a report name, because I used the wrong query, and the test caught it.

I checked the dialog in both themes and with a screen reader, which announced the list as a list.

The longer text made the dialog taller on small phones, so I allowed it to scroll. Priya will review the wording tomorrow.

I deployed it in the evening, and one manager opened the dialog twice and cancelled both times, which seems like the warning did something.

summary: Started the run history details for scheduled reports so each run shows the column set it used, including a note when the set was deleted and the default was used.
body:
The user asked yesterday evening to show the columns used in the run history details, so I started there. The run history table already stores the report id, the start time, the recipient count and the status. It did not store which columns went into the attachment.

I added a column called columns_snapshot to the report_runs table, a JSON array of header names written when the run builds the CSV. A snapshot is better than a link to the set, because sets can be edited or deleted afterwards and the history should show what was really sent. The migration is small and nullable, so old runs just show no columns.

In the details drawer I added a section called Columns used. It lists the headers in order, and for runs that fell back to the default it shows the line 'Default columns, the chosen set was deleted'. That is the case we saw in the report mails of two nights ago. The fallback flag comes from the same code path that picks the set, so there is no second place to get out of sync.

I also checked the permission rule: a manager who can see the run history sees the headers, but the headers are only names, not data, so there is no leak for columns a recipient may not see. Still, I filtered the snapshot to the report owner's permitted columns to be safe, and wrote a test for it.

Vitest has 6 new tests for the snapshot writing, the fallback and the permission filter. All pass locally. Playwright covers the drawer with one test that opens a run and reads the list.

What is left: the drawer for runs with more than 40 columns scrolls badly on narrow screens, and Priya should look at the wording of the fallback note. I did not deploy yet, because the migration should run in the quiet hours.

summary: Fixed the long column list in the run history drawer on narrow screens by capping its height and scrolling inside, and checked it with 60 columns.
body:
The drawer showed all columns in one long list, and with 60 columns the close button moved out of view on a phone-sized window. I gave the list a max height of 40 percent of the viewport with its own scroll, and the header of the drawer stays fixed.

I checked it at 360 and 768 pixels wide and with the keyboard. Tab reaches the list, arrow keys scroll it, and focus returns to the run row when the drawer closes. The screen reader reads the list as a list with a count, which I added through an aria-label.

I also shortened the long header names with an ellipsis and a title attribute with the full name. A Playwright test now opens a run with 60 columns and checks that the close button is visible. Priya will see the wording of the fallback note in the review tomorrow.

summary: Priya reviewed the run history drawer, asked for plainer wording of the fallback note and a count of columns, and both changes are in and deployed with the migration.
body:
Priya looked at the drawer this morning. She found the note 'Default columns, the chosen set was deleted' too technical for dispatchers and suggested 'The saved column set no longer existed, so the standard columns were used'. I changed it to her wording.

She also asked for a count next to the heading, so it reads 'Columns used (12)'. That was a small change in the component and the count is part of the aria-label as well.

The migration for columns_snapshot ran in the deploy at the start of the quiet window. It took under a second, since report_runs has only about 4,000 rows. The first scheduled run after the deploy wrote its snapshot correctly, and I opened the drawer for it to confirm.

Old runs show 'No column information for this run', which Priya accepted. I did not try to rebuild old snapshots, because the sets may have changed since, and a guess would be worse than a blank.

Nothing else is open for this change. The next thing in the report builder backlog is the question of chart sets, which Jonas said can wait.

summary: Investigated why the settings page session list was slow for one admin and found a missing index on the sessions table for the user id lookup, now added.
body:
An admin reported that the session list on the settings page took about three seconds to open. The admin looks at sessions of other users through the invite management, so the query runs often.

EXPLAIN showed a sequential scan over the sessions table, which now has about 38,000 rows. The query filters by user_id and orders by last_seen, and only the primary key and the expiry index existed. I added a composite index on (user_id, last_seen desc).

After the index, the query went from about 40 ms to under 1 ms in the database, and the page opened in 300 ms. The migration used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so that logins were not blocked.

The cleanup job for old sessions deletes by expiry, so it is unaffected. I also checked the write cost: the sessions table gets one update per login refresh, and the extra index is small. No further work is needed.

summary: Answered the user's question whether the report run snapshot adds much storage: about 400 bytes per run, so roughly 1.6 MB for all current runs, which is fine.
body:
The user asked whether storing the column snapshot in every run would grow the database in a bad way. I measured it instead of guessing.

For the 120 runs since the deploy, the average size of columns_snapshot was 410 bytes, with a maximum of 1.3 KB for a report with 48 columns. With about 4,000 runs in total, that is around 1.6 MB.

The growth rate matters more. We have 62 scheduled reports, and most are weekly, so about 70 runs a week and 3,600 a year. That adds roughly 1.5 MB a year, which is nothing for the Render Postgres plan.

I told the user that no cleanup of run history is needed for now. If daily reports become common, a retention of 12 months for the snapshot field could be added, but I would only do it with a real number to justify it. I wrote this down as a short note in the report builder backlog.

summary: Built the first step of chart column sets for Jonas's later wish: only a data model and a read-only list, behind a flag, because the real chart work is not approved yet.
body:
Jonas said earlier that chart sets are wanted later, not now. The user still wanted a safe first step so that the later work does not need a rewrite, so I kept this small and behind a feature flag called chart_sets.

What exists now is a table chart_sets with id, user_id, chart_key, name and a JSON field for the chosen series. It follows the same shape as the column sets table, including the limit of 30 per user, which I put in a shared helper. The helper was copied in two places before, so I moved it into one module.

The API has a GET for the list and nothing else. POST, PUT and DELETE are not built, on purpose. With the flag off, the route returns 404, so the mobile agency sees no change in the API.

I wrote 5 tests for the model and the permission rule that a user sees only their own sets. They pass. The shared limit helper has its own tests, and the column set tests still pass after the move.

What I did not do: no UI at all, and no decision about which charts get sets. ECharts series differ a lot, so the JSON shape for the cost per kilometer chart and the delivery time chart will need a real design with Priya.

I wrote down three open questions for Jonas: which charts first, whether sets are shared inside a team, and whether scheduled reports should embed chart sets. Nothing was deployed with the flag on.

summary: Reviewed the logs after the migration week and found the session cleanup job slowed from 2 to 9 seconds, caused by the new index, and tuned the batch size.
body:
While looking at the nightly logs I saw the session cleanup job took 9 seconds instead of its usual 2. The change started the night after the (user_id, last_seen) index was added.

The job deletes expired sessions in batches of 5,000. With the extra index, each delete has more index entries to update, but that alone should not cost 4x. I checked the logs and found the batch loop ran 8 times instead of 2, because the table had more expired rows than usual after a weekend with many mobile app logins.

So the index was only part of it. I ran the delete in a transaction on a copy of the data and measured: about 1.1 seconds per 5,000 rows with the index, 0.7 without. The rest of the time was the number of expired rows.

I changed the batch size to 2,000 and added a short pause of 100 ms between batches, so that the web requests during the job are not delayed. The total time is a bit longer, about 10 seconds, but the lock time per batch is under 300 ms and the API p95 during the job did not move.

I also added the number of deleted rows and the duration to the log line, which was missing. Tomorrow I will check that the job returns to a normal row count after a normal weekend. No change to the index was needed.

summary: Looked into why two weekly reports had the same recipient listed twice and found the recipients table lacked a unique constraint, which let a double click create duplicates.
body:
A manager got the same weekly report mail twice. At first I suspected the scheduler, since the pause reminder had been added recently, but the run history showed one run for that report.

The run had two rows in report_recipients for the same email address. The mail sender loops over recipients, so the manager got two copies. The edit dialog sends the recipient list on save, and a double click on Save sent two requests that both inserted the same address.

There was no unique constraint on (report_id, email). I first cleaned the data: a query found 7 duplicate pairs across 5 reports. I removed the extra rows by keeping the oldest id for each pair.

Then I added a unique index on (report_id, lower(email)) and changed the insert to ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. On the front end the Save button is disabled while the request runs, which was missing before.

Tests: a new Vitest test posts the same recipient twice and expects one row. A Playwright test double clicks Save and checks one mail address in the list.

The mail sender also deduplicates recipients by lower-cased address now, as a second line of defense for rows created by older code paths. I wrote to the user which five reports were affected, so Jonas can be told if a manager asks.

The fix is deployed. The next scheduled run will show whether any duplicates remain.

summary: Confirmed the recipient fix: the overnight reports went out with no duplicate mails, and the unique index rejected one duplicate insert that the log caught.
body:
Four weekly reports ran overnight. I checked the mail log against the recipients table and found one mail per address in every run, so no duplicates.

The log also showed one rejected insert from the new unique index. It came from an old tab that still had the old Save button, which let a double click go through. The ON CONFLICT clause handled it quietly, and the user saw the normal list after reload.

I looked at whether this needs a message to the user and decided not to add one. The result is what they wanted, one entry in the list. A message would only confuse them.

The five affected reports are clean now. I told the user, and the note for Jonas is ready if a manager asks. Nothing else is open on this.

summary: Planned and built the first part of a cost summary export for the costs page, with the same column set rules, and noted where the large export limit still applies.
body:
The user asked for a CSV export on the costs page, because managers copy the cost table into spreadsheets by hand. I read the costs page code first. It has a table of cost per route and per month, and a summary row on top that is computed in the browser.

The first question was which data the export should contain. The table is aggregated in the API by an SQL view that is refreshed every night, so an export can use the same view. That is better than the browser data, because the summary row would differ otherwise by rounding.

I built a new endpoint, GET /api/costs/export, that takes the month range and an optional route filter. It uses the same permission check as the costs page, which is manager role only. Dispatchers get 403, and there is a test for that.

The CSV has the columns route, month, distance, fuel cost, driver cost, other cost and cost per kilometer. The cost per kilometer is calculated in SQL with a nullif for zero distance, so empty routes show an empty field and not Infinity. That was a bug in the first version of the browser calculation too, which I noticed and noted for later.

The number format is the point where managers differ. Jonas said before that Acme uses a comma as decimal sign in their spreadsheets, so the export has a setting with a default taken from the user's locale. I used a semicolon as separator when the decimal sign is a comma, which is what the spreadsheet program expects.

The export button on the costs page uses the existing export dialog component, without the column set option for now. The costs table has fixed columns, so a set would not make sense here.

I wrote 9 tests: permissions, the number format both ways, the empty route case, the month range and the route filter. All pass.

The limit stays: this export builds the file in memory like the others, and the costs view is small, about 900 rows, so this is fine. If the costs data grows, it has the same timeout problem as the shipments export.

What is left is the review by the user and the wording check with Priya for the number format note.

summary: The user reviewed the costs export and asked to include a totals row and to name the file after the month range, both done and covered by tests.
body:
The user read the diff and had two requests. The first was a totals row at the end of the CSV, because managers want the sum without a formula. The second was a file name with the month range, like costs_2_to_4.csv, instead of costs.csv.

For the totals row I summed distance, fuel cost, driver cost and other cost in SQL with a UNION ALL. The cost per kilometer in the totals row is the total cost divided by the total distance, not the average of the row values. That is the correct number, and I added a comment in the code and a test with two routes of different lengths to show the difference.

There was a question whether a totals row in a CSV is a good idea, because spreadsheet users who sort the data would sort the totals row into the middle. The user decided to keep it and add a setting, 'Include totals row', which is on by default and can be turned off in the dialog. I built the checkbox with a label and a description for the screen reader.

The file name uses the first and last month of the range as numbers. I did not use month names, since the language of the user may differ and month names are hard to parse in file lists. The name comes from the Content-Disposition header, and I tested that special characters in the route filter do not end up in the name.

Tests: 5 new ones, 14 in total for the costs export. The Playwright test downloads a file and checks the last line.

I ran the full Vitest suite, and all 412 tests pass. The lint check found one unused import, which I removed.

I left the deployment for the afternoon so that Priya can look at the dialog first.

summary: Priya approved the costs export dialog with a small change to the totals row label, and the export is deployed and works for the first manager who tried it.
body:
Priya reviewed the dialog on the staging site. She liked the layout, and asked to change 'Include totals row' to 'Add a total line at the end', which is closer to how the dispatchers talk. I changed it in the label and in the test.

After her approval I deployed. The deploy took about four minutes on Render. I then ran an export myself for the last three months, and the file opened correctly in a spreadsheet with comma decimals.

One manager used the export in the evening, and the log shows a 200 with 6 ms of database time and a file of 31 KB. No errors in the client log.

For later: the cost per kilometer bug in the browser summary row is still open, and I noted it in the backlog.

summary: Fixed the cost per kilometer summary on the costs page, which showed Infinity for routes without distance, and aligned it with the SQL used in the export.
body:
While building the costs export I noticed that the summary row in the browser can show Infinity or NaN for routes with zero distance. I took this up now because the export and the page should show the same numbers.

First I reproduced it. A route that was created but had no delivered shipments in the month has distance 0 and a cost of a few euros for the standing fee. The browser divides cost by distance and shows Infinity. In the chart on the same page, ECharts drops the point silently, so the bug was only visible in the table.

The real problem was that the page calculated the ratio in two places. The table cell has its own formatter, and the summary row computes the sum in a reduce. The reduce used the average of the row ratios, which is wrong and differs from the total cost divided by the total distance. The export since yesterday uses the correct formula, so the page and the file disagreed by up to 4 percent on the test data.

I moved the ratio into the API. The view already has the columns, so the endpoint for the costs page now returns cost_per_km with the same nullif as the export, and the totals as one object. The browser only formats the values. That removed about 40 lines of calculation code from the page.

For the empty value I show a dash and not zero, because zero would look like a cheap route. The title attribute says 'No distance in this month' for the screen reader and for hover.

The chart uses the same field now, so a route without distance does not appear as a point. I checked the cost per kilometer chart on narrow screens too, since the legend fix of the ECharts upgrade is recent, and the layout is unchanged.

Tests: the API tests check the nullif and the totals formula with two routes, and a component test checks the dash. I updated the snapshot of the costs table, which changed in the summary row only.

After the change the page and the export show identical numbers for the last 12 months on a test account, which I compared with a script that diffs the two outputs. The difference is 0 for all 214 rows.

One caveat is that the older saved screenshots in the client documentation show the old numbers in the summary row. I told the user so that Jonas does not wonder.

summary: Planned the work to make session rows show the device name and last location in the settings page list, after managers said they could not tell their devices apart.
body:
Two managers wrote to Jonas that the session list on the settings page just shows 'Browser' and a time, so they cannot tell which device to log out. The user asked me to plan the improvement before building it.

I looked at what we store. The sessions table has the user agent string and the IP address, written at login. The list shows only a generic label from a small function that checks whether the string contains 'Mobile'.

The plan has three parts. The first is a better label parsed from the user agent: browser name and version, operating system, and for the mobile app the app name from its own header. The mobile agency's app sends a custom user agent, so that case is easy.

The second is a rough location from the IP address. I looked at options and do not want a third-party call at each page view. A local lookup database would work but adds a file to maintain, and for a dashboard of a logistics firm the city is not very useful anyway, since many dispatchers work from one office. I propose to show the IP address only, partly masked, like 84.12.x.x, and skip locations.

The third part is a name that the user can give to a session, like 'Office laptop'. This needs a new nullable column in sessions and a rename action on the list. It is the most helpful, but the most work.

Order of work: the label first, the rename second, the masked IP last. I estimate the first at half a day, the second at one day.

There is one risk: the user agent parser. I would use a small library, ua-parser-js, and I checked that it is already in the lockfile through another dependency, so no new package is added to the bundle on the server side.

Questions for the user: should the name be shown to admins who view other users' sessions, and should renaming be allowed for the SSO sessions? I assume yes for both and wrote this in the plan.

No code yet. The plan is in the repo notes folder.

summary: Built the readable device label for the session list using the user agent parser, with a special case for the mobile app, and tested 12 sample strings.
body:
I started with the first step of the plan. A new function describeSession in the server code takes the stored user agent and returns browser, version and operating system as a short label, like 'Chrome 124 on macOS'.

The parser is ua-parser-js, which was already in node_modules. I added it as a direct dependency in package.json so that it does not disappear when the other package changes.

For the mobile app the agency's user agent starts with 'AcmeDriver/' and a version. I return 'Driver app 2.3 on Android' or iOS in that case. I asked nothing from the agency, since the string was visible in our own logs.

If the string is empty or cannot be parsed, the label is 'Unknown device', not an error. This happens for old sessions created before the user agent was stored, of which there are 11 rows.

I wrote a test table with 12 real strings from the logs: three Chrome versions, Firefox, Safari on iPhone, Edge, the driver app on both systems, an old Internet Explorer string from a warehouse computer, an empty value and one bot. All 12 produce the expected label.

The API for the session list returns a label field now, and the page shows it as the main text with the time below it. The old generic label function is removed.

I checked the list with the keyboard and the screen reader. Each row reads the label, then the last seen time, then the button 'Log out this device'. I added the label to the button's accessible name, because 5 identical buttons were hard to tell apart.

Next is the rename step. I will need the migration for the name column, and I want to make sure the SSO sessions are covered.

summary: Added the session rename feature with a new name column and an inline edit on the settings page, and the user reviewed the permission rules for admins.
body:
This is the second step of the session list plan. I added a nullable column name to the sessions table with a migration, and a PATCH endpoint at /api/sessions/:id that sets it.

Permissions were the main design question. A user can rename only their own sessions. An admin can see the sessions of other users in the invite management, but cannot rename them, since the names are personal. The user reviewed this and agreed. The endpoint checks the session owner with the id from the current session, not from the request body, and there is a test that tries to rename another user's session and gets 404. I chose 404 over 403 so that the ids cannot be probed.

The name has a limit of 40 characters and is trimmed. Empty means reset to the automatic label. I strip control characters on the server, and React escapes the text on display, so there is no markup risk.

The SSO sessions work the same way. I checked this against the SSO callback fix of the last weeks, which creates a single row per login, so the rename sticks across refreshes of the login. A refresh updates last_seen on the same row and does not touch the name.

The front end has an inline edit: a pencil button next to the label turns the text into an input. Enter saves, Escape cancels, and focus goes back to the pencil button. The saved name appears in bold with the automatic label in a lighter style underneath, so the user still sees the browser.

For the screen reader I use a live region that announces 'Name saved' after saving. I tested this with VoiceOver in Safari. The error case, such as a name that is too long, shows a message tied to the input with aria-describedby.

Tests: 8 new Vitest tests for the endpoint, covering permissions, trimming, the limit and the reset. Playwright has one test that renames a session and reloads the page. All pass, and the whole suite runs in 3 minutes.

The user reviewed the code and asked for one change: a log line when a rename is rejected for permission reasons, because it may show somebody probing the API. I added it at info level without the name text.

The masked IP step is still left, and I will do it tomorrow. I also want to ask Priya about the look of the two-line row.

summary: Added the masked IP to the session list and had Priya review the two-line row, which led to a smaller type size for the automatic label and a deployed final version.
body:
The last step of the session list plan was the masked IP address. The stored IP can be IPv4 or IPv6, so I wrote a small function, maskIp. For IPv4 it keeps the first two parts and shows 84.12.x.x. For IPv6 it keeps the first two groups.

I considered whether masking is needed at all, since the user sees only their own sessions. The reason is the admin view, where an admin sees other users' sessions, and showing full addresses of employees is more than the admin needs. The user agreed and wanted masking for everyone to keep the code simple.

If the IP is behind the Render proxy, the stored value comes from the forwarded header. I checked that the login code reads the first entry of that header, and the stored values in the 40 newest rows look like real client addresses and not the proxy's. That was a worry, and it is fine.

Tests: 7 cases for maskIp, including IPv4 mapped IPv6, a missing value and a garbage string. Garbage returns an empty string and the row shows no address.

Priya reviewed the list on staging. She said the two-line row looked good but the automatic label under the custom name was too prominent and competed with the name. She asked for 85 percent of the text size and a gray that still passes the contrast ratio of 4.5. I checked the gray with the contrast tool, and the color she gave has 4.9 on the white background and 4.6 in the dark theme.

She also asked me to show 'This device' as a small badge for the current session. This was already in the list as plain text, and I changed it to a badge with the same text for the screen reader, so it is not read twice.

I changed the styles and ran the Playwright accessibility checks, which found no issues. Then I deployed in the evening.

After the deploy, I opened the settings page with my own test account and the list showed my three sessions with readable names and masked addresses. The mobile app session showed 'Driver app 2.3 on Android' as expected.

The session list plan is complete with this change. What remains from the idea is a possible notification when a login from a new device happens, which nobody asked for yet, so I only noted it in the backlog.

summary: Checked the logs after four quiet days: no errors from the session list change, and the cleanup job ran in about 10 seconds each night with the smaller batches.
body:
After the weekend I read the logs of the last four days. The session list endpoint had 212 requests, all 200, with a median of 9 ms.

The rename endpoint was called 14 times. Two were rejected for the length limit, and none for permissions, so no probing so far.

The cleanup job ran each night in 9 to 11 seconds with the batch size of 2,000, and the API p95 during the job stayed flat. The deleted row count was 600 to 1,900 a night, which looks normal.

The scheduled reports ran without duplicates, and the pause reminder sent one mail. I saw no client errors in the browser log service. I did not change anything.

summary: Investigated a manager's complaint that the shipments table export of a saved column set had a wrong order of columns, and found the set order was lost in the export for sets edited in a certain way.
body:
A manager said the CSV export of her saved column set had the columns in a different order from the table on screen. I first tried to reproduce it with a fresh set, and the export matched the table. So the problem needed a specific set.

I looked at her set in the database. The set stores two things: a list of visible column keys and a separate order array. When she edited the set, the dialog saved the visible keys in the order of the checkboxes, which is the order of the column definitions, but the order array only when the user dragged a column. A set that was changed by checkbox only had a stale order array that did not include the newly added columns.

The table on screen handles this with a fallback. Columns missing from the order array are appended at the end in their natural position, and the table also respects the manual header click sort rule from last week. The export code did not use that fallback. It used the order array and dropped keys it did not find, or put them first, depending on the code path. In her case two new columns appeared at the front.

The cleanest fix was to use the same function for both. I extracted resolveColumnOrder from the table code into a shared module that takes the visible keys and the order array and returns one list. The export, the report column sets and the table now call it. That also covers the scheduled report attachments, which had the same bug in theory. I checked the 10 report runs with sets since the report column sets were deployed and found that 2 of them had a different order from the screen. Their recipients got the columns in a slightly unexpected order, but all data was there.

I wrote tests for the shared function: an empty order, a partial order, an order with a key that no longer exists, and duplicates. The last case showed another small bug, where a duplicate key in the order array produced a duplicate column. The function removes duplicates now.

The saved snapshot of the run history stores the resolved list, so new runs show the true order. For the two old runs there is nothing to fix, since the snapshot did not exist.

I also wrote a data migration plan to clean stale order arrays, but decided it is not needed, since the shared function handles them on read. Fewer writes to the data are safer.

All 421 tests pass. I did not deploy yet. I want the user to look at the shared module first, since three features depend on it.

summary: The user reviewed the shared column order function, asked for one extra test with a hidden column, and the fix is deployed with a short mail to the affected manager.
body:
The user read the shared module and found the logic clear. They asked for one more test: a key that is in the order array but not in the visible list must not show up. I had that case only implicitly, so I added it as its own test with a clear name.

While writing it, I found the function already did the right thing, since it starts from the visible keys. The test now protects it from a later change.

I deployed after the review. The first scheduled report run after the deploy used the set order from the screen, which I checked by comparing the snapshot in the run history with the table.

The manager who reported it got an export in the right order when I tried her set. I wrote the user a short text for Jonas to forward to her, saying the order is fixed and that two earlier report mails had the columns in another order, with all data included.

summary: Started the accessibility check of the new session list and costs export dialog with a keyboard-only pass and found two focus problems, one fixed and one noted.
body:
The user asked for a keyboard-only pass over the pages changed in the last weeks, since the accessibility fixes are a running topic. I went through the session list, the rename edit, the costs export dialog and the run history drawer using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and Escape.

The session list and the rename edit worked as planned. Focus goes to the input when the pencil is pressed and back to the pencil after Enter or Escape.

In the costs export dialog I found the first problem. When the dialog opened, focus stayed on the Export button behind it, so the first Tab press went to something under the overlay. The dialog component should move focus to the first control. The shipments export dialog does this correctly, but the costs export used a variant with a prop that I did not set. I set autoFocusFirst and added a Playwright test that checks the active element after opening.

The second problem is in the run history drawer. After closing it with Escape, focus returns to the run row, which is right, but if the list was reloaded in the meantime by the auto refresh every 60 seconds, the row element is new and focus goes to the body. This is hard to fix well, since the list rerenders. A fix would be to store the run id and find the row again after the refresh, or to stop the refresh while the drawer is open.

I tried the second option first, because it is simpler, and it worked in my test. But it creates another problem, since the list gets stale when the drawer stays open. For a drawer opened for a minute this does not matter. I did not like deciding it alone, so I left the code as is and wrote the question into the notes for the user.

I also checked the dark theme for the focus ring on the new badge 'This device', and it is visible with a contrast of about 5. The reduced motion setting is respected by the drawer animation.

Tests: one new Playwright test for the dialog. The suite passes.

Open: the decision about the drawer focus after a refresh. I will ask tomorrow.

summary: The user chose to restore focus by run id in the history drawer, so I built it and tested the case where the row is gone after a refresh.
body:
The user answered the question about the drawer: no pause of the refresh, restore focus by id. That keeps the list fresh.

I stored the run id of the row that opened the drawer in a ref. When the drawer closes, the code looks for a row with that id with a data attribute, and focuses it. This is done in an effect after the list rendered, so the new element is found.

If the row no longer exists, for example because the run was removed by a retention rule or a filter changed, focus goes to the heading of the list, which has tabindex minus one. Otherwise focus would fall to the body, which is a problem for screen readers.

I wrote a Playwright test that opens a drawer, triggers a refresh by advancing the timer, closes it with Escape and checks the focused element. A second test removes the row from the mocked data first and checks the heading.

Both pass and the suite is green. I deployed it later with the other changes of the day.

summary: Looked at an error spike in the browser log of 14 errors from one dispatcher and found an outdated cached bundle after a deploy, which a reload fixes.
body:
The browser log service showed 14 errors in 20 minutes from one user, all 'Failed to fetch dynamically imported module'. The error comes up when the page tries to load a lazy chunk with a hashed file name that no longer exists after a new deploy.

The user had left a tab open since before the evening deploy, and then opened the costs page, which is a lazy route. The old index.js asked for a chunk of the old build. Render keeps only the files of the latest build.

This is a known issue with Vite and long-lived tabs. For now I added a handler on the router error: if the error message matches the dynamic import failure, the page reloads once, with a flag in sessionStorage so that it cannot loop. Otherwise the error is shown as before.

I tested it by building twice and loading the first build in the browser, then clicking to a lazy page. The page reloaded and showed the route. Without the flag, a missing chunk on a broken deploy would reload forever, so I tested that case too, and it showed the error page after one reload.

summary: Followed up on the browser error spike after the stale bundle and added a version check that shows a reload banner when the deployed build changes, so dispatchers stop running old code.
body:
The stale bundle that caused 14 errors for one dispatcher a few days ago kept bothering me, because a reload fixes it but nobody knows they need one. The dispatcher keeps a tab open all shift, so the page can run old code for many hours after a deploy. I looked at how the bundle is served on Render and found that index.html was cached for a short time by the browser, while the hashed chunk files of the old build were already gone after the deploy. That explains the error: the old page asked for a chunk name that no longer existed and got a 404.

I added a small file, version.json, that the build writes with the commit hash. The app fetches it every 5 minutes and when the tab becomes visible again, and compares the hash with the one compiled into the bundle. If they differ, a slim banner appears at the top that says a new version is available, with a Reload button. I chose a banner over an automatic reload because a dispatcher may be in the middle of editing a column set or filling in a report form, and a reload would lose that.

I also set the cache header of index.html and version.json to no-cache in the Render static settings, so the check cannot read a stale copy itself. The banner has role status so a screen reader announces it once, and it does not steal focus. I wrote a Vitest test for the comparison with three cases: same hash, different hash, and a failed fetch, where nothing is shown. A Playwright test serves two builds in turn and checks that the banner appears and that Reload loads the new chunk.

After the deploy I opened an old tab on purpose, deployed a trivial change, and saw the banner within the next check. Still open: if a chunk request fails before the next check, the user sees the error first, so I noted a follow-up to show the same banner on a failed dynamic import. I will ask the user if that is worth doing.

summary: Wrote up the open focus problem from the accessibility pass on the session list and costs export dialog, fixed the dialog's focus trap, and left the drawer case with a clear note.
body:
The keyboard pass from earlier today found two focus problems. One of them was in the costs export dialog: Tab moved out of the dialog into the page behind it, so a keyboard user could trigger the table underneath while the dialog was open. I replaced the hand-written handler with the shared modal wrapper that the settings page already uses, which traps focus and returns it to the button that opened the dialog.

I tested it by hand with Tab and Shift+Tab, and with Escape at every step. Then I added a Playwright test that opens the dialog, presses Tab 15 times and asserts that the active element is always inside the dialog. The test ran 5 times in a row without flaking.

The second problem is in the run history drawer for scheduled reports. After the drawer closes, focus falls back to the page body instead of the row that opened it. I did not fix it in this session because there are two ways to do it. One is to restore focus to the row by its index, and the other is to restore it by the run id. The index breaks when the list refreshes while the drawer is open, because the rows move.

I wrote this down in the todo list of the project with a short description of both options and the refresh case that decides between them. The user will pick one tomorrow. Nothing else changed in this session, and the fix for the dialog is on main but not yet deployed, because I want to bundle it with the drawer fix.

summary: Sent Jonas the three questions about monthly reports and got the answers: previous month in the file name, mail at 7 in the morning, and the day can be chosen.
body:
Sent the questions from yesterday's plan to Jonas first thing. He answered within half an hour, which made it easy to go on.

His answers: the mail should go out at 7 in the morning local time of the client, the file name should carry the previous month, and managers should be able to choose the day of the month, not only the first. He also said that a report on the 31st should go out on the last day of short months, which is exactly the rule from the scheduler function.

I wrote the answers into the notes next to the plan. The time of 7 in the morning means the scheduler needs the time zone of the client. Right now it uses the server time zone, which on Render is UTC. I checked and the weekly reports already convert with a fixed zone setting, so the monthly ones can use the same setting.

Next is the form on the reports page. I will add a schedule kind choice and a day of month field that only shows for monthly.

summary: Checked the new focus restore in the history drawer against a real list refresh and found that it also works when the drawer is opened from the keyboard on the last row.
body:
After yesterday's change I wanted to test a few more cases of the focus restore in the run history drawer. The first case was opening the drawer with Enter on the last row of a long list. Focus went back to that row after closing, and the row scrolled into view.

The second case was a refresh of the list while the drawer was open. A new run appeared at the top, so every row moved down by one. Because the restore works by run id, focus still went to the right row.

The third case was a run that had been removed by the cleanup of old runs. There the code falls back to the History heading of the page, which is what I intended. I added one test for that fallback.

I also checked it with a screen reader for about ten minutes. It announced the row name after closing the drawer, which is what we want. All 41 tests of the accessibility group pass. There is nothing open from the keyboard pass except the deploy.

summary: Deployed the accessibility fixes for the costs export dialog and the history drawer, and watched the browser log for focus related errors for an hour with nothing found.
body:
I deployed the focus trap of the costs export dialog and the focus restore of the run history drawer together. The build took about four minutes on Render and the version check banner did not show up for the dispatchers who were online, because the change does not alter any API.

The first check was the costs page, where I opened the export dialog with the keyboard on the production site and went through it with Tab. Focus stayed inside and returned to the button on close. The second check was the history drawer with a real scheduled report, which behaved like on my machine.

After that I watched the browser error log for an hour. There were 3 errors in total, all from one old Safari version and unrelated to focus. I noted them but did not act.

The user looked at the deployed result at noon and was happy with it. Priya will get a note that the focus ring on the dialog buttons is now visible for keyboard users only. The accessibility pass for the new session list is complete.

summary: Made monthly report mails use the previous month in the file name and in the data range, and checked it with a dry run on test data for the end and start of a month.
body:
The monthly mail now names its CSV after the previous month, as Jonas wanted, and the data range of the report is the full previous month, from the first at midnight to the last at the end of day in the client zone.

I reused the month range helper that I wrote for the costs export, which already gives a range and a label from a date. The only change was a parameter for the month offset. That kept the format of the names the same between the costs export and the report mails, which Priya liked in the costs review.

I ran a dry run for the edges: a run at 7 in the morning on the first of a month, and on the last day of a month with the clock set by the test. The ranges were right in both. The dry run mode prints the range, the file name and the number of rows, and sends nothing.

The recipient permission limits still apply to the columns, the same as in the weekly reports. I added one test to prove it for a monthly report with a set containing the cost column and a recipient who may not see costs. Still to do: a trial with real mail for the client test account.

summary: Planned and built the first step of a per-user default column set for the shipments table, so managers no longer pick their set after every login.
body:
Several managers told Jonas that they have to choose their saved column set again each time they open the shipments table. Jonas asked if the table could open with a favorite set. I planned a small first step this morning and built it right away.

The data model is one nullable column, default_column_set_id, on the user settings table. It points to a column set of that user. When the set is deleted, the column is set to null by the foreign key, so there is no dangling id. This also matches the warning for deletes that we added for scheduled reports, which I did not need to change.

On the API side, the settings endpoint now accepts and returns the field. It checks that the set belongs to the user, and answers 400 with a clear message if not. I wrote 6 tests for that, including the case of a set owned by another user.

In the UI, the column set dropdown got a small star button next to each set. Clicking it makes that set the default, and the star appears filled. Clicking it again removes the default. The table reads the default at load and applies it unless the URL already carries a set, so shared links keep working.

There was one question about permissions. A set may contain a column that the user can no longer see, for example after a role change. The existing function that filters columns by permission already runs after the set is applied, so the default behaves like any chosen set. I checked this with a dispatcher account and a set with the cost columns, and the cost columns did not show.

I also checked the first load speed. The extra read of the setting adds no query, because the settings are already loaded with the session. The table opened in the same time as before.

The Playwright test logs in, stars a set, reloads and checks the columns, then removes the star and checks the default again. It runs in 6 seconds. The migration is small and was run on a copy of the production data without problems.

What remains: the user has to review the change, and Priya should look at the star button, because it is a new icon in the dropdown. I did not deploy yet.

summary: The user reviewed the claim statement for scheduled reports and asked for the claim to include the instance id in the run row, which helps to read later logs.
body:
The user read the claim change and agreed with the idea of the single update statement. He had one request: write the id of the instance that claimed the run into the run row, so that a future double run, if it ever happens, can be traced without searching the logs of both instances.

I added a claimed by column to the run history table with the Render instance id, or a random id when running locally. The migration is a nullable text column, so old rows are untouched.
