He also asked whether the claim works when the next run time is computed after the mail, because I compute the next time at claim time. I explained that it does: the next time is computed from the planned time, not from the actual send time, so a late run does not shift the schedule. I added a test with a run claimed 20 minutes late to show the next run stays on the planned day.

All tests pass. Deploy is planned after lunch.

summary: Deployed the claim fix and monthly reports to production, with the flag still limited to the test account, and watched the first overlapping deploy for double runs.
body:
I deployed the claim change and the claimed by column. The migration took less than a second and the app came up on the new version without errors in the log.

The point of watching this deploy was the overlap of two instances, which caused the double mail. I set up a test report to run every 5 minutes for the test account, a temporary schedule only for this check, and started the deploy while it was due. In the run history there is exactly one row for that time, and the claimed by value is the id of the old instance, which shows the old one took it while the new one was starting.

Then I did a second deploy a few minutes later, at a due time again, and again one row. That gives me some trust, though two tries do not prove it. The 200-run loop test is the better proof.

I removed the temporary 5-minute report and its history rows afterwards. I kept one row as an example in the notes.

The monthly flag stays on only for the test account. Jonas will pick two managers to try it. Until then I want to check these points:
- that the 7 in the morning mail arrives at the right local time after the next change of the clock in the client zone;
- that the file name month is right on the first of the month;
- that the run history shows the column count for monthly runs.

The third point I checked right now: the run history drawer reads the snapshot of the run, so it works for monthly runs without a change. The first two need time, so I wrote them as reminders in the notes. I also updated the short help text on the reports page, which still said that reports are only weekly.

summary: Looked into why the shipments table was slow to open for managers with large date ranges and found the count query scanned all rows because the filter used a cast on the date column.
body:
Jonas passed on a complaint from a manager that the shipments table takes about 6 seconds to open when the date range is a full quarter. I looked at the request in the API log: the list query itself was 300 ms, but the count query for the paging took 5 seconds.

I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the count query on a copy of the data. It did a sequential scan over about 1.9 million rows. The reason was in the filter: the count used the cast of the pickup time to a date, while the list query compared the timestamp to a range. The index on the pickup time cannot be used with the cast.

The two queries were written at different times. The list was changed to the range form when I did the large table work, and the count was missed. I changed the count to the same range comparison, built from a shared function that makes the where clause, so they cannot drift apart again.

After the change the count takes 40 ms on the same data. I tested the edges of the range: the last day of the range must be included in full, so the upper bound is the start of the next day, exclusive. I compared the count with the number of rows the list returns over all pages for five random ranges, and the numbers matched.

I also searched the code for other uses of the cast on the pickup time and found one in the costs page summary, which reads a smaller table and is fast enough, so I left it and noted it.

I wrote a test for the where clause function with ranges that touch midnight and the clock change day of the client zone. The test found that on the change day the next day start was computed by adding 24 hours, which is wrong for a 23-hour day. I fixed that by building the next day from the calendar date in the client zone instead.

The change is ready and tests pass. I will deploy it in the afternoon with the next batch after the user has a look.

summary: The user reviewed the shared where clause for the shipments count and list, asked for the clock change test to also cover the autumn day, and it is deployed.
body:
The user read the where clause function and liked that count and list share it. He asked about the clock change test: it covered the spring day with 23 hours, and he wanted the autumn day with 25 hours too, because the same mistake could hide there.

I added the test. On that day the start of the next day computed from the calendar date is correct, and the old plus 24 hours code would have given one hour too early in the evening for the other direction. The test fails against the old code and passes with the new one, which I checked by running it against the old function once.

He also asked whether the filter for the status and the carrier uses the same function. It does not, since those are simple equals filters built in another place. I looked and they are fine for indexes, so I left them.

After his okay I deployed. I checked the first requests in the log after the deploy: the count query is now between 30 and 70 ms for the range of a quarter, and no errors appeared.

I also asked the manager through Jonas to try again. A short mail from Jonas confirmed that the table opens quickly now. One last point to keep in mind: the same cast pattern in the costs page summary. It is not slow today, but the table there will grow, so I put it in the list of small tasks.

summary: Investigated a dispatcher report of being logged out twice in one hour and found the session expiry was refreshed only on page loads, not on API calls from an open page.
body:
A dispatcher told Jonas that she was logged out twice within an hour while she was working with the shipments table open. Since the move to server-side sessions the idle timeout is 8 hours and the session should stay alive as long as she works, so this was surprising.

I looked for her sessions in Postgres. Both sessions ended by expiry, not by a manual logout and not by the cleanup job, which I could tell from the expires at value and from the fact that the cleanup only removes rows that were already expired for a day. The sessions were created at the start of her shift and ended about 8 hours later, which does not fit an hour of work... but then I found that the timestamps she meant were from two shifts, both ending at the 8 hour mark, so she was working with the table for the whole time.

The cause was in the session middleware config. The expiry is extended by the rolling option, but only when the response sets the cookie again. Our API routes for the table data return JSON and, because of a small optimization from earlier, they use a path of the cookie that skips setting it for requests with the header for background refresh. The table of the dispatcher polls every 30 seconds with that header. So her page was active all day and the session never got extended.

I checked the code where the header is handled. It was added to avoid sending a Set-Cookie header on every poll. The idea was fine for a bandwidth reason, but it had a side effect on the expiry. The session store updates the expires at column only on touch, and the touch happens in the same code path.

The fix: keep skipping the cookie header on polls, but call the touch of the session on the server, throttled to once per 10 minutes per session so we do not write to Postgres on every poll. The expires at in the row moves forward, and the cookie itself has an expiry far enough in the future with the max age of the idle timeout set at login... I had to decide this carefully: the cookie max age is renewed on regular page requests, which she also makes at least once every few hours, but if she never reloads, the cookie could run out before the row. So I set the cookie expiry to a longer value of 14 days and let the row be the real authority for the idle time.

I wrote tests with a fake clock: a session with polls every 30 seconds stays alive after 10 hours; a session without any request ends after 8 hours and 1 minute; the writes are at most 6 per hour for a polling session. All pass.

This touches the login, so I want the user to review it before deploying. I also noted that the setting page session list shows last active, which will now be more accurate for polling pages.

summary: After review, deployed the session touch fix for polling pages and checked that dispatchers' sessions now stay alive across a long shift with at most six writes per hour.
body:
The user reviewed the session touch change this morning. His main concern was the longer cookie expiry of 14 days: does it mean a stolen cookie works longer? I explained that the row in Postgres decides, and the cookie max age is only how long the browser keeps it. A session whose row has expired is refused whatever the cookie says. He accepted that but asked me to add a test that proves a cookie with a valid max age and an expired row gets a 401. I added it.

He also asked about the throttle: with 10 minutes, does the "last active" in the settings list become less exact? Yes, by up to 10 minutes. I think that is fine for a list that shows the time in a rough way, and the user agreed.

I deployed after lunch... no, before lunch, right after the review. Then I looked at the data. In Postgres I counted updates for the sessions of the dispatchers who had the table open: the write rate per session is about 6 per hour, as designed. The load on the sessions table is small: 31 active polling sessions give about 190 writes per hour in total.

There was one thing to check, the interaction with the cleanup job. The cleanup removes rows expired for more than a day, and a touch only moves expires at forward, so no conflict. The new index on the user id from the session list work is not affected, since the touch only updates the expires and last seen columns.

One session of a manager showed a different pattern: it ended at the 8 hour mark but he had no polling page, only a chart page which does not poll. That is expected, because a chart page does not call the API again until a user action. I asked Jonas to tell managers that the session ends after 8 hours of no action, which was the plan from the start.

I wrote the case into the notes for the session settings: idle timeout 8 hours, polling pages count as activity, throttle 10 minutes. The question of whether polling should really count as activity at all remains, because a forgotten open tab then keeps the session alive forever. That is a security trade-off for Jonas to decide, so I will bring it up with him tomorrow with a proposal: an absolute maximum of 24 hours after login for every session.

summary: Proposed an absolute session maximum of 24 hours to Jonas because polling pages now keep sessions alive, and he agreed with a warning one hour before the end.
body:
I wrote Jonas a short mail about the trade-off from yesterday: a dispatcher tab that polls keeps the session alive forever, which is good for work and bad for a forgotten tab on a shared computer. My proposal was an absolute maximum of 24 hours after login, after which the user must log in again.

He replied that dispatchers work in shifts of at most 10 hours, so 24 hours would never disturb them, and that the managers rarely stay longer than a day. He agreed, with one wish: a warning before the end so that no one loses a half filled form.

So the plan has two parts. The first is the absolute limit, a created at check in the session lookup, which is simple. The second is the warning: the API sends a header with the seconds left when less than an hour remains, and the front end shows a banner with a button to log in again in a new tab. I reused the reload banner from the stale bundle fix for the look.

I built the first part and its tests, with a clock-faked test at 23 hours 59 minutes and 24 hours 1 minute. The warning part is for tomorrow. Nothing is deployed yet.

summary: Built the one hour warning banner before the absolute session limit, using a response header with the seconds left and the same banner component as the reload notice.
body:
The API now adds a header with the seconds left in the session when less than an hour remains until the 24 hour limit. The front end reads that header in the fetch wrapper and shows a banner: the session ends in about N minutes, with a button that opens the login page in a new tab so that the open work stays.

I took care that the banner does not stack with the reload banner. If both apply, the reload notice wins, since a reload would make a new login anyway.

Tests: the header appears at 23 hours and not at 22; the banner text rounds the minutes up; the button has focus handling that follows the accessibility rules from the earlier check. Priya has not seen the wording yet, so I used a plain sentence and marked it for her review.

summary: Deployed the 24 hour session limit and the warning banner, and caught a bug where a login in the second tab did not clear the banner in the first tab.
body:
After the user's okay I deployed the absolute limit and the warning banner this evening, at a quiet time for dispatchers.

To test the whole flow I made a session in a test account with its created at set 23 hours and 5 minutes back. The banner showed up with 55 minutes left. I pressed the button, logged in again in the new tab, and went back to the first tab. The banner was still there. That was the bug.

The cause is simple. After a new login the browser has a new session cookie, so the first tab is also logged in with the new session, but the banner state lives in the page and only changes when the next response arrives without the header. The poll comes every 30 seconds on the table page, so it would vanish in time, but on a chart page without polling it would stay for good.

I made two changes. First, the banner listens to the storage event: the login page writes a small value to local storage after a successful login, and the other tabs clear the banner when they see it. The value holds only a timestamp, nothing secret. Second, when the user comes back to the tab, the visibility change triggers one cheap request to the session endpoint, which refreshes the state.

I tested both ways in Playwright with two pages in the same browser context: login in page two clears the banner in page one within a second. A test for the visibility check follows too.

The cheap request deserves a note. The session endpoint returns the user and the seconds left, and it does not touch the session row because of the throttle, so it adds no writes.

I also looked at what happens for a user who ignores the banner. At the limit the next request returns 401 with the reason session limit, and the front end shows the login page with the sentence that the session ended after 24 hours. Before the change it showed a general sign in message, which would have confused people, so I fixed the text as well.

The local storage value is deleted by the login page of the same tab after a few seconds, so it does not stay around. I checked the storage after a login and it was empty again.

Priya will look at the sentence of the banner tomorrow. Jonas gets a short note that managers are told about the 24 hour limit in the next newsletter of the client.

summary: Priya reviewed the session banner wording and asked for a calmer tone and a visible time, and then the log out of all devices screen got the same limit explanation.
body:
Priya looked at the banner and the login page message from the last deploy. Her points were three: the banner text sounded like an error, the number of minutes should be in a larger weight so that it is quickly readable, and the login page sentence should say that this is normal and for safety.

I changed the banner text to a calmer one, for example that the session ends in 40 minutes for your safety and that a new login keeps your open work. The minutes are bold now. The color changed from the warning red to the neutral info blue of the design system, and the red is kept for the last 5 minutes only.

The login page sentence says that sessions end after 24 hours for the safety of the account, and that signing in again takes a moment. I checked the length on a phone width and it fits in two lines.

While I was there I looked at the settings page, where the session list has an explanation line under the title. It said nothing about the limit. I added one sentence that each session ends after 8 hours without activity or 24 hours after login, whichever comes first. This helps managers understand why a device disappears from the list.

Tests were updated for the new text: three snapshot tests changed and one new test for the red state at 5 minutes. All pass.

The session list also shows when each session was created, so the 24 hour end can be calculated by the reader. I thought about adding an expires time per row, but Priya said the rows are already crowded after the device label and masked IP work, so I did not.

Next, a deploy is planned for the evening with the other small changes of the day. One more point for the notes: the Playwright test for two tabs takes 9 seconds, which is slow, and I will see if it can be shortened by seeding the session directly instead of logging in through the form.

summary: Shortened the two tab Playwright test from 9 to 3 seconds by seeding the session row directly, and checked the whole auth test group for the same slowness.
body:
The two tab banner test was the slowest in the auth group. It logged in through the form twice, and each login runs the password hash at the production cost setting, which is slow on purpose.

I added a test helper that inserts a session row for a given user with a chosen created at time and returns the cookie value, then sets that cookie in the browser context. The form login stays covered by its own test, which is the right place for it. The helper only exists in the test setup and checks the environment name, so it cannot be used in production code. I wrote that check first, and a unit test calls the helper with the production name and expects an error.

The two tab test now takes 3 seconds. To be sure it still tests the real behaviour, I broke the storage event code on purpose and saw the test fail, then restored it.

Then I ran the whole auth group of Playwright tests with timings. There are 14 tests that take 61 seconds together. Six of them log in through the form without needing to. I changed four of them to the helper. The other two test things that depend on the form, like the error text for a wrong password, so they stay.

The group now takes 31 seconds. A side effect is that the tests no longer depend on the hash cost, so they will not become slower if we raise it later.

One test was flaky in the first runs, the one for the logout of all devices, because it created two sessions with the helper in the same millisecond, and the list sorted by created at showed them in a random order. I gave the helper a small offset per call so the order is stable. I ran the group ten times in a row and all passed.

I also updated the short testing notes in the repository with the helper and its rule: use the form only when the form is what is tested.

Deploy of the banner wording changes went out at the same time, and the log was quiet after it.

summary: Answered Jonas's question how many managers and dispatchers were affected by the old session expiry bug, using the session table and the audit rows of last week.
body:
Jonas asked in a mail how many of his people had been hit by the early logout problem that I fixed this week, because he wanted to tell the client's operations lead. I went through the data to give him a number and not a guess.

The sessions table keeps rows for a day after expiry, and the older ones are removed by the cleanup job, so I could not look far back from the table alone. The audit log has a login row for each new session. I counted users who had two or more logins on the same day with the second login less than 9 hours after the first and with the first session having ended by expiry. That pattern would be the symptom: working through a shift and being asked to sign in again.

In the last 30 days, 11 different users showed the pattern at least once, all of them dispatchers with a polling table page. Four of them showed it on three or more days. No manager was in the list, which fits, since the manager pages do not poll... though they would not be affected by the bug in the same way.

I told Jonas that the numbers are an estimate. A user who logged out by hand and logged in again would not be in the list, because I only counted expiry endings, but a user who closed the browser and came back would not be affected either. The 11 users are therefore a floor for the people who were really bothered, and some of them may have had other reasons.

I also gave him the good news that since the deploy of the fix there has been no such second login. That covers only a few days, but the polling sessions have been stable.

He thanked me and said he would tell the operations lead that it was a known problem with a fix, and ask the four most affected dispatchers if they notice a change. I put the query into the notes so it can be run again after a week.

One question remains for later: whether the audit log should keep the reason for each session end. At the moment it must be guessed from the data, and a reason column would make questions like this one simple. I put it on the list but did not start it.

summary: Followed up on the session fix after a quiet stretch of days: no early logouts in the logs, the write rate on the sessions table is steady, and the cleanup job runs in about 10 seconds.
body:
This was the check I had put in the notes for after a few days of the session touch change. I ran the query for second logins within 9 hours after an expiry ending, and the result was empty for all days since the deploy.

The write rate on the sessions table is steady at about 190 to 210 updates per hour, as computed before. The table has about 340 rows, and the cleanup job runs in about 10 seconds each night, the same as before the change. I looked at the slow query log for the sessions table and found nothing above 50 ms.

The 24 hour limit showed up in the logs too: 3 sessions ended by the limit, all from users who had left a tab open overnight. For two of them the banner had been shown, which I saw in the front end event log, and the third was on a phone where the tab was in the background.

Jonas had asked the four most affected dispatchers. Three said it was fine and one had no opinion. No more work is needed here, so I closed the topic in the notes. The reason column for session ends stays on the list of small ideas.

summary: Checked the first monthly report mails sent to two real managers: both arrived at 7 in the morning with the previous month in the file name, and one asked for a second recipient.
body:
Jonas had picked two managers for the monthly reports, and today was the first of the month for their schedule, so the real test came. I looked at the run history early.

Both runs were claimed at 7:00 with a different claimed by value than the weekly runs of last night, which is fine since the instances changed in a deploy. Both mails were sent within 12 seconds. The file names carried the previous month label, and the row counts were 8,412 and 3,977, in line with what the shipments table shows for that month.

I opened the attachments. The column sets were applied in the right order, and the recipient permission limit worked for the manager who has no cost permission: the cost column was missing in his file, as it should be.

One of them wrote to Jonas that he would like a colleague to get the same mail. Adding a recipient is possible in the form today, so Jonas told him how. There is no change needed in the code. I noted that this is the second request of its kind, and that a short help text near the recipients field could save the question, so I added it as a small task.

The run history drawer shows the column count and the set name for both runs. The flag can now go on for all managers once Jonas has told them, which he plans for next week.

summary: Looked into a manager's report that the default column set star was lost after a rename and found the rename endpoint replaced the whole set row, so the reference was fine but the UI cache was stale.
body:
A manager wrote to Jonas that the star on her favorite set disappeared after she renamed the set. I first feared that the rename removed the default in the database.

I reproduced it on my machine. After the rename, the database still had the right default_column_set_id, and a reload showed the star again. So the data was correct and only the screen was wrong.

The cause was in the client. The rename updated the list of sets in the cache with the new object from the API, but the star is drawn from the user settings, which were cached under a different key. The settings kept the old set name and a stale flag, and the star component compared names instead of ids. After the rename the names no longer matched.

I changed the comparison to use the id, which is the right thing anyway. I also made the rename invalidate the settings key, so both caches agree.

I added a test for the rename case. It stars a set, renames it and expects the star to be still filled. It failed before the change and passes now.

The fix is small and on main. I will deploy it together with the review of the star feature.

summary: Fixed the stale column set star after a rename by merging the response into the client cache, and added a regression test for rename followed by reload.
body:
Slot 21 found that the rename endpoint replaced the whole set row, so the default reference in the database was fine but the UI cache showed the old state. Today I fixed it on both sides. The rename endpoint now returns the full updated set including the default flag, and the client merges that response into the cached list instead of invalidating only the single item.

The first attempt was to refetch the list after every rename. It worked, but it made the dropdown flicker and added a request on a slow connection, so I dropped it. The merge keeps the star in place and needs no extra request.

I also looked at the other mutations on column sets: delete, duplicate and reorder. Delete already cleared the default, and duplicate never copies the flag, which is intended. Reorder had the same cache habit as rename, so it got the same merge.

Tests: one Vitest case for the cache merge, and one Playwright case that sets a default, renames the set, checks the star, reloads and checks it again. All 41 tests of the column set group passed in about 20 seconds.

The user reviewed the diff this afternoon and asked for the flag to be part of the response type so that nobody can leave it out later. That is done in the shared types file. The fix is deployed, and I will write to the manager who reported it. Next is a check of the logs tomorrow morning for any rename errors.

summary: Added a second recipient to a monthly report for the manager who asked, and found the recipient limit check counted the owner, so two recipients were wrongly refused at the limit.
body:
The manager whose first monthly mail arrived on time asked for a second recipient, so I started with the report settings form. Adding a recipient in the UI failed with the message 'Recipient limit reached' even though the report had only one address.

I reproduced it on the test account with a monthly report and one recipient. The API returned 409 from the recipients route, and the log showed a count of 2 against a limit of 2. The count query included the owner row, which the weekly reports also have, but weekly reports are usually created with the owner as the only entry, so nobody had noticed.

The limit is meant to be 5 external recipients, as Jonas agreed some weeks ago. The check in recipients.ts compared the number of all rows with 5 minus one, a leftover from an early version in which the owner was stored separately. That meant a report could hold only 4 addresses in total, and in some cases fewer, depending on how it was created.

I changed the check to count only rows where is_owner is false and to compare with 5. I also moved the check into one function that both the create route and the CSV import of recipients use, since the import had its own copy with the same mistake. The unique index from the duplicate recipient fix still protects against double clicks, and I confirmed that a duplicate insert returns the same clear message as before.

I wrote four Vitest cases: the owner only, five external recipients accepted, a sixth refused, and the import of a list that would pass the limit by one. All four pass, and the old test that expected the wrong limit was corrected.

I then checked production data with a read-only query. Two reports had been stopped at 4 addresses, and neither owner had complained. I did not change their rows.

The fix is not deployed yet. The user should review the shared function first, then I will deploy and add the second address for the manager. After that I will send a short mail to the manager to say it works.

Still open is the wording of the limit message, which says 'Recipient limit reached' without naming the number. I noted this for Priya to look at in the next review.

summary: Fixed the recipient limit check for monthly reports so the owner no longer counts, and two recipients are accepted at the limit, with tests for the edge.
body:
Yesterday's change for the manager who asked for a second recipient showed that the limit check in the report scheduler counted the owner as a recipient. With a limit of three, a report with an owner and two extra recipients was refused at the second one. I read the validation in server/reports/recipients.ts and found it compared the length of the merged list, owner included, against the limit.

The limit was meant for extra recipients only, as Jonas confirmed when we set it. I changed the check to count the extra addresses and to ignore the owner, and also to ignore duplicates, because the same address added twice was counted twice. The error message now says how many extra recipients are allowed instead of a bare number.

I added four Vitest cases: owner only, owner plus the limit, owner plus one over the limit, and a duplicate of the owner address. The last one first failed, because the owner address typed in a different case was seen as a new recipient. I lowercased addresses before the comparison and the case passed.

I also checked the UI form. It showed a counter of 'x of 3' that used the same wrong count, so it said 3 of 3 when only two extras were added. I fixed it to use the shared function from the server package so both agree.

Then I ran the whole reports test group, 58 tests, all green. A dry run on test data with three recipients produced three mails in the log. Nothing is deployed yet. The manager's report has two recipients set by hand in the database, and I will leave those rows alone. Next is a review by the user and a deploy this afternoon.

summary: The user reviewed the recipient limit fix, asked for the owner check to ignore case in the UI too, and the change went to production with a note to the manager.
body:
The user read the diff of the recipient limit fix this afternoon. The logic was fine for him, but he saw that the UI form still compared addresses with case, so a typed owner address in capitals would pass the form and only be caught by the server. He asked for the shared function to be used there as well.

I moved the normalizing into the shared helper and used it in the form's validation. The form now shows the message 'This is the owner address' at once. I added a component test for it.

After that I ran the unit tests and the Playwright test that adds a recipient, both green. The deploy to Render took about four minutes. I then created a test report with the owner and two extras on the test account and watched the log. The scheduler accepted it and the dry run showed the right number of mails.

I wrote a short mail text for the manager that says the second recipient works now and that the owner does not count toward the limit. The user sent it himself. One point stays open: the limit of three is fixed in code, and Jonas may want it per client later. I noted that in the backlog file and did not change it.

summary: Checked the logs after the recipient fix and found the second recipient mails went out at 7 in the morning with no refused saves and no new errors.
body:
This morning I looked at the scheduler log of the 7 o'clock run. The manager's report went to both addresses, and the mail provider showed both as delivered. No save of a recipient list was refused since the deploy yesterday evening.

I also searched the audit rows for the validation error code. There were zero hits, where the week before there had been two. The test account report with three recipients ran as well.

The browser log had no new errors from the report form. I found nothing to change and closed the topic. The recipient limit stays in code for now.

summary: Built the second step of the per-user default column set, a settings page entry to choose or clear the default, and handled sets that were deleted after being chosen.
body:
The first step of the default column set stored a default set id on the user, and the table applied it after login. There was no place to change it except the star in the table toolbar. Today I added an entry on the settings page: a select with the saved sets of the user and an option 'No default'.

The harder part was the deleted set. If a manager deleted the set that was their default, the user row still pointed to it. The table then asked for a set that did not exist and showed an error toast. I looked at three ways. A foreign key with on delete set null was the cleanest and needed one migration. The second was to check in code, which would leave old bad rows. The third was a cleanup on delete only. I chose the foreign key and wrote migration 0047, which first nulls all dangling ids and then adds the constraint.

The first run of the migration on a copy of the production data nulled 3 rows. That matched what I expected, because three managers had deleted sets in the past weeks. The migration took under a second.

On the client, the select reads the sets from the same query cache as the table toolbar. After the lesson of the stale star last week, I made the mutation update that cache by merging the response instead of invalidating it. I tested rename, delete and clear in that order with a reload after each.

I wrote Vitest tests for the endpoint: set default, clear default, set a default of another user's set, which must return 403, and delete of a default set. The third case first returned 200, because the endpoint only checked that the set existed. I added the owner check, and the test passed. Shared sets, which belong to a team, may be chosen by any member, so the check allows those too.

A Playwright test now logs in as a manager with a default and checks that the columns are in the saved order at once. It ran in 6 seconds. Left to do: the wording of the settings entry, which I will show Priya, and a deploy behind the existing flag.

summary: Priya's review of the new default column set entry led to a clearer label and a hint, and the feature was deployed to the managers' flag group.
body:
I sent Priya a screenshot of the settings entry. She replied within the hour with three points. The label 'Default set' was unclear, because managers think of 'views', so it should say 'Column set shown after login'. The 'No default' option should be written as 'All standard columns'. And a short hint was needed under the select.

I changed the labels and added the hint: 'You can change this at any time with the star in the table.' Priya also asked that the select show the set name and the number of columns in grey. I added that with the count taken from the set rows, and it needed no new query.

On the keyboard pass, the select worked with arrow keys and the label was read by the screen reader with the hint through aria-describedby. I tested that with VoiceOver for a minute and it read both in the right order.

Then I deployed. The flag for the default column set was set for the group of managers, not for dispatchers, since only managers use saved sets. The deploy took four minutes, and I opened the page with a manager test account and set a default, reloaded and saw the right columns.

I watched the log for 30 minutes. One 404 appeared for a set id that a manager had deleted in another tab. It was handled by the new null logic and the table fell back to standard columns, which is what I wanted. I noted a possible small improvement, a toast that says 'Your default set was removed', but it can wait.

The next step is to tell Jonas that the feature is live for managers, and to look at the use after a few days.

summary: Found why the scheduled report list was slow for managers with many runs, a missing index on the runs table for owner and start time, and added it.
body:
A manager told Jonas that the page with scheduled reports took several seconds to open. I opened the page with his account on a copy of production data and saw the API call for the run history took 2.8 seconds. He has about 9,000 runs, since one report ran every hour in the early weeks of the feature.

I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query. It filtered by owner id and ordered by started_at descending with a limit of 50, and the plan showed a sequential scan with a sort of all his rows. There was an index on report id alone, which the planner did not use for this query.

I added a composite index on (owner_id, started_at desc). With it the same query took 4 ms. I created it with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in migration 0048, so that writes by the scheduler would not block. The table has about 400,000 rows and the build took 11 seconds on the copy.

There was a second finding. The page also requested a count of all runs for the pager, which scanned the whole owner range, 120 ms for the large account. The user had said before that the pager is rarely used, so I changed the count to be capped at 1,000 and the UI shows '1000+'. This keeps the count cheap.

I wrote a test which inserts 2,000 runs and checks that the list returns the newest 50 in the right order and the capped count. I also checked that the hourly runs are not needed in the history after a month, and noted a retention job as an idea. Jonas should decide how long the history should stay, so I wrote a question for him.

I have not deployed yet. The migration is safe to run first, and the code change follows after the review.

summary: Deployed the runs index and the capped count, and the scheduled reports page for the large account now opens in under 300 ms instead of 2.8 seconds.
body:
After the user's review, with only a small comment about the name of the capped constant, I deployed the migration and then the code. The index build on production took 14 seconds and the scheduler kept running during it, with no lock waits in the log.

I opened the page with the large account of the manager. The history call took 9 ms in the server log and the page was ready in about 280 ms in the browser. The count shows '1000+' for him, as planned.

I also checked two other accounts with fewer runs. Both showed the exact count and looked the same as before. The Playwright test for the reports page passed in the pipeline.

I sent Jonas the retention question: should run history older than 90 days be deleted, or kept for the audit? I told him that for now nothing is deleted and the page is fast either way. The monitoring of the slow query log showed no entries for this query since the deploy.

summary: Investigated a failed export of a costs file for one manager and found a currency column formatted with the browser locale, giving a comma where the file needed a dot.
body:
A manager at Acme sent Jonas a costs export that his accounting tool refused to import. Jonas forwarded the file. I opened it and saw that the amounts looked like '1.234,50' in some rows and '1234.50' in others, which is a mix.

I looked at the export code of the costs page. The CSV is built on the client for small tables and on the server for large ones, and the two paths differ. The client path used toLocaleString with the browser locale for the amount column. The server path wrote a plain number with a dot. The manager's browser was set to German, so his export of a small range used commas, and he had made the range large the day before, which gave dots. That explains why the same report had different formats.

The import of his accounting tool wants a dot as decimal separator and no thousands separator. I checked the first version of the export spec from Jonas, and it says the same: plain numbers, a dot, two decimals. So the client path was wrong, and it had been wrong since the costs export was built.

I wrote one function, formatAmount, in the shared package. It uses toFixed(2) on the number of cents divided by 100 with integer math to avoid float errors, and both paths call it now. I added tests with values like 0, 0.1, 1234.5, 1e6 and negative credits, where the credits had been written with a trailing minus in the client path. The shared function writes a leading minus.

The tests found one more thing. The date column in the client path also used the locale, with 'dd.mm.yyyy' for the German browser. The spec says ISO dates. I replaced it with the same ISO formatter that the server uses.

I compared the output of the old and new client paths on 200 rows of test data. Only the amounts with a thousands separator, credits and dates differed, as expected.

Large exports are still slow and can time out, but that is a separate topic and I did not touch it. I will deploy after the user has looked at the diff, and Jonas should tell the manager to export again.

summary: The user reviewed the shared amount formatter, asked for a test with a very large amount, and the costs export fix is deployed with a note for the manager.
body:
The user looked at the formatAmount change tonight. He liked that both paths use one function and asked what happens at amounts above the safe integer range. For cents, that is about 90 trillion in euro, which is far above any real shipment cost, but he wanted the behavior to be defined.

I added a guard: if the amount in cents is not a safe integer, the function throws an error with the value in the message, and the export shows a clear error instead of a wrong file. I wrote a test for it. I also added a test for a null amount, which writes an empty field, because some old rows have no cost.

He also asked whether the totals row of the costs page used the same function. It did not, it summed floats and formatted them with the locale on screen. This is only for display and the spec does not require the dot there, so I left the screen as it was. I added a comment on this in the code so that nobody changes it by mistake.

I ran all tests, 214 in Vitest and the costs export Playwright test, and everything passed. The deploy followed at about 21:30. After the deploy I exported the same range as the manager with the browser set to German, once small and once large, and diffed the files. They were identical apart from the row count.

I wrote a short text for the manager, which the user will send. It says the file now always uses a dot and ISO dates, and that old files should be exported again.

One thing remains: other users might have imported the comma files before, and their tools may have adapted to them. Jonas should ask if anybody did, since the change could break such a setup.

summary: Answered Jonas's question whether anybody imports the costs export, using the audit rows of exports by user, and found only three managers exported costs files in the last month.
body:
Jonas asked whether the format change of the costs export could surprise many people. I searched the audit rows for export events of the costs page over the last 30 days. There were 41 exports from three managers. Two of them exported only once a month, at month end. The third exported weekly.

Of the 41, 29 came from the server path, which always had the dot. Only 12 came from the client path with the browser locale. Those were from two managers. One of them was the one who had complained. I checked the browser language only through the user agent string in the audit rows, and both managers use German browsers.

So at most one other manager might have adapted to the comma format. I wrote this to Jonas with the numbers and suggested he asks that person one question. He said he would call him in the morning. I did not change anything in the code.

summary: Jonas reported that the second manager does not import the costs file at all and only reads it in a spreadsheet, so the format change needs no further step.
body:
Jonas called the second manager who had used the client path. He opens the files in a spreadsheet, and the new format with a dot worked for him after he changed one import setting once. No accounting tool is involved.

Jonas wrote back this evening that the topic is closed. I noted it in the costs export section of the project notes, with the decision that the format is plain numbers, a dot and ISO dates for both paths. No code change was needed.

summary: Noticed that the new toast for a removed default column set was still missing and added a short message with a test, since the fallback to standard columns was silent.
body:
When I watched the log after the default column set launch, one manager had his default removed in another tab and the table fell back to the standard columns without any sign. That is correct but confusing, so I built the small toast I had noted.

The table now checks whether the default set id of the user is null after the server cleared it, and if the previous value in the client cache was a set, it shows 'Your default column set was removed. Showing standard columns.' The toast uses the same component as the reload banner text style, and it is read by screen readers through a polite live region.

I wrote a component test which deletes the set and checks the toast once and not on the second render. The first version showed the toast twice because of the strict mode double effect in development, so I moved the message trigger into the mutation callback. The test passed after that, and I ran the Playwright test for the settings page as well. The change is small and I will deploy it with the next batch.

summary: Looked at why some scheduled reports ran two minutes late and found the scheduler tick waited for the previous tick's slow report to finish before starting the next one.
body:
A manager noticed that his 7 o'clock report arrived at 7:02 on two mornings. I looked at the scheduler log. The tick runs every minute and handles the due reports one after another in a loop. A large report from another account started at 7:00 and took 110 seconds, and the manager's report came after it in the loop.

The claim of runs with the instance id works as intended, so there was no double run. The delay came only from the sequential loop. I changed the loop to start due reports with a small concurrency of three, using a simple pool in the code, without a new library. Each report still claims its row before it starts.

I tested with a fake report that sleeps for 100 seconds and two quick ones. Before the change the quick ones started after 100 seconds, and after it they started within the same tick. The pool also catches errors per report, so one failing report does not stop the others, which was already the case through a try block.

I checked the database load. Three reports at once use at most three connections of the pool of ten, which is fine. I will deploy after review and then watch the 7 o'clock run.

summary: The user reviewed the scheduler concurrency change, asked for a cap on connection use during the 7 o'clock peak, and it is deployed with a log line for late starts.
body:
The user asked what happens if many reports are due at 7:00, since most managers choose that time. In production there are about 25 reports due at that minute. With a pool of three, the last ones would still start later, though only by a few seconds in most cases.

He wanted to be sure that the report queries do not take all connections from the API during the peak. I checked the pool settings: the API has ten connections and the scheduler shares them. I added a separate small pool of three connections for the scheduler, so that the dashboard users are not affected. This needed a second pg Pool in the scheduler module and a config value.

I also added a log line that records the delay between the due time and the actual start, with the report id. It makes late starts visible without searching for them. Nobody should have to guess again.

Tests: the pool test with the fake slow report passed, and a new test checks that the scheduler pool is used and the API pool is not. I deployed at about 16:30 and the next real check is the run at 7 tomorrow. I wrote down to look at the delay values then.

summary: Checked the 7 o'clock report run after the scheduler change: all 25 reports started within 4 seconds of the due time and the manager's mail arrived at 7:00.
body:
I read the scheduler log for the morning run. The new delay line showed 25 reports with the largest start delay of 3.8 seconds, and the median was 0.4 seconds. The large report from the other account again took about 105 seconds, but nothing waited for it.

The manager's mail arrived at 7:00 according to the provider's log. The scheduler pool used at most three connections, and the API's own pool showed no waits during that minute.

I saw no errors and no double runs. I closed the topic and left the delay log line in place, as it costs nothing.

summary: Started the work on the slow large CSV exports by measuring where the time goes, and found most of the 40 seconds is spent building the string in memory, without a fix yet.
body:
Large exports of the shipments table remain slow, and Jonas mentioned again that dispatchers wait too long for the full month. Today I only measured, since the timeout fix needs a plan first.

I took a range with 180,000 rows on a copy of the production data and ran the export through the server path with timing logs. The query itself took 3.1 seconds. Mapping the rows to objects took 6 seconds, building the CSV string took 27 seconds, and sending it took 4 seconds. The total was 40 seconds, and the Render proxy cuts requests at 30 seconds, so the file never arrived and the user saw a timeout error.

The memory graph showed the process growing from 180 MB to 1.1 GB during the export. The string concatenation in a loop and the full array of rows both stay in memory until the end. With two exports at once, the instance with 2 GB came close to its limit. This explains an out-of-memory restart that I saw in the Render events two weeks ago and had not understood.

I profiled the CSV function with the Node inspector. The escaping of each field used three regular expressions, even for fields without quotes or commas. That alone was about a third of the CSV time. A quick check showed a test for needing quotes with one indexOf scan could skip them in most cases. I did not change the code yet, because I want to look at the whole flow first.

I also looked at the client path: for ranges below 5,000 rows, the browser builds the file. That is fine and fast.

There are several options for the large path: a background job that makes the file and mails a link, a stream of the response, or smaller pages. A background job needs storage for files and a new UI. Streaming needs a cursor on the query and a change in how headers are sent. I wrote the options and the numbers in a note for the user and will discuss the choice with him tomorrow. For today the result is the measurement and the finding that memory, not the query, is the problem.

summary: Discussed the options for the large export with the user, who wanted the least change that keeps one click, and I built a test harness that measures time and memory of an export.
body:
In the evening I went through the note with the user. He asked what dispatchers actually need: a file now, with one click, and no new page. The mail link option would change how they work, so he leaned against it. He did not want to decide before seeing what is possible within the current flow.

He asked for a repeatable measurement first, so that any change can be compared with the 40 seconds and the 1.1 GB. I built a script, scripts/export-bench.ts, which creates 200,000 shipments rows in a scratch database, runs the export function directly and prints the time per phase and the peak memory from process.memoryUsage. It does not need the server or the proxy.

The first run gave numbers close to the ones from the copy of production: 38 seconds and 1.0 GB peak. The run is stable, with a variance of about 2 seconds between runs, which is enough to see large differences.

I also tried the cheap change for the field escaping as an experiment, outside the main code. With the indexOf check, the CSV phase fell from 27 to 17 seconds. It helps, but the total would still be 30 seconds, right at the proxy limit, and the memory would be the same.

The user noted that the instance restarts matter more than the time. He asked me to check the Render events for restarts caused by memory over the last month. I found three, each at a time when a manager made a large export together with the nightly cleanup job. So the memory problem is real and shows up in production.

We agreed on the next step: to try reading the rows with a cursor and writing the lines into the response as they come, and to compare with the harness. I did not start that today. I put the bench script in the repo with a short readme line, and the numbers of today in the notes so that later entries can refer to them.

There is one risk I wrote down: a stream that fails halfway leaves the user with a cut file and no error. This needs thought on the headers and the end of the file, and I will come back to it.

summary: Upgraded Vite to the next minor version and fixed one plugin warning and a changed default for the dev server host, with the build time falling from 41 to 33 seconds.
body:
Vite had a new minor version with a few fixes that matter to us, so I upgraded it in a branch of the main checkout. The change in package.json was small, and I ran npm install and the build.

The build worked at once and took 33 seconds instead of 41. The bundle size of the main chunk was nearly the same, 612 KB against 615 KB. Vitest uses the same config and ran all 214 tests without change.

Two things needed work. The first was a warning from the React plugin about a deprecated option, 'fastRefresh', that we still set in vite.config.ts. The option has no effect anymore, so I deleted it. The second was a changed behavior of the dev server: it now only accepts requests for known host names. The Playwright tests start a preview on 127.0.0.1 and the proxy of a colleague's setup would use a different name, so I added server.allowedHosts for the local names and left everything else closed.

I checked the production build by serving it locally and clicking through the main pages: the shipments table, the costs page, the report builder and the settings page with the session list. The ECharts chunk is still loaded lazily, as before. The new version check banner for the deploy also worked, because the build id in the HTML is the same mechanism.

One point I looked at with care: the source maps. We upload them to the error tracking on deploy. The file names changed slightly with the new hash length, and the upload script matched them with a glob that is still right. I did a test upload to the staging project and a test error showed the original line.

Then I ran the Playwright suite against the preview, 46 tests, and two failed. Both failures were timing, in the report builder drag test, and they passed on the second run. I ran the group five times and they passed each time, so I do not think the upgrade caused them. I noted the test as flaky.

The branch is ready for a review. I will deploy it after the user has read the diff and watch the error log for an hour.

summary: The user reviewed the Vite upgrade, asked me to pin the flaky drag test cause, and I found the test clicked before the chart finished its animation.
body:
The user was fine with the Vite change, but he did not like to leave a flaky test unexplained. He asked me to look at the report builder drag test before the deploy.

I ran it 20 times with tracing on and it failed 3 times. The traces showed the same pattern: the test starts the drag on a chart card while the ECharts animation of the card is still running, and the card moves by a few pixels. The drop target is computed from the first position, so the drop lands on the wrong slot.

There was no change from the upgrade in this. The test was flaky before as well, but the faster build made the page ready sooner and the problem slightly more likely. That fits the timing of the two failures.

I fixed the test by waiting for the chart to be idle. The chart component sets a data attribute 'data-ready' on the card after the 'finished' event of ECharts, and the test waits for it on all cards before the drag. I did not turn off the animation in the test, because I want the test to use the real component.

After the change, 40 runs in a row passed. I also looked for the same pattern in other tests and found one more in the legend click test that I changed the same way.

I will deploy after lunch, since this change is only in test code.

summary: Deployed the Vite upgrade and watched the logs; a stale service worker cache of one dispatcher caused one error, which the reload banner resolved without a report.
body:
After the lunch I merged the Vite branch and deployed to Render. The build took 35 seconds in the pipeline, and the deploy was ready in about three minutes.

I first opened the dashboard with a manager account and a dispatcher account on the new build. Everything loaded, charts appeared, and the reload banner showed up in an old tab I left open, as designed. A click on the banner loaded the new version.

The error tracking got uploads of the source maps, and I triggered a test error to confirm that the stack trace pointed to the right file and line. It did.

In the first hour, there was one new error group. A dispatcher's browser tried to load a chunk with the old hash, which failed with 'Failed to fetch dynamically imported module'. This is the case the version banner was built for. The dispatcher had a tab that was open for hours, and he clicked on the costs page before the banner check. The banner appeared a minute later and the error did not come again from him.

I considered making the chunk load error itself trigger a reload. A small handler on the 'vite:preloadError' event could show the same banner at once. Vite emits this event when a preload fails, so it is simple. I wrote that handler: it shows the reload banner and does not reload automatically, because a user may have a form open. I added a test which dispatches the event on window and expects the banner.

I also checked the memory and the response times of the API after the deploy and they were as before, since the server code did not change. The browser log of the later hours showed no more chunk errors.

I left a note in the project notes about the upgrade: the Vite version, the removed option, the allowed hosts and the fixed test. The next upgrade to look at is the React minor version, which has some deprecation notes I want to read first. The export work comes next, as agreed.

summary: Tried the cursor based streaming of the shipments export in the bench harness and got the memory from 1.0 GB to 90 MB, but the response headers and the failure case still need a design.
body:
Tonight I used the bench script to try the first version of the streaming idea in a scratch file, outside the production route. The export function now opens a cursor with pg-cursor, reads 2,000 rows at a time, and writes CSV lines to a writable stream.

The result on 200,000 rows was good: peak memory of 90 MB, against 1.0 GB, and the total time of 14 seconds, of which the first bytes arrived after 0.3 seconds. The first bytes matter for the proxy, since a response that has started is not cut by the 30 second limit in the same way.

Three things are still open. First, the Content-Disposition header must be set before the first byte, so errors that happen later cannot send a JSON error. Second, a failure in the middle needs a defined end: I think the best way is to destroy the response so the browser shows a failed download, instead of a file that looks complete. Third, backpressure, which I tested by piping into a slow stream and saw the memory stay flat.

I did not wire it into the route yet. The harness code lives in a draft file and the numbers are written down. The production fix is for the next session.

summary: Read the React minor upgrade notes and found two deprecations that affect the dashboard, both in a small chart wrapper, and listed the steps for the upgrade.
body:
Before the next upgrade I read the notes of the new React minor version. Most items do not touch us, but two do: a deprecated way of reading refs in the old class based wrapper of the ECharts component, and a changed warning for state updates after unmount.

I searched the code for the first pattern and found it in one file, src/components/EChart.tsx, which is used by every chart. The wrapper can be a small function component with a ref and an effect, which also removes the data-ready workaround partly. The second item showed up in two places where a polling hook sets state after the page is gone.

I wrote the list of steps in the notes: bump the version, rewrite the wrapper, fix the two hooks with an abort flag, run the full tests, and check the charts by eye. I estimate half a day. I did not change code today.

summary: Upgraded React to the next minor version, replaced the two deprecated patterns in the chart wrapper, and the build and unit tests pass, with the browser tests still to run.
body:
Following the notes I read a few days ago, I started the React minor upgrade in the main checkout. The package bump itself was small: react, react-dom and the type packages moved together, and the lockfile change was clean.

The first deprecation was in src/components/ChartWrapper.tsx, where a legacy ref callback was used to hand the DOM node to ECharts. I replaced it with a plain useRef and an effect that creates the chart and disposes it on cleanup. The second was a state update inside a resize observer callback that ran during render in strict mode and printed a warning. I moved it into an effect with a stable callback.

After the change the dev console showed no more warnings on the shipments page, the costs page and the report builder. Vitest ran 412 tests with one failure, a snapshot of the chart wrapper that contained the old ref attribute. I checked that the new snapshot differed only in that attribute and updated it.

The production build took 33 seconds, the same as after the Vite upgrade, and the bundle size changed by less than 1 KB. I also tried the date picker and the legend toggles by hand, and the charts resized correctly when the window changed.

The Playwright run is still open. I started it once, but the drag test failed on a timeout, and I could not tell yet whether it comes from the upgrade or from the old animation timing, so I stopped to look at it fresh. Next I will run the browser tests twice on a clean checkout and compare with the previous version. Nothing is deployed yet.

summary: Found that the failing drag test after the React upgrade also fails on the old version, so it is a timing problem in the test and not caused by the upgrade, and fixed it.
body:
I ran the Playwright suite on a clean checkout of the version before the React upgrade, as planned. The chart drag test failed there as well, in three of ten runs, so the upgrade was not the cause.

The test dragged a chart selection right after the page opened, and the data arrived a moment later and redrew the chart. The selection then went to a chart that was just replaced. In the log I could see two renders of the series within 200 ms.

I changed the test to wait for the loading indicator to disappear and for the series count to be stable before it drags. It passed 30 runs in a row on the new React version and 20 on the old one.

The rest of the suite passed with the upgrade, 58 tests in about 4 minutes. I pushed the upgrade with the test fix and wrote a short note in the pull request about the two replaced patterns. The deploy will follow after the user has looked at it.

summary: The user asked for a design of the audit row and the per-user limit for the planned streamed export, and I wrote both down as a plan and tried the numbers on the bench.
body:
The user read my notes on the streaming experiment this morning and the sketch of the server route. The bench run had shown the memory dropping a lot with a cursor, but nothing of this exists in the real route yet, and the export still builds the whole file in memory. He had two requests for the design before I start to build it.

The first was the row count in the audit row. At the start of an export the row stores no count, so I wrote down that the row should be updated at the end of the stream with the number of lines written and the duration. For a failed stream it should get the status 'failed' and the lines written so far. This would help to read the logs later, in the same way as the instance id on the report runs.

The second was a limit on parallel large exports per user, because a user who clicks three times would start three streams, and with the current route three full files in memory at once is even worse. I proposed a small in memory counter per user id with a maximum of two, where a third request gets a 429 with a short message. The counter would be decremented in a finally block, so that aborted exports do not block the user. I wrote a first test for this with three requests at once, and for now it is only a failing test that describes the behavior.

What is still open is the response headers and what the client link should show when a stream breaks in the middle. I will go on with these questions next, and nothing of the streaming is planned for a deploy yet.

summary: Worked on the design of the streamed shipments export and tried the audit row on the bench, with nothing built for the real route yet.
body:
The user and I looked at the streamed shipments export as an idea this morning, and it is still a plan and a bench experiment. Nothing has been changed in the real export handler, and nothing is ready for a deploy window.

I ran the bench harness again against a production-sized copy of the shipments table, reading the rows through a database cursor and writing them out line by line. Memory stayed near 90 MB, and the first bytes reached the test client in under a second. This matches the earlier bench runs, so the cursor approach looks sound with the full table, though it only runs in the harness.

The user asked what the audit row should hold. I wrote a draft design: the user id, the start time and the final row count, plus a status field. A cancelled download should leave a row marked as aborted with the count of rows sent so far. I tried this in the harness with a fake client that drops the connection halfway, and the aborted row came out as drafted. The design still has to be written into the real handler, and the response headers are not decided.

I did not look at the exports of the managers on the costs page, because those use a different query path and are small. The current export of the dispatchers still builds the whole file in memory and takes about 40 seconds for the large tables, and for the biggest ones it can still run into the gateway timeout.

One open point: a very slow client could keep a database cursor open for a long time, so I noted a cap on cursor lifetime as something the design needs. Next I plan to turn the draft into a branch of the handler and ask the user to review it.

summary: Planned a time limit for the export cursor after a throttled bench test showed a slow download holding a database connection open for 4 minutes.
body:
I went through the bench harness runs and the timings from the test data for the streamed shipments export. Nothing is live yet, so I wrote down what I expect the real numbers to look like and what I still need to check. The largest file in the harness, about 210,000 rows, finished in a few seconds where the old in-memory build took about 40. Memory in the bench stayed flat, which was the main goal.

The case that worries me is a slow client. In a throttled test I simulated a dispatcher on a weak mobile connection downloading 60,000 rows over about 4 minutes, and the cursor and its database connection stayed open the whole time. The connection pool for the API has only 10 slots, so a few of these at once could starve the dashboard pages.

I looked at two ways to handle it. The first is to read rows in batches and wait for the response to drain before the next batch, which the streaming code already does in the bench, so the cursor cannot be released any earlier that way. The second is a time limit on the cursor: after 2 minutes the route ends the stream with an error line and the audit row says aborted. I prefer the limit since it protects the pool and the user can just retry on a better connection.

I have not built it yet. I wrote the plan in the task notes together with the numbers from the throttled test, and I will ask the user whether 2 minutes is acceptable for the largest files before I start.

summary: Planned a fix for a long-lived export cursor: the plan was to cap the cursor time at 2 minutes and to mark an aborted CSV clearly, with nothing changed in the route yet.
body:
I spent the session on a plan for the CSV export, because large exports are slow and the cursor of one export can stay open far too long. In the current setup one dispatcher on a bad connection could keep a database connection busy for minutes, and nothing in the route puts a limit on that. I did not change the route today. I wrote a short proposal and sent it to the user.

The idea is a 2 minute timer that starts when the cursor opens. When it fires, the route stops reading, releases the connection and ends the stream. The risk I described is that ending the stream quietly would give a CSV that looks complete. So the proposal says the route should write a last line, `# EXPORT INCOMPLETE: time limit reached after N rows`, before it closes. A spreadsheet would show that line in the last row, and a script that parses the file would fail on it, which is a better result than a silent cut.

For the audit row I proposed a status field with the values done, aborted by client and time limit. The final row count would hold the rows sent before the stop. A migration for the status column would use a default of done, so the old rows stay correct.

I also sketched the tests. A unit test with a fake cursor and a fake clock would check the last line, the status and that the connection is released once. A Playwright test would throttle the download to a few kilobytes per second and set the limit to 5 seconds through an environment variable. It would check the marker line and a toast on the page.

The open question is the download link. It is a plain anchor, so the page cannot know about a failure. I noted that the page already polls the audit row after a download, which may be enough to show the toast, and I will check that when I start.

I asked the user whether 2 minutes is the right limit. The answer was that 2 minutes is fine as long as the dispatcher sees a clear message and nothing looks like a complete file when it is not. I will start the work next.

summary: Answered Jonas's question whether the managers' costs exports use the streamed route: not yet, they still build the file in memory, but they are small.
body:
Jonas asked in the evening whether the managers' costs exports got faster too, since one of them mentioned a quick download. I checked the code. The costs export uses its own query path and still builds the file in memory, so it did not change.

The quick download was just the size: the costs files have between 300 and 2,000 rows and take under a second. The largest costs export in the audit rows of the last month had 4,100 rows and took 1.4 seconds.

I told Jonas that there is no reason to move the costs export to streaming now. If the costs page later gets exports with tens of thousands of rows, the same route can be reused, and I added a note about this to the export task list.

summary: Wrote a design note for extending CSV export to the other tables, checked each export for size and query shape, and decided the delivery times export should come first.
body:
Late in the evening I used the quiet time to think about what comes after the shipments export. Large exports still build the whole file in memory, and the dashboard has five more CSV exports besides the shipments one. I went through each of them to see which would profit from a different approach.

The numbers from the audit rows of the last month: the shipments export has up to 210,000 rows, the delivery times export up to 90,000, the driver list 400, the costs export 4,100, the report run history 12,000, and the user list under 100. Only the first two are large enough to hurt. The others finish in a second or two with the memory approach. The shipments export is the one that times out at the gateway for the biggest tables and is slow for everyone, so it stays the main problem.

The query shapes differ. The shipments export is a single select with filters, so a cursor would fit it directly. The delivery times export aggregates per day in a subquery and sorts the result, which means the database must finish the aggregation before it sends the first row. Reading it through a cursor would help the memory there, but the first byte would still come late, maybe 3 to 4 seconds. That is acceptable, though the user should know.

I also looked at how the current export code is organized. The handler mixes three jobs: building the query from the table filters, writing CSV lines with the escaping, and holding the whole result before sending it. For a cursor-based version I would like to keep the query building and the row mapping separate, so that each export only supplies a query and a mapper. The CSV escaping is already in the shared formatter that the costs fix touched, so that part is reusable.

The plan I wrote down has three steps. First, split the handler into those parts while the existing export tests keep passing, with no change in behavior. Second, move the shipments export to a cursor, and measure time and memory in the bench harness with a table above 200,000 rows. Third, do the same for the delivery times export, and decide whether the report run history needs it at all; I think not, since 12,000 rows is small.

I did not start any code. Other work is still waiting for the user's review, and I do not want to stack another change on it. I put the note into the task list, with the row counts, so that the user can see why only two exports are on the list.

summary: Scheduled report emails now survive a failed send: the job records each attempt per recipient and retries only the ones that failed, so no manager gets a report twice.
body:
A manager told Jonas that a weekly cost report never arrived while a colleague got it, and the logs showed the mail provider had returned a 451 for one recipient in the middle of a batch. The old job looped over all recipients and threw on the first error, so the run was marked failed and the whole schedule was picked up again later. That meant the recipients before the failure got a second copy, and the ones after it got nothing in the first run.

I added a table report_deliveries with schedule_id, run_id, recipient and status. The job now creates one row per recipient before sending, sends each mail on its own, and marks the row sent or failed with the error text. A run counts as done when no row is pending, and a failed row is tried again up to three times with a growing delay.

The unique key on (run_id, recipient) is what stops duplicates. If the job crashes in the middle and restarts, it reads the rows of the same run and skips everything marked sent. This also makes the clock-change problem from last week less likely to come back, because a recomputed run gets a new run_id only when the schedule really changed.

I wrote tests for three cases: one recipient fails once and then succeeds, one fails for good, and the job is killed after two sends and restarted. All pass. A failed recipient now shows on the schedule page as a small red note with the last error. Open point: nobody is told when a recipient has failed for good, so the next step is a short mail to the schedule owner. I also still have to check how the migration behaves on the production table of old runs, which has no run_id for most rows.

summary: Scheduled report emails went out an hour off for managers in two time zones because the cron ran in server time; schedules now store an IANA zone and compute the next run from it.
body:
A manager reported that the daily cost report arrived at 07:00 instead of 08:00 after the clocks changed. The cause was in the scheduler: next_run was computed from a cron string evaluated in the Render server time zone, which is UTC. The schedule form never asked for a zone.

I added a timezone column to report_schedules with a default of Europe/Berlin, since nearly all Acme users sit there, and a few rows for the Lisbon depot were set by hand. The next-run calculation now uses the cron-parser library with the tz option. The form got a zone select that defaults to the browser zone.

I wrote a migration that fills the column for existing schedules and recomputes next_run. I ran it against a copy of the production data first. 41 schedules were touched, and 6 of them moved by an hour.

Vitest now has a test that walks a schedule across the clock change and checks that the local hour stays the same. The email footer also shows the zone, so a manager can see which time the schedule uses. I will watch the next morning's sends in the logs.

summary: Wrote the email schedule fix into the release notes and answered Jonas's question about why two reports arrived on the clock-change morning: the old run and the recomputed run both fired.
body:
Jonas asked why two managers got the same report twice on the morning after the schedule migration. I looked at the scheduler log. The migration recomputed next_run, but the job that had already been picked up before the deploy still ran with the old value.

So each of the two schedules fired once with the old time and once with the new one. The reports were identical, so there was no data problem, only a duplicate email.
