I added a last_sent_at check to the job. It skips a schedule if it was sent within the last 10 minutes. This is a cheap guard, and a unique key on schedule and run slot would be cleaner. I put that on the list but did not do it now.

I wrote a short note for Jonas that explains the duplicates as a one-time effect of the migration. The release notes now mention the zone select and the guard.

summary: Session cleanup job was deleting sessions that were still active because it compared against created_at instead of last_seen_at; fixed and covered with a test.
body:
A dispatcher said she was logged out in the middle of a shift, about eight hours after she signed in. The nightly cleanup job removes old rows from the sessions table. Its query used created_at with an 8 hour limit, so every session older than that was removed, active or not.

The session middleware already updates last_seen_at on each request, throttled to once per minute. I changed the delete to use last_seen_at and a limit of 14 days idle. The absolute lifetime of 30 days stays on created_at.

I checked the numbers on a staging copy. The old query would have deleted 212 rows and the new one deleted 37, which matched the rows that had really been idle.

A Vitest integration test now inserts three sessions: one fresh, one idle for 15 days and one old but active. Only the idle one may disappear. I also put the job's deleted count in the log line, so a jump will be easy to see.

The dispatcher was told to sign in once more. Nothing else is needed from her. Next I want an index on last_seen_at, because the delete takes a full scan now.

summary: Added an index on sessions.last_seen_at and batched the cleanup delete, which cut the nightly job from about 9 seconds to under 1 second on production.
body:
This follows the cleanup fix of two days ago. With the corrected query the job did a sequential scan on the sessions table and deleted everything in one statement. That took about 9 seconds on production and held locks long enough to slow a few logins.

I created the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, in its own migration file, because the migration tool wraps files in a transaction by default and that would have failed. The tool needed the no-transaction flag for this one file.

The delete now runs in batches of 500 ids with a short pause between them. After the deploy the job ran in 0.8 seconds, and it removed 64 rows.

I also looked at the table size. It holds about 5,400 rows, which is small, so the index is more for later growth than for now. The query plan shows an index scan.

One thing I did not change: the job runs at 03:00 UTC, and the scheduled reports start around 05:00. They do not overlap, so I left it.

summary: Built the session list on the settings page: each device row shows browser, last seen and a revoke button, with the current session marked and protected from revoking itself by accident.
body:
The settings page now has a section called Active sessions. The API got GET /api/sessions, which returns the rows of the current user, and DELETE /api/sessions/:id. The user agent string is parsed on the server with ua-parser-js, so the client gets a browser and an OS name.

The current session is flagged with current: true and the button for it says Log out here and not Revoke. A revoke of another row deletes it from Postgres, and that device's next request gets a 401 and goes to the login page.

I first tried to show the IP address too. Render puts the client IP in X-Forwarded-For and the Express trust proxy setting was off, so every row showed the proxy. I turned trust proxy on with one hop. I checked the result against my own requests.

A check ensures the user can only delete their own sessions. The first version of the route looked up the id without the user_id condition. The test I wrote for it caught this, and the query has the condition now.

Playwright covers the flow with two browser contexts: revoke in one, and the other lands on the login page. Priya still has to look at the spacing of the rows.

summary: Priya reviewed the session list and asked for relative times and a clearer current-device badge; both are in, and the empty state is now handled.
body:
Priya went through the session list on staging. Her points were small. The last seen column showed a full timestamp, and she wanted relative text like 5 minutes ago. The current device needed a badge and not only a different button label.

I used Intl.RelativeTimeFormat, so there is no new dependency. The text refreshes when the page regains focus, otherwise it would go stale in a long-open tab.

The badge is a small green pill with the text This device. I moved the row of the current session to the top of the list.

While checking the empty state I found that a user with only the current session sees one row and a dangling heading for other devices. That heading is now hidden when there are no other sessions. Priya approved the result on the staging link.

summary: Started the Log out of all devices action: the endpoint deletes every session of the user except, optionally, the current one, and the button is still missing.
body:
The API now has POST /api/sessions/revoke-all with a body field keepCurrent. It deletes the user's rows in one statement and returns the count. With keepCurrent true, the current session id is excluded in the WHERE clause.

I put it behind the same auth middleware as the other session routes and wrote three Vitest cases: keep current, drop everything, and another user's sessions untouched. All three pass.

The settings page button is not done. I want a confirm dialog first, and Priya has not said which wording she prefers. I will pick a default tomorrow and let her change it later.

summary: Finished Log out of all devices with a confirm dialog, and a password change now ends all other sessions too, which closes a gap a manager had pointed out.
body:
The button on the settings page opens a dialog that says what will happen and has a checkbox, Keep me signed in here, checked by default. It calls the revoke-all endpoint from the previous entry and shows the count of ended sessions in a toast.

While testing I noticed that changing the password left other sessions alive. A manager had asked about this a while ago, and I had noted it. The password change handler now calls the same revoke function with keepCurrent set to true. A Vitest case checks that a second session gets a 401 after the change.

The SSO managers have no password, so the handler does not apply to them. Their button works as before.

Playwright got a test: sign in on two contexts, press the button in the first, and the second is sent to the login page. The test was flaky at first because the second context made a request before the delete was committed. I waited for the toast before checking the second context, and it is stable now.

A small thing remains in the text: the toast says 1 sessions for a single row. I fixed the plural with Intl.PluralRules. Deployed in the evening, and the logs show no errors so far.

summary: Large CSV exports of the shipments table still hit the 30 second Render timeout above roughly 150,000 rows; measured where the time goes before touching anything.
body:
Two dispatchers reported failed exports for a full quarter of shipments. I reproduced it on staging with 180,000 rows: the request ended with a 502 after 30 seconds. The server log shows the query itself returning in about 2.1 seconds.

The rest is the building of the file. The handler loads all rows into an array, maps them to objects with formatted dates and costs, joins them into one string and sends it. Peak memory in the Node process went to about 900 MB in my run, and the garbage collector spent a visible share of the time.

I tried two cheap things to see the effect. Moving the date formatting out of the per-row path into a cached formatter saved about 3 seconds. A raised timeout is not possible, because the Render proxy limit applies in front of Node.

So the saving does not reach the 30 seconds for the biggest cases. The real problem is the shape of the code, not a slow line. I did not change the handler yet.

For now I added a message in the UI. Above 100,000 rows the export button asks the user to narrow the date range. This is a stopgap, and I wrote the numbers in the ticket for Jonas. The proper fix needs a bigger change, and I want to plan it separately.

summary: Upgraded Vite to the next minor version; the build works and dev start is faster, but one plugin warning about a deprecated option remains.
body:
I raised Vite and @vitejs/plugin-react to the latest minor versions. npm install went through without conflicts, and the Vitest config needed no change.

The cold dev start went from about 2.8 seconds to 2.1 seconds. The production build took the same time as before, around 19 seconds, and the bundle size changed by less than 1 percent.

The build prints a warning about a deprecated option in the ECharts manual chunk setup in vite.config.ts. It still works. I will clean it up when I next touch the chunking.

Playwright passed in full on the preview build, 48 tests.

summary: Fixed the costs page showing totals that did not match the table below it, because the chart summed a rounded column and the table summed exact cents.
body:
Jonas noticed that the total on the costs page said 118,402 and the table footer said 118,397. The difference looked small but the managers compare these numbers.

The API for the chart aggregates cost_rounded, a column that a former import step fills with whole euros. The table uses cost_cents. Over thousands of shipments the rounding adds up to a visible gap.

I changed the chart query to sum cost_cents and divide by 100 in the API response. The ECharts tooltip formatter now rounds only for display. The monthly bars and the headline total use the same endpoint, so they agree with each other as well.

I checked the totals for the last six months against the table. All of them match to the cent now.

The cost_rounded column is still used by one old report. I left it and added a comment in the schema file. Removing it needs a look at that report, and it is not urgent.

I wrote a Vitest test with three shipments of 10.40, 10.40 and 10.40, where the rounded sum would be 30 and the exact sum is 31.20. It passes. I also checked the currency format for the German locale, where the thousands separator is a dot, and the labels are right.

summary: The schedule page now tells the owner when a report could not be delivered to a recipient after all retries, with the address and the reason in a short mail.
body:
This was the open point from the delivery tracking work. Until now a recipient who failed for good only showed as a red note on the schedule page, and nobody looks at that page unless they are in the settings anyway.

I added a step at the end of a run: if any report_deliveries row is still failed after the third attempt, the job collects them and sends one mail to the schedule owner. The mail lists the addresses, the error text of the provider in plain words, and a link to the schedule. It sends one mail per run, not one per recipient, so a bad distribution list does not flood the owner.

The errors needed some sorting. A 451 or a timeout is described as a temporary problem on the side of the mail provider. A 550 is described as an address that does not exist, with the hint to remove it from the schedule. Anything else gets the raw text, shortened to 200 characters.

I tested it with a stub provider that fails chosen addresses, and the mail came out right for a mixed case. Priya looked at the layout and asked for the subject to start with the report name, which I changed. One thing is left: the owner mail itself can fail, and today that only goes to the log. I left it like that on purpose, since a second alert mail would only repeat the problem.

summary: Planned the CSV export rewrite: the options are a streamed response or a background job with a download link, and the streamed response was picked as the simpler first step.
body:
Since the timeouts above 150,000 rows are a recurring complaint, I wrote down the options before writing code.

Option one is a background job. The user starts an export, a worker builds the file, stores it and sends an email with a link. It solves any size but needs file storage, a job table, cleanup of old files and a new piece of UI. That is a week of work.

Option two is to send the rows while they are read. The handler would open a cursor on Postgres, write each batch to the response and never hold the whole file. Memory stays flat, and the first bytes reach the proxy quickly, so the 30 second limit is no longer a problem as long as data keeps flowing. It changes one handler and no UI.

Risks of option two: the response headers go out before an error can happen, so a failure in the middle gives a cut file. The client has to notice that. Also, the table filters must be applied the same way as now, so the query builder has to be shared between the table and the export.

I checked that pg-query-stream works with the pool we use, in a small script against staging. It read 180,000 rows with a flat memory use of about 60 MB.

I will start with option two and keep the job idea for later if exports grow much bigger. Nothing is changed in the app yet. I shared the plan with Jonas, who only cares that the button works.

summary: Extracted the shipment filter query builder into a shared module so the table API and the future export handler apply exactly the same filters.
body:
This is the first step of the export plan from earlier today. The table endpoint built its WHERE clause inline in routes/shipments.ts, and the export handler had its own copy with small differences. One difference I found: the export ignored the carrier filter when it was combined with a status filter.

I created server/queries/shipmentFilters.ts. It takes the parsed filter object and returns a SQL fragment and a parameter array. All values are passed as parameters, as before. Sorting is a separate function, because the export needs a stable order and not the user's sort.

The table route uses the module now. I replaced the inline code and ran the existing tests. 63 Vitest tests pass without edits, which was the goal.

I then added tests for the combinations that were not covered: carrier with status, a date range with an open end, and an empty filter. The carrier plus status case failed at first because of a missing parenthesis around an OR group. That bug existed in the old table code too, and it returned too many rows for a few users. I fixed it in the module.

The export handler still uses its own copy. I will switch it in the next step, and I did not want to mix the two changes in one commit.

I also wrote a short comment at the top of the module about the parameter order, because the export will append a cursor limit after the filter parameters.

summary: Looked at how the managers' SSO login behaves when the identity provider is slow, and found only a missing loading state, no real fault.
body:
A manager said that the SSO button did nothing for several seconds. I tested it with the network throttled. The redirect to the provider works, but the button gave no feedback while the request to our /auth/sso/start endpoint was pending.

The endpoint itself answers in about 80 ms. The delay was the provider's page. I still added a disabled state and a spinner to the button, so a second click cannot start a second flow.

Nothing else changed. I told Jonas that the wait lies on the provider's side.

summary: Switched the CSV export handler to the shared filter module and read rows through a cursor, with the response write not yet streamed to the client; memory is down but the timeout is still there.
body:
This continues the export work from earlier today. The handler now uses buildShipmentFilters from the shared module, so the export matches the table, including the carrier and status combination that was wrong before.

I replaced the query with a pg-query-stream cursor and a batch size of 2,000 rows. Rows are formatted one batch at a time. However, the batches are still pushed into an array that gets joined at the end, because I wanted to check the cursor on its own first.

Results on staging with 180,000 rows: peak memory fell from about 900 MB to about 310 MB, and the time went from 30+ seconds to 24 seconds. That is under the limit, but only just, and a file twice as big would fail again. So the cursor alone is not the fix.

The remaining step is to write each batch to the response as it is read, with the right headers and backpressure handling. I have not done this yet.

I committed the cursor change on its own, with a message that says it is a step. The temporary UI message about narrowing the range above 100,000 rows stays for now.

Open question for tomorrow: how to signal an error after the headers have been sent. One idea is a final line in the file, but that would be a strange thing for a CSV in Excel. I will look at what other exports do.

summary: Added the accessibility fixes for chart label contrast and a skip link, which closes the last two findings of Acme's audit.
body:
The two open points from the audit were the contrast of the grey chart labels and the missing skip link.

The labels used #9aa0a6 on white, which has a ratio of about 2.6. I changed the ECharts theme to #5f6368 for axis labels, which gives 6.0, and the legend text got the same colour. The dark theme was checked as well: the labels there are light grey on near black and were already above 7.

I added a visually hidden link Skip to main content as the first focusable element in the layout. It becomes visible on focus and moves focus to the main region, which got tabIndex -1 for this purpose.

Priya looked at the new label colour and found it a bit heavy in the small multiples. We settled on #666d73, with a ratio of 5.3. This is still above the 4.5 limit.

I ran axe in Playwright over the dashboard, shipments and costs pages. There are no violations now. One warning about a duplicate landmark label on the costs page remains. That is a small thing, and I renamed one label so it is unique.

I sent the list of changes to Jonas for Acme's own records.

summary: A user with two browsers saw sessions listed twice after an SSO login, because the callback created a new session row even when the cookie already pointed to a valid one.
body:
A manager showed me the Active sessions section with two rows for the same Chrome on the same laptop. Both had a last seen of a few minutes ago.

The SSO callback always calls the session create function after the provider returns. If the browser still has a valid session cookie, for instance from a password login done earlier, the old row stays and a second row appears. The cookie is replaced, so the old row can never be used again, but it sits there until the cleanup job removes it after 14 days idle.

I changed the callback to read the current session first. If one exists, it is deleted in the same transaction as the creation of the new one. This also rotates the session id at login, which is a good thing to do anyway because it prevents session fixation.

The password login route had the same pattern, so I moved the logic into one function, replaceSession(userId, req), and both routes use it. A Vitest test signs in twice with the same cookie jar and counts the rows. It expected one and the old code gave two.

The existing duplicates were cleaned with a one-off query. It removes rows of the same user with the same user agent and IP where the older one has not been seen for an hour. That deleted 23 rows. I looked at the list before running it, and none belonged to a user with another device.

I checked in the logs afterwards that the SSO callback does not show errors. All fine.

summary: Answered a question from Jonas on how long a user stays logged in: sessions end after 14 days idle or 30 days in total, and a revoke acts immediately.
body:
Jonas asked for a plain statement of the login times, because Acme's security contact wanted it in writing.

A session row in Postgres lives as long as the user uses the dashboard. It is removed after 14 days without a request, with last_seen_at as the measure, or 30 days after it was created, whichever happens first. The nightly job does the deletion, but the middleware also rejects an expired row at once, so the job is only cleanup.

When a user revokes a session, uses Log out of all devices, or changes the password, the rows are deleted and the next request of that device gets a 401. There is no delay and no list of dead tokens to wait for.

The mobile app uses the same sessions now, and its drivers show up in the list with the app's user agent string.

I wrote this in a short paragraph and sent it to Jonas.

summary: Prepared the CSV export for streaming by checking the pool, the proxy limit and the error behaviour, without changing how the response is written yet.
body:
This is the step before the one I left open last time. The handler still builds the response the old way, but I spent the session on what streaming will need, so that the change itself is small when I get to it.

First I measured the current state on staging with 180,000 rows. The handler reads through the cursor now, so memory is lower than before, but the response is still written only at the end. The first byte arrives after about 25 seconds and the whole file after 29. That is just under the 30 second gateway limit, which explains why larger tables fail and smaller ones pass by a hair. A test with 600,000 rows ran into the timeout every time.

Then I wrote down what the next step has to do. The response needs Content-Type text/csv and Content-Disposition, the header line should go out at once, and each row needs to be formatted by a Transform. I want to use stream.pipeline and not a loop with res.write, because a loop that ignores the return value would queue batches in the socket buffer on a slow connection. I made a small script that simulates a slow client, so I can see the memory curve later and compare it with the current numbers.

I also listed the things that must stay the same: fields with commas, quotes or line breaks are quoted and quotes are doubled, the file begins with a UTF-8 byte order mark so that Excel reads the umlauts, and dates and costs use the same formatters as the table.

The error case is still a question. If the stream fails in the middle, the status code has already gone out. I see two options: end the file with a visible marker, or destroy the socket so that the browser reports a failed download. I will ask Jonas which one the dispatchers would understand better.

The pool is the last open point. A long-running cursor holds a connection for the whole export, and the pool has 10. I looked at how many exports the dispatchers start at the same time in the logs, usually one or two, but the scheduled reports can add more. I will think about a limit before anything is deployed.

The temporary UI message about narrowing the range stays for now.

summary: Investigated how parallel CSV exports would use the connection pool on staging and planned a concurrency limit, without building it yet.
body:
The export handler reads rows through a cursor now, so I wanted to know what a download would cost the pool once the response is streamed. A streamed export would hold one pool connection for as long as the download runs. With the pool at 10, a few dispatchers exporting at the same time could block the dashboard's other queries.

To get a baseline I ran the current handler on staging with eight parallel exports of 180,000 rows and a loop of normal table requests next to them. The table requests rose from about 60 ms to more than 2 seconds, and some waited for a connection until they failed. The exports are slow and each one holds a connection for a long time, so the effect is already visible, and streaming would make the holding time even longer.

I sketched a fix on paper and have not written it. A small semaphore in the export route with three slots seems enough. A fourth request would wait up to 10 seconds and then get a 429 with a message to try again in a moment. The slot has to be released in a finally block and also when the client closes the connection, so that an aborted download does not leak it. I will test that by killing curl in the middle of an export.

I also looked at Render's Postgres plan and it allows a pool of 15 instead of 10. I would only change that together with the limit, so I noted it for the next release and did not touch the setting.

Next I will build the semaphore on a staging deploy and repeat the same load test. Before anything goes to production I want to export the full shipments table there once more and watch the memory graph during the run. The three-slot limit should go into the runbook note next to the proxy idle limit.

summary: Planned the error handling for the CSV export streaming: checked what Express allows after headers are sent and wrote down how a failed cursor should signal the client.
body:
The CSV export still builds its response the old way, so large files still hit the gateway timeout. Before changing how the response is written, I looked at what happens when a query fails halfway through a stream. Once headers are sent, Express cannot change the status code any more, so a failure after the first batch can only be signalled in the body or by closing the connection. If nothing is done, the client gets a short file that looks complete, and for a dispatcher that is worse than a clear error.

I wrote down the plan. On a cursor error the handler should destroy the response, so the browser reports a failed download instead of a finished one. It should log the export id, the user and the number of rows written so far. I also thought about a final row check that counts the rows written and compares them with a count query run before the stream starts. If they differ by more than the rows added meanwhile, it would log a warning. That would only be a log at first, because shipments are inserted all the time and a hard failure would give false alarms.

I tried the failure on a scratch route with a fake cursor, to see what Chrome does when the response is destroyed after a few batches. It shows a network error, which is what we want. The real handler is not touched yet.

Open points for the next sessions: a Vitest test with a fake cursor that throws on the third batch, a friendlier message in the table toolbar, and a check with the real Render timeout on staging. I will not change the limit on concurrent exports. The export problem is still open and nothing is streamed to users yet.

summary: Planned how to test a CSV export of 200,000 shipments on staging, since large exports still time out at the gateway and no streaming change exists yet.
body:
I looked at the export handler again today. It builds the whole file in memory and sends it at the end, so any export over about 200,000 rows hits the 30 second gateway timeout. I have not changed how the response is written.

To see how bad it is, I wrote down a test plan for staging. I will load the shipments table with about 200,000 rows and export with no filter, then watch the memory of the API process and the time to the first byte. I expect the first byte to come only when the whole file is ready, which is what causes the timeout. I also noted the sizes to try: 50,000, 100,000 and 200,000 rows, so I can see where the timeout starts.

I wrote a small seed script that creates the extra shipments with realistic dates, costs and driver names. It ran on a local database and made 200,000 rows in a few seconds. I have not run it on staging yet, because Jonas's team may be looking at the data there, and I want to tell them first.

I also read how the Render proxy treats responses. It looks like it closes a connection that has had no bytes for a while. That matters for any later change, so I added it to my notes as a question to test, not as a fact.

Next I will ask Jonas whether the managers export on slow or mobile connections, and then run the plan on staging. I will also check the connection pool limit, because parallel exports could starve normal requests.

summary: Investigated why the streamed CSV export on staging gets cut near the end of a 200,000 row file, and found the proxy idle gap as the likely cause, without changing the handler yet.
body:
Yesterday's staging run showed that the export started at once but the connection died close to the end of a 200,000 row file. Today I looked at the timing of the batches and found that the last stretch of rows contains the wide shipments with long notes, which made the cursor reads slower than the proxy idle limit. In a few places there were gaps of more than 55 seconds between two writes. The proxy in front of Render closes a connection that sends nothing for about a minute, which matches the cut exactly.

I tried a smaller batch size of 500 rows instead of 2,000 on a scratch copy of the handler. That helped the average gap but did not remove the longest ones, so I dropped it and went back to 2,000. I also thought about writing a blank line between batches to keep the connection busy. That would corrupt the CSV, so I rejected it at once.

What I plan instead is a small timer in the export handler in server/export/stream.ts. If no batch has been written for about 15 seconds, it would flush the response so the proxy sees traffic, and it must not add anything to the CSV body, so the file stays byte-identical to the non-streamed output. I wrote down how I will check this: export 50,000 rows from both paths and compare them with diff and cmp. The timer also has to stop cleanly when the client disconnects, so I sketched a test for the abort case with a fake clock in export.stream.test.ts, but I have not written the timer itself.

For now the 200,000 row file on staging still does not finish. Memory of the API process stayed flat around 180 MB during the failed run, and the limit of three concurrent exports from the pool check still applies.

What is left is the timer and its tests, a rerun of the 200,000 row file on staging, a real browser check with the managers' slower connections, and a note in the runbook about the idle limit. I will also ask Jonas for one of his larger real exports later.

summary: Wrote the runbook note on the proxy idle limit for the CSV export work and planned a log line for the longest gap between writes, without changing how the export is sent.
body:
Wrote a section in docs/runbook.md about the proxy idle limit of about one minute and why the streamed CSV export will need a flush timer. The streaming work is still being tried on staging, and the proxy cut a connection near the end of a large export, so I wrote the reasoning down while it is fresh. If someone later sees a timer that looks like dead code and removes it, large exports would break again near the end. The note says where the export code lives in server/export/stream.ts and what the idle gap looked like on the staging run with 200,000 rows. I also drafted the comment that would go above the timer, two sentences with the same reasoning. I have not put it into the code yet, because the exact interval is not settled and I do not want a comment that states a number I may still change.

To make the next problem visible earlier, I sketched a log line for the end of each export: row count, total duration, peak memory and the longest gap between two writes in milliseconds. I measured by hand on staging to see what values to expect. A 20,000 row export had a longest gap of 1.2 seconds, a 100,000 row export 3.8 seconds, and the 200,000 row export 9.5 seconds. These are well below the proxy limit, but the 200,000 row run was still cut near the end, so the gap alone does not explain it and I need to look at the idle time on the proxy side too.

One detail surprised me. The longest gap grows with the number of rows because the cursor query sorts by shipped_at and the later pages need more skipping. I checked the query plan and the index on shipped_at is used, so it is not a missing index. I noted it as a possible later improvement and did not touch the query.

I also searched the production logs for exports that failed in the past week. There were two, both from a manager who closed the tab, so nothing there points to a new fault. The runbook note is only a draft for now. The export is not finished: I still want managers to try large exports before I call it done, and nothing about it is ready to ship.

summary: Checked why the sessions table shows a few rows with no user agent after SSO logins and found they come from the identity provider's back-channel check, not from real devices.
body:
While looking at the session list on the settings page I noticed that a few managers have a row with an empty browser name. Priya had asked for a clearer device label, so an empty label looks like a defect in her design too. I wanted to know if it is a real bug or just data.

I queried the sessions table for rows where user_agent is null or empty. There were 14 of them out of about 900 active rows, and all 14 belong to users who log in with SSO. The created_at times of these rows are a few hundred milliseconds before the real session of the same user.

The cause is in the SSO callback. The identity provider calls a health check URL on the same route with its own client, which carries no user agent header, and the callback created a session before it checked the state parameter. The real browser then arrived and created a second row. This is related to the duplicate sessions I fixed a few days ago, but that fix only looked at the cookie.

I moved the state check before the session creation, so a call without a valid state returns an error and creates nothing. I added a test that sends a callback without a state and expects zero new rows. A second test sends a valid callback and expects exactly one row.

The 14 old rows are harmless and the cleanup job removes them after the idle limit, so I did not write a migration. The session list also shows a neutral label of Unknown device for any row that still lacks a user agent, so nothing looks broken. I will check the count again next week to see that no new empty rows appear.

summary: Asked Jonas to have his managers try large CSV exports and report any interrupted download, and listed what is still open before the export work can be called finished.
body:
I wrote to Jonas to ask whether two or three of his managers could try big exports on staging this morning, the kind that used to fail at the gateway timeout. I gave him a short list: open the file in Excel, check that the last row is there, and tell me at once if a download stops with an interrupted message.

While waiting I went through my task list for the export. The streamed handler runs on staging and the pool limit of three concurrent exports is set, but the proxy idle gap near the end of the largest files is not fully understood yet. I do not want to close anything until a 200,000 row file has finished without a cut.

I started a log line that records the longest gap between writes for each export, so that I can see what the proxy sees instead of guessing. I also began a short runbook note about the idle limit and how a keepalive could work.

A background job with a download link for exports that take minutes stays on the nice to have list. I did not start it. For now the export items stay open in my list until the managers report back and the staging run is clean.

summary: Answered Jonas on whether a deactivated user is logged out at once: yes, because deactivating deletes their session rows in the same transaction.
body:
Jonas asked what happens when he deactivates a dispatcher who is logged in at that moment. I read the invite and user admin code to be sure and not answer from memory.

The deactivate endpoint sets active to false and deletes all rows in sessions for that user inside one transaction. The session middleware looks the row up on every request, so the next request of that person gets a 401. There is no delay.

I checked it on staging with two browsers: I deactivated the test user in one and clicked in the other, which went to the login page at once.

One gap: a user who is deactivated while an SSO login is in progress could get a new session from the callback. The callback checks the active flag, so it is closed in practice. I sent Jonas the short answer.

summary: Added a test that the SSO callback refuses deactivated users, since the answer to Jonas relied on that check and nothing tested it.
body:
While answering Jonas I found the active flag check in the SSO callback had no test. I wrote one with Vitest: a deactivated manager arrives from the identity provider with a valid assertion and the callback must answer with an error page and create no session row.

The test passed on the first run, so the code was right. I also added the opposite case, an active manager, to make sure the test can fail.

The error page text was a generic message. I changed it to say that the account is deactivated and to contact an admin at Acme.

summary: Started the scheduled report preview: the owner can now see the next five run times in their own time zone before saving a schedule.
body:
After the time zone bug, Jonas asked for a way to check a schedule before it goes live. I added a preview under the schedule form.

The API gets a new endpoint, POST /schedules/preview, that takes the cron expression and the IANA zone and returns the next five run times as ISO strings with the zone offset. It uses the same function as the job that computes the next run, so the preview cannot disagree with reality.

The form calls it with a small debounce when the cron field or the zone changes, and lists the times in the zone chosen. Invalid cron text shows an inline error with the parser message.

I tested the clock-change case with a zone and a daily 02:30 schedule. The preview shows the day when 02:30 does not exist and the job runs at the next valid time, and the preview says so with a note on that row.

Still to do: the note text needs Priya's view, and the mobile layout of the list is cramped. Tests exist for the endpoint and for the debounce.

summary: Priya reviewed the schedule preview and asked for a calmer layout and clearer wording for skipped times; both changes are done and the preview is ready to ship.
body:
Priya looked at the preview on staging and sent three points. The list of five times looked like an error log, the note about skipped times used the word nonexistent, and the zone field was too far from the preview.

I changed the list into a plain two column layout, with the date on the left and the time and offset on the right, in the normal text color. The first row is marked as the next run.

The note now says that this time does not occur on that day, so the report runs at the next valid time. Priya liked that more.

I moved the zone select directly above the cron field, so the order is zone, timing, preview. The form tab order follows it, which I checked with the keyboard.

On mobile the preview stacks, and the offset goes on a second line in a smaller size. I checked it at 360 pixels width with Playwright screenshots.

I updated the snapshot tests, and all of the suite passes. The preview ships with the next release.

summary: Upgraded React to the next minor version; the test suite passed, and the only change needed was a type fix in the chart wrapper component.
body:
I raised React and the type packages to the newest minor. The install was clean.

TypeScript complained in the ECharts wrapper: a ref callback returned a value, which the new types do not allow. I changed the callback to a block body that returns nothing.

Vitest passed fully, 412 tests. Playwright had one failure in the date picker test, which turned out to be a timing issue and not related; it passed on rerun and I noted it as flaky.

I clicked through the shipments table, the costs page, the report builder and the settings page in dev mode and saw no console warnings. The production build size changed by under 1 kB.

I left the Vite plugin deprecation warning for another time.

summary: Prepared the schedule preview for release after Priya's review, and wrote down what to check for the slow large CSV exports before touching them.
body:
After Priya's review I finished the last wording fixes for skipped times in the schedule preview and read the diff once more. The preview shows the next five run times in the owner's own time zone, and I added a test for a manager in a zone with a clock change, since that is the case most likely to go wrong. The test passes locally. I have not deployed it yet; I want to look at it on staging once more first, and write the runbook note for the release.

I also spent some time on the large CSV exports, which are still slow. Jonas said his managers can run them, but the exports of more than 200,000 rows are close to the gateway timeout of 30 seconds, and I do not like that. I only read the handler and wrote down what it does: it builds the whole file in memory and sends it at the end, so nothing goes out for a long time. I changed nothing in it. I noted two ideas for later, to look at how the rows are read and what the gateway does with a response that is silent for a long time, and I will decide after I have measured a large table on staging.

Tomorrow I will deploy the schedule preview on its own and tell Jonas when it is live.

summary: Planned the log in with SSO session lifetime for managers: they should follow the same idle and total limits as password users, and the plan lists three code changes.
body:
Jonas asked why a manager logged in with SSO stayed logged in longer than a dispatcher last week. I checked the sessions table for both and found the SSO sessions had no last_seen_at update, since the touch happens in the cookie path only.

The SSO callback creates the row with last_seen_at at the time of login. The middleware then updates it only when a request has the older cookie format, which SSO sessions never have. So the idle timer never moved, but the cleanup used created_at plus 30 days, so such sessions could live up to 30 days even when idle.

Wait, this is the opposite of the long idle bug: they live longer than 14 days idle. The cleanup job looks at last_seen_at, which stays at login time, so these sessions end 14 days after login, not later. The manager had logged in again by habit, which made it look longer.

So the real fault is smaller: active SSO managers are logged out after 14 days even if they use the dashboard daily. That is annoying for them. I wrote down three changes: update last_seen_at in the middleware for every session, throttle the update to once per minute to spare the database, and add a test for each login path.

I started with the middleware. The touch is a single UPDATE with a where clause on last_seen_at older than a minute, so most requests write nothing. I measured the cost on staging at under 1 ms.

The tests are written but I have not run the SSO path against the real identity provider yet. That is the next session.

summary: Verified the session touch change against the real SSO provider on staging: an active manager now stays logged in past 14 days of simulated time.
body:
I used a staging manager account and logged in through the identity provider. Then I made requests and checked last_seen_at in the sessions table.

The value moved on requests after a minute, and did not move for requests within the same minute, as designed.

To simulate 14 days, I ran the cleanup job with a shifted clock parameter I added for tests. The active session stayed, while a second SSO session that made no requests was deleted.

The password login path behaved the same way, so both paths share the code now. I also checked the revoke button on the settings page: it still ends the session at once.

I wrote the result into the pull request. A short reminder: the 30 days total limit still applies, and nothing changed there.

summary: Built the first step of the report builder v2 column picker, where users drag columns into order, and left saving the layout for later.
body:
The report builder v2 starts with the column picker. In v1 the column order was fixed, and managers asked to choose and order columns for their own reports.

I built a list component with two panes: available columns on the left and chosen columns on the right. Items move with a button or with drag and drop, and the order of the chosen pane is the order of the columns in the report. Keyboard users can move an item with the arrow keys while holding alt, after the accessibility audit taught us to check this.

The component keeps its state as an ordered array of column keys. A key that is unknown, for example a column removed in a later version, is dropped on load with a console warning.

I used the dnd-kit library, which was already a dependency for the table header. This avoided a new package. The bundle grew by 2 kB.

Tests: Vitest for the reducer that moves items, with seven cases such as moving to the first place and moving the last item. A Playwright test drags a column and checks the order in the preview table.

What is missing: saving the layout per report, the default set of columns for new reports, and the preview uses sample data only. I will connect the layout to the report model next, which needs a column in Postgres for a JSON array.

Priya has not seen the component yet. I will send screenshots once saving works.

summary: Saved the report column layout in Postgres as a JSON array with a migration, and the report builder now reloads reports with the chosen order.
body:
I added a migration that creates a columns column of type jsonb on the reports table, with a default of an empty array. Existing reports get an empty array, and the code treats empty as the old fixed order. That keeps every saved report working.

The API validates the array on save: only known column keys, no duplicates, between one and 20 entries. A bad request gets a 400 with the first problem in the message.

On load, the builder maps the keys to column definitions and passes them to the picker. If the saved layout is empty, it fills the default list.

The scheduled report job also had to learn the new order, since it renders the same table into an email attachment. I found it called the old function with a fixed list. I changed it to read the report's columns and use the same helper as the builder. I tested this with a scheduled report that has columns in reverse order, and the CSV header in the mail matched.

I ran the migration on a copy of the production database. It took 40 ms for about 300 reports.

There are now 18 new tests. One failed at first because a test fixture had a column key with a typo, which showed that the validation does work.

Next I need to send Priya screenshots and decide what the default columns for a new report are. Jonas may have an opinion; I will ask him which five columns his dispatchers use most.

The export of large tables follows the saved layout too, since it uses the same helper. I checked a 100,000 row export with a custom order and it was correct.

summary: Added the column width and sort order to the saved report layout, so a report in the builder v2 reloads exactly as the manager left it, not just with the column order.
body:
Managers using the report builder v2 pointed out through Jonas that their saved reports remember the column order but not the column widths, and the sort order is lost too. They have to fix the same two things every time they open a report. That is a small gap but it makes the saved layout feel unreliable.

The layout is stored as a JSON array of column keys in Postgres, from the migration of a few days ago. I changed the shape to an array of objects with key, width and an optional sort direction. A plain array of strings would not hold the width, and a second column for widths would have split one idea into two places.

The migration converts every existing layout in one UPDATE, turning each key into an object with a default width of 140 and no sort. I ran it on a copy of the production data first. All 212 saved reports converted, and I compared the column order before and after with a script, with no differences.

The API reads both shapes for one release, so an old client tab that still sends strings does not break the save. I wrote a small normalizer in the report layout module for this and covered it with five unit tests, including an empty layout and an unknown key.

In the builder, dragging the column edge now updates the width in the layout state, and clicking a header cycles through ascending, descending and none. The row preview of 20 rows uses the same sort, so what the manager sees matches what the export and the scheduled report will produce. I checked that the CSV export applies the saved sort through the shared filter module, and it does.

One problem showed up in the Playwright test: the width reset when the browser window was resized because the grid recalculated from defaults. I fixed it by treating the stored width as a minimum only when no width was saved. What is left is a decision on whether dispatchers who view a shared report can change the widths for themselves. I will ask Jonas about that tomorrow.

summary: Added real row previews to the report builder: the first 20 rows load from the API with the current filters and column order.
body:
The preview used sample data until now. It now calls a new endpoint, GET /reports/preview, with the filters and column keys and returns 20 rows.

The endpoint uses the shared shipment filter module from the export work, so the rows follow the same rules as the table and the export. That was the reason for extracting it, and it paid off here: no new filter code was written.

The preview refreshes after a half second pause when the filters or the columns change. A small loading state keeps the old rows visible and dims them, to avoid flicker.

I limited the query with a statement timeout of three seconds, so that a broad filter on the large table cannot hang the preview. On a timeout the user sees a message to narrow the filters.

The tests cover the endpoint with filters and an unknown column key, and one Playwright test changes the order and checks the first row header.

Open: the preview shows dates in UTC, while the table shows the user's zone. I will fix that next.

summary: Fixed the report preview showing dates in UTC, and found the same slip in the scheduled report attachment, which now also uses the schedule's zone.
body:
The preview rows showed delivery times in UTC while the table showed the user's zone, so the same shipment looked a few hours off. The new endpoint returned raw timestamps and the client formatted them with a helper that defaults to UTC.

I changed the client to pass the user's zone from the settings, the same helper the table uses. The preview now matches the table row by row, which I checked with five shipments.

The odd part came when I looked at the scheduled report attachment, since it uses the same row renderer. It formatted times in server time. This is a leftover of the zone issue from the schedule fix: the next run time was fixed, but the data in the file was not.

The job now formats timestamps in the schedule's IANA zone. I added a test with a schedule in a zone with a large offset and checked the first cell of the CSV in the mail.

I told Jonas that reports sent before this change have times in server time, and that new ones follow the schedule zone. He said the managers had not noticed, since most are in one zone.

The filter values for dates in a report are stored as local dates. I tested a report that filters on delivery date near midnight, and the result was correct in both zones I tried.

I also added a line to the release notes. The remaining work for builder v2 is sharing a report between managers, which I have not planned yet.

All tests pass, 441 now.

summary: Wrote a short plan for sharing reports between managers: a shared flag and a read-only copy, without per-user permissions for now.
body:
Jonas wants managers to share a report with colleagues. I wrote a plan before coding.

The simplest model is a shared flag on the report. A shared report is visible to all managers of the same client, read-only for everyone except the owner. A manager can copy a shared report to their own list and edit the copy.

I rejected per-user permissions for now. They need a join table, a picker for users and an audit trail, and Jonas said that all managers at Acme trust each other.

Changes: one boolean column with a migration, a list filter in the API, a Shared badge in the list, and a Copy action. Scheduled sends stay with the owner.

I asked Jonas whether dispatchers should see shared reports. He will decide with the managers.

summary: Implemented the shared flag and copy action for reports; dispatchers do not see shared reports until Jonas decides.
body:
I added the migration for a shared boolean on reports with default false and updated the list endpoint. A manager sees their own reports and the shared ones of the same client.

The update endpoint checks the owner before any change, and returns 403 otherwise. I wrote tests for a non-owner trying to edit and to delete a shared report; both are refused.

The Copy action creates a new report with the same columns and filters, an own owner and shared false. The name gets a suffix with the word copy.

In the UI the list shows a Shared badge, and the toggle sits in the report settings of the owner. Dispatchers get no change, because their role excludes the feature.

Tests pass. Priya will look at the badge next.

summary: Jonas decided that dispatchers may view shared reports but not copy them, so the role check was widened for reading only.
body:
Jonas came back with the managers' answer: dispatchers should see shared reports, since they often need the same numbers, but they should not copy or edit.

I changed the list endpoint so that the dispatcher role also gets shared reports. The copy and update endpoints still require the manager role. I added tests for a dispatcher: list works, view works, copy returns 403.

In the UI the Copy button is hidden for dispatchers, and the report page opens in a read-only mode with the builder controls disabled. I checked that the read-only mode still allows the CSV export, since the dispatchers use it.

Priya reviewed the Shared badge and asked for a lighter color; I changed it to the neutral gray used for other tags.

One issue came up in testing: a dispatcher opening a shared report by the direct link to the builder saw the form briefly before the redirect. I made the route check the role before rendering.

All tests pass. I also added a line about this to the release notes for Jonas.

summary: Added a test that dispatchers can open a shared report but get a 403 on the copy endpoint, so Jonas's rule from this afternoon is pinned down.
body:
Jonas decided earlier that dispatchers may read shared reports but not copy them. The role check was widened for reading only, and nothing proved the copy side stayed closed. I added two API tests in the reports suite: a dispatcher GET on a shared report returns 200, and a POST to the copy endpoint returns 403.

I also added a test that a dispatcher still gets 404 on a report that is not shared. All three pass. The copy button is hidden for dispatchers in the UI, but the tests call the API directly so the rule does not depend on the UI.

Nothing else changed in the role code.

summary: Built the first version of the costs page breakdown by customer, with a table and one bar chart fed by a new aggregate endpoint, and left the period comparison for later.
body:
The costs page so far only showed a total per month. Jonas wants managers to see cost per customer, so I started with the data. A new endpoint, GET /api/costs/by-customer, takes the same date range and filters as the shipments table, which means it uses the shared filter module from last week. It returns customer id, name, shipment count, and the summed cost in cents.

The query groups on customer and joins the shipments table to the customers table. On the staging copy with 200,000 shipments it ran in about 310 ms, which is fine. I looked at the plan and it uses the existing index on delivered_at, so I added no index.

On the front end I added a CostsByCustomer component with a sortable table. Next to it is an ECharts bar chart of the top 10 customers. Both read the same query result through one hook, so they cannot disagree.

Money values come as integer cents and are formatted only at the edge. I used the existing currency formatter, so the euro sign and separators follow the user's locale. Rounding happens once, in the formatter.

The empty state needed some thought. A range with no shipments returns an empty array, and the chart showed a blank box. I added a plain message for that case.

I wrote unit tests for the aggregate query with three customers and one customer with zero shipments, which must not appear. I also added a Vitest test for the hook. The full suite passes.

Still open: comparing with the previous period, and the CSV export of this table. I will ask Priya for the layout of the comparison before I build it. Today's work is not shipped yet and sits behind the existing costs page flag.

summary: Reviewed the costs by customer page on staging and fixed three problems: a sort that treated costs as text, a clipped chart label, and a missing total row.
body:
After the first build this afternoon I opened the page on staging with real-sized data and went through it as a manager would.

The first problem was the sort. Clicking the cost column ordered 900 before 12000 because the table sorted the formatted strings. I changed the column to sort on the raw cent value and kept the formatted text only for display. The shipment count column was fine.

The second was the chart. Long customer names were clipped at the left edge of the bar chart. I set the grid to contain labels and truncated names after 24 characters with an ellipsis. The full name shows in the tooltip.

The third was that the table had no total row. Managers will compare it with the monthly total on the same page, so a difference would raise questions. I added a footer row with the sum of the returned rows. It matched the monthly total on staging for three different ranges.

While checking the totals I found that shipments without a customer were dropped by the inner join. They were 41 rows out of 200,000 on staging. I switched to a left join and show them as one line called Unassigned, so the totals now agree exactly.

I added a test for the unassigned case and updated the snapshot of the table. The suite passes.

The comparison with the previous period is still waiting for Priya's layout.

summary: Added the previous period comparison to the costs page after Priya's layout: each customer row shows the change in percent, and a missing earlier period shows a dash instead of infinity.
body:
Priya sent the layout for the comparison this morning. It is small: one extra column with the change against the previous period of the same length, in a muted colour for a decrease and a stronger one for an increase, plus an arrow shape so colour alone does not carry the meaning.

On the API side, the by-customer endpoint now takes compare=previous. It computes the earlier range as the same number of days directly before the chosen start. The query runs twice and the results are merged by customer id in the handler. A single query with conditional sums was possible, but the two-query version was easier to read and test. Both ran in under 400 ms on staging.

The edge cases took most of the time. A customer with no cost in the earlier period would give a division by zero. The API returns null for the change in that case and the table shows a dash. A customer who had cost before and none now shows minus 100 percent, which is correct.

Ranges that cross a daylight saving change were a worry, because a range in days is not always the same number of hours. I compute the earlier range in calendar days in the user's zone, the same way the report preview was fixed last week, so a day is always a day.

The change is rounded to one decimal place on the server and sent as a number. The UI shows it with the locale's decimal sign.

I added tests for four cases: normal change, new customer, vanished customer, and a range across a clock change. All pass.

I also updated the chart. A second, lighter bar per customer shows the previous period, and the legend says which is which. Priya's layout asked for this and it looks fine with ten customers.

Not done: the CSV export of this table and the help text on the page. I will do the export next, using the shared export handler.

summary: Planned the CSV export for the costs by customer table, with its columns, number formats and filters, and found that the aggregate query is the awkward part.
body:
The costs table needed an export, so I spent the session working out what it should look like before writing any handler code. The current export builds the whole file in memory and is known to be slow for large tables, but the costs result is small, bounded by the number of customers, around 900 for Acme. So the plain export path is good enough for this page, and I did not touch the slow large-table problem here.

I wrote down a costs-by-customer definition with five columns: customer, shipments, cost, previous cost, change. The aggregate query is the awkward part, because the comparison column needs the earlier period next to the current one. I sketched it as one grouped query with a left join on the previous range, so that a missing earlier period gives an empty value and not a division by zero, in line with the dash on the page.

I also decided on the formats now, so they do not surprise anyone later. The change column will be a plain number with a dot as the decimal sign, named change_percent, and not a rounded value with a percent sign inside, because spreadsheets read that as text. Jonas uses a spreadsheet tool, so I will check the file in it. Costs will be written as decimal euros with two places, not cents, and the header will say so.

For the filters, the plan is to call the shared filter module, so the export uses the same range and customer filters as the screen. Then I can compare the file with the page for a few ranges and check that the totals match to the cent, including the Unassigned row.

Tests I want to write: column order and header, the decimal format, an empty result giving only the header line. I also need to find out whether the current export has a limit on parallel exports that this one should follow.

Remaining for the costs page: the help text and a check of the page with the dispatcher role, who should not see costs at all. I will look at that tomorrow.

summary: Fixed the costs page so shipments with no customer land in an 'Unassigned' row instead of vanishing from the by-customer totals, which now match the page's grand total.
body: While testing the costs by customer view against a staging copy, the sum of the customer rows was lower than the grand total at the top. The aggregate endpoint joined shipments to customers with an inner join, so shipments without a customer were dropped. I changed it to a left join and grouped the null customer into one row labelled Unassigned, sorted by cost like the others. The total row and the bar chart use the same query, so they agree now. I added a test with three shipments, one of them without a customer, that checks the rows add up to the total. The comparison column for the Unassigned row is still to be checked.

summary: Wrote the help text for the costs page and prepared the by-customer view, the comparison and its export for a deploy, with the role fix still under review.
body:
I wrote the short help text that Priya and Jonas asked for. It says what the comparison period is, that unassigned shipments are shown on their own line, and that exported costs are in euros with two places. Priya shortened two sentences and moved the text into a collapsible hint under the title.

Then I went through the costs work once more on staging to see what is left before it can go out: the by-customer table and chart, the previous period comparison, the CSV export, and the role fix on the routes. Nothing is merged or deployed yet. The role fix still needs one more test, because I want to be sure a dispatcher gets a 403 on every costs route and not only on the main one.

On staging the new endpoint answered in a median of about 280 ms over a few dozen calls, with no errors. I ran two exports to check the file contents and the euro format. Both looked right, and the column with the comparison lines up with the page. I did not touch the session logs.

I told Jonas the page is not live yet and sent him the example range I tested with, so he can look at it on staging with the managers. I will plan the deploy for after the role test passes and after Priya has seen the hint in its final place.

summary: Investigated reports from managers that the session list in settings showed a device as active for weeks after they stopped using it, and found the last-seen time was only updated on login.
body:
Jonas passed on a comment from a manager: the session list on the settings page showed a laptop as last active three weeks ago, although she used that laptop daily. It looked like a display bug, and I started there.

The settings page reads last_seen_at from the sessions table and formats it as a relative time. The formatting was right. So the column itself was stale.

I searched for writers of last_seen_at. There was one, in the login handler. The touch that extends the idle timer, which I changed for SSO sessions on staging a few days ago, writes expires_at but not last_seen_at. So a session that stayed alive by use kept the time of its first login. The idle expiry worked, which is why nobody noticed until someone read the list.

The fix is a small change in the touch function: set last_seen_at to now in the same update that moves expires_at. The cost is one more column in a write that already happens, so no new query.

I thought about write volume next. The touch runs on most requests, and I had throttled it earlier to once per five minutes per session. That throttle stays. A last-seen time that is up to five minutes old is fine for a list of devices, and I wrote this in a comment above the function.

A test came first. It creates a session, advances the fake clock by ten minutes, makes a request, and expects last_seen_at to move. It failed before the change and passes after. A second test checks that two requests within five minutes cause one update.

For existing rows there is nothing to repair. They will correct themselves the next time the owner uses the session. Sessions that are no longer used will keep their old time, which is true.

I also looked at the SSO path, because the touch for SSO sessions was verified earlier on staging. It shares the same function, so it is fixed too. I confirmed it with a staging manager session after a simulated hour.

One more thing I noticed: the session list marks the current device with a label, based on a comparison of session ids. That works and did not need change.

The fix is merged and waits for the next deploy. I will tell Jonas to ask the manager to look again after a day of use.

summary: Answered Jonas on whether the costs page numbers can differ from the finance export: they can for unassigned shipments, and the page now says how they are counted.
body:
Jonas asked why a number on the costs page was a little higher than the figure he gets from the finance department's own export for the same month.

I compared the two. The difference was 3,420 euros, and it came from shipments with no customer. Our page counts them in the line called Unassigned and in the total. The finance export lists only invoiced customers, so it leaves them out.

I checked this by summing the unassigned line on staging for the same range, which gave exactly the difference. The remaining rows matched to the cent.

There are 41 such shipments on staging, and Jonas said production has a few hundred. They are mostly test shipments from the drivers' app and some manual entries without a customer. I do not know yet whether they should count as cost.

I told Jonas the facts and proposed two options: keep them in the total as now, or add a switch to hide them. He said he would ask the finance team before deciding.

In the meantime I extended the help text with one sentence saying that unassigned shipments are included in the total. The change is text only and I deployed it with the session fix.

summary: Deployed the last-seen fix for the session list and confirmed on production that an active manager's device now shows a current time.
body:
The last-seen change went out this morning together with the help text sentence about unassigned shipments.

To check it, I looked at the sessions table for my own manager test account on production. Before the deploy its last_seen_at was eight days old. After a few clicks in the dashboard it moved to the current time, and a second click a minute later did not change it, which shows the five-minute throttle works.

I also counted updates per minute on the sessions table for an hour. The rate was the same as before the deploy because the touch statement is unchanged apart from one column.

The session list page in settings shows the new time as a few minutes ago. I asked Jonas to have the manager who reported it look again tomorrow.

summary: Planned the cleanup of the reports table before report sharing goes wider, after finding duplicate saved layouts and orphaned schedules, with five steps and a rollback note.
body:
Sharing reports between managers has been live for a while, and I wanted to see how the data looks before more people use it. I ran a few queries on the staging copy of the reports and schedules tables.

Three things showed up. First, 112 reports have the same owner, name and layout and were saved within seconds of each other. They are double clicks on the save button. Second, 9 schedules point to a report that was deleted, because the delete route removed the report but not its schedules. Third, 31 copies of shared reports exist whose original is gone, so they have a copied_from value that points to nothing.

The duplicates are the most visible to users. A manager sees the same report twice in the list. The orphaned schedules are the most risky, because the scheduler will try to send an email for a report that does not exist. The log has errors for that, about nine per run.

I wrote a plan in five steps.

Step one is to disable the save button while a save is running, so no new duplicates appear. Step two is to add a unique-ish guard on the server: a save with the same owner, name and layout hash within ten seconds returns the existing report. Step three is to change the delete route so that it deletes schedules in the same transaction. Step four is a one-time migration that removes the orphaned schedules. Step five is the cleanup of duplicates, which I will not do automatically.

For the duplicates I want a dry run first. The script prints the groups and which row it would keep, the oldest one, and which rows it would drop. Jonas should see the list before anything is deleted, because a manager might have renamed a copy on purpose.

For copied_from I propose to set the value to null when the original is gone, and not to delete the copies. A copy is a report in its own right. I will add a foreign key with on delete set null so this stays true from now on.

The rollback note: before the migration I take a dump of the reports and schedules tables and keep it for 30 days. The migration runs in one transaction. If the counts after it are not as predicted, 9 fewer schedules and no other changes, it rolls back.

I estimate steps one to three at half a day and step four at an hour. I start with the guard and the delete route, since they stop the problem from growing.

summary: Disabled the report save button during a save and made the server return the existing report on an identical save within ten seconds, which stops new duplicates.
body:
This is steps one and two of this morning's plan for the reports table.

On the front end, the save button in the report builder now goes into a pending state as soon as it is clicked and stays disabled until the request ends. A failed save enables it again and shows the error. Before, there was no pending state, so a double click sent two requests.

On the server, the save handler computes a hash of the layout JSON, with keys in a fixed order so equal layouts give equal hashes. It looks for a report with the same owner, name and hash created in the last ten seconds. If it finds one, it returns that report with status 200 and does not insert. A save that differs in any of the three fields creates a new row as before.

I stored the hash in a new nullable column, layout_hash, with a migration. Existing rows have null, which is fine because only recent rows are compared.

Tests: two identical saves in a row give one row and the same id. Two saves with different names give two rows. A save after eleven seconds, with the clock faked, gives two rows. A race test with two parallel requests gave one row in 20 runs. For this the check and the insert run in one transaction with an advisory lock on the owner id.

All the report tests pass. I did not deploy yet because the delete route change should go out with it.

summary: Made deleting a report remove its schedules in one transaction and added the on delete set null rule for copied reports, then wrote the migration that clears nine orphaned schedules.
body:
This is steps three and four of the plan. I did the delete route first.

The route used to delete the report row and nothing else. The scheduled reports table has a report id column without a constraint, so the schedules stayed behind. I changed the route to open a transaction, delete the schedules of the report, then delete the report, and commit. If either step fails, nothing is deleted.

Then I added constraints so the database enforces what the route does. The schedules table gets a foreign key to reports with on delete cascade. The copied_from column gets a foreign key to reports with on delete set null. The route's explicit delete of schedules remains, because I want the code to say what happens, but the constraint is the safety net.

Adding the foreign keys would fail while the orphans exist, so the order in the migration matters. First it deletes schedules whose report does not exist. Then it sets copied_from to null where the target is gone. Then it adds the constraints.

Before writing it, I ran the select form of both statements on the staging copy. The first matched 9 rows and the second matched 31 rows, as the plan said. I used the select output as the expected counts in the migration's checks.

The migration raises an error and rolls back if the first delete removes a number other than the number found by a count at the start of the same transaction. That sounds redundant, but it catches a change in data between the dry run and the real run, since someone may delete a report in between.

I ran the migration on a fresh restore of the staging dump. It took 90 ms. Then I ran it a second time to check that it can run twice without harm. The second run deleted nothing and the constraints were already there, so it skipped them.

I wrote tests for the route: a report with two schedules is deleted and both schedules are gone, a report with a copy leaves the copy with copied_from null, and a failure in the report delete, forced with a mocked error, leaves the schedules in place.

I took a dump of the production tables before deploying, as the plan says, and put it in the backup folder with a note of the retention. The deploy ran the migration. The log showed 9 schedules removed and 31 references cleared, and the next scheduler run had no errors for the first time in weeks.

Step five, the duplicate cleanup, is next. I will write the dry run script and give Jonas the list.

summary: Wrote the dry run script for duplicate reports, which found 112 duplicates in 64 groups, and sent the list to Jonas without deleting anything.
body:
Step five of the plan is the duplicate cleanup. As agreed, the first version only reports.

The script groups reports by owner, name and layout JSON. For layouts it compares the JSON values, since the new hash column is empty for old rows. Within a group it sorts by creation time and marks the oldest as the one to keep.

On production it found 64 groups with 112 extra rows. Most groups have two rows, the largest has six. I looked at the largest. It belongs to a manager who obviously clicked save several times while the page was slow.

I added two safety rules to the script. A row is never marked for deletion if it is shared, because someone else may have a link to it or have copied from it. A row is also not marked if a schedule points to it. With these rules the number of rows that would be removed dropped from 112 to 97, and the 15 protected rows are listed separately so that Jonas can see why they stay.

The output is a CSV with the group, the owner's email, the report name, the created time, and the planned action. I wrote it to a file and did not put it into the repository, since it has user data.

I sent the CSV to Jonas with a short explanation: nothing has been deleted, 97 rows would be removed, 15 would stay, and the reports kept are always the oldest. I asked him to look for a name where a manager might have meant to keep two versions.

The real run will need a flag, and the script will refuse to run without a dump taken in the last hour. I will add those once Jonas answers.

summary: Wrote a dry run check for the reports cleanup that compares counts before and after on a copy of production, and it found one schedule that the plan would have deleted by mistake.
body: Before the real cleanup of duplicate reports, I restored last night's dump into a scratch database and ran the five planned steps there. The script prints counts per step: reports, schedules, shared flags and copied reports. Four steps matched the plan exactly. In the schedule step, one schedule belonged to a report that was marked as a duplicate, but the schedule itself had been edited and had a different recipient list. The plan would have deleted it together with the duplicate. I changed the rule so that a schedule is moved to the kept report when its recipients or its time differ from the schedule of the kept report. Only schedules that are identical in both are deleted. I ran the whole thing again on the scratch copy. This time the counts of schedules were 12 removed and 1 moved, which I wrote into the plan. I also checked that copied reports still point to a valid original after the merge. Two copies pointed to a duplicate that would have been removed, so the script now re-points them first. The rollback note got a new line about restoring the moved schedule from the dump. I wrote down the queries for the counts so that they can be run again on production after the cleanup. I did not touch production in this session. The next step is to send the changed list to Jonas, because the moved schedule is a change to what he already approved.
