summary: Ran the approved cleanup of 97 duplicate reports and 12 duplicate schedules on production, after Jonas confirmed the list, with a dump first and counts that matched the plan.
body:
Jonas answered after lunch. He went through the CSV and the schedule list and confirmed both, with one exception: a manager had two versions of a report named Weekly summary on purpose, and they differ only in a hidden column. The script treats them as duplicates because the layout JSON is equal except for column order, which my comparison ignored. I had a bug.

The cause was that I normalised the JSON by sorting keys at every level, including the array of columns. Arrays keep their order in JSON, and the order is the meaning of a layout. Sorting the keys of objects is right, sorting arrays is wrong. I fixed the normaliser so arrays keep their order, and the same function is used by the new layout_hash on the server. That means the hash from this morning also had the flaw. I checked: it uses a stable key order for objects only, and arrays are untouched, so the hash was right and only the script was wrong.

After the fix the dry run on production found 94 rows, not 97. The three differing ones belong to the manager Jonas mentioned. They are now kept. The 15 protected rows were unchanged.

The real run needs the two safeguards I planned, so I added them first. A flag, --apply, switches from the dry run to deleting. The script refuses to apply unless a dump file of the reports table younger than one hour exists.

I took the dump, checked its size and that it restores into a scratch database, and then ran the script with --apply. It works in one transaction per group, so a failure leaves earlier groups done and later ones untouched. The output said 94 reports deleted in 61 groups.

I ran the dry run again straight after. It reported zero duplicates, apart from the protected ones.

The schedules went the same way. The dry run found 12 extra rows in 11 groups, the apply removed 12. The scheduler's next run sent one email per schedule, which I verified in the mail log for the 11 affected managers.

I also ran the query for orphaned schedules and copies again and found none, so the constraints from earlier hold.

The dump stays for 30 days, as the plan says. I wrote a short summary of the numbers for Jonas: 94 reports and 12 schedules removed, 3 reports deliberately kept, 15 protected. I put the script into the tools folder with a README line saying it needs a dump and a flag.

This finishes the cleanup. The guards on both forms should stop new duplicates, and I will check the counts again in a week.

summary: Noticed the sessions cleanup job logged a slower run than usual and found it was only a one-time large batch after a long weekend of SSO logins, not a regression.
body:
In the evening I looked at the job logs for other reasons and saw that the old sessions cleanup took 11 seconds, where it normally takes under one.

I checked whether the cleanup had changed. The last change to it was months ago. The query deletes rows past their expiry in batches of 1,000, and the log showed 38 batches this time, against two or three usually.

The number of rows explained the time. Many managers had logged in by SSO on a single day for a training, and their sessions expired together after the idle limit. About 37,000 rows came due in one night, mostly from the identity provider's back-channel checks that each create a row.

I ran explain on the delete. It uses the index on expires_at, and each batch took about 280 ms. That is about 11 seconds in total, as logged, so nothing is slow per row.

The next night's run was normal again. The table has no sign of growth: its size is the same as a week ago.

I did not change anything. One thing for later: the back-channel rows could be avoided, since they are not real devices, but that is the finding from last week and has low priority. I made a note in the journal so that the next person reading the logs does not chase this.

summary: Answered Jonas on how many users have more than three active sessions and whether log out of all devices is used, with counts from production.
body:
Jonas asked two questions in one message: how many users have a lot of devices logged in, and whether anyone uses the log out of all devices button.

For the first I counted active sessions per user, where active means not expired and seen in the last 14 days. Of 412 active users, 301 have one session, 83 have two, 22 have three, and 6 have four or more. The highest is nine, a dispatcher manager who shares a front desk computer login across several browsers. I did not name the user in the answer, just the count.

For the second I searched the audit log for the event of the button. In the last 90 days it was used 14 times by 11 users. In six cases it was followed within a minute by a new login, which looks like someone cleaning up and then continuing. In the others the user did not come back that day, which matches a lost device.

I also checked whether it worked in the 14 cases: for each, the sessions of the user other than the current one were gone from the table, and the current one was kept. So the revoke works as described to Jonas earlier.

I gave Jonas the numbers in a short list. He said the six users with four or more sessions are interesting for the security question the Acme IT department asked, and I offered a note on limiting the number of sessions per user. He wants to think about that.

I did not change anything in the code.

summary: Started the accessibility pass on the report builder column picker, fixing keyboard dragging and announcing moves to screen readers, which the audit had not covered.
body:
The audit by Acme closed with the chart contrast and the skip link, but it did not look at the report builder v2, which is newer. I went through the column picker with the keyboard only to see what a user without a mouse would find.

The result was poor. The columns can only be reordered by dragging, so a keyboard user cannot change the order at all. Focus also disappeared after a drop, and no text told a screen reader what happened.

I added a keyboard path. A focused column item takes Space to pick it up, the arrow keys to move it up or down, and Space again to drop it, with Escape to cancel and put it back. The same functions that the drag handler calls do the moving, so mouse and keyboard end up in the same state.

For announcements I added a visually hidden live region. It says things like: Customer picked up, position 3 of 8; Customer moved to position 2; Customer dropped at position 2. The text lives in the translation files so it can be translated like the rest.

Focus now stays on the moved item after a drop. Before, the list re-rendered with new keys and the focus went to the page body. I fixed that by keeping the key stable per column id and not per position.

I tested with the keyboard in the browser and with VoiceOver on the Mac. The announcements were read in the right order, though VoiceOver read the position twice once, because the live region was updated with the same text twice. I made the update skip equal strings.

Tests: a Vitest test for the move functions at the first and last positions, where the item must not leave the list, and a Playwright test that picks up a column, moves it twice, drops it and checks the order in the saved layout.

Still to do: the buttons for the column width and the sort order, which I have not checked yet, and the labels of the row preview table.

summary: Finished the accessibility pass on the report builder: labels for the width and sort controls, a caption for the row preview, and a fix for a focus trap in the column dialog.
body:
This continues the keyboard work from earlier today, on the rest of the builder.

The width control was a slider without a label. A screen reader read only the value. I added an aria-label that includes the column name, like Width of Customer, and an aria-valuetext in pixels. The sort toggle was an icon button with no text, so it now has a label that states the current state: Sorted ascending, press to sort descending.

The row preview table had no caption, and its header cells had no scope. I added a caption that says Preview of the first 20 rows, and scope=col on the headers. A preview that is still loading now sets aria-busy on the table, and when it finishes the live region says that 20 rows loaded.

Then I found something worse. The dialog for adding a column trapped the focus wrongly. Tab went from the last button back to the browser address bar instead of the first element of the dialog, and Escape did not close it. I looked at the dialog component and saw that it was a div with a role of dialog and no focus handling. I switched it to the existing modal component that the settings page uses, which already handles the focus trap, the Escape key, and returning focus to the button that opened it.

That component needs a title for the label. I passed the visible heading of the dialog, so the name is read when it opens.

Colour was the last thing. The selected column in the picker was shown by a blue background alone. I added a check mark and a bold weight so that the state does not rely on colour, and checked the contrast ratio: 5.1 to 1 for the text on blue, which passes.

I ran axe through the Playwright tests on the builder page. Before the work it reported 11 violations, mostly labels, and now it reports none. I added the axe check as a permanent test for this page so that new controls cannot slip in without labels.

The full test suite passes. I will ask Priya to look at the check mark and the bold weight, since the look of the picker is hers.

I wrote a note for Jonas that the builder now works with the keyboard, in case one of Acme's users needs it.

summary: Priya reviewed the builder's new check mark and focus ring and approved them with one change, then I shipped the accessibility work and checked axe on the live page.
body:
Priya looked at the builder on staging this morning, for the check mark, the bold weight, and the focus ring that I made more visible while testing the keyboard path.

She liked the check mark but found the bold weight made the column names jump in width when selected, which moved the neighbouring items. That is a true flaw that I had not noticed with short names. We tried a medium weight and the jump was almost gone, but not entirely. In the end I kept the normal weight and let the check mark and a two pixel left border carry the state. Contrast and the non-colour cue stay satisfied.

The focus ring was a thin dotted line in the first version. She asked for a solid two pixel ring in the brand colour with an offset, which gives a ratio of 4.6 to 1 against the white background. I changed the shared focus style in the theme file, so it also changes other pages slightly. I looked at the settings page and the tables, and they looked fine to both of us. The dark theme needed its own colour for the ring because the brand colour is too dark there. I used the lighter variant, with a ratio of 6.3 to 1 on the dark background.

One more detail from Priya: the live region text should be short. She suggested dropping the total in Customer picked up, position 3 of 8. I kept the total, since it helps to know where the end is, but shortened the wording of the drop message.

After these changes I ran the whole suite, including Playwright with the axe check, and everything passed. I merged and deployed.

On production I opened the builder with the keyboard and moved three columns, then saved and reloaded. The order was kept. I ran axe through the browser extension on the live page too, and it found no violations.

The session list and the other pages were not touched, apart from the focus ring colour. No errors appeared in the logs in the first hours.

I wrote a line for Jonas about the change and added the builder to the list of audited pages for the next Acme audit, together with the date. No findings are open at the moment.

summary: Checked the same accessibility points on the costs page and fixed three: the table sort buttons had no state, the chart had no text alternative, and the comparison arrows lacked labels.
body:
Right after the builder, I used the same method on the costs page that I shipped a few days ago, since it is also new and not part of the audit.

The sort buttons in the table headers did not tell the state. I added aria-sort to the header cells, with ascending, descending or none, and made the buttons inside them keep a plain label with the column name. The state is now read as sorted ascending when the user focuses on the header.

The bar chart was a canvas with nothing for a screen reader. ECharts has an aria option that creates a description from the data, and I switched it on with a short title, Cost per customer for the top 10 customers. The generated text was long but usable. Besides that, the table next to the chart has the same numbers, so a screen reader user has a full alternative. I added a sentence before the chart that says so, and a link that jumps to the table.

The comparison column used arrows drawn as icons, with colour for increase and decrease. The shapes did serve as a non-colour cue, but the icons were hidden from screen readers, so they said nothing. I added visually hidden text like Up 4.2 percent, Down 1.0 percent, and No earlier data for the dash. The visible number stays the same.

The unassigned line had a small problem: it was in italics to look different, which means nothing for a screen reader. I added the word Unassigned to the row header as a plain label, which was there already, so no change was needed apart from checking that it was read.

Axe found four violations on the page before the work, two missing labels and two for the table headers, and none after. I added the axe check to the Playwright test of the costs page.

A last point was the keyboard path in the hint that holds the help text. The collapsible hint toggled on click but not on Enter, because it was a div with a handler. I replaced it with a button and aria-expanded, and the hint now behaves as expected with the keyboard.

I ran the whole suite and it passed. The changes are small and I deployed them together after a quick look at the page with the keyboard and VoiceOver. The comparison text was read correctly for increases, decreases and the dash.

No open points remain for the costs page. The next audited item on my list is the settings page, with the session list and the revoke buttons.

summary: Wrote the rollout notes for report sharing, listing what managers see, what dispatchers see, and which support questions to expect in the first week.
body:
After the cleanup of the reports table and the accessibility pass, report sharing was ready to go wider, so I wrote a short rollout note for Jonas. It says managers can set the shared flag and copy a shared report. Dispatchers can open a shared report but get a 403 on copy, as Jonas decided.

I added three expected questions with answers: why a copied report does not follow changes to the original, why a deleted original leaves the copy in place, and why a schedule is not copied. The schedule point matters, because a copy that silently sent emails would surprise people.

I checked each claim against staging with a manager account and a dispatcher account. One sentence in the first draft was wrong: copies keep the column widths, not only the order. I corrected it. Jonas will forward the note to the managers tomorrow. Nothing in the code changed in this session.

summary: Found that scheduled report emails for shared reports went out under the owner's role, so a dispatcher recipient could receive data the role check hides, and fixed the check.
body:
Jonas asked whether a dispatcher who receives a scheduled report by email sees the same columns as in the app. I traced the scheduler code in server/jobs/scheduledReports.ts and found it builds the attachment with the report owner's role, not the recipient's.

For most reports this made no difference. The costs-based reports are a manager-only topic, though, and a manager could add a dispatcher address as a recipient. The dispatcher would then get a file the app would never show them.

I wrote a failing test first: a manager-owned costs report with a dispatcher recipient. The test expected the attachment to be refused and it was not. The fix passes the recipient's role into the query builder and skips the recipient when the role may not read the report. The skipped recipient is logged with the report id.

I also changed the schedule form. When a manager types an address that belongs to a dispatcher account, the form shows a warning that the person will not get this report. External addresses without an account still work as before, because those are the common case for Acme's customers' contacts.

The test suite passed with the new case, and I ran the scheduler against a copy of production data in dry mode. It found four schedules that would now skip a recipient. I listed them for Jonas instead of changing them. He will decide whether to ask the managers to remove those addresses. I did not deploy yet, because a skipped recipient changes what people receive, and Jonas should know first.

summary: Jonas approved the recipient role check for scheduled reports and I deployed it, with a note to the four managers whose schedules skip a recipient.
body:
Jonas replied to the list of four schedules and said skipping is correct. He will tell the managers himself, so I did not send any email from the app.

I deployed the change to Render after the pipeline passed. Then I looked at the scheduler log for the next run, which was at noon. It processed 38 schedules, sent 37 attachments in total to the expected recipients and logged four skipped recipients, each with a report id that matched my list.

One detail I checked on purpose: the attachment for a skipped recipient is not generated at all, so there is no wasted export. The run time was the same as before.

I added a line to the help text of the schedule form so the warning is explained. Left open: a recipient who changes role later is only checked at send time, which is fine.

summary: Deployed the recipient role check for scheduled shared reports, then verified on production that dispatcher recipients get only what the role allows.
body:
Slot 3 shipped the recipient role check yesterday, and this session was the follow-up on production. The goal was to prove that the fix works for real schedules, not only in the tests, and to see whether any email was lost by mistake.

I started with the schedules that have a shared report. There are 52 of them, and 9 have at least one dispatcher as a recipient. For those 9 I ran the send job in dry mode against production data. The job now builds one email per recipient and applies that recipient's role instead of the owner's role. The dry run listed 11 recipients that would be skipped, and I compared the list with the one I sent to the four managers. It matched exactly, so no schedule is skipped that I did not announce.

Then I checked what a dispatcher sees. I made a test dispatcher account and added it as a recipient to a copy of a shared costs report. The attachment held only the columns the dispatcher role may read. The costs by customer columns were gone, and the email body said that some columns were left out because of the role. Before the fix the same email carried the full table.

I also looked at the edge cases:
- A schedule whose only recipient is a dispatcher and whose report is all hidden columns now sends nothing and writes a log line with the schedule id. I left this as is, because an empty attachment would only confuse people.
- A recipient who is not a user of the dashboard, an external email address, is treated like a dispatcher. That is the safer default, and I noted it in the rollout notes.
- A recipient whose role changed since the schedule was saved is read fresh at send time, so a promoted dispatcher gets the full report on the next run.

After that I read this morning's production run in the logs. 38 schedules ran, 38 sent, and the run took about the usual time. Two emails had the skipped recipient note, both for schedules that belong to managers I had written to. No bounce and no error came up.

One small thing is left. The settings page still shows a recipient list without any hint that a dispatcher will get fewer columns. I wrote that down as a small task and asked Priya for a wording for the hint. Next I will watch the support inbox for a week, as the rollout notes say, and only then close the topic.

summary: Checked the 401 counts after deploying the session expiry fix: SSO users no longer drop out after two hours, and the login dialog was used six times without lost work.
body:
I looked at the logs of the last evening and this morning. Before the fix there were about 25 unexpected 401 responses per day from SSO users. Since the deploy there were three, all from sessions created before it.

The new login dialog opened six times. In five cases the user logged in again and the request was retried. In one case the user closed the tab. No report state was lost in the logged cases.

I saw no change in the cleanup job duration. I closed the topic and noted in the help text that sessions last 8 hours of inactivity for everybody.

summary: Built the first version of the saved filter presets for the shipments table, stored per user in Postgres, with a menu to save, apply and delete them.
body:
Dispatchers asked for a way to keep their usual filters, like one depot with late shipments only. I planned the smallest useful version: a preset has a name, a JSON object of the filters and the owner. No sharing for now, since report sharing has just been rolled out and I do not want two sharing models at once.

The migration adds a table filter_presets with user_id, name, filters jsonb and created_at, and a unique index on user and name. The API has three endpoints: list, create and delete. Create returns a 409 on a duplicate name, and the UI shows that as an inline message.

On the front end I added a Presets button next to the filter bar. It opens a menu with the saved names, a Save current filters entry and a delete icon per row. Applying a preset sets the same URL parameters the filters already use, so the back button and links keep working.

One problem came up quickly. The date filter stores a relative range, like last 7 days, as well as absolute dates, and I first saved the absolute dates that were resolved at that moment. A preset for the last 7 days would then show last week forever. I changed the saved shape to keep the relative form as it is and resolve it when applied.

I also had to decide what happens when a preset refers to a depot that was removed. The filter bar now drops unknown values and shows a small notice that one value no longer exists.

Tests: four API tests for the endpoints and ownership, plus a component test for the relative date case. Playwright covers saving, reloading and applying a preset. The button label and menu are keyboard reachable, following what I learned in the accessibility pass.

Still open are renaming a preset and a limit on how many a user may save. I will ask Priya how the menu should look with more than ten entries.

summary: Added a limit of 20 filter presets per user and a rename action, after Priya asked for a menu that still works with many entries.
body:
Priya looked at the presets menu and said ten entries is already long, and that a menu of 40 would be useless. We agreed on a limit of 20 per user, with a message that names the limit when it is reached.

The API now returns a 422 with a clear code when the user has 20 presets. The UI turns the Save entry into a disabled line that explains why. I added a test that creates 20 and checks the 21st fails.

Rename was added as a PATCH endpoint. It uses the same unique rule on the name, so a rename to an existing name returns 409. In the menu, rename is a small pencil that switches the label to an input. Escape cancels and Enter saves.

Priya also asked for the active preset to show a check mark, as in the report builder. I reused that component. When the current filters differ from the preset by even one value, the check disappears, which I compare with a sorted JSON string.

The menu list now scrolls after eight rows. I tested keyboard focus inside the scroll area with the arrow keys. Next is deploying behind no flag, since the feature touches nothing existing.

summary: Deployed the filter presets, then fixed a bug in which a preset with a depot filter showed all shipments after a page reload because the depot ids were compared as numbers and strings.
body:
I deployed the presets in the morning. Within an hour a dispatcher wrote to Jonas that her preset for one depot showed everything after reloading the page. I could reproduce it with a preset saved from the URL.

The cause was a type mismatch. When a user picks a depot in the UI, the filter holds a number. When it comes from the URL it is a string. The preset saved the number, and the apply step wrote it to the URL, which is fine. After reload the state held a string, the check for known depots used strict equality against numbers, and the value was dropped as unknown. The filter bar then showed no depot filter at all.

The notice about removed values did not show up either, because the drop happened before the code that counts dropped values. That made the problem silent.

I changed the known-value check to compare as strings, and moved the counting before the drop so both cases are visible. I wrote a test that loads the table from a URL with a depot id, and one with a depot that does not exist.

I also checked the other filters for the same slip. The status filter uses strings everywhere and was fine. The customer filter has the same number and string problem as depots, and I fixed it in the same function.

Before deploying the fix I looked for affected presets in the database. The stored JSON was correct in every row, so no data repair was needed. I deployed the fix after the tests passed and asked the dispatcher to try again. She confirmed it works.

Lesson for me: normalize ids at the edge when reading the URL, not in each filter. I left a note in the code and put the cleanup on my list.

summary: Normalized filter values once at the URL boundary of the shipments table, so depots, customers and statuses no longer need their own string and number handling.
body:
After yesterday's preset bug I did the cleanup I had noted. All filter state used to be parsed in several places. Now one function, parseFilters in src/table/filters.ts, reads the URL and returns typed values, with ids as strings throughout.

I removed the three local conversions in the depot, customer and status filter components. They now take the strings as given. The chart pages use the same filter code for their queries, and I checked that the API accepts strings for ids, which it did.

The tests for the filters passed unchanged, which was the point. I added a table-driven test for parseFilters with 12 inputs, including an empty value, a repeated parameter and an unknown key.

I clicked through the shipments table, the costs page and the report builder preview with a depot filter. They all showed the same counts for the same filter. No visible change is expected, and none was found.

summary: Answered Jonas on how many managers use filter presets in the first week: 14 of 31 saved at least one, with a median of two presets each.
body:
Jonas asked whether the presets were worth the effort. I queried filter_presets on production, grouped by role.

The result: 41 presets from 19 users. Of the 31 managers, 14 saved at least one, and of the dispatchers 5 did. The median is two presets per user, and the highest is seven. Nobody is near the limit of 20.

The most common saved filter is a single depot with a status. I wrote the numbers and the query in a reply and made clear the first week mostly shows curiosity, so a second look in a month is more useful.

summary: Investigated why the shipments table feels slow for dispatchers with very wide date ranges and found the count query scans the whole table, then added an index and a capped count.
body:
A dispatcher complained that opening the table with the range of the last year takes about six seconds. I measured the API: the list query for 50 rows took 90 ms, but the total count took 5.4 seconds.

I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a copy of production. The count used a sequential scan over 2.1 million shipment rows, because the planner expected most rows to match the date range and the depot filter has low selectivity. The list query could stop after 50 rows, which hid the problem.

Two changes came out of this. First, an index on shipments (depot_id, created_at), which helps the common case of one depot. With it, the count for one depot and one year fell to 700 ms. Second, for ranges where the count would exceed 10,000 rows, the API now counts at most 10,001 rows with a limited subquery and returns a flag that the total is a lower bound.

The UI shows 10,000+ in that case, and the pager shows next and previous without the last-page link. I checked with Jonas's team's use that nobody jumps to the last page of a large result.

The index build took 40 seconds on the copy. I used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY for production so writes do not block. I wrote the migration with a note that it cannot run inside a transaction, and the migration runner needed a flag for that. Adding the flag took longer than the index itself.

I wrote tests for the capped count with a small cap set by config, so the test does not need 10,000 rows. I also checked that sorting by cost still uses its own index and is not made slower.

After deploying to staging the table with the one-year range opened in 400 ms. The costs page uses different queries and is unchanged. Next I will watch the production index build and the slow query log.

summary: Ran the concurrent index build on production for the shipments table and checked the slow query log, which no longer lists the count query.
body:
I ran the migration on production in the evening when few dispatchers were active. The build of the index on shipments (depot_id, created_at) took 2 minutes 10 seconds, longer than on the copy, with no lock waits and no errors from the API during the build.

After the build I checked that the index is valid with a query on pg_index, since a failed concurrent build leaves an invalid index. It was valid.

Then I ran EXPLAIN on the real count query for a depot and a year. It uses the new index, and the actual time was 640 ms. The unfiltered case for all depots still takes about 2 seconds with the cap, which is acceptable. It stops at 10,001 rows instead of scanning everything.

I waited for the traffic of the evening and read the slow query log, with the threshold at 1 second. Before the change it had about 30 entries per day for the count query. In the two hours after, it had none from the table.

One new entry appeared, from the scheduled report job, which runs a similar count for its summary line. That job does not need an exact total either, so I put it on my list instead of changing it at night.

I also updated the help text for the table: it now explains that 10,000+ means more than ten thousand matches and that a narrower filter shows the exact number.

Open items are the report job count and a check of the disk size of the index, which is 180 MB. That is fine for now.

summary: Investigated why the nightly scheduled report job is slow and planned to reuse the capped count from the shipments table for the summary line.
body:
The slow entry from the report job in the log looked real, so I spent the morning on it. Each schedule runs a count for the line that says how many rows the report has, and for wide reports this is the slowest step.

I looked at the capped count function that came with the table work and checked that it can be called from the report job without the table's URL filter handling. It can, as long as the filters are passed in the normalized form. I have not changed the job yet. The plan is to call the capped count for the summary line and to word it as more than 10,000 rows when the cap is hit. The attachment must still contain all rows, so I will not touch that part.

I ran the job against a copy of production and timed it as a baseline: 11 minutes 20 seconds for 38 schedules. Most of that time sits in the count for the wide schedules, and the rest is in the larger exports, which I know are slow and which I will not look at yet.

I wrote down what to check once the change exists: compare the attachments of old and new versions byte by byte for five schedules, add a test for the wording of a count under and over the cap, and make sure the email still uses the schedule's time zone for the date, which was fixed earlier.

I asked Jonas whether the wording more than 10,000 rows is fine for the managers, and I am waiting for his answer before I write the code.

summary: Read the morning scheduled report run on production after the capped count change: all 38 schedules sent and the total run took 3 minutes 40 seconds.
body:
The first run after the change was clean. All 38 schedules sent, and four recipients were skipped as before for the role check, with the same report ids as in my list.

The summary line showed more than 10,000 rows for seven reports and exact counts for the others. I opened two of the emails sent to Jonas's test address and the text read well.

The run took 3 minutes 40 seconds, a bit faster than the test on the copy. The database showed no long queries during it.

One manager replied to an email to ask what more than 10,000 rows means. I pointed her to the help text of the table, which says the same. I will add a short sentence to the email footer so it is explained there too.

summary: Started the upgrade of Vite and its plugins to the next major version, got the dev server and build running, and listed three breaking changes still open in the tests.
body:
Vite has a new major version, and the changelog mentions dropped support for older Node versions, which Render already is above. I created an upgrade commit in the main checkout and bumped vite, the React plugin and Vitest together, since their versions are linked.

The install worked with one peer dependency warning from a chart helper package, which I ignored for now because it only complains about the range. The dev server started at once, and the first page rendered.

The production build then failed with an error about a deprecated option, build.polyfillModulePreload in vite.config.ts. I replaced it with the new modulePreload setting. The next build passed and produced a bundle 3 percent smaller than before: 1.41 MB before the gzip step, 1.37 MB after.

I compared the output chunks. The ECharts chunk was split a bit differently, and the main chunk lost about 20 KB. Nothing was missing, and the lazy loaded report builder chunk was still separate.

Vitest was the harder part. Out of 412 tests, 9 failed. I sorted them into three groups. Five fail because the mocked module path for the API client changed with the new resolver, two fail on a snapshot of CSS class names that changed order, and two fail on a timer test that depends on the fake timer behavior.

I fixed the mock paths and the snapshots in about half an hour. The timer tests were not quick. They test the idle dialog that I wrote for the session expiry, and they use advanceTimersByTime with a promise inside. The new Vitest handles pending promises differently, so I need to switch to the async variant of the timer call.

I did not finish this. Two tests still fail and I did not run Playwright at all. The commit stays local until all pass.

Things to check next: the Playwright run against the new build, the source maps on Render, and the sentry upload step in the build script, which uses a Vite plugin that may need its own upgrade.

summary: Fixed the last two failing timer tests for the new Vitest by switching to the async timer helpers, so the Vite upgrade has a green unit suite.
body:
The two failing tests were for the idle dialog. They advanced fake timers and then checked that the dialog appeared, but a promise inside the handler had not resolved by then.

I changed both to advanceTimersByTimeAsync and awaited it. The first passed at once. The second still failed, and the reason was that the test also used a real fetch mock that returned after a real delay. I replaced it with a mock that resolves immediately.

All 412 tests passed after that, in 38 seconds against 44 before. I ran the suite three times to be sure the timer tests are not flaky, and it was green each time.

I also ran the type check, which passed. Playwright comes next, since it needs the production build served locally.

summary: Ran Playwright against the Vite upgrade, found a broken CSS import order that made the dark theme flash light on load, and fixed it before merging.
body:
I built the app and served it locally for the end-to-end tests. 58 of 61 scenarios passed at first. Three failed, all in the theme tests.

The failing step was a check that the page background is dark right after load for a user with the dark theme saved. In the new build it was light for a moment. A screenshot taken at the first paint showed a white flash for about 150 ms.

I looked at the generated HTML and the CSS. The new Vite version emits the CSS of the lazy theme file after the main one, and the base styles set a light background on the body. Before the upgrade, the theme file was inlined into the first chunk by the way the old version ordered imports.

I had two options. The first was to keep depending on the order, which is fragile. The second was to set the theme class on the html element in a tiny inline script in index.html, before any CSS loads, and to base the background on that class. I chose the second.

The inline script reads the saved theme from local storage and sets a data-theme attribute. The base CSS now uses the attribute for the background color. If nothing is saved, it follows the system setting, as before.

I made sure the script has no dependency and runs in less than a millisecond. The content security policy on Render allows inline scripts with a hash, so I added the hash to the header config, which I had nearly forgotten. Without it the script would be blocked in production and the test would not have shown it, because the local server has no such header.

To check this, I added a Playwright test that serves the build with the same policy header. It passed with the script and failed without the hash, which proves the test is useful.

After this all 61 scenarios passed. I also checked the dark theme by eye on the shipments table, the costs page and the report builder. No flash was visible, even with the CPU throttled to four times slower.

Next are the source maps and the Sentry plugin, then a staging deploy.

summary: Checked that the Sentry plugin and source maps still work with the new Vite, using a deliberate error on staging, and found the plugin needed a minor version bump.
body:
The Sentry plugin printed a warning about the new Vite, but the upload worked. To be certain I deployed the branch to staging and threw an error from a hidden test button.

The event reached Sentry, but the stack trace was not mapped for one chunk. The plugin version was one minor release behind and did not know the new chunk naming. After the bump, the same test gave a readable trace with file names and lines.

I removed the test button, and the upgrade is ready to merge tomorrow after one more look at the bundle sizes.

summary: Merged the Vite upgrade after a last staging check and deployed it to production, with a smaller bundle and no change in the error rate in the first hours.
body:
I read through the diff once more: config changes, the inline theme script with its hash, the plugin bumps and the test fixes. Then I ran the whole pipeline on the branch, and all of it was green.

On staging I opened the main pages with the dark and the light theme and with a cold cache. The first load was a bit faster, 1.6 seconds against 1.8 on the throttled profile.

I merged and deployed. Render built it in about three minutes. The first thing I checked on production was the response header with the policy hash, which was present.

I watched Sentry for two hours. The error rate was the same as the week before, and the traces had readable lines. Nobody reported a flash of light theme.

I left a short note in the repository readme about the inline script and its hash, since changing that script means updating the header.

summary: Looked into the request from Jonas to show the last login time per user on the settings page, and found the data exists in the sessions table but SSO logins write it differently.
body:
Jonas wants managers to see when each invited user last logged in, because they invite many people and some never start. I checked what data exists.

The session rows hold created_at and last_seen. Created_at is a good stand-in for login time, but it shows only the live sessions, because the cleanup job removes old ones. So for a user whose last session was cleaned up three weeks ago, the page would show nothing.

That means a separate column is needed. I planned to add last_login_at to the users table and to set it in both login paths. The password login and the SSO callback have different code, which I know from the expiry problem, so I looked at both and wrote a shared function, recordLogin(userId), called from each.

The migration adds the column with null as default. I wrote a backfill that sets last_login_at from the newest existing session where there is one. For users without a session it stays null and the page will say Never or No recent login. I cannot tell these two apart, so the text is No login recorded.

The settings page for managers gets a new column in the user table, sorted by that value, with a relative time and the exact time in a tooltip. I added the time zone from the user's settings, which I did not forget this time.

One privacy question came up. Dispatchers must not see the column, and the API should not send it to them at all. I made the field part of the manager response only and tested that a dispatcher request returns no such key.

Tests: the two login paths each set the value, the backfill is idempotent, and the dispatcher test. The Playwright test for the settings page was updated.

I have not deployed it. Jonas should confirm the wording, and the backfill needs a dump first.

summary: Ran the backfill for last_login_at on production after a dump and checked that 143 of 171 users got a value, with the rest showing no login recorded.
body:
Jonas approved the wording, so I took a dump of the users table first. Then I ran the migration and the backfill in one go. It took under a second.

The result: 143 users got a value from their newest session, and 28 had no session left and stayed null. I looked at a sample of the 28 and found 19 who were invited but had never accepted the invitation, which makes sense. The other 9 are older accounts, probably inactive.

I checked that running the backfill a second time changes nothing. The count was the same.

The settings page showed the new column for a manager account and no column for a dispatcher account. Sorting by last login put the null values at the end, as I wanted.

summary: Added a reminder action next to users who never logged in, so managers can resend the invitation email in one click, with a limit of one per day per user.
body:
With the new column, managers saw 19 users who had never accepted an invite. The next obvious step was a way to resend the invitation. Before this, they had to delete and invite again.

I added a Resend button for users without a recorded login who still have a pending invitation. The endpoint creates a new invitation token, which replaces the old one, and sends the same email. The old link then no longer works, which I explained in the confirmation text.

To stop mistakes and abuse, there is a limit of one resend per user per day. The API returns a 429 with the time when the next one is possible, and the button shows that time as a disabled hint. I store the last send time on the invitation row.

The email template needed no change, but I found that the link text said Accept your invitation and the expiry of seven days was hard coded in the text, while the code used a config value. I made the text use the config value so they cannot differ.

Tests: the resend replaces the token, the old token fails, the limit works, a user with a login cannot be resent, and a dispatcher gets 403. I tested on staging with a real mailbox, and the email arrived in a few seconds.

Accessibility: the button has an accessible name that includes the user's email, so a screen reader does not hear Resend 19 times without context.

I deployed this in the late evening. The effect of the first real use will show tomorrow, when Jonas tells the managers.

summary: Checked the first day of invitation resends: managers sent 11, five of the users have logged in since, and no email bounced.
body:
I looked at the invitation table and the mail provider's log this morning. Eleven resends were made yesterday evening and at night, by four managers. The limit blocked two attempts, both by one manager who pressed the button twice, and the 429 hint showed as designed.

Of the 11 invited users, five have logged in since, which the new last_login_at column confirms. That is a better rate than I hoped for. Two emails went to addresses at one customer's domain, and neither bounced.

I read the log for errors in the resend endpoint and found none. The old tokens were rejected correctly in three cases where users clicked an old link, and they saw the page that says the invitation has been replaced.

That page was plain, so I changed its text to tell the user to look for the newest email, and to ask their manager if none came. It is a small copy change, tested with the existing page test.

Next I will leave the feature alone for a week and look at the numbers again. If many users still do not log in, the problem is probably the email and not the dashboard.

summary: Checked the settings page last-login column on a narrow screen and fixed the truncated email addresses, which hid the resend button on small laptops.
body:
Jonas mentioned that on his laptop the resend reminder button next to users who never logged in was cut off. I reproduced it at 1280 pixels wide in the main checkout. The email column had no max width, so long addresses pushed the actions column out of the card.

I gave the email cell an ellipsis with a title attribute and let the actions column keep its minimum width. I checked widths of 1024, 1280 and 1440 in the browser and added one Playwright screenshot check for 1024. It passed, and I deployed it. Priya looked at the screenshot and had no remarks.

summary: Started the work on cost breakdown by depot on the costs page, which Jonas wants for the monthly review, and settled the query and the first chart on staging.
body:
Jonas asked for a view of delivery costs per depot, split into fuel, driver time and tolls, because the monthly review currently uses a spreadsheet. I began by reading how the costs page gets its numbers. It calls /api/costs/summary, which groups by week and has no depot dimension.

I wrote a new endpoint, /api/costs/by-depot, that takes the same date range and returns one row per depot with the three cost parts. The first version joined costs to shipments and then to depots, and on staging with a full year of data it took 2.8 seconds. The plan showed a sequential scan on the cost lines table.

The cost lines table has an index on shipment_id but not on the booking date, and the date filter was applied after the join. I rewrote the query to filter cost lines by date first in a subquery and then join. That brought it to 310 ms on staging.

I checked that the totals agree with the existing summary. For the last full quarter the sum over all depots was 1,284,730.12 and the summary page showed the same number. Two depots had cost lines with a null depot because of old imports. I put them in a row called Unassigned instead of dropping them, so the total still matches.

For the chart I used a stacked horizontal bar in ECharts, one bar per depot, sorted by total. The first version had 23 bars and looked crowded. I limited it to the top 10 by default with a link to show all, which Priya had asked for in the older costs designs.

I wrote Vitest tests for the mapping of rows to series, including the Unassigned row and an empty range. A Playwright test loads the page with seeded data and checks the bar count. All tests passed locally.

What is left is the table below the chart with the same numbers, the export of it, and the label colors, which need a check by Priya. I did not deploy yet, only staging. Next I will build the table and ask Priya about colors.

summary: Added the depot cost table below the chart and found that sorting by cost sorted the formatted strings, so 9,000 came after 10,000, and fixed it.
body:
I continued the depot costs work with the table under the stacked bar chart. It shows depot, fuel, driver time, tolls and total, with the total sorted descending by default.

While testing the sort buttons on staging I saw that clicking sort on fuel put 9,420 below 10,350. The table component sorted by the cell text, because the column definition used a formatter that returned strings and the sort read the rendered value. The older costs table did not show this because its values were passed as numbers with a cell renderer.

I changed the column definitions so each column has a raw numeric accessor and a separate format function. The sort now uses the accessor. I added a Vitest test with 9,000 and 10,000 as the first case, and a case with the Unassigned row, which should always stay last regardless of the sort direction. That second rule was new, and I put it in the comparator.

I also checked the accessibility points that I fixed last week on the costs page. The new sort buttons use the same aria-sort state, and the table has a caption with the date range. axe found no problems on the page locally.

The number format shows the currency without decimals in the table and with two decimals in the tooltip of the chart. Jonas had said in the past that managers dislike cents in overviews, so that fits. I wrote it down in the component as a comment with the reason.

I deployed it to staging and let Jonas look at it at lunch. He asked for one change, a column for cost per shipment, because depots of different sizes cannot be compared by totals. That needs the shipment count per depot, which the query can return with one more count, so I will do it next.

summary: Added cost per shipment to the depot costs view, which needed a shipment count per depot, and found the count was inflated by multi-leg shipments until I counted distinct ids.
body:
Jonas wanted a cost per shipment column on the depot table so depots of different sizes can be compared. I added a count of shipments to the by-depot query and divided the total by it.

The first numbers looked wrong. One depot showed a cost per shipment of 4.10 while the dispatchers say a typical shipment costs around 11 to 14. The count was too high. Shipments with several legs have several cost lines, and my join produced one row per line, so a shipment with three legs was counted three times.

I changed the count to count(distinct shipment_id). The same depot now showed 12.35, which fits. I compared three depots by hand with a manual query on the staging copy and the numbers agreed to the cent.

Two other things came up. First, a depot with zero shipments in the range but some cost lines, for example a late invoice, would divide by zero. The API now returns null for the cost per shipment in that case and the table shows a dash. Second, the sort on this column must treat null as smallest, so I extended the comparator test.

I also changed the chart. A second chart mode can switch between total cost and cost per shipment, using the same data. I used a small segmented control instead of two charts, since the page is already long. Keyboard focus and the labels follow the same pattern as the range control.

The Vitest and Playwright runs were green. I deployed to staging and sent Jonas the link. He will check it with the numbers from his spreadsheet. If they match, it goes to production in the next days, together with the export of the table.

summary: Jonas compared the depot costs with his spreadsheet and found one depot off by 3 percent, which was a currency rounding difference in how I summed the lines.
body:
Jonas sent a list of eight depots from his spreadsheet and the view on staging agreed for seven. One depot was off by about 3 percent, 41,230 in the spreadsheet against 42,480 in the view.

I looked at its cost lines. The depot had many tolls booked in a foreign currency, converted at booking time into a stored euro amount. My query summed the stored amount, but the spreadsheet recalculated with the monthly rate, so his number was the one that differed. The existing summary page also sums the stored amount, so the view is consistent with the rest of the dashboard.

I explained this to Jonas with the three largest lines. He agreed the stored amount is right for the reports and that the spreadsheet will be dropped. I added a note under the table that amounts use the rate at booking time. No code change was needed apart from this text.

summary: Added a CSV export button to the depot cost table, reusing the table export helper, and noted that exports of this size are fine since the table has at most a few dozen rows.
body:
The depot table needed an export, as Jonas had asked. I used the existing client-side CSV helper that the other tables use, since this table has only one row per depot, so around 25 rows.

The helper takes column definitions, so I passed the raw numeric accessors and not the formatted text. That way the CSV has plain numbers and Excel can sum them. The Unassigned row is exported as the last row. I added a test for a depot name with a comma and a quote, which the helper escapes correctly.

I did not touch the large exports. Those still time out for very big shipment tables, and that is a separate problem that I have on the list. This export is small and not affected.

I deployed the depot costs view to production after Jonas confirmed his numbers. I checked the page once on production with a real range and the by-depot endpoint answered in 290 ms.

summary: Investigated reports of dispatchers being asked to log in again after a laptop wakes from sleep, and found the session cookie was refreshed only on page loads, not on background polling.
body:
Two dispatchers wrote to Jonas that the dashboard asks for a login after they come back to a laptop that slept. The sessions last 12 hours with a sliding expiry, so a short sleep should not matter. I started with the production logs for one of the two users.

Her session row had a last_seen_at from 07:40 and an expiry of 19:40, which is correct. But after wake-up, at 10:55, the first request returned 401. So the session was still valid in the table, yet the request failed.

The cause was in the cookie. The server sets the cookie with a max age of 12 hours only when the session is touched, and I had made the touch happen on normal API calls. The dashboard also polls a lightweight status endpoint for the shipment counter every minute. That endpoint was excluded from the touch, to save database writes, which I did when the cleanup job was written. That is fine for the table, but the browser cookie had an absolute expiry set at the last touch from a normal call. For users who left the dashboard open on the shipments view, only polling ran, and the cookie expired in the browser while the row stayed valid.

I reproduced it locally by setting the cookie max age to two minutes and keeping only the polling active. After two minutes the browser dropped the cookie and the next call returned 401, as for the dispatcher.

The fix is to have the polling endpoint refresh the cookie but not write to the database more than once every five minutes. I added a check on last_seen_at with a five minute threshold in the session middleware, and the response sets the cookie header each time. The write load stays almost the same, since the extra writes are limited to one per five minutes per session.

I wrote a test with a fake clock that runs polling for 13 hours and checks that the session survives, and that a session without any call for 12 hours and a minute is expired. Both passed. The middleware tests for the older behavior also passed.

I did not deploy yet. I want to look at the write numbers on production for a day first, using the staging copy of the traffic pattern, and then deploy in the morning so I can watch it.

summary: Wrote the pre-release checklist for the depot cost view and ran it on staging, which caught a cost total that ignored the selected date range on the CSV button.
body:
Jonas wants the depot costs page ready for his monthly review, so I wrote a short checklist and ran it against staging this morning. It covers the totals, the sorting, the cost per shipment column, the CSV button and the empty states.

Most items passed at once. The chart, the table and the cost per shipment agreed with each other for three different date ranges, and they still matched Jonas's spreadsheet after the rounding fix from last week.

The CSV button failed one check. When the date range was changed after the page loaded, the export still used the range from the first load, because the helper captured the filter values when the component mounted. A manager could therefore download a file whose total differed from the table on screen. This is the kind of mismatch Jonas would notice in the review.

I changed the button to read the current range from the URL state at click time instead of at mount. I added a Vitest case that changes the range and checks the query parameters of the export call. I also ran the same flow by hand with a range of one week and one of a full quarter, and the totals in the file matched the table both times.

Two smaller things came up. The empty state for a depot with no costs in the range showed a zero with a currency sign, which looks like data, so it now shows a dash. The tab order skipped the sort buttons in the table header on one browser, which I traced to a stray tabindex and removed.

I did not deploy yet. The checklist is in the repository notes so it can be reused for the next page. Next I will show the page to Priya for the spacing of the chart legend, then release it.

summary: Checked the 401 counts on the first full working day after the cookie refresh: none on the status endpoint, so the sleep logout problem is closed.
body:
I counted the 401 responses on the status endpoint for today until noon. There were none, against about 15 on a normal working day before the change.

The overall 401 count for the API was 22, which is in line with normal expired and logged out sessions. I looked at the five users with the most 401s and each of them had used log out of all devices or had an expired session after a long absence. None of them were the sleep case.

I told Jonas that the two dispatchers should not see the problem again. The write load on the sessions table is still about 6 percent higher than before, and I left the five minute threshold as it is.

summary: Began the report builder v2 option to group rows by depot and week, and found the grouping happens in the browser, which gets slow above about 20,000 rows, so I moved it to the API.
body:
Jonas asked for grouping in the report builder, so a report can show shipments per depot per week with subtotals, not only flat rows. I started with a version in the browser, since the builder already loads the rows for the preview.

It worked on small ranges. With a quarter of data, around 38,000 rows, the preview froze for about four seconds while grouping and the page used 400 MB of memory in the profiler. A flat preview shows only the first 50 rows, which is why this had not shown before; grouping needs all rows.

So I moved the grouping into the API. The report endpoint now accepts a group_by list, with depot, week, month, customer and status as allowed values, and builds a group by query. I validated the list against a fixed set, so no column name from the request goes into the SQL text. Subtotals use the same query with a rollup, which Postgres supports directly.

The response has one row per group with the chosen sums and counts. For the quarter of data it takes 180 ms. The preview in the browser only draws what it gets, with expandable groups.

The builder UI got a small section called Group by with up to two levels. I limited it to two because three levels made the preview hard to read, and Priya agreed in her mock-ups. The order of levels can be changed with up and down buttons, which are keyboard friendly, following last week's accessibility work.

The saved report definition has a new field for the grouping. Old reports have none and load as flat. I wrote a migration that adds a nullable json column and I checked that the old reports still open. I also checked that scheduled reports use the same definition, so a grouped report can be sent by email, but the email rendering of groups is not done yet. For now the scheduled job skips grouping and sends the flat version, which would be misleading, so I added a guard that refuses to save a schedule for a grouped report until the email part exists.

Tests are green, 14 new Vitest cases for the query builder, including a hostile column name that must be rejected. The next step is the email rendering of groups and the CSV export of grouped reports.

summary: Wrote the email rendering for grouped reports, with a subtotal row per group, and lifted the guard on schedules after sending test mails to three clients.
body:
The scheduled reports build their email from the same rows as the web report, so I extended the renderer for groups. Each group becomes a header row with the group name, its rows below, and a subtotal row in bold.

Email clients are picky. I used a plain table with inline styles, as the existing mails do, and no nested tables. I sent test mails to Gmail, Outlook on the web and Apple Mail. In Outlook the subtotal rows lost their top border, so I changed the border to a background color which survived in all three.

The CSV attachment of a grouped report has one extra column with the group name and the subtotal rows marked in a column called row_type. I chose this over blank lines since people load these files into Excel and need to filter them.

I removed the guard against schedules for grouped reports and added a test for it. Next I will ask Jonas which managers should try the grouping first.

summary: Fixed a column picker bug in the grouped reports that dropped the group-by setting when a saved report was duplicated, after a manager reported two copies behaving differently.
body:
A manager told Jonas that a duplicated report did not group rows like the original. Jonas passed it on this morning, and I reproduced it on staging in a few minutes.

The duplicate action copied the columns, filters and sort order of a saved report but built the new record from a list of fields that was written before grouping existed. The group-by levels were therefore left out, and the copy opened as a flat table. The original was never affected, and no data was lost.

Instead of adding the missing field to the list, I changed the duplicate action to copy the whole stored definition and then overwrite only the name and the owner. That way the next option added to reports will not be dropped in the same way. I added a test that creates a report with every option set, duplicates it, and compares the two definitions apart from name and owner.

I then checked production with a read-only query for reports whose names end in the copy suffix and that have a flat definition while a report with the same columns has grouping. It found nine candidates, but I cannot tell which of them were meant to be flat. I did not change them. I listed the nine with their owners for Jonas, so that he can ask the managers whether they want the grouping restored.

The fix is merged and deployed, and I opened a copy of a grouped report on the live page to confirm it keeps its levels. I will look at the list again once Jonas has answered.

summary: Answered Jonas on how many saved reports use grouping after two weeks and which levels people choose, with counts from production.
body:
Jonas asked whether the grouping is used, since he wants to decide if the next step should be pivot tables. I ran counts on production for the reports with a group definition.

Of 412 saved reports, 37 use grouping, created by 15 users. Of the 37, 22 use one level and 15 use two levels. By level, depot was used in 24 reports, week in 19, customer in 11, month in 6 and status in 3.

The most common two level combination is depot and week, in 9 reports. Four of the grouped reports are scheduled, and the schedules ran without errors. I also looked at how often the grouped reports are opened. In the last 14 days the 37 grouped reports were opened 213 times, about 5.8 per report, against 3.1 per report for flat reports. That is a rough number, since the groups were mostly created by active users.

I sent Jonas the counts in a short table. My view is that people use the simple case, and the pivot would be a larger step for a small group. I suggested to wait a month and ask the 15 users what they miss.

summary: Reviewed the shipments table scroll performance with 10,000 rows loaded and found that the row height was measured on every render, then cached it.
body:
A dispatcher with a very slow laptop said the shipments table stutters when scrolling after loading many pages. I loaded 10,000 rows on staging and recorded a profile in the browser.

The scripting time per frame was around 28 ms, which is too high for smooth scrolling. Most of it was in a function that measures the row height for each visible row on every render, by reading offsetHeight. This forces a layout each time. With 40 rows visible that adds up.

The table uses virtual scrolling with a fixed estimate and a correction after measurement. I changed the row component to measure once after mount with a ResizeObserver and store the height by row id. Renders then read the stored height. Rows with wrapped text still get the right height since the observer fires when the content changes.

After the change the frame time was around 7 ms in the same recording. I tested again with a throttled CPU at four times slower, which gave 19 ms, still acceptable.

I checked the dark theme and the compact density setting, since both change the row height. The observer handles the change, and I added a Playwright test that switches density and checks that the scroll position stays on the same row.

A small side effect: the sticky header had a flicker on the first scroll in Safari. It was from the same layout work and is gone now.

I deployed this and asked the dispatcher to try it. She said that scrolling is better but still not perfect on her laptop. The remaining cost is the cell renderers, mainly the status badges, which are re-created. I will look at memoizing them next.

summary: Memoized the status badge and date cells in the shipments table and measured the result with a script that scrolls through 5,000 rows, cutting frame time on a throttled CPU by half.
body:
After the row height fix, the dispatcher still saw some stutter, so I looked at the cell renderers. The profile showed the status badge component and the date formatter as the biggest remaining parts, each taking around 3 ms per frame on the throttled CPU.

The date formatter created a new Intl.DateTimeFormat object for every cell. Creating this object is slow compared to using it. I moved it into a cache keyed by locale and time zone, so one object is shared. This alone took about 2 ms off.

The status badge had props that were new objects on each render, such as a style object and an icon element, so React memo had no effect. I made the style map a constant outside of the component and passed only the status string. Then I wrapped the component in memo. Renders of the badge dropped, since scrolling changes which rows are visible but not the status of a row.

To measure without guessing I wrote a small Playwright script that loads 5,000 rows, scrolls through them in steps, and collects long frames using the performance observer. It runs with a CPU throttle of four. Before the changes there were 212 long frames over the run. After the row height fix 96, and after the cell work 41. That is a good number to keep as a reference.

I did not add the script to the normal test suite, since timing tests are flaky on shared runners. I put it in the scripts folder with a note on how to run it and what the numbers were.

I checked for functional changes. The badge still shows the right color for the five statuses, and the tooltip with the status time works. The Vitest snapshot of the badge changed only in the removed inline style, which I updated. The accessibility check was unchanged.

I also looked at the filter presets menu, because it renders the table state. It was not part of the slowness.

I deployed it and asked the dispatcher again. She said it feels smooth now, even with long ranges. I will close this topic. If other dispatchers complain, the next idea would be to reduce the number of columns shown by default, but that would be a product decision for Jonas.

summary: Looked at a Sentry alert about failed scheduled report emails and found one recipient address had a typo that the provider rejected, then added address validation in the schedule form.
body:
Sentry reported an error from the scheduled report job: the email provider returned a 422 for one message. I opened the event and found the recipient address ended with .con instead of .com.

The schedule form accepted any text with an at sign. The job continued with the other recipients, so only that one mail was lost, and the error was logged but not shown to anyone. The schedule belonged to a manager who had added the address three weeks ago, so he missed three reports.

I added a proper email check to the form and to the API, using the same validator as the user invites. It does not catch .con, which is a valid pattern, so I also added a warning for a few common typos of top level domains, shown as a hint, not an error.

For the failed sends, the job now records the error on the schedule row, and the schedule list shows a small warning icon with the text. I wrote to the manager and fixed the address with his agreement. Tests pass and I deployed the change.

summary: Planned the work on the CSV export of large tables, noting where the timeouts come from, and did not change code yet, since the fix needs a decision about the file build.
body:
Dispatchers keep reporting that exporting the whole shipments table to CSV for a long range fails after about 30 seconds. I used the time to look at the cause and write a plan, with no code change.

The export endpoint runs the same query as the table without the page limit, builds all rows in an array in memory, converts them into one CSV string and then sends it. For a range of a year, about 400,000 rows, the query takes 6 seconds, the string building another 14 seconds, and memory grows to over 600 MB on the Render instance. The reverse proxy cuts the request at 30 seconds, and on the largest ranges the process also runs out of memory and restarts.

I tried it on staging with 400,000 rows and saw exactly this. The log showed the memory growth and then the restart of the instance.

Options I wrote down:
- Raise the proxy timeout. This only moves the limit and does not help with memory.
- Make the export a background job that stores a file and sends a link by email. This works but is a bigger feature with storage and cleanup.
- Send the rows as they are read, without holding all of them. This keeps memory flat and the first bytes arrive quickly, so the proxy does not cut it.

I think the third is the smallest step with the biggest effect, but it needs a database cursor, and the current database layer returns whole result sets. I need to check that the pool can hold a connection for the duration of a download, and what happens when the client closes the connection in the middle.

I also noted that a very large export could still be slow for the user, but at least it would not fail. I will talk to Jonas about whether a background job is still wanted later.

Nothing was changed today. The plan is in the notes file for the project, with the numbers above, and I will start with a small test of a cursor read on staging.

summary: Asked by Jonas whether the old cookie-era session code can be removed, I checked that no route still reads the legacy cookie name and listed two leftovers.
body:
Jonas had heard that the codebase still contains old login code and asked if it can go. I searched the repository for the legacy cookie name and the old middleware.

No route reads the legacy cookie any more. There are two leftovers: a config option for the old in-memory store that is never set, and a test helper that creates a login the old way but is used by only one skipped test. I wrote both on the list.

I removed the config option and the skipped test with its helper in a small change, and the suite still passes. I did not touch the sessions table code, which is in use.

summary: Tried a database cursor read for the large shipments export on staging and measured memory and first byte time, with the result that reads work but the file build was not changed yet.
body:
Following the plan of the day before, I tested whether a cursor read is possible with our database layer, without changing the export itself. The goal was to find the numbers and the problems.

I used the pg-cursor package, which works with the pool we already have. In a throwaway script on staging, I opened a cursor for the 400,000 row query and read in batches of 2,000 rows. The memory of the script stayed around 90 MB for the whole run, against over 600 MB before. The first batch arrived after 0.4 seconds.

The total read time was 7.5 seconds, a bit longer than the 6 seconds for the one shot query, which is normal for batches. I tried batch sizes of 500, 2,000 and 10,000. The time was 9.1, 7.5 and 7.3 seconds, so 2,000 is a good middle with low memory.

The important point is that a cursor needs a connection of its own for the whole read, inside a transaction. The pool has 10 connections. If a download is slow because the user has a poor connection, the connection stays busy. I tested five parallel cursors with a deliberately slow consumer and the normal dashboard requests still worked, but with ten of them the dashboard would stall. So the number of parallel exports needs a limit. A limit of three at the same time, with a clear error message for the fourth, seems right for the size of Acme. Dispatchers are not many at the same moment.

I also tested what happens when the client closes the connection. The cursor was not closed in my first script, and the connection leaked until the transaction timeout. The fix is to listen to the close event of the response and call cursor close. With that, the connection returned to the pool in under 100 ms in my test.

Another question is the transaction itself. A cursor needs a transaction, and a long one holds back vacuum for tables it reads. For 8 seconds that is acceptable. I set a statement timeout of 120 seconds for the export connection so a stuck read cannot hold it forever.

I wrote the results into the notes file together with the batch size table. The risk I see is the code that writes the CSV, which must now work row by row, including the escaping and the header, and the quote handling for fields with line breaks. The existing helper builds the whole text in one go, so I need a version that works on batches.

Nothing was deployed. Tomorrow I will write the batch version of the CSV writer and test its output against the old one byte by byte, so I know that the files are the same.

summary: Wrote a batch-based CSV writer for the shipments export and compared its output to the old helper on 50,000 rows, finding a difference in how dates with time zones were written.
body:
I wrote the CSV writer that works on batches of rows, as planned. It writes the header once, then escapes and joins each row, and returns a string per batch that can be written out. It shares the escaping function with the old helper, so quotes, commas and line breaks behave the same.

To check this I wrote a test that takes 50,000 rows from the staging copy, runs them through the old helper and through the new writer in batches of 2,000, and compares the results byte by byte. The first run failed.

The difference was in the date columns. The old helper received rows after the formatting step of the API, which converts timestamps into the depot time zone and writes them as local text. The cursor read returns the raw timestamps, so the new writer wrote them in UTC with a Z suffix. Dispatchers would have seen different times in the file than on the screen, which is exactly the kind of mistake that is noticed too late.

I moved the conversion into a function that works on a single row, used by both paths, so the old helper and the new writer apply the same code. The test passed after that. The row count, the header and the last row also matched.

A second difference came from null values. The old path wrote an empty field and the new writer wrote the text null for one column, because the formatting function was skipped for nulls in the new path. The shared row function fixed this as well, and I added a test with a row full of nulls.

I also checked numbers. The cost columns are decimals that arrive as strings from Postgres, and the old path converted them with two fixed decimals. The shared function keeps that.

The encoding is UTF-8 with the byte order mark that Excel needs for names with umlauts. The old response added the mark at the start. In the new writer the mark must be written only once, before the first batch. I put it in the header step and tested it with a depot called Düsseldorf.

All of this is still only in a branch of the working copy, not connected to the endpoint. The next step is to connect the cursor and the writer in the route, with the limit of three parallel exports and the cleanup on close. I expect that to be the final change, and I will test it on staging with the 400,000 row range first.

summary: Planned the streaming CSV export route, read how the cursor and batch writer could fit together, and tested only the batch writer on staging.
body:
I spent the session preparing the export route and did not change the route itself. The goal is to stop building the whole file in memory, but the route still uses the old helper, and I left it that way.

First I wrote down what the route will have to do. It checks the permissions and takes the same filters as the table. It will need a limit on parallel exports, and I proposed three to Jonas in a short message, with a 429 and a message to try again in a minute when the limit is reached. He had no objection, but he wants the support note to say clearly what dispatchers will see.
