Then I read the code around the connection pool. A read only transaction with a statement timeout of 120 seconds looks right for the long reads, and I checked that the pool has enough connections for three exports plus the normal dashboard traffic. It does, with a few to spare. I also noted the points that need care later: waiting for the drain event when the response buffer is full, and closing the cursor and giving the connection back when the client closes the response.

On staging I only ran the batch writer alone, on a table of 400,000 rows, to see how it behaves with batches of 2,000 rows. It wrote the lines correctly and the process memory stayed low in that test, but this did not go through any route, so it says little about the real behavior. I compared its output with the old helper on 50,000 rows, and the lines matched.

I have not written the counter of running exports, the cancel handling or the toast in the frontend. Nothing is deployed and the export route is unchanged. Next I want to connect the cursor and the writer in a branch-free local change and test the error cases before anything goes near staging.

summary: Planned the test and review work for the CSV export change, ran the existing suites against the current export code and listed what a streaming version would need to check.
body:
Ran the full suites to see where the export tests stand before the streaming work starts. The Vitest suite passed, but I noticed that an older export test reads the response body by waiting for a single data event and compares it to the expected text. That works today because the whole file is built in memory and sent in one piece. If the rows ever come in batches, the body will arrive in several chunks and this test would see only the first one. I noted that the test should collect the chunks until the end, which is how a browser handles a download anyway, and left it as it is for now.

Playwright passed as well. I opened an export in the browser and then in Excel to have a baseline. The umlauts were fine, the dates matched the table and the cost columns could be summed. Whatever changes in the file build has to keep exactly this result.

I also looked through the export handler for the database side and found that the statement timeout is set with a session command. On a pooled connection that setting would stay after the connection goes back to the pool, so a transaction-local setting would be safer. I wrote that down for the change and did not touch the code yet. I also want a log line with the row count and the duration for each export, so the real sizes in production become visible.

The decision about the file build is still open, so no release is planned. The next step is to talk it through with Jonas and then start with the cursor read on staging.

summary: Planned the note for Jonas about how the large CSV export would change for dispatchers, and checked with him whether three parallel exports would be enough.
body:
Before any release I drafted a short note for Jonas that he can pass on to the dispatchers. It describes the plan for the large export, which is not live yet. The content is:

- Large exports should no longer end in an error after half a minute. The download is meant to start at once and the file grows while it is loaded.
- The file should look the same as before, with the same columns, the same local times and the same number format. I still have to confirm the time zone dates, since the batch writer differed from the old helper on those.
- Only three exports may run at the same time for the whole dashboard. If a fourth person tries, they would see a message to try again in a minute.
- A very large range can still take 10 to 20 seconds, and depending on the browser the download may only show up when the file is finished.

I also wrote what support should ask if someone reports a problem: the range, the filters and the time of day. The plan is that the server log shows each export with its row count and duration, so those answers can be matched to a log line.

Jonas asked whether three is enough. I told him that Acme has about 40 active dispatchers and that exports of this size are rare, around ten a day over the last weeks according to the logs of failed attempts. If the message shows up often, the limit can be raised, since the expected limit is the database connections and not memory. He was happy with this.

I also noted for myself that the scheduled report attachments use their own path and would not be touched by this work. They are small enough, but I will check them when the next large schedule is added.

Nothing is released yet; the work is still being tried on staging.

summary: Prepared the streaming CSV export for its production release by checking the Render setup and planning what to watch afterwards.
body:
The streaming export is not in production yet, so today I prepared for the release and decided what to look at once it goes out. On staging the API instance stayed between 140 and 170 MB with a 400,000 row export, where the old file build pushed it above 600 MB on a similar table. I want the same numbers from production, so I opened the Render metrics page for the API instance and noted the current memory baseline, so I can compare it after the release.

I also went through the logs of the old export route to find the largest recent exports. One dispatcher export of about 180,000 shipments took close to a minute with the old code, which is near the gateway limit, so I will look for a request like that first. I wrote down how to find it in the logs by route and row count.

The limit of three parallel exports needs a message for the fourth request. I checked that the text about waiting for a free slot is clear and that the support note for Jonas matches it. I did not see anything in the support inbox about exports today.

Next I want to look at the Sentry filter for the export route so it is ready before the release, and to note the normal Postgres connection count, about 12, so I can check after the first peak that the temporary cursor connections are released. Nothing was released today, and the only changes were small edits to the support note.

summary: Planned how the large CSV export should behave when a dispatcher closes the tab, after measuring that a big export currently times out and holds memory.
body:
Large exports from the shipments table have been slow for a while, and before changing anything I wanted to know what a failed download costs us. I ran a 400,000 row export on staging with the current route, which builds the whole file in memory before sending it, and watched the API process. Memory climbed to several hundred MB for that single export, and the response only started after the whole file was built.

Then I killed the browser tab after about ten seconds to see what happens on a closed connection. The API kept building the file regardless. Nothing in the route listens for the close event of the request, so the work runs to the end and the result is thrown away. With several dispatchers exporting at the same time, a few abandoned downloads could keep the API busy for everybody.

I wrote down what a better route would need. It should read the rows from a database cursor in batches instead of loading them all. It should limit the number of exports that run in parallel, probably to three. It should release the cursor, the connection and its slot when the client goes away or when an error happens in the middle, not only on the normal end. I have not written any of this yet. I only listed it in the export notes with the numbers from staging.

I also noted an open question for later. A half written CSV can look complete to some spreadsheet programs, and I need to decide whether a marker row on error is worth it or whether the browser showing a failed download is enough.

Next I will try a plain cursor read on staging to measure memory and the time to the first byte, before touching the route. I will talk to Jonas about the parallel limit once I have those numbers.

summary: Started the work on a scheduled report that skips empty results, because Jonas said managers get mails with a table of zero rows on quiet weeks.
body:
Jonas forwarded a complaint from two managers who receive the weekly late shipments report even when there were no late shipments. The mail then contains only the header row. They find it confusing.

I looked at the scheduler code. It runs the saved report, renders the mail and sends it, with no check of the row count in between. The report runner already returns the count, so the check is easy to add.

The question is what the setting should be. I see three options: always send, skip when empty, or send a short note saying nothing to report. I think the third is best for managers who want to know the schedule still works, but Jonas should decide. I wrote the options in a short message to him with a mock of the note.

In the meantime I added a column skip_when_empty to the schedules table with a default of false, so nothing changes for existing schedules. The migration ran on staging without trouble.

I also looked at how many schedules would be affected. Of the 38 active schedules, 9 are on filters that often give few rows, and for three of them the last month had at least one empty run.

The form change comes next, and the mail text for the note. I did not touch the runner yet.

summary: Added the skip-when-empty switch to the schedule form and the runner, and tested the three cases with a seeded report that has no rows.
body:
Jonas answered quickly and chose both options: a checkbox to skip empty reports, and when it is off, the mail gets a line saying that there are no rows for the period. So I built that.

In the schedule form I added a checkbox with a short help text. It is saved in the new skip_when_empty column. In the runner, after the report returns, the code checks the row count. If it is zero and the box is checked, it logs a skipped run and sends nothing. If it is zero and the box is not checked, it renders the no-rows text instead of the empty table.

I seeded a report with a filter that matches nothing and wrote Vitest cases for the three paths: rows present, empty and skipped, empty and note. The run history on the schedule page needed a status for skipped, otherwise it looked like a failure. I added a grey label.

One detail was the subtotal row of grouped reports. For an empty grouped report the renderer printed a total row of zeros. I made it print nothing when there are no groups.

I ran the scheduler on staging with the test report and got the expected result in all three cases. The mails looked fine in the test inbox.

I will look at the run history label on a narrow screen later, and then release.

summary: Reviewed how the session list on the settings page handles a user with many old sessions, and found it loads every row and shows expired ones too, so I limited it.
body:
A manager mentioned that the page with the list of devices is slow and long. I checked the account on staging with the same shape of data. This user had 214 session rows, most of them expired and not yet removed by the cleanup job.

The endpoint returned all rows of the user. The page then drew all of them, with the parsed user agent for each. The request took 380 ms and the page needed another second to render.

Two things were wrong. First, expired sessions should not be shown at all, since the user cannot do anything with them. Second, even active sessions should have a sane upper limit.

I changed the query to filter on expires_at greater than now and to order by last_seen descending. I added a limit of 50 and a line in the response with the total number of active sessions. The page shows a note when there are more than 50.

The parsed user agent is now cached per distinct string in the request, since many rows share the same one. This cut most of the parsing time.

I also checked the log out of all devices button. It deletes by user id, so it removes expired rows too, which is fine and in fact helps with the clutter.

The cleanup job runs nightly and removes rows that expired more than seven days ago. I looked at why that user still had 200 rows. They were all within the last week, because a script of theirs logs in every few minutes. I asked in the summary for Jonas whether that is expected. It looks like an integration of the client that logs in again each time instead of keeping a session.

After the change the endpoint answered in 40 ms and the page rendered at once. I wrote a Vitest test for the filter and the limit.

The integration user remains an open question. I will ask Jonas who runs that script.

summary: Asked Jonas about the script that logs in every few minutes, and learned it is a client's spreadsheet macro, so I noted a possible API key later and changed nothing now.
body:
Jonas replied this evening about the account with the 214 sessions. It is a logistics planner at Acme who pulls the shipments into a spreadsheet with a macro. The macro logs in with the email and password each time it refreshes, every five minutes during the working day.

That explains the rows. It is harmless for the database now that the list is limited and the cleanup works, but it creates a login event each time, and those show in the last login column and the audit view.

I see two ways to handle it. One is a read-only API key for such integrations, which is a real feature and needs a design. The other is to tell the planner to reduce the refresh rate. Jonas will talk to the planner about the rate. I wrote the API key idea into the backlog notes with the reasons.

I also checked the login rate limit. The macro does not hit it, since five minutes is far below the limit.

No code changed in this session. The notes in the repository now have a short entry about this integration so that I find it again.

summary: Prepared the export cleanup on close and the skip-when-empty schedules for release, running the full test suites and a staging check of both.
body:
Today I got two changes ready that have been waiting: the cleanup when the client closes an export download, and the skip-when-empty option for schedules. Neither is released yet.

First I ran the Vitest suite and the Playwright suite on the branch. All 612 unit tests passed. One Playwright test of the schedule form failed because it looked for the form by the old number of checkboxes. I fixed the selector to use the label text, and the suite is green now.

Then I did a manual check on staging. I started an export and closed the tab, and the connection count fell back. I ran a schedule with the skip option and saw the skipped label in the history.

I wrote down the plan for the release. The migration for skip_when_empty only adds a column with a default, so it is safe to run on production before the deploy. The deploy through Render should take about four minutes. I want to watch the logs for an hour afterwards, mainly the export route and the morning scheduler jobs.

I told Jonas that both changes are ready and that the managers will be able to switch on skipping in their schedules once they are live. He is fine with waiting until I have the logs in view.

Next is the half-written file question, what a client should get when the connection breaks in the middle of a download. I decided to leave it for now.

summary: Looked at the Playwright run time, which grew to 14 minutes, and found two slow specs that log in through the form every test instead of using a stored session.
body:
The Playwright suite in CI now needs about 14 minutes, and it was 9 minutes a few months ago. I looked at the report with the timing per spec.

Two specs, for the settings page and for the reports, log in through the form in each test. That is about 40 logins. The other specs reuse a stored state from a setup step.

I moved both to the stored state and kept one test for the form login itself. The two specs now take 2 minutes instead of 6. The whole run is at 10 minutes.

I will look at the sharding of the suite another time.

summary: Built the first part of an API key for read-only integrations after Jonas agreed, with hashed keys, a scope field and a settings page to create and revoke them.
body:
Jonas talked to the planner and the answer was that the macro cannot easily be changed in its rate, but a key would be welcome. He asked for something simple that managers can create themselves. So I started the work on read-only API keys.

Design decisions, in short:
- The key is a random string of 32 bytes, shown once at creation.
- Only a SHA-256 hash is stored, with a prefix of eight characters to find the key in the list.
- Each key has a name, an owner, a scope (only read for now), a created time, a last used time and a revoked time.
- A key acts as its owner for permissions, but only for GET routes.

I wrote the migration for the api_keys table and the lookup middleware. The middleware reads the Authorization header with the scheme ApiKey, hashes the value and loads the row. A revoked key gives a 401. A non GET request with a key gives a 403 with a clear message.

The middleware sits before the session middleware, so a request with a key does not create a session row. That solves the original problem of the many rows and the many login events.

I also wrote the routes to create, list and revoke keys under the settings. Creation returns the plain key once. The list shows prefix, name, last used and status.

Tests: I wrote Vitest tests for the hash lookup, for the 401 on revoked keys, for the 403 on a POST, and for the fact that no session is created. All pass.

A question came up about the last used time. Updating it on every request would write to the database a lot, since the macro calls often. I update it at most once per minute per key, by comparing with the loaded value.

I also compared the timing of the lookup against a wrong key and a right prefix, to see if there is a timing difference. I used a constant time comparison of the hashes to be safe.

Still missing is the page in the frontend and the documentation for the planner. I will do these next. Nothing is released yet, and the middleware is only active on staging.

summary: Added the settings page section for API keys with a create dialog that shows the key once, and a revoke button with a confirmation.
body:
The backend of the API keys was done earlier this evening, so I wrote the frontend part. The settings page got a new section called Integrations, visible to managers only.

The list shows name, prefix, last used and status, and a revoke button. A click on revoke opens a confirmation that names the key, since revoking breaks the macro of whoever uses it.

The create dialog asks for a name only. After saving, a second view shows the key in a monospace field with a copy button and a clear text that it cannot be shown again. The dialog cannot be closed by a click outside, to avoid losing the key by accident.

I used the existing modal component and the table style of the user list. Priya's spacing tokens are used, so the section fits the rest of the page.

I wrote a Playwright test that creates a key, copies it from the field, calls the API with it and checks the response, then revokes it and checks the 401. It passes on staging data.

One small bug was that the copy button used the clipboard API, which fails on non secure origins. Staging is secure, so it worked, but I added a fallback with a text selection.

The documentation for the planner is the next step.

summary: Wrote a one page guide for using an API key from a spreadsheet macro, tested it against staging, and found that the date range needs explicit parameters.
body:
The planner needs a way to use the key, so I wrote a one page guide. It explains how to create the key, which header to send and which routes can be read.

To be sure the guide works I made a small VBA style macro example and also tried the same call with curl. Both use the header Authorization: ApiKey followed by the key. The shipments route answered with the JSON as expected.

One problem showed in the test. Without a date range the shipments route uses the default of the dashboard, the last 30 days, which surprised me when comparing counts. The guide now says to always send from and to, and gives the format as ISO dates.

I also added the page size limit to the guide, since the route returns at most 1,000 rows per page and the macro would need to go through the pages. For bigger pulls I first wanted to point to the CSV export, but large exports are still slow and can run into the gateway timeout, so the guide says for now to keep the pulls small and to page through the route. I will revisit that line when the export is better.

I sent the guide to Jonas for the planner. The key feature is still only on staging. I plan to release it after the planner has tried it there once.

summary: Released the API keys to production after the planner tried the macro on staging, and watched that the session rows from that account stopped growing.
body:
The planner tried the macro against staging with a key and it worked, with one fix to the date parameters, so I released the API keys.

The migration for the api_keys table ran first. Then the deploy went through in about four minutes. I created the key for the planner myself from a manager account and sent it over a secure channel through Jonas.

After the planner switched the macro, I watched the sessions table for that user. Before, it grew by about 12 rows an hour in the working day. Over the first three hours there was no new row. The last used time of the key updated as expected, once per minute at most.

The last login column for that user will show the old time from now on, which is correct, since no login happens anymore.

I also checked the Sentry events for the new middleware. There were none. The 403 for non GET requests has not occurred.

I will let the cleanup job remove the old rows over the coming week.

summary: Investigated why the costs page is slow for the yearly range, found a query that summed over all lines without a depot index, and cut it from 6 seconds to 700 ms.
body:
A manager said the costs page takes a long time when the range is a full year. I reproduced it on staging with a copy of production data. The request for the depot breakdown took about 6 seconds.

I ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the query. It scanned the cost_lines table sequentially, 2.3 million rows, then joined with shipments and grouped by depot. The planner did not use any index since the only index on cost_lines was on shipment_id.

I tried an index on (depot_id, booked_at) with the amount included. The plan changed to an index scan. The time came down to 1.4 seconds, but the join with shipments was still costly.

The join was there only to filter by shipment status. Cost lines of cancelled shipments are excluded. I moved the status into a column cancelled on cost_lines, kept in sync by the code that cancels a shipment, and backfilled it with one update. The query no longer joins shipments for the sum.

With both changes the request took 700 ms for the yearly range and 90 ms for a month.

I checked the result against the old query on five depots and three ranges. The sums were identical to the cent.

The backfill touched 2.3 million rows, so I ran it in batches of 50,000 on staging. It took about four minutes. For production I will do the same outside the working hours.

The code that cancels a shipment now sets the flag in the same transaction. I wrote a test for it and for the reverse case of a restored shipment.

The index creation on production should use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, so that writes are not blocked. I wrote the migration that way and noted that it cannot run inside a transaction, which the migration tool needs to be told.

I did not release yet. I want to run the batches on production tonight or tomorrow after a dump.

summary: Ran the cost_lines index and the cancelled backfill on production in batches after a dump, and measured the yearly costs request at 640 ms.
body:
This morning I took a dump of production first, then ran the migration. The concurrent index build took about three minutes and writes were not blocked. I saw no slow queries in the meantime.

Then I started the backfill of the cancelled flag in batches of 50,000 rows with a pause of 200 ms between batches, to keep the database calm. It took five minutes in total. The row counts matched the number of cost lines of cancelled shipments, which I verified with a separate count query: 41,870 on both sides.

After that I deployed the code that uses the flag and the new query. The deploy was uneventful.

I measured the yearly range request five times. The times were between 610 and 690 ms. The monthly range took about 80 ms.

I asked the manager who reported it to try again, and the answer was that it feels instant now.

One leftover is that the old query is still in the code for the CSV export of cost lines, and uses the join. It is not slow, since it reads a narrow range. I noted it for later.

summary: Answered Jonas on how many API keys exist after three weeks and which routes they call, with counts from production logs.
body:
Jonas asked whether the keys are used beyond the planner. I looked at the api_keys table and the access logs.

There are four keys. Two belong to the planner, one old and one new after a reissue, and the old one was revoked. Another belongs to a manager of the north depots, and one was made by Jonas for a test.

Calls with keys over the last week were about 9,400. Of these, 8,900 went to the shipments route, 400 to the costs route and the rest to the depots list. No call got a 403, so nobody tries to write.

The manager of the north depots pulls costs once a day. That fits a small sheet.

I told Jonas that usage is low and healthy and that I see no need for more scopes now.

summary: Investigated why the shipments CSV export shows some shipments twice and found the join to cost_lines as the likely cause, without changing anything yet.
body:
A dispatcher wrote that the shipments CSV has some shipments twice, with the same id. I took the example from her message, a shipment with two cost lines, and ran the export query on staging. The same shipment came out as two rows.

The export joins cost_lines to add a cost column. For a shipment with two lines the join gives two rows, so this is a plain one to many join. I looked at the export helper too. It deduplicates the rows by id in memory before writing the file, which explains why nobody saw the problem in the past: the helper hid it. Large exports are still slow and I know that, but that is a separate problem and I did not touch it today.

I checked how many production shipments are affected: 3,100 of about 410,000 have more than one cost line. So about 0.8 percent of the rows can show up twice in a full export, and the number of extra rows depends on how many lines a shipment has.

The filters of the export use the same query base. I ran each of them, status, depot and date range, with the seeded data on staging. None of them adds another one to many join, so the cost lines are the only source of duplicates.

I also looked at the table view in the dashboard. It uses a different query with a lateral aggregate and shows one row per shipment, so it is not affected.

My plan is to aggregate the cost lines in a subquery grouped by shipment_id and join that, so there is one row per shipment by construction. I wrote down a Vitest integration test to add first: a seeded shipment with three cost lines, expecting exactly one row and the summed cost. It should fail on the current query. I will compare the new output with the old helper on a sample of rows before anything goes out. I will answer the dispatcher with the cause for now, and later I will check which exports of the last days may contain duplicates.

summary: Investigated duplicate rows in the shipments export, traced them to a join over cost lines, and prepared the fix and a check of which exports were affected.
body:
A dispatcher and then a manager reported that the shipments export sometimes had more rows than the table on screen. I looked into it and found the cause: when a shipment has two cost lines, the export query joins the cost lines directly, so the shipment appears once per line. The cost column of such a shipment then counts twice in a sum.

I wrote the fix on a branch of the main checkout, replacing the join with an aggregated subquery that sums the cost lines per shipment. I have not released it yet. The full test suites still have to run, and I want one more look at the query plan on a large range first.

Then I wanted to know who might have received files with duplicates. The export route logs the user, the filters and the row count of each export. I started a script that reruns each logged export with the fixed query, counts the rows, and compares them with the logged count. It runs against a copy of the data and only reads. The first test on a handful of exports showed differences of one to three rows for single-day pulls, which fits the idea that only shipments with several cost lines are affected. The complete run over the exports of the last days is still to do.

I also thought about why the tests did not catch it. The test data has one cost line per shipment, so the join never multiplied anything. My plan is to add a second seeded shipment with several cost lines to the shared fixture, so that other tests using the export query cover the case too. I also want a check in the export tests that the number of rows equals the number of distinct ids. It is cheap and it would have caught this.

I wrote down for Jonas what I know so far, and that I will bring him a list of users and files once the script has run, because the two managers who export whole months are the ones who may have wrong cost totals in their sheets.

summary: Reviewed the log out of all devices flow after a manager said it did not log out the open session on the phone, and found the phone session was created after the click.
body:
A manager reported that after pressing log out of all devices, his phone was still logged in. This sounded like a real bug, so I traced it.

The route deletes all session rows of the user, then clears the cookie of the current request. I tested it on staging with two browsers. Both were logged out at their next request, as expected.

Then I asked for details. The manager said that the phone showed the dashboard still after the click. I looked at his sessions in the table. There was a session on the phone created two minutes after the logout of all devices.

The cause is the login screen on the phone browser. The page was still open with the dashboard. After the deletion, the next background poll got a 401. The app then showed the login form, and a password manager filled it in automatically and submitted it. So the phone logged in again at once.

That is not a bug of the logout, but the result looks like one. I considered two things. One is a message on the login page after a forced logout, saying that the session was ended on another device, so that the user understands. The other is to ask for the password again, which the password manager would do anyway.

I built the first. The 401 response now contains a reason, either expired or ended_by_user. The login page reads it from the query string after the redirect and shows a short text for the second case.

I wrote a Playwright test with two browser contexts. One of them logs out of all devices, then the other makes a request and must land on the login page with the text.

The poll interval of the dashboard is 60 seconds, so the second device can take up to a minute to notice. I left it as it is.

I wrote an explanation for the manager. He understood and said the new text would have helped.

The change is on the branch for tomorrow's release.

summary: Released the message after forced logout and checked in staging and production that the reason value reaches the login page for both ended and expired sessions.
body:
Today I released the change with the reason on the 401. Before the release I ran the Playwright test for the forced logout again, together with the whole suite. All passed.

After the deploy I checked production with two of my own sessions. I ended one with the log out of all devices button and let the other poll. After about 40 seconds the second browser showed the login page with the text that the session was ended on another device.

I also checked the normal expiry. I set the expiry of a test session in the database to a minute ago. The next request returned 401 with the reason expired, and the login page showed the plain text asking to log in again, as before.

One thing I found was that the mobile app also reads the 401 response. The new field is only added to the JSON body, so the app should ignore it. I sent a short note to the agency to be sure, since they parse the body in one place.

The agency answered within the hour that their code only checks the status code. So there is no problem.

I closed the item on my list. The next piece is the review of the report builder performance, which I will start another day.

summary: Profiled the report builder preview with 30 columns and found that every keystroke in the filter field reran the preview query, so I added a debounce and request cancellation.
body:
Priya noticed while testing that the report builder lags when she types in a filter field with many columns selected. I profiled it in the browser with a report of 30 columns on staging.

Every keystroke fired a request to the preview endpoint. Typing a word of eight letters gave eight requests, and the responses arrived out of order sometimes, so the table showed the result of an older text for a moment. The preview query is not cheap with many columns, about 400 ms.

I made two changes. First, a debounce of 350 ms on the filter inputs, so only the final text triggers the query. Second, an AbortController for the request in flight, so a new request cancels the old one in the browser.

On the API side, I checked that an aborted request stops the query. It did not, since the query ran to its end anyway. I added the same close handler as in the export, which cancels the query through pg when the client disconnects. A cancelled preview now frees the connection at once.

I measured with the same typing script. Before there were 8 requests and the last response at about 3.1 seconds after the start. After, there is one request and the result is there after about 0.8 seconds.

The out of order display is gone, which I checked by throttling the network and typing fast.

I wrote a Vitest test for the hook that debounces and cancels, using fake timers, and a Playwright test that types a word and counts the requests, which must be one.

The date picker in the builder has the same pattern. I looked at it and it only changes on selection, so no debounce is needed there.

I will release this with the next batch. Priya will check the feel of it on her side tomorrow.

summary: Priya tried the debounced report builder and said the preview now feels fine, but the delay made the loading state look stuck for a moment, so I added a pending indicator.
body:
Priya tested the report builder on staging this morning. Her comment was that typing is smooth now, but after she stops, nothing happens for a third of a second and then the table changes, which looks like a freeze.

That is the debounce. I added a small pending indicator, a thin bar above the preview table that appears as soon as the text changes and goes away when the result is shown. The table content is dimmed slightly in the meantime.

I kept the old rows visible while waiting. Before they stayed without any sign that they were outdated.

I checked the accessibility side. The bar has aria-busy on the preview region, so a screen reader gets a hint that content is changing. I used the existing styles of the loading bars of the charts.

Priya looked at it again and was happy with it.

summary: Released the report builder debounce with the pending bar and ran a check on production with a 30 column report, seeing one request per typed word and no stuck connections.
body:
I released the debounce, the cancellation and the pending bar. The suites passed and the deploy took about four minutes.

On production I built a report with 30 columns and typed a filter word at a normal speed while watching the network panel. There was one request per word. I also typed a word and then changed it quickly, and the first request showed as cancelled in the panel.

Then I looked at Postgres. I counted the active queries from the preview endpoint during the test with pg_stat_activity. There was never more than one at a time, and no query stayed after I closed the tab.

I also asked the logs for the average preview time of the last hour, which was 410 ms, similar to before. So only the number of requests changed.

Nothing else showed in Sentry. I told Priya that it is live.

summary: Checked the nightly session cleanup job after a run that took 11 minutes, and found it deleted in one statement, so I changed it to delete in batches.
body:
The monitoring showed that last night's session cleanup took 11 minutes, where it took seconds before. I looked at the job and its log.

The job deletes sessions that expired more than seven days ago with a single DELETE. Last night it removed about 310,000 rows. Most of these were from the macro account before the keys, plus the usual logins of everyone else. A statement of this size holds locks and creates a lot of dead tuples at once, and the session lookups on the login path slowed down during that time. I saw a small peak of response times for logins in that window.

I rewrote the delete to run in batches of 5,000 with a short pause. It selects the ids with a limit and deletes them by id, in a loop until nothing is left. The log now prints the total and the time.

I tested on staging by creating 300,000 expired rows and running the job. It finished in about 90 seconds with no visible effect on the login time, which I measured with a loop of logins during the run.

Because the macro account no longer creates rows, the normal nightly volume should drop to a few thousand, so the batches will rarely matter. It is still the safer way.

I added a Vitest test with a small batch size to check that the loop ends and removes only the expired rows. I will release it with the next deploy.

summary: Released the batched session cleanup and confirmed with the first night run that it removed 2,900 rows in a few seconds with no peak in login times.
body:
The batched cleanup job went out with this morning's deploy. I looked at the first run, which happened last night on the version from staging data, and checked it again against production by running the job manually once.

The manual run removed 2,900 expired rows in 4 seconds, in one batch only. The log printed the total and the duration as intended.

I watched the login response time during the run in the metrics and saw no peak. The table size on disk is also stable, since the dead tuples are cleaned up by autovacuum now in smaller amounts.

I closed the item. The work on the old query in the cost lines export is still on the list, as a small cleanup for later.

summary: Reviewed the whole login path after the batched cleanup release and listed what still touches the sessions table, with two small fixes made and three items parked
body:
After the batched cleanup went out this morning, I went through every place that reads or writes the sessions table to see whether anything else could cause a load peak. I found four: the login route, the session middleware that refreshes last_seen, the settings session list, and the cleanup job itself.

The middleware wrote last_seen on every request. For a dispatcher with the dashboard open and polling, that was an update every few seconds on the same row. I changed it to write only when the stored value is older than one minute. In a staging run with 20 simulated dispatchers the update count fell from about 2,400 per minute to 40.

The second fix was in the settings session list. Its query ordered by last_seen without an index on user_id plus last_seen, so for users with many rows it sorted in memory. I added the composite index in a migration and the plan went from a sort to an index scan.

Three things I parked. First, the login route does a bcrypt compare before checking whether the account is locked, which wastes time on locked accounts. Second, the session row stores the user agent as free text with no length limit. Third, the cleanup job has no metric for how many rows it removed, only a log line.

I ran the Vitest suite for the middleware and the Playwright login specs, and both passed. The index migration is small, but I will run it on production in a quiet hour and not right away. I wrote the three parked items into the notes file so they do not get lost.

Next step is the release of the last_seen throttle with the index, then a look at the production update counts the day after. I also want to check that the forced logout flow still sees a fresh last_seen, since it uses that value to decide which session is the current one. I read that code and it uses the session id, not last_seen, so it should not be affected. Still, I will add one test for it to be sure.

summary: Released the last_seen throttle and the session list index, and production session updates dropped by about 95 percent in the first hours
body:
I ran the index migration on production at the quiet evening hour, and it took under a second because the sessions table is small after the batched cleanup. Then I released the last_seen throttle.

I compared the update counts from the Postgres statistics before and after. Before, the sessions table saw about 1,900 updates per minute at the evening level. After the release it saw about 90. The login time stayed the same, around 220 ms at the median.

I added the test I had planned: a session that is touched twice within a minute keeps the first last_seen, and one touched after two minutes gets a new value. It passes. I also checked that the log out of all devices flow still marks the current session correctly, and it does.

One side effect: the session list on the settings page can now show a last active time that is up to a minute old. I looked at it with Priya's design in mind, and since the page shows minutes already, nobody would see the difference. I left the text as is.

Tomorrow I will look at the parked items, starting with the locked account check before the bcrypt compare.

summary: Moved the locked account check before the password hash compare in the login route and measured that locked accounts no longer cost any hashing time
body:
One of the items I parked yesterday was that the login route compared the password hash first and looked at the lock only after. A locked account that gets many attempts therefore burned CPU for no reason.

I moved the lock check to before the compare. The response must not reveal whether the account exists, so the locked case now returns the same message and the same status as a wrong password. To keep the timing similar I kept a dummy compare for unknown emails, which was already there, and did not add one for locked accounts, since locked accounts are known to exist and the lock message is already shown to the user by the login page after the first block.

That last point needed a check, so I read the login page code. It shows a hint for locked accounts that comes from a separate endpoint after a successful email check, so the behavior is consistent with what I did.

I wrote three Vitest cases: wrong password on an open account, any password on a locked account, and unknown email. All three return in the expected way, and I mocked bcrypt to count calls. The locked case made zero calls, the other two one each.

In a local test with 200 attempts on a locked account, the total time dropped from about 14 seconds to under 0.3 seconds. That is the whole gain, and it matters mostly if someone attacks a locked account.

I did not release yet. I want to bundle it with the length limit for the user agent field, which is the next small item. The full test suite passed locally. The diff touches only the login route and its test file.

summary: Limited the stored user agent of a session to 255 characters and found one odd row of 9 KB in production that came from a bot scan
body:
The second parked item was the user agent column, which had no limit. I looked at the production data first and found the longest value was 9,100 characters, a row from a scan against the login route, probably a bot sending junk in the header.

I added a cut at 255 characters when the session is created. I did not change the column type, because a migration for a type change on that table adds risk for no gain; the application cut is enough. The session list on the settings page shows a short device name parsed from the string, so the cut does not change what users see.

I wrote a test with a 10,000 character header and checked that the stored value has 255 characters and that the parsed device name is still correct for a normal Chrome string.

I also cleaned the one odd row with an update statement after checking that it belonged to an already expired session. I ran it in a transaction and looked at the count before the commit: one row.

The release of this change and the lock check is planned for after lunch. Nothing else was touched.

summary: Released the locked account check and the user agent limit together after a full test run and a short check on staging
body:
I ran the full Vitest suite and the Playwright login specs, and both passed. The Playwright run took 9 minutes now, since the stored session helper from the earlier work is used in most specs.

On staging I tried four cases by hand: a normal login, a wrong password, a locked test account, and a login with a very long user agent set through curl. The response codes and messages matched what I expected, and the session row of the long agent had 255 characters.

Then I released to production. I watched the login endpoint for a quarter of an hour. The median stayed at about 220 ms, there were no new errors, and the count of failed logins was normal for the time of day.

The third parked item, the metric for the cleanup job, is still open. I will do it next because it is the only one that helps with the next incident, and the other two are done now.

summary: Added a count and duration for each nightly session cleanup run, written to a small table and shown in the admin health page
body:
The cleanup job only wrote a log line, and the log lines roll off after a few days on Render. I wanted the numbers to stay, so I added a small table, cleanup_runs, with started_at, finished_at, rows_deleted and batches.

The job now inserts one row at the end of each run. If it fails in the middle, it writes the row with the numbers so far and an error text, so a failed run is visible and not just missing. I wrote the migration and the insert in the same style as the other jobs.

The admin health page already has a section for the report scheduler. I added a second section that shows the last ten cleanup runs with the duration and the count. I kept the design plain and used the same table component as the scheduler section, so Priya does not need to review it.

Tests: one for a normal run with 25 expired rows and a batch size of 10, which gives three batches and a count of 25, and one where the delete throws on the second batch. Both pass.

I ran the job on staging by hand and the row appeared with 340 deleted rows in 4 batches, taking 0.8 seconds. The health page showed it right away.

One question I considered is how long to keep the run rows. At one per night, a year is only 365 rows, so I did not add a cleanup for the cleanup table. I wrote a comment in the job saying so, in case that changes.

I will release this tomorrow morning with the other small changes. That finishes the review items from the session path, and I will tell Jonas that the login work has no open loose ends for now.

summary: Worked through the three parked items from the login path review and fixed the one that mattered: the logout route ran two session deletes where one is enough.
body:
The login path review of the last days left three parked items. I started with the logout route, which deleted the session row and then ran a second delete by user and session id. The second statement never matched anything, so I removed it and kept the single delete.

The second item was the session lookup on every request. It selects the whole row, including the user agent and the data column, although the middleware only needs the user id, the expiry and the last_seen value. I changed the select to those three columns. On staging the lookup time dropped from about 1.8 ms to 1.1 ms in a local loop of 10,000 requests.

The third item was a doubt about whether the expiry check happens in SQL or in Node. It happens in SQL with a comparison against now(), so clock differences between the API and the database cannot let an expired session through. I added a short comment in the middleware so that nobody moves it to Node later.

I ran the unit tests of the auth folder and the Playwright login specs. All of them passed. The change is small and I did not release it alone; it waits for the next release together with the throttle work.

Two items stay parked: a rename of the sessions table columns, which would need a migration for no real gain, and a check of the cookie settings on the staging domain. I will look at the cookie settings when Jonas asks for the new subdomain.

summary: Wrote a short test that proves an expired session is refused even when its cookie is still sent, closing the doubt from the login review.
body:
After the lookup change I wanted a test that pins down the expiry behaviour, since the review had only read the code. I wrote an integration spec in the API tests that creates a session row, sets its expiry to one minute in the past, and calls a protected route with the cookie.

The route answered 401 with the reason value expired, which is what the login page uses for its message. I added a second case with an expiry one minute in the future, which answers 200. A third case covers a session row that was deleted, and it answers 401 with the reason ended.

While writing the test I noticed that the seed helper created sessions with the expiry in local time of the test machine. That would have made the spec flaky on a machine in another time zone. I changed the helper to write UTC explicitly and reran the spec ten times without a failure.

The whole auth suite now takes 9 seconds. I did not touch any production code in this session. The spec runs in the normal Vitest command, so it needs nothing in the CI setup.

summary: Added the weekly cost summary as a fixed template in the report builder with parameters for depots and number of base weeks
body:
The report builder keeps its templates in a list of definitions, each with a name, a column set and a query function. I added a new definition called weekly cost summary that calls the query from yesterday.

It has two parameters: the depots, as a multi select that uses the same component as the costs page, and the number of base weeks, a number from two to eight with a default of four. I changed the query to take the base weeks as an argument and not as the fixed value.

The builder form hides the free column editor for fixed templates, since it makes no sense there. I added a flag fixed to the definition and made the form check it. The preview works as before, including the debounce and the pending bar from the earlier work.

A test checks that the preview of the template returns the expected columns and that changing the base weeks to six changes the base count. It passes.

I did not touch the scheduling, since it takes any definition. Tomorrow I will try a scheduled mail with the template on staging and look at how the table renders in the mail clients Jonas uses.

summary: Checked the scheduled mail of the weekly cost summary on staging, and fixed the percent column and the dash for null values that rendered badly in the mail table
body:
I created a schedule for the new template on staging with three depots, sent to my test mailbox and to Jonas's test address. The mail arrived and the table was readable, but there were three problems.

First, the percent column showed values like 0.0734 and not 7.3 percent. The web preview formats them with a column format function, but the mail renderer uses its own path and ignored it. I made the mail renderer use the same format function, and the column now shows 7.3 percent with one decimal.

Second, null values showed as the word null in the mail. The web preview shows a dash. This was the same cause, the two paths for formatting. After the fix both use the dash.

Third, negative differences, meaning lower costs, showed in the same color as positive ones. For costs, a rise is bad and a fall is good, but the other templates show a rise as green, as with revenue. I added a direction field to the column definition with the values up_is_bad and up_is_good, and the mail and the preview color the number accordingly. The default stays as it was for the existing templates.

I checked how the table looks in the web mail of my test account and in the desktop client that Jonas told me he uses. The inline styles held in both. The column widths were a little narrow in the desktop client, so I set a minimum width for number columns.

I also sent a schedule with skip-when-empty switched on and with a depot that has no costs. The mail was sent because the zero rows still count as rows, which is the right behavior here: a depot with zero costs is a result, not an empty report. I noted this in the template description so nobody is surprised.

Tests I added:
- the formatting function used by the mail path
- the direction field giving the expected color class
- a snapshot of the mail table for two depots

The snapshot test needed some care because the numbers must be stable. I used the seeded data and fixed the date in the test through the clock mock, and it passes in repeated runs.

The full suite ran in about 4 minutes for Vitest and passed. Playwright I did not run because no UI flow changed except the template list.

Open points: Priya should look at the colors, since I chose them by eye and I am not sure that the green and red work for color blind readers. There is an accessibility item on the list from earlier work, so I will ask her to check this one together with it. I also have not asked Jonas to look at real numbers yet; that is the last step of the plan.

The branch is still local. I will push it after Priya's answer, and release after Jonas confirms the numbers.

summary: Checked the mobile app sessions after the duplicate phone finding and measured that one active driver creates about 14 session rows per day.
body:
The finding that each app start of the mobile app creates a new session needed numbers before I could suggest anything to the agency. I counted session rows in production by user agent for the last week. The app user agent made up 71 percent of all new rows.

One active driver created about 14 rows a day, because the app is started after every phone lock of some minutes. Most of these rows are never used again, they just live until the cleanup job removes them. The batched cleanup handles the volume without trouble, so this is not an emergency.

The login route itself is the part to improve. It could reuse a still valid session of the same device when the app sends a stable device id. The app does not send one today. I wrote a short proposal with the header name, the rule that a session is reused only when the user and the device id match, and the effect on the session list.

I also checked the other option, which is to keep the app logged in with the existing session until it expires. The app agency said before that it does this for the cookie, but the app drops the cookie when the operating system clears its storage. That fits the numbers.

I sent the proposal to Jonas so that he can pass it to the agency. Nothing changed in the code yet.

summary: Added a device id header to the login route behind a flag, so a session is reused for the same user and device, and tested it with a fake mobile client.
body:
While the agency looks at the proposal, I prepared the server side so that the change can go live quickly. The login route now reads an optional X-Device-Id header. When the header is present, the user matches, and an unexpired session with the same device id exists, the route returns that session instead of creating a new row.

I added a nullable device_id column to the sessions table with a partial index on user id and device id for rows that have one. The migration ran on staging in under a second. The feature sits behind an environment flag that is off by default, so production behaves as before.

I tested with a small script that logs in ten times with the same device id and the same user. With the flag on, it produced one session row, and with the flag off, ten. A second device id for the same user produced a second row, as intended.

The settings session list now shows one entry per device for these users. I checked that the log out of all devices flow still removes every row of the user, including the ones with a device id.

What is left is the app change by the agency and a limit on the length of the header, which I will add next.

summary: Looked at the URL parameters of the costs page for a link from the summary mail, and found that the depot filter is stored by name and breaks when a depot is renamed
body:
I wanted to know if a link from the summary mail to the costs page can be made reliable. I read how the costs page puts its filters into the URL and how it reads them back.

The date range is stored as two ISO values and works well. The depot filter, however, is stored as a comma separated list of depot names, for example depots=North,South. When I looked at the code I found it matches names against the depot list on load, and silently drops any name it cannot find.

This is a problem for two reasons. A depot that Acme renames makes old links lose that depot without any message. And names with a comma or special characters would break the list. I checked the production depot list and found one name with an ampersand and none with a comma, so the second case is only theoretical today.

I tried it: I renamed a depot on staging and opened a bookmarked URL. The page showed the other depots only, and nothing told me that one was missing. That is the kind of thing that makes a manager believe a number is the total when it is not.

The fix is to put the depot ids in the URL and not the names. I wrote the change so that the page reads both forms: ids are preferred, and names are still accepted for old bookmarks and mapped to ids on load. After the load it rewrites the URL to the id form with replace, so the history has no extra entry.

When an id or a name is unknown, the page now shows a small notice above the filters that says which value was ignored. I used the same notice component as the one for forced logout reasons, to keep the look consistent.

Tests:
- URL with ids gives the right selection
- URL with old names gives the right selection and is rewritten
- URL with one unknown value shows the notice and keeps the rest
- name with an ampersand survives the round trip

The first and second pass. The fourth failed at first, because the encoding of the ampersand was double applied in my helper. I fixed the helper, and since ids are numbers, the case matters only for old links.

I also searched the code for other places that build links to the costs page. There are two: the dashboard tile and the export dialog. Both use the old name form. I changed them to use ids.

I did not release this today. It touches the URL handling of a page that managers use daily, so I want a second look tomorrow with a fresh mind and a Playwright spec that opens an old bookmark.

The link in the summary mail can use the id form once this is released. I wrote that as the next step, and it will be a small change to the mail renderer, which already knows the depot ids of the schedule.

summary: Wrote the Playwright spec for old costs page bookmarks with depot names and one with a renamed depot, and both pass on staging data
body:
I wrote the spec I planned. It opens the costs page with an old URL that has depot names, checks that the selection shows the right depots, and checks that the URL was rewritten to ids.

The second case renames a depot through the settings API in the test setup, opens a URL with the old name, and checks that the notice appears and names the ignored value. After the test it renames the depot back, in a finally block, so staging data stays clean.

The specs use the stored session helper, so they do not log in through the form, and the two together run in about 20 seconds.

Both passed on the second run. The first failed because the notice appeared a moment after the chart was drawn, and my assertion looked too early. I changed it to wait for the notice element.

The release is planned for tomorrow morning.

summary: Limited the device id header to 64 characters and a safe character set, and added tests for odd values after last session's change.
body:
The device id header from the last session accepted any string, which is the same mistake as the 9 KB user agent. I added a check in the login route that allows 8 to 64 characters from letters, digits and dashes. A value that does not match is ignored and the route creates a normal session, so a bad header never blocks a login.

I wrote tests for an empty header, a header of 200 characters, a header with spaces and one with a semicolon. All four log in normally and store no device id. A valid UUID is stored and reused as before.

I also made the column a varchar of 64 so the database enforces the same limit. The migration ran on staging again without problems. The full API suite passed.

The flag is still off in production. I will switch it on once the agency confirms the app sends the header.

summary: Looked into why the settings session list shows the same phone twice for some managers and found that each app start of the mobile app creates a new session
body:
A manager told Jonas that her settings page showed her phone three times, and Jonas passed it on. I looked at her session rows on production, with her permission through Jonas, and saw three live sessions with the same user agent string, created on three different days, all from the same IP range.

The cause was in the login route. The mobile app does not keep its session id after it is closed on some phones, and logs in again with the stored credentials at each start. Each login creates a new session row, and the old one stays until it expires. So the list is correct, but it shows one device as several.

I checked how many users are affected. A query for users with more than two live sessions with the same user agent and the same /24 network gave 41 users out of about 600. Of these, 30 use the mobile app. The rest are desktop users with a browser that clears cookies at exit.

I thought about three options. The first is to identify a device by a device id that the app sends, and reuse the session for it. That needs the other agency to change the app, and I do not control their schedule. The second is to merge sessions on login when user agent and network match, by deleting the older ones. This is risky, since two people on the same office network with the same browser string would be one user anyway, but one user with two real devices of the same model on the same Wi-Fi would lose a session without knowing.

The third option is to do nothing to the data, and group equal entries in the list. A group would show the device name, the count, and the last active time of the newest one, and the revoke button would end the whole group.

I chose to build the third option now and to ask the agency about the first. The third changes only the display and the revoke of a group, and it can be removed if the agency adds device ids.

The implementation: the list API still returns every row. The frontend groups by user agent plus the /24 of the IP, shows the newest last_active, and a small label such as 3 sessions. The revoke action sends the ids of the group. I kept the current session marked, and the group that contains it shows the label this device and cannot be revoked as a whole, only the other rows of it.

That last rule took thought. If the current session is in a group of three, the revoke should end the other two and keep the current one, so the user is not logged out by cleaning up. I wrote this as a test.

Tests:
- grouping of rows with equal and different networks
- the current session in a group is kept on revoke
- a group of one behaves as before

The tests pass. I did not run Playwright yet.

I also wrote a message for the agency, short and in plain words, describing what we see and asking whether the app can send a stable device id in a header. I gave it to Jonas to forward, since he has the contact. I proposed an optional header name and said that nothing breaks if it is missing.

The release is for tomorrow, after Playwright and a look from Priya at the group label.

summary: Looked at why the weekly cost summary mail shows depots in a different order than the page, and made both sort by depot name.
body:
A manager said the order of the depots in the weekly cost summary mail differs from the costs page. The page sorts by name in the browser, while the mail runner takes the rows in the order the query returns them. That order changes whenever Postgres picks another plan.

I added an explicit order by depot name to the summary query. The costs page keeps its own sort, so both now agree. I compared the mail and the page for three depots lists on staging and the order matched each time.

The percent column rounded to one digit in the mail and to two on the page. I did not change the page, because Jonas said the mail should be short. I wrote the difference into the template notes.

I added a test that renders the mail with shuffled input rows and checks the sorted output. The mail tests passed and the change is ready for the next release.

summary: Released the sorted depots in the cost summary mail and checked the first scheduled send on production against the costs page.
body:
I released the sorted depot order together with the device id limit after a full run of Vitest and Playwright. Both passed with no change to the run time.

The first scheduled summary mail went out in the evening. I compared its table with the costs page for the same weeks and depots. The order and the totals matched for all rows.

One manager has a saved summary with only two depots. It rendered correctly and sorted by name. I saw no errors in the runner log.

Nothing else is open on this topic.

summary: Audited which API routes still create sessions for requests that only need to read, and found that the health check and the public status route did so.
body:
After the API keys release and the session growth from the spreadsheet macro, I wanted to be sure no other caller creates session rows without a reason. I counted new session rows in production over three days and grouped them by the route that created them. Almost all came from the login route, as expected.

Two other sources showed up. The health check route that Render calls every 30 seconds had the session middleware mounted before it, and the middleware created a row when a request had no cookie. That produced thousands of rows per day, which the cleanup removed again. The public status route did the same.

I moved both routes above the session middleware in the Express setup, so they never touch the sessions table. I also checked that no other route under the public prefix depends on a session. None does.

I tested by calling both routes 100 times without a cookie on staging and counting rows before and after. The count stayed the same. Login and logged-in routes behaved as before.

The nightly cleanup log should now show smaller counts. I will compare the numbers after a few nights.

summary: Stopped the public status and health routes from creating session rows, and counted that these two routes had added about 1,100 rows per day in production.
body:
The audit of two days ago showed that the health check and the public status route went through the session middleware and created a row for every request without a cookie. Today I fixed that and measured the effect. The monitoring service of Render calls the health check every 30 seconds, and an uptime tool that Jonas set up calls the status route every minute, so the rows added up quickly.

First I looked at how the middleware is mounted. It was registered once for the whole app, before the routers, so every route got it. I moved the mounting so that it applies only to the routers that need a login: the API router, the settings routes and the report routes. The health check and the status route are now registered before the middleware and never see it.

The second step was a flag in the middleware, saveUninitialized, which I set to false for the remaining routes. With that, a session row is only written when something is stored in the session, such as a login. Before, an anonymous request to the login page created a row too. I checked that the login form still works, because the CSRF value is kept in the session and needs the row to exist before the form is posted. It does, because the value is written when the form is rendered, so the row is created at that moment.

Then I wrote the tests. One test calls the health check ten times and asserts that the count of rows in the sessions table did not change. A second test does the same for the status route. A third test loads the login page once and asserts that exactly one row exists afterwards, because of the CSRF value. All three pass, and the existing suite of 412 tests passed as well.

On staging I counted the rows by hand. Before the change, the table grew by about 2 rows per minute with no user active. After the change it grew by none over a period of 30 minutes. The Playwright login specs ran too and passed.

For production I counted the rows without a user id that were created in the last 7 days. There were about 7,700, which is about 1,100 per day, and none of them was ever used for a login. They are all expired or will expire with the normal cleanup, so I did not delete them by hand. The nightly job will remove them in batches, as it does now.

One thing is left. The mobile app item from the audit is still open, since each app start creates a new session, and the device id work from last week only covers part of that. I will look at it separately and did not change anything for it today. The release of this change is planned for tomorrow, together with a note for Jonas that the count of anonymous rows should go to near zero.

summary: Wrote a short summary of the session cleanup and middleware work for Jonas, with the numbers that show the effect and the open mobile app item.
body:
Jonas asked for a plain summary of what the session work of the last weeks changed. I wrote it in a few paragraphs without the technical details.

The main points were these. Sessions that are never used again are removed in batches every night, and it no longer slows down logins. The health check and the status route no longer create rows, which cut the nightly deleted rows to about a fifth. The last_seen throttle reduced session updates by about 95 percent.

The open item is the mobile app. Each app start still creates a new session until the agency sends the device id header. The server side is ready behind a flag.

I sent the note to Jonas in the evening.

summary: Checked the other saved schedules and reports for stale all-depot lists and converted the 6 that had the full list at creation time
body:
After the fix in the evening I ran a query on production over all schedules and saved reports that have a depot filter. There were 14 with a depot filter. For each one I compared the stored id list with the current list of depots.

Six of them contained the full list of the depots at the time of creation, and four of those six were missing at least one depot that exists now. The other two were created recently enough that the lists were still complete. The remaining eight have a manual selection, with fewer depots than the full list, and I left them alone.

Before I changed anything, I wrote the six rows with their old JSON into a backup file. Then I asked Jonas by message about the four with missing depots, since the owners may have chosen the list on purpose. For three of them he knew the owner and said the intent was all depots. For the fourth, a report of a regional manager, he was not sure, and I did not touch it.

So I converted five: the three confirmed, plus the two that were still complete, which are safe to convert because the result is the same today and stays right later. I used an update that sets the all flag and removes the id list, in a transaction, and checked the row count of five before the commit.

I opened the three with the changes on production in the preview as the owner and compared the depot count in the table with the costs page: they now show all depots, including the new ones.

For the one left open, I added a line in the notes file with the report id and a reminder to ask Jonas on the next call.

I also changed the report builder so that a saved report with the old full list gets a small hint when it is opened: the selection has all depots as of its creation, with a button to make it follow new depots. That is a quick way for a user to fix it by themselves. I did not release the hint yet, since I want Priya to look at the wording.

The work on this topic is nearly done. The remaining items are the hint, the one open report, and a look at how the new depot creation could warn that schedules with a fixed list exist. I do not think the last one is needed now.

summary: Started on the mobile app session reuse: with the device id flag on in staging, a fake client now keeps one session row across ten app starts instead of ten rows.
body:
The open item from the summary for Jonas was the mobile app creating a new session on every app start. The device id header went in behind a flag a few days ago, so today I turned the flag on in staging and ran the fake mobile client against it.

The client logged in ten times with the same user and the same device id. Before the flag it left ten rows in sessions; with the flag it left one, and its expires_at moved forward each time. A second device id for the same user created a second row, as intended.

Then I tried the cases that could go wrong. A login with the header but a wrong password created no row. A login for a different user with the same device id created a new row and did not take over the first user's session. That last case matters on shared phones, and the lookup already uses user id and device id together, so it held.

One gap showed up. When the old session had already expired but the cleanup job had not yet removed it, the login reused the expired row and the new cookie was refused right away. I changed the lookup to ignore rows with expires_at in the past and create a new one in that case. I added a test for it in the login route spec.

The full Vitest run passed afterwards, 412 tests. The flag stays on in staging only. Next step is to ask the mobile agency whether their app always sends the same id after a reinstall, because that decides how many old rows are left behind.

summary: Started on the stale session problem for the mobile app: sessions that expire while the app is in the background make the first call after resume fail with a 401.
body:
The mobile agency reported that drivers sometimes see an error on the first screen after returning to the app. I reproduced it with the fake mobile client on staging by creating a session, waiting past the idle limit and then calling the shipments route. The API answered 401 with the reason value 'expired', which is correct, but the app treated it as a hard failure instead of sending the driver to the login. That part is on the agency side, so I did not touch it.

What I could check was how often the case happens. I queried the logs of the last two weeks for 401 responses with the reason 'expired' on routes called with the mobile user agent. There were 212 of them, spread over 37 drivers, and 160 came in the first minute after the app was opened. That fits the picture of an app that wakes up with an old cookie.

I also looked at whether the idle limit is too short for drivers. It is 12 hours of inactivity, and the absolute limit is 30 days. A driver who finishes a late shift and starts the next morning can pass the idle limit easily. With the device id change now live, a driver logging in again reuses the same row, so the cost of a forced login is small for the database.

I wrote down two options for Jonas. One is a longer idle limit for sessions that carry a device id, say 48 hours. The other is a silent renewal call that the app makes at start, which would need work from the agency. I prefer the first because it is one line of config and needs nothing from them.

Nothing is changed yet. I added the 401 counts to my notes and opened a short message for the agency that describes the exact response body and the reason values, so they can handle 'expired' with a login screen. Next I want to ask Jonas whether a 48 hour limit for drivers is acceptable from a security view on the Acme side.

summary: Checked the admin health page after two weeks of cleanup run counts: runs take 3 to 6 seconds and remove between 2,500 and 3,100 rows a night.
body:
I looked at the table that stores the count and duration of each nightly session cleanup run, as shown on the admin health page. The runs stay between 3 and 6 seconds, and the deleted counts are between 2,500 and 3,100 rows per night. That matches the drop after the status route fix.

One run was longer, 14 seconds, and it was the night after the big manager import when many sessions were created. It was still in batches and login times showed no peak.

I did not change anything. I noted that when the device id flag goes live, the nightly count should fall, and that this is a simple way to see the effect.

summary: Set the idle limit for sessions with a device id to 48 hours after Jonas agreed, and tested that web sessions keep the 12 hour limit.
body:
Jonas answered this morning that 48 hours is fine for drivers, as long as managers and dispatchers on the web keep the shorter limit. So I made the idle limit depend on whether the session row has a device id. The value comes from a new setting, SESSION_IDLE_HOURS_DEVICE, with a default of 48, next to the existing one for the web.

The change sits in the session middleware where the expiry is checked and where last_seen is updated. I had to be careful with the last_seen throttle from a few weeks ago. The throttle only writes if the stored value is older than a few minutes, and the expiry check uses the stored value, so the check had to use the limit of the row and not a global one. I wrote that as a small function that takes the row and returns the limit in milliseconds.
