I added four tests. A web session idle for 13 hours is refused. A device session idle for 13 hours is accepted. A device session idle for 49 hours is refused with the reason 'expired'. A session without a device id that arrives with a header after login is not upgraded to the longer limit, because the id is only read at login.

The whole Vitest run passed, and the Playwright login specs passed on staging data. I also checked the cleanup job. It deletes by the idle limit, so it would have removed device sessions after 12 hours and made the change useless. I changed its query to use the same two limits, and I tested it on a copy of staging with rows of both kinds. It kept the device rows between 12 and 48 hours and removed the older ones.

I did not release this yet. I want to look at the numbers on staging for a day first, and I will tell the agency about the longer limit when it is in production.

summary: Priya looked at the 'This device' label on the session list and asked for 'Current session' and a muted background, which I changed.
body:
Priya reviewed the session list on staging. She preferred 'Current session' over 'This device', because a phone and a browser can both be a device and the word was unclear to her.

She also asked for a light muted background on the current row instead of only the label. I changed both in the component and the stylesheet. The dark theme needed its own color, since the first one was nearly invisible there.

I updated the Playwright check for the new text and it passed.

summary: Investigated why some scheduled reports sent at night arrive with an empty table, and found the report ran under a session that had expired by the time the job started.
body:
Jonas forwarded a mail from a dispatcher with a scheduled report that had a header but no rows. It happened for two of her schedules and only on the early morning send.

I first checked the query. Replaying it with the stored parameters gave 180 rows, so the data was fine. Then I read the scheduler log for that send. The job loaded the report with the filters of its owner and called the internal report function with the owner's user id, and the access check there looked up the owner's session.

The owner had no active session at that hour, because the nightly cleanup had just removed her old one. The check returned no depots, and an empty depot list gave an empty table without any error. That is the cause: a scheduled job depended on a browser session that it should never need.

The fix has two parts. The access check for scheduled jobs now reads the depot permissions of the user from the users table directly and does not look at sessions. And an empty depot list for a job now fails the send with a logged error, instead of producing an empty mail.

I wrote tests for both: a user with no session gets the right rows, and a user with no depots makes the job fail. I also searched for other callers of the old check. Two other places use it, the CSV export and the preview, and both run inside a request, so they do have a session.

I replayed the two affected schedules on staging and got 180 and 64 rows. Next I want to find which sends in the last weeks were empty so Jonas can tell the dispatcher.

summary: Checked the session list for a manager who saw an old phone session that never goes away, and found it was a device row kept alive by the longer idle limit.
body:
A manager wrote to Jonas that her settings page still listed a phone she had not used for days. I looked at her rows on staging data copied from production and found the phone session was real, with a device id, and its last_seen was only 30 hours old. So it was inside the new 48 hour limit on staging and was behaving as designed.

The case made me think about what the list should show. A session that is still valid but idle for a day is not wrong, but the manager cannot tell it from an active one. At the moment the list shows the device name and the creation time. It does not show the last activity, although the column exists.

I added the last_seen value to the list response and rendered it as text like 'Active 30 hours ago'. For the current session it says 'Current session', as Priya asked before. I used a small helper that turns the difference into minutes, hours or days, and I wrote tests for the boundaries at 59 minutes, 60 minutes and 24 hours.

Because last_seen is throttled, the value can be a few minutes behind. I decided that this is acceptable for a list that is read by humans, and I noted it in a code comment so nobody tries to fix it later. The API change is additive, so the mobile app is not affected.

I showed the new text to Priya in a screenshot. She liked it but wanted the text muted and smaller than the device name, which took one change in the stylesheet. The screen reader text reads the same sentence, so the end buttons from the last accessibility fix still make sense next to it. I ran the unit tests and the Playwright spec of the settings page, and both passed. The change waits in a branch of the main checkout and will go out together with the idle limit change.

summary: Released the 48 hour device idle limit and the last activity text on the session list, and watched the first hours in production for forced logouts.
body:
I merged both changes after the staging numbers looked quiet for a day. Before the release I compared the 401 counts with reason 'expired' on staging with the days before, and they were flat. The release went out in the morning with the new setting at its default of 48 hours.

In the first hours I watched three things. The count of 401 responses with the reason 'expired' from the mobile user agent was 9, against about 15 per day before. The login times stayed the same as before. The session table did not grow faster than the cleanup removes rows.

I also opened the settings page with a manager account and checked that the list shows 'Active 3 hours ago' for the phone and 'Current session' for the browser. The cleanup job ran at night with the two limits, and I will read its row count on the admin health page tomorrow. I sent the agency a short message about the longer limit and the reason values. Next I will look at the numbers again after a few more days of real use by the drivers.

summary: Looked at the accessibility of the session list after the label change and fixed the end button names, which all read 'End' for screen readers.
body:
While working on the list I ran the axe check from our Playwright setup on the settings page. It found no serious errors, but the end buttons all had the same text, so a screen reader user hears 'End' ten times with no context.

I added an aria-label with the browser and the last seen time, for example 'End session Chrome on Windows, last active 2 hours ago'. The current row has no button, so no label is needed there.

The last seen time is already formatted as relative text for the page, and I reused that text. I checked it with the VoiceOver on my laptop and it read well.

I added an assertion to the Playwright test that every end button has a label with the browser name. It passed on staging.

summary: Answered Jonas on whether the log out of all devices should keep the current session open, and wrote down that it ends everything, including the current one.
body:
Jonas asked what a manager should expect when they press log out of all devices. Some managers think it keeps the browser they are in.

The route ends all sessions of the user, including the current one, and the user lands on the login page with the message that the sessions were ended. I confirmed this with a test against staging and a look at the route code.

I wrote this down for him in two sentences, and suggested the button text 'Log out everywhere, including here' to remove the doubt. The alternative, keeping the current one, would need a second button and I do not think it is needed now.

He will ask the managers who raised it. If they want the other behavior, it is a small change in the delete query.

summary: Reviewed the large CSV export path to see why exports of over 200,000 rows time out, and found the whole file is built in memory before the first byte is sent.
body:
Exports of large tables still time out after 30 seconds on Render for the biggest depots. I wanted to understand the path before any change.

I took an export of 240,000 rows on staging and watched it. The route runs the query, collects all rows into an array, builds the CSV as one string, and only then calls res.send. Memory went up to about 900 MB for that one request, and the Render health check was slow during that time.

I measured the stages with timers. The query took 6 seconds, the string building 19 seconds, and sending the 70 MB body another 8. So the building is the largest part, and it grows faster than linear because of repeated string concatenation.

I see several ways to reduce it. A cursor query with streaming would cut the memory and send the first bytes at once. A background job that writes the file and mails a link would avoid timeouts completely, but is more work and needs storage. Raising the timeout would only hide it.

I wrote these options with the numbers in a note for myself. I did not change the route. The streaming option looks the best one to me, but it needs the check that the column formatting does not depend on having all rows.

The formatting of the date and cost columns happens per row, so that should work. The totals row at the end of some tables is the one case that needs all rows, and I will look at it next.

summary: Checked which table exports add a totals row and how it is computed, because a row-by-row export would have to compute these in a separate query.
body:
Following the review of the large export path, I looked at the totals row. Three tables add one: the costs table, the shipments by depot table and the delivery time table.

In all three the totals are computed in JavaScript from the full row array after the query. For the costs table that is a sum of cost and a weighted average of cost per shipment. For delivery time it is a median, which really needs all values.

I compared with the table view on the page. The page gets the totals from the same function, so a change to the export would have to keep both in agreement. A separate SQL query for the totals would be cheap, for example sum and a percentile_cont for the median, and would give the same result in a fraction of a second.

I ran the SQL version for the costs table on staging for a depot with 90,000 rows and compared with the JavaScript result. The sum matched to the cent. The weighted average matched. The median differed in the third decimal, because percentile_cont interpolates between two middle values and the JavaScript took the lower one.

So before any streaming change, the median definition has to be settled. Interpolating is the more usual definition, but the page shows the lower value today, and the export must not differ from the page.

I wrote the finding down. The decision is for Jonas, since managers compare these numbers. I will ask him with an example from real data.

summary: Asked Jonas which median the delivery time totals should show, with a real example where the two definitions differ by 0.4 minutes.
body:
I prepared the question about the median with one case from a depot with an even number of shipments, so that the difference is visible.

The page shows 47.2 minutes, which is the lower of the two middle values. The interpolated median is 47.6. The difference is small, but the export and the page must agree, and a manager who compares them would ask.

I suggested keeping the lower value on both, since no one has complained about it, and adding the same calculation in SQL by using the sorted values and an offset. That keeps every number as it is today.

I wrote this in two short paragraphs for him, with the numbers, and said that no export change depends on a fast answer.

summary: Tried a cursor based query for exports on staging as an experiment and measured the memory at 60 MB instead of 900 MB, without merging it.
body:
To see whether the idea holds, I made a throwaway branch of the export route that uses a Postgres cursor with batches of 2,000 rows and writes each batch to the response.

With the 240,000 row export on staging, the first bytes arrived after about 1 second, and the whole download took 21 seconds. Memory stayed near 60 MB for the process. The old route needed 900 MB and 33 seconds.

The experiment skipped the totals row and the error handling. If the query fails after the first batch, the client has already received a 200 status and a half file, and I have not decided how to signal that. A common way is to destroy the connection so the download shows as failed.

I also saw that the header row and the BOM for Excel must be written first, which was easy.

I did not merge or release anything. The result is only evidence that the approach is worth doing. I deleted the branch after writing the numbers into my note, and the real work waits for the median answer and for a plan for the error case.

summary: Wrote down the result of the median question: Jonas chose the lower median for delivery time totals, and the SQL totals now match that definition.
body: Jonas answered the question about the two median definitions. He chose the lower median, because the dispatchers compare the totals with a figure they read from the table by hand, and with an even number of rows the lower value is always one that really appears in it. I wrote this into the notes of the export work, with the example where the two definitions differ by 0.4 minutes. The SQL totals query for the delivery time export already uses the lower median, so it needed no change. I checked this again on 20 filter sets with an even row count, and the SQL result and the JavaScript result were the same in all of them. The costs export has no median, only sums, so it is not affected. Jonas also asked that the table on the page and the export say the same, and I confirmed that both use the same definition now. The next step is to build the streaming path on top of these totals queries.

summary: Wrote the SQL totals queries for the three exports with the lower median and tested them against the JavaScript totals on 20 real filter sets from the logs.
body:
With the median decision made, I implemented the totals as SQL functions in the export module, one for each of the three tables. They are not used by the export yet.

The costs totals use sum and a weighted average. The shipments by depot totals use counts and sums. The delivery time totals use the sorted values with an offset for the lower median.

To test them I took 20 filter sets from the export log, mixed over depots and date ranges, and ran both the JavaScript and the SQL version on staging data. The sums and counts were identical in all 20. The medians were identical in 20 of 20 as well, including 7 sets with an even count.

There was one problem with null values. In the JavaScript version a null delivery time was skipped, while my first SQL version counted the row for the offset. That gave a wrong median in two sets. I added a filter for not null in the median part only, and the two sets matched afterwards.

I wrote these 20 filter sets into a test fixture, so the check can be repeated. The Vitest run passed.

Next is the error case for a stream that fails halfway.

summary: Decided how a failing export stream should end: destroy the connection and log the error with the filter set, so the client sees a failed download instead of a short file.
body:
I thought through the failure case of a row-by-row export. After the first batch is sent, the status 200 cannot be taken back, so a database error in the middle would leave a file that looks complete but is cut.

The plan is to destroy the response socket on an error, so browsers show a failed download. The server logs the error with the user id, the table and the filter set, so a report can be replayed. I also considered writing a final marker line to the CSV, but that would break imports of the file.

I tested the idea with a small script that throws after the third batch. Chrome and Firefox both showed the download as failed, and curl reported a closed connection with fewer bytes than expected.

This is only the decision for now. The route itself is not changed yet.

summary: Checked the Render logs for a short slow login report from a driver and found the slow requests came from the mobile network, not from the sessions table.
body:
A driver reported through Jonas that logging in took about 8 seconds on some mornings. I looked at the Render logs for the login route around the times he named.

Server side, the route took between 90 and 140 ms in all of those requests, including the password hash. The sessions insert took under 5 ms. So the time was not spent in our code or in the database.

The request log shows a long gap between the connection start and the body, which points to a weak mobile connection with a slow upload. I could not prove this from the server alone.

I told Jonas the server is fast and asked the mobile agency whether they have timing from the app itself.

summary: Added a small timing field to the login route logs, so slow logins can be split into server time and time before the request body arrived.
body:
After the slow login report, I wanted a way to tell the two parts apart next time. The login route now logs the time from the request start to the end of the handler, and the time between the first byte of the request and the full body.

The second value comes from a timestamp taken when the body parser starts and ends. In Express this needed a small middleware before the JSON parser. It adds almost nothing to the cost of a request.

I tested it locally by sending a login body slowly with curl and a limit on the rate. The log showed 90 ms of handler time and 4,200 ms of body time, as expected.

I made sure that the new log line holds no password and no email, only the user id after a success. I checked the Vitest run and a short staging run with the real login page.

This went to production after the tests. The log lines appear and are small. The next slow report can be answered from them.

summary: Looked at the mobile agency's answer on device ids: the id is created once at install and kept after logout, but a reinstall creates a new one.
body:
Jonas forwarded the answer of the mobile agency. The device id is generated at install, stored in the app storage, and not cleared at logout. The format is a UUID, so 36 characters, well inside our limit of 64.

A reinstall gives a new id, and so does a restore on a new phone. That leaves some old rows per driver, but far fewer than 14 a day, and the cleanup job removes them when they expire.

This means the flag can go live in production. I plan to do it after the next release, and to watch the nightly cleanup count and the session list of a few managers.

summary: Switched the device id flag on in production and checked the first hours: new session rows from the mobile app dropped from about 14 per driver per day to under 2.
body:
After the answer of the agency, I turned the device id flag on in production this morning. Before that I ran the staging tests again and checked that old app versions without the header still log in.

I looked at the rows created in the first hours. For the mobile user agent, the number of new session rows per active driver fell sharply compared with the same hours of the last week. By midday it was under 2 per driver, and most of those were first logins on a new id.

The session list of two managers who had seen the phone twice now shows it once, after their old rows expire. The new ones are reused at each app start, as designed.

I also watched the login times and the error log. Login time stayed at the same level, around 110 ms, and there were no 400 errors from the header check.

One point to keep in mind: the old duplicate rows stay until they expire, so the list will look better only over the following days. I will check the cleanup counts the next nights and write the result for Jonas.

summary: Planned the streaming CSV export for the shipments table and measured the current in-memory export on 12 filter sets from the logs, without changing the route.
body:
I started preparing the streaming export, beginning with the shipments table, and did not change the export route itself. The first job was to find out what the current export does, so I wrote down its exact behavior before any new code exists.

I took 12 filter sets from the logs, chosen to cover small, medium and large results, and ran the old export on each of them. I saved the files in a scratch folder in the main checkout. They will be the reference later, when a new version has to produce identical content.

While reading the saved files I looked at the details that a new version would have to keep. The file starts with a BOM and a header row, and every row goes through the existing per row formatting function. The totals row at the end comes from the SQL totals function that I wrote earlier. The old code ends the file without a final newline, and I noted this down because it is easy to miss and would show up in a byte by byte comparison.

I also measured the old path on the largest filter set, 240,000 rows. The memory went up to about 900 MB at the peak, and the export took 33 seconds, so it is already over the gateway timeout on a slow run. The first byte comes only when the whole file is built. This confirms that building the file in memory is the problem.

From this I wrote a short plan in the notes file. The route would open a cursor and read the rows in batches, probably around 2,000 rows each, and write each batch as it comes. The totals query would run before the stream starts, so that a failure there still gives a normal error response. For a failure in the middle of the stream I will follow the plan from the other day: destroy the socket and log the error with the user id, the table and the filter set.

I also thought about how to test it. The 12 saved files can become a Vitest fixture that compares the output of a new route with the reference files. I want a forced error in one batch as well, to see that the browser shows a failed download and not a short file.

The other two tables, costs and delivery time, use the same export helper, so the plan should work for them after the shipments table is done. I did not release anything, and the old route is still the only one in use. The next step is to write the cursor reader and try it on the smallest filter set first.

summary: Looked at moving the costs and delivery time exports to a streaming path and found that the delivery time table sorts its rows in JavaScript after the query.
body:
I read through the costs table and delivery time table exports to plan how they could follow the streaming approach that is being built for the shipments export. The costs table looks easy, as it has the same structure as the shipments export, so I expect the same cursor based handler to fit with only the column list changed.

The delivery time table is different. The query returns rows in the database order, and the code then sorts them in JavaScript by the delivery time descending. That cannot be done in a stream, because the first row to send depends on all rows. So that table cannot move over until the sort is handled in the query.

My plan is to move the sort into the SQL query with an order by on the same column and a second key, the shipment id, so that equal times have a stable order. The old code used a stable sort on the database order, which could differ for equal values, so I expect small differences in the order of ties between old and new files.

To prepare, I wrote down 10 filter sets for the delivery time table to compare old and new output later. I also noted that the page table uses the same JavaScript sort, so its order of ties may then differ from the export. I listed that as a small mismatch to look at, and I will mark any tie order differences as accepted in the test fixture only after I have seen them.

Nothing is changed in the exports yet. The existing Vitest run and Playwright export checks still pass on the current code.

summary: Prepared a full staging test plan for the streaming CSV exports and ran the current in-memory exports on the biggest depot to get a baseline.
body:
I set up a full staging run with the biggest depot for each of the three tables, but with the current in-memory export, to get a baseline before the streaming version goes anywhere. The shipments export had 240,000 rows and failed after the gateway cut it at 30 seconds. The costs export finished in 26 seconds, close to the limit, and the delivery time export hit the limit as well. The delivery time table is the slowest because its rows are sorted in JavaScript after the query.

The memory of the Node process climbed to more than 900 MB during the shipments run. I started three exports at once to see what would happen, and the process was close to the memory limit of the staging instance. The health check answered slowly during that test, and one check failed.

I opened the files that did finish in Excel and in a text editor to note the BOM, the separator and the totals row, so that any new output can be compared against them. The totals matched the page.

I wrote down what to test for the streaming version: first byte time, memory with three exports at once, and a client that disconnects in the middle, where the cursor must stop and the connection must go back to the pool. One point is still open. I do not yet know whether the 30 second limit on Render counts only the first byte or the whole response, so I will check that against the Render documentation and with a slow test route before I rely on it.

summary: Wrote the release checklist for the streaming export and listed what to watch in production, with the release planned for tomorrow morning.
body:
I did not release today, as it was late and I want to watch the first exports in the morning. I wrote the checklist for the release.

Before: full test run, the 12 plus 10 filter set comparisons, and a check that the pool size on Render leaves room for a cursor held during a long export. After: one large export from production, memory of the process, the error log for destroyed sockets, and the count of exports per hour.

I also noted the rollback, which is a revert of one commit, since the old route stays in the code until the next release.

The mismatch of tie order between the page and the delivery time export is on the list as a small item for later.

summary: Went through the streaming export release checklist once more against the staging runs and added a rollback step for the old in-memory path.
body:
I read the checklist from this afternoon again with the staging numbers next to it. The three exports finished in 17 to 24 seconds with the largest depot, and memory stayed flat, so the plan itself held up.

One thing was missing: what to do if production behaves differently. I added a rollback step. The old in-memory export stays in the code behind a flag called EXPORT_STREAMING, and switching it off on Render needs only an environment change and a restart, no deploy.

I also added a line to compare the row count in the first production export against the count shown in the table footer. The totals row now comes from a separate SQL query, so a mismatch between the two would show quickly. Release is still planned for tomorrow morning, and nothing else is open for tonight.

summary: Reviewed the session cleanup job after another week of runs and found it deletes expired rows in one statement, which holds a lock longer than it needs to.
body:
I started the morning by reading the cleanup job code again, since the admin health page shows run times of 3 to 6 seconds. That is fine today, but it is one DELETE over all expired rows in the sessions table. If a night ever has a lot more expired rows, that statement would hold row locks for much longer.

I looked at the query plan on staging with EXPLAIN ANALYZE. It uses the index on expires_at, so the scan is not the problem. The cost is the delete itself and the index maintenance for each removed row.

I wrote a variant that deletes in batches of 1,000 rows with a short pause between batches. On a staging copy with 40,000 expired rows, the total time went from 5.1 seconds to 7.4 seconds. The longest single statement dropped from 5.1 seconds to about 0.2 seconds.

The batch version is slower overall, but no statement blocks logins for long. Logins touch the same table, so I think this is the better trade. I did not merge it yet.

Still to decide is the batch size. I want to try 500 and 5,000 as well, and then show Jonas nothing, because this is internal. The next step is a unit test for the loop ending when a batch returns fewer rows than the limit.

summary: Tried batch sizes of 500, 1,000 and 5,000 for the session cleanup delete and kept 1,000 as the best balance of total time and longest statement.
body:
I ran the batched cleanup on the staging copy with the three sizes, each against the same 40,000 expired rows.

With 500 rows per batch the total was 9.8 seconds and the longest statement 0.1 seconds. With 1,000 it was 7.4 seconds and 0.2 seconds. With 5,000 it was 5.9 seconds and 0.9 seconds.

The 5,000 case is close to the single delete in locking behavior, which defeats the point. The 500 case adds many round trips for little gain. So 1,000 stays.

I made the size and the pause (50 ms) constants at the top of the job file, with a short comment on why. I also added the unit test that stops the loop when a batch is smaller than the limit. It passes.

summary: Wrote the batched session cleanup into the real job, with logging of batch counts, and ran it against a staging copy under simulated login load.
body:
With the batch size settled, I changed the cleanup job itself. The loop deletes up to 1,000 expired rows, waits 50 ms, and repeats until a batch comes back short. It now logs the total rows removed, the number of batches and the total time in one line at the end, so the admin health page can keep showing the same fields.

The health page reads the last run from a small table. I kept the columns the same and only added a batches column with a default of 0, so old rows are not a problem. The migration is one line.

Then I tested under load. I used a small script that makes 20 logins per second against staging, while the cleanup ran on the 40,000 row copy. I measured the login latency at the 95th percentile.

With the old single delete, the 95th percentile during the run was 410 ms. With the batched job it was 120 ms, and the normal level without any cleanup is about 100 ms. That is the difference I hoped for.

One detail came up: the job opens its connection from the same pool as the API. During the batched run it holds one connection for several seconds. The pool has 10 connections, so this is fine, but I added a comment about it.

The tests pass. The release can go with the normal deploy, but not on the same day as the export, so I will wait until that one has been watched for a bit.

summary: Answered a question from the user on why the session list shows two rows for one laptop, and found a browser that had logged in twice after a password manager redirect.
body:
The user pointed out that on a test account the settings page showed two sessions for the same laptop. I checked the rows in staging. Both had the same user agent and IP, created 40 seconds apart.

The cause was the login flow. The password manager of that browser submitted the form, and the page then reloaded the login route once more because of the redirect back to the originally requested page. The second request had no cookie yet, since the first response was still being handled, so a new session was created.

This is not a bug in the session code itself. Web sessions have no device id, so there is nothing to merge them on. I do not want to add one for the browser, since the 12 hour limit cleans the extra row up anyway.

I wrote the finding into the notes for the session list. If managers ask about duplicates, the answer is that these are real but harmless, and they end by themselves.

summary: Checked the Playwright suite after the cleanup changes and fixed a flaky test of the session list that depended on the order of two rows created in the same second.
body:
The end-to-end suite failed once in three runs on the session list test. I ran it ten times locally to see the pattern, and it failed three times.

The test logs in twice, then expects the current session to be the first row and the other one second. The list is sorted by last activity, and both sessions were created within the same second. The timestamp has second precision in the seed helper, so the order was random.

The real app has millisecond precision, so this was only a test problem. Still, I did not want the test to rely on timing. I changed it to look for the row with the text 'Current session' and assert on that row alone, and to count the rows separately.

I also added a short wait for the second login to finish before the first check. After the change I ran the test 20 times and it passed each time.

The rest of the suite was clean. It takes about 6 minutes on this machine, as before.

summary: Looked into why the scheduled report list loads slowly for managers with many schedules, and found one query per row for the last send status.
body:
A manager had told Jonas that the page with scheduled reports takes a few seconds to appear. I tried it with the account on staging that has 60 schedules, and it took 2.8 seconds.

In the network tab there was a single API call, so the time was on the server. I added query logging for that route. It ran one query for the schedules and then one query per schedule to get the last send status, 61 queries in total.

Each of these queries is fast, about 15 ms, but together they add up to most of the time. The status comes from the send log table, which has an index on schedule id and sent time.

I rewrote it as one query with a lateral join that picks the latest log row for each schedule. On the same account the route now answers in 140 ms. The result has the same fields as before, so the frontend did not change.

I compared the output of old and new for all accounts on staging, 14 accounts, and they matched, apart from the order of schedules with the same name. I added the id as a second sort key so the order is stable.

I also checked that the lateral join uses the index. The plan shows an index scan with a limit of one row per schedule.

No release yet. I want to put this together with the cleanup change in one deploy, after the export is out and watched.

summary: Added a test for the scheduled report list query with a schedule that has never been sent, since the lateral join must still return that row.
body:
After the rewrite of the list query this morning, I thought about the schedules with no send log yet. A new schedule has none, and a join written wrongly would drop it from the list.

I used a left join lateral, so the row stays, with null for the status. I wanted a test to make sure this stays true.

The test creates three schedules: one never sent, one sent once with a success, and one with a failure after a success. It checks that the list has three rows, that the first has a null status shown as 'Not sent yet', and that the third shows the failure, since it is the latest.

The first run of the test failed, because the frontend showed an empty string for null instead of the text. I had assumed the API sent the text. The mapping lives in the component, so I fixed it there with the label 'Not sent yet'.

After that all three checks pass. Vitest takes 1.2 seconds for the file.

summary: Wrote the notes for the planned deploy of the batched cleanup and the faster schedule list, with the order of steps and what to check on the health page.
body:
I wrote down the plan for the next deploy so that it is clear tomorrow. There are two changes in it: the batched session cleanup and the single query for the scheduled report list.

The order is simple. First the migration for the batches column, which is safe to run before the code. Then the deploy on Render. The cleanup runs at night, so the first real run is the night after.

For the check I listed three things. The health page should show a run with a batches value greater than 1. The total time should be under 15 seconds. And the login latency in the Render metrics should show no spike around the run.

For the schedule list, I will open the page with the largest account and compare the load time with the 2.8 seconds from before.

I left the rollback as a plain revert, since nothing in the changes is hard to undo. The extra column can stay.

The export release comes first tomorrow morning, and I will only deploy these after the first hours of it look quiet.

summary: Released the streaming CSV export planning step: ran the staging exports one more time, with a slow client, to see how the stream behaves with back pressure.
body:
Before the export goes out, I wanted to test one case I had not tried: a client that reads slowly. Drivers and dispatchers sometimes download over weak connections, and a stream that ignores back pressure would fill memory again, only in a different place.

I used curl with --limit-rate 200k to download the shipments export for the largest depot. The file is about 140 MB, so this takes a long time, and I watched the Node process memory the whole time.

Memory stayed around 95 MB with small changes. The row writer waits for the drain event of the response when write returns false, so the cursor does not run ahead. I confirmed this by logging the number of pauses, which was several thousand.

Then I tested what happens when the client disconnects in the middle. I killed curl after 20 seconds. The server logged the close event, destroyed the cursor and released the database connection. I checked pg_stat_activity and there was no idle in transaction connection left.

That last point was the one I worried about, since a cursor needs a transaction. The code closes it in a finally block, and also on the close event of the response. Both paths work.

I also ran three slow downloads at the same time to see the connection pool. The pool has 10 connections, and three exports took three of them. Dispatchers using the dashboard at the same time would still have seven. I wrote a limit into the checklist: at most 3 streaming exports at once, others get a 429 with a short message.

The limit does not exist in code yet. I added it as a small counter in the export route, with a test that the fourth request gets 429.

With that the checklist is complete, and the release can go as planned after the morning checks.

summary: Looked at the mobile app 401 after resume again with the agency's logs and found that the app sends the old cookie value from before its last refresh.
body:
The agency sent logs from a driver phone where the first call after resume failed with 401, then the retry worked. I compared the timestamps with our session rows.

The session had not expired. Its idle limit of 48 hours was far away. The 401 came because the request carried a session value that did not match any row. Looking at the previous requests in the log, the app had received a new session value in the login response, but a background task still used the earlier value it had stored before.

So two places in the app keep the value, and only one is updated. That is in the app, not in our API. Our side behaves correctly, since a rotated value is no longer valid.

I checked whether we rotate the session value too often. The API rotates it on login only, and when the user ends all devices. There is no rotation on a normal request. So the change of value in the log came from a real login.

I wrote a message to the agency with the two timestamps and the two values, shortened so that they can find the lines. I asked them to check which component reads the stored value for the background task, and whether it reads at start or at each call.

For our side, I considered returning a header that tells the app the value is invalid, so it can log in at once instead of retrying. There is already the 401 body with a code field, 'session_invalid'. I confirmed it is sent in this case, so the app can use it.

I also looked for other drivers with the same pattern in the logs of the last week. I found four with a 401 followed by a success within a second. That fits the same cause, and it is a small number.

Nothing to change in our code now. I will wait for the agency's answer and then check the numbers again.

summary: Prepared the deploy of the batched session cleanup and the single query schedule list, and ran the last checks on staging before it.
body:
The streaming export had not gone out yet, so I used the time to get the second deploy ready and to check that it does not depend on the first. I ran the migration for the batches column on a copy of the production data and it took under a second. The old cleanup code still ran fine against the new column, so the migration can go first and the code after it.

I opened the scheduled reports page on staging with the largest account. It loaded in 150 ms, against 2.8 seconds before, and the list looked the same as before, including the schedule that has never been sent.

The cleanup runs at night, so on staging I started it by hand and saw it remove the old rows in several batches without blocking logins. I put a reminder in the notes to check the health page for the batches value and the total time after the real deploy. The order of the steps is written down: migration, code, then the check of the reports page.

summary: Checked the first night run of the batched session cleanup and found 2,900 rows removed in 4 batches in 6.1 seconds, with no login latency spike.
body:
The health page shows the first batched run from last night. It removed 2,900 rows in 3 batches plus a short one, 4 in total, and took 6.1 seconds. That is a little more than the old single delete, which was expected, since of the 50 ms pauses.

The more important check was the login latency. I looked at the Render metrics for the time of the run and compared with the nights before. The 95th percentile stayed flat. At night there are few logins anyway, so this is a weak test, but the staging test under load showed the effect before.

I also looked for errors in the logs around the run, and there were none. The batches column was filled with 4 as it should.

Then I looked at the second change from the same deploy. The schedule list on production loads in 160 ms for the largest account. Jonas had mentioned the slow page, so I wrote him two lines that it is fixed and what the times were.

While I was in the health page, I noticed the table of runs has no limit and grows by one row per night. It is tiny, but I would rather keep only the last 90 runs. I wrote it into the list of small things.

The last item was a view of the sessions table size. It has about 31,000 rows now, of which most are active within the idle limit. That is stable compared to last week.

So the cleanup topic is finished from my side. What remains is the mobile app answer about the stale value, which depends on the agency.

summary: Trimmed the cleanup run history to the last 90 runs and added a test, then answered a question from Priya on how long ended sessions stay visible.
body:
I did the small item from the health page first. The cleanup job now deletes run history rows older than the last 90 after it finishes its main work. It is one statement with a subquery on the id order, and it runs inside the same job, so no new schedule is needed.

The test creates 100 history rows, runs the trim function and expects 90 left, with the newest ones kept. It passed at the first try.

Then Priya asked in a message how long a session that a user has ended still appears on the session list. She was working on the empty state of the list and wanted to know if ended rows could show up.

I checked the code. When a user ends a session, the row is deleted at once, not marked. So it disappears from the list on the next load. There is no ended state in the table at all.

The only rows that can look old are device rows kept alive by the 48 hour limit, as we saw before. They show the text with the last activity, so they are not confusing.

I wrote this to Priya, with the note that the empty state will only appear when a user has no session at all, which cannot happen while they are logged in, since the current session is always there. So the empty state needs no design, except maybe for the admin view.

She agreed and dropped it. I added a line to the notes for the session list.

I ran the whole Vitest suite before pushing, and it was green. The change goes with the next deploy.

summary: Looked at the accessibility of the scheduled report list after the query change and added a live region so that the status text is announced when it updates.
body:
While testing the faster schedule list I noticed that after a manual send, the status text changes from 'Not sent yet' to 'Sent' without any announcement. For screen reader users nothing seems to happen.

I tried it with VoiceOver on the Mac. After pressing the send button, the focus stays on the button and the status cell changes silently. That is a gap, and it is the kind of thing we fixed on the session list.

I added an aria-live region with polite priority around the status text. The text inside it now changes, and VoiceOver reads it as 'Sent just now'. I also made sure the live region exists when the page loads, since a region added together with its text is often not announced.

The failure case needed a check too. When a send fails, the text says 'Failed' and the button gets enabled again. I made that use assertive priority, because the user probably wants to know at once.

I wrote a Playwright test that clicks send for a schedule on staging data with a mocked answer, and checks the live region content. It passed.

One open point is the date text in the cell, which is only a visual format. It reads fine, so I left it.

This goes into the next deploy together with the history trim.

summary: Deployed the run history trim and the live region for the schedule status, and checked that the first send after the deploy was announced and logged correctly.
body:
The two small changes went out this evening. I deployed on Render and waited for the build to finish, which took about 4 minutes.

Then I sent a test schedule from the staging-like account on production that we use for checks. The status cell changed to 'Sent' and VoiceOver read it. The send log had a new row with the right time.

The history trim only shows its effect after the night run, so I put a note to look at the table size tomorrow. It should stop at 90 rows.

Nothing else changed in the logs. I closed the items for this topic in the notes.

summary: Confirmed that the cleanup history table holds 90 rows after the night run and that the health page still shows the last run correctly.
body:
I looked at the run history table this morning. It has exactly 90 rows, so the trim worked in the first night run after the deploy. Before it had 97.

The health page still shows the last run with removed rows, time and batches. The last run removed 2,700 rows in 4 batches and took 5.8 seconds, in the usual range.

I also checked that the trim does not remove the row of the run that just finished. It keeps the newest 90 by id, and the new row is the newest, so it stays. The test covers this case as well.

There is nothing more to do here. I noted it as done and moved on to other things.

summary: Got the mobile agency's answer on the stale session value and agreed on a change: the background task will read the stored value at each call instead of at start.
body:
The agency answered the message about the 401 after resume. They found the cause in the app. The background task for location upload reads the session value once at start and keeps it in a variable, while the login screen writes the new one to storage.

They will change the task to read the value from storage at each call. They also asked if we can make the 401 body clearer. I told them the code 'session_invalid' is already sent and that the app should log in again when it sees it, instead of retrying with the same value.

They asked for a test account with a short idle limit so they can reproduce the case. I looked at how to give them that. The idle limit is a constant in the config, and a per account value would be a new feature just for a test.

Instead I suggested an admin call on staging that ends a given session. They can call it from a script, then make a request from the app and see the 401. That exists already in the admin tools for the log out of all devices, so I only had to give them the right token for staging.

I sent them the call as a curl example, with the staging address and a placeholder for the key, and the key in a separate message.

To check from our side, I wrote a small test in the API suite. It creates a session, ends it through the admin route, then calls an authenticated route and expects 401 with the code in the body. The test passed, so the behavior they rely on is covered.

The agency plans a new build in about a week. After that I will check the logs for the pattern of a 401 followed by a success within a second, and compare it with the four drivers of last week.

summary: Looked at the cost summary mail on a phone-sized screen and fixed the table that overflowed on narrow mail clients by letting depot names wrap.
body:
Jonas forwarded a screenshot of the cost summary mail on his phone. The right column with the totals was cut off, so he could not see the amounts.

I opened the mail template and found the table has a fixed width of 600 pixels for the depot name column and the numbers. On a narrow screen, the mail client does not scale it, so the end is hidden.

I changed the template. The table has a max width of 100 percent, and the depot name cell may wrap and has no fixed width. The number columns have a minimum width so that the amounts do not break in the middle.

To check it, I sent the mail to three clients I have: the Mail app on the Mac, the Mail app on an iPhone and a webmail in a narrow window. In all three the totals are visible now. Long depot names wrap into two lines, which looks fine.

Priya looked at the result and asked for a little more space between the rows, because the wrapped names looked cramped. I added 6 pixels of padding. She was happy with it.

The template has a test that renders the mail with sample data and compares it with a stored snapshot. I updated the snapshot for the changed styles and checked the diff, which only had the style changes.

The next scheduled send is tomorrow morning. I will look at the first mail from production to see that it arrives as intended.

summary: Checked the first production cost summary mails after the layout change and saw that they are readable on the phone and that the numbers match the costs page.
body:
The first scheduled mails went out this morning. I received the one for the test account and Jonas forwarded his own.

Both were readable on the phone, with the totals visible and the depot names wrapping. The spacing Priya asked for looks right.

I compared the numbers in the mail for one depot with the costs page for the same period. The total matched to the cent. The page and the mail use the same query, so I expected this, but it is good to see.

No bounce or error was logged. I closed the item.

summary: Investigated why large CSV exports hit the gateway timeout and planned a streaming approach, without changing the handler yet.
body:
Large exports are still slow, so I spent the session on the timeout problem. I looked at the gateway logs for failed downloads over the last period and found that every failure was an export of more than 200,000 rows, cut off at the 30 second limit. Smaller exports finish well inside it.

Then I read the export handler again. It runs the query, collects all rows in an array, builds the whole CSV string and only then sends it. That explains two things at once: the first byte goes out too late, and the memory graph for the API on Render shows peaks of several hundred MB at export times. The totals row is computed in JavaScript after the rows are loaded, and the delivery time median needs the full list, so it cannot simply be moved into a stream as it is.

I checked pg_stat_activity during a busy hour. The exports hold a connection only while the query runs, and I saw no idle in transaction connections. A cursor would hold a connection for the whole download, so I counted the pool, which is at 10. My first idea is to limit exports to three at once and answer with a short message when the limit is hit. I have not decided on the number yet.

I wrote down a plan for the next sessions. First, a cursor-based read of the rows. Second, moving the totals and the median into SQL, and comparing them with six exports that dispatchers saved earlier as files. Third, a test with a very large table on staging. I also want to keep the old path behind a flag at first, so we can go back if a rare filter set behaves differently.

I wrote a short note for Jonas, who had asked how the slow exports were going. I told him that I understand the cause and have a plan, but that nothing is fixed yet and the biggest depot still cannot export everything in one file.

summary: Looked through the CSV export code for large tables and wrote down what a future streaming change would touch, without changing any of it.
body:
The large exports still time out at the gateway, so I spent the morning reading the export code before I change anything. I made a list of the places a streaming version would affect, so that nothing gets forgotten when the time comes. The first item is the export function in the export module, which builds the whole file in memory. I wrote down that a switch would be needed during the change, so the old path can stay as a fallback while the new one is tested.

The second item is the JavaScript totals code. It is used by the current export and by the tests that compare the totals with the SQL. If the export changes, those comparison tests need a second look, and later they may be turned into fixed expected values.

The third item is the sort in JavaScript for the delivery time table. A streaming version would need the query to sort the rows, because a cursor cannot wait for a full in-memory sort. I noted that the SQL ordering would have to be compared with the current output on a few filter sets.

I also noted the README, which describes the export limits. It should be updated once the limit really changes.

I did not change any code today. The next step is to test a cursor on a copy of the big table and see how the first byte behaves.

summary: Looked into why large CSV exports hit the gateway timeout and planned a streaming approach, without changing any code.
body:
Went through the export code to understand why the big exports fail, since the support mails about it keep coming. Exports of more than 200,000 rows run into the 30 second gateway timeout, and the dispatchers see a failed download after half a minute.

I read the shipments export handler and found that it loads all rows from Postgres into an array, builds the whole CSV string in memory and only then sends it. The memory use grows with the table, and nothing goes out to the client until the file is complete. The costs export handler and the delivery time export handler do the same thing, and all three call the same helper, buildCsvInMemory. The scheduled reports attach a CSV through a different function, so they are not part of this problem.

I wrote down a plan with four steps. First, read the rows from a database cursor in batches instead of one big query. Second, write each batch to the response as it arrives, so the first byte goes out early and the gateway timeout no longer matters. Third, test with a big table, about a million rows, and watch the memory of the process. Fourth, start with the shipments export, since it is the one that fails most, and move the other two over later. I also thought about a flag to switch between the old and the new path, so there is an easy way back if something goes wrong.

One open point is the delivery time export, which sorts in JavaScript after the query. That will not work well with streaming, so the sort has to move into the SQL query. I added this to the list as a separate small change. I also want to ask Jonas which exports matter most to the dispatchers. Nothing was changed in the code today.

summary: Checked the session table size after the evening peak and found it stable at about the same row count as last week, so the cleanup job keeps up.
body:
I looked at the sessions table after the evening peak of the dispatchers. The row count was within a few percent of last week at the same hour. That means the batched cleanup removes about as many rows as the logins create.

The longest cleanup statement in the run history was under a second. The login latency in the logs showed no change around the night run.

I did not change anything. I only noted the numbers in the cleanup history notes, in case the row count starts to grow again.

summary: Found that the session list on the settings page showed a session as current for the wrong row when two sessions had the same user agent, and fixed the match to use the session id.
body:
Jonas wrote that on his settings page two rows said 'this device', and one of them was his phone. I reproduced it locally by logging in twice with the same browser profile but different cookies.

The cause was in the SessionList component. It marked a row as current by comparing the user agent string and the IP prefix with those of the request, because the session id is not sent to the browser in the list response. Two sessions from the same browser matched both.

The API route now adds a boolean isCurrent to each row, computed on the server by comparing the row id with the id of the session of the request. The component only reads that field. I removed the user agent comparison from the front end.

I added a Vitest test for the route with three sessions, one of them current, and a component test that renders two rows with equal user agents and expects exactly one 'this device' label. Both pass.

There is one side effect. The 'log out of all other devices' button used the old match to hide itself when only one session existed. It now uses the count of rows where isCurrent is false, which is simpler and gives the same result in the normal case.

I ran the Playwright test of the session list, and it passed. The deploy is planned for the next release together with the small fixes of this week.

summary: Built a first version of the delivery time export without the JavaScript sort, moving the ordering into the SQL query, and compared the output with the old one on 10 filter sets.
body:
The delivery time table sorted its rows in JavaScript after the query, which was noted during the streaming work. That sort breaks the streaming idea, because the rows must be read before the first one can be written. I started to move the ordering into the query.

The old code sorted by depot name with a locale compare, then by planned time. Postgres sorts by the collation of the database, and that was the first difference I found: names with umlauts came in a different order. I checked the collation of the database and it is en_US.UTF-8, while the JavaScript compare used the German locale.

I tried two options. The first was ORDER BY with COLLATE "de-x-icu" on the depot name. The second was to add a sort key column to the depots table. The second option needs a migration and a backfill, which is too large for this change. I took the first.

The query now has ORDER BY depot_name COLLATE "de-x-icu", planned_at, shipment_id. I added the shipment id as the last key, because two rows with the same planned time came out in changing order between runs of the old code.

I compared the new output with the old export on 10 filter sets, line by line. Eight were identical. Two differed in the order of rows with equal planned time, which is the case the old code did not define. I think the new order is the better one, as it is stable.

The explain output showed a sort node on 1.2 million rows that used the disk. An index on depot_name and planned_at did not help with the collation, so I left the sort in the database. The time to first byte is still short for small filters, but for the full table the sort comes first. I will measure that on staging next and write down the result.

summary: Measured the delivery time export with the database sort on staging: first byte after 2.4 seconds on the largest depot, which is acceptable, and finished in 21 seconds.
body:
I ran the new delivery time export on staging with the largest depot, about 1.2 million rows, three times. The first byte came after 2.4, 2.2 and 2.6 seconds. The total time was 21, 20 and 23 seconds.

The wait at the start is the sort, which Postgres does before it sends rows. It is long enough to see, but far below the 30 second gateway limit. The memory of the API process did not grow during the runs.

I also tried a variant with an index on (depot_id, planned_at) and sorting by depot name only in the application for the small groups. It saved about half a second and made the code more complex, so I dropped it.

The output of the three runs was identical byte by byte. I compared the new file with the old export after sorting both with the same command, and only the order of the equal rows differed, as before.

What is left: a test that checks the order for names with umlauts, and the removal of the JavaScript sort. I did both in the branch. The test uses six depot names and expects the German order.

I will release this together with the cleanup of the old path, so that the rollback flag still exists when the change goes out.

summary: Wrote the reply for Jonas on why the manager SSO login shows a second consent screen sometimes, which happens only after the identity provider session has ended.
body:
Jonas asked why some managers see a consent screen twice in a day. I looked at the SSO logs of the last week for the cases he named.

In all of them, the identity provider session had ended between the two logins, which is set to eight hours on the Acme side. After the end the provider asks again for consent, and our code cannot change that. Our own session of the dashboard was not the cause.

I checked that our callback does not ask for a new consent by itself. The authorization request sends prompt=none only for the silent check, and the normal login sends no prompt parameter, so the provider decides.

The reply to Jonas says that it comes from the provider setting, and that the IT of Acme can raise the limit if they want fewer screens. I added the lines of the log that show the pattern, so he can show them to his IT.

No code change was needed.

summary: Read through the shipments export handler and planned how to remove its in-memory CSV path, checking where the flag and the small-table check are used.
body:
I started to prepare the cleanup of the export code, with the shipments handler first because it has the most traffic and the clearest logs. I did not change any code yet. The streaming path is already in place next to the old one, and the plan is to remove the old path in small steps once the streaming change for large exports has been released and watched for a while.

I read the handler and wrote down what a removal would touch: the branch that builds the file in memory, and the flag read in that handler. The flag is also read in the other two handlers, for costs and delivery times, so it has to stay in the environment until those are done. That keeps the rollback step for them.

I ran the Vitest suite for the exports on the current code to see what depends on the old path. Everything passes today, but one test sets the flag to false to test the old path. It will fail once the branch is gone, and I plan to delete it, since it tests code that will not exist any more. The comparison test between old and new output still uses the helper, so it stays until the helper is removed at the end.

I also ran the Playwright test that downloads a shipments export with a filter and checks the first lines. It passes on the current code and will be my check after the change.

One detail I found: the handler has a check for the row count that switches to the in-memory path for small tables, under 1,000 rows, because it was faster. I measured the timing on a few small tables, and streaming takes about 40 ms more at most. That is not worth a second path, so the check should go too, together with the branch.

The plan is to do the shipments handler first, then the same change for costs and for delivery times, then the helper and the flag. I plan to start with the shipments handler later today or tomorrow, and the rest next week.

summary: Found the scheduled report scheduler could start twice after a deploy restart and sketched a claim column on the schedule row to stop duplicate mails.
body:
Following Jonas's report that some scheduled report mails arrive twice, I read the scheduler code again before changing anything. The scheduler wakes every minute, selects the schedules that are due, renders the report and sends the mail, and only then writes last_sent_at. During a deploy, Render keeps the old instance alive for a short time while the new one starts, so both instances run the same due-query within the same minute.

I confirmed this against the logs of the last three duplicates. In each case the two send log lines came from different instance ids, 4 to 9 seconds apart, and each was within two minutes of a deploy. A single instance never sent twice, so the retry logic and the mail provider were ruled out.

The fix I sketched is a claim on the schedule row. The due-query becomes an UPDATE that sets a new claimed_at column to now() for rows where it is null or older than 10 minutes, and it returns only the rows it claimed. Postgres row locks make sure that only one of two simultaneous instances gets a given row. After a successful send the job clears the claim and writes last_sent_at, and after a failure the claim simply expires.

I wrote the migration for claimed_at as a nullable timestamp, with no default and no backfill, so it is safe to run before the code change. I also wrote a Vitest test that starts two scheduler ticks at once against a test database with one due schedule and expects exactly one send. It failed on the current code, as it should.

Not done yet: the real change in the scheduler, the 10 minute expiry needs a check against the slowest report render, which was about 40 seconds last week. Next I will implement the query, run the migration on staging and force a restart during a due minute to watch it.

summary: Prepared the costs and delivery time exports for a later move to streaming by listing the callers of the in-memory helper and checking the sort change, without changing any handler yet.
body:
No export handler has been switched to streaming yet, so I spent the session getting the shipments, costs and delivery time handlers ready for that change. I did not touch their code paths.

The delivery time handler needed the most attention. It still has the JavaScript sort, and I had already built a version that moves the ordering into the ORDER BY of the query. I compared the output of both on a set of filters, including the names with umlauts, since the database collation could order them differently from the JavaScript sort. The umlaut test passed on the new query. I wrote down that the branch with the sort has to go when the handler is switched, but I left it in place for now.

Then I searched for every user of the buildCsvInMemory helper, because I want to know what breaks before I delete anything. The search found two more users than I expected: a script in the tools folder that dumps a table for support, and the legacy comparison test. For the script I sketched a version that reads rows from a cursor and writes them to a file stream. It looks shorter than the old code, but it is not committed. The legacy test will have to be deleted together with the helper, so I added both to my notes for the cleanup.

I also thought about the flag that chooses between the in-memory path and the small-table check. If a later deploy stops reading it, a rollback to the previous version would still need it in the Render environment. My plan is to keep it in the environment for one more release after the code change, mark the config entry as unused, and remove it in the release after that.

I ran the whole Vitest suite on the current state as a baseline: 412 tests, all green. The Playwright export tests for the three tables passed too. Last, I ran the costs and delivery time exports on staging with the largest depot to have numbers to compare against: 22 and 21 seconds. The plan is to start with the handlers next, write the release notes, and only then think about when to deploy, probably after the evening peak.

summary: Prepared the export cleanup on staging and checked the old and new export paths against each other, with nothing deployed yet.
body:
I prepared the export cleanup after the evening peak and kept it on staging. Nothing went to production today.

I ran the shipments, costs and delivery time exports on staging, two of each, and all six finished. The largest took 19 seconds on the biggest depot, close to the earlier measurement, so the database sort still looks acceptable. Large exports are still slow in production for now, and I did not change how the file is built there.

The tools script for support also needed a check. I ran it for one small table against staging and compared the file with a normal export, and the two were equal.

There was one client disconnect in the staging logs, which is normal for a closed tab. No other errors showed up.

Tomorrow I will go through the list of what the cleanup removes, write down the steps for the deploy and the rollback, and ask Jonas for a quiet time after the evening peak. The flag in the environment stays for now.

summary: Investigated a report from Jonas that scheduled report mails sometimes arrive twice, and traced it to two overlapping runs of the scheduler after a deploy restart.
body:
Jonas forwarded two mails of the same weekly report that arrived within a minute. I looked at the scheduler log for that morning.

The scheduler runs inside the API process and wakes every minute to find schedules that are due. At the time of the mails, a deploy had just restarted the service, and for about 40 seconds the old and the new instance ran at the same time on Render. Both woke, both found the schedule due, and both sent it.

The code marked a schedule as sent after the mail was handed to the mail service, not before. So the second instance still saw it as due.

I changed the flow to claim the schedule first. The query now does UPDATE ... SET claimed_at = now() WHERE id = $1 AND (claimed_at IS NULL OR claimed_at < now() - interval '10 minutes') RETURNING id, and only the instance that gets a row sends the mail. After the send, last_sent is written, and the claim is cleared. If the send fails, the claim ends after the 10 minutes and the next run tries again.

I wrote a test that starts two scheduler ticks at the same moment against the same schedule and expects one mail. Before the change the test sent two, so it does show the bug.

I also checked the earlier cases. In the last month, three more double sends were in the logs, and all three were within a minute of a deploy.

A migration adds the claimed_at column, nullable, so it is safe to run before the code. I did not deploy yet, because the migration should go first. I will do both in order tomorrow morning.

summary: Ran the claimed_at migration and deployed the scheduler claim change, then watched a deploy restart on purpose to see that only one mail goes out.
body:
I ran the migration for the claimed_at column on production first. It took a few milliseconds, as the table has under 400 rows.

Then I deployed the scheduler change. To test the case from the report, I created a test schedule that was due in two minutes and sent only to my own address, and triggered a second deploy while it was due, so that two instances overlapped.

The logs showed both instances waking within the same second. One log line said claimed, the other said already claimed, skipping. One mail arrived.

I ran it a second time with a failing mail send, by pointing the test schedule to an address that the mail service rejects. The claim stayed for the ten minutes, and the next tick after that tried again, as intended. The schedule was not lost.

After the tests, I deleted the test schedules.

I checked the real schedules for the next morning. Fourteen were due, and I will look at the logs to see that each went out once.

I also added a line to the health page that shows the number of schedules with a claim older than the limit. It should be zero all the time, and if it is not, a send is stuck.

The notes for the change are in the release file. The one open question is whether the scheduler should move out of the API process into its own worker. That is a larger change, and I wrote it down for a later planning day instead of starting it.

summary: Planned the removal of the in-memory CSV export path and the unused export flag, and drafted the README section on exports, without deploying or removing anything yet.
body:
I went through the export code again to plan the cleanup. The in-memory CSV path is still in the shipments, costs and delivery time handlers, and large exports are still slow and still hit the 30 second gateway timeout above 200,000 rows. Nothing about that is fixed yet, and I did not touch any handler today.

I listed where the export flag is read. It is checked in the shipments handler and next to the small-table check, and the costs and delivery time exports go through the same helper. My plan is to keep the small-table path as it is for now and compare the old and new paths on staging once more. I want to know how the delivery time query behaves for the largest depot, since that one is the slowest on staging.

I made a short plan for the flag. First check that the previous version is no longer needed as a rollback target. Then change the variable in the Render environment and expect one restart. Then delete the config entry from the code. I did not change anything in the environment today.

I started on the README section on exports as a draft. It should describe only the streaming path, with a note on why the delivery time query sorts in the database. The draft is not committed yet.

The cleanup list from earlier has one more item, a check of the staging environment for the same flag. I looked at the staging variables and found that the flag is set there too, so it goes on the list for the same round.

The export cleanup is far from closed. The handler changes, the flag removal in both environments and the README change are all still to do.
